en: The Kaiyuan Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings, Volume One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu Year.
Preface: Now, the emergence of catalogues was intended to distinguish the true from the false and clarify right from wrong, and to record [the names of] persons...
Distinguishing between ancient and modern eras,
he indicated the number of fascicles and sections;
he gathered up what was omitted or lost and excised what was redundant or superfluous.
I desire that the orthodox teachings be systematically organized so that the golden words have a coherent thread;
thus, the essential principles may be clearly presented, with their governing themes and key points laid out for ready observation.
However, the Dharma-gates are profound and subtle, and the net of transformation is vast and expansive.
As the years passed and eras succeeded one another during successive translations,
the texts were frequently lost and scattered, leaving the scrolls disordered;
furthermore, certain individuals occasionally added spurious and false elements.
Consequently, these have become so intermingled that it is difficult to investigate their origins;
for this reason, former sages and Confucian scholars compiled these topical records (*tiaolu*).
Of those that survive today, there are approximately six or seven families of texts.
Nevertheless, it has not yet reached the ultimate source and still contains many omissions and deficiencies.
I, Sheng, though of mediocre and shallow capacity, have long devoted myself to its study;
I have examined its various points of agreement and difference and pointed out its strengths and weaknesses.
This collection of volumes has now been completed,
so that it may avoid any discrepancies.
I hope that all wise scholars will deign to examine it in detail.
I bow my head to the Sugata, the Honored Muni, the Unsurpassed Great Being, and the Tamer of Men;
I also pay homage to the pure and wondrous Dharma of the Three Vehicles, as well as the Sangha of the Eightfold Assembly of Arhats.
Having compiled this catalogue of scriptures to protect the citadel of the Dharma, I pray that the Triple Gem will bestow compassion and grant me secret protection.
I only pray that the lamp of the Dharma shall shine long through the night, so that deluded followers may thereby attain the clarity of wisdom;
may the True Dharma abide for a long time in this world, and by relying upon its study, may they swiftly ascend to the Unsurpassed Stage.
From the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Han, the year being Dingmao.
Reaching the year of Gengwu, the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang Emperor Shiwu,
a total of six hundred and sixty-four years had passed.
During this interval, one hundred and seventy-six individuals, both monastics and laypeople, engaged in the transmission and translation of scriptures.
The holy teachings of the Tripitaka of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles that were translated,
along with the collected biographies of sages and worthies and those of unknown translators,
total two thousand two hundred and seventy-eight works.
In total, there are seven thousand forty-six fascicles.
Those currently in circulation that lack original texts are all included within the aforementioned number.
The new catalog comprises twenty fascicles.
The opening is divided into general and specific sections.
The general record compiles and summarizes the multitude of sutras;
the specific record classifies them according to their vehicles and treasuries.
Each of the two catalogs consists of ten fascicles.
Within them, there are further seven topical sections;
I shall first set forth the outlines, and the remaining contents will follow in their proper order.
General Compendium of the Various Scriptures, Volume One.
The above covers all translations and expositions from the Han to the Tang dynasties,
detailing the reigns of the emperors as well as the personal histories of the translators.
The various teachings produced herein are arranged according to the chronological sequence of their authors rather than following the order of the Tripiṭaka; furthermore,
a catalog is appended to record the similarities and differences between the new and old versions.
The Supplementary Catalogue of the Piṭaka of the Vehicle, Part Two.
Within the above supplementary catalogue, there are seven distinct divisions.
First: those that have been translated and for which the original texts exist.
Second, there are translations for which the original texts do not exist;
third, various sectarian lineages have diverged;
fourth, redundancies and complexities have been excised.
Five: Supplements to Omissions.
Six: Re-examination of Doubts.
Seven: Perversion and Heresy Disturb the Correct.
Within these seven gates, the distinctions between the Two Vehicles and the various classifications of the Tripitaka are fully detailed;
furthermore, the specific characteristics of each school are clearly elucidated.
This comprehensive record is divided into ten fascicles.
From the first [chapter] to the tenth, these are the coarse and prominent outlines; if each were explained in full detail, they would be contained within the tenth fascicle.

Fascicle One lists the biographies of the translators—both monastic and lay—of the sūtras, precepts, and *karmavācanā* produced during the Han and Wei dynasties, as well as those of works whose translators were lost in earlier or later versions, including supplementary entries.
Fascicle Two lists the monastic and lay translators of the Wu and Jin dynasties.
The scriptures, precepts, and other works produced by individuals, along with various newly and formerly lost translations, are appended as before;

this concludes the third volume of the Biographies of Translators. The fourth volume covers the Eastern Jin, the two reigns of Fu Qin, and the dynasties of Yao Qin, Western Qin, Former Liang, and Northern Liang, including the scriptures, vinayas, and śāstras produced by monastics and laypeople, as well as the biographies of newly and formerly lost translations, following the same format as before.
Volume Five: The sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras translated by monastic and lay translators of four dynasties, as well as newly compiled and previously lost translations;

Volume Six: The sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras translated by monastic and lay translators of the Qi, Liang, Northern Wei, and Northern Qi dynasties, as well as newly compiled and previously lost translations.
Volumes Seven through Nine: Volume Seven contains the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras, as well as the Newly Compiled Collection of Lost Translations of Sūtras and Vinayas;
Volume Eight contains the Sūtras, Vinayas, Śāstras, and biographical records produced by monastic and lay translators during the three dynasties of Northern Zhou, Chen, and Sui;
and Volume Nine contains the Sūtras, Vinayas, Śāstras, and biographical records produced by monastic and lay translators of the present dynasty.
The first ten scrolls consist of a detailed record of the number of fascicles and the similarities and differences among the various ancient catalogs;
these are divided into ten scrolls from the eleventh to the twentieth. A rough outline of these contents is provided in detail within the tenth scroll.

Volumes Eleven and Twelve: A Catalogue of the Translated and Existing Texts of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka—Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras—along with an Account of the Translators and Their Eras. Volume Thirteen:

A Catalogue of the Translated and Existing Texts of the Śrāvaka Piṭaka—Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras—as well as the Collections of the Noble Ones and Biographies, also including an Account of the Translators and Their Eras.
Volume 14: Catalogue of Mahāyāna Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras for which there are translations but no extant texts; Volume 15:
Catalogue of Hīnayāna Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras, as well as the collected works of sages and saints, for which there are translations but no extant texts; Volume 16:
Catalogue of separately circulated branches of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras, and separately derived works of the collected writings of sages and saints.
Volume Seventeen of the Catalogue: Abridgment of Redundant Entries and Separate Listings of Scriptures with Identical Texts but Different Titles;
Deletion of Duplicate Entries; Supplementing Omissions and Recovering Lost Works;

and the New Compilation and Inclusion of Previously Missing Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras from the Great Zhou Canon Catalogue, as well as Newly Translated Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Sūtras, Vinayas, Śāstras, and Collections of Biographies.

Volume 18 of the Catalogue of the Tibetan Canon: A Further Detailed Examination of Doubtful Works, a Catalogue of Spurious and Deceptive Texts that Confuse the Authentic with the False, and Newly Compiled Spurious Scriptures along with the Catalogues of Various Collections of Excerpts.
Volume 19: Catalogue of Mahāyāna Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras Included in the Canon.
Volume 20: Hīnayāna Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras, and the Collections of the Noble and Holy Ones.
Catalogue of the Transmission into the Tibetan Canon, Part 1: Compendium of Various Scriptures, Volume One, Section One. Upper Part of the Compendium of Various Scriptures.
From the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming (dingmao) to the first year of the Yankang era of Emperor Xian (gengzi) of the Later Han dynasty, when the Liu clan ruled from Luoyang.
In total, there were eleven emperors over a period of one hundred and fifty-four years.
Twelve individuals, both monastics and laypeople,
produced various sūtras and vinayas, as well as the new and old collections and various sūtras of unknown translators.
In total, there are two hundred and ninety-two works comprising three hundred and ninety-five fascicles;
among these, ninety-seven works totaling one hundred and thirty-one fascicles are extant, while one hundred and ninety-five works totaling two hundred and sixty-four fascicles are missing.
The *Houhan jinglu* (Catalogue of Scriptures of the Later Han) states therein that those [scriptures] which directly refer to the "Emperor" are authentic,
while those that also exclude his name are spurious.

The dates are established according to the chronological records of two families— the Tang dynasty *Sili* (Minister of the Court of Judicial Review) Zhen Luan and the *Chengjun* (National Academy) *Boshi* (Doctor) Wang Dao-gui— refined for the Later Han period.
[There were] one fascicle of one scripture by the śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga, and four fascicles of ten [scriptures] by the śramaṇa Zhu Falan.
The *Five-Scroll Sūtra* translated by the śramaṇa Xuánlújiāchèn (Dharmakṣema), twenty-two works totaling sixty-seven scrolls;

the collection of sūtras translated by the śramaṇa Ān Shìgāo, ninety-five works totaling one hundred fifteen scrolls; the collection of sūtras and vinaya translated by the śramaṇa Zhú Fóshuò, two works totaling three scrolls;
and the collection of sūtras translated by the upāsaka Ān Xuán, two works totaling three scrolls. All [were] translated by śramaṇas.
One collection by Zhi Yao consisting of eleven sections and eleven fascicles; one collection by the śramaṇa Kang Ju consisting of one fascicle;
five collections by the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao totaling eight fascicles; six collections by the śramaṇa Kang Mengxiang totaling nine fascicles;
one collection on Sūtras and Vinaya by the śramaṇa Zhu Dalie consisting of two fascicles; and one collection by the śramaṇa Tanguo consisting of two fascicles.

One hundred and forty-one works in one hundred and fifty-one fascicles, comprising fifty-nine works in seventy-six fascicles translated by various unknown translators from both earlier and later periods;
eighty-two works in eighty-two fascicles collected from earlier sources; and one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Forty-two Sections* newly appended.
In the tenth year of the Yongping era, the year Dingmao, at the Baima Temple, [this was] [translated] together with Dharmaratna.
The first translation is recorded in the old catalogues as follows: "One fascicle of one volume, titled *The Forty-two Sections*, by Emperor Xiaoming;
its manuscript still exists.
[It was brought by] the śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga."
Some call him Zhu She Moteng;
others call him Shemoteng.
Various records preserve both names, leaving it uncertain which is correct.
The reasons why he was not translated previously have already been fully set forth.
He was a person from Central India of the Brahmin caste;
from his youth, he was intelligent, erudite, and widely learned.
Possessing the power of reflection and excelling in his mastery of the Sūtras and Vinaya,
he once traveled to a small kingdom in Western India,
where he was invited to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
Shortly thereafter, a neighboring state raised an army and advanced; yet,
just as they were about to enter the borders,
they were obstructed by unforeseen circumstances and unable to proceed.
The military forces of that country, suspecting the presence of some extraordinary artifice, secretly dispatched envoys to spy upon him;
they saw only the ministers sitting at ease together, listening to his exposition of the Mahāyāna sūtras on the methods for protecting the state through the Mingdi (明地) Spirit-Kings.
Thereupon, that country requested peace and sought the Dharma.
In the seventh year of the Yongping era, a Jiazi year,
Emperor Ming dreamed of a golden man sixteen feet tall, with a sun disc upon his crown, its radiance blazing brilliantly as he flew before the palace hall.
The next day, he extensively questioned his ministers about this divine anomaly.
Fu Yi, a man of broad learning, came forward and offered this response:
Your servant has heard that in the Western Regions there is one who has attained the Way,
known as the Buddha.
That which Your Majesty dreamed of must surely be him.
The Emperor agreed with this.
He issued an edict dispatching Langzhong Cai Yin, Langjiang Qin Jing, and the student of the Classics Wang Zun, along with seventeen others— eighteen people in total—
to travel to India to seek out and investigate the Buddha-dharma.
In the country of the Great Yuezhi, he met with Kāśyapa Mātanga.
At that time, Cai Yin and others earnestly entreated Mātanga,
who subsequently came with them to Luoyang.
Emperor Ming received him with great appreciation and hospitality.
The Buddhist scriptures he had brought and the painted images he had acquired were loaded onto white horses and transported together to Luoyang.
Consequently, the monastery was established and named the Baima Temple (White Horse Monastery).
Monasteries were established in competition across various regions to repay the kindness of the white horse.
It is said that the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* was translated at the Baima Monastery by An Shigao.
Initially, [the scriptures] were sealed within the fourteenth chamber of the Stone Chamber at the Lan-tai Library.
From that time forth, the teachings of Śākyamuni arose in succession like clouds,
and śramaṇas and lay devotees followed one after another to transmit and translate them.
I have compiled this based on the catalog;
he is thus the patriarch of the sūtras and the Dharma in the land of Han.
The old catalog states:
This sutra was originally an excerpt from a foreign scripture, initially derived from a major compendium.
It condenses the essential points to guide the laity,
resembling the eighteen chapters of the Classic of Filial Piety (*Xiaojing*).
This is recorded in the *Jiulü* (Old Catalogue), Zhu Shixing’s *Hanlù* (Han Dynasty Catalogue), and Sengyou’s *Chū Sānzàng Jì* (Collection for the Translation of the Tripitaka), among others;
it is not included in Dao’an’s catalogue.
Dharmaratna [Kāśyapa Mātanga] considered that because the Great Transformation had only recently been transmitted, people had yet to have deep faith.
He harbored profound insights but did not translate many works;
instead, he extracted the essential points of the sutras to guide the common people of his time.
He eventually passed away in Luoyang.
The details of its origins and provenance are fully recorded in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* (Record of the Han) and the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Daosheng sought out the source and beginning of these records in order to describe the intent behind the translation of the scriptures.
For the arrival of translated scriptures, there must necessarily be a historical cause and context.

Therefore, I have collated various accounts to broaden the range of diverse information. Although this makes the text somewhat prolix, the matters concerning the *saṃgha* are complete herein. The *Daśabhūmi-pratisaṃyukta-saṃyojana-cchedana-sūtra* (Ten Stages Sutra on Severing the Fetters) in eight fascicles—or four fascicles—is also called the *Daśabhūmi-prathama-niḥsaraṇa*.

It was first translated by Zhu Fonian from the same original text as the *Daśabhūmi-pratisaṃyukta-saṃyojana-cchedana-sūtra*. Its appearance in the thirteenth year of the Yongping era is recorded in the *Zhu Shixing Hanlu*, the *Gaoseng zhuan*, the *Changfang lu*, and other catalogs. The *Dharmasāgara-kośa-sūtra* (Sutra of the Dharma-Ocean Treasury) in one fascicle—some versions omit the character "kośa" (treasury)—was first translated from the same original text as the *Dharmasāgara-sūtra*. It is mentioned in the *Gaoseng zhuan*, the *Changfang lu*, and other records. The *Buddha-pūrva-yoga-sūtra* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Former Deeds) in five fascicles was translated in the eleventh year of the Yongping era. It is mentioned in the *Gaoseng zhuan*, the *Changfang lu*, and other records. The *Buddha-janma-sūtra* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Birth) in one fascicle is mentioned in the *Gaoseng zhuan*, the *Changfang lu*, and other records. The above comprises four works totaling fifteen fascicles.
The originals for these were all missing.
The śramaṇa Zhu Falan was also a native of Central India;
he claimed to have recited several tens of thousands of chapters of sūtras and śāstras by heart.
He served as a teacher to the scholars of India.
At that time, when Cai Yin arrived in that country,
Zhi Lan entered into an agreement with Kāśyapa Mātanga to travel together for the purpose of proselytizing.
They subsequently followed one another to the assembly;
however, as that disciple was detained,
Lan traveled by a different route and arrived there.
Having arrived in Luoyang, he stayed with Yan Foteng.
In a short time, he became proficient in the Chinese language.
Initially, he translated the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* together with Foteng.
Foteng passed away.
Daolun himself translated four works, including the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃgraha-sūtra*.
Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Former Han, black ash was found at the bottom of Kunming Lake after it had been dredged.
He questioned Dongfang Shuo.
Shuo replied,
"This is not within my knowledge."
"You may ask the Hu people from the Western Regions.
Once Dharmaratna had arrived, he was questioned about this; Dharmaratna replied:
"This is the ash from the time of the kalpa-conflagration.
Such was the testimony of Shuo,
which many came to believe.
Furthermore, when the envoy Qin Jing returned from the kingdom of Yuezhi, he obtained a statue of Śākyamuni Buddha.
This was the fourth image carved by the master who had previously fashioned the sandalwood image for King Udayana.
Upon its arrival in Luoyang, the Emperor immediately issued an edict ordering it to be reproduced in painting.
He was enshrined on the Qingliang Terrace and at the Xianjie Mausoleum for offerings;
from that time until the present, his paintings have been widely circulated.
Later, Lan passed away in Luoyang.
At that time, he was over sixty years of age.
Furthermore, the records of Sengchang and others state that it is not the case that Lan translated the *Two Volumes on the Two Hundred and Sixty Precepts Combined with Variants*.
A detailed examination of the titles reveals that they were not translated by Lan.
A thorough investigation into their similarities and differences is described below in the "Catalogue of Missing Texts.
The *Daoxing banruo boluomi jing* (Ten Fascicles) is titled *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-dao*.
The *Xing jing* (Practice Sutra) is also called the *Bore daoxing pin jing* (Sutra on the Chapter of the Practice of Prajñā), consisting of eight fascicles;

its initial appearance was identical to the *Mingdu xiaopin* (Shorter Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom) and the fourth assembly of the *Dabanruo* (Great Prajñā). It appeared on the eighth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Guanghe era, as recorded in the catalogs of Min and Yu.
The *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing* (Sutra of the Immeasurable Pure Equal Enlightenment) in two fascicles is also simply called the *Wuliang* (Immeasurable).
The *Jing jing* (Sutra on Purity), Volume Two, is identical in its original text to the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*, the *Ratnakūṭa-bhadrakalpika-anantāyus-parivarta*, and others;
it appears in the *Wu lu* (Record of Wu) as the *Akṣobhya-buddhakṣetra-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated in the first year of the Jianhe era, or in one fascicle.

Its initial appearance is identical to the *Akṣobhyatathāgatasyavyūha-parivarta* in the *Ratnakūṭa*; it appears in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* (Record of Han) and in the *Seng [zhuan]* (Biographies of Monks).

The *Yùlù* (Record of the Canon) also states that there is a *Fó xuéchéng pǐn jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of Bodhisattva Training in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya), or one volume of the *Fó yí rì móní bǎo jīng* (Sūtra of the Sun-Mani Jewel Bequeathed by the Buddha).

Master Ān said it belongs to the Vaipulya section; when first translated, it was identical in text to the "Pǔmíng Púsà Huì" (Assembly of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhā) in the *Bǎojī* (Ratnakūṭa), having the same title as the "Gǔpǐn" (Ancient Chapter). It is also called the *Yírì shuō bānrě jīng* (Sūtra of the Sun Explaining Prajñā).
The *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, also known as the *Mahāyāna-ratnavyūha-sūtra*. It appears in the catalogs of Sengyou and Changfang.
The *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles, also known as the *Sarvabuddhābhimukha-vihāra-samādhi-sūtra*.

An old catalog states it is the *Mahāpratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*, or in two fascicles, translated in the second year of the Guanghe era. Its initial publication was concurrent with that of the *Mahā-*.
The *Jixian hu jing* (Sutra on the Protection of the Assembly of Worthies) and others are identical to the original texts; see the *Nie Daozhen lu* and the *Wu lu*.
The one-fascicle *Dousha jing* (Kāśyapa-parivarta) appears in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Wu lu*; it is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Names" from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The two-fascicle *Dunzhentuo suowen jing* (Sutra on the Questions of Indradatta) begins by stating: "The Sutra on the Jewel Tathāgata Samādhi as Asked by Indradatta"; it is an old [translation].
The Catalogue states that the *Dundubhissara-nirghoṣa-rāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra* consists of either three fascicles;

its initial translation was the same text as the *Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, though it is not seen in Dao’an’s catalogue, while it is found in Zhu Shixing’s Han-lu and Sengyou’s catalogue.

The *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* consists of two fascicles; its initial translation was the same text as the *Samantaprabhāsa-samādhi-sūtra* and others, and it is found in Sengyou’s catalogue, attributed to Master Dao’an.

The claim that it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama* is incorrect. The *Nèizàng Bǎibǎo Jīng* (Sūtra of the Hundred Treasures within) in one fascicle is also called the *Nèizàng Bǎipǐn* (Hundred Chapters within);
its initial translation differs slightly from that by An Shigao. Master Dao’an stated it belongs to the Vaipulya section; this is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.
The *Wénshūshīlì Wèn Púsàshǔ Jīng* (Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Bodhisattva Stations) in one fascicle is also simply called the *Wènshǔ Jīng*; this is seen in [Sengyou’s] *Mù* (Catalogue).

Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji* and the *Wulu* state that Master Dao’an says this *Zapiyujing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables) in one fascicle, containing eleven items, belongs to the Vaipulya section.
Sengyou states it was translated by an unknown translator; Fajing notes it is found in the *Bielu*. The above are extant; the following are missing.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* in twenty-seven fascicles: its initial translation is the same text as those produced by Dharmakṣema and others.
Li Kuò’s record states that there is one fascicle of the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, which is a re-translation of the latter ten chapters.
Yòu possesses this one fascicle, but not the three-fascicle version; this is seen in Jìngtài’s record. Alternatively, it is titled with the "Da" (Great) character as the third appearance.

Yòu’s record states that on the eighth day of the tenth month of the second year of Guānghuá, the two-fascicle or one-fascicle *Fan banniehuan jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) was first produced from the Sanskrit.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and others share the same original text as seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Han-lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*.
It was formerly called the *Hu-ban*, now revised as the *Fan-xiang-yi jing* (One fascicle); its initial appearance is recorded in Fa-shang’s *Lu*. The *Sarvadharma-vīrarāja-sūtra* (One fascicle);
its initial appearance is recorded in Fa-shang’s *Lu*. The *Prabhāsa-samādhi-sūtra* (One fascicle); its initial appearance is recorded in Fa-shang’s *Lu*.

Sengyou states that it appears in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record), while Daoan’s record does not; Sengfang says it is also seen in the *Wu lu* (Wu Record). The *Bo ben jing* (Original Scripture of the Star) in two fascicles first appeared in the *Sengyou lu*;
the *Shou lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama-sūtra) in two fascicles was translated on the eighth day of the second month of the third year of the Zhongping era.
It is also said to be in three fascicles, appearing in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* (Han Record) as well as the *Wu lu* and the *Sengyou lu*. The *Da...* [text ends].

*Fangbian bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Repaying Kindness through Expedient Means), one fascicle; listed in the *Wu lu*. *Ajātaśatru-rāja pṛcchati pañcānantarya-sūtra* (Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru’s Inquiry into the Five Heinous Offenses), one fascicle;

also called the *Ajātaśatru-rāja sūtra*. Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Chángfáng lu*. *Dhyāna-sūtra*, one fascicle; its initial appearance, according to Zhìfáng, is recorded in the *Bié lu*.
*Ayuwang taizi huaimu yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Aśoka’s Crown Prince Blinding His Eyes), one fascicle; [recorded] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Since King Aśoka did not appear until more than one hundred years later, these were not spoken by the Buddha; alternatively, they may have lacked the word "sūtra" when they first appeared.
This is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The above twenty-three sections comprise sixty-seven fascicles.
Eleven sections, comprising twenty-six fascicles, are currently extant within the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*. Twelve sections, comprising forty-one fascicles, are missing.
The śramaṇa Lokakṣema—
also simply called Zhi Chen—
was a native of the Yuezhi people.
His conduct was pure and profound, and his nature was open and quick-witted.
He was renowned for his diligent observance of the Dharma and precepts;
he recited the various sutras with the resolve to propagate the Teaching.
During the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling, he traveled to Luoyang.
This spanned from the first year of Jianhe under Emperor Huan (the Dinghai year) until the third year of Zhongping under Emperor Ling (the Jinyin year).
In Luoyang, he translated twenty-three scriptures, including the *Daoxing* [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra],
having accurately captured their original intent without adding any embellishments.
He may truly be called a master who skillfully proclaims the essentials of the Dharma and propagates the Way.
The lay follower from Henan, Meng Fu, and Zhang Lian received this orally.
As for the old translation that renders it as "Hu Ban niepan," I have privately found it unclear.
Since the time of the early translations of the scriptures, virtuous scholars have served as scribes (bishou).
Whenever he reached a point where the language needed to be translated, there was no instance in which he did not remark, "I am translating from Hu into Han.
Now, "Hu" refers to the various border-dwelling tribes such as the Xianyun and Qiang among the five regions of India; it is for this reason that they are now called "Hu."
How could this have anything to do with India?
It is profoundly relevant to Chu and Yue;
how can one not examine this in detail?
However, all the sūtras spoken by the Buddha are collectively referred to as "Brahma-texts" (fanben).
"Brahma" (fan) means "purity" in this language.
Long ago, at the beginning of the kalpa, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the Brahma-world descended here.
In that land, there were those who fed on the fat of the earth;
their bodies became so heavy that they could no longer move about,
and consequently, they eventually became human beings.
He was the progenitor of the Five Heavens;
his title was established by following their celestial designation.
Just as they refer to him as "Hu."
How can this principle be established?
It is simply that they call it "Sanskrit," just as we here refer to it as "Han" (Chinese).
This indeed has its basis and is not an error; for instance,
in former times, monks all referred to their secular surnames.
During the Fu Qin era, there was the śramaṇa Dao’an,
who stood out as preeminent among his contemporaries and possessed a profound, transcendent realization.
Having shaved his head and entered the monastic life, he succeeded to the lineage of Śākyamuni’s sons, though with a different father.
How could one say this is merely a matter of inherited tradition?
Now that we have left the household life, it is appropriate that all titles be called "Śākya.
Furthermore, when translating the *Caturāgama*, the text indeed states: [as follows].
Those who have left the household life from the four castes are all of one Śākya lineage.

The multitude all sighed in admiration and submission; these four castes are: first, the Kṣatriya; second, the Brāhmaṇa; third, the Vaiśya; and fourth, the Śūdra. This was during the era of the Jin and Qin dynasties.
He compiled and edited the catalogs and annotated the various scriptures,
styling himself a "Celestial Model" (*Miti*) for posterity;
it was as if he were translating from the Hu language into the Qin language.
There are five losses and three difficulties not to be altered.
Is this not, perhaps, a universal human limitation that prevents one from reaching perfection?
From the time of the former dynasties onwards, wherever there were foreign (Hu) words, they have now all been changed to Sanskrit characters.
I hope there will be no errors so that those who discuss this may attain the correct understanding.
Furthermore, among the records of Zhi Chen’s translations compiled by Changfang and others,
there is additionally one fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
Now, as for the *Buddhāvatamsaka-maṇi-ratna-sūtra*, since it shares the same original source [as other versions], it is not appropriate to issue it again.
Furthermore, upon examining its phrasing and terminology, it was not translated by Dharmakṣema;
among the separate catalogs, it is all classified as a work of lost translation.
Now, following the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue) as the authoritative source, the *Chenlu* (Chronicle of Prophecies) has excluded it.
The *Mahāyāna Vaipulya Prajñā Sūtra*, one fascicle, was first translated alongside the *Ratnakūṭa: Maitreya’s Inquiry on the Eight Dharmas*.
*The Sūtra on the Prince’s Longing for His Soul* (Taizi mumo jing), one fascicle; same original text as seen in the Catalogue of Changfang; first appearance in the *Collection of the Six Pāramitās*.
*The Sūtra on the Elder’s Son’s Restraining [Himself]* (Zhangrezizi zhi jing), one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra on Restraining*; same original text as the *Sūtra of the Boy Śreṇika*, etc.;
first appearance as seen in the Catalogue of Changfang. *The Mañjuśrī Inquiry into the Dharma-body within the Ratnakūṭa Samādhi* (Baoji sanmei wenshu wen fashen).
*Sūtra in One Scroll*, also titled *The Sūtra on Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into the Dharmakāya within the Reliquary of the Sun-Jewel Samādhi*.
Its initial appearance was as the same text as the *Sūtra on the Essential Nature of the Dharmadhātu*. See the *Chángfáng Lù* (Record of Dharma Abode).
*Sūtra on the Samādhi of Self-Vow*, one scroll. A note beneath the title states: "The fourth chapter, 'Individual Realization,' excerpted from the 'Pure Conduct of Bhikṣus. Its initial appearance."
It is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, that translated by Dharmarakṣa; see the *Chángfáng Lù*.

The *Wēnshì Xǐyù Zhòngsēng Jīng* (Sūtra on the Bathing of the Assembly of Monks in the Warm Chamber), one fascicle, is also simply called the *Wēnshì Jīng*; its initial appearance is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.

The *Míngdù Wǔshí Xiàojiào Jīng* (Sūtra of the Fifty Evaluations of the Perfection of Wisdom), two fascicles, is also simply called the *Míngdù Xiàojiào* or the *Wǔshí Xiàojiào*; it appeared in the first year of the Yuánjiā era.
The *Foyin sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha-Seal Samādhi), one fascicle, first appeared in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*.

The *Badarenjue jing* (Sūtra of the Eight Great Persons’ Awakening), one fascicle, appears in Changfang’s *Lu*. The *Shelifu huiguo jing* (Sūtra of Śāriputra’s Repentance), one fascicle—also simply titled *Huiguo jing*—first appeared in Changfang’s *Lu*.
The *Renben yusheng jing* (Sūtra on the Human Root Desire for Birth) [one fascicle]... [appears in Changfang’s *Lu*].

Volume [X], translated in the second year of the Yongjia era; the tenth volume of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, a different translation with commentary by Dao’an, found in Zhu Shixing’s *Han-lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*.

The *Śikṣānanda-ṣaḍ-abhimukha-praṇāma-sūtra*, one volume—also known as the *Śikṣānanda-ṣaḍ-diś-pūjā-sūtra*—translated from the eleventh volume of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, a different translation, found in the *Chang-a-han*.

The *Fánglù* (Catalogue of the Canon) records that the *Cháng āhán shíbàofǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Ten Retributive Dharmas of the Long Āgama) in two fascicles—also known as the *Duōzēng dào zhāng jīng* or simply the *Shíbào jīng*—is found in the ninth fascicle of the *Cháng āhán*.
It is also noted in ancient catalogues that it is an alternative translation from the *Cháng āhán*, as seen in Sengyòu’s catalogue.
The *Yīqiè liúshè shǒuyīn jīng* (Sūtra on the Retention of Causes for All Flows) in one fascicle is found in the second [fascicle] of the *Zhōng āhán*.

The *Ji lu* (Old Catalogue) states that this scroll is a different translation [of the same text]. The *Wu lu* (Wu Dynasty Catalogue) calls it the *Yiqie liu she jing* (Sūtra on the Encompassment of All Outflows);

it is also called the *Liu she shou yin jing* (Sūtra on the Guarding of Causes for the Encompassment of Outflows), or simply the *Shou yin* (Guarding of Causes), or the *Liu she* (Encompassment of Outflows), or the *Yiqie liu she shou jian* (Encompassment of All Outflows and Guarding of Views).

It is recorded in the two catalogues of Zhu Shixing and Sengyou as a one-fascicle *Sidi jing* (Sūtra of the Four Truths), appearing as the seventh fascicle of the *Zhong ahan* (Madhyama Āgama) with a different translation. It is found in the *Seng*.

Sengyou’s Record states that the claim [the *Benshang yizhi jing*] was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama* is perhaps an error. The *Benshang yizhi jing*, one fascicle, appears as the tenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation in Sengyou’s Record states that the *Benshang yizhi jing* and the *Yuanben zhi jing* share the same original text;
it is also written with the character "yī" (猗). This is seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* and Sengyou’s Record; this is the Dharma.
*Fajing* (Dharma-Scripture), one fascicle; translated from the twenty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, a variant translation, appearing in the records of Zhu Shixing and Sengyou.

*Loubu fenbui jing* (Sūtra on the Distribution of Leaks), one fascicle; translated from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, a variant translation, appearing in the Han Records of Zhu Shixing and the records of Sengyou.
Master Daoan stated that it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, but this may be an error.
*The Brahmin’s Son: A Sutra on the Unwavering Affection for One’s Deceased Child*, one fascicle;
translated from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; a variant translation seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Sutra of the Householder Daśaśāṭaka of Aṣṭagrāma*, one fascicle;

translated from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; a variant translation seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Sutra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma*, one fascicle; also titled *Pǔ* [Universal].
*Yijing* (義經), also titled *Jufaxingjing* (具法行經); the *Pufa yi* (普法義) is called the *Sheli* (舍利);
*Jufaxing Shelifu* (具法行舍利弗)—the remainder is the same as [the previous entry]. It is said to have been translated from the *Madhyamāgama*. Translated in the second year of the Yuanjia era;
it is the same text as the *Guangyi famen jing* (廣義法門經). Seen in the records of Shi Xing and Sengyou. *Boluomen bisijing* (婆羅門避死經), one fascicle; translated from the *Ekottarikāgama*.

The *Ahan* (Āgama), Volume 23: A single-fascicle translation of the *Anāthapiṇḍika-vaśīkaraṇa-sapta-putra-sūtra*, listed in the *Chángfáng-lù* as a variant translation, appearing in the forty-ninth fascicle of the *Zēngyī āhan*.
A single-fascicle *Ānanda-tóngxué-jīng* (Sūtra on Ānanda’s Fellow Students), titled as being from the *Zēngyī āhan*;
upon examination it is not found there, though it is listed in the *Chángfáng-lù* as seven [entries].

*Chu san guan jing* (Sūtra on the Three Contemplations), one fascicle; extracted from the *Saṃyuktāgama*, comprising thirty sūtras in total from beginning to end, as they are designated by their titles from the outset.
Alternatively, it exists in two fascicles, translated in the first year of the Yuanjia era, as seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* and Sengyou’s catalog.

*Wu yin piyu jing* (Sūtra of Similes for the Five Aggregates), one fascicle; sometimes the character "pi" (simile) is omitted. Also known as the *Shui mo suo piao jing* (Sūtra on Being Drifted by Water Foam); extracted from [the Āgamas].
The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume Ten; see the *Zhu Shixing Han Lu* and the *Sengyou Lu*.
The *Dharmacakra-pravartana Sūtra*, one fascicle—also called the *Dharmacakra-vartana Sūtra*—is a variant translation from the fifteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
its latter portion is identical to its original text while the former differs. See the *Sengyou Lu*. The *Aṣṭāṅgamārga Sūtra*, one fascicle; appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The twenty-eighth volume of the Āgama contains various translations found in the two catalogs of Sengyou:
the *Mātṛceṭī-sūtra* (one fascicle), also known as the *Māzōu-nǚ* or the *Ānàn wèi gǔdào nǚ huò jīng*, which appears in the Changfang Record;
its initial translation was the same text as the *Matangga-jing*. Also included is the *Guǐ wèn Mùlián jīng* (one fascicle), whose initial translation is likewise recorded.

The *Yù èguǐ bàoyìng jīng* (Sutra on the Retribution of Hungry Ghosts) shares the same original text as [the following works], according to the *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Dharmananda): the *Ānán wèn shì fó jíxióng jīng* (Sutra of Ananda’s Inquiry into the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha), one scroll;
also titled the *Ānán wèn shì jīng* (Sutra of Ananda’s Inquiry into Serving) or the *Shì fó jíxióng jīng* (Sutra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha);

these appear in the *Chángfáng lù*. Its initial translation is the same original text as the *Ānán fēnbié jīng* (Sutra of Ananda’s Separation). The *Nàinǚ qǐyù yīnyuán jīng* (Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Maiden Nala and Jīvaka), one scroll.

The first fascicle appears with or without the characters "caused by no conditions" (wú yīn yuán); it is also simply titled *The Sūtra of the Woman Nà* (Nǎi nǚ jīng). It is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.

*The Sūtra on Teaching and Transforming Hell through the Retribution of Karmic Offenses* (*Zuìyè yīngbào jiàohuà dìyù jīng*), one fascicle; its initial appearance is sometimes called *The Sūtra on the Retribution of Hells* (*Dìyù bàoyìng jīng*).

It is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. *The Sūtra of Resolute Intent* (*Jiānyì jīng*), one fascicle; its initial appearance is also known as *The Sūtra of Resolute and Right Mind* (*Jiānxīn zhèngyì jīng*), and it is also called *Resolute Mind* (*Jiānxīn*).

The *Dà ān bān shǒu yì jīng* (Sūtra on the Great Ānāpāna-smṛti) in two fascicles, or one fascicle, or without the characters "shǒu yì" (mindfulness), or simply titled *Ān bān*, is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.
Master Seng’an stated that it is the "Small Ānāpāna," and he provided a commentary upon it.

The *Sēngyòu lù* separately records one fascicle of the *Dà ān bān*, and the *Chángfáng lù* further records one fascicle of the *Ān bān*; both are considered duplicates. This is noted by Shìxíng and Sēngyòu.
Li Kuò’s *Three Records* list the *Yin chī rù jīng* (Śraddhā-pratipatti-sūtra) in two fascicles, or one; Sengyǒu states that "Chí-rù" (Pratipatti) was erroneously omitted.
It is also called the *Yīn chí rù*; Master Ān provided its commentary. The *Fáng Record* lists the *Yīn chí rù* separately from the *Chú chí rù*, which is an error.
The *Chùchù Jīng* (Sūtra on Various Places) in one fascicle appears in both the records of Huishìxíng and Sengyǒu. The *Mà [Jīng]* (Sūtra of Abuse) appears in the *Chángfáng Record*.
*Yijing* (Sūtra on the Mind), one fascicle; listed in the Chángfáng lù. *Fēnbié shān'è suǒqǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Distinction of the Arising of Good and Evil), one fascicle;
listed in the Chángfáng lù. *Chūjiā yuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Leaving Home), one fascicle; also titled *Chūjiā yīnyuán jīng*; listed in the Chángfáng lù.
*Axiáng zhèngxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Right Practice of Aṅga), one fascicle; also titled *Zhèngyì jīng*; listed in the Chángfáng lù. *Shíbā nílí jīng* (Sūtra on the Eighteen Nirayas), one fascicle.
*Juǎn* (also known as *Shíbā dìyù jīng*), one fascicle; listed in the *Chángfáng lù*.
*Fǎshòu chén jīng*, one fascicle; listed in the *Sēngyòu lù*. *Cánxíng fǎxiǎng jīng*, one fascicle; listed in both the *Sēngyòu lù* and the *Bǎochàng lù*.
*Chángzhězǐ àonǎo sānchù jīng*, one fascicle; also titled *Chángzhě yāonǎo sānchù jīng*, or simply *Sānchù*.
The *Nǎo jīng* (Sūtra on Annoyance); seen in Changfang’s record; one fascicle; sometimes the character "king" (*guó*) is omitted from the title *Qiánduō guówáng jīng*.

The *Fùmǔ ēn nán bào jīng* (Sūtra on the Difficulty of Repaying Parental Kindness); also called *Qín bào*; seen in Changfang’s record; Changfang states it was translated from the *Madhyamāgama*, but it cannot be found there.
The *Jiǔ héng jīng* (Sūtra on the Nine Untimely Deaths); one fascicle; Changfang states it was translated from the *Saṃyuktāgama*, but it cannot be found there. Seen in Changfang’s record.
*Fanglu Chanxing Sanshiqijing* (The Thirty-seven Sūtras on the Practice of Dhyāna Recorded by Fang), one fascicle; sometimes the character "pin" (chapter) is added, as seen in Baochang’s record.

*Fanjie Baoying Qingzhongjing* (Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of Retribution for Violating Precepts), one fascicle; it appears in the *Mulian Wen Vinijing* (Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana’s Questions on the Vinaya), also titled *Fanjie Zuibao Qingzhong* (Lightness and Heaviness of the Guilt of Violating Precepts), or simply *Mulian Wen Jing* (Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana’s Questions);
see Changfang’s record. *Dabiqiu Sanqian Weiyingjing* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Deportments of a Great Bhikṣu).

It consists of either two fascicles or four fascicles, also titled *Dà-sēng-wēiyí-jīng* (Sūtra on the Dignified Conduct of the Great Saṃgha). Fáng states that he saw it in the *Bielù* (Separate Catalogue);

however, according to Sēngyòu’s *Shīyìlù* (Record of Lost Translations), it was divided into two sections with two fascicles each. In the *Bielù*, these were combined, but now only two fascicles remain, while the other three are no longer extant.

The *Dàodì-jīng* (Sūtra of the Stages of the Path) in one fascicle appeared early on; sometimes the character "Da" (Great) is prefixed to its title, as it is the same as the *Xiūxíng-jīng* (Sūtra on Practice).
An excerpt from the original foreign abbreviated version with the commentary of Dao’an; seen in Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue) and all other catalogues, it is stated to be in two fascicles.
According to Master Dao’an’s preface, there are seven chapters in total, and this first fascicle contains the full text. *The Scripture on Kāśyapa’s Compilation*, one fascicle;
its initial appearance is recorded in Changfang’s catalogue. *The Abhidharma Sūtra on the Five Dharmas*, one fascicle; alternatively, it may not exist.
The *Xingzi jing* (also known as the *Abhidharma-duḥkha-prajñā-sūtra*) was seen by Sengyù in the monastic records; the above portions are extant, while those below are missing.

The two-fascicle *Wuliangshou jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra) was first translated and is identical in substance to the "Infinite Life Assembly" (*Wuliangshou hui*) within the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*; this is what the Fáng family says.
The *Yúànhuàn sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Illusion-like Samādhi) in two fascicles, or one fascicle, is seen in the *Bié lù* (Separate Record);

its initial appearance was identical to the *Ráojí shànzhùyì huìděngběn* (Version of the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra on the Assembly of the Well-Abiding Mind), as noted in the *Chángfáng lù* (Chángfáng Record). The *Yuèdēng sānmèijīng* (Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra) in one fascicle is an alternative translation of the seventh chapter of the *Dà yuèdēngjīng* (Great Moon Lamp Sūtra), as seen in the *Chángfáng lù*.
The *Shī'èr yīnyuánjīng* (Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination) in one fascicle, whose initial appearance is also recorded as follows: [text continues].
*Wencheng shier yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Heard in the City); one fascicle, listed in Sengyou’s *Neizang jing lu*.
Second appearance; also titled *Neizang baipin* or *Baibao*. Translated in the twelfth month of the second year of the Yuanjia era. Listed in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu*.
*Sibukeye jing* (Sūtra on the Four Unobtainables); one fascicle. First appearance; some versions lack the character "ke" (unobtainable). Listed in Changfang’s *Lu*.
*Yao wang yao shang pusa guan jing* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata), one fascicle; first appeared in the *Chángfáng lù*.

*Kōng jìng tiān gǎnyìng sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Response of the Emptiness-Purity Heaven), one fascicle; the old catalogs call it the *Kōng jìng sānmèi jīng*; first appeared in the *Chángfáng lù*.

*Zú féng zéi jié yī dài zhòu jīng* (Sūtra on the Incantation for Binding Robes and Belts When Encountering Bandits), one fascicle; appears in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Zhòu zéi jīng* (Sūtra on the Incantation Against Bandits), one fascicle. (1)
The *Nāmavidhvaṃsanamārakṣaya-mantra* (The Incantation for Expelling Harmful Demons) is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*; it is also listed twice in Sēngyòu’s *Shīyì lù* under the same title, *Zhòuzé*.
Only one version remains here: the *Shí sìyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Fourteen Intentions), one fascicle;
the old catalogs state it is the *Púsà shí sìyì jīng*, as seen in Sēngyòu’s *Lǜfǎ sānmèi jīng*, one fascicle, which first appeared in Fǎshàng’s catalog.

*Daoyi faxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Path of Intention), two fascicles or one fascicle; recorded in the catalogs of Dao’an and Sengyou. Faxiang says it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
*Dà shí’èrmén jīng* (Great Twelve Gates Sūtra), two fascicles or one fascicle; translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Contains the commentary by Master Dao’an;
recorded in the catalogs of Baochang and Sengyou. *Xiǎo shí’èrmén jīng* (Small Twelve Gates Sūtra), one fascicle; translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Recorded by Master Dao’an.
The Master’s commentary is found in Baochang’s Record and Sengyou’s Record. There is one fascicle of the *Saptadharma-sūtra*;
old records state it is either the *Abhidharma-saptadharmaprakaraṇa-sūtra* or simply the *Saptadharmaprakaraṇa-sūtra*, as seen in Sengyou’s Record. Fang states it is extracted from the *Dīrghāgama*.

There is one fascicle of the *Bahu-dharmacakra-sūtra* (or *Bahu-dharmacakra-adhyāya-sūtra*); old records lack the character "dao" (path), referring to it as a variant version of the *Daśavipāka-sūtra*.

The *Fajian Changfang Lu* states that the *Yijue lü jing* (Scripture on the Decisions of Meaning for the Vinaya), one fascicle—sometimes omitting the word "scripture"—or also called the *Yijue lü fahang jing*, was translated by An Gong and is found in the *Chang ahan*.

It appears in Sengyou’s catalog as forty-four miscellaneous sūtras in two fascicles; some say it consists of forty-four miscellaneous sūtras. Since its specific title is not clearly manifest, [it remains unrecorded].
Regarding which sūtra [this corresponds to], Master Dao’an stated it was extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

It is found in Sengyou’s catalogue as the one fascicle, one hundred and sixty chapters of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; the old catalogues state it is the one fascicle, one hundred and sixty sections of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, also found in Sengyou’s catalogue.
The *Śatruñjaya-sūtra* (She-tou-jian jing) is one fascicle, found in the old catalogues; its second appearance also states it is the *Śatruñjaya-śāstra* (She-tou-jian taizi ming), twenty [chapters].
The *Aṣṭanakṣatra-sūtra* also mentions it; the *Prabhāvatī-kumāra-aṣṭāviṃśati-nakṣatra-sūtra* also mentions it; the *Vyāghrakarṇa-sūtra*;
the *Vaiḍūryarāja-sūtra*, one fascicle—some call it the *Ruli* (Liu-li) [Sūtra]; it is said to have been produced from the *Ekottarika-āgama*, but it is not found upon inspection;
the *Pañcamukha-dhyāna-yoga-upāya-sūtra*, one fascicle—initially appearing in the *Chángfáng-lù* (Catalogue of Dharma-pitaka); the *Kumāra-svapna-sūtra*, one fascicle.

The first fascicle appears in Changfang’s *Lu* (Catalogue) as the *Chanjing* (Dhyāna Sūtra) in two fascicles; the second appearance in [Changfang’s] *Lu* states it is seen in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue).

The *Hengshuijing* (Sūtra of the Ganges) in one fascicle first appeared with the title *Hengshui*; the *Bushuojiejing* (Sūtra on Not Preaching the Precepts) is seen in Fashang’s *Lu*. The *Baochang Lu* states:

the *Hengshui Jiejing* (Ganges Precept Sūtra) and the *Huiguo Fajing* (Sūtra on the Method of Repentance) in one fascicle are seen in Changfang’s *Lu*. The *Wufajing* (Sūtra of the Five Dharmas) in one [fascicle]...

One fascicle of the *Wuxing jing* (Sūtra on the Five Practices) is recorded in the *Sengyou lu*. One fascicle of the *Xiaobanniepan jing* (Minor Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa) is recorded in the *Changfang lu*;
Changfang states it is found in the *Bielu* (Separate Record).

The śramaṇa Anqing, whose courtesy name was Shigao,
was the crown prince of the chief queen of the King of Parthia. From childhood,
he harbored a pure and filial devotion, exhausting his sincerity in the care and support of his parents.
His benevolence, rooted in compassion, extended even to the most lowly creatures;
his speech and conduct were as precise as if following a compass and square.
Furthermore, he was diligent and quick-witted in his studies, applying himself with resolve to his learning.
There were no foreign classics that he did not master.
He was proficient in the phenomena of the seven luminaries and the five elements,
as well as the divinations of wind-angles and cloud-objects.
He calculated the waxing and waning of the calendar, thoroughly exhausting all its variations;
furthermore, he possessed profound mastery of medical arts and was exceptionally skilled in acupuncture and moxibustion.
By observing a patient’s complexion, he could diagnose their ailment, and his administration of medicine invariably brought salvation.
Even down to the cries of birds and beasts, he knew their intentions by hearing their sounds.
Once, while traveling, he saw a flock of cranes and suddenly said to his companions,
"The cranes say there must be someone bringing them food."
Shortly thereafter, he indeed achieved this;
everyone marveled at it, and thus his reputation for extraordinary talent spread throughout the Western Regions.
Neighboring countries, both far and near, all revered and esteemed him.
Although Gao lived as a layman, he observed the precepts with rigorous austerity.
He continuously provided the gift of Dharma through public lectures and assemblies.
Later, when the king passed away, he was about to succeed to the throne.
He then reflected deeply upon suffering and emptiness, developing a sense of weary detachment from his physical vessel.
Once his period of mourning was completed, he abdicated the kingdom to his uncle and left the household life to cultivate the Way.
He extensively mastered the Piṭaka of the Sūtras and was particularly proficient in the study of the Abhidharma.
He recited and upheld the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, exhausting its subtle mysteries.
Subsequently, he traveled abroad to propagate the teachings, visiting various kingdoms.
In the beginning of the reign of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty, he first arrived in the Eastern Land (China).
Possessing high talent and quick-witted insight, he could grasp the meaning upon hearing it once.
Not long after his arrival, he became thoroughly proficient in the Chinese language.
Lamenting that the True Dharma was declining, he extensively undertook the work of translation and propagation.
Tao Gao thoroughly investigated principle and exhausted his innate nature, thereby personally recognizing his past karmic conditions;
there were many divine traces that the world could not fathom.
Initially, Gao claimed that in a previous life he had already been the prince of Parthia (Anxi).
Together with the sons of the elders in his country, he left the household life.
While wandering for alms,
he encountered donors who were unsuitable.
Each time this occurred, he would vent his resentment and harbor hatred;
although Gao repeatedly admonished and exhorted him,
he ultimately did not reform.
After more than twenty years in this manner,
he took leave of his fellow students, saying:
"I shall go to Guangzhou to settle my karmic retribution from previous lives."
"You, Minister, are learned in the sutras and diligent, not lagging behind me;
yet your nature is prone to anger and resentment.
When your life ends, you shall receive an evil form."
"If I attain the Way, I shall certainly deliver you.
Subsequently, he departed for Guangzhou,
where he encountered great chaos due to bandits and rebels.
While traveling on the road, he encountered a youth who spat in his hand,
drew his sword, and said, "I have truly caught you!
He laughed loudly and said:
"I am here to repay you from afar because I owed you in my past lives.
Your anger, therefore,
is simply the intention [of your mind] from a previous existence."
He then extended his neck to receive the blade with an expression free of fear.
The bandits subsequently killed him,
while onlookers lined the road.
All were struck with wonder at this marvel;
yet this divine consciousness returned to become the crown prince of the King of Anxi,
who is none other than the present-day Shigao.
Having traveled extensively throughout China to propagate the teachings and complete his mission of expounding the sutras,
he encountered the turmoil of Guanzhong and Luoyang at the end of Emperor Ling’s reign;
he then took up his monk’s staff and journeyed south to Jiangnan.
"I shall pass through Mount Lu to visit my former fellow student.
Upon arriving at the temple of the Xutang Lake,
he found that this temple had long possessed divine power.
When merchants and travelers offered prayers, the wind would divide into upper and lower currents so that no one was detained.
Once, there was someone who begged for a divine bamboo staff;
before permission had been granted, he took it by force.
The boat immediately capsized and sank;
the bamboo returned to its original place.
From then on, the boatmen revered and feared him, none of whom failed to be struck with awe.
More than thirty ships of his traveling companions offered sacrificial victims and prayed for blessings.
The deity then descended and spoke through the invoker, saying:
"There is a śramaṇa on board; you may call him up."
The guests were all struck with amazement and requested that Gao enter the temple.
The deity addressed Gao, saying:
"In the past, in a foreign land, I went forth from home and studied the Way together with you."
He was fond of practicing charity but was by nature prone to anger; he is now the deity of the Yangting Temple.
Within a circumference of one thousand li, all is under my jurisdiction.
Because of his former practice of giving, his precious treasures are exceedingly abundant.
Because of my anger, I have fallen into this divine retribution.
Now that I see my fellow student, my grief and joy are beyond words;
my life will end within days.
His form was hideous and large;
if he were to die here, he would defile the rivers and lakes,
so he should instead be taken across the mountains to the marshes of the west.
"I fear that after this body perishes, I shall fall into hell.
I possess a thousand rolls of silk and various precious objects;
you may use these to establish the Dharma and construct a stupa, so that I may be reborn in a favorable realm."
Gao said, "I have come specifically to save you; why do you not manifest your form?
The spirit replied:
His appearance was so extremely hideous that everyone would surely have been terrified.
Gao said, "Just go out among the crowd; they will not find it strange."
The deity emerged from behind the bed with its head;
it was a great python,
and its tail could not be seen for its length.
He approached the Buddha’s knees;
the Buddha turned toward him and recited several verses of praise in Sanskrit.
The serpent wept with grief like falling rain, and in a brief moment, he vanished once more.
Gao immediately took the silk goods, bid them farewell, and departed.
As his fellow travelers hoisted the sails,
the python again emerged from its body, climbed the mountain, and gazed upon the multitude.
He raised his hand, and only then did the light vanish.
In the space of a mere instant, he had reached Yuzhang.
He immediately used the temple's assets to establish Dongsi Temple.
After Gao departed, his spirit immediately passed away.
At dusk, a young man came and knelt upright before Gao on the boat.
Having received his blessing and vow, the youth suddenly vanished.
Gao said to the boatmen, "The young man just now was none other than the deity of the Xuting Temple; he has finally been liberated from his evil form."
Thereupon, the temple deity vanished and ceased to manifest any further spiritual efficacy.
Later, people saw a dead python in a marsh to the west of the mountain,
its head and tail spanning several li.
The present-day She Village in Xunyang Commandery is that very place.
Later, when he arrived again in Guangzhou,
he found that the young man who had previously harmed him was still there.
Gao Jing went to his home and recounted the events of their past karmic retribution.
He further described their long-standing affinity, and as they faced each other with joy, he said,
"I still have remaining karmic rewards."
I shall now go to meet Bi Du in Kuaiji.
The traveler from Guangzhou realized that he was no ordinary man;
his mind was suddenly enlightened, and he felt deep remorse for his previous transgressions.
Hou provided him with provisions as they traveled eastward together, eventually reaching Kuaiji.
Upon arriving, they entered the marketplace, where a riot was breaking out;
those engaged in the fray mistakenly struck Gao on the head.
He passed away at that very moment.
A traveler from Guangzhou repeatedly witnessed these two karmic retributions and subsequently applied himself with diligence to the Buddha-dharma, recounting the circumstances in detail.
Those who heard of or learned of this, both far and near, could not help but lament;
it clearly demonstrates that the three periods of time possess verifiable evidence.
From the second year of the Jianhe era of Emperor Huan (Wuzi) until the third year of the Jianning era of Emperor Ling (Gengxu), more than twenty years had passed.
He translated ninety-five Mahāyāna sūtras, including the *Mahāyānopadeśa*, among others;
their principles and meanings were clearly analyzed, and their phrasing was both authentic and correct.
His style was eloquent yet not flowery, refined yet not rustic.
May all readers study this work with tireless devotion.

The *upāsaka* An Xuan was a native of the kingdom of Parthia (Anxi).
His character was upright and pure, and he possessed a profound mastery of philosophical principles.
He upheld the Dharma and the precepts without the slightest transgression,
and through his extensive reading of the various sutras, he had mastered many of them.
During the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, he traveled to Luoyang as a merchant.
Having rendered meritorious service, he was titled Commandant of Cavalry.
By nature, he was serene, tranquil, gentle, and respectful.
He constantly made Buddhist affairs his primary concern.
Gradually refining his command of the Han language, he resolved to propagate the scriptures.
He frequently engaged in discussions on the principles of the Way with śramaṇas.

He was what the world calls a Commandant (Duwei). In the fourth year of the Guanghe era (the Xin-chi year), Yan Fu drew up a list of the texts he had translated. Among them were the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* and others, which he co-translated with the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao. In the first year of the Jian’an era, he again co-translated the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* with the śramaṇa Zhu Falan.
