Xuán orally translated the Sanskrit text while Fútiao took it down in writing;
thus the principles were captured and the phonology made correct, exhausting the subtle purport of the sutra.
The beauty of this "sculptor of Ying" was extolled by later generations.
Dharmarakṣa stated that the *Fajing* and the *Fotiao* were produced based on their joint translation.
Furthermore, he referred to the *Ahan koujie* as being translated by An Shigao.

This is a case where the same family name leads to confusion regarding the identity of the translator. Since the old catalog records him as Anhou (An Hou), his oral interpretation likely also refers to Shi Gao’s second translation.

The *Chengju guangming dingyi jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance), also called the *Chengju guangming sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance) or simply the *Chengju guangming jing*, is the second translation;
it appears in the catalogs of Zhu Shixing, Zhi Mindu, Sengyou, and others.

The *Lu* (Catalogue) and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* record the *Anuruddha-aṣṭānussati-sūtra* in one fascicle, or simply the *Aṣṭānussati-sūtra*, also titled the *Dhyāna-practice of Mind-Restraint Sūtra*.
The old catalogues state that the *Dhyāna-practice of Mind-Examination* is an alternate translation found in the eighteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
There is also the *Sūtra on the Three Marks of Horses* in one fascicle, also called the *Good Horse Has Three [Marks]*.
The *Xiāng jīng* (Sūtra on Characteristics), translated by Fáng [Zhēn] from the thirty-third fascicle of the *Zá āhán jīng* (Saṃyukta Āgama);

also known as the *Jiàn wǔlù mǎ yǒu bā tài pì rén jīng* (Sūtra on Seeing Eight States of Horses Compared to Humans) in one fascicle, or simply the *Mǎ yǒu bā tài jīng* (Sūtra on the Eight States of Horses), also titled the *Mǎ yǒu bā bì è tài jīng* (Sūtra on the Eight Evil States of Horses).
Translated by Fáng [Zhēn] from the thirty-third fascicle of the *Zá āhán jīng* (Saṃyukta Āgama). It is recorded in the *Wǔlù* (Records of the Wu Kingdom) that it was seen [there].
*Wulu Xiaodaodi jing* (The Scripture on the Minor Path of the Earth), one fascicle. Fang says he saw it in the *Wulu*; it existed prior [to his time] but was subsequently lost.

*Wencheng Shier yinyuan jing* (The Scripture on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Spoken by Mañjuśrī), one fascicle. This is the second translation; it is the same text as the *Shier yinyuan jing* translated by An Shigao.
Fang says he saw it in the *Wulu*. *Damojie jing* (The Mahāmāyā Sūtra), one fascicle. Sometimes the character "Da" (Great) is omitted. Or...
The first fascicle of [the *Lalitavistara*] is the same text as the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*; Fang says he saw it in the *Wu lu*.
The *Ratthapāla-sūtra*, one fascicle, is from the thirty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; it is a different translation; Fang says he saw it in the *Wu lu*.
An says it is from the Vaipulya section, though this may perhaps be an error. The *Xiao benqi jing* (Shorter Sūtra of the Origin of the Buddha), two fascicles; some say—

*Xiuxing benqi* (The Original Arising of Practice), also called *Suxing benqi* (The Original Arising of Past Practice); the title was later supplemented with the characters "Jin jia" (Recently Added).
Its initial publication was identical to the *Ruixing benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Original Arising of Auspicious Signs), as seen in the old catalogs and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
*Duoluo youposai jing* (Sūtra of the Fallen Upāsaka), one fascicle; also called *Youpise*; Fang says he saw it in the *Wu lu* (Records of Wu). Total: ten works, eleven fascicles, small [size].
The first five sections and five fascicles of the *Daodi jing* (Scripture on the Path) currently exist; the latter five sections and six fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Zhiyao was a man from the Western Regions.
He was profoundly learned in the various classics and possessed a subtle understanding of their most profound mysteries.
In the second year of Zhongping of Emperor Ling’s reign (the year Yichou), ten scriptures including the *Juguangming jing* were translated at Luoyang.

In Changfang’s catalog and others, there is also the *Shouzhi wenfo shisi shi jing*; however, some versions lack the character "Fo" (Buddha). I personally saw its original manuscript, which was actually an excerpt from a scripture already compiled within the *Bieli shenglu*.
This has been deleted and is not included here.

One fascicle of the *Questioning on the Matters of Hell Sūtra* (Diyùshì jīng) is found in Zhu Shixing’s *Han-lù* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Kangchen (or Kangchen; it is unclear which version is correct) was a native of the Western Regions.
His heart was set on traveling to convert others, and his will was dedicated to spreading the teachings.
In the fourth year of the Zhongping era of Emperor Ling (the Dingmao year), he...
In Luoyang, he translated the *Questioning on the Hells Sūtra* (*Yiqiandiyu jing*).
Its language was direct and its principles profound, without further embellishment.

He also translated the two-fascicle *Sūtra of the Supreme Pure Alms-round of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī* (*Roushou pusa wushang qingjing fenwei jing*), also known as the *Sūtra of Resolving All Dharmas as Illusory Transformations Samādhi* (*Jueliao zhufa ruanhua sanmei jing*), which was among the first to appear.
The *Mahāprajñā-nāgaśrī-bhāga* (or similar title), one fascicle; identical to the original text, as recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
The *Huishang Púsà Wèn Dàshànquán Jīng* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Huishang Asking about Great Skillful Means), two fascicles;

its initial translation is identical to the *Ráozǎ Jīng*, "Chapter on the Mahāyāna Skillful Means" from the *Ratnakūṭa*, though some versions lack the word "Bodhisattva," or it appears as one fascicle, as recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. The *Gǔ Wéimójié Jīng* (Ancient Vimalakīrti Sūtra).
The first fascicle appears in the *Gǔlù* (Ancient Catalogue) and Zhusi Xing’s *Hàn lù* (Han Dynasty Catalogue); it is the same text as the Tang translation of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
The *Sìyì jīng* (Sutra on the Intention of Thought), also called the *Yìyì jīng* (Sutra on the Increase of Thought), appeared first in the *Chángfáng lù* (Changfang Catalogue).

The *Púsà nèixí liùbōluómì jīng* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Internal Practice of the Six Pāramitās) was stated by Master Dao’an to have been issued from the Vaipulya section; some say it is [contained within] the "Internal" section.
The *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* also speaks of "internal and external"; this is recorded in Changfang’s catalogue.

Of the five works totaling eight fascicles mentioned above, the first four consist of seven fascicles whose original texts are missing, while the latter one consists of one fascicle which is currently extant.

The śramaṇa Yan Fotiao also stated that Fu-tiao was a native of Linhuai Commandery; this is consistent with the records of Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue) and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, and it is incorrect for those such as the śramaṇa Changfang to record him as a lay believer (*qingxinshi*).
In her youth, she was exceptionally intelligent and fond of learning; her faith and wisdom were innate.
She subsequently left the household life to cultivate the Way, became proficient in translating the scriptures, and was held in high esteem by her contemporaries.
She was ordained in the fifth year of Zhongping of Emperor Ling’s reign, the Wuchen year.
In Luoyang, he translated five scriptures, including the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Śūraṅgama*.
The world has praised the three—An Houshu, Duwei Fotiao, and others—for their translation work, declaring them difficult to emulate.
Master Dao’an praised the translation produced by Zhu Fodiao as being concise rather than prolix, maintaining the original’s elegance and ingenuity.
Furthermore, the catalogues of Sengchang and others record an additional *Sūtra on Kāśyapa Interrogating Ānanda*.
It is also said to have been translated by Buddhayaśas;
I personally examined its original manuscript, which was a compilation of various sūtras containing several items of information.
The *Sui zhong jing lu* (Catalogue of Scriptures Compiled During the Sui Dynasty) states that this was extracted from the *Za piyu jing* (Miscellaneous Parables Scripture).
However, both An Shigao’s and Nie Chengyuan’s catalogues include this scripture;
thus, the compilers of the *Sui lu* were mistaken.
Since this is a separately produced excerpted scripture,
it should not be counted among the translations of the authentic canon.
Furthermore, the *Śrāmaṇera-daśajñāna-sūtra* states:
The preface composed and annotated by Fodiáo is neither the word of the Buddha nor does it contain the original text.
Now both of these have been deleted.
The *Śāriputra-Maudgalyāyana-catur-vīthi-saṃcāra-sūtra*, one fascicle, is a variant translation found in the forty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*;
see the separate record. The *Udāna-varga* (or *Qǐxìng xíng jīng*), two fascicles, is also titled *Yánjì sùyuán*.
The *Sūtra* is seen in the *Wulu* (Records of Wu), where the title reads: *Fannwang jing* (Brahmajāla Sūtra) in two fascicles, first appearing in the *Wulu*, or in three fascicles.
The *Siddhārtha Sūtra* in one fascicle appeared in the first year of the Xingping era. A second translation appears in the seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
it differs slightly from the version translated by Shigao. It is seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Han lu* (Han Records). Ta... [text fragment]

The *Zi ben qi xuying jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising of Auspicious Responses) in two fascicles is also called the *Xuying benqi* (Original Arising of Auspicious Responses); it is the second [text] produced, sharing the same source as the *Guoxian yinguo jing* (Sutra on Causes and Effects in Past and Present).
Fang says he saw it in the *Sanzang ji* (Record of the Tripitaka), yet in Sengyou’s *Sanzang ji*, Meng Xiang’s translation is titled *Zhongbenqi* (Middle Original Arising) and not *Xuying benqi*.
The *Baofu jing* (Sutra on Receiving Blessings) in one fascicle is also called *Fubao* (Recompense of Blessings). It is seen [in the catalog].

According to the *Wulu* (Records of Wu), there are six sections totaling nine fascicles: the first two sections, comprising three fascicles, are extant as the *Xingqi xing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Practice);
the latter four sections, comprising six fascicles, are missing from the original.
[Compiled by] the śramaṇa Kang Mengxiang.
He was originally a native of Kangju,
renowned for his wisdom and learning.
He arrived [in China] from the first year of the Xingping era of Emperor Xian (Jiaxu) to the fourth year of the Jian'an era (Jimao).
In Luoyang, he translated six works, including the *You sifu jing* (Sūtra on Wandering through the Four Crossroads).
Master Dao’an remarked:
"The translations produced by Meng Xiang flow with a majestic and elegant brilliance."
This is sufficient to soar into the profound and mysterious realm.

The *Xiuxing benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Acts of Practice), in two fascicles, is recorded in the third volume of the *Shixing lu* (Record of Shixing). It was produced alongside the *Ruizheng benqi jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses and Original Acts) and others; it shares the same title as the *Suxing benqi* (Original Acts of Past Conduct). This one work, in two fascicles, is extant.
The śramaṇa Zhu Dalì was a man from the Western Regions.
He delighted in traveling afar and felt no dread of hardships or dangers.
In the third month of the second year of the Jiàn’ān era of Emperor Xiàn (the Dingchūl year), he departed.
The *Sūtra on the Original Acts of Practice* was translated in Luoyang.
Its Sanskrit manuscript had also been brought from the kingdom of Kapilavastu by Dharmaphala and Kang Mengxiang.

Kang Mengxiang translated the *Zhongbenqi jing* (Sutra of the Middle Origination) in two fascicles, also known as the *Taizi zhongbenqi jing* (Sutra of the Middle Origination of the Prince); it is recorded in the *Shixing lu*. The title at the beginning of the sutra states: "Extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. This one work in two fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Dharmaphala was a man from the Western Regions.
His learning encompassed both the inner and outer teachings, and his understanding penetrated both the ultimate and conventional truths.
Carrying Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras, he arrived in Luoyang from the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
The *Madhyamāgama-sūtra* (Zhong benqi jing) was translated in the twelfth year of the Jian’an era of Emperor Xian, the Dinghai year.
Kang Mengxiang transcribed the language;
in the *Neidian lu*, it is recorded that Tan’guo and Mengxiang produced this work together.

It is incorrect to subsequently merge this with the *Mingxiang* (Allegory of the Prince’s Manifestation) and the *Benqi Ruinying* (Auspicious Responses to the Origin of the Prince) into a single volume;
the two scriptures are entirely different and cannot be combined.
Daoyou said:
As for the *Zhongbenqijing* translated by Kang Mengxiang,
this is based solely on its shared textual content with other scriptures.

The seven-fascicle *Dafangbian Fobaoen Jing* and the one-fascicle *Mahāyāna Baoyan Jing*— the latter also known as the "Chapter of Mahākāśyapa"— were the second translations, produced alongside the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*.

The *Ming Pusa Hui* (Assembly of Bodhisattvas) and other texts state that these were combined into a single volume during the Jin dynasty; the Jin records are followed here as preserved by Sengyou. They include: the *Mahāyāna-ratnavyūha-sūtra* (one scroll);
the *Amitābhabuddhagāthā-sūtra* (one scroll—some editions omit the word "sūtra"); the second edition of the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra* (one scroll);

the first edition of the *Buddhapratimā-sūtra* (one scroll), which is identical to the *Atilokottara-sūtra* translated in the Tang dynasty; also known as the *Udayanarāja-buddhapratimākaraṇa-sūtra* or the *Pratimākaraṇa-nidāna-sūtra*; and the *Pratimānirmāṇa-sūtra*.

*Fóbào jīng tóngběn ānzhái shénzhòu jīng* (Sūtra on the Blessings of Merit, Same Text as the Sūtra of the Spirit-Spell for Securing the Dwelling), one fascicle; also called *Ānzhái zhòufǎ jīng*. Sengyou says it is also called *Ānzhái zhòu shòu shíshàn jiè jīng* (Sūtra of the Spirit-Spell for Securing the Dwelling and Receiving the Ten Good Precepts), one fascicle.

*Kùyīn jīng* (Sūtra of the Aggregate of Suffering), one fascicle; translated from the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Zhōngāhán jīng* (Madhyama Āgama). *Yìmó rǎoluàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Disturbance by Māra), one fascicle;

also known as *Bìmó shì Mùlián jīng* (Sūtra on the Evil Māra Testing Maudgalyāyana) or *Mówáng rù Mùlián lánfù jīng* (Sūtra on the Demon King Entering the Belly of Maudgalyāyana); translated from the thirtieth fascicle of the *Zhōngāhán jīng*. *Shāmínijì jīng* (Sūtra on the Precepts for Śrāmaṇerikās), one fascicle.

One fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the word "Sūtra. *The Questions of Upāli on the Buddha’s Sūtras*, one fascicle; alternatively, it is called *Upāli’s Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. *The Treatise on the Analysis of Merit*, four fascicles;

alternatively, it is called *The Sūtra on the Analysis of Merit*, or three fascicles, or five fascicles. *The Essential Methods of Dhyāna for Rebuking Desire*, one fascicle; its title reads *The Essential Methods of Dhyāna, Chapter on the Contemplation of the Internal Body from the Section on Verses*. *The Sūtra on the Verses of Internal Body Contemplation*, one fascicle;

alternatively, it lacks the word "Verses. *The Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables*, two fascicles; also known as *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Saving Sentient Beings*. *The Sūtra of the Names of Six Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle. It is recorded that these were included in the Canon.
The names of the six bodhisattvas should also be recited and maintained. The above is preserved; the following is missing.

One fascicle of the *Amitābha Buddha Gāthā*, first translated from the Sanskrit original, consisting of four fascicles. Formerly called the "Hu-ben" (Central Asian manuscript), it has been newly revised as "Fan" (Sanskrit).

It appears to have emerged during the Chang'an period. Four fascicles of the *Transformation Sūtra of the Thousand-Year [Nirvāṇa]*, also known as the *Qiansui* (Thousand-Year) Sūtra, which appeared one thousand years after the *Nirvāṇa*.

The *Biàn jīng yòu* states: "One scroll of the *Biàn jì* [Record of Transformations] from within the first millennium after the *nirvāṇa*; two scrolls of the *Zhū jīng fó míng* [Names of Buddhas in Various Scriptures].

I now suspect these are the *Bù sīyì gōngdé jīng* [Sutra of Inconceivable Merit], the *Sān qiān fó míng jīng* [Sutra of the Names of Three Thousand Buddhas] in one scroll, and the *Chēngyáng bǎi qīshí fó míng jīng* [Sutra of the Praising of the Names of One Hundred and Seventy Buddhas] in one scroll, which is also simply titled *Bǎi qīshí fó míng*. I now suspect these originated from the *Chēngyáng gōngdé jīng*."
*The Scripture on the Names of the Buddhas of the Southern Virtue Region*, one fascicle (formerly titled *The Scripture of Zhicheng Temple*, which is incorrect;
this is merely a record of the temple’s name and not an alternative title for the scripture). *The Scripture on the Names of Buddhas for Eradicating Sin and Attaining Merit*, one fascicle.
*The Scripture on the Methods of Practice Spoken by Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle. This is a dhāraṇī scripture [concerning] the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.

*Qiu shen banruo tuangxiang jing* (Sutra on Seeking the Image of the Profound Prajñā), one fascicle; *Shouchi foming budu edao jing* (Sutra on Receiving and Maintaining the Names of Buddhas to Avoid Falling into Evil Paths), one fascicle;

*Wulong zhoudu jing* (Sutra of the Five Dragon Mantras Against Poison), one fascicle; *Qu xueqi shenzhou jing* (Sutra of the Spirit-Mantra for Taking Blood and Qi), one fascicle—formerly recorded as *Xuezhou zhuzhai zhufa jing* (Sutra of the Blood-Mantra and Methods for Cursing Thieves), one fascicle.

The fifty-nine works above are all found in Sengyou’s *Shiyì lù* (Record of Lost Translations). These fifty-nine works comprise seventy-six fascicles;

It is said that there were originally five fascicles, but now only four remain;

thus, of the names of the seventy-six bodhisattvas, sixteen sections comprising twenty-six fascicles are extant under the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*, while forty-three sections comprising fifty fascicles are missing.
The records of Sengchang and others state that these were lost translations from the Later Han period,
totaling one hundred twenty-five works in one hundred forty-eight fascicles.
Now, having meticulously collated the remaining sixty-six works in seventy-one fascicles, it is found that they are not of lost origin.
The detailed circumstances are set forth as follows:

*The Sūtra of the Sun-Moon Mani Jewel Left by the Buddha*, translated by Zhi Chen of the Han; *The Sūtra on the Birthplace of Bodhisattvas*, *The Sūtra of Various Difficulties Regarding the Sun*, and the above two sūtras, translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu;

In the later records of lost translations, these works were again included; however, upon close examination, it appears that this sutra is neither a work of lost origin from the Han dynasty nor one produced by Zhi Qian. It seems rather to have been translated by Master Kumārajīva and others during the Yao Qin period and onwards. For now, it is classified as a work of lost origin within the Qin records.

Some translations have reliable sources,
while others give rise to doubts regarding their authenticity;
since we have now investigated and identified their foundations, it cannot be said that the Han dynasty lost the original source.
Fearing that a re-compilation of the old versions would result in excessive complexity,
I have now standardized them all.
Changfang’s Record states:
The above one hundred and twenty-five works, totaling one hundred and forty-eight fascicles,
were all compiled by the Vinaya Master Sengyou from the *Chū-sanzō-ki* (Record of the Tripitaka).
They are derived from two ancient catalogs and the catalog of Dao’an, though their original sources have been lost.
Furthermore, the newly collected volumes of various scriptures translated by unknown translators are extremely numerous.
When collating these various catalogs, those that are corrupt and defiled are many;
as they intermingle and overlap, it is truly difficult to establish a definitive classification.
Without having seen the actual scripture, one reads its title in vain;
there are those who have entered [the path] and those from whom it originated, yet for those who have not entered, there is no translation.
Examining its origins, it is not as if they lack a source.
Since this has been deferred for many years, I have appended it here at the end.
I hope that those of broad learning may one day encounter the original source,
so that it might be corrected and recovered as a reliable authority.
Yingcheng [stated] that one should cause the waves and billows of the Dharma-ocean to subside;
however, this statement by Changfang cannot currently be relied upon.

*The Sūtra of the Difficulties of the Elder of the Four Castes*, one fascicle (the old catalog calls it *The Sūtra of the Elder of the Four Castes*);
*The Sūtra of the Refutation of the Buddha*, one fascicle; *The Essential Chapters from the Daodi Jing*, one fascicle (also called *The Minor Path*).

Regarding the *Dì jīng* (Earth Sūtra), it is currently suspected that the version translated by Zhi Yao consists of one fascicle titled *Shù liàn yì zhāng* (Chapter on Refining the Mind through Calculation). An old catalog states this is the *Shù liàn jīng*.

Master Dao’an claimed that the two aforementioned sūtras were derived from the *Chūshēng jīng* (Sūtra of Birth). Sengyou, however, has examined the current *Chūshēng jīng* and found no chapter with this name.
Thus, of the eighty-two works and eighty-two fascicles [previously listed], the first three sūtras beginning with the *Bāpō jīng* are extant; the remainder are all missing.
These are all the "Classical Scriptures" (Gu Dian Jing) collected by Master Dao’an from within Sengyou’s catalog;
since it refers to them as "classical," they clearly belong to a remote antiquity.
Now, these have been compiled among the texts of the late Han period, which I consider to be a loss of their original source.
Master Dao’an’s original catalog of classical scriptures comprised ninety-two sutras in total;
I have now searched through various catalogs for the remaining ten sutras.
Some are attributed to the primary translator while others are separately produced;
since these are already recorded therein, they are excluded here.
Together with the previously mentioned fifty-nine works in seventy-six fascicles translated by those of unknown translators, [the total is as follows].
In total, there are one hundred and forty-one works comprising one hundred and fifty-eight fascicles;
all are said to have lost their origins during the Han dynasty.
The Cao Wei dynasty of the Cao clan was based in Luoyang; from the first year of the Huangchu era of Emperor Wen (Gengzi) until the second year of the Xianxi era of Emperor Yuan (Yiyou),
a total of five emperors reigned for forty-six years.
The sūtras, precepts, and karmavācanās produced by the five śramaṇas comprise twelve sections in total.
Altogether there are eighteen fascicles; among them, four sections totaling five fascicles are extant, while eight sections totaling thirteen fascicles are missing.

[The extant works are: one section in one fascicle on the *Vinaya* by the Cao-Wei śramaṇa Dharmakāla; three sections in four fascicles on the *Sūtras* and *Karmavācanā* by the śramaṇa Saṃghavarman; one section in one fascicle on the *Karmavācanā* by the śramaṇa Dharmaratna; five sections in seven fascicles on the *Sūtras* by the śramaṇa Bai Ting; and two sections in five fascicles on the *Sūtras* by the śramaṇa An Faxian. There is also one fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika-śīla-mātṛkā*, which first appeared in the *Weishi lu* (Record of the Wei Dynasty) by Zhu Daozu. This latter work, consisting of one fascicle, is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmakāla (translated as "Dharma-time" in Wei) was a native of Central India.
His family had been immensely wealthy for generations and constantly cultivated the merit of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Since his youth, Kāla was exceptionally gifted and perceptive;
his physical appearance surpassed that of ordinary men, and when he read a book even once, he thoroughly mastered both its literary style and its meaning.
He was well-versed in the four Vedas and mastered all aspects of wind,
clouds, constellations, diagrams, prophecies, and the shifting movements of fortune;
he claimed that the principles and patterns of the world were entirely contained within his own mind.
At the age of twenty-five, he entered a monastic residence to study.
There he happened upon the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* by Dharmatrāta;
he took it up for a brief look, but found it utterly incomprehensible.
As he reverently and repeatedly examined them, his confusion and bewilderment increased all the more.
He then sighed, saying:
"I have accumulated learning for many years."
I have long aspired to the ancient classics and wielded my skills with ease through the scriptures;
yet, I could not conceive of their meaning twice, nor did I need to read their phrasing more than once.
Now, beholding these Buddhist texts, they suddenly transcend the limits of my understanding.
The principles were profound and contained further essential insights;
thereupon, he took his credentials into the quarters and requested a bhikṣu to provide a brief explanation.
Consequently, he attained a deep realization of cause and effect and gained a subtle mastery of the three periods of time.
Only then did he realize that the Buddhist teachings are vast and expansive, beyond what secular texts can reach.
He consequently renounced worldly glory to leave the household life and practice with diligent austerity,
reciting the sutras of both the Mahayana and Hinayana, as well as the various sections of the Vinaya.
He always valued traveling to convert others and did not delight in remaining in one place.
In the third year of the Huangchu era of Emperor Wen (the Renyin year), he arrived in Luoyang;
at that time, although the Buddha-dharma existed within the borders of Wei, [it was not widespread].
Yet the influence of the Way has declined and been corrupted;
there are even members of the Sangha who have not yet received the precepts of taking refuge,
regarding the mere shaving of their heads as sufficient to distinguish them from the common folk.
Furthermore, although their fasting and repentance rituals were similar to those of sacrificial offerings,
once Kālaya had arrived and extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma,
the monks requested that he produce the *Vinaya*.
Because the Vinaya-piṭaka was composed in verse with verbose and extensive phrasing,
it would certainly not have been adopted had Buddhism not yet flourished.
Consequently, in the second year of the Jiaping era (Jia-wu) of Emperor Fang of the Qi dynasty, he [began the work].
At the Baima Monastery in Luoyang, he produced the *Sengqi jieben* (Mahāsāṃghika-Prātimokṣa) and its essential precepts to provide for his daily needs.
Thereupon, he further assembled Indian monks and established the *karmavācanā* ritual for conferring the precepts;
it was from this that the Vinaya tradition first began in the Eastern Land (China).

Kāla’s final whereabouts are unknown. *The Sūtra on the Questions of the Householder Ugga* (one or two fascicles), the third translation, also titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Practice as Asked by Uggarava*;

it appeared in the fourth year of the Jiaping era. It is found in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei Record* and is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa*, specifically as the nineteenth assembly. *The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* (two fascicles), the fourth translation; it is found in Zhu Dao’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* and Baochang’s *Record*. It differs slightly from the version translated by Shi Huijiao. Furthermore, it is the same text as the *Immeasurable Life Sūtra* in the *Ratnakūṭa*. *The Miscellaneous Karma of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (one fascicle); its title reads *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya Section: Miscellaneous Karma*, beginning with the "Binding of the Precept Field. Newly appended. These three sections comprise four fascicles, and their texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Kang Seng-kai was a native of India.
He studied the various sūtras extensively and thoroughly elucidated their profound meanings.
In the fourth year of the Jiaping era, the Ren-shen year, he...
At Baima Monastery in Luoyang, he translated three works, including the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states that he translated four works, though their specific titles are not fully recorded.
This is confirmed by the *Weijin lu* (Records of the Wei and Jin) by Zhu Daozu, as well as the catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang from the Liang dynasty.
Furthermore, the three catalogs by Changfang, Daoxuan, and Jingmai all state that there were two recensions;
as for the other two, since their names are not apparent,
they have not been seen upon collation.
Now I have further obtained one fascicle;
however, one sutra remains missing,
and though I have searched for it, I have not yet found it.

The *Dharmaguptaka-karman* in one fascicle; its title reads *Karman*, one fascicle, extracted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. It begins with the "Binding of the Great Boundary" (*mahā-sīmā-bandha*). This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei lu*. This one work in one fascicle currently exists.
The śramaṇa Dharmatāta— also called Tandi—
is known as Fashi (Dharmatāta) in the Wei language.
He was a native of the country of Parthia.
A master student of the Vinaya-piṭaka who had attained profound mastery of its subtlest mysteries,
he arrived at Luoyang in the first year of the Gao-gui Xiang-gong era (the Jiashu year).
At the Baima Monastery, he translated the *Dharmaguptaka-karman* in one fascicle.

*The Sutra of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment*, two fascicles; the fifth [fascicle] was produced and corresponds to those translated during the Han dynasty by Zhi Chen and others, as well as the "Immeasurable Life Assembly" (*Wuliangshou hui*) of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
While the texts are identical, the phrasing differs. This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* and Sengyou’s *Catalogue*.
Furthermore, the *Sutra of Śūraṅgama* (*Chashulai jing*), one fascicle; one version lacks the character "Cha" (叉). Sengyou’s catalogue records it as "You" (又).
First appearing in the catalogs of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou:

*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Cultivation* (one fascicle), also titled *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Practice as Asked by the Elder Vaiśya*, or alternatively *The Scripture on the Elder’s Practice*.

Second, appearing in the two catalogs of Shixing and Baochang: *The Scripture on the Elimination of Calamities and Afflictions* (one fascicle), appearing in the catalog of Sengyou; first appearing alongside [the previous title].
The *Chujin zaihuān jīng* (Sūtra on Eliminating Fear and Calamity), a duplicate version of the *Shòulényán jīng* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra) in two fascicles, fifth in its appearance;

this is identical in content to the version translated during the Han dynasty by Zhi Chen and others, though the wording differs. This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jìnshì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Sengyou’s catalog.
These five works, totaling seven fascicles, are all currently missing.
The śramaṇa Baiyan was a man from the Western Regions.
His talent and brilliance were unsurpassed by his generation, and his profound understanding exceeded that of his contemporaries.
In the third year of the Gānlù era of Gāoguǐxiānggōng, which was the Wùyín year, he...
While traveling and teaching in Luoyang, he stayed at Baima Monastery and translated five sections of scriptures, including the *Wuliang qingjing jing* (Sutra of Immeasurable Purity).
According to the records of Sengchang and others, there was also one fascicle of the *Pingdengjue jing* (Sutra of Equal Enlightenment).
It is also said to have been translated by Bo Yan.
This present scripture is none other than the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing*;
however, because its title was either expanded or abbreviated, it was no longer retained [in the canon].

The *Rāmaka-sūtra* in three fascicles is found in the four catalogs of Zhu Daozu, Baochang, Fashang, and Lingyou; it is a small portion of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in two fascicles was first issued [as a separate work], and subsequently, the initial chapters of the abbreviated version of the great text were issued as these two fascicles. These two works are recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei-lu* (Wei Dynasty Catalog). Both sections comprise five fascicles in total, and their original texts are currently missing.
The śramaṇa An Faxian was a man from the Western Regions.
His mastery of the arts and learning was profound, and his wisdom and understanding were particularly lofty.
Carrying his mendicant’s staff, he traveled through various lands, arriving here from afar.
He translated two scriptures, including the *Rāmāyaṇa*,
both of which various catalogs attribute to the Wei dynasty,
though they do not specify the reign of which emperor.
Now, these are appended at the end.
Furthermore, the *Bie lu* (Separate Record) also contains various scriptures of unknown translators;
these are all listed following the *Wu lu* (Record of Wu).
*Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll One; Part One of the General Catalogue.
*Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu Year.
The second part of this general compendium of various scriptures, Volume One, Part Two:
The States of Sun and Wu; the House of Sun of Wu.
Formerly, the capital was at Wuchang.
Later, when the capital was established at Jianye, he followed Sun Quan’s posthumous title as Emperor Wenzu, the Great Ancestor.
From the first year of Huangwu (Renyin) until the fourth year of Tianji (Gengzi) under Sun Hao, he received no posthumous title.
In total, under four successive rulers, fifty-nine years passed.
Five individuals, both monastics and laypeople,
produced various translated scriptures, including those whose translators were lost.
In total, there are one hundred and eighty-nine works comprising four hundred and seventeen fascicles;
among these, sixty-one works in ninety-two fascicles are currently extant, while one hundred and twenty-eight works in three hundred and twenty-five fascicles are missing.
The Wu dynasty śramaṇa Vighna compiled two collections of six fascicles each; the śramaṇa Zhu Lüyan compiled four collections of six fascicles each;
the upāsaka Zhi Qian compiled eighty-eight collections totaling one hundred and eighteen fascicles of sūtras and vinaya;
the śramaṇa Kang Senghui compiled seven collections totaling twenty fascicles of sūtras; and the śramaṇa Zhi Jiangliangjie [compiled] one...
The section on the six fascicle scriptures includes eighty-seven works totaling two hundred and sixty-one fascicles translated by various unknown translators during the Wei and Wu dynasties.

Among them are the *Aksayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra* in four fascicles; its initial translation was identical in substance to the *Aksayamati-nirdeśa* and the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin, as recorded in the two separate catalogs of the Wu dynasty.
Also included is the *Dharmapada* in two fascicles, [the latter] being the first [of its kind].
The *Chū* (translated as "Emergence") is also called the *Dharmapada-saṃgraha*, compiled by the Venerable Dharmatrāta and translated jointly by Zhu Foyan and Zhi Qian;
this is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. The *Wu lu* (Record of Wu) states that Zhu Juan is unknown. Thus, there are two sections totaling six fascicles:
the *Dharmapada-sūtra* in two fascicles currently exists, while the *Aksayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* in four fascicles is missing.
The śramaṇa Vighna (translated as "Obstacle" in the Wu [Chinese] language) was originally a person from India.
For generations his family had followed heterodox paths, regarding fire worship as supreme.
At that time, there was an Indian śramaṇa who had studied the Hīnayāna and practiced many magical arts.
As he was traveling a great distance and evening approached, he wished to seek lodging for the night at the house of the Nans.
Since the host family followed a heterodox path, they harbored suspicion toward the Śramaṇas;
consequently, they placed them outside the gate on the open ground to sleep there.
At night, the Śramaṇa secretly applied incantations and esoteric arts.
He caused the fire upon which the family relied to suddenly vanish.
Thereupon, the entire household came out together to entreat the śramaṇa to enter their home for offerings.
The śramaṇa, in turn, used his incantations to transform the fire so that it would reappear.
Having witnessed that the śramaṇa’s supernatural powers surpassed his own,
Nandika conceived a profound faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma;
he then abandoned what he had previously served and left the household life to pursue the Way.
Relying on this śramaṇa as his preceptor,
he studied the Tripiṭaka and became profoundly skilled in the four Āgamas;
wherever he traveled to convert and teach in various kingdoms, there was no one who did not revere him.
Together with his companion Zhu Lüyan, he departed from the Western Regions and arrived in Jiangzuo.
In the third year of Sun Quan’s Huangwu era, the Jiachen year,
at Wuchang Commandery, he and Zhu Lüyan translated two sections of the *Acchara-mati* (Aśokadattā) Sūtra and other scriptures.
However, as both Zhi Nan and Yan were not yet proficient in local dialects,
there were considerable omissions during the translation from Sanskrit;
their intent lay in the fundamental meaning, and their phrasing was relatively plain and unadorned.

The *Madengjia jing* (Mātṛkā-sūtra) in three fascicles is recorded in the *Fashang lu*; it was translated jointly by [Dharmakāla] and Zhi Qian. It shares the same original text as the *Shetoujian jing* and others, or consists of two fascicles; this is the fourth translation. The *Samojie jing* (Samudra-sūtra) in one fascicle was first recorded in the *Shixing lu*; it shares the same original text as the *Fenhuotuanwang jing* but is a different translation. It is also known as the *Sumoti nü jing*, the *Nanguo wang jing*, or the *Shuhetuanwang jing*. The *Foyi jing* (Buddha-physician Sūtra) in one fascicle was translated jointly with Zhi Yue; it is not a complete canon but an abridgment from a larger sūtra. Some call it the *Foyiwang jing*; it is recorded in the *Baoshang lu*. The *Fanzhi jing* (Brahmacārin Sūtra) in one fascicle is recorded in the *Shixing lu*. The above four works comprise six fascicles; of these, the first three consist of five fascicles and are extant, while the last one consists of one fascicle and is missing.
The śramaṇa Zhu Lüyán was a native of India.
His understanding and practice were pure and rigorous, and he was extensively learned in both Buddhist and secular learning.
He traveled through the territories of Wu together with Weiqinan.
After the death of Vighna,
in the second year of the Huanglong era of Sun Quan, the gengxu year,
he translated four scriptures, including the *Mātṛkā*, at the capital of Yangzhou.
Their names appear differently in various catalogs;
some call them Jiangyan (將炎),
while others call them Chiyen (持炎).
Some call it the *Lüyan* (律炎);
it is not clear which is correct, so both are listed here for reference.
The *Damingdu Wujing Jing* (大明度無極經) consists of four fascicles; it was the second [translation] produced, though some versions consist of six fascicles and are simply titled *Damingdu* (大明度).
The *Sūtra* is identical in its original text to the *Daoxing Xiaopin* (Shorter Version of the Practice of the Way) and other works;
it is recorded in the *Weiwu Lu* by Zhu Daozu as well as in the catalogs of Sengyou and others. Within the two-fascicle *Amituo Jing*, the internal title reads:
*Buddhabhāṣita Sarvabuddha Amitābha San-xie Sanfo Saqi-dan Guodu Ren Dao Jing*, Fascicle Three; it is also titled *Wuliangshou*. This is seen in the records of Zhu Dao[zu].

The two catalogs of Master Sengyou differ slightly from those of Shi Heng and others. The *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-sūtra* (一卷) is also simply titled the *Mūla-karman-sūtra*, and is alternatively called the *Śuddhacaryā-parivarta-sūtra*.
This is a separate translation of the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śuddhacaryā-parivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
It appears in the catalog of Sengyou; it is an error for the *Changfang-lu* to list the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" separately outside of the *Mūla-karman-sūtra*. [End of] Wei.

*Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, two fascicles; also titled *The Teaching on the Inconceivable Dharma-gate Spoken by Vimalakīrti*, or alternatively *The Sūtra on the Buddha-Dharma Universally Entering the Gate of the Path Samādhi*, translated secondly [during the Wu dynasty].
It appears in three fascicles in the records of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou, with slight differences from the translation by Bo Fazu and others of the Han period.
*Huiyin Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Wisdom-Seal Samādhi), one fascicle; also simply called *Hui*.

The *Yinjing* (Seal Sūtra), also known as the *Baotianhuiyin Sanmeijing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom of the Precious Field), was originally translated from the same source as the *Rulai Zhiyin Jing* (Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Seal of Wisdom);

it appears in both the *Jiaozu lu* and the *Sengyou lu*. The *Jiuse lu jing* (Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer) in one fascicle was translated from the *Liudu ji* (Collection of the Six Pāramitās) and is found in alternative translations;

it appears in the *Fashang lu*. The *Laonuren jing* (Sūtra of the Old Woman) in one fascicle, according to Master Dao’an, was translated from the *Abhidharma*; it is listed in the *Wu lu* (Wu Record). It is direct [authentic].

The *Sūtra on the Old Woman* (also known as the *Sūtra on the Old Mother*). Its initial appearance is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue; a version titled the *Sūtra on the Calf* (*Vatsa-sūtra*) in one fascicle appears in Faxiang’s catalogue.
Its first appearance was concurrent with the *Sūtra of the Radiant Milk Buddha* (*Kṣīraprabhāsa-buddha-sūtra*), among others.

The *Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under a Peepal Tree* (*Bodhi-vṛkṣa-mūle dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-cintā-sūtra*) in one fascicle appears in Fazang’s catalogue. Its third appearance was concurrent with the Tang translation of the *Ārya-pratītyasamutpāda*.

*Daojing dengtongben liao ben shengsi jing* (The Scripture on the Path, Identical to the Original and Clarifying the Original of Birth and Death), one fascicle. Master An stated it was the *Chusheng jing*.

Sengyou examined the five-fascicle *Sheng jing*, but this title does not appear therein; he saw it in the *Sengyou lu* as being the same original text as the *Dao mian jing* (Rice Seedling Scripture) but issued separately.

Daoqian personally annotated it and composed a preface. Master An’s preface states: "Issued at the end of the Han dynasty; Daoqian annotated the *Longshi nü jing* (Scripture of the Dragon-Giving Woman), one fascicle."
The initial edition was the same text as the *Nāgadatta-bodhisattva-pūrvayoga-sūtra*. Sengyou states that it is recorded in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalog) but is not found in Seng'an's catalog;

one fascicle of the *Bajixiang shenzhou jing* (Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Divine Spells). In some initial editions, the character "shen" (divine) is absent, or it is called the *Bajixiang jing* (Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones), which is the same text as the *Bayang shenzhou jing* (Sūtra of the Eight Yang Divine Spells).
Fazang states that he saw it in ancient catalogs as the *Wuliangmen weimi jing* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Gates of Subtle Mystery).

The *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Chí jīng), one fascicle, is also simply called the *Subtle and Secret Dhāraṇī Sūtra* (*Wēimì chí jīng*), with the alternative title *Sūtra on Attaining the Way, Subduing Māras, and Obtaining All-Knowledge*.
Its initial translation was identical in substance to the *Sūtra on the Holding of the Gate of Producing Immeasurable Doors* (*Chūshēng wúliàngmén chí jīng*).

This is seen in the two *Qin* catalogs by Sengrui and the *Catalog* by Sengyou. Alternatively, there is the *Huājī dhāraṇī Divine Spell Sūtra* (*Huājī tuóluóní shénzhòu jīng*), one fascicle, which appears in the *Bǎochàng* catalog.
*Wushenzizi yu Huazhuituoluoni dengben chizhou jing* (The Scripture on the Mantra for Holding the Same Text as the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī*), one fascicle.
Its first appearance is recorded in the *Changfang lu*; it is said to be the same text as the *Daluolinni po jing*. It is also said to have been translated by Tuo-lin-ni-po.

*Shihuimei jing* (The Scripture of the Secret and Profound), one fascicle. Its second appearance; some say "Secret and Profound" (*Shihuimei*) is an alternate name for the *Bodhisattvamārga* (The Path of the Bodhisattva).

The tree is also called the Bodhi Tree (the Tree of the Way). Regarding the *Samādhi of Seeing the Path on the Bodhi Tree*, Sengyou and others of the three catalogs—Dao'an, Zhi Min-du, and Sengyou—record it. Sengyou states:
"This sūtra is the *Bodhisattva-dao-shu* (Bodhisattva’s Tree of the Way) or *Bodhisattva-sheng-di* (Birthplace of the Bodhisattva) Sūtra, one fascicle;

it is also titled the *Chamojie* (Kṣamāvatī) Sūtra. Its initial appearance is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wu-lu* (Record of Wu) and Sengyou’s catalog. The *Bo-jing* (Sūtra of the Parable of the Wise Man), one fascicle, is also called *Bo*.

Sengyou’s *Chao jing* (Excerpts from the Scriptures) states: "The single fascicle of the *Bo jing* (Upasaka Sūtra) is the second edition; it appears in Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Lu*) and the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalogue).

The single fascicle of the *Yueming pusa jing* (Candraprabha Bodhisattva Sūtra)—sometimes with the word 'samādhi' added—also known as the *Yueming tongzi jing* (Candraprabha Boy Sūtra) or the *Yueming tongnan jing* (Candraprabha Youth Sūtra), appears in Sengyou’s Catalogue.
The single fascicle of the *Sanpin dizi jing* (Sūtra on the Three Grades of Disciples) is also known as..."
The *Disciples’ Three Grades of Learning Sūtra* (Tǐzǐ xué yǒu sānbèi jīng) is recorded in the Chángfáng lù;
the *Lǜfǎ sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Vinaya and Dharma), one fascicle, is also simply titled the *Lǜfǎ jīng*, its second appearance being recorded in the Chángfáng lù;

the *Fànzhì Ābá jīng* (Sūtra of the Brahmin Ābá), one fascicle, also known as the *Ābá mónnà jīng*, is listed in the Ān lù as simply the *Ābá jīng*, and is also called the *Fó kāijiě fànzhì ābá jīng*.
The *Bān jīng* (Sūtra of Bān) appears in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*; it is seen in the *Chángfáng lù* as a variant translation.
The *Fàn wǎng liùshí'èr jiàn jīng* (Sūtra of the Sixty-two Views of the Brahma-net), one fascicle—also titled the *Fàn wǎng jīng*—is noted by Fáng as being found in a separate catalog;

it appears in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* as a variant translation. The *Qī zhī jīng* (Sūtra of the Seven Knowledges), one fascicle—or alternatively titled the *Qī zhì jīng*—is seen in the *Chángfáng lù* as appearing in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
*Āgama*, Volume One: *The Sūtra on the Original Account of Śreṇika*, one fascicle (not recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue;
alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Causes of the Five Aggregates*; Sengyou’s catalogue states it was extracted from the twenty-fifth [section] of the *Madhyamāgama*).
A different translation seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Wu Lu* and Sengyou’s catalogue. *The Sūtra on the Root of All Dharmas*, one fascicle: extracted from the [twenty-fifth section] of the *Madhyamāgama*.
Twenty-eight alternative translations are recorded in the *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Dharma-ling): 1. *Bìmó shì Mùlián jīng* (Sūtra on the Evil Māra Tempting Maudgalyāyana), one fascicle;

also known as *Mó rǎoluàn fáng* (The Māra Who Disturbs the Dwelling); said to be found in the old catalogues. 2. *Làitāhuólúo jīng* (Sūtra of Rāṣṭrapāla), one fascicle; translated from the *Zhōng āhán jīng*, fascicle thirty;
an alternative translation, also called *Luóhàn Làitāhuólúo jīng* (Sūtra of the Arhat Rāṣṭrapāla). This was translated by Zhīyào of the Later Han dynasty.
Slightly different from the above, it appears in the third volume of the *Madhyama Āgama* (translated by Yào Wǎn). Sēngyòu states that it is recorded in the *Bié lù* but is not found in the *Ān lù*.
There is one fascicle of the *Brahmāyu-sūtra*, also written as *Yú*; it is seen in the records of Dàozǔ and Sēngyòu.

It appears in the forty-first volume of the *Madhyama Āgama* as a different translation of the *Zhāijīng* (Fasting Sūtra), also known as the *Chízhāijīng* (Holding the Fast Sūtra); it is seen in the *Bié lù*.
Recorded in the *Sengyou lu* as the fifty-fifth sutra of the *Madhyamāgama*,
translated differently as the one-fascicle *Sumati-dārikā-sūtra*. Recorded in the *Changfang lu* as the twenty-second sutra of the *Ekottarikāgama*,
translated differently as the one-fascicle *Anātma-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (also appearing as *An-ātma* or *Zi-shou yi-bu zi-shou jing*), translated from the *Saṃyuktāgama*.

Included in Volume Eleven; a variant translation seen in the *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Dharma-Repository). *Wǔ mǔzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Five Mothers and Sons), one fascicle, seen in the *Chángfáng lù*.

Its initial appearance was as the same text as the *Shāmíló jīng* (Sūtra of Śamīla). *Tàizǐ ruìyìng běnqǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Auspicious Response and Original Arising of the Prince), two fascicles, translated during the Huángwǔ era.
Its fourth appearance is also titled *Tàizǐ běnqǐ ruìyìng* (Auspicious Response and Original Arising of the Prince), or simply *Ruìyìng běn* (Auspicious Response and Origin).

The version produced by Qi differs slightly from that translated by Meng Xiang; it was transcribed by Xie Qiang of Chenjun and Zhang Xi of Wujun, and edited by Huan Xiang, Prince of Hedong of the Wei dynasty.
It appears in the two catalogs compiled by Sengyou of Shixing.

The *Sūtra of the Dragon King Brothers* (one scroll), also known as the *Nan Dragon King Sūtra* (sometimes omitting the character "Wang"), or the *Jiang Dragon King Sūtra*, first appeared in the *Chang [Ahan Jing]*.

*Fánglù Zhǎngzhě Yīnyuè Jīng* (The Sūtra of the Elder Yīnyuè Recorded by Fáng), one scroll; also called *Zhǎngzhě Yīnyuè Bùlánjiāshè Jīng* (The Sūtra of the Elder Yīnyuè and Bùlánjiāshè) or simply *Yīnyuè Jīng*.
Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Qīnǚ Jīng* (The Sūtra of the Seven Daughters), one scroll; also called *Qīnǚ Běnjīng* (The Original Sūtra of the Seven Daughters).
Master Ān states it was extracted from the *Āpítán* (Abhidharma). Its initial appearance is recorded in the *Sēngyòu Lù*. *Bāshī Jīng* (The Sūtra of the Eight Teachers), one scroll.
The *Zhujiaozu Wulu* and the *Sengyou Lu* record that the *Pingshawang Wuyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Five Vows of King Piṅgala) was first translated in one fascicle;
it is also written with the character "ping" (flask), and is alternatively titled the *Fushajiewang jing*. It is recorded in the *Changfang Lu*.

An Gong stated that it was originally from the *Madhyamāgama*, but upon verification, it is not found there. The *Yizu jing* (Sūtra on the Meaningful Footsteps) in two fascicles is recorded in the *Zhujiaozu Wulu* and the *Sengyulu*.
In the first compilation of Sengyou’s *Chanyan lu*, there were sixteen scriptures, including:
the *Sumati-gṛhapati-sūtra* in one fascicle—also titled *Huizhufuqian* and alternatively titled *Rulai suoshuo shixian zhongsheng jian*;
the *Ānansishi jing* in one fascicle, found in Sengyou’s catalog as well as the *Bielu*; and the *Weishengyuan jing* in one fascicle.
The *Sūtra on the Four Vows* (Sīla-vrata-catuṣka-sūtra), one fascicle, is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Brāhmaṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle, is recorded in the *Zhú Dàozǔ Wǔlù* and the *Sēngyòu lù*;
Fáng states it is found in the *Bièlù*. The *Xiègǒu jīng* (Rabid Dog Sūtra), one fascicle, is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.
The *Sūn Duōyézhì jīng* (Sūn Duōyézhì Sūtra), one fascicle, is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*, though some call it the *Fànzhì Sūn Duōyézhì jīng*.

Master Daoan stated that the *Jie xiaozai jing* (Sūtra on the Extinguishing of Calamities through Precepts), also known as the *Jie xiaofu zai jing*, in one fascicle, was translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*;
this is seen in the *Jiulü*. The *Zuanji baiyuan jing* (Collected Sūtra of One Hundred Karmic Causes) in ten fascicles is seen in the *Neidian lu*.

The *Pusa benyuan jing* (Sūtra of the Original Causes of the Bodhisattva) in two fascicles—also known as the *Pusa benyuan ji jing*—is either in two or four fascicles; it was [translated by] the Indian Śramaṇa... [text ends].
*Men sengqiesina zhuan jian* (The Compilation of Men Sengqiesna on Views), one fascicle;

recorded in the *Changfang lu*. Only the first part exists; the following is missing. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle; sometimes without the word "Mahā"; recorded in the *Baoshang lu*.
*Fajing jing* (Dharmādarśa-sūtra), two fascicles; sometimes one fascicle. This is the second edition; Sengyou states it was translated by [An]shigao.
I have examined the *An-lu* (An’s Catalogue) among the supplementary records and found it not there;

furthermore, the *Chang-fang-lu* and other catalogues list another work, the *Yujia Zhangzhe Jing* (Ugra-paripṛcchā-sūtra) in two fascicles, also said to be translated by Qian, which is identical to this present scripture and should not be recorded twice.

The *Ajieshiwangnü Ashuda Pusa Jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Āśudatā, Daughter of King Ajātaśatru) in one fascicle first appears in the *Chang-fang-lu*. The *Achamo Pusa Jing* (Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra) in four fascicles—
The third edition of the *Xiǎo Āchāmò jīng* (Sūtra of Akṣayamati) in two fascicles, found in the *Wùlù*, is identical in text to the version translated by Vighna, differing only slightly;
it is recorded in the *Bièlù* and the *Sēngyòulù*. Since it has been designated with the prefix "Small" (*xiǎo*), it should not be the same text as the preceding sūtra.
The *Dàbānníhuán jīng* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) in two fascicles is the third edition; this is an abridgment of the introduction to the extensive version, consisting of the section on lamentation.

This chapter consists of two fascicles; it differs slightly from the last three sheets [of the standard version]. According to Zhu Daozu’s *Wu lu*, Master An stated that it was extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Sengyou states that the current *Dīrgha Āgama* differs from this. The *Sūtra of the Three Chariots Summoned by the Buddha* in one fascicle is recorded in the *Changfang lu*;
it is said to have been extracted from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, specifically from the second fascicle, the "Parable" (*Upamā*) chapter, concerning the "Unadorned Woman."
*Sūtra* (one fascicle). Its first appearance is recorded in the *Baochang lu*. *Sūrya-sūtra* (one fascicle), also called *Sūrya-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
Its third appearance is the same text as that translated by Bai Yan and others; it is recorded in the *Zhu Daozu Wulu* and the *Sengyou lu*.
*Bodhisattva-xingxing-jing* (one fascicle). Its first appearance is recorded in the *Baochang lu*. It expounds upon the Way for both the clergy and the laity.

*Yejing* (Sutra on Karma), one fascicle. First appearance in the *Jiulù* (Old Catalogue); some versions lack the character "ye" (karma). *Fangdeng Shoulengyanjing* (Prajñāpāramitā Śūraṅgama Sūtra), two fascicles.
Translated during the Huangwu era. Second appearance; same text as that produced by Zhi Qian and others of the Later Han. Appears in Zhu Daozu’s *Wùlù* (Wu Catalogue) and the *Ānlù* (An Catalogue).

The latter lacks the characters "wúyòu" (without benefit) and "fāngděng" (vaipulya), stating instead that it is seen in the *Bièlù* (Separate Catalogue) and the *Wéimíng* (Vimalakīrti). Two fascicles.
*Shi ji jing* (Ten Verses Sūtra), one fascicle; first appearance—some editions omit the word "sūtra"—listed in Sengyou’s *Lu*. *Fa mie jin jing* (Sūtra on the Extinction of the Dharma), one fascicle;
first appearance—some say *Fa mo jin*, others say *Kong ji pusa suo wen jing* (Sūtra Asked by the Bodhisattva Śūnyatāśānta)—listed in Changfang’s *Lu*.
*Qi fo shen zhou jing* (Sūtra of the Divine Spells of the Seven Buddhas), one fascicle; one version omits the word "sūtra"—listed in Changfang’s *Lu*. *Maha jing* (Mahā-vidyā).

*Jinjing* (Sutra on Progress), one fascicle; also called *Dajingjinjing* (Sutra of Great Diligence); listed in the Changfang lu. *Dafangdeng jing* (Great Vaipulya Sutra), one fascicle; not recorded by Daoan;
Sengyou states it is seen in the *Bielu* (Separate Record). *Fosongshangsu xing sanshi jie jing* (Sutra of Thirty Verses on the Buddha’s Conduct Above), one fascicle;
sometimes the word "sutra" is omitted; listed in the Sengyou lu. *Sishier zhang jing* (Sutra in Forty-two Sections), one fascicle; second edition.
It differs slightly from the translation by Kāśyapa Mātanga; its phrasing and meaning are highly correct, and its diction is worthy of admiration (see the *Bie lu*).
The *Chan miyao jing* in four fascicles—sometimes omitting the word "jing" (sūtra)—first appeared in the *Wu bie lu*.
The *Jianyi jing* in one fascicle—also called the *Jianxin jing*—is listed as the second appearance in the *Changfang lu*. The *Quanjin xue dao jing* in one fascicle is the first [entry].

The first appearance of the title *Benwu quan* (Fundamental Non-existence Exhortation) is seen in Changfang’s record as one fascicle of the *Hengshui jiejing* (Sutra on the Precepts of the Ganges), though some versions lack the character "jie" (precepts).

The second appearance is in the old records as one fascicle of the *Qiloujing* (Sutra on the Seven Leaks). Changfang states it is also found in the *Bielu* (Separate Record) as one fascicle of the *Huiguo fajing* (Sutra on the Method of Repenting Transgressions), though some versions lack the character "fa" (method);
it is also known by the alternative title *Xushi fang shi baili huiguo wen* (Text on the Sequence for the Ten Directions’ Prostrations and Repentance), as recorded in Sengyou’s catalog.
*The Sutra on the Virtues of the Wise*, one fascicle; listed in the *Monk You’s Catalog*. *The Sutra on the Brahmin’s Binding Purity*, one fascicle;
listed in the *Catalog of Changfang*. *The Sutra of King Aji*, one fascicle; listed in the *Catalog of Changfang*.

*The Sutra of the Parable of King Weilou and the Lion’s Crossing*, one fascicle; one version lacks the word "parable"; listed in the *Catalog of Changfang*. *The Sutra of King Landata*, one fascicle. (1)
The *Maudgalyāyana-guṇa-sūtra* (also known as the *Maudgalyāyana-hetu-pratyaya-guṇa-sūtra*) is recorded in the *Wulu*.
The *Śata-avadāna-sūtra* in one fascicle is recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Pañca-skandha-vastu-sūtra* in one fascicle is recorded in the *Changfang lu*.
The *Māra-nirmita-bhikṣu-sūtra* in one fascicle is recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Uttara-mātṛ-sūtra* in one fascicle; according to one version, it lacks the word "mother."
*Zijian sengyou lu*: *Renmin qiuyuan jing*, one fascicle; seen in the *Changfang lu*. *Xingxiu fangbian jing*, two fascicles;
also called *Xingxiu fangbian chan jing*; seen in the *Wulu*. *Faju jing*, two fascicles;
the second edition; also called *Faju ji*; seen in the *Bielu* and the *Sengyulu*. The above totals eighty-eight works, one hundred [fascicles].
The *Weirizhan jing* (Sūtra on Miscellaneous Difficulties) consists of eighteen fascicles and fifty-one sections totaling sixty-nine fascicles; these are currently extant.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra* section consists of thirty-seven sections totaling forty-nine fascicles; these are missing from the original.
The Upāsaka Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming,
also known as Yue,
was a native of the Great Yuezhi.
His grandfather, Fadu, led several hundred people from his nation to submit to Han rule during the reign of Emperor Ling;
he was subsequently appointed General of the Household for Leading the Well-Governed.
At the age of seven, Yue played with a bamboo horse at a neighbor’s house.
He was bitten by a dog, which shattered the bone in his shin.
A neighbor wished to kill the dog to take its liver and apply it to the wound.
Yue said:
Heaven created this creature to guard and bark for man.
If you do not go to your master’s house, the dog will never bite you;
thus the fault lies with me and does not concern the dog.
If even killing it would not lead to recovery, it should not be done;
how much less so when it provides no benefit to me while inviting great sin in vain?
Furthermore, as animals lack consciousness, how can they be held accountable through reason?
Because of this, his neighbor was moved by the sincerity of his words and consequently ceased killing [animals] altogether.
At ten years of age, he studied the Chinese classics;
at thirteen, he studied the Brahmanical scriptures.
He was also exceptionally refined and proficient in the spoken languages of the six kingdoms.
During the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling, Zhi Chen translated the scriptural canons.
There was also Zhi Liang, whose courtesy name was Jiming.
Zi studied under Chen;
Xuanqian, in turn, received instruction from Daoliang.
He read widely through the scriptures and classics, becoming thoroughly proficient in them all.
He was well-versed in many worldly arts.
His physique was slender, tall, dark, and emaciated;
his eyes were mostly white with yellow irises.
At that time, people spoke of him in verse, saying:
"Zhi Lang’s eyes are yellow; though his frame is slender, he is a treasury of wisdom.
Originally, he had revered the Great Dharma and refined his mastery of the essential meanings of the sutras.
At the end of Emperor Xian’s reign, the House of Han fell into great chaos.
He fled to Wu with several dozen fellow villagers;
on the day they first set out, he possessed nothing but a single blanket.
There was a traveler who followed him; it was extremely cold and he had no blanket.
Yue called the traveler to sleep with him, but when the night was half over, the traveler snatched the blanket away and departed.
The next morning, his companions asked where his robe was;
Yue replied,
"Last night it was taken by a guest."
His companions all said,
"Why did you not inform us?
He replied:
"If I were to report you, I would surely condemn you for the crime of robbery.
How could it be right to kill one person for the sake of a single garment?
Those who heard this, both far and near, were all filled with admiration and submission.
Later, when Sun Quan, the ruler of Wu, heard of his extensive learning and talent, he summoned him for an audience.
He then questioned him on the profound and obscure meanings within the scriptures;
Yue responded with such spontaneity that he resolved all difficulties without hesitation and never failed to prevail.
Wu was greatly pleased and appointed him as a *boshi* (doctor).
He was sent to instruct and guide the Crown Prince, receiving exceptional favor and honor.
Although the Great Teaching had been propagated, many of the scriptures were in Sanskrit, and there was no one who could understand them.
Being proficient in both Chinese and non-Chinese languages,
he then collected various manuscripts and translated them into the Wu dialect.
This work spanned more than thirty years, from the second year of Huangwu (Gui-mao) under Sun Quan to the second year of Jianxing (Gui-you) under Sun Liang.
He translated eighty-eight works, including the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,
skillfully capturing the sacred meaning while ensuring the phrasing and style were elegant.

Furthermore, based on the *Amitāyus-sūtra* and the *Madhyama-āgama’s Mahāvadāna-sūtra*, he composed three sets of *brahmaghoṣa* (Buddhist chants) consisting of linked verses in praise of the Bodhisattvas.
He annotated the *Mūlasaṃsārasūtra*,
and all [of these works] were circulated in the world.
Later, the Prince ascended the throne.
He subsequently retired to Mount Qiong’ai, where he did not engage in worldly affairs.
Following the Daoist monk Zhu Falan, he further refined his practice of the five precepts.
All those with whom he traveled and associated were exclusively śramaṇas.
Later, he passed away in the mountains at the age of sixty.
Emperor Sun Liang of Wu wrote to the assembly of monks, saying: "Zhi Gongming did not survive his illness."
His conduct was characterized by profound simplicity from beginning to end, such that one cannot help but feel deep sorrow for him.
He was thus cherished by his contemporaries. As for the number of fascicles in the scriptural collection produced by Xuanqian, various accounts differ.
Sengyou’s *Sanzang jiji* records only thirty-six works;
Sengyou’s catalog, as recorded in the *Xianchuan*, states that twenty-seven scriptures were produced;
yet Huijiao’s *Gaoseng zhuan* lists forty-nine scriptures.
The *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Dharma Master Chángfáng) records one hundred and twenty-nine works.
However, many of those listed therein are separate recensions or duplicate entries under different titles.
We have now deleted them according to their sequence, as described below.
The *Mṛgaśīrṣa-sūtra* is identical in text to the *Mṛgajā-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin;
the *Śunīṣa-sūtra* is also identical to the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa; and the *Pravrajyā-guṇa-sūtra* currently exists in two versions:

one is a translation from the Qin period included in the Qin catalog, and the other is excerpted from the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, now included in the separate section on miscellaneous births (*bie sheng lu*).
The *Vajra-paryavadāna-sūtra* is also called the *Vajrasamādhi-mūla-viśuddhy-aniruddha-avikāra-sūtra*.

It is recorded in the *Lost Translations of the Later Han* (Hou Han Shi Yi Lu) with detailed textual evidence showing it was not produced by Zhi Qian; it is now reclassified and appended to the Qin records.
Also included are the *Mahāmaitry-aparihāṇa-sūtra*, the *Ratnāvalī-paripṛcchā-dvātriṃśan-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, and the *Mārakanyā-buddha-dharma-deśanā-śravaṇa-sūtra*.
The *Attaining a Male Body Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on Great Compassion Never Diminishing*, and two others—these three sūtras are all from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*;

the *Sūtra on the Accomplishment of Great Compassion by Ratnasāgara-śānta-mati* is from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Vipula* is the separately circulated *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows*;
the *Sūtra of King Mādhava* is from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*; and the *Sūtra on the Buddha [Teaching] Hārītī*...
The *Wild Ghost Preaching the Dharma Sūtra* (also known as the *Hāritī Sūtra*); the *Sūtra on the Withered Tree* from the *Madhyama Āgama*;

the *Sūtra on the Hawk and Falcon Hunter* (sometimes prefixed with the character "Da" [Great]); and the *Sūtra on the Matter of the Owl*. These three sūtras, including the *Withered Tree*, are all from the *Ekottara Āgama*.

The *Sūtra on Form and Impermanence*, the *Sūtra on the Exhaustion of All Outflows* (sometimes without the character "Wu" [Non-), the *Sūtra on the Snowy Mountains Having No Monkeys*, or alternatively titled... [text ends].

The Sūtra on the Monkey (or the Sūtra on the Absence of the Word "Non-existence"), the Sūtra on Mother and Son, the Sūtra on Impurity Contemplation, the Sūtra on the Three Kinds of Excellent Horses, the Sūtra on the Four Kinds of Excellent Horses,
the Sūtra on the Shortness of Life, the Sūtra on the Grass and Turtle in the River, the Sūtra on the Five Dharmas by Which a King Endures Long in the World,
and the Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching to the Heretic Susīma on Renunciation of Desire; these constitute eleven [sections] beginning with the impermanence of form.
The *Sūtra on What Belongs to Me* and the *Brahmin Sūtra* both appear in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. The aforementioned two sūtras both appear in the *Udānavarga*.

The *King Ke-tan Sūtra* appears in the *Arthavargīya*. The *Sūtra on the Heretic Seniya’s Teaching of Deliverance* and the *Sūtra on Delivering the Brahmin*—the aforementioned two sūtras—are excerpts from the Hīnayāna.
The *Blind Turtle Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on the Brahmin Questioning the Buddha about the Increase and Decrease of the World*, and the *Sūtra on the Three Fish Losing [Their Way]* [are also included].

The *Jingshui jing* (Sutra on the Watercourse), the *Ganlu dao jing* (Sutra on the Path of Ambrosia), the *Jiang qian fanzhi jing* (Sutra on the Descent upon a Thousand Brahmins), the *Fanzhi zi si dao bai jing* (Sutra on the Death of a Brahmin’s Son and the Ruin of Rice),

the *Hu kuyi jing* (Sutra on Guarding Speech and Mind), the *Fanzhi wen fo shi jing* (Sutra on the Brahmin Asking the Buddha about His Teacher), the *Fashi sheng jing* (Sutra on the Superiority of Dharma-Giving), the *Shuishang pao jing* (Sutra on Bubbles on Water), and the ten sutras beginning with the *Xie bie jing* (Sutra of the Blind Turtle)— all these appear in the *Chuyao jing*. Furthermore,

the *Xiuxing ci jing* (Sutra on the Practice of Loving-kindness) appears in the *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Treatise on the Stages of Cultivating the Path), and the *Duotuo gouzi jing* (Sutra on Saving the Puppies).

The *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables* (Jīng chū zá pìyù) comprises thirty-eight sections and thirty-eight fascicles, including the *Sūtra on Great Compassion Without Diminution* (Dàcí wújiǎn jīng) and others;
the catalogs of Fajing and others all state that these were translated by Bo Yan.
Now, according to the two catalogs of the Sui dynasty’s *Zhongjing lu* (Records of the Scriptures) and the newly compiled *Biesheng chaojing deng* (Extracted Scriptures of Separate Translations),
these works were all excerpted from various scriptures;
they do not properly qualify as part of the total count of translated works.
Since the *Shí-lù* (Records of Reality) currently exists, I have deleted all [duplicate entries] from it.

The *Liù-dù jí jīng* (Sūtra of the Collection of the Six Perfections), in eight fascicles—or nine fascicles—is also called the *Liù-dù wú-jí dù jīng* (Sūtra of the Infinite Perfections), the *Dù wú-jí jí* (Collection of the Infinite Perfections), or the *Zá wú-jí jīng* (Miscellaneous Sūtra of the Infinite Perfections).
These titles are seen in Zhúdào-zǔ’s *Wú-lù* (Record of Wu) and Sēng-yòu’s *Lù* (Catalogue). Old records state: [text continues].
The *Zapiyujing* (Sutra of Mixed Parables) in two fascicles is found among the old titles in the Buddhist canon but is not listed in Sengyou’s *Chángfáng lù*.

It is also called the *Zapijijing* (Sutra of the Collection of Mixed Parables), though sometimes the character "ji" (collection) is omitted. This is seen in the *Gāosēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) and the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Wǔpǐnjīng* (Sutra of Five Chapters) in five fascicles is not recorded as such in Sengyou’s catalog;
it is stated that there are ten chapters in total. The third chapter is identified by Sengyou as being the *Xiǎopǐn bōrě* (Shorter Prajñāpāramitā).

In Sengyou’s Catalogue, it is recorded that the *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra* in two fascicles is an alternative translation of the "Ratna-keśa" chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, or is simply called the *Viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra*.

It is said to have appeared during the period of the "Red Birds" (the Wu dynasty). The *Upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* in one fascicle is identical in substance to the *Anupūrva-upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* and others;
