Now, as for the remaining twenty-three works in thirty fascicles,
some have a verifiable source for their translation.
Some have alternative names or different titles;
some are extracts from larger works;
others are suspected of being apocryphal and not authentic.
Now, these have all been deleted to avoid redundancy;
they are fully described below.
Since this [text] is already included within the four-fascicle *Avaivartika-cakra-sūtra* translated during the Northern Liang dynasty (the translator is lost), it is known that this is [a duplicate].

Sengyou’s *Chonglü* (Revised Catalog) states: "Master Dao’an [noted] that this is a different version of the scripture from those in the Liang region; it currently exists in the Liang catalog, so it has been removed from this [present] collection.

*Xiǎoběnqǐjīng* (Smaller Sūtra on the Origins), two fascicles. Translated by Zhi Yao of the Later Han. *Sìbèijīng* (Sūtra of the Four Classes), also called *Sìbèidízǐjīng* (Sūtra of the Disciples of the Four Classes) or *Sìbèixuéjīng* (Sūtra of the Training of the Four Classes).
The *Fǎshànglù* (Catalog of Fashang) states it was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. *Dáihuīsānmèi* (Samādhi Attaining Wisdom).
The *Sūtra on the Ten Matters of the Bodhisattva’s Practice* asked by Mañjuśrī, one fascicle; another name for the *Moon Lamp Sūtra*;
also known as the *Sūtra on the Concentration of Mind in the Practice of Dhyāna* or the *Sūtra on the Examination of Mind in the Practice of Dhyāna*;

the *Sūtra on the Eight Recollections of Aniruddha*, another name for the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī*, two fascicles—which is precisely the *Sūtra of the Pure Almsround of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī*. This is it.
The *Nāmadheya-mātra-saṃkṣepa-pāramitā-sūtra* (or *Pāramitā-upamā-sūtra*) in three or four fascicles; the *Śikhaṇḍin-rāja-sūtra* (sometimes written with the character "ni" instead of "shi");
the *Kumāra-dharmamati-sūtra* (sometimes written with the character "hui" instead of "zhi"); the two sūtras beginning with *Śikhaṇḍin*, which appear in the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃcaya-sūtra*;
the *Kāmuka-pārṣṇi-kramaṇa-sūtra*, which appears in the *Arthavargīya-sūtra*; and those falsely attributed to persons.

The *Dàojīng pínǚ tīngjīng shéniè mìngzhōng jīng* (The Scripture on the Poor Woman Listening to the Sutra and Dying from a Snake Bite); also known as the *Pínǚ tīngjīng shéniè mìngzhōng shēngtiān jīng* (The Scripture on the Poor Woman Listening to the Sutra and Dying from a Snake Bite, Reborn in Heaven);

the *Guówáng chīfúren jīng* (The Scripture of the King and the Foolish Lady); the *Mài zhìhuì jīng* (The Scripture on Selling Wisdom); the *Chūshòudào jīng* (The Scripture on First Receiving the Way);

the *Xué jīng fú jīng* (The Scripture on Learning the Sutras and Merit); the *Xuéfú gòng shì yī jīng* (The Scripture on Learning Merit, All Being One Scripture); the *Bā bù sēngxíng míng jīng* (The Scripture on the Names of the Eightfold Practice of the Sangha); and the *Huàpì jīng* (The Scripture of Transformative Parables), also known as the *Huà* (Transformation).

The *Upamā-sūtra*, the *Sūtra on Deceitful Names and Other Topics* (the eight sūtras), both appear in the *Saṃyukta-avadāna*; the *Sūtra on the Five Hundred Brahmins Asking about Existence and Non-existence*,
the *Sūtra of the Five Hundred Brahmans*, the *Sāha-bodhisattva-sūtra* (also known as the *King Sāha-bodhisattva-sūtra*),
and the *Hui-ding-pu-bian-shentong-bodhisattva-sūtra* (also known as the *Hui-ding-pu-bian-guotu-shen*).

The *Tong pusa jing* (Sutra on the Universal Bodhisattva), the *Pin nü jing* (Sutra of the Poor Woman), also known as the *Pin nü Nanda jing*; the *Aqiu na jing*, also known as the *Aqiu na Samādhi jing*;
and the five sutras including the *Wubai boluomen deng* (The Five Hundred Brahmins)—these are all listed in the *Yiwei lu* (Record of Doubtful and Spurious Works).
Regarding the Western Jin: the Sima clan ruled from Luoyang; it is also called the Northern Jin, beginning with Emperor Wu’s first year of the Taishi era.
From the year of Yǐyǒu (135 CE) until the fourth year of the Jiànxīng era of Emperor Mǐn (252 CE),
a total of four emperors and fifty-two years elapsed.
There were twelve individuals, both monastics and laypeople.
The various sūtras, precepts, compendiums, and newly or formerly translated scriptures of unknown provenance comprise a total of three hundred and thirty works in five hundred and ninety fascicles;
of these, one hundred and fifty-six works in three hundred and twenty-one fascicles are extant, while one hundred and seventy-seven works in two hundred and sixty-nine fascicles are missing.
The *Collection of Sutras and Precepts* by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa: one hundred and seventy-five works in three hundred and fifty-four fascicles.
The *Collection* by the śramaṇa Kanglouti: one work in one fascicle. The *Collection of Sutras* by the śramaṇa An Faqin:
five works in sixteen fascicles. The *Upāsaka-sūtra* by the śramaṇa Mokṣala: one work in thirty fascicles.
Two sections of five fascicles of sutras by Zhu Shulan; sixteen sections of eighteen fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Bai Fazang;
four sections of twelve fascicles of sutras compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Fali;
forty sections of fifty fascicles of sutras and vinaya by the śramaṇa Shi Faju; and two sections of three fascicles of sutras by the lay devotee Nie Chengyuan.
The lay devotee Nie Daozhen [translated] twenty-four sections in thirty-six fascicles of sūtras and vinaya;
the śramaṇa Zhi Fadu [translated] four sections in five fascicles of sūtras; the śramaṇa Yu Falüyan [translated] one section in one fascicle of sūtra;

and fifty-eight sections in fifty-nine fascicles (or fifty-five sections in fifty-six fascicles) of various previously and newly translated works of unknown translators, with three [sections] newly appended.

The *Guangzan Banruo Boluomi Jing* (Sutra of the Radiant Praise of the Perfection of Wisdom), in fifteen fascicles, was originally compiled in three fascicles; its initial edition consisted of ten fascicles.
It shares the same root text as the second assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the "Great Chapter on the Emission of Light" (*Prabhāsa-parivarta*).
It is also titled the *Guangzan Mahāprajñā Sūtra*, comprising twenty-seven chapters in total. Translated on the twenty-fifth day of the eleventh month in the seventh year of the Taikang era.

The *Miji Jingang Lishi Jing* (Sūtra of the Secret-Trace Vajra-wielding Malla) in seven fascicles—alternatively recorded as five, four, or eight fascicles—was translated on the eighth day of the tenth month of the first year of the Taikang era. It is also simply referred to as the *Miji Jing*.
It appears in the three catalogs of Zhi Mindu, Zhu Daozu, and Sengyou; it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection.
The *Bodhisattva-svapna-sūtra* (Dream Sutra) in two fascicles, spoken during the third assembly, is recorded by Fashang;

it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* and renamed the "Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras. Fashang’s record states it was produced by Hu Gong, but a detailed examination of the text reveals this is not the case;
for now, we shall rely on Fashang’s record as definitive. The *Bodhisattva-ratnaśikhara-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in two fascicles is also known by another name.

The *Catalogue of the Old Records* for the *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra* simply calls it the *Ratna-śikhara-sūtra*; this is a separate translation of the "Ratna-śikhara" chapter from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.

It appeared on the fourteenth day of the seventh month of the first year of the Tai-xi era. According to the two records by Dao-zhen and Seng-you, it is now included as the forty-seventh assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
The *Pumen-pin-jing* (Universal Gate Chapter Sutra) in one fascicle was also initially called the *Pumen-jing*. It was... [text ends]... with the same.

The *Ratnakūṭa-mañjuśrī-samantamukha-parivarta* and others share the same original text as the *Pātra-jātaka-sūtra*, one fascicle, which was translated by Nie Daozhen on the eleventh day of the first month in the eighth year of Taikang;

this is recorded in the *Sengyou lu*. The old records state that the *Pātra-śarīra-pratilambha-sūtra* was translated on the first day of the eighth month in the second year of Tà'ān, and it shares the same original text as the *Ratnakūṭa-garbha-vyākaraṇa-parivarta*. These are now extant.

The *Wenshushili futu yanjing jing* (Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-pariśuddhi-sūtra) in two fascicles, also simply titled the *Yanjing jingtu jing* or the *Fotu yanjing jing*, was translated in the first year of the Taixi era.
Its initial appearance was identical to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* section on the "Prophecy for Mañjuśrī," as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jinshi zalu*. It is listed in the records of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.

Furthermore, according to Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Chu sanzang jiji*), there is the *Yujialuoyue wen pusa xing jing* (Sūtra on the Questions of the Householder Ugga on the Bodhisattva Practice) in one fascicle;

it is also called the *Yugajiangzhe jing* (Sūtra of the Elder Ugga), which is the same as the *Dayujia jing* (Great Ugga Sūtra) in two fascicles. The fourth [version] was translated by An Xuan and corresponds to the *Fajing* and the *Baoji Yugajiangzhe hui* (Assembly of the Elder Ugga from the Ratnakūṭa).
This is seen in the three catalogues of Dao’an, Min Du, and Sengyou. It is also known as the *Huanshi* (The Illusionist).

The *Renxian jing* (One fascicle), also known as the *Renxian huanshi jing*. Its initial appearance was identical to the "Chapter on Bestowing the Prediction upon the Illusionist" in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*;
this is recorded in the *Nie Daozhen lu* and the *Sengyou lu*. The *Sumati jing* (One fascicle).
Its initial appearance simply titled it the *Sumati pusa jing*; its textual content is identical to the "Chapter on Wondrous Wisdom" in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. This is recorded in the [same catalogs].
*Ajātaśatru-rājñī-duhitṛ-āśudharmā-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated during the first year of the Jianwu era by Nie Daozhen, Zhu Daozu, Sengyou, and others.
Recorded in the three catalogs of Nie Daozhen, Zhu Daozu, and Sengyou; it is also called the *Ajātaśatru-dauhitṛ-sūtra* or the *Aśudharmā-dauhitṛ-sūtra*.
It appears in the catalogs of Zhenmin and Sengyou; it is separately preserved in the two catalogs of Sengyou and Fang, though not in others.
The *Youshi jing* (Sutra on the Woman Who Gave Away Her Body) recorded by Sengyou further includes the *Ajashai wang nü jing* (Sutra of the Daughter of King Ajātaśatru); both of these are erroneous.
The *Lijushi nü jing* (Sutra of the Woman Vimaladatta), one fascicle, first appeared on the second day of the twelfth month of the tenth year of Taikang.

It is the same text as the *Raoji wugou shi hui* (Assembly of Vimaladatta from the Ratnakūṭa). It is found within Dao’an’s and Sengyou’s two catalogs; furthermore, it is not included in the *Neidian lu*.
The attribution of the *Gou shi ying bian jing* (Sūtra on the Discernment of Defiled Offerings) is an error; it was translated by Daozhen, as is evident from what follows.

The *Ru huan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Illusion-like Samādhi) exists in two fascicles, or alternatively in three or four fascicles, and is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Section on the Assembly of the Well-Abiding Mind), according to Sengyou’s catalogue.
The *Taizi shuhu jing* (Sūtra of the Prince Brushing Teeth) exists in one fascicle; its initial appearance is recorded in Faxiang’s catalogue.
The *Ratnakūṭa: Assembly of Prince Ajātaśatru*, etc., identical to the *Upāyakauśalya Sūtra* (The Great Skillful Means) inquired by the Bodhisattva Prajñottara, in two fascicles;
the second edition, or alternatively in one fascicle, was produced on the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the sixth year of the Taikang era.
It is also called the *Mahopāyakauśalya Sūtra*, or the *Prajñottara-bodhisattva Sūtra*, or the *Sukauśalyopāya Sūtra*, or the...

*Sūtra on the Infinite [Virtues] of Skillful Means for Delivering Others* (Shànquán fāngbiàn suǒ dù wújí jīng), recorded in the *Jiànzhēn* and *Yòu* catalogs; *Sūtra on the Original Vows Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva* (Mílè púsà suǒwèn běnyuàn jīng), one fascicle.
First issued on the eleventh day of the fifth month in the second year of the Tà'ān era. Translated [by Dharmarakṣa]; some editions omit the two characters "suǒwèn" (asked).
It is also called the *Mílè běnyuàn jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Original Vows) and alternatively the *Mílè nán jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Questions). It is identical to the *Ratnakūṭa* [section].

Regarding the *Acintyaprabhāsa-sūtra* (A-ch'a-mo ching) in seven fascicles—also known as the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* (Wu-jin-i) in the Jin translation, or alternatively in four or five fascicles—Sengyou’s three catalogs record it as being among those translated during the reign of Emperor Le. It is the third translation from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.
It was produced on the first day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Yuanjia era; some versions include the characters "Bodhisattva" [in the title], as seen in Sengyou’s second catalog.
The two catalogs of Sengyou record the *Anantamukha-parivarta* (Wujin yi jing) in four fascicles; this is an error. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* (Da ai jing) consists of eight fascicles.
The old catalog states that the *Tathāgata-mahākaruṇā-sūtra* was begun on the seventh day of the seventh month in the first year of Yuankang and completed on the twenty-third day of the eighth month.
It contains twenty-eight chapters and is a separate translation of the initial section of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* (Daji jing), consisting of either six or [eight] fascicles.
Volume seven contains the *Zhu Daozu Jin Shi Za Lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty by Zhu Daozu) and the *Sengyou Lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou).

It includes the *Bao Nü Suowen Jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Precious Woman) in three volumes, which was translated on the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Taikang era. This is a variant translation of the "Precious Woman Chapter" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, though it is also sometimes recorded as being in four volumes.

It is also simply titled the *Baonü Wen Hui Jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Precious Woman on Wisdom), and is further known as the *Baonü Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra of the Precious Woman’s Samādhi). This is seen in the *Dao An Lu*.

The *Wuyan tongzi jing* (Sutra of the Silent Boy) in two fascicles—also called the *Wuyan pusa jing* (Sutra of the Silent Bodhisattva)—is an alternative translation of the "Silent Chapter" (*Avakīrṇa-kusuma-parivarta*) from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*;
it is sometimes recorded as one fascicle and is found in the catalogues of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.

The *Pusa shizhu xingdao pin* (Chapter on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Path) in one fascicle is an alternative translation of the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; it is found in the records of the Sui dynasty śramaṇas.

The *Fajing lu*, the *Shizhu jing*, and the *Yufang lu* state directly that the "Ten Abodes of the Bodhisattva" is precisely this "Chapter on the Practice of the Path. It is the *Jianbei yiqiezhide jing* (Sutra on the Gradual Preparation of All Wisdom Virtues) in five fascicles;
it is also titled the *Shizhu jing* (Sutra of the Ten Abodes) or the *Dahui guangsanmei jing* (Sutra of the Great Wisdom Light Samadhi), or [in ten fascicles].
It was translated on the twenty-first day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Yuankang era. This is the "Ten Grounds Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika*) from the *Avataṃsaka*.

According to the catalogs of the Nie Daozhen and Sengyou records, there is a *Samādhi Asked by the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra* in two fascicles—also known as the *Samādhi of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*, or simply the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*—or in three fascicles.
This is a variant translation of the "Ten Samādhis" chapter of the new *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. It is noted that this chapter did not exist in the old translations, as seen in the Sengyou record.

*Laixingxian jing* (Sūtra on the Manifestation of Arising), four fascicles; also known as *Xingxian ruyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Manifestation of Illusory Arising). Translated on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Yuankang era.
This is a variant translation of the "Tathāgatagotra-nirdeśa" and "Daśakṣānti" chapters of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, as recorded in the bibliographies of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.
*Dushi pin jing* (Sūtra on the Chapter of Delivering the World), six fascicles; also known as *Dushi jing* (Sūtra on Delivering the World).
Alternatively, there is a five-fascicle version produced on the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Yuankang era;

this is a variant translation of the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, as seen in the records of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou. The *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* in two fascicles was first translated;

it shares the same source text as the *Sui* dynasty translation of the *Catuḥ-kumāra-sūtra*. In some versions the character "pari" (般) is absent, while others have three fascicles or refer to it as the *Mahā-parinirvāṇa*.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Nīhuan jing) appeared on the twenty-third day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Taishi era. It is recorded in both the two catalogs of Daozhen and Sengyou.
The *Puyao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Radiance), eight fascicles, also titled *Fangdeng benqi* (Origins of the Vaipulya); Master An states it belongs to the *Fangdeng* division.
It was translated at Tianshui Temple in the fifth month of the second year of the Yongjia era by the śramaṇas Kangshu and Bai Faju; this is the second translation.
According to the records of Sengzhēnyòu, there were three versions [of this scripture]:

the *Zhèngfǎhuá jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) in ten fascicles—also called the *Fāngděng zhèngfǎhuá*—or in seven fascicles consisting of twenty-seven chapters, translated on the tenth day of the eighth month in the seventh year of the Tàikāng era.
The third translation was received by brush by the lay devotees Zhāng Shìmíng, Zhāng Zhōngzhèng, Niè Chéngyuǎn, and others; this is recorded in the two records of Sengzhēnyòu.
*Record of the Mahāvaipulya Śikhin-rāja Sūtra*, one fascicle. Initially translated by Master Dao’an, it is classified within the Vaipulya section.
It is also simply called the *Śikhin-rāja Sūtra*, alternatively titled the *Vimalakīrti-putra-praśna Sūtra*, and also known as the *Susīma-kumāra Sūtra*; thus, there are four titles in total.
This is recorded in the catalogs of Zhi Mindu and Sengyou. [It concerns] the Buddha ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother.
The *Sūtra* in two fascicles was first translated; it is also said to be in three fascicles and is titled the *Buddha Ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Sūtra*.

It is the same text as the *Dao Shenzu Jing* and others, appearing during the Taishi era according to the records of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou. The *A-vi-yue-zhi-che Jing* (Avivartika-cakra-sūtra) in three fascicles was first translated;
it is also said to be in four fascicles or simply the *A-vi-yue-zhi Jing* (Avivartika-sūtra), appearing in the fifth year of the Taikang era.

On the fourteenth day of the tenth month of this year, it was brought forth at Dunhuang as a different translation of the same text as the *Avaivartika-sūtra* and the *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-śuddha-sūtra*, as seen in the *Zhenyou lu* and other catalogues.
It consists of three fascicles of the *Samādhi of the Collection of All Virtues*.

An earlier record states that it was initially called the *Sūtra on the Equal Collection of All Virtues*, or simply the *Sūtra of Equal Collection*, and corresponds to the *Collection of All Meritorious Virtues*.

The *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra* (Holding the Mind Sūtra of the Brahmā Deva) exists in versions identical to the original or in two fascicles, as recorded in the *Nie Daozhen lu* and the *Sengyou lu*.
It consists of four fascicles, also known as the *Zhuangyan Fofa* (Adorning the Buddha-Dharma) or the *Dengyu Zhufa* (Equal Mastery of All Dharmas), comprising seventeen chapters;

alternatively, it appears in six fascicles. When first translated, it was sometimes titled with the addition of the characters "Suowen" (Questions) or simply called the *Chixin jing* (Holding the Mind Sūtra). This occurred in the seventh year of the Taikang era.
On the tenth day of the third month, transcribed by Nie Chengyuan from an old manuscript.
According to the three catalogs of Sengyou, this *Dharanimdhara-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-skandha-dhātu-āyatana-mārga-jñāna-vibodhana-sūtra* consists of four fascicles.

It is stated that when it was first translated, it consisted of three fascicles and shared the same original text as the *Dharanimdhara-sūtra*, though they were different translations. This is recorded in Sengyou’s catalog as having been brought from various regions.
*The Scripture on Equal Learning* (Dengxue jing), one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Saṃghavarman; alternatively, it lacks the character "wu" (without).

Its initial appearance was identical to the *Scripture on the Universal Dhāraṇī of Vaipulya*. This is recorded in the catalogues of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou. *The Scripture on Mañjuśrī Manifesting the Treasure Treasury* (Wenshushili xian baozang jing), three fascicles.
Its initial appearance sometimes lacks the character "xian" (manifest). It is identical to the *Scripture on the Jewel Casket of Vaipulya* (*Fangguang baoqie jing*).
In the tenth month of the sixth year of the Taishi era, [this work] was produced; it consists of either two fascicles or is simply titled the *Ratnagarbha-sūtra* (Bǎozàng jīng).

It is found in Sengyou’s catalogue (*Sengyòu lù*) and in Changfang’s catalogue (*Chángfáng lù*). It is a grave error to separately record a *Ratnagarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles, as there is no such work.

There is also the *Anuttararatnasamādhi-sūtra* (Wújí bǎo sānmèi jīng) in one fascicle. When first produced, it was sometimes called the *Anuttararatna-sūtra* (Wújí bǎo jīng), which shares the same original text as the *Ratnatathāgatasamādhi-sūtra*.
On the third day of the third month in the first year of the Yongjia era, it was issued; see the *Bielu* (Separate Record) and the two records by Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.
The *Puchao sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence), three fascicles, second issue; or four fascicles, also titled the "Ajātaśatru-rāja-parivarta" (Chapter on King Ajātaśatru).
Issued on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month in the seventh year of the Taikang era; or the word "samādhi" is omitted, or the character "plus" (加) is added above.
The *Wen shu shi li an lu* states that there is another edition of the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, which is not found in the two catalogs by Sengzhao and Sengyou;

the *Wu suo xiwang jing* (Sūtra on Having No Hopes), one fascicle, is the second edition—sometimes written with the character "悕" (*xī*) instead of "希" (*xī*)—also known as the *Xiàngbù jīng* (Elephant-Step Sūtra), which shares the same root text as the *Xiàngyè jīng* (Elephant-Axle Sūtra) and others, as recorded in the catalogs of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.
Furthermore, there is the *Dà jìng fǎmén jīng* (Sūtra of the Great Pure Dharma-Gate).
The title of the scroll reads: *The Great Purity Dharma-Gate Chapter, Part One: The Scripture on the Questions of the Girl Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī and the Instruction of the Youth Mañjuśrī*.
Its initial translation was identical to the *Mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*.

It appeared in the world on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Jianxing era, according to the two catalogs by Nie Daozhen and Sengyou. It is a teaching that accords with skillful means.

A sūtra in two fascicles, also titled *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Transforming the Female Body*, or alternatively *The Sūtra of Skillful Means* (the old catalogues refer to it as *The Sūtra of the Girl Following Skillful Means* or *The Sūtra of the Girl Adapting to Skillful Means*).
This is the second appearance [of this text], or it may consist of one fascicle. It is found in the two catalogs of Dao’an and Sengyou;

however, its separate preservation in the two catalogs of Sengyou and Huiyuan under the title *The Sūtra of the Girl Adapting to Skillful Means* is an error. *The Sūtra of the Prince Washing His Face*, one fascicle.
The third [section] contains the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*, scroll four, an alternative translation; some editions read *Mupò* (Mùpò).
It is recorded in Sengyou’s *Lù* (Catalog) as the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* in one scroll, first appearing under the title *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra*, also known as the *Śin-ni* (Shēnrì) Sūtra;
it shares the same text as the *Kṣemadatta-gṛhapati-sūtra*, etc., according to Sengyou’s *Lù*. Also, the *Kṣīraprabha-buddha-sūtra* in one scroll, number three.
The second translation is also called the *Kṣīraprabhā-sūtra*; it is a different recension of the same text as the *Vatsa-sūtra*, etc., according to Sengyou’s catalogue.

The *Vimaladatta-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle is the second translation; it is also titled the *Garbha-kośa-sūtra* and is the same text as the *Strīvivarta-sūtra*, etc., according to Nie Daozhen’s catalogue.
Both Sengyou’s and [Dao]fang’s catalogues record the *Garbha-kośa-sūtra* as being this very *Vimaladatta*.

*The Sūtra of the Virtuous Woman: A Definitive Compendium*, one fascicle; first appearance. Some say it is the *Sūtra of the Decisive Dhāraṇī*, which shares the same root text as the *Sūtra on Slandering the Buddha*;
see Sengyou’s Catalogue. *The Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Sole Testimony and Self-Vow Samādhi*, one fascicle;
also called the *Sūtra of the Grasping Testimony and Self-Vow Samādhi*, or the *Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Self-Vow Samādhi*; second appearance.
It shares the same original text as the *Han An Shigao Zishì sānmèi jīng* (The Scripture on An Shigao of Han’s Self-Vow Samādhi), according to Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Sēnyòu lù*).

The *Lóngshī púsà běnqǐ jīng* (The Scripture on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Longshi) in one fascicle—formerly recorded as the *Lóngshī běnjīng* or the *Lóngshī nǚjīng*—is a second translation that shares the same original text as the *Lóngshī nǚjīng*, according to Sengyou’s Catalogue.
The *Bāyáng shénzhòu jīng* (The Scripture of the Eightfold Yang Divine Spells) in one fascicle is likewise [a translation].

It is stated directly that the *Bāyáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Eight Yangs), fascicle two, is an alternate translation of the same text as the *Bāshìjiǎng zhòu jīng* (Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Mantras);

this is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Yúlán pén jīng*, one fascicle, is also called the *Yúlán jīng*; it is an alternate translation of the same text as the *Bàoen fèngpén jīng* (Sūtra on Repaying Kindness by Offering Bowls), as recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.
The *Sì bùkědé jīng*, one fascicle, is a second translation, appearing in the *Niè Dàozhēn Zhèndù*.
*Fannü Shouyi jing* (The Scripture of the Brahmin Woman Shouyi), one fascicle; first translated. Also titled *Shouyi nü jing*. Recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.
*Baowang jing* (The Jewel Net Scripture), one fascicle; first translated. Also called *Baowang tongzi jing*. Recorded in the catalogues of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou.
*Bodhisattvaxing wushi yuan shen jing* (The Scripture on the Fifty Circumstantial Accounts of the Bodhisattva’s Deeds), one fascicle; first translated. Recorded in the old catalogues.

The *Bodhisattva-yuan-shen-wu-shi-shi-jing* (Sūtra on the Fifty Matters of the Bodhisattva’s Contemplation of the Body) is also known as the *Wu-shi-yuan-shen-xing-jing* (Sūtra on the Fifty Contemplations of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of the Body);

these titles are found in the records of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou. The *Xuzhen-tianzi-jing* (Sūtra of the Son of Heaven Xuzhen) in three fascicles was first translated, though it may have been in two fascicles;

it is also titled with the addition of the words "Suowen" (Questions), or simply the *Wen-si-shi-jing* (Sūtra of Questions on Four Matters). On the eighth day of the eleventh month of the third year of the Taishi era, at... [text ends]

The *Anwenhui deng zhuan* (Biographies of An Wenhui and Others) produced at the Baima Monastery outside the Qing Gate in Chang’an was transcribed by Nie Chengyuan and others, completed on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month;

it is recorded in the catalogs of Sengdao and Sengyou. The *Hai Longwang jing* (Sutra of the Dragon King of the Sea), four fascicles (originally perhaps three fascicles), was first translated on the tenth day of the seventh month in the sixth year of Taikang; it is recorded in the catalog of Nie Daozhen.

Furthermore, according to Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji*, there is the *Foyao ji jing* (Sūtra of the Essential Collection of the Buddhas) in two fascicles; the Indic title is Buddhāsaṃgīti, though it is also simply called the *Yaoji jing*.
Its initial appearance is recorded in Sengyou’s catalog. There is also the *Xianjie jing* (Sūtra of the Worthy Kalpa) in thirteen fascicles, titled *Bada jie sanmei* (Bhadrakalpa Samādhi);

in the Jin language, it is called the *Xianjie dingyi jing* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Worthy Kalpa). It was translated on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the first year of the Yongkang era.
Recorded by pen as dictated by Zhao Wenlong upon its initial translation; it appeared in either seven or ten fascicles according to the two catalogs of Daozhen and Sengyou.
It was mistakenly recorded as the *Bāntuójié sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Bhadra-kalpa) in the separate catalog of [Dao]fang and others.

The *Hóngdǎoguǎngxiǎn sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Broad Manifestation of the Propagation of the Way), in four fascicles, is also known as the *Ānòudá Lóngwáng Suǒwèn Juézhū Húyí Qīngjìng Pǐn* (The Questions of the Dragon King Anavatapta: The Chapter on Resolving All Doubts and Purifying [the Mind]). It is also...
The *Vajrapraśna-samādhi-sūtra* (also titled *Jin'gang wen dingyi jing*), consisting of twelve chapters or two fascicles, was translated in the third month of the second year of the Yongjia era.
It appears in the records of Sengyou and Zhenyu; its inclusion in the *Neidian lu* as a separate entry under the title *Anutara-sūtra* is an error.
The *Cittavidyā-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Cittavidyā-brāhmaṇī-bhikṣuṇī-bhakta-śeṣa-dāna-sūtra*—is recorded in the catalog of Sengyou. [It has since] been lost.
*Shifang ming jing* (Sutra on the Darkness of the Ten Directions), one fascicle; issued on the fourteenth day of the eighth month of the Guangxi year.

Some say it is titled *Shifang mie ming jing* (Sutra on the Extinction of the Darkness of the Ten Directions); seen in the records of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou. *Lumujing* (Sutra of the Deer Mother), one fascicle;

there is also a separate *Luzijing* (Sutra of the Deer Child) in one fascicle, which is identical to this; seen in the record of Sengyou. *Mo’e jing* (Sutra of Māra’s Rebellion), one fascicle; Taikang [era].
On the second day of the twelfth month of the tenth year, at the Si-baima Monastery in the city of Luoyang, [this text] was produced with Nie Daozhen acting as the scribe;
this is recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue) and the postscript to the scripture.

One scroll of the *Jing de Taizi jing* (Prince De-guang Scripture), also called the *Laituo heluo Suowen Jing* (Scripture of the Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla), was produced on the thirtieth day of the ninth month of the sixth year of the Taishi era; this is recorded in the [catalogues].
The *Record of Zhu Daozu* and the *Record of Sengyou* list the *Banniehuan hou guanla jing* (One Scroll) in one volume;
it is also called the *Banniehuan hou sibei guanla jing* or simply the *Guangxiang jing*, as seen in the *Changfang lu*.
The *Sibei jing* (One Scroll) in one volume is also called the *Sibeidi zi jing* or the *Sibeixue jing*, as seen in the *Fashang lu*.
*The Scripture on Future Transformations*, one fascicle; also known as *The Scripture on Future Transformations of Consciousness*.
Seen in Sengyou’s two catalogs. *The Scripture on the Almsround of Past Buddhas*, one fascicle; the old catalog calls it *The Scripture on the Almsround of Buddhas of Past Ages*.
Seen in Sengyou’s catalog. *The Mañjuśrī Scripture on the Pure Vinaya*, one fascicle; first appearing, it is also simply called *The Pure Vinaya Scripture*. [Translated during the] Taikang era.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the tenth year, at the Baima Monastery, [the text] was produced. Previously, he encountered a śramaṇa from the Western Regions who recited the manuscript;
subsequently, there were several more chapters, but that person had forgotten them. Only what he remembered was proclaimed, with Daozhen serving as the scribe.

This is seen in the two records (*Lù*) by Zu and You. One fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-pāpadeśanā-sūtra* was first translated; some added the character "Shili" (Śāriputra), and it is also called the *Mañjuśrī*.

The *Wǔtǐ huìguò jīng* (Sūtra on Repenting with the Five Limbs) is listed in Sengyou’s catalogue; the *Líshuì jīng* (Sūtra on Leaving Sleep), one fascicle, is an alternative translation from the twentieth fascicle of the *Madhyamāgama*, as seen in the Changfang catalogue;
the *Shòusuì jīng* (Sūtra on Observing the Uposatha), one fascicle, is an initial alternative translation from the twenty-third fascicle of the *Madhyamāgama*, as seen in the Changfang catalogue;
the *Lèxiǎng jīng* (Sūtra on the Perception of Pleasure), one fascicle, is from the second [fascicle] of the *Madhyamāgama*.
The *Jianchang-fu-lu* records sixteen alternative translations: one scroll of the *Zunshang jing*, translated from the forty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
one scroll of the *Yijing*, translated from the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
and one scroll of the *Yingfa jing*, also translated from the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*. All are recorded as alternative translations in the *Jianchang-fu-lu*.

The translation is recorded in Changfang’s *Lù* (Catalogue). It is one fascicle titled *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra*, sometimes written with the character for "demon" (*mó*) instead of "finger" (*yǐ*), or called the *Zhǐjì Jīng* (Finger-Crest Sūtra), or the *Zhǐmàn Jīng* (Finger-Garland Sūtra);
it appears as a variant translation in the thirty-first section of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
One fascicle titled *Lìshì Yishān Jīng* (Sūtra of the Worthy Man Moving the Mountain), also simply called the *Yishān Jīng*, is found in Sengyou’s catalogue.
*The Sūtra on the Four Unprecedented Dharmas*, one fascicle; an alternative translation of the thirty-sixth *Ekottarika Āgama*.
It is also titled *The Sūtra on the Four Non-existent Dharmas* (*Wúfǎ*) or *The Sūtra on the Four Unprecedented [Dharmas]* (*Sìwèiyǒufǎ*).

It is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. It is also an alternative translation of the thirty-sixth *Ekottarika Āgama*: *The Sūtra on the Seal of the Noble Dharma* (*Śrīdharmamudrā-sūtra*), one fascicle. Its Indic name is *Acchadhammavimutti*.
Extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 3; alternatively titled the *Dharmābhāva Sūtra* or the *Prajñāmudrā Sūtra*.
Translated on the fifth day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of Yuankang at Jiuquan Commandery. Recorded by pen by Zhu Fashou. Appears in the three catalogs of Daozhen, Baochang, and Sengyou.
One fascicle of the *Śatruñjaya Sūtra*; the title states that "Śatruñjaya" is rendered as "Prince" (*Taizi*) in the Jin language. Twenty [verses].
The *Aṣṭama-bhikṣu-sūtra*, also known as the *Vyāghrī-śruti-sūtra*, is of the same textual lineage as the *Mātangī-sūtra*.

It is the fifth [text] produced; it differs slightly from the version translated by Dharmakṣema during the Han period. As seen in Dao’an’s catalogue, Sengyou states: *The *Vyāghrī-śruti-sūtra* (also titled *The Sūtra on the Desires that Cause Calamity*), one fascicle.
First produced in the first month of the third year of the Tàian era. Translated by Daozhenwangzong. Recorded by Sengyou.*
*The Sūtra of King Vimalacakra*, one fascicle; second edition, also known as *The Sūtra of Liu-li*; listed in Sengyou’s Catalogue. *The Sūtra of Birth*, five fascicles;
first edition, also in four fascicles; issued on the nineteenth day of the first month in the sixth year of the Taikang era;
contains fifty-five sūtras; listed in Nie Daozhen’s Catalogue and Sengyou’s Catalogue. *The Sūtra of Distinction*, one fascicle; formerly said to be identical to [the above].
It is incorrect to claim that the *Ānanda-vibhaṅga-sūtra* and others are identical to this [text].

According to the *Chángfáng-lù*, there is the *Svayambhū-nidāna-sūtra of the Five Hundred Disciples*, one fascicle, translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Tà'ān era; some say it is the *Svayambhū-nidāna-sūtra of the Buddha’s Five Hundred Disciples*.
An old catalogue calls it the *Svayambhū-pūrvāpara-nidāna-sūtra of the Five Hundred Disciples*, and it is also called the *Five Hundred* [Disciples Sūtra].

*The Disciple’s Original Arising* (Dizi benqi jing), one fascicle; listed in the two catalogs of Sengyou as *Jian dao zhen seng*. *The Original Scripture of Mahākāśyapa* (Da jiaye ben jing), one fascicle;

also called *The Scripture of Kāśyapa*, listed in the catalog of Sengyou. *The Scripture on Self-Inflicted Harm* (Zi qin jing), one fascicle; An Kang states it was extracted from the *Abhidharma*; listed in the catalog of Sengyou.

*The Scripture on Contemplating the Body* (Shen guan jing), one fascicle; stated to be extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; upon examination, it is not found therein. Listed in the catalog of Sengyou. *The Scripture on Longevity* (Chang jiu jing), one fascicle; listed in the catalog of Sengyou.
In Sengyou’s *Chusanzang jiji*, the first fascicle of the *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Treatise on the Stages of Cultivating the Path) is titled *Yuzhejiabomijing*;
it was translated during the second year of the Taikang era (281 CE) on the twenty-third day of the second month, and consists of seven fascicles and twenty-seven chapters.
A third version of this same work is simply titled *Xiuxing jing*. Both titles are recorded in Sengyou’s catalog as well as in the *Faguang jing*.
One fascicle; found in the *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Dharma-rooms). The portion from "seen above" onwards is missing.
The *New Fāngguǎng jīng* (New Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in ten fascicles is also called the *Xiǎopǐn* (Shorter Version), or in seven fascicles.

Sengyou states that it was translated again as the *Xiǎopǐn* in the eighth year of the Tàishǐ era; this fourth appearance is the same text as the old *Dàoxíng jīng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra). The *Fáng lù* further records the *Xiǎopǐn*.

The mention of "seven fascicles" is an error; this is not the version found in the two catalogs of the Jōyu-bō collection. Previously, one or two fascicles of the *Ninnō-hannya-kyō* (Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā) were missing.
On the first page of the thirty-first sheet, the original manuscript states: "Seen in the miscellaneous records of the Jin dynasty.
The *Muryōju-kyō* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra), two fascicles, also known as the *Muryō-seijō-byōdō-kaku-kyō*, [was translated] in the second year of the Yongjia era."

On the twenty-first day of the first month, the sixth translation was produced; its text is identical to that of the versions translated during the Han dynasty by Lokakṣema and others, though there are differences in their views.
This is recorded in the *Zhudaozu lu* and the *Sengyou lu*. Regarding the three-fascicle *Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra*, it first appeared in the *Changfang lu*.
Regarding the two-fascicle *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*, Master Dao’an’s record states that it was translated again.

The *Mèi jīng* (Faint Sutra), fascicle 5; first appearing in Sengyou’s catalogue. The *Púsà shí dì jīng* (Bodhisattva Ten Stages Sutra) in one fascicle, also called the *Dà fāngguǎng jīng* (Mahāvaipulya Sutra) or simply the *Shí dì jīng*;
first appearing in Sengyou’s catalogue. The *Sà yún fēn tuó lì jīng* (Sarvabuddhavaṃśa Sutra) in six fascicles, translated in the first year of the Taishi era;
recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jìn shì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty), entry 2; also recorded in the Sui catalogue.
The entry "Sàtán Yúnzhě" (薩曇芸者) is likely an error; it does not appear in Sengyou’s Record (*Chu sanzang jiji*).

There is one fascicle of the *Weimojie suoshuo fofamen jing* (維摩詰所說法門經), translated on the first day of the fourth month in the second year of the Tà'ān era; this is the fourth appearance [of this title], as seen in Niè Dàozhēn’s record.

Sengyou’s Record simply lists it as the *Weimojie jīng* (維摩詰經). Furthermore, Sengyou’s Record includes the *Shān Weimojie jīng* (刪維摩詰經); Sengyou states that his intention was to [distinguish] the former...

The *Xianju jing* (Sūtra on Dwelling in Solitude), one fascicle, is an excerpt of omitted verses from the *Weimo chanzhong hu* (Vimalakīrti’s Profound Protection). It is a different translation of the same text as the *Beihua jing* (Sūtra of the Lotus of Compassion);
its initial appearance is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue. Furthermore, there is the *Ajase wang jing* (Sūtra of King Ajātaśatru) in two fascicles;
this is the fourth appearance of the text, as seen in Sengyou’s catalogue. If one follows Dao’an’s catalogue, however, it lists only the "further appearance" of the *Ajase wang jing*.

The *Wú pǔchāo sānmèi* (Samādhi of Universal Transcendence) is recorded twice in both Sengyou’s and Fajing’s catalogs; since the Sanskrit original is identical, it is not appropriate to list it again.
The *Mílé chéngfó jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya Attaining Buddhahood), one fascicle, was first translated under the name *Mílé dānglái xiàshēng jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Future Descent).
It was translated in the second year of the Tà'ān era and consists of seventeen sheets, as seen in the records of Niè Dàozhēn and Sengyòu. [It concerns] the twelve links of dependent origination.
*Yuan jing* (Sutra on Conditions), one fascicle; the fourth translation, also titled *Sishou shi'er yinyuan* (Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Pippala Tree).

See Sengyou’s Record. *Wenshi xiyu zhong seng jing* (Sutra on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in a Warm Chamber), one fascicle; the second translation, also simply titled *Wenshi jing* (Warm Chamber Sutra).
See Nie Daozhen’s Record and Sengyou’s Record. *Bai fo ming jing* (Sutra of the Names of One Hundred Buddhas), one fascicle; the first translation. Not recorded by Sengyou.
The *Guānshìyīn dàshèzhì shòujué jīng* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta), one fascicle; first appeared during the Yuánkāng era.
It is also simply titled *Guānshìyīn shòujì jīng* (Sūtra on the Record of the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara) and is found in the catalogs of Niè Dàozhēn and Sēngyòu.

The *Yǒngfú dìng jīng* (Sūtra of the Heroic Subduing Samādhi), two fascicles; Master Ān stated that this was another appearance of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. [It was] in the fourth month of the first year of Kāng.

The ninth day, transcribed by Nie Chengyuan; the sixth translation. Regarding the *Jiandao zhen seng* (Record of True Monks Who Have Seen the Path) by Sengyou, the two catalogs of Sengyou and Daofang further record two fascicles of the *Shoulengyan* (Śūraṅgama), which is an error.

There is also one fascicle of the *Wusi yi guang haotong pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Child Bodhisattva of Inconceivable Light), also called the *Wusi yi haotong jing* (Sūtra of the Inconceivable Child), and also named the *Wusi yi guang jing* (Sūtra of Inconceivable Light); these were in the old catalogs.
It is simply called the *Child Scripture* (*Tongzi jing*). According to Sengyou’s *Lu*, it consists of two fascicles and was translated in the first month of the seventh year of the Taishi era;
its initial appearance is also recorded as being in three fascicles, or simply as the *Chāorìmíng jīng*.
It is found in Nie Daozhen’s *Lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*. The *Zhàomíng sānmèi jīng* (one fascicle) is also an initial translation found in Sengyou’s *Lu*.

*Weiming sanshi ji jing* (The Sutra of the Thirty Verses on the Sole Illumination), one fascicle; sometimes without the word "jing" (sutra). This second edition is identical to the version translated during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian, as recorded in the *Changfang lu*.
*Famojin jing* (The Sutra on the Exhaustion of the Dharma), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Kongji pusa suowen jing* (The Sutra Asked by the Bodhisattva Emptiness and Quiescence).
This second edition is the same text as that translated by Zhi Qian, though it is also referred to as the *Famiejin jing* (The Sutra on the Extinction of the Dharma). As seen [in the catalogues].
*Sengyou lu*: *Zhushenzhou jing* (Scriptures of Various Divine Spells), three fascicles; seen in *Sengyou lu*. *Wenshushili pusa jing* (Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Sūtra), one fascicle;
seen in *Changfang lu*. *Xiaoyuqiejing* (Shorter Ugra Sūtra), one fascicle; different from the *Dayuqiejing*; seen in *Sengyou lu*, though some versions write the character "jia" (迦) instead.
*Zhu fangfo ming gongde jing* (Sūtra on the Merits of the Names of Buddhas in All Directions), one fascicle; "gongde" (merits) is not present in [Dao]yǒu's record.
*The Scripture on the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*, one fascicle; recorded in the catalogs of Sengyou and Changfang, though the title "Scripture" (jing) is absent in Sengyou’s record.
*The Scripture on the Eighty Minor Marks as Asked by Ciren*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Scripture on the Eighty Minor Marks*;
recorded in the catalog of Dao’an and the catalog of Changfang. *The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of the Thirty-two Major Marks*, one fascicle.
One fascicle; alternatively called the *Bodhisattva-triṃśad-dvātriṃśat-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*. Recorded in the catalogs of Dao’an and Changfang. The *Śuddha-vyūha-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle;
also known as the *Xushi jing* (Sūtra on the Introduction to the World). Recorded in the catalog of Sengyou. The *Ratnadatta-dārikā-sūtra*, one fascicle;
also known as the *Sumati-dharmasamaya*. Recorded in the catalogs of Sengyou and Daozhen. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-kulapati-sūtra*.

*Zi jing* (The Scripture on the Son), one fascicle; recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*. *Lijou gai jing* (The Scripture on the Stainless Canopy), one fascicle; recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*. *Huiming jing* (The Scripture on Wisdom-Light), one fascicle;

recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*. *Zhongyou jing* (The Scripture on the Multitude of Blessings), one fascicle; recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*. *Sanzhuan riming jing* (The Scripture on the Three Turnings of Sunlight);
Sengyou’s *Lu* states it is the *Yueming* (Moonlight). Recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*. *Shidengzang jing* (The Scripture on the Tenfold Treasury), one fascicle; recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*.

*Yùlù jué dàosú jīng* (Sūtra Resolving Matters for the Clergy and Laity), one fascicle; recorded in Sengyǔ’s catalog. *Zhí zhòng déběn jīng* (Sūtra on Planting the Roots of All Virtues), one fascicle;
recorded in Sengyǔ’s catalog. *Xiǎofǎ mòjìn jīng* (Sūtra on the Extinction of the Lesser Dharma), one fascicle; recorded in Sengyǔ’s catalog. *Měngshī jīng* (Sūtra on Fierce Giving);
the old catalogs call it *Měngshī dàozhì jīng*; recorded in Sengyǔ’s catalog. *Mùlián shàng jìngjūtiān jīng* (Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana Ascending to the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens), one fascicle.

One fascicle, titled *The Sutra on the Method for the Bodhisattva’s Fasting* (or lacking the character "sūtra," or lacking the character "method"). Also known as the *Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Correct Fasting*, the *Sutra on Maintaining the Fast*, or the *Sutra on the Method for the Fasting of the Bodhisattva Bhadraśrī*. It first appeared in the records of Sengyou and Fazang. Longfang notes it was found in the *Collection of the Buddha’s Past Deeds* (*Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*). One fascicle. (From the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Volume 12). It is recorded that this work was translated by Zhu Fakai during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Liu Song dynasty. Regarding those works of outstanding quality from successive generations that are largely identical with minor differences, they are seen in the *Nie Daozhen Lu* and the *Sengyou Lu*.

One fascicle. Translated on the twelfth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yongning era;

the first translation. Master An remarked that it did not resemble the version produced by Master Hu. It appears in the records of Nie Daozhen and Sengyou. *The Scripture of the Five Dreams of the Buddha as a Bodhisattva*, one fascicle.

Sengyou states it is the *Piyu sanbai shou jing*, found in Sengyou’s catalog. Fang states it is found in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalog). Above.

One hundred and seventy-five works in three hundred and fifty-four fascicles; *Faguang jing* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of Dharmas), ninety-one works in two hundred and eight fascicles, currently extant;
*Xin daoxing jing* (New Sūtra on the Practice of the Way), eighty-four works in one hundred and forty-six fascicles, missing from the original.
The śramaṇa Zhu Tanmoluocha—
whose name means "Dharmarakṣa" in the Jin language—
was originally a native of the country of Yuezhi.
His original surname was Zhi,
and his family had resided for generations in Dunhuang Commandery.
At the age of eight, he left the household life and took the foreign śramaṇa Zhu Gaosuo as his teacher.

He subsequently adopted the surname Zhu. Before the Qin and Jin dynasties, śramaṇas mostly followed their teachers in adopting their surnames; later, because of Maitreya and Dao’an, they all collectively adopted the surname Shi. He could recite ten thousand words of scripture daily, and he was able to master them upon a single glance.
By nature he was pure and noble, and his conduct was refined and austere.
With a steadfast resolve for learning, he sought out teachers even ten thousand *li* away;
thus, he extensively studied the Six Classics and allowed his mind to roam through the Seven Canons.
Although worldly affairs such as praise and blame never entered his heart,
it was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin that temples and sacred images were first venerated in the capital.
At that time, the profound Vaipulya sutras were still confined beyond the Onion Range (the Pamirs).
Consequently, Senghu was filled with lamentation and resolved to propagate the Great Way;
he thus followed his master to the Western Regions, traveling through various kingdoms.
He thoroughly studied all thirty-six types of foreign languages and scripts;
he mastered their glosses, phonetics, meanings, and character forms, understanding them all completely.
He then brought back a vast collection of Sanskrit scriptures to China.
From Dunhuang to Chang’an,
and later reaching Luoyang and traveling to the region east of the Yangtze River,
he translated and transcribed [the texts] into the language of Jin along the way.
From the Jingsu year of the second year of Emperor Wu’s Taishi era (366 CE) to the Guiyou year of the first year of Emperor Min’s Jianxing era (421 CE),
he brought forth one hundred and seventy-five scriptures, including the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Praise of Light* (*Guangzan banruo jing*).
The lay devotee Nie Chengyuan,
along with his son Daozhen, Zhu Fashou,
Chen Shilun, Sun Bohu, Yu Shiya, and others.
Together they all received and protected his instructions, taking up their pens to carefully edit and revise [the texts].
Yet Hu was diligent in his endeavors, making the propagation and transmission [of the teachings] his sole vocation;
throughout his life, he labored at copying and translating without ever complaining of weariness.
That the sutras and dharmas have spread widely throughout the Eastern lands is due to the power of his protection.
In his later years, he lived in seclusion deep in the mountains;
there was a clear mountain stream where he constantly took water for washing and rinsing.
Later, a woodcutter came and defiled the water's edge, which dried up in an instant.
Guhu then paced back and forth and sighed, saying:
Because people lack virtue, they have caused the clear spring to cease its flow.
If the water were to dry up forever, there would truly be no means for it to sustain itself;
it simply must be moved elsewhere.
When he finished speaking, a spring flowed forth, filling the ravine.
Such were the manifestations of his profound sincerity.
Thus, Zhi Dun composed a eulogy for his portrait, saying:
Master Hu was serene and tranquil, his virtue profound and beautiful;
he would chant softly, as the distant valleys and parched springs murmured their waters.
Master Hu was born with a lofty and noble nature; he washed his feet in the shifting sands and grasped the ultimate mysteries.
Later, he established a monastery outside the Qing Gate in Chang’an and applied himself with diligence to the practice of the Way.
Thereupon, his virtuous transformation spread far and wide, and his reputation covered the four quarters;
several thousand monastics all venerated him as their master.
When Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty fled west to Chang’an,
the Guanzhong region fell into desolation and the common people were forced to migrate.
Senghu, along with his disciples, sought refuge by traveling eastward until they reached Mianchi.
He fell ill and passed away at the age of seventy-eight.
It is said that during the reigns of Emperors Huai and Min, he once again produced translations of sutras and commentaries.
When Emperor Hui traveled west to Chang’an, [he followed him].
Master Hu fled the chaos to the east and died at Mianchi; perhaps this was not yet his destined end.
Master Hu had lived his entire life in Dunhuang, and his transformative teachings spread everywhere.
People of the time all called him the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva."
Some records refer to him as the Bodhisattva of Mozhī (Yuezhi),
while others call him the Bodhisattva of Tiānzhú (India);
these are all ways of honoring his virtue and extolling his title.
As for Dharmarakṣa,
his name was translated in this land as *Dharmarākṣa*;
it is the Western Sanskrit designation.
However, the *Liang sengyou lu* and the *Sui fajing lu* list them as two separate individuals, claiming that each produced a distinct scripture; this is not entirely accurate.
Now, having carefully examined various catalogs:
The number of sutras translated by Dharmarakṣa is indefinite;
in Sengyou’s *Chū-sanzō-ki-shū*, their count is even more numerous.
Now, upon careful investigation and collation, it appears that most are derivative or apocryphal sutras.
There are some works not translated by Master Hu that cannot be counted among the authentic translations;
for the sake of an accurate record, they have been deleted in their entirety as described below.

Regarding the *Sūtra on the Previous Life of Siṃhacandra Buddha*, various catalogs such as those of the Fang family state that it was translated by Master Hu, though the word "original" (or "master") may be absent. Details are provided therein.

The *Wen* (Text) is not a translation from the present; it was compiled in the *Qin lu* (Catalogue of the Qin Dynasty). The *Fashu jing* (Dharma Society Sūtra) has a commentary by Shi [Sheng] that marks it as doubtful;

having personally seen its manuscript, I find it to be a human composition, and thus I now include it in the *Yilu* (Record of Doubtful Works). The *Bao nü wen hui jing* (Sūtra of the Jewel Maiden’s Inquiry on Wisdom), the *Fan wang bian shen jing* (Sūtra of the Brahma King’s Transformation of Body)—these two sūtras are derived from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.
The *Si zai zhong tong jing* (Sūtra of the Four Sovereign Supernatural Powers) is derived from the *Īśvararāja-sūtra*. The *Vajragarbha* [is derived from the same source].
The *Bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra* is excerpted from the *Zhanbei jing*; the *Guangshiyin jing* is excerpted from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
the *Ratnādityaprabha-bodhisattva-sūtra* is also called the *Ratnādityaprabha-bodhisattva-prcchā-padmalokadhātu-vyūha-sūtra*, excerpted from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
the *Samantamukha-kumāra-bhūta-sūtra*—sometimes written with the character "溥"—is excerpted from the *Samantābhibhū-sūtra*; and the *Sulambana-sūtra*.
The *Aśvavarga-sūtra*, the *Maitreya-as-a-Woman-sūtra*, the *King Māndhātṛ-sūtra*, and the four sūtras beginning with the *Sulambha* all appear in the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*.
The *Bodhisattva-pāpadeśanā-dharma-sūtra* sometimes omits the word "sūtra. The *Nāgārjuna-daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* cites the *Puruṣāgamanasūtra*, which is also called the *Puruṣāgamana-sūtra*.
There are also the *Puruṣasya-kāmopapatti-sūtra* and the *Daridra-sūtra*. What [is there]?
The *Dukha-sūtra* and the *Daridra-ādi-dvaya-sūtra* both appear in the *Madhyama Āgama*; the *Saptaratna-sūtra* appears in the *Ekottara Āgama*;
the *Vaidyarāja-sūtra*, the *Sivirideva-rāja-bhikṣu-gāthā-sūtra*, and the *Caturvidha-puruṣa-sūtra*—these three sūtras beginning with the *Vaidyarāja-sūtra*—all appear in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
and the *Viveka-sūtra* and the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* (also known as the *Buddhacitta-dhāraṇī*).

The *Abushijing* (Sutra on the Belly-Servant), *Mijujing* (Sutra on the Honey-Preparation), *Zazanjing* (Sutra of Miscellaneous Praises), and *Xianjujing* (Sutra on Dwelling in Solitude)—these five sutras are all extracted from the *Chushengjing*.

The *Nürenyuchihuangmijing* (Sutra on Women’s Lust, Fervor, and Confusion) and the *Duowenjing* (Sutra on Much Hearing) and *Wuyijing* (Sutra on Awakening the Mind)—these three sutras above are all extracted from the *Chuyaojing*.
The twenty-seven sutras from the *Bao-nü* (Jewel Woman) section below are all separately excerpted sutras derived from major collections.
Now, all of these have been deleted.

One fascicle of the *Zhong jing mulu* (Catalogue of the Scriptures) was compiled by Master Hu himself; it was not a translation from an Indic original, and as it is listed within the *Xù mulu* (Continued Catalogue), it is no longer preserved. One fascicle of the *Shí èr yóu jīng* (Sūtra of the Twelve Wanderings) first appeared [in this collection]; the aforementioned one work in one fascicle was originally missing.
The śramaṇa Qiángliánglóuzhì— whose name means "True Joy" (Zhēnxǐ) in the Jin language—
was a man from the Western Regions.
His aspirations were expansive and unrestrained,
and he held the propagation of the Dharma close to his heart.
In the second year of Emperor Wu’s Taikang era, the year of Xinchou (281 CE).
Translated in Guangzhou.
One fascicle of the *Shier you jing* (Sūtra of the Twelve Wanderings) is recorded in the *Shixing lu* and the *Baochang lu*.

The four-fascicle *Daoshenzu wuji bianhua jing* (Sūtra of the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way), the second [translation], is also known as the *He daoshenzu jing* (Combined Sūtra of the Divine Footsteps of the Way).

Alternatively, there is a three-fascicle version which is a different translation of the same text as the *Buddha Ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother* translated by Zhu Fahu;

this is recorded in the *Zhu Daozu Lu*. There is also a seven-fascicle *A-yu-wang Zhuan* (Biography of King Aśoka), sometimes with the character "Da" (Great) prefixed to it, also called the *Da A-yu-wang Jing* (Great Aśoka Sūtra), or a five-fascicle version.
Its initial translation is the same text as the *Yù-wáng-jīng* (Aśoka Sūtra) translated during the Liang dynasty, titled *Guāngxī*.

The śramaṇa Baiyuan, whose courtesy name was Fazǔ, was originally surnamed Wàn.
A native of Hénèi, his father Wéidá was renowned for his refined scholarship and elegance;
he declined all appointments offered by the provincial and regional governments.
From his youth, Zu conceived the aspiration for the Way and petitioned his father to leave the household life.
His arguments were so earnest and compelling that his father could not resist him;
he subsequently changed his attire and followed the Way.
Zu’s talent and intellect were exceptionally brilliant and lucid, surpassing all others.
He could recite eight or nine thousand words of scripture daily;
he investigated and savoring the Vaipulya sutras, he entered their profound subtleties with marvelous ease.
The secular *fensuo* (classical texts) were extensively encompassed by him.
He subsequently constructed a vihāra in Chang’an, making the study and exposition of the teachings his primary vocation.
Monastics and laypeople who took him as their spiritual guide numbered nearly a thousand.

The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) in six fascicles, the second translation; also called the *Daluotan jing*.

It is recorded as being the same text with a different translation as the fourth division of the *Chang ahan jing* (*Dīrgha-āgama*) and the *Jishi jing*; it differs slightly from the five-fascicle version translated by Dharmarakṣa.
It appears in Sengyou’s catalog as either five or eight fascicles. The *Faju piyu jing* (Udānavarga-avadāna-sūtra) in four fascicles, the second translation.
One title is the *Dharmapada-mūla-paryāya-sūtra*, also called the *Dharma-upamā-sūtra*; it consists of either four fascicles or six fascicles and was produced jointly by [Tang] Li and Faju;
it appears in Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Sengyou lu*). One fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*;
the old catalogues call it the *Buddhagarbha-vaipulya-sūtra*; it first appeared in Sengyou’s Catalogue. The above four works comprise twelve fascicles; the first three...
The first section consists of eleven fascicles and is currently extant; the latter section consists of one fascicle and is missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Falì was a person of unknown origins.
His wisdom and path were broad and eminent;
his priority was to awaken sentient beings.
During the era of Emperor Hui, he...
Together with Dharmakara and others, he translated four scriptures, including the *Sarvadeva-kṣetra* (諸德福田), at Luoyang.
The one-fascicle *King Udayana Sūtra* (*Udāyana-rāja-sūtra*) is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa Udāyana-rāja-parivarta*; its initial appearance is recorded in the *Cháng-āhán-jīng* (長阿含經).
*Fanglu qianshi sanzhuan jing* (Sūtra on the Three Turnings of Previous Lives), one fascicle; first recorded in the *Changfang lu*, it shares the same original text as the *Yinse nü jing*.

*Ajātaśatru-rāja-vyākaraṇa sūtra* (Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Receiving the Prediction), one fascicle; first recorded in the *Changfang lu*, it shares the same original text as the *Cailian wei wang jing*.
*Guanxi foxingxiang jing* (Sūtra on Bathing the Buddha’s Image), one fascicle; its initial appearance is also said to have been on the eighth day of the fourth month.
The *Riju-guan jing* (Directly Spoken Sutra on Empowerment) is also simply called the *Guan jing*; it is of the same text as the *Mahāsthāmaprāpta-sūtra*, according to the *Changfang lu*.

The *Hengshui jing* (Sutra on the Ganges River), one fascicle, is also called the *Henghe yu jing* (Sutra of the Parable of the Ganges); it is an alternative translation from the ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, according to the *Changfang lu*.
The *Dingshengwang gushi jing* (Sutra on the Story of King Mūrdhaja), one fascicle, is also simply called the *Dingshengwang jing* (Sutra of King Mūrdhaja); it is extracted [from the canon].
*Qiuyujing* (Sūtra on Seeking Desire), one fascicle; translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, chapter 11; listed in the *Changfang Lu* as a variant translation.

*Kuyinyingshijing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Aggregate of Suffering), one fascicle; translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, chapter 22; listed in the *Changfang Lu* as a variant translation.
*Zhanpabiqiujing* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Campā), one fascicle; alternatively [titled]...; listed in the *Changfang Lu* as a variant translation from the *Madhyama Āgama*, chapter 25.
*Zhanpo chujing* (The Sutra on the Birth in Campā), one fascicle; translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter 29; listed as a variant translation in the *Chángfáng lù*.
*Fuyin jing* (The Sutra on Subduing Lust), one fascicle; translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter 30; listed as a variant translation in the *Chángfáng lù*.

*Shujing* (The Sutra on Counting), one fascicle; translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter 35; listed as a variant translation in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Pósìní wáng tài...* (The [Sutra on] King Prasenajit’s... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

*The Sūtra on the Dust and Earth Covering the Body after the King’s Demise*, one fascicle; translated from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama* with a variant translation, as recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
Furthermore, there is the *Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Mourning for His Mother*, which is identical to this *Sūtra on the Dust and Earth Covering the Body*.
There is also the *Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha to Make Offerings*, one fascicle, also known as the *Bīn*.

The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* in one fascicle, translated by Bāzhù; listed in the Chángfáng Lù as a variant translation of the twenty-sixth section of the *Ekottarika-āgama*, largely identical with minor differences to the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* by Zhú Fǎhù.

It appears in the thirty-first section of the *Ekottarika-āgama*. The *Nandika-sūtra* in one fascicle; listed in the Chángfáng Lù as a variant translation from the third section of the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.

*Ten Fascicles*, translated differently; seen in Changfang’s Record. *Xiangyingxiangke Jing* (Sutra on Corresponding Characteristics), one fascicle; produced as a separate translation from the *Za Ahan Jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama);
seen in Changfang’s Record. *Manfa Jing* (Sutra on Arrogance), one fascicle; the second production, identical in text to the *Ahan Fenbie Jing* (Sutra on the Analysis for Ānanda) and others;
seen in Changfang’s Record. *Fahai Jing* (Sutra on the Dharma-Ocean), one fascicle; the second production, identical to the *Hai Ba* [Sutra].

The *Dejing* (Scripture on Virtue) shares the same original text as that recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. The *Ajātaśatru-rāja-wèn wǔnì jīng* (Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Asking about the Five Heinous Crimes), one fascicle;
second appearance, recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. The *Lóuyún rěnrù jīng* (Sūtra on Rāhula’s Forbearance), one fascicle; alternatively titled simply the *Rěnrù jīng*, recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
The *Fó wèi niánshào bǐqiū shuō zhèngshì jīng* (Sūtra on the Buddha Explaining Righteous Matters to Young Bhikṣus), one fascicle, recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. The *Shāhé*... [text fragment].
*The Sūtra on the Merits of a Bhikṣu*, one fascicle; Fang says it was seen in the Old Catalogue. *The Parable of the Herd of Cows*, one fascicle;
seen in the Catalogue of Baochang. *The Sūtra on a Bhikṣu Attempting Suicide to Avoid the Evil Reputation of a Woman*, one fascicle;
seen in the Catalogue of Baochang. The above are extant; those below are missing.
*Fútián jīng* (Sūtra on the Field of Merit), one fascicle; also known as *Zhūdé fútián jīng* (Sūtra on the Field of Merit for All Virtuous Ones).

This second edition differs slightly from that translated by Fali; it is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jìn lù* (Catalogue of the Jin Dynasty). *Zhūpúsà míng jīng* (Sūtra of the Names of Bodhisattvas), two fascicles;

recorded in Changfang’s catalogue. *Zhèngyì jīng* (Sūtra of Correct Meaning), one fascicle; recorded in Changfang’s catalogue. A note in the catalogue states: "The second edition is not yet clear as to which [text] it is."

The *Ming Dishi Shijing* (Sutra on the Gift of Indra) in one fascicle, translated during the early period, is recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) in eight fascicles is the third translation;
it is a variant translation of the fourth section of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Jishi jing* (Sutra on the Record of the World).

It is largely identical to the version produced by Dharmarakṣa and Dharmasthiti. Previously, [the text] was produced jointly with Dharmasthiti, but because Dharmasthiti’s understanding was not yet complete, he expanded upon it; this is seen in the *Min* [catalog].
*The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana*, one fascicle; first appeared in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*The Sūtra of the Poor Old Man*, one fascicle; first appeared in the *Fǎshàng Lù*. *The Sūtra on Fragility*, one fascicle; seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*The Sūtra of the Simile of the Great Snake*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Great Snake Sūtra*. Fáng states it is seen in the "Old Catalogue."
*Ārhat-Kāḷodāyin Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the character "Ārhat" (according to the *Chángfáng Lù*).
*Nakhakha-Parigṛhīta-mṛttikā-upama Sūtra*, one fascicle; also called *Nakhakha-Gṛhīta-mṛttikā Sūtra*. Fáng states it is found in the old catalog.
*Śrāmaṇyaphala Sūtra*, one fascicle; found in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Sattva-anabhyudgata-tridhātu Sūtra*, one fascicle; found in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*Qiúyù shuōfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Request for the Exposition of the Dharma), one fascicle; listed in the Chángfáng lù. *Lóxún yù jīng* (Sūtra of the Parable of Rāṣṭrapāla), one fascicle;

currently suspected to be an alternative title for the *Luómíshòu jīng* (Sūtra of Rāṣṭrapāla) found within the *Biéshēng jīng* (Separately Produced Sūtras); listed in the Chángfáng lù. *Yíjiào fǎlǜ jīng* (Sūtra of the Dharma-Regulations of the Bequeathed Teaching), three fascicles;

also titled *Yíjiào fǎlǜ sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Dharma-Regulations of the Bequeathed Teaching), or simply *Yíjiào sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching); alternatively, it consists of two fascicles.
According to the *Shixing lu* (Record of Beginnings and Flourishing), the above forty works comprise fifty fascicles;

twenty-four works comprising twenty-four fascicles were translated by the Bhikṣu Biyun; and sixteen works comprising twenty-six fascicles currently exist as extant texts, while the remaining ones are missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Faju was also of unknown clan and lineage;
his capacity was lofty and eminent, and he harbored the intention to travel and transform others through his teachings.
At the beginning of Emperor Hui’s reign, he collaborated with Fali to produce translations of the scriptures.
After Fali passed away, Daohui subsequently translated forty sections of sutras, including those concerning King Udayana, on his own.
Furthermore, the records of Sengchang, Fang, and others list various other sūtras, all claiming they were translated by Zhu Fajü.
However, these are all sūtras produced through separate recensions; the cataloguers have erroneously attributed them to him.
They shall now all be deleted, as described below.
The *Sūtra on Time and Non-Time* is also simply called the *Sūtra on Time*; according to the postscript of this sūtra, it was not translated by Fa Ju, as described below.

The *Sūtra on the Demoness Hearing the Buddha’s Teaching and Attaining a Male Body* is from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*. The *Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Compassionate Bhikṣu* is from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

The *Sūtra on Past Deeds* and the *Sūtra on Holding the Alms Bowl*—these two sūtras are both from the *Samādhi of Universal Transcendence*. The *Sūtra on Using Gold to Redeem Sins at Mount Tai* and the *Sūtra on Devadatta Teaching Others to Commit Evil*—these two... [text ends]

The sūtras include the *Ṣaḍpāramitā-samuccaya*, the *Buddha-dharṣaṇa-aṅgulimāla-prajā-pramoda-sūtra*, and the *Aṅgulimāla-pravrajyā-sūtra* (also known as the *Strī-maraṇa-sūtra*; the latter two titles are likely errors). These two [latter] sūtras are both included in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*.

There is also the *Vaidehī-putra-candramas-rātri-pṛcchā-bhāryā-sūtra* (alternatively titled *Devamanuṣya-niḥsaraṇa-sūtra*). From the *Dīrgha-āgama*, there are the *Puṇyakriyā-sūtra*, the *Durgati-sūtra* (also named *Duṣṭāśaya-sūtra*;

the title *Yāśaya-sūtra* is likely an error), and the *Krodhopaśamana-sūtra* (in the catalog, the names *Durgati* and *Duṣṭāśaya* are listed together, which is incorrect). Also, the *Krodhopaśamana-sūtra*.
The *Mṛdvīka-sūtra*, the *Upāli-sūtra*, the *Nāma-sūtra*, the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*, and the seven sūtras on meritorious conduct (*puṇyakriyā*)—all these appear in the *Madhyama Āgama*.

The *Śakuntaka-upama-sūtra*, the *Kāṣṭharāśi-dahana-sūtra* (also known as the *Mahāśuṣka-vṛkṣa-sūtra*), the *Rājā Prasenajit upasaṃkrāmati pañcabhir īryāpathaiḥ-sūtra*, and four sūtras including the *Śakuntaka-upama-sūtra* from the *Ekottara Āgama*—all these appear in the *Ekottara Āgama*.
Furthermore, there are the *Viśvadeva-sūtra*, the *Carmavastu-bhikṣu-upama-guru-roga-sūtra*, the *Buddha bhikṣūn uddiśya śira-dāha-upama-sūtra*, and the *Udāyin vṛkṣopaviṣṭa-sūtra*.

The Sūtra on Tranquility and Subjugation; the Sūtra on Great Power Spoken by the Buddha for the Bhikṣus; the Sūtra on Developing Disgust for the Four Great Elements and the Physical Body; the Sūtra on Different Faiths and Different Desires; the Sūtra on the Three Dharmas Spoken by the Buddha for the Bhikṣus;
the Sūtra on the Parable of Leaves Regarding Quantity; the Sūtra on the Extremely Deep, Precipitous, and Difficult Places Spoken by the Buddha for the Bhikṣus;

the Sūtra on Not Contemplating the World Spoken by the Buddha for the Bhikṣus (alternatively titled the Sūtra on Not Contemplating the World or the Sūtra on Contemplating the World); the Sūtra on the Impurity of the Sentient Being’s Body; the Sūtra on the Mutual Bondage of the Eye and Form; and the Sūtra on the Bhikṣu’s Detachment from Form.

The Sutra on Abandoning Worldly Affairs; the Sutra of the Simile of the Infant; the Sutra on the Appearance of the Seven Jewels of a Wheel-Turning Sage King in the World; the Sutra on Turning Toward the Deviant and Contrary to the Dharma; the Sutra of the Simile of the Farmer;

the Sutra on the Five Kinds of Calamities Arising for One Who Trusts Others; the Sutra on the Few and Many Precepts; the Sutra on the Beginningless Fundamental Limit; the Sutra on an Arhat Meeting King Bimbisāra; the Sutra on the Venerable Godhika’s Solitary Contemplation;

the Sutra on People Afflicted by Epidemic Receiving the Three Refuges; the Sutra on the Flowing of the Ganges River; or the Sutra of the River of Ashes from Flowing Tree Ashes, also known as the Simile of the River of Dust and Ashes.
It is an error for these two titles to be recorded separately in the *Yujing lu* (Record of Parables). These include:

the *Sūtra on the Death of King Prasenajit’s Grandmother*, the *Sūtra of the Golden Casting Parable*, the *Sūtra of the Wooden Pestle Parable*, the *Sūtra of the Elder’s Illness at the Goldsmith’s Monastery*, the *Sūtra of the Parable of the Flock of Sheep*, the *Sūtra on Walking the Middle Way*, the *Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Daughter Passing Away and Visiting the Buddha*, the *Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Asking the Buddha about Names*, the *Sūtra on the Upāsaka’s Death*, and the thirty-five sūtras beginning with the *Sūtra of Universal Giving*.
All of these appear in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the *Bhikṣu-piṇḍapāta Sūtra*, the *Upananda Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra on Living by Wrong Means*.

The Sūtra on the Individual Aspirations of the Bhikṣus; the Sūtra on the Exegesis of Harmony and Difficulty; the Sūtra on the Illness of a Bhikṣu; the Sūtra on Fearlessness; the Sūtra on the Simile of Poisonous Herbs; the Sūtra on the Simile of Poison; the Sūtra on the Simile of the Horse;

the ten sūtras beginning with the Bhikṣu’s Almsround—all of which are from the *Chusheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth); the *Piyu liuren jing* (Sūtra of Parables on the Six Men); the *Chu ma yi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaning of Insults); the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-wen-chenhen-cong-he-sheng jing* (Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Asking Where Hatred Arises from);

the *Mahābhikṣu jing* (Sūtra of the Great Bhikṣu); the *Tiduolü jing* (Sūtra on the Simile of Devadatta); the three sūtras beginning with *Ajātaśatru*; the *Xiaosheng chao jing* (Abridged Sūtra of the Hīnayāna); the *Zhantan tuta jing* (Sūtra on Anointing the Stūpa with Sandalwood); the *Chubaiyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Emergence of One Hundred Conditions); and the *Wuchang* (Impermanence).

1. The Sūtra on a Bhikṣu Seeking Witnesses 2. The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Abhaya 3. The Sūtra on the Impermanence of the Bhikṣu 4. The Sūtra on the Bhikṣus Asking the Buddha Why He Abandoned the World to Study the Path 5. The Sūtra on the Buddha Visiting a Sick Bhikṣu and Refusing the Elder’s Invitation 6.

The Sūtra on a Bhikṣu Practicing Dhyāna Who Passed Away and Was Reborn in Heaven 7. The Sūtra on Heedlessness 8. The Sūtra on Bhikṣus of Shallow and Deep Learning 9. The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Kṛtī 10. The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Pāli Slandering the Holy Life 11.

The Sūtra on the Worldly Benefits of the Northern Region 12. The Sūtra on King Virūḍhaka Attacking the Śākyas 13. The Sūtra on How Faith Can Cross the River 14. The Sūtra on the Three Types of Sentient Beings

The *Worldly Deeds of Evil Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on the Wise and Clever Bhikṣu*, the *Sūtra on the Difficulty of Encountering the Dharma*, and the *Sūtra on Devadatta Asking about the Buddha’s Complexion*—these seventeen sūtras from the section on "Impermanence" (*Anitya*) are all extracted from the *Udānavarga*.

The *Sūtra on the Morning Meal* is extracted from the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (or *Yogācārabhūmi*). The eight sūtras from the section on "The Demoness" onwards, including the *Sūtra of the Simile of the River Xū*, are all excerpted from the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* (or *Mahāsūtra*);
they are recorded in the *Biéshēng lù* (Separate Birth Record) and have been excluded here.

The *Chāorìmíng sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Surpassing the Sun’s Radiance), two fascicles; the second [version] was translated separately, or is simply called the *Chāorìmíng jīng*, or consists of three fascicles. This sūtra was first translated by Master Hu from the Sanskrit original, but its phrasing and meaning were cumbersome and redundant. Daosheng subsequently refined and organized the prose and verses, revising them so they surpassed the previous version. This is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gāosēngzhuàn*) and Sengyou’s *Catalogue* (*Mùlù*). The *Yuènán jīng* (Sūtra of Overcoming Difficulties), one fascicle—also known as the *Nánzhǎngzhě jīng* (Sūtra of the Elder Nanda) or simply the *Nán jīng* (Sūtra of Difficulties)—was first translated and appears in the *Chángfáng lù*. These two works, totaling three fascicles, both have extant manuscripts.
The lay devotee Nie Chengyuan was clear-headed and talented,
possessing a sincere commitment to the Dharma.
When Master Hu brought forth the scriptures, Chengyuan frequently assisted in correcting the wording and also served as the scribe to record the master’s instructions.
Later, during the reign of Emperor Hui, he personally translated two scriptures, including the *Chāorìmíng jīng* (Sūtra of Surpassing the Sun’s Radiance).
Furthermore, the catalogues by Zhìshēng and others state that Chéngyuǎn additionally translated the *Jiāshè qì Ānán jīng* (Sūtra of Kāśyapa Rebuking Ānanda).
This is merely a miscellaneous collection of parables and not a separate translation.
