Furthermore, it is a grave error for the three catalogs of the Han period—those of Fotiao, An Shigao, and this Chengyuan—to all include it.

*Vimaladattā-bodhisattva-vibhaṅga-pratibhāna-sūtra*, one fascicle; the second translation, identical in substance to the *Dharmarakṣa-vimaladattā-sūtra*, also titled *Vibhaṅga-pratibhāna-pratidāna*. It is now included as the thirty-third assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*. Other records state it was translated by Zhu Fahu, but this is an error, as seen in the *Changfang lu*. *Sarvabodhisattva-buddha-mūla-karma-sūtra*, one fascicle (some versions omit the word "Sarva"). This is a variant translation of the "Pure Conduct" chapter (*Śīla-paṭala*) of the *Avataṃsaka*. See the *Changfang lu*. *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle. See the *Changfang lu*. *Bodhisattva-pūrvotpatti-sūtra*, one fascicle (some versions omit the character "qi"). See the *Changfang lu*. *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle. See the *Changfang lu*. *Bodhisattva-śīla-upavāsa-sūtra*, one fascicle; the second translation. See the *Changfang lu*. The above [titles] currently exist; those below are missing.

*The Scripture on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva of the Vaipulya*, one fascicle; the second translation, which is largely identical with minor differences to that by Dharmarakṣa, as recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.
*The Scripture on the Ten Dharma-Abodes of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle;

a different translation of the "Ten Abodes Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the third translation, as recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *The Scripture on the Ten Abodes*, twelve fascicles; this is the *Daśabhūmika* [chapter] of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The second translation of this fascicle, which appears in the *Chángfáng lù*, is the *Bōsà yuánshēn wǔshí shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Fifty Matters of the Bodhisattva’s Physical Origins), one fascicle;
its second translation is largely identical with minor differences to the *Wǔshí yuánshēn jīng*.

The *Guānshìyīn shòujì jīng* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara), one fascicle, is a second translation appearing in the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Zhūfó yàojí jīng* (Sūtra on the Essential Collection of All Buddhas), two fascicles— [End of fragment]
2. *Bodhisattvapraṇidhānasūtra* (One fascicle), recorded in the Chángfáng lù; *Bodhisattvapañcacakṣuradhigamadharmasūtra* (One fascicle), recorded in the Chángfáng lù;
the character "jing" (sūtra) is missing from the manuscript by Yòu, or it is said that the text contains the "five eyes";
*Bodhisattvamārgacaryāṣaddharmasūtra* (One fascicle), recorded in the Chángfáng lù; *Bodhisattvaprathamabhūmisūtra* (One fascicle), recorded in the Chángfáng lù.

In the *Chángfáng lù*, it is recorded that there is one fascicle of the *Bōsà shí dào dì jīng* (Sūtra on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva), which states it was a previous translation of the *Bōsà shí dì* (Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva).
There is also one fascicle of the *Wénshǔshīlì yǔ Líyì nǚ lùn yì* (Discourse between Mañjuśrī and the Woman Liyi), which closely resembles the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Furthermore, there is one fascicle of the *Bōsà zá xíng fǎ* (Dharmas of the Miscellaneous Practices of the Bodhisattva) recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. [The text continues with] the *Bōsà suǒ...* [recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*].

*Xiing sifafa jianjuan* (One fascicle on the Practice of the Four Dharmas), listed in the Chángfáng Record; *Bosha suming jing* (Sūtra on the Past Lives of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle, listed in the Chángfáng Record;
*Wenshushili jinglü jing* (Mañjuśrī Sūtra on the Pure Vinaya), one fascicle, a second translation slightly differing from that translated by Dharmarakṣa, listed in the Chángfáng Record;

*Bosajie dusou tanwen* (Text on the Platform for Solely Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts), one fascicle, listed in the Chángfáng Record; *Bosha chanhui fa* (Method for the Bodhisattva’s Repentance).
One fascicle; titled *Yichu ben* (Variant Edition), recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The above twenty-four works comprise thirty-six fascicles.
Of these, the first six works totaling six fascicles are extant under the section "Mahāvaipulya" (*Dafangguang*). The remaining eighteen works totaling thirty fascicles are missing.
The lay devotee Nie Daozhen was the son of Chengyuan.
Father and son were both pure and enlightened, and they both took the transmission of the Dharma as their vocation.
This period spanned from the beginning of Emperor Wu’s Taikang era to the end of Emperor Huai’s Yongjia era.
During that interval, in addition to the scriptures he consulted, received, and had Dharmarakṣa transcribe,
after Dharmarakṣa’s death, Zhu Fonian himself translated twenty-four sūtras, including the *Vimaladattāparipṛcchā* and the *Pratibhānamati*.
Master Hugu truly lived up to his title.
He was quite skilled in literary composition, and his phrasing and meanings were distinct and brilliant.
Furthermore, the catalogs of Sengzao and others list twenty-nine additional scriptures, which also claim to have been translated by Daozhen.
Since these are all excerpts from separate translations of the sutras, they have been deleted and are no longer preserved. [Included here are:

"The Bodhisattva’s Offering and Vow Made at a Stupa," "The Sutra on the Recollection of the Dharma Master," "The Lion’s Gait," and "The Thunderous Voice of the Bodhisattva. [Also included is] "The Inquiry of the Bodhisattva on Arousing the Resolve."
The *Sūtra on the Three Dharmas of Bodhisattvas*, the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Offerings and Other [Practices]*—these three sūtras are all from the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-pariśuddhi-sūtra*;
the *Dharma of Bodhisattva Generosity and Repentance* is from the *Vinaya-viniścaya-sūtra*;
the *Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Admonitions as Asked by King Vaśavartin Bodhisattva* (also known as the *Bodhisattva-śīla-kāya-vaśitā-sūtra*); and the *Bodhisattva-pradarśana-caryā-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Initial Resolve*, the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Wuyanyan’s Propagation of the Dharma*, the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Wuyanyan*,
the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Essential Practice of the Unobstructed Dharma-Gate*, the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Guangwei Constructing a Ladder of Seven Jewels*,

and seven other sūtras including the *Sūtra of the Sovereign King Bodhisattva*— all these were translated together with the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Wish-Fulfilling Supernatural Powers*.

The *Sajie Zizai Jing* (Sūtra on the Sovereignty of Bodhisattva Precepts), the aforementioned two sūtras from the *Zizaiwang Jing* (Sūtra of the King of Sovereignty), the *Jiyin Pusa Wen Wuzhuo Jing* (Sūtra on the Five Turbidities Asked by the Bodhisattva Jiyin)—

also known as the *Jiyi Zhuanlun Shengwang Fachen Qingtu Jing* (Sūtra on the Resolve for a Pure Land Made by the Wheel-Turning Sage King Jiyi)— the aforementioned two sūtras from the *Beihua Jing* (Sūtra of the Compassionate Flower),

the *Dayun Mizang Pusa Wen Dahan Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Great Ocean Samādhi Asked by the Bodhisattva Dayun Mizang)— from the *Dayun Jing* (Great Cloud Sūtra), and the *Pushou Tongzi* (Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta).

The *Zhenjing* (True Scripture) appears in the *Puchao jing* (Sutra of Universal Transcendence); the *Rutong pusa jing* (Sutra of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī)—sometimes omitting the word "Bodhisattva"—appears in the *Liudu ji jing* (Compendium of the Six Pāramitās);

the *Basiridawang yu fayaṅjuemolu jing* (Sutra of King Prasenajit Wishing to Attack Aṅgulimāla) appears in the *Aṅgulimāla jing*; the *Daguangming pusa baisishibazhi yuan jing* (Sutra of the One Hundred Forty-Eight Vows of the Bodhisattva Mahāprabhāsa);
the *Pusa liufaxing jing* (Sutra on the Sixfold Practice of the Bodhisattva); and the *Pusa benyuanxing jing* (Sutra on the Original Vow-Practice of the Bodhisattva).

The *Pin jing* (Chapter Sutra), the *Pusa kuxing jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Ascetic Practices), the *Pusa he shuimian jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Rebuke of Sleep), the *Pusa he jia guo jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Rebuke of the Faults of the Household), the *Daguangming jing* (Sutra of Great Radiance), and five other sutras—these six are recorded in the *Yulü* (Records of the Canon) as being excerpts;

they are now all classified as Mahāyāna excerpted sutras. The *Pusa jie yaoyi jing* (Sutra on the Essential Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts) is extracted from the *Dizhi jing* (Bodhisattvabhūmi Sutra).
The *Pusa wufa xing jing* (Sutra on the Fivefold Practice of the Bodhisattva) concerns the easy practice for a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
Regarding the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra* and the aforementioned two sūtras, both appear in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The *Cakravartin-rāja-saptaratna-paripūrṇa-sūtra* appears in the *Za ahan zhong jing mulu* (Catalogue of Various Āgama Sūtras) in one fascicle; it was compiled by Daozhen himself and is not a translation from a Sanskrit original.
It is listed among the "Prefaces and Records" (*xùlù*) but no longer exists. Furthermore, the catalogues of Sengchang and others state:
The Upāsaka Weishi Du,
during the reign of Emperor Hui,
produced the two-fascicle *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mārgacaryā-sūtra*, which says:

The *Sengyou lu* states that various catalogs all record the *Dàoxíng jīng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāpāramitā-sūtra) as being in two fascicles, translated in brief by Weishidu from an old version. Since this was a condensation of an existing scripture rather than a separate translation from a Sanskrit original, it is not a distinct version.
It is now included in the *Jiesheng lu* (Record of Additional Translations) and no longer exists here.

The *Shi tongzi jing* (Sūtra of the Deceased Boy), one fascicle, is the fourth appearance; it is also titled the *Zhangzhe zhi jing* (Sūtra of the Elder’s Prohibition) or simply the *Zhi jing* (Sūtra of Prohibition).
It is also titled *The Sūtra on the Departure of the Bodhisattva* (or simply *The Sūtra on Departure*). Five versions are largely identical, differing only in their separate translations and titles;
this is noted in Baochang’s *Record*. *The Sūtra on the Son of a Good Family*, one fascicle: its initial translation was the same as that produced by Jītamitra and Zhú Nántí.
It appears in the thirty-third section of the *Madhyama Āgama* as a variant translation, according to Zhī Mǐndù.
The *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by Zhu Daozu and Baochang and others, is the third appearance;
it is identical in content to the *Prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* translated by Zhu Fahu, as seen in the *Zhu Daozu lu* and the *Baochang lu*.
The *Daśakuśala-daśākuśala-sūtra* in one fascicle appeared for the first time, as recorded in the *Zhu Daozu Jin lu* and the *Bao... lu*.
The catalog records the following: four sections totaling five fascicles; two sections totaling two fascicles, including the *Śrīkumārabhūta* and others;
and two sections totaling three fascicles, including the *Vidyamāna Mañjuśrī-ratnakośa* and others, which are missing texts.
The śramaṇa Zhī Fǎdù, whose origins are unknown, translated four works,
including the *Śiśupālavadhāna-sūtra*, during the first year of the Yongníng era (the *xīn-yǒu* year) of Emperor Huì’s reign.
Furthermore, according to the catalogs of Sengyou, Changfang, and others:

during the reign of Emperor Hui, the śramaṇa Zhimin-du combined the two versions by Zhi Chen and Zhi Qian with the two versions by Zhu Fahu and Zhu Shulan, making four versions; Changfang’s catalog further added one version by Bai Yan to make five. Now, based on Sengyou’s catalog and the *Hejing ji* (Record of Combined Scriptures), there are only four versions combined, as there is no version by Bai Yan. The *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra* consists of eight fascicles, though Sengyou says it may be five fascicles; it combines three versions: those by Zhi Qian and the two Zhu translators, Zhu Fahu and Zhu Shulan. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* consists of five fascicles.
Since this was neither a separate translation from a Sanskrit original nor does its original text exist, it has been deleted and not included in this catalogue.
The *Time and Non-Time Sūtra* (or simply the *Time Sūtra*), one fascicle, is recorded in the postscript to the canon; this one work in one fascicle currently exists as an extant manuscript.
The śramaṇa Jīvarāja was a man from a foreign land. He translated one scripture,
the *Jie shifei jing* (Sūtra on the Proper and Improper Times).
The postscript states:
"The foreign Dharma Master Yueluoyan held the manuscript in his hand and translated it orally himself."
The Daoist monk Yu Qian of Liangzhou, or perhaps Yu Tian, transcribed this record within the city.
Fang and others all maintain that it is an error to claim that Dharmaprajña translated it;
furthermore, its imperial era remains unknown.
Furthermore, these are appended to the records of the Western Jin dynasty:

the *Bhadrakalpika-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* in one fascicle, and the *Pañca-puṇya-sūtra* in one fascicle—these three works comprise three fascicles, all of which are currently missing. According to the catalogues of Senglang and others, these were translated anonymously during the Western Jin dynasty; they constitute eight works in fifteen fascicles in total.
The two separate catalogs [of Sengyou] both provide single annotations stating that these works appeared during the Yuankang era, though the translators are not explicitly named.
Having examined various catalogs in detail, I have found no definitive evidence;
therefore, these individual items remain distinct cases of lost translations.
Now, having examined the various catalogs and consulted the textual contents of the remaining five sections totaling twelve fascicles,
it is evident that they all have reliable sources and are not translations of lost works.
I shall provide a detailed account of their origins.

They are listed as follows: *The Scripture on the Chapter of Transcending the World*, six fascicles; *The Scripture of the Dragon King Anavatapta*, two fascicles. These two scriptures, which are alternative titles for the *Scripture on the Samādhi of the Broad Manifestation of the Propagation of the Way*, were translated by Dharmarakṣa. *The Scripture of the Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury*, two fascicles—also titled *The Great Vaipulya Scripture on the Subtle Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising*, or simply *The Scripture on the Nature-Arising of the Tathāgata*. This is the "Nature-Arising of the Tathāgata" chapter of the old *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. It was already lost during the Later Han period, yet it has been re-recorded here; this is a grave error. It is now appended to the "Record of Separate Productions. *The Scripture on the Ground of Continuous Liberation and the Pāramitās*, one fascicle; translated by Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty. *The Scripture on the Three Grades of Disciples*, one fascicle—an alternative title for the *Scripture on the Three Grades of Disciples*; translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The following have been newly appended to this record.
*The Sutra of Prince Hehu*, one fascicle; the second [translation], identical in text to the *Sutra of Prince Shuhu*.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one fascicle; the old catalogues call it *Sayun Puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or simply *Puṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is a partial variant translation of the "Jeweled Stupa" and "Devadatta" chapters of the *Lotus Sutra*. *The Sutra of the Alms Bowl*, one fascicle.

One fascicle of a sutra; this is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Raising the Alms Bowl" from the *Puchao jing* (Sutra of Universal Transcendence). Fascicle One. Master Dao’an states it belongs to the Vaipulya section.
The *Bodhisattva Shan jing* (Sutra of the Bodhisattva Śyāma), one fascicle—also called the *Xiaozizi Shan jing* (Sutra of the Filial Son Śyāma) or simply the *Shan jing* (Śyāma Sutra).

Fascicle Two. An alternative translation of the *Changshouwang jing* (Sutra of King Long-life), one fascicle, translated by Fachang. It appears in the second fascicle of the *Liudu ji jing* (Collection of the Six Pāramitās).

*Zhujing* (Sūtra on Abiding), one fascicle; *Xianshui yu jing* (Sūtra of the Simile of Salt Water), one fascicle—the old catalog states this is the *Xianshui poyu jing* (Sūtra of the Simile of Salt Water) from the first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, a different translation;
*Douzhao jing* (Sūtra of Douzhao), one fascicle—appears in the forty-fourth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, a different translation;
*Shewei guowang mengjian shishi jing* (Sūtra of the King of Śrāvastī Dreaming Ten Things), one fascicle—also simply called the *Shimeng jing* (Sūtra of the Ten Dreams).
The *Jiùlù* (Old Catalogue) states that the *Śrāvastī-rāja-daśasvapna-sūtra*, also known as the *Prasenajit-rāja-daśasvapna-sūtra*, is found in the fifty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*;
it is a variant translation. Master Dao’an says it appears in the *Abhidharma-yuyā-sūtra* in one fascicle, also known as the *Yuyā-sūtra*.
Its initial translation was identical in text to the *Aśokadatta-sūtra* and others; it was translated during the Xì period.
*The Sutra of the Son* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sutra on Filial Sons Repaying Kindness*; *The Sutra of Aṭaḥḍakī* (one fascicle);

*The Sutra of King Pūrṇabhadra* (one fascicle); *The Sutra on the Enshrinement and Burial after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sutra of the Bhikṣu Teacher* or *The Sutra of the Teacher Bhikṣu*;
*The Sutra of Hārītī* (one fascicle); *The Sutra of King Brahmadatta* (one fascicle).
*The Sūtra on the Verses on the Extinction of Phenomena Spoken by Kātyāyana*, one fascicle;
alternatively titled *The One Hundred and Twenty Chapters of Verses on the Extinction of Phenomena Spoken by the Buddha’s Messenger, the Bhikṣu Kātyāyana*, or simply *The Verses of Kātyāyana*.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Treatment of the Body*, one fascicle (sometimes without the word "Buddha"); the old catalog states it is the *Sūtra on the Treatment of the Body*, and other records agree that its purport concerns treatment.

One fascicle. The old catalog states it is the *Buddha-zhi-yi jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha Governing the Mind); other records are identical to the above. It currently exists; the following [entries] are missing.

One fascicle of the *Mile danglai sheng jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Future Birth). Its initial appearance was the same text as the *Mi-le lai-shi jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Coming), but it has been lost.
*Li Yue jing* (Sūtra of Li Yue), one fascicle; second edition, identical in substance to the *Yueguang Tongzi jing* (Sūtra of the Youth Candraprabha) but differing in its conclusion.

*Liao ben shengsi jing* (Sūtra on the Clarification of Birth and Death), one fascicle; identical in substance to the *Shèngjī jīng* (Śālistamba Sūtra). *Neizang dafangdeng jing* (Inner Treasury Mahāvaipulya Sūtra), one fascicle;
currently suspected to be the *Fozang dafangdeng jing* (Buddha-treasury Mahāvaipulya Sūtra). *Xiao Ajieshi jing* (Minor Ajaśatru Sūtra), one fascicle. *Xiao Xulai jing* (Minor Sūryodana Sūtra).
*Ekottarika-sūtra*, one fascicle. Master An said it was extracted from the Vaipulya section; today it is suspected to be the *Ānanda-ekottarika-sūtra*.

*Maitreya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Master An said it was extracted from the Madhyama Āgama. *Dhūmāyana-sūtra*, one fascicle. Master An said it was extracted from the Madhyama Āgama. *Saptavastuka-sūtra*, one fascicle.
Master An said it was extracted from the Madhyama Āgama. *Rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra*, one fascicle. Master An said it was extracted from the Madhyama Āgama.
*Ura-sūtra*, one fascicle; Master An states it was translated from the *Ānanda-saṃyukta-āgama*. *Huanyu-jing* (Sūtra on Joy), one fascicle;

the *Fajing lu* states it is called *Quanyu* and was translated from the twenty-second chapter of the *Madhyama-āgama*. *Shisi-jing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Kinds of Birth and Death), one fascicle; I now suspect this is the *Shengsi-jing* (Sūtra on Birth and Death) in twelve sections.
*Qifu-jing* (Sūtra on the Seven Wives), one fascicle. *Ananbindi sishi shi-jing* (Sūtra on Ānanda-Binduka’s Four Seasonal Offerings), one fascicle.
The old catalog states: *Ānanda-bhṛgu-cāturmāsa-dāna-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Saptaratha-sūtra*, one fascicle.
Now it is suspected that this refers to the *Saptaratha-upamā-sūtra* from the *Madhyama-āgama*. *Samudra-aṣṭa-dharma-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Duskarādi-prathama-sūtra*, one fascicle. The old catalog states: *Ānanda-kāśyapa-pratyeka-prathama-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Vailopa-sūtra*, one fascicle.
The *Jiulù* (Old Catalogue) states: *Wéiliúwáng jīnglǐ jiānán jīng* (One Scroll), *Jiālǐduōwáng jīng* (One Scroll), and *Fànzhì shásūn jīng* (One Scroll).
The *Gǔlù* (Ancient Catalogue) states: *Fànzhì ànxùn jīng*, *Bōdáwáng jīng* (One Scroll), *Bēixīnyìyì jīng* (One Scroll), *Qùdùshìdào jīng* (One Scroll), and *Chángzhě wēishì* [jīng] (One Scroll).
*Sūtra* in one fascicle; *Dhī-ṭīkā-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Devadatta-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Haridra-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Pakṣa-sūtra* in one fascicle;
*Saptadhā-bhāga-śarīra-sūtra* in one fascicle (alternatively titled *Vibhakta-kāya-pratipatti-vinaya* in one fascicle);
*Siddham-mu* in two fascicles; *Kalyāṇa-dharma-pratyaya* in one fascicle; *Mukha-paramparā-kalpa-utpāda-nirodha* in one fascicle; *Ghaṇṭā-koṭana*.
Dharma: one fascicle. The above comprises fifty-five works in fifty-six fascicles. *Zhìyì jīng* (Sūtra on Governing the Mind):
the first nineteen works in nineteen fascicles are extant; the latter thirty-six works in thirty-seven fascicles are missing.
Sengyou’s Record of the Liang states:
Among the scriptures whose translators were lost in Master Dao’an’s catalog, only those recorded by Sengyou—such as those by [Dao]fang and others—are preserved, while all others are missing.
Sengyou records that there were a total of one hundred and forty-two scriptures whose translators were lost according to Master Dao’an’s catalog.
Now, having examined the various catalogs regarding the remaining eighty-seven works, it is found that most bear the names of their translators;
some are separate excerpts from sutras or biographies composed by individuals.
Since these have reliable sources, they have been deleted and not included here.
Since Seng'an does not specify the era,
we shall for now place this work at the end of the Jin dynasty.
Together with the three previously mentioned lost translations from earlier periods, there are now three works in three fascicles.
In total, there are fifty-eight sections comprising fifty-nine fascicles.
It is said that these were all lost to the source during the Western Jin dynasty.
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Fascicle Two, General Catalogue Part Two.
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Scroll Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu year.
Part Three: General Compendium of the Records of the Multitude of Scriptures, Upper Part, Section Three.
The Eastern Jin (Dōngjìn) was ruled by the Sima clan with its capital at Jiankang (Jiānkāng), also known as the Southern Jin (Nányìn).
It spanned from the first year of the Jiānwǔ era of Emperor Yuán, the *dingchū* year, until the second year of the Yuánxī era of Emperor Gōng, the *gēngshēn* year.
In total, there were eleven emperors over a period of one hundred and four years.
Sixteen individuals, both ordained and lay,
translated sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, as well as various newly and formerly collected scriptures of unknown translators.

In total, there are one hundred and sixty-eight sections comprising four hundred and sixty-eight fascicles; of these, eighty-five sections comprising three hundred and thirty-six fascicles are extant, while eighty-three sections comprising one hundred and thirty-two fascicles are missing.
The *Three Collections of Fourteen Volumes of Sūtras* by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Śrīmitra;
the *Two Collections of Seven Volumes of Sūtras* by the śramaṇa Zhi Daogen; the *Sixty-one Collections of Sixty-three Volumes of Sūtras* by the śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan;
and the *Five Collections of One Hundred and Eighteen Volumes of the Vinaya-piṭaka* by the śramaṇa Gautama Saṃghadeva.
*Jinglun jiaofa* (Sūtra-śāstra Instructional Methods) by the śramaṇa Kālodaka: one fascicle; *Xian sheng ji* (Collection of Worthies and Sages) by the śramaṇa Kang Daohuo:
three fascicles; various sūtras by the śramaṇa Buddhabhadra: thirteen works totaling one hundred twenty-five fascicles;
*Jinglü lunji* (Collection of Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras) by the śramaṇa Dharma: two fascicles; *Lüyao* (Essentials of the Vinaya).
The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Matters) in two sections and five fascicles by Upagupta;

the collection of sūtras, precepts, and treatises in seven sections and twenty-six fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Faxian; the sūtras in thirty-three sections and forty-five fascicles by the śramaṇa Jītamitra;
the sūtras in two sections and five fascicles by the layman Zhu Nanti; and the work in one section and one fascicle by the śramaṇa Zhu Fali.
The *Sāṃghika Śramaṇa Shi Song* compiled three works in three fascicles; the *Śramaṇa Shi Tui* compiled one work in one fascicle;

the *Śramaṇa Shi Fayong* compiled one work in one fascicle; and forty new and old works by various anonymous translators totaling forty-eight fascicles, consisting of two works in three fascicles from the old collection and thirty-eight works in forty-five fascicles from the new collection.
*The Great Consecration Sūtra*, twelve fascicles (or nine fascicles according to catalogs that omit the character "Great"; details unknown). Fang states it was seen in the *Zalu*.
*The Sūtra of the Divine Incantations of the Great Peacock King*, one fascicle; seen in the catalogs of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou.
Initially, there was *The Sūtra of Miscellaneous Divine Incantations of the Peacock King*, one fascicle; seen in the catalogs of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou.

Record of the Second Section: The three parts above comprise fourteen fascicles; the first part consists of twelve fascicles and is extant, while the latter two parts consist of two fascicles and are missing.
[Compiled by] the Śramaṇa Śrīmitra.
Luo Jin’s words were auspicious.
His friend was the son of a Western Region king who,
being destined to inherit the throne, had instead yielded the kingdom to his younger brother.
An-quai was a descendant of Taibo.
Having subsequently awakened his mind through divine inspiration, he became a śramaṇa.
Tanmi possessed a lofty and brilliant natural disposition, and his spirit and bearing were transcendent.
If he were confronted with such things directly, they would immediately manifest before him;
how much more so for those who were clever, eloquent, and awakened by his words?
He first arrived in this land during the Yongjia era of the Western Jin dynasty.
He subsequently crossed the river to the left bank and stayed at Jianchu Monastery.
When Prime Minister Wang Dao saw him once, he marveled at him,
considering him one of his own kind.
For this reason, their names became renowned:
Taiwei Yu Yuangui and Guanglu Zhou Borin.
Xie Youyu, Grand Master of Ceremonies,
and Huan Moulun, Minister of Justice,
were both renowned scholars of their generation.
Having seen him, he sighed repeatedly throughout the entire day;
opening his breast, he established a profound bond of affinity.
Dao once went to visit Tanmi.
Huiyi untied his sash and lay prostrate, yet he understood the words with divine insight.
At that time, Bian Wangzhi, the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, was also on friendly terms with Huiyi; shortly thereafter, Wangzhi arrived.
Huiyi then adjusted his collar, composed his countenance, and sat upright to face him.
Someone asked him the reason for this,
and Mi replied,
"The Prince’s character and conduct are such that he expects others to be like himself."
"Xuanbiao Bian’s command of standards and his method of examining things were precisely what made it so. Thereupon,
the gentlemen sighed in admiration that his spirit was so pervasive and vigorous, and that everything had found its proper place."
The Grand Master of Justice Huan once wished to compose a preface for the *Mì* (Honey),
but after a long time he had not succeeded.
Some have said:
"Śrīmitra may truly be called outstanding and brilliant.
Thereupon, Huan sighed with deep admiration, regarding him as the ultimate pinnacle of those who set forth titles.
At that time, the Great General Wang Chuchong was in the South;
having heard that the various lords of the Zhou dynasty all held him in high esteem, he too came to value him.
He suspected that he had lost his way,
but upon seeing the honey himself, he was filled with joy and rushed forward; once there,
he offered his devotion with complete sincerity.
The Prince once said to Mi,
"In foreign lands, there is only you as a ruler.
Mi smiled and replied:
"If it had been me who was like you gentlemen today, how could I have remained here?
At that time, he considered this a clever retort.
By nature, Mi was lofty and simple, and he did not learn the Jin language.
Whenever I engaged in discourse with these gentlemen,
although it was conducted through interpreters,
they grasped the spirit and understood the meaning, conveying the full depth of what was expressed.
He considered himself to be naturally gifted and transcendent, beyond the comprehension of ordinary people.
Mi was skilled at maintaining incantations and rituals;
whatever he directed toward always proved effective.
The people of that time called him the Dharma Master of the High Seat (*Gaozuo Fashi*).
During the reign of Emperor Yuan, he translated three scriptures, including the *Abhiṣeka-sūtra*.
He also taught his disciple Molixun the high-pitched chanting of Sanskrit hymns (*brahmaghoṣa*).
The oral transmission has been passed down to the present day.
At over eighty years of age, he passed away during the Xiankang era;
when the eminent officials heard of it, they mourned him with such deep sorrow that their tears flowed.
Huiyi was constantly practicing *dhūta* austerities east of Shizigang.
Having passed away, he was buried here because Emperor Cheng admired his character.
He established a monastery at Shu-chaseng-kuo.
Later, there was a śramaṇa from Guanyou who came to travel in Jiankang.
He then established a monastery on the site of the tomb.
Xie Kun of Chen County assisted in completing this undertaking;
to commemorate these past events, it was still called Gaozuo Monastery.

*The Sutra on the Attainment of Fruition by the Bodhisattvas of the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya*, two fascicles; translated during the Taikang era, the second translation, which is largely identical with slight variations to the version translated by Zhi Chen of Han, as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*. *The Vaipulya Lotus Sutra*, five fascicles; translated in the first year of the Xiankang era, as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*. This is the fourth appearance [of this text] and is the same original as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa. The above two works comprise seven fascicles in total; the original manuscripts for both are currently missing.
The śramaṇa Zhidao’gen traveled through various regions, cultivating the Way and benefiting sentient beings.

In the first year of Emperor Cheng’s Xiankang era, the year of Yiwu (365 CE), he translated two sections of the *Akṣobhyavyūha-sūtra* and other scriptures. The catalogs of Changfang and others all state that the *Akṣobhya-buddha-sūtra* was translated during the Taikang era. However, the Taikang era belonged to the reign of Emperor Wu of the Western Jin, which was nearly sixty years prior to the Xiankang era; it is unlikely that the same person could have produced scriptures in both reigns across such a vast interval of time. This must be a scribal error, and it is most likely that [the original date] was Xiankang.
*The Scripture on the Prediction Bestowed upon King Utpalavaktra for Plucking Lotus Flowers*, one fascicle;

also simply titled *The Scripture on King Utpalavaktra*, second translation, identical in origin to the *Scripture on the Prediction Bestowed upon King Ajātaśatru*. *The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī-bhājana*, one fascicle;
also called *The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī-mantra of the Bhājana*, second translation, identical in origin to the *Scripture on the Divine Mantra of the Dharapada* and others.
The *Benfang Lu* (Record of the Main Office) states that apart from the *Dalinbo Jing*, there additionally exists the *Chiju Shenzhou Jing*, which is incorrect.
There is also the one-fascicle *Maniluo Dan Jing*, also called the *Maniluo Dan Shenzhou Jing*. There is also the one-fascicle *Xuanshi Batuo Suoshuo Shenzhou Jing*;
the record states that the word "phantom" (*huàn*) is not present in the text spoken by Batuo, though it may be written as "lame" (*pó*), and is also called "wave" (*bō*).

The *Tuogulü* states: the *Huàn wáng fántuó jīng* (Sūtra on King Bhaṭṭa) and the *Jìzhì guǒ jīng* (Sūtra on the Fruits of the Śramaṇa), one fascicle each, are from the seventeenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* as alternative translations;

the *Tiěchéng nílí jīng* (Sūtra of the Iron City Hell), one fascicle, is from the twelfth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, being the same text as the *Wǔtiānshǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Five Divine Messengers);
the *Ānòufēng jīng* (Sūtra of the Anupama Wind), one fascicle, is the same as the *Yányìcì*. These are from the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Included herein is the *Ekottarika-āgama* version, the *Brahmacārin Āḷāra Questions the Honored One on Lineage Sūtra* (1 fascicle), also known as the *Āṣāḍha*;
it is a variant translation of the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama-āgama*.
Also included is the *Niraya Sūtra* (1 fascicle), also known as the *Madhyama-āgama Niraya Sūtra*; it is a variant translation of the fifty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama-āgama*.
*Śīlaguṇagandha-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Śīlaguṇa-sūtra*; translated from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
*Caturniraya-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Caturmahānirayabhavana*; recorded in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record) with the note that Sengyou states it is of lost translation;
translated from the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*. Alternative translation by King Pili-xian.
*The Ten Dreams of the Bhikṣuṇī*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Xianni*. Translated from the fifty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
*The Sūtra on Being Drifted by Water Froth*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on the Great Mass of Froth in a River*, or *The Parable of the Froth*.
This is the same text as the *Parable of the Five Aggregates*, translated from the tenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*Yujie jing* (The Scripture on Yujie), one fascicle; also known as *Jiangzhe yi fo shuo zifu wujing jing* (The Scripture on the Elder Visiting the Buddha to Speak of His Daughter-in-law’s Lack of Reverence) or *Yujie nü jing* (The Scripture on the Woman Yujie).
Second translation; same text as the *Asoka jing*. *Wuku zhangju jing* (The Scripture on the Five Sufferings and Their Verses), one fascicle; first translation;
also known as *Zhutian wuku jing* (The Scripture on the Five Sufferings of the Various Heavens), or *Wudao zhangju jing* (The Scripture on the Verses of the Five Realms). First translation.

*Fuchuzuigaiyulefofajing* (Sutra on Floating Away the Coverings of Sin and Delighting in the Buddha-Dharma), one fascicle; also called *Zaiai* (Self-Love) Sutra, or *Zaiai-buji'aijing* (Sutra on Self-Love and Non-Self-Love).
Fáng says he saw it in the Old Catalogue. *Zhongxinjing* (Sutra of the Central Mind), one fascicle; also called *Zhongxinzhengxingjing* (Sutra on the Correct Practice of the Central Mind).

The Old Catalogue calls it *Dazhongxinjing* (Great Central Mind Sutra) or *Xiaozhongxinjing* (Small Central Mind Sutra). Fáng’s catalogue states it is extracted from the *Liudujijing* (Collection of the Six Pāramitās). Now [extant].

*Jian wujian zhengjing* (Examination of Non-Viewing of the True Sutra), one fascicle; also known as *Shengsi bianshi jing* (Sutra on the Transformation of Consciousness in Birth and Death); *Dayu shi jing* (Sutra on the Matter of the Great Fish), one fascicle;
*Anan qimen jing* (Sutra of Ānanda’s Seven Dreams), one fascicle—or simply called *Qimen jing* (Sutra of the Seven Dreams);

*He diao anan jing* (Sutra of the Hārītī Anāgāmin), one fascicle—also known as *He diao*, or written with the character "ke"; *Xin sui jing* (Sutra of the New Year), one fascicle; *Biqiu ting shi jing* (Sutra on the Bhikṣu Hearing of Almsgiving), one fascicle.
Volume One: The Sūtra on Listening to the Bhikṣu’s Teaching of Alms; The Sūtra on Mahākāśyapa Attending the Buddha at His Parinirvāṇa. One scroll.
Also titled *The Sūtra on Kāśyapa Attending the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*. The first part exists as preserved above; the following is missing.
*Vatsa-sūtra*, one fascicle—also called *Vatsaputra-sūtra*; third translation, same text as the *Kṣīraprabhā-sūtra*. *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*, one fascicle;
third translation, same text as that translated by Ki-yǒu (Kumārajīva). *Saptabuddha-parigṛhīta-tailamantra-sūtra*, one fascicle;
listed twice in Sengyou’s *Chū sānzàng jìlù*, once under two different titles. One version states it is a distinct text.
*The Scripture on the Vow-Mantra of the Mother of the Great Deity*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Divine Mantra of the Dharma-Vow of Eran*, one fascicle;
*The Scripture on the Divine Mantra for Resolving the Calamity of the Sun*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Divine Mantra of the Six Deities’ Names*, one fascicle;
*The Scripture on the Divine Mantra of Tanthila’s Sesame Oil*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Sesame Oil Mantra*, one fascicle; *The Divine Mantra of Maṇiroha*, according to the catalog.

*Mo jing* (Māṇavikā Sūtra), one fascicle; *Yiwang weilouyan shenzhou jing* (Sūtra of the Divine Incantation of the Physician King Vairocana), one fascicle—also known as the *Anan suowen yiwang weilouyan shenzhou jing*;

*Longwang zhushuyu jing* (Sūtra of the Dragon Kings’ Incantation for Bathing with Water), one fascicle; *Shiba longwang shenzhou jing* (Sūtra of the Divine Incantations of the Eighteen Dragon Kings), one fascicle;

*Qingyu zhou jing* (Sūtra of the Incantation for Requesting Rain), one fascicle; *Zhiyu zhou jing* (Sūtra of the Incantation for Stopping Rain), one fascicle; *Qinshui jing* (Sūtra on the Offering of Water).
One fascicle of the *Māyākāra-Acirajñāna-mantra-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Jala-mantra-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Bhaiṣajya-mantra-sūtra*;
one fascicle of the *Viṣa-mantra-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Kāla-vyādhi-mantra-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Bāla-mantra-sūtra*; and one fascicle of the *Danta-mantra-sūtra*.
[These] were recorded again in the *Yù Shī-yì-lù* (Record of Translations by Unknown Persons) as one additional text with the same title, though its colophon states it is different.
*Benyi yunzhong chishi zhouyaya tongjing* (The Sutra on the Incantation for Toothache by the One Who Originally Spoke of Insects and Teeth), one fascicle; Yu states it is of lost translation.

Another copy is recorded with the same title as this, though titled *Yiben* (Alternative Version), or alternatively as *Chitong zhoutongjing* (Sutra of the Incantation for Toothache and Eyeache), one fascicle, and *Wuyan wenjing* (Sutra of the Text on the Five Eyes), one fascicle;
these are now suspected to be the "Method for Seeking the Five Eyes" produced by Nie Daozhen.
*The Text on the Precepts for Upāsakas and Upāsikās Who Have Renounced Desire through Alternative Names*, one fascicle; also known as *The Text on the Twenty-two Precepts of Complete Practice*.
*Sutra on the Retribution of Karmic Offenses*, one fascicle; same text as the *Sutra on the Teaching and Transformation of the Hell of Karmic Retribution for Offenses*, second edition.
*Sutra of the Eight Teachers*, one fascicle; second edition. *Sutra of King Piṇḍola’s Five Vows*, one fascicle; second edition.
Volume One: The *Puṣya-rāja-sūtra*, Second Edition. The *Arthavargīya-sūtra* in two volumes; Fang [Yun] states it is seen in the *Wu-lu* (Records of Wu) and is also called a separate edition.
Second Edition: The *Daśakuśala-daśākuśala-sūtra* in one volume; the second translation; the *Wu-lu* states it is a separate edition.
Master An states it is extracted from the *Abhidharma-dhyāna-prakriyā-sūtra*. The *Brahmā-deva-gaṇanā-śāstra* in one volume.
One fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Affairs of the Various Heavens* (formerly recorded as the *Sūtra on the Various Heavens and Earths*); one fascicle of the *Śāriputra-vinaya Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra*;
and one fascicle [of the *Prātimokṣa*] compiled in the sixth year of the Taiyuan era by the three masters Saṃghapure, Dharmadhara, and Zhu Sengshu.
This single fascicle is seen in Baochang’s catalogue as the second edition of the three-part collection of the three hundred and sixty precepts.
Preface to the *Héyì* (Combined and Differentiated) in two fascicles, with the title augmented by the characters "Dàbǐqū" (Great Bhikṣu).
On the twentieth day of the sixth month in the sixth year of the Tàiyuán era, at Xiè Zhèn-xī Temple, the assembly combined [the texts] and examined them with great care.

Regarding the old catalogs and the *Bǎochàng lù*, the sixty-one works totaling sixty-three fascicles on the right—including the twenty-four works totaling twenty-four fascicles currently extant under the heading "The Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa"—are as follows.
The *Vatsa-sūtra* (犢牛經), parts 37–39 in three volumes; these texts are missing.
Translated by the śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan (竺曇無蘭), which in Jin Chinese means Fǎzhèng (法正).
A man from the Western Regions,
he arrived at the capital of Yang during the sixth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu, the *xin-si* year, and remained until the twentieth year,
the *yi-wei* year. During this time, at Xie Zhenxi Temple in Yangdu, he translated sixty-one scriptures, including the *Fajing jing*, the *Weiwang jing*, and others.
I have consulted the *Chángfáng lù*.
Furthermore, the *Chángfáng* and other catalogs list forty-eight additional scriptures,
which are likewise said to have been translated by Fǎzhèng.
Since these are all excerpts from separate translations or are of doubtful authenticity and spurious,
they have all been deleted.

As described below, the *Jiuhu shenming jing* (Sūtra on Saving and Protecting Life) also states: "The *Jiuhu shenming ji renbing kuyi jing* (Sūtra on Saving and Protecting Life and Relieving Humans from the Calamities of Illness) was included in the Zhou catalog among the authentic scriptures;

however, the old catalogs state it is spurious. Following the old tradition, it is now included here. The various devas question the Tathāgata regarding the prohibitions that must not be transgressed."

The *Sīsi Jing* (Scripture on Contemplation) and the *Jian Shui Shijie Jing* (Scripture on Seeing the Water World)—these two scriptures are both from the *Daji Longwang Jueyuan Wulong Shenzhou Jing* (Great Assembly Scripture on the Dragon King’s Vow and the Five Dragon Deity Spells) and the *Dajiangjun Shenzhou Jing* (Scripture on the Great General’s Divine Spells). The aforementioned two scriptures are also found in the *Guanjing Wuwu Jing* (Scripture on the Consecration and Non-Ego).

They appear in the *Puchao Jing* (Scripture of Universal Transcendence) and the *Milan Jing* (Scripture of Milinda), the latter also written as *Milian*, and is also called King Milinda of the Heaven.
The *Ānanda-nianmi-jing*, the *Milan-jing*, and other such scriptures—these three sutras—are all included [in the canon].

The *Xiánjié qiānfó míngjīng* (Sutra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa) states in its preface: "The *Xiánjié jīng* (Sutra of the Bhadrakalpa) speaks of two thousand one hundred *pāramitās*, with Krakucchanda Buddha as the foremost.
This *Qiānfó míng* (Names of the Thousand Buddhas) has a separate translation in which Kanakamuni Buddha is [placed first].
Regarding the *Saptatriṃśat-pakṣa-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment), Master Dao’an stated it was translated from the Vinaya scriptures.
Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Chu sanzang jiji*) records that it was compiled in the sixth month of the year of Bingshen (the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty) at Xie Zhenxi Temple.
It also includes the *Trāyastriṃśa-deva-vana-vihāra-sūtra*, the *Bhikṣu-pañca-dharma-niraya-praveśa-sūtra*, and the *Śaikṣaka-vikṣipta-citta-sūtra*.
The three preceding sūtras are from the *Ekottarika Āgama*: (1) "The Sūtra on the Great Heat Hell Spoken by the Buddha for the Bhikṣus";
(2) "The Sūtra on Śakra Devānām-indra Visiting Maudgalyāyana and Emitting Light"; (3) "The Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Seeing a Being of Gigantic Stature with Burning Iron Wrapped Around Its Body";
(4) "The Sūtra on Seeing a Being Whose Entire Body Was Coated with Excrement"; and (5) "The Sūtra on a Being with an Iron Mill atop Its Head, Blazing with Intense Fire."
However, there are the *Sūtra on the Śyena Bird*, the *Sūtra on Being Seized by a Hawk*, the *Sūtra on the Ten Dharmas Accomplishing Evil Karma and Entering Hell*, the *Sūtra on the Snake’s Gait*,
the *Sūtra on a Bhikṣu Bathing and Encountering a Devaputra Emitting Light*, the *Sūtra on the Heavens Wishing to Fight with the Asuras*, the *Sūtra on Śakra Devendra Receiving the Precepts*,
the *Sūtra on a Bhikṣu Asking the Buddha about the Causes and Conditions of Śakra Devendra*, and the *Sūtra on the Four Heavenly Kings*.
The *Rājā Loka-cārikā Sūtra*, the *Buddha-dṛṣṭa-brahmottara-śīrṣa Sūtra*, the *Śakra-maitracitta-saṃgrāma-jaya Sūtra*,
the *Devatā-ratna-pratiṣedha Sūtra*, the *Aśoka-rāja-mārgadruma-pūjā Sūtra*, the *Sākṣāt-kriyā-pravartana Sūtra*, the *Śīla-saṃprayukta-dharma Sūtra*,
and the *Dhyāna-paripūrṇa Sūtra*— these twenty sūtras, beginning with those spoken by the Buddha for the bhikṣus, are all extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The *Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra*, the *Kūrma-markaṭa-sūtra*, the *Vetāla-śuka-kāka-sūtra* (or the *Śakuni-sūtra*), the *Śrāvaka-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Khara-uṣṭra-sūtra*,
the *Kauśala-deśa-śakuni-rāja-sūtra* (or the version without "deśa"), the *Mayūra-sūtra*, and the *Dampati-sūtra*— these eight sūtras, beginning with the *Āṭānāṭīya*,
are all contained within the *Udāna-varga*. Furthermore, the *Go-sahasra-sūtra* is included in the *Caryā-piṭaka*.
The *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra*, the *Hastināga-sūtra*, and the *Go-yūtha-sūtra*—these three sūtras appear together in the *Chuyao jing*.
The *Nāraka-sattva-parasparopaghāta-sūtra* appears in the *Xiuxing daodi jing*.

The two sūtras concerning the "Red-beaked Crow" (*Raktatuṇḍa-kāka*) and the "Ānanda-unnāla-mātṛ-sūtra" appear in the *Zapiyu jing*. This concludes the second [fascicle] of the sixty-fascicle *Madhyama Āgama*.

The translation was produced in fifty-eight fascicles; it began on the tenth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Long’an era at Dongting Temple and was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month of the second year. This is the same text as that translated by Dharmānanda.
The śramaṇa Doci acted as the scribe for the oral transmission. This is seen in Daozu’s Record. The *Ekottarika Āgama* in fifty-one fascicles is the second translation.
In the first month of the first year of the Long’an era, [this work] was brought out; it differs slightly from that by Nandi. Zhu Daozu acted as the scribe.
It is not fixed at either forty-two or thirty-three fascicles, though there are also versions consisting of sixty fascicles, as seen in the records of Zhu Daozu and Baochang.
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* consists of four fascicles; some call it the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. The author is the Venerable [Dharmaśreṣṭhin].
Dharmottara composed [this work]; in the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era, it was translated at Mount Lu by Dharma Master Huiyuan, with Daozi receiving the oral transmission.
It is recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue). The *Dharmapada-śāstra* in two fascicles was also produced for Dharma Master Huiyuan at Mount Lu in the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era;
this second translation is largely identical to that by Nandimitra, differing only slightly, though some versions consist of three fascicles.

The *Bielu* (Separate Catalog) states there is one fascicle; alternatively, it is simply called the *Sanfadu wulun* (Treatise on the Three Dharmas of Measurement), sometimes omitting the character "lun" (treatise) or titled as a *jinglun* (sutra-treatise);
see Sengyou’s catalog. The *Jiaoshou biquni fa* (Method for Instructing Bhikṣuṇīs) is one fascicle; Faxiang says it is seen in the *Bielu*, and it is also said to have been produced at Mount Lu.
Thus, these five works comprise one hundred and eighteen fascicles in total; the first four works comprise one hundred and seventeen fascicles in their original form.
The latter one-volume version is missing.
The śramaṇa Gautama Saṃghadeva— “Saṃghadeva” meaning “Multitude of Gods” (Zhòngtiān) in the Jin language— ...
Some call him Tihe;
this is due to a corruption of the pronunciation.
He was a native of Kaśmīra.
Entering the Path to study, he traveled far to seek out an enlightened master.
His learning encompassed the Tripiṭaka, which he had mastered and committed extensively to memory;
he was particularly proficient in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, penetrating its most subtle nuances.
He constantly recited the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*, sighing over and savoring its meaning day and night,
regarding it as the treasury of the Way.
He was a man of brilliant character and profound discernment.
His deportment was mild and respectful;
he was dedicated to instructing others with sincere diligence.
During the Jianyuan era of the Fu Qin dynasty, he came to Chang’an to propagate the teachings of the Dharma.
The two sections of his translated treatises are fully recorded in the *Qin lu*. Later,
during the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era (the *xinmao* year) of the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to propagate the teachings in the region south of the Yangtze River.
Previously, Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu had been devotedly diligent in the sublime scriptures,
extensively collecting the treasury of the sutras;
with an open mind and a seat prepared for guests, he looked out in expectation for eminent visitors from afar.
Upon hearing that he had arrived, [the Emperor] immediately invited him to Mount Lu.
In that same year, he requested [Vasubandhu] to translate the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*.
Vasubandhu then, at the Prajñā Terrace, [began his work].
Holding the Sanskrit text in his hand,
he proclaimed the language of Jin orally;
he eliminated floridities while preserving the substance, striving to exhaust the fundamental meaning.
What is transmitted today is likely its text.
In the first year of the Long’an era of Emperor An’s reign, the year Dingyou,
he came to travel in Jiankang.
Among the princes and dukes of the Jin dynasty, as well as the eminent men of refined culture, there were none who did not attend his gatherings and pay him their respects.

At that time, the Minister of the Household and Commander of the Eastern Army, Marquis of Dongting, Wang Xun of Langya—according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, the *Record of Sengyou*, and the *Record of Changfang*—stated that Wang Xun’s preface to the *Zhonghan jing* was actually written by Wang Yuanlin; Yuanlin was likely a courtesy name for Xun. He possessed refined faith and wisdom, and he upheld the True Dharma.
He established a vihāra and widely invited a multitude of students.
Once Deva arrived,
Sengxun immediately extended an invitation to him.
He continued to lecture on the Abhidharma in that residence;
eminent monks gathered there in great numbers.
As for Deva’s doctrinal principles, they were refined and his phrasing was clear and analytical, as he expounded upon the profound depths of the meaning.
The assembly was all delighted and attained awakening.
That winter, Sengxun gathered more than forty śramaṇas learned in doctrine, including Shi Huichi and others,
and again invited Vasubandhu.
In the translations produced at that monastery, two Āgamas were added;
the Kapiśa śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa held the Sanskrit manuscripts,
while Deva translated them into the language of Jin.
It was only completed by the following summer.
The śramaṇa Daoci of Yuzhou received the oral dictation,
while Li Baotang and Hua of the Wu region transcribed it together.
In both Lushan and Jiankang,
Deva translated five sections totaling one hundred and eighteen fascicles.
Having traveled extensively among both Chinese and foreign lands, he was thoroughly conversant with their customs.
He was composed and quick-witted,
skilled in conversation and laughter;
his reputation for spiritual transformation was heard everywhere.
His final whereabouts are unknown.

One fascicle of the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra* (Twelve Wanderings Sutra), the second translation, differs slightly from that translated by Kang Senghui; this is noted in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* and Baochang’s *Catalogue*. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, its manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Kālodāyin— translated into Chinese as Shishui (Time-Water)—
was a man from the Western Regions.
Hongyu was a man of skillful means who traveled through various kingdoms while cherishing the Way.
In the seventeenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu, the Renchen year,
he translated the *Dvādaśavyākaraṇa-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Twelve Wanderings), one fascicle.

*Yìyì jīng* (Scripture on Increasing the Intention), three fascicles; the second instance of its appearance. According to *Zhū Dàozǔ’s Jìnshì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty), it was in two fascicles according to *Zhú Shíxíng’s Hānlù* (Han Records), with the translator not being specified. This one work in three fascicles is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Kang Daohe possessed the dignity of moral virtue and served as a model for all beings.
In the Jingshen year of the twenty-first year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu (396 CE),
he translated one scripture, the *Yiyi jing* (Scripture on Increasing the Meaning),
in sixty fascicles. Originally, it was first produced as fifty fascicles, which were later divided by subsequent generations.
The śramaṇa Zhīfǎlǐng obtained the Sanskrit original from Khotan. On the tenth day of the third month in the fourteenth year of the Yànxí era, he translated it at Dàoqiáng Temple;
it was completed on the tenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Yuánxī era. Fǎyè acted as the scribe.
It is recorded in the two catalogs by Sēnzuò and Wǎngyòu. There is one fascicle of the *Sūtra of Holding the Door to the Infinite Emanations*, also known as the *New Mìmì*.
The *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* translated at Mount Lu is the fifth appearance; it is identical in its original text to the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* translated by Zhi Qian.
This is seen in the two catalogs of Sengzhuo and Fajing; the separate entry for the *New Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in the catalog of Daoxuan and others is an error.
The *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, one fascicle—also simply called the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*—is the third appearance; [translated] in the Yuan [era].

In the second year of the Xihé era, at Daochang Monastery, he translated the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra* (also known as the *Guanfo sanmei jing*) in ten fascicles—or, according to some accounts, eight fascicles.
This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi zalu* and Sengyou’s catalog. It was also produced during the Song dynasty; furthermore, he translated four fascicles of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
It consists of ten fascicles, though some say thirty; the Sanskrit original was brought from the kingdom of Magadha by Faxian.
In the eleventh month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era, it was translated at Douchang Temple together with Faxian, as recorded in the catalogue of Zhu Daozu.

Because the [catalogue of] Sengyou is based on the record of Faxian, it states that they translated it together. There is also one fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣu-śīla-mūla*, which is also called the *Maha*... [text truncated].
The second part of the *Mahāsāṃghika-śīla-sūtra* was produced at Daochang Monastery; this is recorded in Baochang’s catalogue.
Sengyou is included in Faxian’s catalogue; both Sengyou and Juexian jointly produced these works, which are cross-referenced in both records.
Furthermore, two fascicles of the *Dharmatrāta-dhyāna-sūtra*—also titled *Yugacchāra-bhūmi*, translated as "The Stages of Cultivation"—were produced at Mount Lu.
The *Aśubhabhāvanāsūtra* (also titled the *Sādhanopāyabhāvanāsūtra*). Sengyou states that this *Bhāvanāsūtra-sādhanopāya* consists of seventeen chapters;

it is listed in Sengyou’s catalogue. The *Mañjuśrīpraṇidhānasūtra*, one fascicle—sometimes with the character "gāthā" added [as *Mañjuśrīpraṇidhānagāthāsūtra*]—was translated at Douchang Temple in the second year of the Yuanxi era.
It appears in both Sengyou’s and Baochang’s catalogues following the aforementioned sutra.
The record states that when the fourfold assembly of foreign lands pays homage to the Buddha, they frequently recite this sutra to make vows and seek the Buddha-way.
The *New Sutra of Immeasurable Life* in two fascicles was translated at Daochang Temple in the second year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty;
it appears in the records of Sengyou and Baochang as the eighth translation, which is identical to those produced by An Shigao, Zhi Qian, Zhi Chen, and Seng Kai.

*The Sutra on the Original Vows and Deeds of the Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle (also simply titled *The Sutra on Original Deeds*), found in the *Jingxing pin* (Chapter on Pure Conduct) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
noted in the catalogs of Sengyou and Daofang; included in the Great Zhou Canon, now missing, yet preserved here.
*Sutra on the Six Pāramitās*, one fascicle; noted in the catalogs of Sengyou and Daofang. *Treatise on the Expedient Mind*, one fascicle; [the above] together [with the previous].

The *Fayeyu* (Record of the Propagation of the Dharma) appears in the *Chūsōden* (Biographies of Eminent Monks). It first appeared as the four-fascicle *Kokon igyō kyō* (Sutra on Past Causes and Effects);
Fang states it is seen in the fifth volume of the *Betsuroku* (Separate Record). To the right, these thirteen works comprise one hundred twenty-five fascicles.

Under the heading *Monjushihon* (Vows of Mañjuśrī), eight works comprise one hundred sixteen fascicles; these are currently extant. Under the heading *Muryōju* (Amitāyus), five works comprise nine fascicles; these are missing.
The original [text] was by the śramaṇa Buddhabhadra,
which in the Jin language means "Awakened Virtue."
His original surname was Śākya;
he was a native of Kapilavastu and a descendant of King Amṛtodana.
His grandfather, Dharmadeva— translated into Chinese as Fātian— once traveled for trade in Northern India and settled there.
His father, Dharmasūrya— translated into Chinese as Fārì— died in his youth.
Xian was orphaned at the age of three.
After living with his mother for five years,
he lost her as well and was raised by his maternal relatives.
His great-uncle Kumāralīta,
having heard of his intelligence and acumen,
was also moved by pity for his orphaned and destitute state.
He was then welcomed back and ordained as a śrāmaṇera.
Upon reaching the age of seventeen,
he and several fellow students made the practice of recitation their primary vocation.
While the entire assembly took one month,
the Venerable One finished reciting it in a single day.
His teacher marveled, saying:
Xian was the equal of thirty men in a single day.
Upon receiving full ordination, he practiced with diligent effort;
he studied the various scriptures extensively and attained mastery in many areas.
In his youth, he gained renown for his mastery of meditation and the Vinaya.
He once traveled to Kaśmīra with his fellow student Saṃghadatta, where they lived together for many years; although Saṃghadatta admired his brilliance and talent, [the latter remained steadfast].
Yet he had not yet ascertained who this person was.
Later, while sitting in meditation with the door closed in a private chamber, he suddenly saw Xian arrive;
startled, he asked where he had come from.
He replied,
"I have gone briefly to Tuṣita to pay my respects to Maitreya.
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Buddhatā knew him to be a sage,
yet had not fathomed his depth;
later, she repeatedly witnessed the holy man’s supernatural transformations.
He then made a reverent inquiry and only then learned that he had attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
He constantly desired to travel abroad to propagate the teachings and observe the customs of various lands.
There was a monk from the Qin dynasty named Zhiyan who traveled west to Jibin,
where he beheld a community of Dharma practitioners and pure monks.
He then looked eastward with a sigh of regret and said,
"Among my peers, there are those with the aspiration for the Way,
yet they do not encounter a true master from whom they may gain awakening."
He immediately consulted the people of the kingdom as to who was capable of propagating the transformation in the eastern lands.
They all replied,
"There is one named Buddhabhadra."
He was born in the city of Nāgarī in India;
his lineage had maintained the tradition for generations of following the Way and studying its teachings.
When he reached the age of childhood, he left the household life.
Having already mastered the sūtras and śāstras,
he received some instruction from the Great Meditation Master Buddhajīva,
who was also in Kaśmīra at that time.
He then said to Yan:
"As for one who can uphold the discipline of the monastic community and propagate the teaching of Chan,
Buddhabhadra is that man."
Since Yan insisted that he must endure the hardships,
Xian was moved by compassion and granted his request.
Thereupon, he left the community, took leave of his teacher, packed his provisions, and traveled eastward.
Having traveled for three years through the vicissitudes of winter and summer,
he crossed the Pamir Mountains and passed through six kingdoms;
the rulers of these lands admired his mission of distant transformation.
He devoted his entire heart and resources, including his salary,
and upon reaching Jiaozhi, he boarded a ship and traveled along the coast.
After passing beneath an island, he arrived.
The Sage pointed to a mountain with his finger and said,
"You may stop here.
The ship's captain replied:
A traveler on the road treasures the passing days, for favorable winds are difficult to encounter;
thus, one must not stop.
He traveled more than two hundred li.
Suddenly, the wind shifted and blew the ship back toward the island.
Only then did the people realize his divine power;
they all took him as their teacher, following his every move. Later, when a favorable wind arose, his companions all set sail.
The worthy one said,
"It must not be moved.
Thereupon, the ship's captain desisted.
Subsequently, those who set out first were all simultaneously defeated and destroyed.
Later, in the midst of a dark night, he suddenly ordered all the ships to depart together,
but none were willing to comply.
The worthy man himself rose to haul in the mooring ropes, and the single ship set sail alone.
Before long, the pirates arrived;
those who remained were all plundered and killed.
Shortly thereafter, he arrived at Donglai Commandery in Qingzhou.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an,
he immediately went there to follow him.
Daosheng was greatly delighted and discussed the characteristics of dharmas with Kumārajīva;
they probed the profound and subtle mysteries, gaining much insight and benefit.
Thereupon, Daosheng said to Kumārajīva:
"What you have explained does not go beyond what people already expect;
yet how is it that you have attained such a high reputation?
Kumārajīva replied:
"It is simply because I am old.
Why must one necessarily be able to produce elegant discourse?
Whenever Kumārajīva encountered points of doubt or difficulty, he invariably consulted with him to reach a resolution.
At that time, Yao Xing, the ruler of Qin, devoted himself single-mindedly to the teachings of the scriptures and supported more than three thousand monks;
these monks frequently came and went between the palace and the imperial gates, busying themselves extensively with worldly affairs.
Only the worthy maintain stillness and do not conform to the multitude.
Later, he said to his disciples:
"Yesterday I saw five ships setting sail together from my native village."
Shortly thereafter, his disciples spread the news to outsiders.
The veteran monks of Guanzhong all considered this to be a display of heterodoxy intended to delude the masses.
Furthermore, while Xian was in Chang’an, he extensively propagated the practice of dhyāna.
Those from the four quarters who delighted in tranquility all arrived, drawn by his reputation.
Yet, their engagement with the study was varied in depth,
and their realization of the Dharma differed in intensity.
Deceitful and hypocritical individuals took advantage of this to act with guile and sophistry.
One disciple, having practiced contemplative cultivation for a short time,
claimed for himself that he had attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
The worthy man did not immediately investigate the matter,
and consequently, rumors spread and he was subjected to great slander and vilification,
on the verge of facing an unforeseen calamity.
Thereupon, some of the disciples hid their names and departed in secret,
while others scaled walls and fled by night;
within half a day, the assembly had almost entirely dispersed.
Fazhan remained composed and initially paid no heed to this.
At that time, the veteran monks Sengqie and Daoheng said to Fazhan,
"Even the Buddha did not permit [his disciples] to speak of the Dharma they had attained themselves."
Previously, it was said that five ships were approaching,
but this proved false and without substance.
Furthermore, among the disciples, mutual deception and confusion arose, leading to conflicting accounts.
"Since you have violated the Vinaya and your views differ from reason, it is appropriate that you depart at once; do not remain for long.
The Venerable said:
"My body is like a drifting duckweed; it is very easy for me to go or stay.
I only regret that my inner aspirations have not yet been fully realized, which makes me feel a sense of melancholy.
Thereupon, he set out together with over forty disciples, including Huiguan.
His countenance remained composed and showed no sign of distress from the outset.
Those who recognized the truth all sighed in lamentation together.
The mourners, both monastics and laypeople, numbered several thousand.
Upon hearing that [Kumārajīva] had departed, Yao Xing was filled with regret and said to Daoheng:
"The śramaṇa Fóxian has come here to travel with the Way,
desiring to proclaim the Bequeathed Teachings."
That these words remain sealed and unspoken fills me with profound lamentation.
How can the fault of a single utterance cause ten thousand men to be without a guide?
The Emperor then issued an edict ordering him to be pursued.
Buddhabhadra said to the messenger, "I truly understand the imperial favor; I shall not wait for further orders."
Thereupon, leading his companions, he set out under the cover of night toward the south.
The śramaṇa Huìyuǎn of Mount Lú had long admired his reputation and virtue;
he thus dispatched an envoy to the Guān region to deliver a letter of invitation. When [Dharmakṣema] later arrived at Mount Lú, he rejoiced as if meeting an old friend.
Huiyuan esteemed him for his virtue.
His expulsion was caused by his disciples.
As for the prediction concerning the five ships, it refers specifically to those who were of like mind.
Furthermore, he was not in violation of the Vinaya.
He then dispatched his disciple Tanyong to deliver a letter to the Yao ruler and the monastic community of Guanzhong to resolve the matter of his suspension.
Daoyuan subsequently requested the translation of various sutras on meditation and *abhidharma*.
Xian’s aspiration lay in traveling to convert others, and he sought no settled comfort.
After staying at the mountain for about a year,
he again traveled west to Jiangling.
He encountered the captain of a foreign ship and subsequently inquired of him;
it was indeed one of the five ships from India that he had previously seen.
The local gentry and commoners of the entire region vied with one another to come and pay their respects.
He would not accept any offerings made to him.
Carrying his alms bowl, he went on his rounds for food regardless of whether the donor was noble or humble.
At that time, Yuan Bao of Chenjun served as the Chief Secretary to the Grand Marshal of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty.
When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty went south to campaign against Liu Dun,
Bao followed the imperial headquarters to Jiangling.
There, the disciple Huiguan of the eminent general went to Bao to beg for food.
Liu Bao was by nature neither respectful nor trusting, and he treated him with extreme scantiness.
Before he had even finished his meal, [the monk] took his leave;
Liu Bao said:
"It seems not yet sufficient; please remain for a short while longer.
Xian said, "The donor's intention to give is limited."
Therefore, what has now been provided is already exhausted.
Bao immediately called his attendants to bring more rice,
but the rice was indeed finished.
Baofa was deeply ashamed.
Shortly thereafter, he asked Huiguan,
"What kind of person is this śramaṇa?"
Guān said,
"His virtuous capacity is so lofty and remote that it cannot be measured by ordinary people.
Bǎo deeply marveled at this extraordinary quality and informed the Grand Marshal.
The Grand Marshal invited him to a meeting and treated him with profound reverence,
providing him with the most abundant offerings and provisions.
Shortly thereafter, the Grand Marshal returned to the capital.
Please return with him and settle at Daochang Temple.
His noble deportment and ritual practices were simple and unadorned, differing from those of the Chinese customs.
His aspirations and temperament were pure and far-reaching, possessing a refined and profound elegance.
The Dharma Master Sengbi of Yangdu wrote in a letter to the śramaṇa Baolin:
"The Meditation Master of Douchang possesses a truly great resolve."
"He is truly a man of such refined elegance, a king of India indeed.
Such was the acclaim he received.
Prior to this, there was the śramaṇa Zhī Fǎlǐng.
In the kingdom of Khotan, he obtained the Sanskrit original of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* consisting of thirty-six thousand stanzas,
which had not yet been translated or propagated.
This was in the fourteenth year of the Yixi era.
Meng Yi, the Interior Governor of Wu Commandery,
and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard,
immediately requested Xian to serve as their master translator.
He then took the Sanskrit manuscript in his own hand and,
together with more than one hundred people, including the śramaṇas Faye, Huiyan,
and Huiyi, translated and finalized the text at Daochang Temple.
The meaning of the text is harmonized across both Chinese and foreign traditions, and its subtle essence perfectly captures the spirit of the sūtra;
thus, the Huayan Hall still exists at Daochang Temple today.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Faxian obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in India and again requested Buddhabhadra to translate it.
From the second year of Long’an during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty (wùxū) until the second year of Yongchū of the Song dynasty (xīn yǒu),
Xuán resided at two locations: Yángdū and Lúshān.
He translated a total of thirteen works, including the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and others,
thoroughly investigating their profound purports and perfectly exhausting the meaning of the texts.
Xian entered nirvāṇa in the sixth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.

He was seventy-one years of age. Furthermore, the two catalogs by Sengyou and Hui Chang state that Buddhabhadra produced the *Xin weimimi chijing* (The New Sūtra of the Subtle and Secret Retention). The term "new" (*xin*) is attached because this is not included among the paired translations; it is added to distinguish it from the earlier translation by Zhi Qian. There are also the *Bodhisattva Shizhu jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva) and the *Benye jing* (Sūtra on Original Acts); these two sūtras are both separate chapters of the *Avataṃsaka*. Since Buddhabhadra had already translated the main body of the *Avataṃsaka*, it was inappropriate for these sūtras to be issued separately. Regarding the *Benye jing*, although its name appears in the *Zhou ruzang lu* (Catalogue of Works Entered into the Canon during the Zhou Dynasty), I have not yet seen the actual text, so I shall preserve its entry for now. As for the *Shizhu jing*, I have deleted it and do not establish it as a separate work.
*Zawen lushi* (Miscellaneous Questions on Vinaya Matters), two fascicles; first appeared in the *Changfang lu*. This one work in two fascicles is missing from its original.
Translated by the śramaṇa Dharma (translated into Chinese as "Dharma") during the Jin dynasty.
He was well-versed in the Vinaya teachings.
On the second day of the third month of the fourth year of the Long’an era (the Gengzi year) of Emperor An’s reign,
he [passed away] at the monastery of Wang Fadu, the Minister of the Secretariat, in Yangdu.
More than twenty virtuous monks, including the śramaṇa Śākya Sengzūn and others,
requested that the preface to the *Zawen lushi* (A Collection of Questions on Vinaya Matters) be placed at the beginning of the volume,
clarifying how the property of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha may intermingle with one another.
The distinctions between these sections are extremely important and must be carefully guarded against confusion.

The *Vinaya-nidāna* (序) in three fascicles of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (十誦律)—also referred to as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-nidāna*—is now included within the final three fascicles of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. This is incorrect; the so-called *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya-bhāṣya* (毘尼誦) mentioned by Fáng [Daoxuan] refers to the *Sūtra-saṃgraha* (善誦), which consists of four fascicles and corresponds to the tenth section (*daśama-bhāṇavāra*) of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. This is seen in the *Lùjì záwèn* (律事雜問) in two fascicles recorded in the *Ānshìlǐ Lùjì* (二秦錄). Regarding the second category, the *Zhònglù yàoyòng* (眾律要用) in two fascicles, also recorded in the *Ānshìlǐ Lùjì*: of these two works totaling five fascicles, the former, the *Vinaya-nidāna* in three fascicles, is extant; however, the latter, the *Lùshì záwèn* (律事雜問) in two fascicles, is originally missing.
The śramaṇa Vimalākṣa—
translated into Chinese as Wugouyan (Stainless Eye)— was a native of Kaśmīra.
He was grave and serene, possessed of great resolve.
Having left home at a young age, he practiced the Way with austere discipline and achieved great accomplishment;
he served as a guide for others and was thus known at the time as the "Blue-Eyed Vinaya Master" (Qingyan Lishi).
Previously, he had propagated and expounded the Vinaya-piṭaka in Kucha.
Scholars from the four directions vied with one another to go and study under him;
Kumārajīva was among those who participated at that time.
When Kucha fell, [the situation changed].
He then fled to Khotan. Shortly thereafter,
he heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an extensively propagating the treasury of the sūtras,
and he further desired that the supreme categories of the Vinaya might also spread throughout the eastern lands.
Thereupon, carrying his staff and alms-bowl, he traversed the shifting sands and braved dangers to enter the East.
In the eighth year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty, he arrived in Guanzhong.
Kumārajīva received him with the reverence due to a teacher.
Faxia also met Kumārajīva by chance when he was far away.
When Kumārajīva passed away,
Faxia [arrived] during the Yixi era of Emperor An.
He then traveled east of the pass and stayed at Shou-chun, halting at Shijian Temple. There,
disciples of the Vinaya gathered like clouds as he vigorously propagated the monastic discipline.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* in fifty-eight fascicles translated by Kumārajīva has its final section,
known as the *Bhikṣu-bhāṇavāra*, which elucidates the methods for receiving the precepts as well as various matters concerning the accomplishment of wholesome dharmas.
Selecting the essential meanings of these [texts] was called "reciting well" (*su-paṭhita*).
Later, "reciting well" was further refined into "reciting the Vinaya" (*vinaya-paṭhita*);
thus, both names continue to exist.
Furthermore, three fascicles of the *Vinaya Preface* were separately issued and placed at the end, resulting in a total of sixty-one fascicles.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Catalogue of Changfang* claim that the first fifty-eight fascicles were expanded to sixty-one; this is not entirely accurate. Regarding the three fascicles of the *Vinaya Preface*, some modern editions of the scripture place them after the ninth recitation and before the tenth recitation, corresponding to fascicles 55, 56, and 57; however, this is incorrect. Upon examining the ancient version of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they are located after the tenth recitation, corresponding to fascicles 59 through 61. Therefore, the present edition follows the ancient manuscript as the correct version.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled south to Jiangling and sat in summer retreat at Xin Temple,
where he lectured on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Having mastered the Jin language, he was exceptionally adept at conveying and interpreting its meaning.
The wondrous foundation of non-action was extensively revealed.
At that time, those who analyzed the texts to seek the underlying principles gathered like a forest;
those who clarified the articles and understood the prohibitions were likewise numerous.
The extensive propagation of the Vinaya-piṭaka was due to the power of [Buddhabhadra].
Later, he produced the *Zawen lushi* (Miscellaneous Questions on Vinaya Matters) in two fascicles.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states that Daochang Huiguan acted as the scribe. It records that Huiguan deeply encompassed the essential principles [of the Vinaya] and compiled his notes on the gravity of internal prohibitions into two fascicles, which he sent back to the capital. When monks and nuns examined them, they vied with one another to transcribe them. At that time, those who were ignorant had a proverb: "The vulgar speech of Beiluo was skillfully recorded by Huiguan; the people of the capital copied it so diligently that the paper became as precious as jade. What is now called the *Zawen lushi* (Miscellaneous Questions on Vinaya Matters) is precisely this work: Huiguan, having doubts regarding the teachings, consulted Beima on various matters as they arose, recording what he heard and compiling it into two fascicles for circulation in the world.
