This was not a separate Sanskrit manuscript translated by Beima; the version attributed to Dharmaruci is also this very same text, though it was erroneously attributed by the compilers.
Chāyǎng was virtuous and fond of seclusion; he abandoned clamor and distanced himself from the mundane world.
In the winter of that year, he returned once more to Shíjiàn in Shòuchūn, where he passed away at the monastery.
He was seventy-seven years old.
Regarding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* in six fascicles, the preface states that it is also known as the *Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* in ten fascicles;
this fourth translation was produced at Daochang Monastery on the first day of the tenth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era, together with Juexian.
Bao Yun acted as the scribe, completing the transcription on the second day of the first month of the fourteenth year.

According to the records of Daozu and Sengyou, there are three fascicles—or perhaps two—of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which is an alternative translation of the first section of the *Dīrgha-āgama*, the *Cankrama-sūtra*.
Various catalogs state that this is the *Vaipulya-nirvāṇa* revealed by Xian; it is not the same as the aforementioned *Mahā-nirvāṇa-sūtra* with additions.
The *Fangdengzi* (大方等字) is a text on the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna; as its phrasing appears to be a literal translation, it has been used here as a substitute for it.
The *Zazang jing* (雜藏經), one fascicle, is the second [text] produced; it is the same version as the *Guishun Mulian Egui Baoying jing* (鬼問目連餓鬼報應經).
This is seen in the two catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang. The *Shisengqi Biquni Jieben* (十誦比丘尼戒本), one fascicle, is also produced from the *Bhikṣuṇī-Prātimokṣa*.
The *Lüti Mùchā Sēngqí Jìběn* (Sārvastivāda Vinaya-mātṛkā) translated jointly by [Saṃghavarman] and Juéxián; recorded in the Chángfáng Lù.

The *Lìyóu Tiānzhú Jìchuán Yījuǎn* (One-fascicle Record of Travels in India), also known as the *Fǎxiàn Chuán* (Biography of Faxian), which records the accounts of Faxian’s own travels to and from India;
recorded in the Chángfáng Lù. The *Zá Āpítán Xīn* (Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya) in thirteen fascicles, the second translation produced during the Fúqín period by Saṃghadeva.

The works produced by [Dharmakṣema] and others are identical to the original texts; see Sengyou’s Catalogue. Fáng states that Xuán and Juéxián co-translated the *Fó yóu Tiānzhú jì* (Record of the Buddha’s Travels in India) in one fascicle;

see Sengyou’s Catalogue. Of the seven works totaling twenty-six fascicles listed above, the first five works comprising twelve fascicles are extant, while the latter two works comprising fourteen fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Faxian,
whose original surname was Gong,
was a native of Wuyang in Pingyang.
It is revealed that he had three elder brothers;
the second of them died when [the father] was still a child,
which caused his father great alarm.
When he reached several years of age, he was sent forth to leave the household life.
After residing there for several years, he fell gravely ill and was on the verge of death;
consequently, he was escorted back to the monastery, where he recovered after staying for two nights.
He was unwilling to return home;
his mother wished to see him but could not find him,
so she built a small hut outside the gate to accommodate his coming and going.
At the age of ten, he encountered the sorrow of his father's death.
His uncle, because his mother was a widow with no one to rely on,
compelled him to return to secular life.
Xian said,
"It was not because I had a father that I left home;
it was precisely because I wished to distance myself from the dust and depart from the mundane world that I entered the Way."
His uncle approved of his words and desisted.
Shortly thereafter, his mother passed away; his filial nature exceeded that of ordinary men.
Once the funeral rites were completed, he immediately returned to the monastery.
Once, while he was harvesting rice in a field with several dozen fellow students,
some hungry bandits appeared intending to seize the grain.
All the śrāmaṇeras fled in all directions.
He remained alone and spoke to the thieves, saying:
"If you wish for grain, take as much as you desire.
However, it is because you did not practice generosity in the past that you have been born into this life of hunger and poverty."
Now you are again seizing people from them;
I fear this will become even more severe in future lives.
It is because I am already concerned for you that I have spoken thus.
Having finished speaking, he immediately returned.
The bandits abandoned the grain and departed.
Among the several hundred monks, there was none who did not express deep admiration and submission.
Having received the full precepts, his resolve and conduct were pure and bright, and his ritual observances were orderly and solemn.

the Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Hundred Knot Divine Kings Protecting the Body; the Sūtra of the Divine Kings Guarding and Stabilizing the Left and Right of Palaces and Residences;
the Sūtra of the Four-Directional Divine Spells on the Causes and Conditions of Tombs and Graves; the Great Divine Spell of the Sealing of the Subduing of Māras; and the Māniradanda [Spell].
The *Mahādevī-mantra-sūtra*, the *Sūtra of the Mantra for Summoning the Dragons of the Five Directions and Subjugating Pestilence*,
the *Brahmadeva-vidyā-sūtra*, and the *Puguang-jing*— the eleven works totaling eleven fascicles listed above were all translated by Śrīmitra.
The *Mahābhiṣeka-sūtra* from the first to the eleventh fascicle, and the *Yijiao-sanmei-jing* in two fascicles (also known as the *Yizhang-sanmei-jing*).

The *Yijiao Sanmei Falü Jing* (Sūtra on the Dharma-Regulations of the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching), translated by Dharmakṣema of the Western Jin; it is also included among the spurious records.

There is also the *Anagāmi Sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by Zhiyan of the Song; it is likewise included among the spurious records. There is also the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya Sūtra* in two fascicles, sometimes simply called the *Adbhuta Sūtra*;
it has already been translated twice, with one version extant and the other missing. [Also listed: *Dhyāna-samādhi-upāya-anupūrvi*.
*Fajing* (Dharmapada), translated by An Shigao of the Later Han; *Qifo shenzhou jing* (The Divine Incantations of the Seven Buddhas), translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu;

*Xianzhe wufu jing* (The Sutra on the Five Blessings of the Worthy), translated by Bai Fazhu of the Western Jin; *Manilodan shenshou wang'an jing* (The Sutra on the Manilodan Deity’s Incantation for Examining the Ground), translated by Zhu Tanwulan (the title may omit the character "Wang");
*Benxing liuboluomi jing* (The Sutra on the Original Acts of the Six Pāramitās), translated by Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* translated by Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty; the *Sangui-wujie-jing*; the *Shenwang-ming-jing-chao*;
the *Guanding-jing*; the *Dingyi-sanmei-jing*; and those extracted from the *Shizhu-duanjie-jing*. The following are newly appended to this catalog.
*The Sutra on the Definitive Vinaya* (Jueding pinijijing), one fascicle; also known as *The Destruction of All Consciousness*.

This was the first translation, a different version of the same text as the *Upāli’s Assembly in the Ratnakūṭa*. Daoxuan states that various catalogs all record it as having been produced at Dunhuang, though the translator is not specified.
Tradition says it appeared during the Jin dynasty, though it is unclear under which emperor. *The Sutra on Maitreya’s Arrival*, one fascicle; number [ ].
Three translations by Saṃghavarman: the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born* (Mile xiasheng jing), which is the same text as [the version by] Kumārajīva;

the *Sūtra on the Rice Seedling* (Daomian jing), one fascicle, which is the same text as the *Sūtra on the Understanding of Birth and Death* (Liaoben shengsi jing); the *Sūtra on the Merit of Constructing Images* (Zaoli xingxiang fubao jing), one fascicle, which is the same text as the *Sūtra on Making Buddha Images* (Zuo fo xingxiang jing);
and the *Sūtra on Repaying Kindness by Offering Bowls* (Ba’en fengpen jing), one fascicle, which is the same text as the *Ullambana Sūtra* (Yulanpen jing).

*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita*, one fascicle; *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Flower-Cluster*, one fascicle—these two preceding sūtras are the same original text with different translations;
*The Six-Syllable King of Mantras*, one fascicle, which is the same original text as the *Six-Syllable Divine King of Mantras*;
*The Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means of the Good Dharma*, one fascicle; *The Secret Goodness of the Vajra*.

*Mentuo luo ni jing* (Mentāraṇī-sūtra), one fascicle; the first two sūtras are the same text with different translations. *Pusa benxing jing* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Bodhisattva), three fascicles.
*Qifo suoshuo shenzhou jing* (Sūtra of the Divine Spells Spoken by the Seven Buddhas), four fascicles; the first fascicle states that it was spoken by the seven Buddhas and eleven bodhisattvas.
*Da tuoluoni shenzhou jing* (Great Dhāraṇī Divine Spell Sūtra). *Salu guo jing* (Sūtra of the Kingdom of Salu), one fascicle; also called the *Salu guowang jing* (Sūtra of the King of Salu).

The *Parnirvāṇa Sūtra* (Bānnièhuán jīng), in two fascicles—also simply called the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* or the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*—is an alternative translation of the first part of the *Cankrama Sūtra* (Cháng āhán chūfēn yóuxíng jīng).
Among the various collections, the single-fascicle version contains only the upper fascicle and lacks the lower fascicle.
The *Yuánběnzhì jīng* (Yuánběn zhì jīng), in one fascicle, is an ancient alternative translation from the tenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*Lai shi shi jing* (Sūtra on the Times of Future Lives), one fascicle; translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, volume thirteen, alternative translation. *Fan zhi ji shui jing* (Sūtra on the Brahmin’s Calculation of Water Purity), one fascicle;

translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, volume twenty-three, alternative translation. *San gui wu jie ci xin yan li gong de jing* (Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, Five Precepts, Compassionate Mind, and Renunciation), one fascicle;
translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, volume thirty-nine, alternative translation. *Jian* (The Arrow).

*Yujing* (The Parable Sutra), one fascicle; translated from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyamāgama*. *Shishi huowu fubao jing* (Sutra on Receiving Five Kinds of Meritorious Rewards for Bestowing Food), one fascicle;
also titled *Shiseli jing* (Sutra on Bestowing Color and Strength) or *Fude jing* (Sutra on Merit);

translated from the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Ekottarikāgama*. *Manyuzi jing* (Sutra of Pūrṇa), one fascicle; listed among the works of lost translators by Sengyou as having been translated during the Jin dynasty.
It is stated that this was formerly included in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, volume thirteen; it is a separate translation of the one-volume *Mādrī-dārikā-vimocana-ṣaḍvastu-sūtra*.
This is the fifth appearance [of this text], which is the same as the *Mātangī-sūtra* and the *Śikhā-vinodana-sūtra*.
There is also the one-volume *Preta-vipāka-sūtra*, the third appearance, also known as the *Maudgalyāyana-bhāṣita-naraka-preta-hetu-sūtra*.

The *Yuanjing* (Sutra on Conditions) and the *Guiwen Mulian jing* (Sutra of the Ghosts Questioning Maudgalyāyana) share the same root text as the *Dedao ticheng xizhang jing* (Sutra on the Ladder to the Path and the Staff),
one fascicle, titled "The Twelfth Chapter on the Staff" from the *Dedao ticheng jing*, or simply called the *Xizhang jing* (Staff Sutra).

The *Senghu jing* (Sutra of Saṃgharakṣita), one fascicle— also known as the *Senghu yinyuan jing* (Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of Saṃgharakṣita) or the *Yinyuan senghu jing* (Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of Saṃgharakṣita)— concerns the purification of offerings.
*Sūtra* in one fascicle; *Khadira-Indrāraṇi-sūtra* in one fascicle (the character "huàn" is sometimes used, and it is also written as "xuán");
*Anuttara-sthāna-sūtra* in one fascicle; *Nidāna of the Householder Lu-zhi* in one fascicle; *Sūtra of the Five Kings* in one fascicle;
*The Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras, Together with Their Dignified Conduct* in one fascicle (also called *Śrāmaṇera-dignified-conduct-precept-text* or *Śrāmaṇerī-vinaya-text*).
*Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu-sūtra*, one fascicle;

*Aśoka-rāja-avadāna-sūtra*, one fascicle—titled *Tianzun shuo Aśoka-rāja-avadāna-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Parables of King Aśoka Spoken by the Heavenly Honored One); as the ancient scriptures refer to the Buddha as the "Heavenly Honored One," this is actually spoken by the Buddha;
*Zhuanjì sānzàng jí zázàng zhuan* (Biographies of the Compilation of the Tripiṭaka and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka), one fascicle, also called *Zhuàn*.
The *Tripiṭaka-sūtra*, the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra*, and the *Maitreya-buddhatva-kāla-sūtra* in one fascicle (not recorded by Sengyou;
second appearance, same text as the *Maitreya-āgamanasūtra*, etc.; see Baochang’s record).
The *Bodhivṛkṣa-samādhi-sūtra* in two fascicles (second appearance, same text as the *Śrīsamādhi-sūtra*; see Zhimindu’s record). The above.
Of the thirty-eight sections comprising forty-five fascicles, the final two sections totaling three fascicles are missing; the remainder are all extant.
This consists of the first thirty-six sections totaling forty-two fascicles.
All of these are scriptures seen in the Tripiṭaka collections,
yet their translators remain unknown;
they are omitted from the catalogs of lost translations and have not been recorded there.
These appear to be scriptures from a distant era;
therefore, they have been compiled at the end of the Jin period so that nothing may be omitted.
Including the two sections in three fascicles previously lost and translated anonymously,
there are a total of forty sections in forty-eight fascicles,
all of which are said to have their origins lost during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The Fu Qin dynasty of the Fu clan was based in Chang’an; it is also called the Former Qin. It began with Fu Jian, posthumously titled Emperor Ming, in the first year of Huangshi, the *xinhai* year.
It lasted until Fu Deng, who received no posthumous title, in the ninth year of Taichu, the *jiawu* year.
In total, during the reigns of five emperors over a period of forty-four years,
six śramaṇas translated various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras.
In total, there are fifteen sections comprising one hundred and ninety-seven fascicles.

Among these, seven sections totaling sixty-five fascicles are extant; eight sections totaling one hundred and thirty-two fascicles are missing. The library records state that the *Huangshi* era year 1 (Jia-yin) and the *Yanchu* era year 1 (Ding-you) differ from the chronological tables of various houses by two years. Subsequently, based on Master Dao’an’s added preface and a verification of the sexagenary cycle (*jiǎzǐ*), it was found that the library records were in error.
The Śramaṇa Dharmadhara of the Fu Qin [dynasty] translated three sections in three fascicles: the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and the *Vidhi-maṇḍala*.

The Śramaṇa Kumārabuddhi translated one section in two fascicles: the *Saṃyukta-āgama*. The Śramaṇa Saṃghabhūti translated three sections in twenty-seven fascicles: the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and other treatises.

The Śramaṇa Dharmapriya translated one section in five fascicles: the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*. The Śramaṇa Saṃghadeva translated two sections in four [fascicles]: the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and other works.
The *Śāstra in Sixteen Fascicles* by the śramaṇa Dharmanandin; the *Collection of One Hundred and Fourteen Fascicles of Sūtras and Śāstras of the Five Schools*;
the *Ten Recitations Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa*, one fascicle—also called the *Ten Recitations Mahābhikṣu Prātimokṣa*, first appearing in Sengyou’s catalogue;
the *Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprātimokṣa*, one fascicle—also called the *Ten Recitations Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa*, second [recitation].

The *Chūshōroku* (Catalogue of the Sangha) records a one-fascicle work titled *Kyōju bikuni nissai danmon* (Text on the Two-Year Ordination Platform for Bhikṣuṇīs), though some versions omit the character "ni" (bhikṣuṇī).
Sengchun obtained the Sanskrit original in the kingdom of Kucha; Buddhanian acted as the oral translator and Huichang served as the scribe.
This is recorded in the *Baoshanglu*. These three works comprise three fascicles in total, and their manuscripts are currently missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmadhara,
also called Shi (Attendant);
in the Qin language, Fahui (Dharma-Wisdom).
Another was called Fahai.
A man from the Western Regions,
he was skilled in upholding the Vinaya-piṭaka and had profoundly mastered the Sūtras.
During the third year of the Jianyuan era, the *dingmao* year, and the fourth year, the *wuchen* year, under Emperor Fu Jian— who was posthumously titled King Zhuanglie Tianwang—
he translated three works, including the *Śāriputra-vinaya-mātṛkā*, at Chang’an.
Zhú Fóniàn translated the words orally, and Huìcháng recorded them in writing.
In Sēngzhào’s *Preface to the Monastic Precepts*, it says:
"Fóniàn transcribed the Sanskrit text."
Daxian served as the translator and Huidang acted as the scribe.
Regarding the Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa,
Sengyou’s catalogue states:
During the reign of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Sengchun obtained a Sanskrit manuscript in the kingdom of Kuci in the Western Regions.
Upon arriving in Guanzhong, he commissioned Fonian, Dharmapriya, and Huichang to produce a Chinese translation together.
I have carefully examined the records of Sengchangfang and others;
they all designate Huichang as the primary translator,
who translated this work together with Dharmagupta and Zhu Fonian.
Now, as for the Qin monk Huichang, he had never traveled to India.

Although Chang co-translated the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa* with him, the original manuscript was actually that of Dharmabuddhin; Chang served as the scribe and translated it alongside the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa*.
What distinguishes this? This is specifically to highlight that wisdom is constant.
By examining its origins and its culmination, the matter becomes clear.
Because Dharmaruci was the primary translator while [the author] constantly served as his assistant,
it was included in Dharmaruci’s catalog.
The *Huìcháng bùbié* exists [separately].
The two-fascicle *Sīāhán mùchāojiě* (Excerpts from the End of the Four Āgamas), also titled the *Sīāhán mùchāojīng*, is recorded in Sēngyòu’s catalog; this one work in two fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Kumārabuddhi— translated into the language of Qin as "Child Enlightenment"—
was a man from the Western Regions.
In the eighth month of the eighteenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the year of Renwu,
he translated the *Ahan mu chao* (Extracts from the Āgamas) in one fascicle at the Ye Monastery.
It was completed in the eleventh month of winter.
The Buddha-dhiti held the Sanskrit manuscript; Buddhasmṛti and Buddharakṣa translated it into the Qin language.
The śramaṇas Sengdao, Sengrui, and Tanjiu acted as scribes.

This is the *Saṃghabhedavastu-śāstra* (or *Saṃghabhadra-sūtra*) compiled by the Bodhisattva Saṃghabhadra, in ten fascicles; it is also called the *Vasu-mitra-sūtra*, or [in other versions] twelve fascicles.
In fourteen fascicles (or thirteen fascicles), begun on the fifth day of the third month in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era and completed on the thirteenth day of the seventh month.
Translated by Baoteng, Nandi, and Deva holding the original text, with Fonian interpreting and Huisong recording the oral transmission;
as recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu*. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* in fourteen fascicles (sometimes without the character "wu" [treatise], also called *Vibhāṣā*).
The *Abhidharma* (also called *Vaipulya*) consists of either fifteen or nineteen fascicles.

It was translated from the fourth month to the end of the eighth month of the nineteenth year of the Jianyuan era. Nanti recorded the Sanskrit text, Fotuoluoche translated it, and Minzhi served as the scribe.
This is noted in Sengyou’s catalogue. The *Sangharakṣasa-saṃgīta-sūtra* consists of three fascicles; some say [it is by] Sangha...
The *Kālakārṣa-saṃgraha* (伽羅剎集) was first produced in five fascicles; its translation was completed on the thirtieth day of the eleventh month in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era.
Translated by Buddhasmṛti (佛念), with Huisong (慧嵩) receiving the oral transmission in writing; this is recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue as having been produced at Shiyang Monastery in Chang’an.
It is also said that Buddhagupta (佛護) transmitted and translated it. These three sections comprise twenty-seven fascicles, and their manuscripts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Saṃghabhūti,
also called Bhūti; in the language of Qin,
this means "Manifestation of the Multitude."
A native of Kaśmīra,
he possessed a resolute and profound character.
He traveled extensively to seek out renowned masters, cultivating his practice until he attained the highest level of mastery.
He read widely across many classics and was particularly proficient in the Abhidharma treatises.

He could recite the *Vibhāṣā* from memory and had mastered its subtle principles—this refers to the *Vibhāṣā*, not the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. He constantly set his mind on traveling to various regions to observe local customs and propagate the Dharma.
At the end of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, he entered Guanzhong.
Previously, the Mahayana scriptures had not yet spread widely,
while the study of dhyāna and śamatha-vipaśyanā was very prevalent.
Upon his arrival in Chang’an, everyone hailed him as a master of the Dharma.
Zhao Zheng, styled Wenyue, was a Secretariat郎 (lang) under Fu Jian;
he was widely learned, possessed great talent, and held the Great Dharma in the highest esteem.
I have heard that in foreign lands, the *Vibhāṣā* is the tradition most practiced and studied,
and that Saṃghabhūti could recite it from memory;
thus, I offered him the fourfold offerings and requested him to translate the Sanskrit text.
From the seventeenth year of the Jianyuan era, the year of Xinsi,
until the twenty-first year, the year of Yibyou, Fotudeng,
together with the renowned and virtuous Dharma Master Shi Dao’an and others, [collated the scriptures].
The three sections beginning with the *Vasumitra* were translated by the śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou,
with the foreign śramaṇa Fotudeng acting as interpreter.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Minzhì Huìsōng;
transcribed by the Secretariat Drafter Zhào Wényè;
and collated and verified together with Ān Gōng Fǎhuó.
Bhadrapāla’s precepts and virtue were upright and severe; he was serene and aloof from the mundane world.
The monastic community in Guanzhong took him as their model.
Later, his final whereabouts remained unknown.
Buddhatrāta was a man of unknown nationality.
His virtuous deeds were pure and refined, and he had thoroughly mastered the Buddhist scriptures.
Having traveled extensively throughout the Central Kingdom for a long time, he was proficient in the language of Qin.

Regarding the translation of the Sanskrit text, which was highly acclaimed in his time, various catalogs such as those by Sengyou and others all state that the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* was translated by Saṃghadeva. However, based on the preface to the treatise by Master Dao’an, it states that it was translated by Saṃghabhūti; we shall take this as correct. Furthermore, the fourteen-fascicle *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* mentioned in the various catalogs of Sengyou and others is precisely this same *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra* (or *Sūtra on the Excerpts of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā*) in five fascicles—sometimes without the character "shā" (*śāstra*), or in seven fascicles; also called the *Prajñā* [Sūtra], the *Subhūti Chapter*, or the *Cháng'ān Chapter*. It is the sixth translation, identical in substance to the *Dàoxíng*, *Xiǎopǐn*, and *Míngdù* [versions]. This is recorded in Sēngruì’s *Qín Lù* (Two Qin Records) and Sēngyòu’s *Lù*. This one work in five fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Dharmapriya (曇摩蜱),
whose name means "Dharma-love" in the language of Qin,
was a person from India.
Of clear intelligence and refined character, he set his mind upon the propagation of the Great Dharma.
In the eighteenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the Renwu year,
he translated one fascicle of the *Prajñā-saṃgraha-sūtra*.
Translated by Buddhagupta; Buddhagupta is the same as Buddhaloṣṭa.
Transcribed by Huijin and verified by Master Daoan.
The common tradition states:
Regarding those [texts] that share the same root as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Prabhāsa*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā-stava*, one might fear that an investigation of them has not yet been thorough.

The *Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra* (Treatise in Eight Chapters) consists of thirty fascicles; alternatively, it may omit the word "treatise" (*lun*), or consist of twenty fascicles, or be called the *Kātyāyanīya-abhidharma*, or the *Abhidharma-sūtra*. Its first eight chapters were originally the same root as the *Jñānaprasthāna* translated during the Tang dynasty. It was produced on the twentieth day of the fourth month in the nineteenth year of the Jianyuan era and completed on the twentieth day of the tenth month; this is seen in Sengyou’s catalogue. The *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* consists of sixteen fascicles; initially it consisted of thirteen fascicles. It was produced in Luoyang at the end of the Jianyuan era; this is seen in Sengrui’s *Biographies of the Two Qin* and Sengyou’s catalogue. Of these two sections totaling forty-six fascicles, the former section of thirty fascicles currently exists, while the latter section of sixteen fascicles is missing.

The śramaṇa Saṃghadeva—also called Tihé or Saṃghatīpó—is a name that differs merely in its phonetic pronunciation, like the dialects of Chu and Xia; in the language of Qin, it means "Assembly of Devas.
He was a native of Kaśmīra.
He was of the Gautama clan.
In the nineteenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, the year of Guiwei,
he traveled to Chang’an.
The śramaṇa Fǎhuá requested that it be translated;
it began in the nineteenth year [of the Jianyuan era] and was completed at the end of the Jiànyuán period.

Two treatises, including the *Abhidharmāṣṭagrantha*, were produced; among them, the fourteen-fascicle *Vibhāṣā*—which, according to Master Dao’an’s preface, was translated by Saṃghabhūti—is excluded here.
This [present work] was translated and transmitted by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou.
Huilong and Sengmao transcribed it by dictation;
Faho clarified its essential meaning;
and Master Daoan composed the preface.
Later, in the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,
he traveled to Mount Lu and then proceeded to Jiankang,
where he further produced translations of sutras and treatises.
This is exactly as revealed in the *Jin lu* (Records of the Jin Dynasty).
The fifty-nine fascicles of the *Madhyama Āgama* were produced in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era; this is the first translation, with Zhu Fonian acting as the scribe (*bishou*).
This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi za lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue), as well as the *Ekottara Āgama*.

The first translation consisted of fifty fascicles; it was produced from the summer of the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era (the Jiashen year) until the following spring, at which point it was reduced to forty fascicles.

It was translated by Buddhabhadra (*Fonien*) and orally received by Tanhong (*Tansong*). This is evidenced by Master Dao’an’s preface to the sutra, as well as the records of Sengrui, Sengyou, and Baochang.
Sengyou states that the thirty-third and twenty-fourth fascicles [of the original] were likely erroneous, and that they should instead be titled *Sanfadu* (The Threefold Dharma-Degree).

*Treatise on the Two Truths*, two fascicles; first translated, some say it is the *Treatise on the Three Dharmas*. The characters differ slightly from those translated by Saṃghadeva during the Jin dynasty;
see the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Collected Works of Saṃgharakṣa*, two fascicles; composed by Saṃgharakṣa seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
first appeared in the *Bǎochàng Lù*. *The Story of King Aśoka’s Son Who Destroyed His Eyes*.

*Yuan jing* (Sūtra on Conditions), one fascicle. Third edition, produced at Cheng in Anding during the sixth year of Jianchu (the *xinmao* year) of the Yao Qin dynasty, for Yao Min, Minister of the Secretariat.
Begun on the eighteenth day of the second month and completed on the twenty-fifth.

Translated by Fonian, who also composed the preface. Recorded in the *Er Qin lu*. This should properly be included among the Later Qin records; here it is appended according to the majority of sources. The above comprises five works.
Of the one hundred and fourteen fascicles, the first four parts consisting of one hundred and thirteen fascicles are missing;
the final part, consisting of one fascicle, is extant.
The śramaṇa Dharmanandi—translated into Chinese as Faxi (Dharma-joy)—[translated this].
A native of the country of Tukhāra,
he left secular life in his youth;
being of keen intelligence, he attained maturity early and devoted himself to the study and recitation of the scriptures.
He devoted himself with single-minded concentration to his professional practice,
thoroughly examining the Tripiṭaka and reciting from memory the two additional Āgamas within it;
his vast knowledge and extensive learning left nothing unrefined.
Consequently, those both near and far within the realm all came to respect and submit to him.
From his youth, he traveled abroad, visiting various countries;
he often maintained that the essence of propagating the Dharma lay in proclaiming what had not yet been heard.
Therefore, braving the distant shifting sands and carrying his treasures, he traveled eastward;
in the twentieth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era,
he arrived in Chang’an.
Nandi’s scholarly achievements were already eminent and his reputation for the Way was widespread.
Fu Jian received him with profound respect and provided him with generous offerings and support.
Previously, the various scriptures of the Central Land had not yet included the four Āgamas.
Zhao Zheng, the Governor of Weiwei and a trusted minister of the Jian clan, whose resolve was deeply rooted in the treasury of the Dharma,
then joined with Master An to petition for the translation of the scriptures.
Zhao Zheng assembled monks learned in the doctrines within the city of Chang’an.
The Sanskrit manuscript was transcribed twice before the translation finally began;
Founian acted as the oral interpreter.
Huisong recorded the dictation.
It was transcribed from the twentieth year of Jianyuan of Fu Jian (Jia Shen) to the sixth year of Jianchu of Yao Chang (Xin Mao).
This collection includes five sections of translated scriptures, such as the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
After this, [Dharmarakṣa] returned to the Western Regions, and his final whereabouts remain unknown.
*Catalogue of the Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll Three, General Catalogue Part Three.
Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu, Volume Four, Section Seven:
A General Compendium of All Scriptures, Part Four, compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the Western Regions during the Gengwu year.

The Yao Qin dynasty was established by the Yao clan with their capital at Chang’an; it is also referred to as the Later Qin. It began with Yao Chang, who was posthumously titled Emperor Shaowu, in the first year of the Baique era (Jia-shen).
It ended with Yao Hong, who received no posthumous title, in the third year of the Yonghe era (Ding-si).
In total, over the course of thirty-four years under three successive rulers, five śramaṇas produced a combined total of ninety-four works, comprising six hundred and twenty-four fascicles.

Of these, sixty-six works totaling five hundred and twenty-eight fascicles are extant; twenty-eight works totaling ninety-six fascicles are missing. According to the postscript to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the third year of Hongshi (the year of Xinchou) was the date of completion. Wang Daogui states it was Gengzi, while another version also records it as Xinchou. Fang and Zhen Luan further differ by one year. Here, I follow the postscript of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as the definitive authority and have arranged the texts in their proper order.
The Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of the Yao Qin translated twelve divisions comprising seventy-four fascicles of sūtras and vinayas;
the Śramaṇa Kumārajīva compiled seventy-four divisions comprising three hundred and eighty-four fascicles of sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras;
the Śramaṇa Puṇyatāra [translated] one division comprising fifty-eight fascicles of vinaya; and the Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas [translated] four divisions comprising eight... [fascicles].
The fourteen-fascicle *Sūtra and Vinaya* by the śramaṇa Dharmayaśas consists of three sections totaling twenty-four fascicles.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃyojana-prahāṇa-sūtra* (Ten Stages Sutra on Severing the Bonds) is in ten fascicles;

its preface states it is titled *Vijayaparipṛcchā-bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-mala-vyudāsa-saṃyojana-prahāṇa-sūtra*, also known as *Daśasahasra-sūryaprabhā-samādhi-samāpatti*, or alternatively *Daśabhūmi-saṃyojana-prahāṇa*. It is also found in either eleven fascicles or...
In fourteen fascicles, the second edition appeared, as recorded in the *Sanqin lu*, the *Gaoseng zhuan*, and the *Sengyou lu*.

The *Bosha yingluo jing* (Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa-sūtra) in twelve fascicles—also known as the *Xianzai bao* (Present Retribution)—appeared in the seventh month of the twelfth year of the Jianyuan era of the Fu Qin dynasty;
it is also recorded in the *Erqin lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan* as having appeared in either thirteen, fourteen, or sixteen fascicles.

According to Sengyou’s *Chū sanzō ki shū* (Collection for the Transmission of the Tripitaka), the *Bodhisattva-chu-t’ai ching* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Abiding in the Womb) consists of five fascicles;

its opening states that the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb and preached the *Kuang-pu ching* (Extensive Universal Sutra). It is also simply called the *T’ai ching* (Womb Sutra), appearing in either four or eight fascicles according to the *Erh-ch’in lu* (Record of the Two Qin Dynasties) and the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
The *Chung-yin ching* (Sutra of the Intermediate State) consists of two fascicles, as seen in the *Erh-ch’in lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*.
Sengyou’s Catalog records the *Bodhisattva-yaṣṭi-mūla-karma-sūtra* in two fascicles, also simply called the *Yaṣṭi-mūla-karma-sūtra*;

it first appeared in Changfang’s Catalog. The *Vinaya-naiyāyika* in ten fascicles—also known as the *Śikṣā-hetu-pratyaya-sūtra*, the *Vinaya-naiyāyika-sūtra*, or the *Śīla-phala-hetu-pratyaya-sūtra*—was transcribed by the śramaṇa Tanjing; it was seen by Master Dao’an.
Preface to the Sūtra: On the twelfth day of the first month of the fourteenth year of the Jianyuan era (Renwu) of the Fu Qin dynasty, twenty fascicles of the *Chuyao jing* were produced;
it is also called the *Chuyao lun*, or in nineteen fascicles. It was produced in the nineteenth year of the Jianyuan era of the Fu Qin dynasty, as recorded in the *Erqin lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*.
It is listed in the catalogs of Sengyou, Baochang, and others, and currently exists.
The following portion is missing.
The *Dharanidhara-bodhisattva-sūtra* in three fascicles, the second translation, is identical in substance to the *Dharmarakṣa-dharani*, the *Dharanidhara*, and the *Lokaprajñapti* by Kumārajīva;
this is recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Mahāvaipulya-nirnimitta-sūtra* in five fascicles is also titled the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, or alternatively [in four fascicles].
The *Fangdeng Dayun* (Vaipulya Mahāmegha) in three fascicles, translated by Dharmakṣema, shares the same original source; its initial appearance is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.

The *Pusa puchu jing* (Bodhisattva-sarvaviṣaya-sūtra) in three fascicles is also recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Shisong biquni jie suochu benmo* (Origins of the Ten Recitation Bhikṣuṇī Precepts) in one fascicle was the third translation;
Saṃghaputra obtained the Sanskrit manuscript in the country of Kuci, and Buddhasmṛti translated the text. Later, it was revised by Zhu Fonian.
Fata revised and corrected it; it is recorded in Baochang’s catalogue.

*The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Fayi’s Self-Inflicted Blindness*, one fascicle—also called *The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of King Aśoka’s Son’s Self-Inflicted Blindness*, the third version—is found in Sengyou’s catalogue.
The above twelve works, totaling seventy-four fascicles, and the seven works from the *Udānavarga* (Chuyao) totaling sixty-one fascicles, are extant and currently held.
The thirteen fascicles of the *Renxia wubu* (Five Sections for Commoners) are missing.
The śramaṇa Zhu Fonian was a native of Liangzhou.
He left home to become a monk at a young age, his aspirations and practice being pure and steadfast.
Outwardly harmonious and inwardly luminous, he possessed a penetrating and敏敏 (penetrating) discernment.
He recited and studied various sutras and had a general familiarity with the external classics.
He was particularly proficient in the glosses and explanations of the *Cangjie* and *Yaya* lexicons.
From his youth, he delighted in traveling to various regions to observe local customs;
his family lineage had long resided in Xihe, and they were thoroughly conversant with the dialects of those lands.
He explained the phonology and meanings of both Chinese and non-Chinese terms without exception;
thus, although his reputation for scholastic expertise was lacking,
his fame for extensive learning was widely renowned.
During the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan’s reign,
there were Dharmadhara, Kumārabuddhi, and Saṃghabhūti.
Devaṃdara and others arrived in Chang’an; Master Dao’an,
Zhao Zheng, and others requested that they translate various scriptures.
At that time, none among the renowned and virtuous were able to transmit and translate [the scriptures].
The assembly all recommended Kumārajīva as a master of illumination.
Since the time of Dharmarakṣa and Zhi Qian, [he was the preeminent one].
None surpassed him in mindfulness.
During the two reigns of the Fu and Yao dynasties, he was the preeminent master among translators;
thus, the monastic community in Guanzhong all held him in high esteem.

Reflecting upon the two reigns of Fu Jian and Yao Xing, [it appears that] among the twelve sections of sutras such as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga* translated by him, the ten-volume *Daśabhūmi-vibhaṅga-sūtra* preserved separately in Dao An’s catalogue is erroneous; for there is no distinction between the two meanings of "staying" (*zhu*) and "ground" (*di*). Thus, we now retain the *Daśabhūmika* and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga*, having deleted the latter. Later, he fell ill and passed away in Chang’an.
People far and near, both white and black, all sighed with regret.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in forty fascicles—also known as the *Dapin Banruo Jing* (Large Version Prajñā Sūtra)—is what Daoyou calls the "New Dapin Jing.
This third edition was translated based on the same manuscript as the *Fangguang* [Prajñā], consisting of either thirty or twenty fascicles.

Four [fascicles], or twenty-seven; translated on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the fifth year of Hongshi (the *guimao* year), and completed on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the sixth year.

As seen in the *Qin lu* and the *Sengyou lu*, the ten-fascicle *Xiaopin banruo boluomi jing* lacks the characters "xiaopin" (small version) in its title; Sengyou [noted] that it is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
The *New Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Xīn xiǎopǐnjīng) is identical in its original text to the *Dàoxíng míngdù jīng*; it is the seventh translation, consisting of either seven fascicles.
It was produced from the sixth day of the second month in the tenth year of the Hongshi era until the thirtieth day of the fourth month, according to the *Lù of the Two Qin* and the *Sēngyòu Lù*.
There is also one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, also called the *Jīngāng bōrě jīng*.
Regarding the *Buddha at Śrāvastī*: the first translation is identical in its original text to that produced by Dharmaruci and others during the Yuan-Wei dynasty;
this is seen in the two *Qin* catalogs and the *Sengyou lu*. The *Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomi Jing* in two fascicles is also called the *Renwang Banruo Jing*, or sometimes said to be one fascicle.
The second translation was produced by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty and [others] during the Liang dynasty.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitāmahāvidyāmantra-sūtra* (一卷), also known as the *Mahāvidyāmantra-sūtra*, translated by Paramārtha from the same original source but with different wording, was noted by Fang [Guangchang] in his *Bie lu* (Separate Record).
Its initial translation is identical in substance to the *Prajñāhṛdaya-sūtra* (Heart Sutra) translated during the Tang dynasty;
this is evident from the title on the scroll. It is also recorded in the *Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra* (菩薩藏經) in three fascicles, also titled *Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-sūtra*.
That *Nāga-pṛcchā-sūtra* is also titled the *Mahākaruṇā-citta-sūtra*; it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* as the seventeenth assembly, titled the "Pūrṇa Assembly.
It was translated in the seventh year of Hongshi, in two fascicles.

This second translation is identical in its source text to that produced by Dharmarakṣa, as recorded in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* and the *Sengyou Lu*. The *Subāhu-bodhisattva-sūtra* in two fascicles is now also included in the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The *Ji* (Collection) contains the twenty-sixth assembly, the *Sūmaṭī-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle;
the second edition is identical to the *Ratnakūṭa-mahāprajñā-parivarta*. This is recorded in the *Chángfáng-lù*.
The *Īśvararāja-bodhisattva-sūtra*, two fascicles—sometimes omitting the word "bodhisattva"—was first translated in the ninth year of Hongshi, being identical to the *Veṣṭhitarāja-sūtra*.

In the [X]th year, at the residence of Yao Xian, the Minister of State Affairs, Seng Rui transcribed the text by dictation and composed the preface; this is recorded in the *Er Qin Lu* and the *Sengyou Lu*.

There is one fascicle of the *Zhuangyan Pútíxīn Jīng* (The Scripture on Adorning the Bodhicitta), which is the fourth translation and shares the same source as the *Fahù Púsà Shìdì Jīng* (The Ten Stages Scripture of Bodhisattva Dharmarakṣa).
Fang states that he saw it in the *Bielu*; there is also the *Shìzhù Jīng* (The Scripture on the Ten Abodes) in four or five fascicles.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, "Chapter on the Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika*), was translated by Kumārajīva and Buddhabhadra together; this is recorded in the two *Qin* catalogs and the *Sengyou lu*.

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in eight fascicles, the *Sengyou lu* states that the original *New Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consisted of seven fascicles and twenty-seven chapters, which were later expanded by adding the "Devadatta Chapter" (*Devadatta-parivarta*) to become twenty-eight chapters in the eighth year of the Hongshi era.
In the summer, at the Great Temple (Daisi), [Kumārajīva] produced this translation with Sengrui serving as scribe and composing the preface;

this fifth translation is recorded in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels through the Ages) and the *Sengyou Lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou). The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* consists of three fascicles;
it is also titled *Acintyavimokṣa* or simply *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*. The *Sengyou Lu* states that this new *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* was translated in the eighth year of the Hongshi era.
The sixth translation, produced at the Great Monastery (Daci), was transcribed by the monk Zhao and its preface composed by Sengrui;
it is recorded in both the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Records of the Three Jewels through the Ages) and the *Sengyou Lu*.

The *Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles is also titled *Acintyavyūha-parivarta* or simply *Mahādruma-kinnara-sūtra*; this second translation corresponds to Zhi Chen’s *Tunzhentuo-luo-jing*.

The *Jí yīqiè fúdé sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Collecting All Merit and Virtue) in three fascicles, recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*, is a different translation of the same text as the *Jí zhòngdé jīng* (Sūtra on Collecting Various Merits and Virtues) translated by Zhu Fahu and others; it is the third translation according to the *Zhēnjì sì lù*.

The *Sīyì fàntiān suǒwèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin) in four fascicles, also simply called the *Sīyì jīng*, is described in Sengyou’s catalog as the *Sīyì yì* (Meaning of Viśeṣacintin).
On the first day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of the Hongshi era, the second translation was produced at the Xiaoyao Garden.
It was translated together with Dharmarakṣa, Dharmamitra, Kumārajīva, and Saṃghavarman; all shared the same original text, as seen in the two Qin catalogs and the Sengyou catalog.

The *Lokasthiti-sūtra* consists of four fascicles, also known as the *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*, though it is sometimes in three fascicles. This third edition was produced together with Dharmarakṣa and Dharmamitra.

The *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* (諸法無行經), in two fascicles or one fascicle, is identical in its original text to the *Sarvadharmābhāvasamudgata-sūtra* (諸法本無經) translated by Jñānagupta during the Sui dynasty;
both were first recorded in the two Qin catalogs and the catalog of Sengyou.
The *Amitābha-sūtra* (阿彌陀經), also known as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (無量壽經), in one fascicle, was [translated] in the fourth year of Hongshi.
On the eighth day of the second month, the first translation was produced; it is identical in text to the *Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land* translated during the Tang dynasty.
It is recorded in the *Two Qin Records* and the *Monk You Record*. *The Sūtra of Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood*, one fascicle:

the second translation, which is identical in text to Dharmarakṣa’s *Sūtra of Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood*, was produced in the fourth year of Hongshi. It is recorded in the *Two Qin Records* and the *Monk You Record*.

*The Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent and Birth* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sūtra on Maitreya Receiving the Prediction*. It begins by stating that when the Great Wisdom Śāriputra and Maitreya come, it is the same text as [the previous] sūtra;
the fourth edition also calls it *The Sūtra on Maitreya Attaining Buddhahood*, or *The Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood upon Descent*, or simply *The Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood in This Very Life*.
This is recorded in the *Catalogue of the Two Qin Dynasties* (*Er-Qin Lu*) and the *Catalogue of Monk You* (*Sengyou Lu*). [This was translated by] Wenshu.
The *Śrīmañjuśrīparipṛcchābodhicittotpādasūtra*, one fascicle— also simply called the *Bodhisattvasūtra*, alternatively titled the *Gayāśīrṣasūtra* or the *Bodhicittācaraṇasūtra*—
was initially produced as the same text as the *Gayāśīrṣasūtra* and the *Hastikṣaśālāsūtra*.
Its inclusion as a separate *Bodhisattvasūtra*, one fascicle, in the *Catalogue of Scriptures* (*Jingtu*) within Sengyou’s record is an error.

*The Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*, one fascicle; the fourth edition, also titled *The Great Golden Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī Sūtra*, produced at the Xiaoyao Garden, including the complete methods for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*). [Dao]fang states that he saw it in the *Bielu*.
*The Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, three fascicles (or two fascicles), also simply called the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; the *Sengyou Lu* states: [it was translated by Kumārajīva].
The ninth fascicle of the New Śūraṃgama Sūtra, which is identical in text to the Fangdeng Shoulengyan Yongfu Ding Jing (Śūraṃgama Samādhi of Heroic Subjugation Sūtra),
is recorded in the Catalogue of Monk You as the *Asaṃkhyeya-prabhāsa-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (One Fascicle).
It is also called the *Asaṃkhyeya-prabhāsa-bodhisattva-bhāṣita-sūtra*, and also the *Acintya-prabhāsa-kumāra-bodhisattva-sūtra* (Fascicle Two).
The *Huashou jing* (Flower-Hand Sūtra), thirteen fascicles— also known as the *Huashou jing*,
alternatively titled the *Shezhushangen jing* (Sūtra on Gathering All Roots of Goodness) or the *Shezhufude jing* (Sūtra on Gathering All Merits)—

in ten, eleven, or twelve fascicles, was translated in the eighth year of Hongshi by Zhu Fahu from the same original text as the *Wusi yi haotong jing* (Sūtra of the Inconceivable Child). It is recorded in the *Changfang lu* (Catalogue of Changfang) and appears in the two Qin records.

The *Sūtra on the Brief Exposition of the Buddha’s Final Instructions at the Time of His Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Last Words* (*Yijiao jing*)—is recorded in the *Sengyou lu*.
The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas*, one fascicle, is recorded in the *Fashang lu*.
The *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, two fascicles—the second edition produced in the eighth year of the Hongshi era at Caotang Monastery—[totaling] three thousand [characters].
The Master [Kumārajīva] last produced this one chapter; the Sanskrit manuscript contained sixty-one chapters in total.
Upon completion of the translation, three hundred people, including Tanyong and others, simultaneously received the Bodhisattva precepts. Sengzhao received the *Jianjing* (Preface to the Scripture).

The *Fozang jing* (Buddha-treasury Sūtra), also known as the *Xuanze zhufa jing* (Sūtra on the Selection of All Dharmas), consists of four fascicles—or alternatively three or two—translated in the seventh year of the Hongshi era.
On the twelfth day of the sixth month, two copies of the *Qingjing pini fangguang jing* (Sūtra on the Pure Vinaya Vaipulya) in one fascicle were discovered;

this is the third appearance [of this text], recorded in the *Shiqi apitan lun* (Treatise on the Seventeen Abhidharmas), the *Monk You Lu* (Catalogue of Monk You), and identical in content to the *Wenshu jinglü jing* (Mañjuśrī Sūtra on the Pure Vinaya).

Also discovered was the *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) in one hundred fascicles—also known as the *Dazhidu jing lun* (Sūtra-Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) or the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The treatise consists of either seventy fascicles or one hundred ten fascicles;

it was translated at the Xiaoyao Garden during the summer of the fourth year of Hongshi and completed on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the seventh year, as recorded in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels through Successive Dynasties) and the *Sengyou Lu* (Catalogue of Sengyou).

It is also noted that there is a four-fascicle version titled the *Zhonglun* (Treatise on the Middle), or alternatively the *Zhongguan Lun* (Treatise on the Middle Way), consisting of eight fascicles, which was translated at the Great Monastery in the eleventh year of Hongshi.
The preface composed by Sengrui is recorded in the *Erqin lu* and the *Sengyou lu*, as well as in the earlier *Dazhidu lun*.
The *Shiermen lun*, one fascicle, was composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

it was translated at the Dasi Monastery in the tenth year of the Hongshi era, with the preface composed by Sengrui, as seen in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Baochang lu*. The *Bailun*, two fascicles, [was composed by] Deva.

The *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-śāstra* (or *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*) in fourteen fascicles was composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; it was translated in the sixth year of the Hongshi era and its preface was written by Sengzhao.

This is recorded in the *Records of the Two Qin* (*Er-Qin-lu*) and the *Record of Sengyou* (*Sengyou-lu*). Alternatively, it may be titled *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, or it may consist of twelve or fifteen fascicles;
this is recorded in the *Changfang-lu*. The *Mahāvyūha-sūtra-śāstra* in fifteen fascicles is also listed, though some versions omit the title.

The *Sūtra on the Letter* (Jīngzì), composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, consists of ten fascicles; it is listed in the Chángfáng Catalogue. The *Treatise on Generating the Bodhicitta* (*Fāpútíxīnlùn*) consists of two fascicles;
some call it the *Sūtra on Generating the Bodhicitta* (*Fāpútíxīnjīng*), and others refer to it as a "sūtra-treatise" (*jīnglùn*); it is listed in Lǐ Kuò’s catalogue.

The *Sūtra on Tending Cattle* (*Fàngniújīng*), also called the *Sūtra on Herding Oxen* (*Mùniújīng*), consists of one fascicle; it is an alternative translation of the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Fáng states this.

I have seen the *Bie lu hai ba de jing* (Separate Record of the Sutra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean) in one fascicle; this third edition is identical in text to the *Fa hai jing* (Sutra on the Dharma-Ocean).

I have also seen the *Chan mi yao jing* (Sutra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna) in three fascicles in the record of Fashang—some omit the character "jing" (sutra), calling it the *Chan mi yao fa* (Secret Essentials of Dhyāna)—or in four fascicles, which is identical in text to the edition translated by Zhi Qian and others;
this is the second edition. Fang states that he has seen the *Deng zhi yin* (Record of the Lamp’s Index) in the Separate Record.
*Yuanjing* (Discourse on Conditions), one fascicle; recorded in Li Kuò’s catalog. *Shisong Biqiu Jieben* (Ten Recitation Bhikṣu Precept Manual), one fascicle;

also called the *Shisong Bōluómótí Chájiejing* (Ten Recitation Prātimokṣa Precept Sūtra). This third edition is identical in text to those produced by Dharmagupta and others; recorded in Sēngyòu’s catalog.
*Chéngshí Lùn* (Tattvasiddhi Śāstra), twenty fascicles—or twenty-four, sixteen, or fourteen; translated during the Hongshǐ era.

On the eighth day of the ninth month of the thirteenth year, Yao Xian, the Grand Chancellor, requested [the scripture] to be brought forth; it was completed on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the fourteenth year.
Tan Gui and others received this work, which was composed by Harivarman nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.

It consists of three fascicles, titled the *Zuochan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation), also known as the *Pusa chanfa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Dhyāna Methods). It was first translated upon its initial emergence.
It is simply called the *Chan jing* (Sutra on Dhyāna), or the *Chan fa yao* (Essentials of the Dharma of Dhyāna), or the *Aranya xichan fa* (Method for Practicing Dhyāna in the Āraṇya);

The śramaṇa Kumārajīva—“Jīva” meaning “Child-Life” in the language of Qin, and also known as Kumārajīva—was given his name by combining elements from both his parents' names, as it is common in foreign naming conventions to base them upon one's father and mother. His father was named Kumārayāna, and his mother’s name was Jīvā; thus, he took these two names together to form his own.
He was a man from India whose family had served as ministers of state for generations.
Kumārajīva’s grandfather was Datta.
He was unconventional and stood out from the crowd, his reputation being esteemed throughout the realm.
His father, Kumārajīva’s paternal uncle Jūmoyán, was intelligent and possessed noble character;
when it came time for him to succeed to the相位 (prime ministerial position), he declined the appointment and left the household life.
Crossing the Pamir Mountains to the east,
the King of Kucha heard that he had renounced glory and abandoned secular life;
he held him in profound reverence and admiration.
He went out from the outskirts of the city to welcome him and invited him to serve as the National Preceptor.
The King had a younger sister who was twenty years of age.
His talent was awakened and his intellect sharp;
whatever he saw once, he could master,
and whatever he heard but once, he could recite.
Furthermore, her body had a red mole, a sign that she would give birth to a son of wisdom.
Although various states sought her hand in marriage, none succeeded.
When King Yan saw her, his heart was filled with desire, and he wished to take her as his consort.
When the king heard this, he was greatly delighted and compelled him to take her as his wife.
Subsequently, Kumārajīva was born.
While he was in the womb, his mother’s wisdom and understanding were twice as great as usual.
He went to the Great Kaniṣka Monastery to listen to the sutras.
Suddenly, he spontaneously mastered the language of India;
in his challenging questions and inquiries, he invariably exhausted the depths of their profound meaning.
The assembly all marveled at this with admiration.
The arhat Dharmaghoṣa said,
"This woman must surely be carrying a wise child."
He recounted for him the evidence regarding Śāriputra’s time in the womb;
subsequently, Kumārajīva was born,
possessing a precocity like that of a divine being.
After Kumārajīva was born, he forgot his previous words.
Some time later, his mother left the household life to practice the Way and attained the first fruit of sainthood.
At the age of seven, Kumārajīva also left the household life together with him;
receiving the sūtras from his teacher, he recited a thousand gāthās daily,
each gāthā consisting of thirty-two syllables.
The work comprises thirty-two thousand words.
Having completed his recitation of the Abhidharma as transmitted by his teacher,
he attained spontaneous understanding of its meaning, such that there was no subtle point that was not fully clarified.
At that time, the people of Kucha,
seeing that his mother— the King’s daughter— received such great offerings and honors,
took Kumārajīva along with them to avoid her.
At the age of nine, Kumārajīva proceeded to Kaśmīra,
where he encountered the renowned and virtuous Dharma Master Bandhudatta,
who was the younger cousin of the King of Kaśmīra.
Profound and pure, he possessed a vast capacity for understanding;
there was nothing among the Tripiṭaka and the nine divisions of the scriptures that he did not thread together with meticulous detail.
He could also recite a thousand verses daily.
His reputation spread throughout various countries.
Once Kumārajīva arrived, he served him as his teacher and subsequently recited the *Madhyama Āgama* and the *Dīrgha Āgama* from within the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*.
It totaled four million words.
Every time Kumārajīva engaged in debate with Dharmadatta, he deeply admired and respected him,
and his reputation reached the King.
The king immediately invited him inside and assembled the non-Buddhist masters of logic to engage him in mutual debate and refutation.
When their breaths first met,
the non-Buddhists disparaged him for his youth, claiming that his words were somewhat unorthodox.
Kumārajīva seized this opportunity to humble them.
The non-Buddhists were defeated and humbled; filled with remorse, they remained speechless.
The King, increasingly respectful and awed, provided daily a pair of goose carcasses, three *dǒu* each of non-glutinous rice and flour, and six *shèng* of ghee.
Furthermore, as a supreme offering to the foreign country,
the monks residing at the temple dispatched five senior monks and ten śrāmaṇeras to attend to and sweep the grounds, serving like disciples.
He was thus held in such high esteem.
When he reached the age of twelve, his mother took him back to Kucha.
Upon arriving in Mozhī (Yuezhi),...
On the northern mountain there was an arhat who,
seeing this, marveled at it and said to his mother:
"You must always protect him.
If this śrāmaṇera does not break the precepts by the age of thirty-five,
he shall greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma and deliver countless people."
He was no different from Upagupta;
had his precepts not been incomplete, he would have been incapable of such deeds.
He could at best be described as a Dharma Master of brilliant talent and refined insight.
When Kumārajīva arrived at the kingdom of Kucha, he carried the Buddha’s almsbowl upon his head.
He thought to himself, "The shape of this bowl is exceedingly large; why is it so light?"
It was so heavy that he could not bear its weight;
he let out a cry as he lowered it.
His mother asked him the reason for this.
He replied,
"It is because my mind has conceptual discrimination that the bowl appears to have weight.
In the kingdom of Kashgar, Kumārajīva recited the Abhidharma.
The six *pāda* treatises, the various gateways,
the *Ekottarika Āgama*,
and his return to Kucha brought his fame to cover all the kingdoms.
At that time, the assembly of monks in Kucha, numbering over ten thousand, suspected him was no ordinary person;

Consequently, he was not included in the sequence for offering incense.
He then extensively studied the four Vedas, the treatises on the five sciences, and the scriptures of the non-Buddhists;

attaining such profound insight into auspiciousness and misfortune that his words were as infallible as a tally.
By nature he was straightforward and forthright, not strictly adhering to minor rules of propriety;

yet Kumārajīva remained self-possessed in his mind and never took it to heart.
Later, he studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Vimalākṣa and received instruction in the Mahāyāna from Sūryasoma,
whereupon he exclaimed:
In the past, I studied the Hīnayāna;
it was like a person who, not recognizing gold, mistook brass for something exquisite.
Thereupon, I extensively sought out the essential meanings.
He recited the Madhyamaka-śāstra, the Śata-śāstra, the Dvādaśamukha-śāstra, and other works.
After some time, Kumārajīva’s mother took her leave to travel to India;
she said to Bai Chun, the King of Kucha:
"Your kingdom will soon decline; I shall now depart.
When he arrived in India, he advanced to attain the third fruit of the path.
As Kumārajīva’s mother was about to leave, she said to him:

Yet, you will derive no personal benefit from this."
"What can be done about this?
Kumārajīva replied,
"The Way of a Mahāsattva is to benefit others even at the cost of one's own life."
"If I must ensure that the Great Transformation spreads to cleanse and awaken the ignorant masses,
I shall have no regrets even if my person must endure the suffering of the cauldrons and furnaces.
Thereupon, he remained in Kucha.
While Zhiwang was at the New Temple and had obtained the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,

Kumārajīva, knowing this was the work of Māra, made his resolve even more firm.
After Māra had departed, Kumārajīva’s name was revealed as "Xiǎn" (Manifest), and he continued to recite and study it.
Later, at the Great Temple of Kukkutapāda, he read Mahāyāna sūtras.
Suddenly, a voice was heard from the air, saying, "You are a wise man; why do you read this?
Kumārajīva replied:
"You are but a minor Māra; it is fitting that you depart at once.
My mind is like the earth and cannot be turned.
Stay for two years."
He recited the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras extensively, penetrating their profound mysteries.
The King of Kucha had a golden lion throne constructed for him and spread it with brocade cushions from Da Qin.
He caused Kumārajīva to ascend and preach the Dharma.
Later, he went to Kaśmīra and fully explained the wondrous meaning of the One Vehicle to his teacher, Bandhudatta.
The Master was moved to realization and submitted his heart;
he immediately paid obeisance to Kumārajīva as his teacher,
saying, "I am the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teacher of my Upādhyāya."
"The Upādhyāya is my teacher of the Mahāyāna.
In the various kingdoms of the Western Regions, everyone was awed by Kumārajīva’s divine brilliance and held him in universal reverence;
whenever he delivered a lecture, [the assembly would gather].
The kings knelt on their haunches beside their seats and commanded Kumārajīva to step upon them;
such was the degree of esteem in which he was held.
Kumārajīva’s Way shook the Western Regions and its fame spread throughout the Eastern Lands.
In the first month of the thirteenth year of the Jiànyuán era of the Fú clan, when the cyclical year was Dīngchū,
the Grand Astrologer reported that a star had appeared in the celestial division corresponding to the foreign lands.
When a person of great virtue and wisdom enters to assist the Central Kingdom,
Yao Jian— who had long heard of Kumārajīva’s reputation— suddenly realized it and said,

Is it not this? In the nineteenth year, Yao Xian dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang and others,

As he was about to depart, he said to Kumārajīva:
"I have heard that there is one named Kumārajīva there who possesses a profound understanding of the characteristics of dharmas and is well-versed in the principles of yin and yang."
"He is the patriarch of that school;
I have long contemplated this.
If you can capture Kucha, I shall immediately dispatch an express messenger to bring Kumārajīva here."
Before Guangjun had arrived,
Kumārajīva said to its king, Baizun:

There will be a formidable adversary.
A person from the east shall arrive at the hour of the Sun (the seventh watch).
You should receive them with respect and not oppose their advance.
Fu Chun did not submit and fought;

By nature, Guang was negligent and arrogant, and thus he had not yet gauged the extent of Kumārajīva’s wisdom and capacity.
Seeing that he was still young in years, they treated him as an ordinary man and mocked him.
As Kumārajīva was thus driven to the limit,
he eventually compromised his integrity.
Some even forced him to ride an ox or mount a vicious horse,
intending to cause him to fall;
yet Kumārajīva always maintained patience, never showing the slightest change in his expression.
Guang felt ashamed and desisted.
On his return journey, Guang stationed his army at the foot of the mountain so that the officers and soldiers could rest.
Kumārajīva said, "We must not remain here; we will certainly face distress.
It is advisable to move the army to the heights of Long."
Guang did not accept [the advice].
That night, as expected, heavy rain fell and a sudden flood arose;

Daowang began to treat him with reverence and wonder.
Kumārajīva said to Daowang, "This is a land of calamity and ruin; it is not fitting to linger here."
"By calculating the numbers and measuring the course of destiny, it is clear we should return quickly.
Along the way, there will surely be a blessed land where we may dwell.

Upon arriving in Liangzhou, he heard that Fu Jian had already died;

Not long after these words were spoken, everything occurred exactly as he had said.

In the third month of the year of the Xin-chou cycle, the third year of Hongshi, a tree with joined branches grew in the courtyard of the ancestral temple.

Xing [considered that] the Buddha-way is profound and subtle; its practice consists solely of goodness, and faith is the excellent ford for escaping suffering and the grand standard for governing the world.

until the fourteenth year, the *Ren-zi* year.

Although the general meaning may be captured, the literary style is profoundly alienated;
it is like chewing food for someone else—not only does one lose the flavor, but the act itself is offensive.
This causes people to vomit and retch.
Kumārajīva once composed a verse in praise of the śramaṇa Fǎhuó, saying:

With his wings broken here, what more could he discuss?

Kumārajīva was a man whose spirit and character were clear and penetrating, and whose lofty bearing rose above the crowd.

At that time, there was the śramaṇa Sengrui,
whom Daoxing greatly admired.

He was intelligent and eloquent, and had studied extensively;
there were few secular texts from the Western lands that he had not read and recited.
Yet, he served as a patriarch for the non-Buddhist outsiders of that foreign country.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong extensively propagating the Buddha-dharma,
he was immediately filled with resolve and said to his disciples,
"How could we allow the teachings of the Śākya clan to be transmitted to Zhendan alone?"
Yet, he caused our orthodox teachings to not yet reach the Eastern lands;
consequently, he traveled far on camelback carrying scriptures to enter Chang’an.
Yao Xing saw that his mouth and eyes were clever and dexterous.
Some were indeed perplexed by this, but the Brahmin Xing then said:
"The ultimate Way has no fixed direction; each honors its own practice."
I have therefore come from afar to request that you compete with the monks of Qin in the power of debate;
whichever side proves superior shall propagate its teachings.
Xing immediately granted his permission.
At that time, the monastic community from all four directions in Guanzhong looked upon one another with a sense of deficiency;
none dared to step forward.
Kumārajīva said to Tanyou,
"This non-Buddhist is exceptionally clever compared to others;
in a contest of speech, he will surely prevail."
How could it be that the unsurpassed Great Way should be made to yield for their sake by those such as us?
This is truly lamentable.
If we were to allow the non-Buddhists to act according to their whims and achieve their ambitions,
it would mean that the axle of our Wheel of Dharma has been shattered;
how could such a thing be permitted?
"As far as I have observed, you alone possess this quality.
Dao Rong reflects that his own talent and capacity are no inferior [to yours],
yet he has not yet fully read the scriptures of the non-Buddhist outsiders from the Western Regions."
He then secretly had someone copy the list of scriptures read by the Brahmin;
upon seeing it once, he could recite it from memory.
Subsequently, he fixed a date to engage in a formal debate.
When Yao Xing personally attended, the high officials all assembled;
monks from throughout Guanzhong gathered from near and far.
At that time, Daorong engaged in debate with the Brahman, matching him point for point.
His sharp eloquence and soaring insights were beyond their reach.
At that time, although the Brahmin realized for himself that his arguments had been defeated,
he still took pride in his extensive learning.
Daorong then arranged the books he had read and further provided a comprehensive discussion of the titles of the classics and histories of the Qin region;
the number of scrolls and fascicles was three times greater than before.
Kumārajīva, seizing the momentum, further mocked him, saying:
"Have you not heard that the Great Qin has vast learning?
Why have you so lightly come from afar?"
The Brahmin felt shame and submission in his heart and prostrated at the feet of Daorong;
within ten days, he departed without further ado.
That the fortune of the image was manifested once again was due to the power of Kumārajīva and Daorong.
Furthermore, while the bhikṣu Beidu was in Pengcheng,
he heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an,
whereupon he sighed and said:
I have been parted from this son in play for over three hundred years;
we have remained in profound obscurity without a set time for reunion,
and can only hope to meet again in a future life.
As Kumārajīva was approaching his death, he summoned his strength to bid farewell to the assembly of monks, saying:
"We met because of the Dharma, yet we have not been able to fully express our mutual intentions.
Now that we are about to part for another world, how can I speak of my sorrow?"
I have, out of my own ignorance, falsely assumed the role of a translator.
If what I have transmitted is free from error,
may my tongue not be scorched or withered after my body is cremated.
He passed away during the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty.
His body was cremated according to foreign rites in the Xiaoyao Garden;
when the firewood was consumed and his form had vanished, only his tongue remained unchanged.
One may trust that the propagation of the Dharma has its signs of efficacy; at the time of Master Kumārajīva’s passing, various records were inconsistent.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states that he passed away on the twentieth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of Hongshi at Chang’an.
Some say seven years;
others say eight years.
The tradition takes eleven as the correct number.
This is not so. According to the postscript to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it states:

"On the eighth day of the ninth month of the year of Shihwei, the thirteenth year of Hongshi of the Da Qin [Later Qin] dynasty, Yao Xian, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, requested that this treatise be translated."
It was completed on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the following year.
According to this, at the end of the fourteenth year,
Kumārajīva had still not passed away.

Furthermore, according to Sengzhao’s memorial to the Qin ruler Yao Xing regarding the "Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa," it states that Zhao was in the service of Master Kumārajīva for more than ten years.
If Kumārajīva produced the scriptures in the fourth year [of the Jianyuan era] and passed away in the eleventh year, this would amount to only eight years.
It has not yet been ten years.
How can it be said that more than ten years have passed?
Therefore, we know that [the work] was merely completed during the Hongshi era.
It is impossible to fix the dates and years with certainty; however, regarding the number of fascicles in the scriptural divisions translated by Kumārajīva,
various accounts differ as to their quantity,
and in the *Chángfáng lù*, the number is even more extensive.
Now, upon careful examination and comparison, it appears that most are separate recensions.
Alternatively, some may have multiple titles for a single work,
or these may be errors introduced by the compilers of the catalogues.
The items are listed as follows.
They are now all deleted.

Regarding the sixty-first fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), Sengyou’s catalog states it was translated by Kumārajīva; [the portion] prior to the first fifty [fascicles] is now deleted.

The first eight fascicles were translated by Kumārajīva; they are not his direct translations but rather renderings of his oral explanations. The final three fascicles were subsequently produced by Vimalākṣa and placed at the end.
These have already been recorded in other catalogs and are not included here.

Regarding the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in twenty fascicles, Fáng states that it is the second translation, as seen in separate records. Now, comparing the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* with the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* (Dapin)...

When the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) was being translated together [with others], there arose an attachment to the old version; when Kumārajīva produced the new version, some claimed that the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Fangguang) was the old version translated by Kumārajīva.

If one asks what this "old version" is, it is clear that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is the new version and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is the old; to record both versions as duplicates is a grave error.
Regarding the twenty-fascicle *Collection of Prajñā Sūtras and Śāstras*, Fang states that he saw it in the *Wu lu*; however, I now maintain that this collection is [the work] in question.

It was Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu who, seeing that the textual passages of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* were so voluminous and accumulated that beginners found them difficult to seek out, abridged the redundancies and trimmed the disorder to ensure the prose and substance were well-formed. He compiled it into twenty fascicles;

it is also called the *Essentials of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Dazhidu lun yaoyue*) or the *Essential Extracts of the Commentary* (*Shilun yaochaoyao*). This is a condensation of the original treatise by Master Huiyuan, not a separate translation by Kumārajīva.

*Yechan fayao* (Essentials of the Yecha Dhyāna Method), three fascicles; the lower volume contains a note stating: "Originally translated in the first year of Hongshi, re-corrected [by Daorong]. Sengrui composed the preface.

Since it says "originally translated" and then "re-corrected," it is inconsistent to retain both names. According to Sengrui’s *Sūtra Preface*, this is the *Zuochan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Sitting Meditation).
*Asuoruo xichan fayao jing* (Āśvaghosa’s Sūtra on the Essentials of Practicing Dhyāna), two fascicles; Fazang states he saw it in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue).

Some claim that this scripture is identical in essence to the *Zuochan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation) but differs in its outward appearance; however, we maintain that this is not so.
This is simply another title for the *Zuochan sanmei jing*. Examining its textual passages from beginning to end, they are largely the same; thus, it is the original version, not a revised edition.
One fascicle of the *Lengqie zhuangyan jing* (The Sūtra of the Adornment of the Garland), recorded by Fang, states that he saw it in Li Kuò’s catalogue and was instructed to conform to the sūtra.
The postscript states that this was translated by Dharmayaśas and not by Kumārajīva; it has now been moved and appended to his record.

*Shíxiānglùn* (Treatise on the True Nature), one fascicle (*Gāosēngzhuàn* says two fascicles). Kumārajīva compiled and produced this for Yao Xing; as it was not a translation from an Indic original, it is omitted [from the standard catalog].
In ancient times, the character "Xìng" (性) was used for "Fóguó" (佛國); the *Yuànxíngfǎdiǎnjīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of Vows and Conduct) was sometimes written as "Shēnghé" (生和) or "Chū" (出).
The Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-pariśuddhi Sūtra; the Buddha-ṣṭhīvana-kāsa-daśadig-vyāpana Sūtra;
the Buddha-samavartana-niḥsṛta-bodhisattva Sūtra; the Mārakarma Sūtra; the Atīta-anantaprabha-viśuddha-buddhakṣetra Sūtra;
the Gaganagañja-bodhisattva-pṛcchā-dhāraṇī-sūtra-kuśala-mūla-pramāṇa Sūtra (also known as the *Puṇya-pramāṇa* Sūtra); the Māra-dharman-dhātu Sūtra; and the Śukra-māra Sūtra.

The King firmly believed in ten sutras: the *Sūtra of Verses on the Buddha’s Disciples Transforming the Son of Māra*, the *Sūtra of the Conversion of Māra*, the *Sūtra of the Demon King Changing His Form*, and the eight sutras beginning with the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Cough*;

these were all derived from the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, the *Dhāraṇī Dharma-gate* from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of the Sixfold Earthquakes*, and the *Sūtra of Bodhisattva Maitreya’s Original Vow to Attain Buddhahood When the Time Arrives*.
The *Buddhavikurvaṇasamayasattvasūtra*, the *Pūrvasyāṃ diśi Supuṣpālokadhātubuddhāsana-prakampasūtra*,

and the *Dhāraṇīsūtra*— these four sūtras appeared together. Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīkasūtra*, the *Śukrarājasūtra*, the *Buddhapūrvabodhisattvahariṇarājasūtra*, and the *Bodhisattvahaṃsarājasūtra*—
these three sūtras, including the *Śukrarāja*, appeared together with the *Ṣaṭpāramitāsaṃgrahasūtra* and the *Amitasukhābuddhakṣetrasūtra*.

It is also called the *Gokuraku-kyō* (Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra); the *Buddha-āmantrita-asura-mahāsāgara-hāni-kyō* (Sūtra on the Buddha Questioning the Asuras Regarding the Decrease of the Great Ocean) is from the *Madhyama Āgama*;
the *Buddha-jikken-sen-fukurin-sō-kyō* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Footprints Showing the Thousand-Spoked Wheel Mark) is from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
