and the three sūtras—the *Buddha-shin-sōji-kyō* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Mind Dhāraṇī), the *Go-niu-ō-kyō* (Sūtra on the Water Buffalo King), and the *Usagi-ō-kyō* (Sūtra on the Rabbit King)—are all from the *Chushō-kyō* (Collection of Birth Stories). [Also included are] the *Hikkyū to Bi Kyō* (Sūtra of the Monkey and the Maidservant).

The *Xi zhì biàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Transformation Caused by Play), the *Wáng hòu wéi qiāngláng jīng* (Sūtra on the Queen Becoming a Dung Beetle), and the two sūtras concerning the *míhóu* (monkey) and others all appear in the *Zá pìyù jīng* (Miscellaneous Parables Sūtra).

The *Bǐqiū yīnggòng fǎxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Dharma Practice of the Bhikṣu’s Receiving Offerings) was classified as a doubtful scripture by Sengyou; it is currently also included in the *Yì lù* (Record of Doubtful Scriptures).
Altogether, there are thirty-five works comprising one hundred and thirty-six fascicles.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* in fifty-eight fascicles was translated on the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of Hongshi at Zhong Temple; this is recorded in the *Qin Lu*. This one work in fifty-eight fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Puṇyatrāta,
whose name means "Flower of Merit" in the language of Qin,
was a native of Kaśmīra.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and was renowned for his observance of the precepts and their regulations.
He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka,
specializing particularly in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya).
He became the preeminent master for foreign teachers.
People of the time all claimed that he had already attained the fruits of sainthood.
In the tenth year of the Hongshi era, he took up his staff and entered Guanzhong.
The Qin ruler Yao Xing treated him with the etiquette due to a guest of honor.
Kumārajīva, in turn, held his precepts and conduct in high esteem and revered him deeply.
Previously, although the sūtras had been transmitted, the Vinaya-piṭaka had not yet been elucidated.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was already well-versed in this school,
everyone thought of him with longing; thus,
on the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of Hongshi (the Jiachen year), they [invited him].
More than six hundred śramaṇas who had gathered for the study of the Dharma invited Dharmatāra to Zhong Temple in Chang'an.
The Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* was recited,
and Kumārajīva translated it into the language of Qin;
two-thirds of the text were successfully rendered.
Tara fell ill and suddenly passed away;
because his great undertaking was not yet completed when the master artisan died,
the depth of their grief and regret surpassed ordinary sorrow.
Next, there was the śramaṇa Dharmaruci from the Western Regions— translated into Chinese as Fale— who had left his home to enter the Way and was particularly renowned for upholding the Vinaya Piṭaka.
In the autumn of the seventh year of Hongshi, he arrived at Guanzhong.
When Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu heard that [Master] Zhi was well-versed in the *vinaya*,
he hoped to obtain a definitive understanding of the Vinaya-piṭaka;
he therefore sent a letter to establish friendly relations, saying:
The rise of Buddhism first occurred in the superior states [of China].
Since its initial dissemination, more than four hundred years have passed,
yet the moral standards and disciplinary forms of the śramaṇas remain particularly deficient.
Recently, the Western Region monk Puṇyatāra, a native of Kaśmīra,
was reciting the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
There was also the Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
A man of versatile talent and broad learning served as the translator; however,
before more than half of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* had been completed,
Puṇyatāra passed away prematurely, and the work was suspended mid-course.
I deeply regret that I was unable to complete this great undertaking; my lamentation is profound.
I have heard by report that you, O Virtuous One, carry this scripture with you at all times.
I am truly delighted to have encountered such a treasure.
When the movement of destiny arrives, how could it be a matter of mere human affairs?
I imagine that you, who propagate the Way for the sake of all beings, will be moved by the times;
when someone knocks at your door, your heart will surely be free from any stinginess.
If one can serve as a follower of the Vinaya studies,
complete this sūtra text,
and reveal the holy life (brahmacarya).
He cleanses their ears and eyes,
ensuring that those who have first entered the stream do not lose the ford to the Unsurpassed.
Those who harbor superior practices find the sun and moon ever more radiant.
This is indeed a profound bounty and a deep virtue;
both humans and deities are moved by it alike.
I pray that you will graciously extend your compassion and not let your former intentions falter.
Once Zhu Faliu received the letter from Huiyuan as well as the earnest invitation from Yao Xing,
he then worked together with Kumārajīva to complete the translation of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
They meticulously examined, verified, categorized, and finalized its regulations.
However, Kumārajīva still regretted that the prose was cumbersome and not yet refined.
Subsequently, as Kumārajīva passed away, he did not have the opportunity to edit and polish it.
Daoyou then resided at the Great Monastery in Chang'an.
Hui-guan wished to invite him to go to the capital of Yangdu.
Zhi said,
"That land has both people and the Dharma."
"It is sufficient to benefit the world.
I shall now proceed to places where there is no teaching of the Vinaya.
Thereupon, he traveled to convert others in different regions.
One knows not where it has gone.
The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle; its initial translation may lack the word "Bodhisattva" and is identical in substance to the *Ākāśagarbha-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
It is a separate division of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*. After [the translator] returned to foreign lands from the Tripiṭaka, he obtained this sūtra in Kaśmīra.

It was sent by a merchant to Liangzhou and seen by Daohui. According to the *Song Qi Lu* and the *Sengyou Lu*, the *Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra* in twenty-two fascicles was translated, beginning in the fourteenth year of Hongshi and concluding in the fifteenth year.

The Śramaṇa Fonian of Liangzhou acted as the oral translator (*yanyì*), while the Śramaṇa Daohan of the Qin state served as the scribe (*bishòu*). This is recorded in the *Sengrui Er Qin Lu* and the *Seng [you] Lu*.
The *Yùlù Gāosēngzhuàn* (Record of Eminent Monks Compiled by Yù) and other sources state that the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya) consists of sixty fascicles;

it is also called the *Tánwúdélǜběn* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya Original), translated in forty-five fascicles, or as some say forty or forty-four fascicles. There are also versions today consisting of seventy fascicles.
It was brought forth in the temple in the tenth year of the Hóngshǐ era, with Huìbiàn serving as the oral translator; this is seen in the *Jìnshì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty).

The *Sifen sengjieben* (Four-Part Monastic Precept Manual) in one fascicle, sometimes omitting the character "seng" (monastic), also known as the *Tanwude jieben* (Precept Manual of the Dharmaguptaka School),
is found in the *Jin shi zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the *Sengyou lu* (Sengyou’s Catalog). The above four works comprise eighty-four fascicles,
and their texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Buddhayaśas—
“Buddha” meaning “Awakened” (Jue) in the Qin language,

and “Yaśas” meaning “Renown” (Cheng)— is sometimes called Juecheng. In the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), he is translated as Jueming (“Awakened Brilliance”), which slightly deviates from the original meaning.
He was a man from the country of Kaśmīra,
born into the Brahmin caste and whose family had followed non-Buddhist paths for generations.
Once, a śramaṇa came to his house to beg for alms.
His father, filled with rage, ordered someone to strike him.
Consequently, the father’s hands and feet became cramped and paralyzed, rendering him unable to walk or move.
He then consulted a diviner.
He replied,
"This is because I have offended a worthy man and the spirits by sitting here.
I now request that this śramaṇa accept my sincere repentance for my transgression."
After several days, he was cured.
Consequently, Yaśas was ordained as his disciple;
at that time, he was thirteen years old.
Once, while traveling with his teacher through a vast wilderness, they encountered a tiger.
The teacher wished to flee and hide,
but Yaśas said:
"This tiger, having already eaten its fill, will certainly not harm anyone.
Shortly thereafter, the tiger departed.
As he proceeded forward, he indeed saw the remains of meat.
The Master secretly marveled at this.
By the age of fifteen,
he could recite five or six ten-thousand-character passages of scripture each day.
The monastery where he resided was constantly occupied with alms-gathering outside, so that his recitation and study were neglected.
There was an arhat who,
valuing his intelligence and acumen, [took him under his care].
He constantly begged for alms to provide for him.
At nineteen, he had recited several million words of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras;
however, by nature he was simple and haughty, and he tended to rely too heavily on his own intellectual insights.
Because he considered himself a teacher of only a few,
he was not held in high esteem by the community of monks;
he was valued merely for his graceful deportment and his skill in conversation.
Those who saw him forgot their deep resentment.
When he reached the age for receiving the full precepts, no one came forward to preside over the ordination platform;
thus, even at the age when one should stand as a teacher, he remained a śrāmaṇera.
He then studied the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) under his maternal uncle.
He became extensively proficient in various worldly arts and techniques.
It was not until he was twenty-seven that he finally received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
He constantly made recitation his primary task, never letting the scrolls leave his hands.
Each time he sat upright to contemplate the meaning,
he was unaware that the day had passed in emptiness.
His single-minded devotion was such as this.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Śālukya.
At that time, the Crown Prince Dharmaputra—which means "Son of the Dharma" in the language of Qin—beheld his dignified and elegant countenance.
When asked where he had come from,
Yaśas replied with eloquence;
the Prince was delighted by this.
He was subsequently invited to reside within the palace,
where he was treated with great honor and generosity.
Later, Kumārajīva arrived and studied under him.
They held one another in great esteem; Kumārajīva followed his mother back to the east, while Guṇabhadra remained behind.
Shortly thereafter, the king passed away and the crown prince ascended the throne.
At that time, Fu Jian dispatched Lü Guang to attack Kucha.
The King of Kucha urgently sought military aid from Kashgar.
The King of Kashgar personally led his troops to rescue him.
He sent Yaśas to remain and assist the crown prince,
entrusting him with the subsequent administration;
however, before the relief army could arrive, Kucha had already been defeated.
When the King returned, he recounted in detail how Kumārajīva had been seized by Guṇabhadra,
whereupon he sighed and said,
"Although I have known Kumārajīva for a long time..."
Our hearts' long-held longing remains unfulfilled;
how could we have expected to meet again after suddenly becoming captives?
We remained parted for over ten years until the King passed away.
Consequently, he arrived in Kucha, where the transformation of the Dharma was flourishing.
At that time, Kumārajīva was in Guzang and sent a messenger to invite him;
[Guṇabhadra] packed his provisions and intended to depart.
The people of the country requested that he remain, so he stayed for another year.
Later, he said to his disciples,
"I wish to seek out Kumārajīva."
"You should pack your things secretly and set out at night so that no one knows.
Your disciple said,
'I fear that if we are pursued by dawn, we will not avoid having to return again.'"
Yaśas then took a bowl of clear water,
cast medicinal herbs into it, and recited several dozen words of incantation.
He gave it to his disciple to wash his feet, and they set out that very night.
By the time dawn arrived, they had traveled several hundred li.
He asked his disciples,
"What have you perceived?"
He replied,
"I have heard nothing but the sound of a violent wind,
and tears have simply flowed from my eyes."
Yaśas then washed his feet with consecrated water and rested.
At dawn the next day, the people of the country pursued him,
but having already traveled several hundred li, they could not catch up.
Xing arrived at Guzang,
while Kumārajīva had already entered Chang’an.
Upon hearing that Xing had reached Guzang, Kumārajīva [sent a messenger].
Fayuan urged Daoxing to welcome him,
but Daoxing did not yet accept him.
Shortly thereafter, he commanded Kumārajīva to translate the scriptural treasury.
Kumārajīva said:
"In propagating the teachings of the Dharma, it is appropriate that both the words and their meanings be perfectly integrated.
Although I have recited the text, I have not yet mastered its meaning."
They had not yet mastered its principles;
only Buddhayaśas had a profound understanding of the essential meaning of the scriptures,
and he was currently residing in Guzang.
I pray that you issue an edict to summon him.
Let his words be examined three times before being committed to writing,
so that these subtle teachings do not fall into oblivion and may be trusted for a thousand years.
Xing followed his advice and immediately dispatched an envoy to invite him.
Although he was presented with generous gifts, he refused them all;
only after repeated messengers had earnestly exhorted him did he finally arrive at Chang’an.
Emperor Xing personally went out to inquire after him.
He established a separate new monastery within the Xiaoyao Garden and provided the fourfold offerings.
He did not accept [offerings],
but partook of only a single meal during his daily alms-round.
At that time, Kumārajīva produced the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
For more than a month, he had been hesitant and wavering,
and had not yet taken up his brush; however,
once Yaśas arrived, [he proceeded].
As they deliberated together to resolve their differences, the arguments and principles were finally settled.
More than three thousand monastics and laypeople all marveled at the excellence of his essential insights.
Shi was a man with red facial hair.
He was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā*,
and thus his contemporaries called him "The Red-Bearded Vibhāṣā Master.
Having served as the teacher of Kumārajīva, he...
He was also called Mahāvibhāṣa.
Although the fourfold assembly offered him robes, alms bowls, and bedding that filled three rooms,
he did not set his mind upon them.
Xing built a monastery south of the city to house him as a source of merit.
Yaśas had previously recited the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya;
Yao Shuang, the Commandant of the Metropolitan Police (or, according to some accounts, Yao Shi), requested that he produce a translation of it.

Xing suspected that there were omissions or errors [in the translations] and thus tested Guṇabhadra by having him recite forty-odd sheets each from the Qiang-language scriptures and medical prescriptions.
On the third day, he took up the text and reviewed it;
there was not a single character in error.
The assembly marveled at his powerful memory.
In the tenth year of Hongshi, the Wushen year,
he translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* along with the *Dīrgha-āgama* and other sūtras;
it was only completed in the fifteenth year, the Gui-chou year.
The śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou translated it into the Qin language,
while Daohan recorded it by pen.
Upon completion of the translation, they dissolved the assembly.
Xing Qin offered Yaśas ten thousand bolts of silk,
all of which he refused to accept.
The Buddha then thought that Daohan should offer one thousand bolts of silk each.
Five hundred śramaṇas of renowned virtue all offered him heavy gifts and alms.
Yaśas later returned to Kaśmīra, and his final destination remains unknown.
The Preface to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: [as cited above].
In the year of Renchen, there was a śramaṇa from the kingdom of Jin named Zhī Fǎlǐng.
Traveling west across the shifting sands with the distant goal of India, his route passed through Yutian.
There he met the śramaṇa Buddhayaśas, a Tripitaka master of the Mahāsāṃghika school who embodied the Mahāyāna.
Talented, brilliant, and widely learned, he was thoroughly versed in the Sūtras and Vinaya;
having mastered the recitation of the Tripiṭaka and the Vaipulya sūtras, he immediately gathered a vast collection of various scriptures within a vihāra in that country.
Returning in the year Wushen, he first arrived at the state of Qin. The ruler of Qin, Yao Xian, joyfully requested that the Vinaya Piṭaka be translated that very year.
At that time, more than three hundred śramaṇas who maintained the Vinaya were assembled at Zhong Temple in Chang’an; [Dharmakṣema] then appointed his disciple Huibian as the translator.
The year *renchen* corresponds to the seventh year of the Jianchu era of the Qin dynasty; the year *wushen* corresponds to the tenth year of the Hongshi era.
Furthermore, there is another account stating that Guṇabhadra, together with Fonian and others, collated the Sanskrit manuscripts brought by Dharmakṣema before translating them.
Various accounts differ slightly, and it is not yet clear which version is authoritative.
Furthermore, according to both Sengzhao’s preface to the *Dīrgha Āgama* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*,
it was stated that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* was translated in the twelfth year of Hongshi.
This may be stated according to the conclusion of the [corresponding] section.
*The Sūtra of Kṣema* (one fascicle), translated during the Long’an era of the Eastern Jin dynasty at Baisha Monastery in Guangzhou for the laywoman Zhang Puming, was included in the Jin Records;
it is appended here following the person [of the translator], as seen in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Chang*.
*Fánglù lèyíngluò zhuāngyán fāngbiàn pǐn jīng* (Sūtra on the Chapter of the Expedient Means of the Adornment of Necklaces of Music), one fascicle;

also known as the *Zhuǎnnǚshēn Púsà wèndá jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions and Answers of the Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Female Body). Third, it is recorded by Lì Kuò that this is identical in text to the *Shùnquán fāngbiàn jīng* (Sūtra on Accordance with Expedient Means) translated by Dharmarakṣa.
According to the colophon at the end of the sūtra, it was brought out by Guṇabhadra; therefore, it has been moved and included here [following] the *Śāriputra-ābhidharma*.

The *Abhidharma-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā-śāstra) in twenty-two fascicles—sometimes titled with the character "wu" (negation), or in twenty fascicles, or in thirty fascicles—was translated together with Dharmagupta at Shiyang Monastery;
the preface was composed by Shi Daobiao. This is recorded in Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji*, Baochang’s *Chusanzangji ji*, and the *Gaoseng zhuan*.
These three works comprise twenty-four fascicles in total; the first work consists of one fascicle, which is missing from the original. Following this...
The two sections, comprising twenty-three fascicles, are extant.

The śramaṇa Dharmayaśas—translated into Chinese as Fǎchēng (Dharmayaśas)—is listed in the *Gaosēngzhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) as Fǎmíng, though this is a semantic error. He was a native of Jibin.
From his youth he was fond of learning;
at the age of fourteen, he was recognized by Puṇyatāra.
As he grew older, his physical bearing was lofty and vigorous, and he possessed a refined spiritual intelligence.
One should peruse the sutras and vinaya to attain clear awakening that transcends the masses;
cultivate the mind within the eight dhyānas and let the heart roam through the seven factors of enlightenment.
People of the time compared him to Pūtimakṣika;
he traveled alone through mountains and marshes, avoiding neither tigers nor rhinoceroses,
dwelling in solitude and contemplating for days and nights on end.
Once, while beneath a tree, he repeatedly reproached himself:
"My years are approaching thirty, yet I have not yet attained the fruit.
How negligent I am!"
Thereupon, for several days he neither slept nor ate,
applying himself with singular devotion and intense austerity to repent for his past transgressions.
He then saw the Heavenly King Vaishravana in a dream.
He addressed him, saying:
"O śramaṇa,
you should contemplate traveling to various regions to propagate the teaching, with the vast salvation of beings as your primary concern."
Why cling to minor details and seek only personal perfection?
The Way relies on manifold conditions and must await the ripening of the time.
To force what is not one's lot will lead to death without realization.
He reflected within himself that he wished to travel abroad to bestow the Way. Thereupon,
he traversed various kingdoms, braving hardships and dangers.
During the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty,
he first arrived at Guangzhou and resided at Baisa Temple.
Yaśas was skilled in reciting the *Vibhāṣā-vinaya*.
People all called him the Great Vibhāṣā.
At that time, there was a laywoman of pure faith named Zhang Puming,
who sought instruction in the Buddha-dharma from him.
Yaśas explained to him the Buddha’s account of his own birth and the dependent origination of phenomena (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
and also translated for him one fascicle of the *Carmavastu* (the Sutra on Leather).
Later, during the Yixi era, he came to Chang’an.
At that time, Yao Xing had usurped the title of emperor and held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem;
upon Yeśa’s arrival, he treated him with profound courtesy and exceptional honor.
There was a time when the Indian śramaṇa Dharmagupta—whose name means "Dharma-treasury" in the language of Qin—came to enter Guanzhong.
Like kind spirits seeking one another, they felt as though they had been old acquaintances.
Consequently, they together produced the *Śāriputrābhidharma*.
In the ninth year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, the year Dingwei, the Sanskrit texts were brought forth.
They remained until the sixteenth year, Jiayin,
when the masters of the scriptures gradually became proficient in the Qin language and were permitted to proclaim the translations themselves.
It was finally completed in the seventeenth year, the year of Yimao (172 CE).
It consists of twenty-two fascicles in total.
Prince Hong of the Qin personally oversaw its management and study.
The śramaṇa Daobiao composed a preface for it.
He also produced one fascicle of the *Lèyíngluò jīng* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra).
Later, Dharmayaśas traveled south to Jiangling.
He resided at Xinsi Temple and extensively propagated the Dharma of Chan.
More than three hundred guests who sought the flavor of tranquility came through the brambles to visit him.
Among all the officials and commoners who came to him, even those who previously lacked faith, [were moved].
All who saw them felt reverence and joy.
He himself said that he had one teacher and one disciple,
both of whom had cultivated their practice and attained arhatship.
The transmitter of this account has lost the names [of these figures].
Furthermore, he once sat in meditation with his door closed at the outer gate when,
suddenly, five śramaṇas entered his room.
Furthermore, there were frequent instances— not limited to one or two— where śramaṇas were seen flying to the tops of trees;
they constantly communicated with the divine while appearing outwardly to conform to the common, ignorant populace.
Although his traces on the Path had not yet been fully manifested,
people of the time all claimed that he had already attained the fruit of sainthood.
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he took his leave and returned to the Western Regions.
Its ultimate end is unknown.

As for Xiqifu of Western Qin, who ruled with his capital at Yuanchuan, it is also called Western Qin; it began from the posthumous title of Xuánliè Wáng (Martially Resplendent Founder) granted to Qifu Guóréng, in the first year of Jiànyì, the year of Yǐyǒu.
Reaching the reign of Qifu Mumo, who died posthumously without a title in the fourth year of Yonghong (the Xinwei year),
a total of four rulers had presided over forty-seven years. During this period,
there was only one scripture translated by a single śramaṇa.
Including the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras translated during the Three Qin dynasties by both new and old translators, there are a total of fifty-six works in one hundred and ten fascicles;
among these, thirty-two works in seventy-nine fascicles are extant, while twenty-four works in thirty-one fascicles are missing.
The *Sūtras* of the Qiqiu Qin dynasty, translated by the śramaṇa Shi Shengjian: fifteen works in twenty-four fascicles;
the newly and formerly translated *Sūtras* of the Three Qin dynasties whose translators were lost: forty-one works in eighty-six fascicles; the works from the old collections:
thirty-four works in seventy-nine fascicles; and the newly appended *Rāmāyaṇa-sūtra* (Luo-mo-jia jing) in three fascicles, which is an entry into the *Avataṃsaka*.

A partial variant translation of the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* is recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The *Sūtra of Prince Sudāna*, one fascicle, appears as a variant translation in the second fascicle of the *Liudujijing*;
it was produced at Xin Monastery in Jiangling with Yu Shuang serving as the scribe. Some say it is titled *Sudāna*;
it should be included in the Jin period according to the *Shixing lu* and *Baochang lu*, and should be appended to the Qin period following the person [to whom it is attributed]. *Śān*.

*The Sutra of the Son* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sutra of the Filial Son Śyāma*, *The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Śyāma*, *The Sutra of Śyāma Spoken by the Buddha*, *The Original Sutra of Śyāma*, and *The Sutra of the Hidden Filial Son*—these are its six titles.

It is the fourth [text] produced from the second fascicle of the *Ṣaḍpāramitā-samuccaya*. Alternative translations are found in the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*. [Also listed in] the *Mahāsthātṛ*.
One fascicle of a sutra, also titled *The Sutra on Bathing Buddha Images* or simply *The Sutra on Bathing the Buddha*, is the second [text] produced;
it shares the same original source as the *Sutra on Washing Buddha Images*. It is recorded in the *Shixing lu* (Record of Shixing).

One fascicle of the *Dharmamukha-sūtra of Boundless Retention*, also known as the *Ananta-sūtra*, shares the same original source as the *Sutra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣavijaya* and others; its initial appearance is recorded in the [same catalog].
*Shixing lu* (Record of Shixing) and *Fashang lu* (Record of Fashang): *Yandao suye jing* (Sutra on the Practice of the Way by Monastics and Laypeople), one fascicle;
the second edition is the same text as that translated by Zhi Qian, as seen in the *Fashang lu*. *Chukong zaihuai jing* (Sutra on Eliminating Fear and Disaster), one fascicle;

the second edition is the same text as that translated by Bo Yan, as seen in the *Shixing lu*. *Xianshou jing* (Sutra of the Wise Head), one fascicle; [seen] in the three records of Baochang, Fashang, and others from Shixing.

The *Mingxianshou furen jing* (Sūtra of the Lady Mingxianshou), one fascicle; also known as the *Ānán fēnbié jīng* (Sūtra of Ānanda’s Discrimination) or the *Ānán wèn shì fó jíxióng jīng* (Sūtra of Ānanda’s Questions on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha);
third, these appear in the *Shixing lu* (Record of Shixing) and the *Fashang lu* (Record of Fashang).

The *Fùrén yùgū jīng* (Sūtra of the Woman Meeting Calamity), one fascicle; also titled the *Fù yùduì jīng* (Sūtra of the Woman Meeting Retribution); appears in both the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*. The above [entries] are seen [in these records].

The following section is missing. There is a *Vaipulya Sūtra on the Lord of Space, Ākāśagarbha* in eight fascicles, also called the *Sūtra Asked by Ākāśagarbha*, or alternatively titled the *Sūtra Encouraging the Bodhisattva’s Adornment of Bodhi*;
it consists of five fascicles. This is a different translation of the "Ākāśagarbha-parivarta" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
It is recorded in the *Jin shi za lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the *Fashang lu* (Record of Fashang), which state that it is identical to the *Rāmaka-sūtra*.
*Ben fei ye pusa suo sheng di jing* (The Sūtra on the Original Non-Being, the Birthplace of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; also titled *Mojie suo wen jing* (The Sūtra of the Questions of Mahākāśyapa).

Second appearance in the *Zhao lu* (Record of Zhao); its chronological relation to other versions is unknown. It was attributed to the Western Qin after the Zhao dynasty was overthrown, as seen in the *Shixing lu* (Record of Shixing).

*Bai jing* (The Sūtra of the Seer), one fascicle. Third appearance in the *Fashang lu* (Record of Fashang). *Tongjiaye jie nan jing* (The Sūtra of Kaśyapa the Child Resolving Difficulties), one fascicle; also called *Tong*.
The *Kāśyapa-sūtra* and the *Kumāra-kāśyapa-sūtra* share the same original text; Sengyou states they were translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama* and transcribed by Yu Shuang.
They are found in the catalogs of Wang Zong, Bao Chang, and Zhi Min-du et al.

The *Qīnǚběnjīng* (Sūtra of the Seven Daughters’ Originals), one fascicle—also titled *Nǚběnxīnmíngjīng* (Sūtra of the Women’s Original Heart-Illumination) or *Qīnǚjīng* (Sūtra of the Seven Daughters)—is the third [text] mentioned in Zhi Min-du’s *Dùlù*.
The above records fifteen collections comprising twenty-four fascicles: ten collections totaling twelve fascicles concerning women meeting with calamity are extant;
five collections totaling twelve fascicles concerning the primary subjects of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) are missing their texts.
The śramaṇa Śākya Śrī-Sthira,
also known as Dharma-Sthira,
was likewise called Master Sthira.
It is not clear which of these accounts is correct, so they are all listed here for reference.
His capacity was vast and universal, and his mind was set on benefiting all beings.
During the Taichu era of the Qifu Qin dynasty...
In the kingdom of Henan, he posthumously conferred the title of King Wuyuan upon Qiangui and translated fifteen scriptures, including the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
Examining the traces of his holy journey and transformative influence,
it is evident that he produced these scriptures wherever he traveled.
Since it has no fixed place of inclusion,
I do not know to which dynastic record it should be appended for verification.
For now, I have recorded it generally according to the *Yifashang* (The Record of the Dharma Above).
The *Shilu* (Record of the Qi-fu Qin Dynasty) states: *Śrāmaṇera Sūtra*, one fascicle;

second edition, same text as the *Five Mothers and Sons Sūtra*; *Sahasa-rāja Sūtra*, one fascicle; *A-da-samādhi Sūtra*, one fascicle (also titled *A-da-xian-wang Sūtra*); *Bhadra-āpatti-deśanā Sūtra*, one fascicle; *Vaipulya-nirṇaya Sūtra*, one fascicle; *Bhikṣu-dvividha-kārya Sūtra*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s record states: "Three matters; the above seven works. Sengyou’s record further notes: "These seven works, totaling seven fascicles, were 'extraordinary scriptures from Guanzhong' by Master Dao'an. Of these, the original for the *Śrāmaṇera Sūtra* exists, while the others are all missing."
The *Chángfáng lù* states:
"All were produced by the śramaṇa Sengyou from the *Sanzàng jílù*,
based on the records of Shi Dao'an concerning the extraordinary scriptures in Guāngzhōng."
It is now appended to the *Shi-qin shi-lu* (Record of the Three Qin Dynasties) as a whole, categorized under the section for works of unknown translators.

The *Fang-lu* (Fajing’s Record) further notes that there is a four-fascicle Sanskrit manuscript of this scripture, with a marginal note stating it likely originated in Chang’an; it was already included in the *Hou-Han shi-yi lu* (Record of Lost Translations from the Later Han).
The entries contained herein were previously recorded;
as they were already included above, they have been omitted here.
The following are newly appended to this record.
*The Sūtra of the Crown Prince Vaira of the Heavenly King*, one fascicle (some editions omit the characters "Heavenly King");
also known as *The Sūtra of the Crown Prince Pīla*. *The Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Great Jewel Accumulation and the Sun*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of the Questions of Dhāgala on the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of Ānanda on the Incantations of Sorcery*, one fascicle; the Old Catalogue states it was translated by Ānanda.
*Sūtra on Being Cursed by the Practice of Sorcery* (formerly suspected to be the *Sūtra of the Mātaṅga Woman* from among the Tripiṭaka);
*Sūtra of the Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain at Rājagṛha*, one fascicle; the old catalog states: *Essential True Sūtra of the Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain at Rājagṛha*;

*Sūtra of the Path of Thought*, one fascicle; *Sūtra of the Buddha at the Bamboo Grove*, one fascicle; *Sūtra of the Dharma for Humans*, one fascicle; *Sūtra of the Meaning of the Path*, one fascicle; *Ā...* [text fragment].

*Yi Bǐqiū Jīng* (The Scripture on the Barbarian Bhikṣu), one fascicle; *Bādé Jīng* (The Scripture on the Eight Virtues), one fascicle—these are now suspected to be the *Hǎi Bādé Jīng* (The Scripture on the Eight Virtues of the Sea);

*Shàndé Jīng* (The Scripture on Good Virtue), one fascicle; *Móhē Jiàntuó Wéiwèilá Jìn xìn Bǐqǐděng Dù Jīng* (The Scripture on the Great Kāṇḍa-vyūha and the Bhikṣus Jìn-xìn and Others Crossing Over), one fascicle;
the old catalog states it is the *Jìn xìn Bǐqǐ Jīng* (The Scripture of the Bhikṣu Jìn-xìn). These fourteen works comprise fourteen fascicles. First, the Prince’s Renunciation.
The *Luojing* (Sūtra on the Net) has its original text, while the remainder of the filial piety texts are all missing.
Sengyou’s catalogue states that these were the "Extraordinary Scriptures from Guanzhong" by Master Dao'an.
The records of Changfang and others all omit this and fail to include it; however,
Sengyou includes the *Miraculous Scriptures from Guanzhong* by Master Dao’an.
In total, there are twenty-four sections comprising twenty-four fascicles; among these, seven sections are listed in the Fang-lu (Fangguang Record).
Now, fourteen additional sūtras are further presented, bringing the total to twenty-one sections.
Regarding the remaining three sections,
catalogs such as those by Sengyou and others all specify the translators;
therefore, they are omitted here.
The *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, one fascicle, is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection as the forty-third assembly;

its title has been changed to the "Assembly of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha. Third, it was translated together with the *Mahāyāna-ratnavyūha-buddhāstamgata-maṇiratna-sūtra* from the same original text but with different translations.
The *Sarvabuddhaviṣayajñānālokalaṃkāra-sūtra*, one fascicle, was first translated together with the [Buddha-]... [text fragment].
Regarding the *Huayan ruru Lai de zhi bushi yijingjie jing* (Avataṃsaka-sūtra:
Entering the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata’s Virtue and Wisdom), it is said that its base text is identical to the *Yu Rulai zhuangyan zhihui guangming ru yiqie fo jingjie jing*.
This claim is entirely erroneous. Furthermore, the eight-fascicle *Dabei fenduoli jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) is also called the *Dasheng bei fenduoli jing*, fascicle two.
First, the *Mahāsuvarṇa-mayūra-rāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle, which is identical in its original text to the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema;
fifth, the *Buddhabhāṣita-mahāsuvarṇa-mayūra-rāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle;

sixth, these two sūtras are identical in their original text to the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgata-rahasya-garbha-sūtra* in two fascicles, which the *Dazhou Catalogue* states is identical to the [previous] *Mahā*...
The claim that the *Vaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* is the same text [as the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*] is incorrect.

The *Vajrasamādhi-bhūta-svabhāva-viśuddhy-avināśy-aniruddha Sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled the *Vajra-viśuddhi Sūtra*—is recorded by the Chángfáng and other catalogs as having been translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty;
it is also listed among the lost translations of the Later Han, but these are both incorrect. Examining the phrasing and sentences now, it appears to be a translation from the Qin period.
Therefore, this *Sīhamāsa-buddha-jātaka-sūtra* (one fascicle) has been moved here;

the *Chángfáng lù* and other catalogs state it was translated by Zhú Fǎhù of the Western Jìn dynasty, but upon examining the wording and phrasing, it does not appear to have been produced by Master Hù, as it resembles translations from the Qín period; hence it has been moved here.
This *Daśa-maṅgala-sūtra* (one fascicle) and the *Sarvajñā-prabhāsa-ṛṣi-karuṇā-hetu-pratyaya-sūtra*... [are likewise moved here].
*Śāka-māṃsa-bhakṣaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Viśuddha-karmāvaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Saṃyuktāgama-vibhāga*, twenty fascicles;
*Pravrajyā-guṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle (not extracted from the *Xianyu jing*);
*Vinayamātṛkā*, eight fascicles (also called the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*); *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, nine fascicles; *Sammitīya-nikāya*.

*Treatise on the Three [Vehicles]* in three fascicles (sometimes without the word "section" [*bu*], or said to be in four fascicles); *Treatise on the Causes and Conditions of Pratyekabuddhas* in two fascicles;

*Treatise on the Eighteen Schools* in one fascicle. The initial translations were identical to the *Treatise on the Different Tenets of the Schools* and others. Master Fang and others all claimed these were translated by Paramārtha, but this is incorrect.
*The Sutra on the Secret Traces of the Vajra-wielding Malla’s Lamentation upon the Buddha’s Entry into Nirvana* in one fascicle.
The *Amidhyājñāna-rākṣasa-saṃgraha* (one fascicle), also known as the *Amidhyājñāna-rākṣasa-sūtra* (or two fascicles).
The above twenty sections comprise sixty-five fascicles;
all are included in the canon.
It appears that several sūtras translated during the Qin dynasty contain characters with the phonetic value of "Qin" (秦); these have not been included in the catalogs of works of unknown translation.
They are now appended here to this catalog of the Qin period.
I hope this may avoid any omissions.
Together with the seven previously lost translations consisting of seven fascicles,
as well as the newly appended "Various Scriptures from Guanzhong" by Master Dao’an, [the total is now complete].
In total, there are forty-one sections comprising eighty-six fascicles;
all are attributed as translations lost during the Three Qin periods.

Former Liang: The Zhang clan of Former Liang resided in Guzang. The *Xinshang yulu* lacks a record of the years; following the record of Zhen Luan, most dates are according to the era names of the Jin dynasty. [The founder] Zhang Gui was posthumously titled Emperor Wu. From the first year of Wenyong, the Xinyou year, until Tianxi received the title of General of the Chariots and Cavalry and Governor of Liangzhou from the Qin in the sixth year of Xian’an, the Jingsi year, there were eight successive rulers for a total of seventy-six years.
A single foreign upāsaka translated these scriptures;
they comprise four sections totaling six fascicles. Among them, one section consisting of one fascicle currently exists, while three sections totaling five fascicles are missing.
The *Sūtra in Six Volumes for the Four Assemblies* by the Upāsaka Zhi Shilun of Former Liang;

the *Sūrala-sūtra* in one volume, which is the same text as the *Sūrala-sūtra* produced by Bo Yan of the Cao Wei, Zhi Qian of the Wu, and Gongde Xian of the Song, as noted in the third postscript of the canon;
and the *Yathābhūta-māyopama-samādhi-sūtra*, produced in the third year of the Xian’an era.
Two fascicles; the fourth [translation] is identical to those by An Shigao, Dharmarakṣa, the *Tathatā-samādhi*, and the *Ratnakūṭa-Sujātārtha-parivarta*.
See the postscript to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*. Translated in the third year of the Xian’an era. One fascicle, the *Jingangshou-jing* (Sūtra of the Golden Light Crest);
the second [translation] is identical to the *Mahāśubha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* by Dharmarakṣa of the Jin dynasty and the [version by] Yaśas of the Sui dynasty.
The *Dharmaviśeṣasaṃgraha-sūtra* (莊嚴法門經), translated in the third year of the Xian’an era [399 CE], is seen to be the same text as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.

According to the postscript of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, two fascicles were produced in the eighth [year] and are the same text as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* translated by Zhi Chen of Han, Zhi Qian of Wu, Bo Yan of Wei, and Dharmarakṣa of Jin.
These four [versions] are recorded in the postscripts of the sutras. Right: four.

One section in six fascicles; the *Sūtra of Sūrata*, one fascicle, currently extant; and five other sections, such as the *Yathā-māyā* (As Like an Illusion), totaling three fascicles, which are missing.
Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Shilun.
He was a person from the Yuezhi.
He had extensively mastered various scriptures and was particularly adept at the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings.
His intention lay in enlightening and transforming others by transmitting what had not yet been heard.
He brought the scriptures and traveled until he reached the land of Liang; when Lord Zhang saw them, he held them in high esteem and requested that they be translated.
In the third year of Xian’an, the *guiyou* year according to the Jin calendar, this was done beneath the Zhanlu Pavilion behind the main hall within the precincts of Liangzhou.
The four sections of the *Sūtra of Sūrata* and other texts were translated;
Baima Yan, the Crown Prince of Kucha, acted as interpreter,
while the Palace Attendant Zhao Xue of XiHai, the District Magistrate Ma Yi, and the Inner Attendant Lai Gongzheng served as the three scribes who recorded the text.
The śramaṇa Shi Huichang and Shi Jinxing were both present at the assembly for its verification.
This was transcribed by those from Liangzhou; no further literary embellishments have been added.

This postscript to the *Sūrala-sūtra* and the postscript to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* should have been produced during the era of Former Liang. It is fortunate that later generations have encountered them, and they are here appended to the collection as a continuation.
The Northern Liang was established by the Juqu clan.
Initially they were based in Zhangye, later moving to Guzang.
From the time of Juqu Mengxun, who was posthumously titled King Wuxuan, until the first year of the Yong’an era, the *xinchou* year.
Reaching the seventh year of the Chenghe era (Ji-mao) under Yao Mengqian, who was enfeoffed as the King of Hexi during the Wei dynasty,
a total of thirty-nine years had elapsed under two rulers.
During this time, nine individuals, both monastics and laypeople, produced translations of sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras.
Including the various scriptures from both the new and old collections whose translators are lost,

there are a total of eighty-two works comprising three hundred and eleven fascicles; among these, twenty-five works totaling two hundred and nine fascicles are extant, while fifty-seven works totaling one hundred and two fascicles are missing.
Twelve fascicles of sutras from two collections by the Northern Liang śramaṇa Shi Daogong;
four fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Shi Fazhong; two fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Saṃghadeva;
and one hundred and thirty-one fascicles of sutras and vinayas from nineteen collections by the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema, collected by Juqu Jingsheng, Marquis of Anyang.
One collection in two fascicles by the śramaṇa Buddhavarman; one collection in sixty fascicles by the śramaṇa Śikṣānanda;
one collection in twenty fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Zhimeng; two collections in four fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Daotai; one collection in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Shi Fasheng;
and fifty-three collections in seventy-five fascicles consisting of various previously and newly translated scriptures of unknown translators.
Volume five: eighteen sections in total; forty-eight works in fifty-seven volumes from the old collection, with two new additions.
The *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (寶梁經) in two volumes is now included within the *Ratnakūṭa*, appearing as the forty-fourth assembly. This is seen in the *Hexi lu* by Zhu Daozu and the *Sengyou lu*.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (悲華經) in ten volumes is the third translation, produced alongside the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* (閑居經) by Dharmarakṣa.
As for the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (translated by Dharmakṣema), the *Beihuajing* (Sutra of the Lotus of Compassion) and others share the same original text.
The library records state that it appears to have been a prior translation which was subsequently revised and edited by Gongsun. I now suspect this is indeed the work produced by Dharmakṣema himself.

Of these two works totaling twelve fascicles, the former, the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Bao liang jing) in one fascicle, still exists; the latter, the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Beihuajing) in ten fascicles, [is also extant].
Volume missing from the original manuscript.
The śramaṇa Shi Daogong,
with a vacant mind and vast application, pursued the Way for the sake of broad benefit.
During the Yong’an era of Mengxun, the King of Hexi under the Northern Liang dynasty, he translated two scriptures—the *Bao liáng jīng* (Jewel Beam Sūtra) and others—at Zhangye for Mengxun.

Regarding the four-fascicle *Dàfāngděng tuóluóní jīng* (Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra), it is also known as the *Wú dàzì yī míng fāngděng tánchí tuóluóní jīng* (The One Without the Character "Great," otherwise titled the Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra) or simply the *Tánchí tuóluóní jīng*. This one work in four fascicles, as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jìnshì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Sengyou’s catalog, still exists today.
The śramaṇa Shi Fazhong was a native of Gaochang Commandery;
he also [arrived] during the Yong’an era.
In Zhangye, he translated one fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* for Mengsun, the King of Hexi.
The *Baochang lu* states:
Translated at Gaochang Commandery;
it is unclear which version is correct.

*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Hui Shang’s Inquiry on Great Skillful Means*, two fascicles—also titled *The Sūtra of Great Skillful Means*, *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Hui Shang*, and *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of Expedient Means*—having four titles in total. All versions are identical. This fifth edition is the same text as the *Sūtra of Great Skillful Means* translated by An Shigao of Han and Dharmarakṣa of Jin, as well as the "Mahāyāna Chapter on Expedient Means" from the *Ratnakūṭa*. This one work in two fascicles is incomplete.
The śramaṇa Saṃghadatta.
In the language of Liang, this means "Abounding in Goodness.
He was a man from the Western Regions.
With his mind set on universal salvation and the transformation and guidance of others held within his breast,
he likewise served as [monk] for Mengsun in Zhangye during the Yong’an era.
He translated one fascicle of the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-sūtra*,
as recorded in the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*.
He also translated the forty-fascicle (or thirty-six-fascicle) *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the fifth translation, in the third year of the Xuanshi era.
Completed on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the tenth year. The Sanskrit original consists of thirty-five thousand verses in full;
what has been translated here amounts to only ten thousand verses or so, being merely one-third of the whole.

According to Zhu Daozu’s *Liang lu* and Sengyou’s catalog, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* comprises thirty fascicles, though it is sometimes simply referred to as the *Da jí jīng* (Saṃnipāta-sūtra), specifically the third part.
The versions translated during the Han dynasty by Zhi Chen and those by Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty share the same original text;
they appear in twenty-nine, thirty-one, thirty-two, or forty fascicles.

This is truly because the initial translations were immediately transcribed with differing divisions of fascicles, as seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Liang lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*: the *Dafangguang Sanjie jing* in three fascicles was first translated.
The *Ratnakūṭa-samaya-trisaṃvara-sūtra* is seen to be the same text as [the *Baoji sanlüyi jing*]; this was recorded by Fashang in his *Beihua jing* (ten fascicles), Part IV.
It is also seen to be the same text as the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is noted in Zhu Daozu’s *Hexi lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*.
Sengyou states that it is a separate record, or that it was produced by Gongshang; now I suspect that Dao, Gong, and Chen are one and the same person.
It is likely that these two versions were not originally identical, as they are recorded in both catalogs.
The four-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* initially comprised eighteen chapters; this is seen in the *Hexi lu* by Zhu Daozu and the *Sengyou lu*.

It is the same text as the newly translated *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which is now included within the eight-fascicle combined edition. These four fascicles, however, are contained in the *Shanfan lu*.
The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-sūtra* in six fascicles—also known as the *Mahāvaipulya-animitta-mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-animitta-sūtra*, or the *Mahāmegha-guhyagarbha-sūtra*;
alternatively titled the *Vaipulya-mahāmegha-sūtra*—exists in versions of four or five fascicles.
It was translated at Neiyuan Temple; this is the second edition, appearing in the records of Sengrui, Li Kuò, and Sengyòu.
*Sanlu fuzhong nü tingjing* (The Sutra on the Woman in the Womb Listening to the Dharma), one fascicle; also known as *Buzhuangjiao nü jing* (The Sutra of the Unadorned Woman).

This is the same text as the *Wugouxian nü jing* (Sutra of the Stainless Virtuous Woman) and the *Zhuan nüshen jing* (Sutra on the Transformation of the Female Body), etc. Third appearance in the *Changfang lu*. *Bodhisattvabhūmiviniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Treatise on the Bodhisattva Stages), ten fascicles;
sometimes the character for "sutra" (*jing*) is omitted. It is also called a *śāstra* (treatise), or the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, or simply the *Bodhisattva* [Sutra].
The *Dìjīng* (Sutra on the Stages), either in eight fascicles, is excerpted from the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;

it is recorded in the *Hèxī lù* by Zhūdǎozǔ and the *Sēngyòu lù*. The *Upāsaka-jīng* (Upāsaka Precepts Sutra), either in seven fascicles—or without the word "sutra"—is the Upāsaka Bodhisattva Precepts;
alternatively, it exists in five, six, or ten fascicles. [It was translated] in the year Bingyin of the fifteenth year of Xuānshí.
From the twenty-third day of the fourth month until the twenty-third day of the seventh month, it was completed. Recorded by the śramaṇa Doyang as pen-receiver.

This is based on the postscript to the sutra and the *Sengyou lu*. One fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Pusa jie ben) is extracted from the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva-bhūmi" (*Dichi jieben*).
This second extraction is identical in text to the *Śīla-sūtra* (Jie ben) produced by Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; a separate record states this.
The *Sūtra of King Mandhātṛ* (一卷), translated at Dunhuang; listed in Sengyou’s *Lu*, it is a variant translation of the eleventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*;
listed in Changfang’s *Lu*. The *Buddhacarita-kāvya* (佛所行讚經傳) in five fascicles—some say the title lacks the character "zhuan" (傳), while others say the title lacks the character "jing" (經);
composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; also known as the *Buddhapūrva-yoga-sūtra* (佛本行經). Listed in the [catalog].
In Sengfang’s Record (*Chángfáng lù*), the entries from "currently extant" onwards are missing.
One fascicle of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*—also titled *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-sūtra*—first appeared in Sengfang’s Record;
it is identical to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* translated by Gongde Xian of the Song dynasty and the *Śrīmālā* within the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The *Renhuì tóngběn luómójī jīng* (The Scripture on the Common Source of Humans and Lumbinī), one fascicle, is the fourth [version] translated by An Faxian and others of the Cao Wei dynasty;

it is the same text as those previously produced, differing only in its degree of elaboration or brevity. It is a small portion of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātupraveśa*) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

According to the Changfang Record, the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* was first produced during the Song dynasty by Guṇabhadra, followed by that of Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei, and later that of the Tang dynasty.
The version produced by Śikṣānanda and others, which is the same text as that seen in the *Chángfáng lù*, is titled the *Sūxūzhēn tiānzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Devaputra Susīma), one fascicle;

it is the second translation, identical to the one produced by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Chángfáng states he saw it in the *Wùlù* (Records of Wu) and further notes it was produced by Kumārajīva, appearing to be a re-translation.
The *Hǎilóngwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Sea Dragon King), four fascicles, may have new characters added; it is the second translation, [identical to] that of Zhu... [Fàn].

The translations produced by Dharmarakṣa include: the *Bodhisattva Sūtra of the Jewel Radiance* (*Gongde Baoguang Pusa Jing*), one fascicle, which appears in the *He-xi Lu* of Zhu Daozu and the *Sengyou Lu*;
and the *Bodhisattva Precept Platform Text* (*Pusa Jietan Wen*), one fascicle, also titled *Upāsaka Precept Platform Text*.
Sengyou refers to it as the *Bodhisattva and Upāsaka Precept Platforms*.
The textual evidence is found in the two catalogs by Sengyou and Baochang. To the right [of this entry], there are nineteen works totaling one hundred thirty-one fascicles;

the *Suxingzan* (Praise on Previous Conduct) above consists of twelve works totaling one hundred eighteen fascicles; the extant *Śrīmālā-sūtra* below consists of seven works totaling thirteen fascicles;
and there are missing texts.
The śramaṇa Dharmakṣema,
also called Tanmochan,
and likewise called Tanmoxian.
This is likely because the Sanskrit pronunciations differ.
Liang states that Dharmaprabha was a native of Central India.
He was of the Brahmin caste.
At the age of six, his father passed away;
his mother supported him by working as a hired weaver.
Seeing that the śramaṇa Dharmayaśas— whose name means "Dharma-fame"— was revered by both the clergy and the laity and received abundant offerings,
his mother envied him;
therefore, she made Chen her disciple.
At the age of ten, he recited dharanis with several of his fellow students;
his intelligence surpassed the rest of the group,
and he could master over ten thousand words of scripture each day.
In his early studies, he mastered the Śrāvaka vehicle and concurrently examined the various treatises of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
His expositions were so precise and eloquent that none could challenge or oppose him.
Later, he encountered the White-headed Meditation Master (*śvetakeśa-dhyānācārya*).
He engaged in debate with Baoshan Chàn;
as their respective practices differed, they contended for ten days.
Although Chàn launched a flurry of sharp criticisms and difficult challenges, [Dao’an] remained steadfast.
The Chan Master, however, ultimately refused to yield.
Daorong was convinced by his profound reasoning and said to the Master:
"Is there perhaps any scripture that may be seen?
The Meditation Master immediately gave him a copy of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* written on tree bark.
Upon reading it, Saṃghabhūti was struck with sudden realization; he then felt deep shame and regret.
Considering that his understanding of the narrow well had long led him astray from the Great Way,
he assembled the community to repent his errors and subsequently devoted himself exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
By the time he reached the age of twenty, he had recited more than two million words of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.
Guṇabhadra’s elder brother was skilled at training elephants for riding;
he killed the white-eared great elephant ridden by the king.
The king was enraged and executed him,
issuing a decree:
"Whoever dares to look upon [the corpse] shall have their three clans exterminated."
His relatives dared not go to attend his funeral, and they buried him while he was still weeping.
The King was enraged and wished to execute Zhanchen.
Zhanchen said:
"The King killed him for the sake of the Dharma;
I buried him out of affection for my kin.
Neither act contravenes the Great Meaning."
When others became enraged and their companions were struck with cold dread,
his countenance remained composed as before.
The king, marveling at his resolve and spirit, subsequently retained him to provide for his needs.
Dharmakṣema was clearly proficient in incantations and esoteric arts;
whatever he directed always proved effective.
He was renowned throughout the Western Regions as a master of great divine spells.
Later, he accompanied the King into the mountains;
when the King became exhausted with thirst and required water but could not find any, [the master intervened].
The Seer then secretly recited mantras over the rock until water gushed forth;
he then praised it, saying,
"This is moved by the gracious bounty of Your Majesty."
Consequently, springs began to flow from parched rocks.
When neighboring states heard of this, they all marveled at the King’s virtue.
At that time, the rains were perfectly regulated, and the common people sang his praises.
The king delighted in his arts and techniques, treating him with profound favor and honor.
However, in recent times, the king’s interest had somewhat waned and his treatment of him grew increasingly perfunctory.
Thereupon, the Seer (Cen) said in anger:
"I shall take water from a jar to the pond, enchant the dragon, and place him inside the jar so that a great drought shall fall upon the world.
The King will surely request my incantations;
thereafter, I shall release the dragon to send down rain. What do you think of being treated with such hospitality?"
He then took a jar and went to create a dragon.
Someone informed on him in secret;
the king grew angry and arrested the Seer.
Fearing execution, Śīkṣānanda took with him the first fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, as well as the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-sūtra*, and fled toward Kucha.
In the kingdom of Kucha, many followed the Mahayana teachings but did not believe in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Consequently, [the Master] proceeded to Guzang and stayed at an inn;
fearing he might lose the original manuscript of the scripture, he placed it under his pillow while sleeping.
Someone dragged him to the ground;
the interpreter was startled and thought he was a thief.
This continued for three nights.
A voice was heard from the air, saying:
"This is the treasury of the Tathāgata’s liberation;
why do you use it as a pillow?"
Dharmakṣema was then filled with shame and realization; he moved it to a high place.
At night, there were thieves who tried to lift it but could not prevail over its weight.
They attempted to lift it several times, yet it remained immovable.
At dawn the next day, Baoyun carried the sutra away without regarding it as heavy.
When the thief saw him, he thought he was a sage.
They all came to pay their respects and offer thanks.
Juqu Mengxun, the King of Hexi, having heard of the Seer’s name,
summoned him for an audience and received him with great generosity.
Mongxun had long venerated the Great Dharma and was intent upon its propagation.
He requested that a copy of this scripture be produced; however, as the prophetic text (jñānapada) had not yet been adapted to the local language and lacked a translator, [it could not be rendered].
Fearing that the words might deviate from the principle,
he did not permit the translation immediately;
thus, after studying the language for three years, he finally translated it.
The first part consists of ten fascicles.
At that time, the śramaṇas Huìsōng and Dàolǎng were peerless in Hexi;
they encountered the proclamation and translation of this treasury of the Dharma.
Shen Xiang was entrusted with the task of translating the Sanskrit text,
while Master Huisong acted as the scribe;
several hundred monastics and laypeople engaged in a spirited exchange of questions and challenges.
When facing critical moments, Śikṣānanda resolved their difficulties without ever encountering any obstruction.

Senglang and others further requested that he produce more of the remaining sūtras—namely, the *Mahāsannipāta*, *Mahāmegha*, *Karunāpuṇḍarīka*, and *Kṣitigarbha*, along with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—in total, nineteen works.
Because the number of chapters in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was incomplete,
Dharmakṣema returned to his country to seek it out;
however, encountering the death of his mother, he remained there for over a year.
Later, while in Khotan, he obtained further manuscript copies of the scriptures;
returning once more to Guzang, he continued the translation, completing them in four fascicles.
Dharmakṣema began the initial translation in the third year of Xuansi, the Jia-yin year.

In the fifteenth year, the Bingyin year, the compilation was completed; Fang states that it was finished in the tenth year of Xuanshi, but this refers to the time when the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was concluded, not other scriptures. According to the postscript to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, it was translated in the Bingyin year; thus, even during those fifteen years, further scriptures were being produced. Dharmakṣema passed away in the third month of the Guiyou year, the third year of Yihé. During the six intervening years, he should have produced even more scriptures, yet they are not mentioned in the catalogs; therefore, the details remain unclear. Dharmakṣema once told Tanyao:
There was a ghost that entered villages and invariably brought about much disaster and pestilence. Xun did not believe this and wished to see it for himself as proof.
Baoshan Chen immediately employed his arts upon Xun.
Upon seeing [the ghost], Xun was struck with terror. Chen said:
"You should purify yourself with sincere sincerity and observe the fasts and abstinences to expel it through divine incantations.
He then recited the incantations for three days and said to Xun:
The ghosts departed toward the north.
Shortly thereafter, tens of thousands died of pestilence beyond the northern borders.
Xu grew increasingly reverent and apprehensive, treating him with ever greater honor and hospitality.
When Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty heard of his spiritual arts, he dispatched an envoy to invite him.
He further warned Daosun, saying:
"If you do not send Chen, I shall immediately deploy troops against you."
Sun assessed his own situation and considered that his state was weak and unable to resist the command.
Furthermore, he feared that the many divinations and omens might be plots devised by Wei against himself.
He was perplexed and distressed as to whether to advance or retreat,
and thus secretly devised a plan to eliminate him.
Initially, when Dharmakṣema had finished translating the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the number of fascicles had already been fixed.
The foreign śramaṇa Dharmaphala said, "This sūtra is incomplete;
its chapters have not yet reached their conclusion.
Kāśyapa Mātanga once sighed with regret and vowed that he would surely seek it out again.
Mong-xun, taking advantage of his [the monk's] pursuit of his own aims,
feigned support for his departure and bestowed upon him a generous gift of precious goods.
Yet, before he had set out for several days, Mong-xun wept and addressed the assembly, saying:
The retribution for karmic offenses is about to arrive;
even the assembly of sages cannot save one.
Because of my original vow, it is not permissible to remain stationary.
After traveling forty *li*,
Xun secretly dispatched an assassin to kill him;
he was then forty-nine years old.
The multitude all mourned him with deep sorrow.
Shortly thereafter, Sun’s attendants frequently saw ghosts and spirits during the day striking him with swords.

In the fourth month, Sun fell ill and passed away. Sun had been harmed by Chen in the third month of the third year of Yihé; that very year, in the fourth month, he met his end through illness. Truly, retribution is not empty, following one like a shadow follows a form. Fang’s claim that Chen lived until the world and died in the fourth year of Shenghe is incorrect. That third year of Yihé corresponds to the second year of Yanhe of the Wei dynasty, the year being Guiyou. Initially, Chen was in Guzang.
There was a śramaṇa named Daojin from Zhangye who wished to receive the bodhisattva precepts from Dharmakṣema.
Dharmakṣema said:
Furthermore, he repented his transgressions and,
with utmost sincerity, practiced for seven days and seven nights.
On the morning of the eighth day, he went to Baoshen to request ordination.
Chen suddenly became greatly enraged;
Jin further reflected,
"It is simply that my karmic obstructions have not yet been extinguished."
Thereupon, for three years, he exerted himself with single-minded diligence, alternating between meditative trance and the study of prophecies.
Within a state of concentration, he beheld Śākyamuni Buddha and various great bodhisattvas bestowing the precepts upon him.
That evening, there were more than ten people staying together with him.
Everyone experienced dreams identical to what Sengjin had seen.
Just as Jin wished to go to Huichan to tell him of this,
he was not yet ten paces away when—
The Seer started in alarm and cried out, "Excellent, excellent! You have already received the precepts;
I shall now act as your witness."
In succession, he explained the characteristics of the precepts before an image of the Buddha.
At that time, the śramaṇa Daolang was renowned throughout Guansi;
it was on the very evening when Daojin received the precepts.
Lang also had a dream of this;
he then sought to become Lang’s dharma-brother, requesting ordination from him at his own lower level of seniority (*śīla-vatsara*).
Thereupon, more than a thousand people followed him to receive the precepts.
The transmission of this dharma has continued down to the present day;
all are the remaining rules of the Prophecy (Kṣaṇa).
A separate record states:
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* must have been brought to this land by the Bodhisattva Iṣvara; subsequently,
it was indeed transmitted and translated by Dharmakṣema.
It is suspected that Paramārtha (Chen) was perhaps no ordinary man.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* in eight fascicles is recorded by Sengyou, Huifang, and others as being translated by Paramārtha;

however, since this is merely another name for the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is not listed separately here. The *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* in five fascicles is likewise recorded by Sengyou, Huifang, and others as being translated by Paramārtha.

The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* (One Scroll): This is currently extracted from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-gaganagañja-parivarta* and circulated separately; it is now recorded in the *Biesheng lu* (Record of Separate Translations) and no longer exists as a separate work here.
*Baoshang lu* states it was translated by [Dharmakṣema] and also says it was excerpted from the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*;
it is likewise recorded in the *Biesheng lu* and does not exist separately. — By Shanxin.
*The Scripture on Women*, two fascicles; *The Scripture on the Path of Non-action*, two fascicles; *The Scripture on the Householder Inviting Monks as a Field of Merit*, one fascicle;

and *The Scripture on the Determination of Sin and Merit*, one fascicle—these four preceding scriptures were all recorded by the Chángfáng et al. catalogues as translations by Dharmakṣema, yet they further note that they are suspected of being apocryphal.
Now, following the old tradition, they are appended here among the doubtful works. The *Essential Explanations of Dhyāna Methods*, two fascicles, is not included herein.
The second edition is identical in its source text to that produced by Kumārajīva; this is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. This one work in two fascicles is currently missing.
[It was translated by] Zhūqú Jīngshēng, Marquis of Ānyáng.
He was the younger cousin of Meng Xun, the King of Hexi.
He was a man of strong will, open-minded, quick-witted, and clear-sighted;
from his youth, he possessed discerning intelligence.
He browsed through various records and was skilled in discourse.
Having received the five precepts in his youth, he applied himself with keen intent to the Buddhist scriptures;
whatever sutras he read, he was immediately able to recite them from memory.
I have always considered that devotion to learning and the pursuit of extensive knowledge to be the preeminent undertaking of a Mahāsattva.
In his youth, he once crossed the Flowing Sands and arrived at the country of Tien (Khotan).
At the Mahādevī Monastery in Jummadi,
he met the Indian Dharma Master Buddhasena— whose name means "Awakening General" in the Liang language— and followed him to inquire about the meaning of the Way.
Sena originally studied the Mahāyāna;
his natural talent was exceptionally outstanding,
and he could recite fifty million verses and was thoroughly proficient in the methods of dhyāna.
Therefore, the various kingdoms of the West refer to him as the "Lion among Men.
Dao’an received from him the various secret and essential arts of the Dharma of Receiving the Throne (abhiṣeka).
He recited the Sanskrit texts orally and returned eastward to Liangzhou.
During the Shunhe era of Emperor Mogaon, one work titled *The Essential Explanation of Dhyāna Methods* (*Chánfǎyàojiě*) was translated.

Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in sixty fascicles—sometimes titled with the characters "Eight Chapters" (*bājiàndù*) at the beginning—was first produced; it is the same text as the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* translated during the Tang dynasty. It has also been circulated in versions of eighty-four fascicles or one hundred and nine fascicles. Compiled by five hundred Arhats more than six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is recorded in the two catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang. This single work in sixty fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Buddhavarman—
alternatively called Buddhabhadra;
in the Liang language, this means "Awakening Armor."
He was a man from the Western Regions.
From childhood, his conduct was upright and straightforward, and his intelligence surpassed that of his peers.
He studied the Tripiṭaka and was particularly proficient in the Vibhāṣā.
He constantly recited and upheld this treatise as his essential core practice.
During the Chenghe era, he arrived at Guzang,
where there was previously a śramaṇa named Daotai.
His resolve and application were firm and resolute.
In his youth, he traveled through the regions east of the Pamirs, visiting various kingdoms,
where he obtained the Sanskrit original of the *Vibhāṣā* in one hundred thousand verses.
Upon returning to Guzang,
he sat with his side-bench vacant and his mind open, yearning for a master of illumination.
He heard that Guṇavarman was devoting his mind to this treatise.
Please provide a translation.
At that time, Juqu Mengxun had already passed away,
and his son Maoqian succeeded him to the throne.
In the fourth month of the middle spring of the fifth year of the Qiánchéng era (the Dingchou year),
at the Xiányù Palace Temple within the city of Liangzhou,
I requested Guṇavarman to translate it.
Tai himself took dictation;
the śramaṇas Huìsōng and Dàolǎng, together with over three hundred monks specializing in doctrinal studies, collated and verified the textual meanings.
This was finally completed in the seventh month of the seventh year, the Jīmóu (Ji-mao) year.
It comprised one hundred fascicles,
for which the śramaṇa Daoyan composed a preface.
Shortly thereafter, Emperor Taizu of the Northern Wei launched a western campaign against Guzang.
The land of Liang fell into chaos, and the scriptures and miscellaneous articles were all consumed by fire;
consequently, forty fascicles were lost,
and only sixty now remain.
Guṇavarman fled the chaos and traveled westward;

his ultimate destination is unknown. The preface states that it was produced in the year Yichou, which corresponds to the fourteenth year of Mengxun’s Xuanshi era, and completed in the year Dingmao, which corresponds to the sixteenth year of Xuanshi. This differs from the catalogue; the reason for this discrepancy remains unclear.

*The Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, twenty fascicles; recorded in the *Jiandao Hui* (Catalogue of the Path of Wisdom) and the *Song Qi Lu* (Record of the Song and Qi Dynasties), and listed as the sixth translation in the *Sengyou Lu*. It is the same text as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema. This one work in twenty fascicles is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Zhimeng was a native of Xinfeng in Jingzhao.
By nature he was upright and intelligent, and he maintained a life of pure and austere conduct.
At a young age, he donned the dharma robes and applied himself to his studies with single-minded devotion; the sound of his recitations continued from night into day.
Whenever he encountered foreign monks speaking of the sacred sites left by Śākyamuni, or heard that the Vaipulya sūtras were spread throughout the Western Regions, [his resolve grew stronger].
I have long been filled with a profound sense of inspiration, directing my thoughts toward distant realms beyond.
I held that ten thousand *li* are but the span of a few inches, and that even a millennium can be pursued.
Thus, in the sixth year of Hongshi of the Yao Qin dynasty, the year of Jiachen, I began this work.
He summoned fifteen like-minded companions and set out from Chang'an,
crossing thirty-six rivers and valleys.
Upon reaching the city of Liangzhou,
he then traveled west out through the Yang Pass and entered the shifting sands for over two thousand li.
The land is devoid of water or grass, and the roads are impassable for travelers.
In winter it is bitterly cold, while in summer it is miasmic and scorching.
When people die, their bones are piled up to mark the path.
Carrying provisions on a camel was extremely arduous and perilous;
he thus traveled through the various kingdoms of Shanshan, Kucha, and Yutian,
observing their customs in detail.
Traveling two thousand li southwest from Yutian,
he first ascended the Pamir Mountains (Congling),
at which point eight of his nine companions turned back.
Mǎng traveled with his companions for over one thousand seven hundred li until he reached the kingdom of Pólún,
where his fellow traveler Zhú Dàoshōng also passed away.
Just as he was about to perform the cremation, he suddenly lost sight of where the corpse was located.
Overcome with intense grief, he sighed in lamentation, struck by the mystery of the situation;
thereupon, exerting his own strength, he moved forward.
Together with four others, he crossed the Snow Mountains three times; there,
the ice cliffs were brilliant white, rising more than a hundred thousand *tan* high,
and they traversed them by flying across the void over bridges made of suspended ropes.
Peering down, its bottom could not be seen; looking up, the sky was not visible.
The cold air was bitterly severe, such that his shadow trembled and his soul shuddered.
He traveled south again for a thousand *li* and reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
They crossed the Sindhu River once more.
The snow mountains rose up even more precipitously than before;
below, there was much miasmic vapor and malevolent spirits that blocked the path.
Many of the practitioners died;
however, with a fierce and sincere mind that penetrated the darkness, he was able to cross the perils and reach the city of Kaśmīra.
Once he arrived at the city of Kaśmīra...
There are always five hundred arhats dwelling in this kingdom,
who constantly travel back and forth to Lake Anavatapta.
Among them is an arhat of great virtue.
Upon seeing that Maṅgala had arrived and come to rest, they rejoiced and praised him.
Maṅgala inquired about the local lands,
and they explained to him the affairs concerning the four devaputras.
These details are fully contained in the *Foguo ji* (Record of the Buddhist Kingdoms).
Faxian previously saw a stone spittoon inscribed with the Buddha’s writing in the country of Qiśa;
he also saw the Buddha’s alms bowl in this same country.
The light and color were deep purple-blue, extending to all four boundaries.
With intense fragrant flowers as an offering, he bowed his head in reverence and made a vow.
If the bowl was indeed appropriate, [he should accept it].
He was able to lift it lightly and then heavy;
once he had shifted it to a heavy weight, his strength could no longer bear it.
Yet, when lowering it onto the table, he again perceived no heaviness.
The path of the mind of enlightenment should be such as this.
Traveling again one thousand three hundred li to the southwest,
he reached the kingdom of Kapilavastu, where he beheld the Buddha’s hair, his tooth, and the bone of his *uṣṇīṣa*.
The Buddha’s shadow and the Buddha’s footprints remain vividly present.
Furthermore, I beheld the Forest of Firm Nirvana and the Bodhi Tree where he subdued Māra;
with intense joy filling my heart, I made offerings for one day.
Furthermore, he used a precious canopy and a great robe to cover the image of the Subduer of Māra.
As he traveled and observed these sites, he investigated their spiritual transformations;
the accounts of the Celestial Ladder and the Dragon Pond are beyond counting.
Later, he arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra,
which was the former capital of King Aśoka.
There lived a Brahmin of great wisdom named Rāyagupta, whose entire clan propagated the Dharma and whom the king held in high esteem.
He constructed a pure silver stupa three zhang high.
Previously, the śramaṇa Faxian had already obtained six fascicles of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra at his house.
When Mengzhi saw him, he asked,
"Is there the study of Mahāyāna in the land of Qin?
He replied, "Everyone studies Mahāyāna."
Rājagṛha was struck with amazement and exclaimed, "How rare! How rare!
Could it not be that a Bodhisattva has come to convert them?"
Mǎng obtained a copy of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in Sanskrit from his home.
He further found a copy of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in Sanskrit as well as other sūtras in Sanskrit.
Vowing to propagate [the teachings],
he then turned back.
In the year of Jiǎzǐ, he departed from India.
Four fellow monks passed away along the way;
only Daomeng and Tanzuan returned together to Liangzhou.
During the Qiánchéng era of the Hè period, they translated the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* into twenty fascicles.
Sengmeng died at the end of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
As Sengsheng subsequently traveled abroad, the itineraries recorded by various śramaṇas sometimes differed from one another;
even the locations of the Buddha’s alms bowl and cranial bone were inconsistent.
One should know that traveling to India was not limited to a single route;
