as the bowl and the skull-cup underwent miraculous migrations when the time came for them to reach different lands,
it is difficult to generalize based on what has been transmitted through reports of sights and hearsay.

The *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra* in two fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara; see the *Fanjing tu*. The *Mahāyāna-praveśa-śāstra* in two fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Sthiramati; see the *Tang jiulu* as well as the *Neidian lu* and the *Fanjing tu*. These two works, totaling four fascicles, are extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Dao Tai possessed a talent bestowed by Heaven; his spirit was lofty and clear,
and his extensive learning led him to take a keen interest in marvelous matters and to investigate foreign languages from afar.
In the past, as the various texts of the Han lands were already complete and the profound principles roughly elucidated,
the only areas that remained unrefined were the Tripiṭaka and the nine divisions of scripture.
Therefore, taking up my staff and braving the perils, I arrived at the west of the Pamir Mountains.
There I examined Sanskrit texts and received the profound meaning of their lofty principles;
furthermore, I obtained the Sanskrit original of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* in over one hundred thousand verses, as well as various sūtras and śāstras.
He returned east to Liang,
where he subsequently met Buddhavarman and together they translated the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Later, Sengtai himself translated two works, including the *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra*. Furthermore, the *Chángfáng nèidiǎn lù* (Longfang’s Inner Scriptures Catalog) states that during the Liang dynasty, there was also the śramaṇa Tanjue, who translated the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányú jīng*) in one fascicle at the kingdom of Gaochang.
This would place it in the twenty-second year of the Song Yuanjia era.
Now, this is not so;

for by the sixteenth year of Yuanjia, the year Jīmōu (459), the Liang state had already ceased to exist—how then could there still have been a translation of scriptures in the twenty-second year, the year Yǐyǒu (465)?
Therefore, we know that both catalogs are in error.

Now, following Jingmai’s *Jingtu*, it is compiled under the era of the Northern Wei. Although both the Song and the Wei were contemporary, with the Song residing in Jianye and the Wei capital at Heng’an, when considered by geography, it properly belongs to the Wei catalog.

*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice of His Body to a Starving Tiger and the Circumstances of the Stūpa’s Construction*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states it is also known as *The Sūtra on Giving One’s Body to a Starving Tiger*. See the postscript at the end of the sūtra. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, its manuscript is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Fasheng was a native of Gaochang.
During the Liang period,
he also translated one fascicle of the *Sūtra on Casting One's Body to Feed a Starving Tiger*.
Therefore, at the end of the *Biography of the Former Eminent Monk Dharmakṣema*, it says:
"At that time, there was also a śramaṇa from Gaochang named Fasheng,
who likewise traveled abroad and composed a four-fascicle biography."
The *Postscript to the Sutra of Casting One's Body to the Starving Tiger* states:
"At that time, having heard the Buddha’s discourse,
the king immediately erected a great stupa at that very spot."
It is called the Stūpa of the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice to the Starving Tiger;
the stūpa is still extant today.
On the mountain slope to the east of it, there are monastic quarters, lecture halls, and viharas.
There were always five thousand monks who received offerings of the four requisites.
At that time, Fa-sheng saw in various countries people suffering from leprosy,
insanity, deafness, blindness, and those with crippled hands, feet, or lameness.
Furthermore, those suffering from various ailments all come to this stūpa to burn incense,
light lamps, smear the ground with fragrant mud,
sweep and sprinkle it clean, and prostrate themselves while repenting.
Hundred ailments were all healed.
Those who had come previously recovered and departed;
subsequently, there were always more than a hundred people arriving at any given time.
This applies to all, regardless of their noble or humble status;
it shall never come to an end.
Now, having carefully examined the texts of the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) and perused the accounts in the scriptures and records:
Fasheng’s travels to the Western Regions were not in vain;
furthermore, since he personally beheld the sacred shrine, his account must be free from error.
If it were not translated by Fasheng himself, how could that scripture have been included there?
Since Zhong was ultimately able to travel to the Western Land himself,
how could he not have transmitted the scriptures and teachings?
When examining the events from beginning to end, the matter becomes perfectly clear.
I have now extensively translated and compiled these records for this collection: 1.

*The Sūtra of the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma* (4 fascicles), also known as the *Sūtra of Non-retrogression*, second translation; identical in substance to Dharmarakṣa’s *A-vui-yue-tche-tche king*. 2. *The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* (2 fascicles, or 1 fascicle). 3. *The Sūtra of Great Forbearance* (10 fascicles). 4. *The Sūtra of the Golden-Wheel King* (1 fascicle). 5. *The Names of the Five Hundred Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa* (1 fascicle). These five works comprise eighteen fascicles in total. Of these, the first two works totaling six fascicles are extant; the remaining three works totaling twelve fascicles are missing.
The records of Changfang and others all state:
"This is the 'New Collection of the Diverse Scriptures of the Liang Region by Śramaṇa Sengyou' compiled by Shi Dao'an."
I have now appended these to the catalog of the Liang dynasty as works of unknown translators, so that the eras,
the presence or absence of prominent translations, the number of fascicles, and the locations from which they emerged may be known.
The following works have been newly appended to this catalogue:
*Upāsikā-śīla-prakāśana-sūtra* (Two fascicles; sometimes the word "sūtra" is omitted and it is simply called *Jingxing jing*);
*Gṛhapati Dharmavatsa-patnī-sūtra* (One fascicle); *Mahāprajāpatī-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* (Two fascicles; also called *Dà*).

The *Ājñātakaunḍinya-pratimokṣa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Ājñātakaunḍinya Receiving the Precepts); the old catalog states: the *Mahāprajāpatī-sūtra*, the *Triprajñā-sūtra* (one fascicle), the *Bodhisattva-samācāra-sūtra* (one fascicle).
Below these, there are missing: the *Catvāri-vaiśāradya-sūtra* (one fascicle) and the *Upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* (one fascicle). The old catalog states:
the *Mañjuśrī-upāya-kauśalya-samādhi-sūtra*, or simply called the *Upāya-kauśalya-samādhi-sūtra* (ten fascicles).
*Ugra-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Saptapada-dhyāna-anuśaṃsā-sūtra*, one fascicle. The old catalog states: *Ugra-saptapada-dhyāna-anuśaṃsā-sūtra*;
*Bodhisattva-daśaugra-sūtra*, one fascicle. [The latter] is now suspected to be the same as the aforementioned *Daśaugra*.
*King Bimbisāra-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Sadasat-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Pañcaśatika-gāthā-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Suyave Country Poor Man* [sūtra], one fascicle.
*Ren jing* (Sutra on Humans), one fascicle; the old catalog states it is the *Xuyeue guo pin ren lin ti tou jing* (Sutra on a Poor Man from the Kingdom of Xuyeue Hiring a Barber).

*Fu mu jing* (Sutra on Floating Wood), one fascicle. *Pai yu jing* (Sutra on the Simile of the Clay Pot), one fascicle. *Yaoguai jing* (Sutra on Strange Spirits), one fascicle. *A ban ji niepan jing* (Sutra on the Nirvana of Abhagnya), one fascicle;
another version reads *Tao she ji niepan jing*. *Si fei chang jing* (Sutra on the Four Impermanences), one fascicle. *Wu shi gai jing* (Sutra on the Five Losses and Coverings), one fascicle.

*Juyan zhenjing* (The Essential True Scripture), one fascicle; *Benwu jing* (The Scripture on Original Non-existence), one fascicle; *Quande jing* (The Scripture on Encouraging Virtue), one fascicle; *Shiwude jing* (The Scripture on the Fifteen Virtues), one fascicle;

*Fumuyinyuan jing* (The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of Parents), one fascicle—this is currently suspected to be the same as the *Fanyuyinyuan jing* (Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of Father and Son); *Huixing jing* (The Scripture on Wise Practice), one fascicle;

*Weishengwang jing* (The Scripture on King Unborn), one fascicle—this is currently suspected to be the *Weishengyuan jing* (Scripture on King Ajātaśatru). [These belong to] the Inner and Outer Non-action (*Anabhisaṃskāra*).

*Sūtra* in one fascicle; *Dào jìng jīng* (Sūtra on the Purity of the Path) in one fascicle; *Qīshì běnmò jīng* (Sūtra on the Origin and End of the Seven Matters) in one fascicle—the old catalog states it was titled *Qīshì běnxíng jīng*;
*Bǎibǎo sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Hundred Jewels) in one fascicle; *Sānchéng jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Vehicles) in one fascicle;

*Qíyù shù jīng* (Sūtra on the Arts of Jīvaka)—the old catalog states it was titled *Qíyù sìshù jīng*; *Wǔgài líyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Coverings and Dispelling Doubts) in one fascicle—this is now suspected to be the *Wǔgài jīng*.
*Gaiyi jieshi xing jing* (Sutra on the Loss of Practice Due to Doubt), one fascicle; *Taizi zhizhi jing* (Sutra on the Prince’s Cessation through Wisdom), one fascicle;

*Daode zhang jing* (Sutra on the Chapters of the Way and Virtue), one fascicle; *Kuxiang jing* (Sutra on the Characteristics of Suffering), one fascicle; *Xufude du jing* (Sutra on Receiving Buddhahood through Attaining Enlightenment), one fascicle; *You jing* (Sutra on Causes), one fascicle; *Fenran huan guo jialuoyue jing* (Sutra of Kātyāyana of the City of Fenranhuan), one fascicle;

*Wuyin shi jing* (Sutra on the Matters of the Five Aggregates), one fascicle; *Yiju fashi jing* (Sutra on Resolving the Meaning of Dharma-Matters), one fascicle; and *Shisi* (Ten Reflections), [one fascicle].

The *Weijing* (Sutra on Solitude), one fascicle; the *Fenbie liu qing jing* (Sutra on Distinguishing the Six Sense-Organs), one fascicle; the *San shi gai jing* (Sutra on the Three Losses and the Coverings), one fascicle;

the *Fo bao san mei jing* (Sutra on the Buddha-Treasure Samādhi), one fascicle; and the *Fazhi nü jing* (Sutra of the Woman Fazhi), one fascicle—these four works totaling six fascicles exist in manuscript;
all others among these forty-seven works and forty-nine fascicles are missing.
Sengyou’s Catalogue states:
"Master Daoan’s 'Different Scriptures from the Liang Region' was omitted and not recorded in the catalogues of Hui Changfang and others."
Now, these are appended to the Liang Catalogue.
Considering them to be of lost translation, Dao’an included them in his "General Record of Extraordinary Scriptures from the Liang Territory," totaling fifty-nine works;
among these, five works were already recorded in the Fang Catalogue.
Now, forty-seven additional sections are presented;
together with the previous fifty-two,
there remain seven sections totaling fourteen fascicles.
I have carefully examined the records of Sengchangfang and others;
all of them have a basis in fact and are therefore not translations of lost works.
For this reason, these have been omitted and not preserved in this record.
Now, the titles and conditions are fully set forth as follows:
*The Sūtra of the Chapter on Subhūti*, seven fascicles; *The Excerpted Sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā* (also known by other titles), translated by Dharmapriya during the Former Qin dynasty.
*The Sūtra on the Manifestation of the Treasure Store by Śubhavyūha*, two fascicles; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
*The Sūtra of the Seven Knowledges* (also titled *The Sūtra of the Seven Wisdoms*), one fascicle; translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu.

*The Sūtra of the Dragon King Nanda* (also called *The Nanda Dragon Sūtra* or *The Sūtra of the Brother Dragon Kings*), one fascicle; translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu under various titles. *The Āṭānāṭiya Samādhi Sūtra*, one fascicle.
The *Ātā-samādhi Sūtra* is an alternative title for the *An-gong Guanzhong Yijing*. It has already been recorded as one fascicle of the *Dà wǔzhuó jīng*;
old catalogs refer to it as the *Dà wǔzhuó shì jīng*, while various records call it spurious; it is now also included at the beginning [of this collection].
First is the *Shǒuzhìwèn shí sì zhāng jīng*, one fascicle; old catalogs call it the *Shǒuzhìwèn fó shí sì yì jīng*, or simply the *Shǒuzhìwèn*.

The *Shou zhi wen shi si shi jing* (Sūtra on the Fourteen Questions Asked by Śūra) is also said to have been translated by Zhi Yao of the Later Han; it is now included as a selected sūtra in the *Bie sheng lu*.
The eight-fascicle *Da fang guang shi lun jing* (Mahāvaipulya Daśacakrakṣitigarbha Sūtra) was first produced and shares the same text as the Tang translation of the *Dizang shi lun jing*.
It appears to be a translation from the Liang period, though it is not recorded in the various catalogues; it is now appended here as part of the thirteenth division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
During the late Liang period, I have striven to avoid omissions; these include both new and old translations,
totaling fifty-three works in seventy-five fascicles,
all of which are recorded as having lost their original sources during the Northern Liang dynasty.
*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll Four, General Catalogue Part Four;
*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu Year.
Part Five: A General Compendium of the Various Scriptures, Volume One, Part Five.

From the first year of the Yongchu era of Emperor Wu of the Liu Song dynasty, the year Gengshen, until the third year of the Shengming era of Emperor Shun, the year Jiwu—the Liu Song dynasty, of the Liu clan, had its capital at Jianye.
In total, there were eight directors for sixty years.
There were twenty-two individuals, both monastics and laypeople,
who produced various sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and miscellaneous collections of translated scriptures whose original translators were lost.

In total, there are four hundred and sixty-five works comprising seven hundred and seventeen fascicles; among these, nine hundred and thirty works totaling two hundred and forty-three fascicles are extant, while three hundred and seventy-two works totaling four hundred and seventy-four fascicles are missing.
The Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas of the Song [Dynasty] translated three sections totaling thirty-two fascicles of Vinaya precepts and *karmavācanā*;
the Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra translated two sections totaling two fascicles of sūtras; the Śramaṇa Dharmamitra translated twelve sections totaling seventeen fascicles of sūtras;
the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda translated ten sections totaling thirty-one fascicles of sūtras; and the Śramaṇa Ratnamegha [translated as follows].
A collection of fourteen sūtras from the four Āgamas, totaling seventeen fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Yebaluo (Jīvaka);

a collection of one treatise, totaling thirteen fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Qiunabamo (Guṇavarman); a collection of ten treatises, totaling eighteen fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Sengqiebamoluo (Saṃghavarman);
and a collection of five vinaya treatises, totaling twenty-four fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Qiunabaduoluo (Guṇabhadra). [Total: fifty fascicles.]
A collection of one hundred thirty-four fascicles of sūtras and śāstras from two sections: one work in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Shi Tanwujie;
twenty-eight works in twenty-eight fascicles of sūtras and vinaya by the layman Juqu Jingsheng;
ten works in ten fascicles of sūtra collections by the śramaṇa Shi Huijian; and two works in seven fascicles by the śramaṇa Gongdezhi.
*Jīng shāmen Shì Sēngqú* (The Scripture of the Śramaṇa Shi Sengqu), one fascicle; *Jīmó shāmen Shì Fǎyǐng* (The Karma of the Śramaṇa Shi Faying), one fascicle;

*Níjiè shāmen Zhú Fǎjuàn* (The Bhikṣuṇī Precepts of the Śramaṇa Zhu Fajian), six works in twenty-nine fascicles; *Jīng shāmen Shì Xiánggōng* (The Scripture of the Śramaṇa Shi Xianggong), one work in two fascicles;
*Jīng shāmen Shì Dàoyán* (The Scripture of the Śramaṇa Shi Daoyan), two works in three fascicles; and the *Jīnglù shāmen Shì Yǒng* (The Scripture and Vinaya of the Śramaṇa Shi Yong).
The Honored One’s three sections, three fascicles of sutras; the śramaṇa Shi Faha’s two sections, two fascicles of sutras and vinaya;
the śramaṇa Shi Xian’s one section, one fascicle of sutras; the śramaṇa Saṃghavarman’s one section, one fascicle of vinaya compendium;
the newly compiled collection of various sutras of lost translation, three hundred and seven works in three hundred and forty fascicles; and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, thirty fascicles.
It is also called the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, or in twenty-four fascicles; the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog) states it is in thirty-four fascicles, which is likely an error.
According to Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu* and Sengyou’s catalog, there is one fascicle of the *Wufen biqiu jieben* (Five-Part Bhikṣu Precept Manual), also called the *Mahīśāsaka-jieben*.
According to Zhu Daozu’s catalog and Sengyou’s catalog, there is also one fascicle of the *Mahīśāsaka-karmavācanā*.

[This] volume is seen in the records of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou; the aforementioned three sections totaling thirty-two fascicles concerning the Vinaya precepts are currently extant, though the *Karmavācanā* (羯磨) is missing.
[Compiled by] the Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas.
In the Song language, his name was Jue-shou (Jñānāyus).
He was a native of Kaśmīra and,
in his youth, received his training in the Mahīśāsaka school.
He was dedicated to the study of the Vinaya-piṭaka and simultaneously mastered the essentials of Dhyāna.
In the seventh month of the first year of the Jingping era (the *guihai* year) of the deposed Emperor Yifu, he arrived at the capital of Yangdu.
Previously, the śramaṇa Faxian had obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya in the Kingdom of Siṃhala.
Before he had finished translating them, Xuancheng passed away.
When the monks in Jianye heard that Kumārajīva was already proficient in this field of study,
they requested him to produce translations of these works.
In the eleventh month of winter of that same year,
he convened at Longguang Temple to translate it;
it was titled the *Wufen lü* (The Five-Part Vinaya).
Kumārajīva held the Sanskrit text;
the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Yutian interpreted the language;
and the Śramaṇa Zhu Daosheng of Longguang and the Śramaṇa Shi Huayan of Dong’an held the writing brush together to verify and correct it.
The State Councilor and Prince of Langya, Yan Liàn of the Song dynasty, served as the patron (dānapati).
The work was completed in the twelfth month of the following year,
at which time he also issued the *Jixin* (Text on the Mind of Precepts) and the *Jiemowen* (Text on the Karmavācanā), among other materials.
These circulated concurrently in the world.
Kumārajīva’s ultimate end is unknown.

The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* (one fascicle), also titled the *Sūtra on the Visualization of Immeasurable Life*, first appeared in the *Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties Concerning Daohui* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. The *Sūtra on the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata* (one fascicle) was second in appearance according to the *Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. These two works, totaling two fascicles, are extant today.
The śramaṇa Qiāngliángyèshē was commonly known during the Song dynasty as Xīyù Rénxìng (Western Region Nature).
He was a man of upright character and few desires.
He was proficient in reciting the Abhidharma and extensively studied the Vinaya;
furthermore, he had mastered a great many other sūtras.
Although he was well-versed in all three piṭakas, he was particularly distinguished in these fields.
He specialized exclusively in the Chan gate;
whenever he engaged in contemplative observation, he would often remain without rising for seven days.
He constantly used the correct reception of samādhi to transform and guide people throughout various kingdoms.
In the first year of the Yuanjia era, a Jiazi year,
Huiyuan braved the desert sands and arrived at Jianye;
Emperor Wen Di Yilong deeply marveled at his extraordinary qualities.
An imperial edict ordered him to reside at Daolin Monastery on Mount Zhong.
The śramaṇa Baozhi honored his methods of dhyāna.
The śramaṇa Senghan requested that he translate the *Contemplation of Immeasurable Life* and the *Medicine King and Medicine Superior [Sūtras]*.
Guānhan served as the scribe.
This was because these two sutras constitute the grand cause for the Pure Land and are the secret arts for transforming obstacles.
Reflecting deeply and savoring its meaning, he circulated it throughout the Song state.
Meng Yi of Pingchang, moved by this influence, held him in profound reverence and provided him with abundant resources.
When Zhiyi was appointed as the governor of Kuaiji, he firmly declined the appointment;
later, he moved to reside in Jiangling.
In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he traveled west to the regions of Min and Shu.
Everywhere he propagated the Way, and students of Chan gathered in great numbers.
Later, he returned and passed away in Jiangling at the age of sixty.
*The Sutra of the Divine Incantation of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha*, one fascicle;

the second translation, identical in text to the *Ākāśagarbha* [Sutra] by Yaśas under the Yao Qin and the *Ākāśagarbha-garbha* [Sutra] by Jñānagupta under the Sui, as recorded in Li Kuò’s *Wei-shi-lu*.
Also, the *Sutra on the Contemplation of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha*, one fascicle, also titled the *Sutra on the Contemplation of Ākāśagarbha*, or simply called *Ākāśagarbha*.

The *Bodhisattva-jñāna-darśana-sūtra* (菩薩經見道慧), one fascicle; recorded in the Song-Qi catalogues and the Sengyou catalogue as the fourth production, which shares the same text as the *Aniṣṭhita-sūtra* (無所希望經);
seen in Li Kuò’s catalogue. The *Dharmavīrarāja-sūtra* (諸法勇王經), one fascicle;
the second production, which shares the same text as the *Sarvadharmaniruttara-rāja-sūtra* (一切法高王經); seen in Li Kuò’s catalogue. The *Strīvivarta-sūtra* (轉女).
*Shen jing* (Sūtra on the Body), one fascicle; the fourth appearance, identical in text to the *Wugou xian nü jing* (Sūtra of the Immaculate Virtuous Woman) and others, according to Li Kuò’s record.

*Guān púxián púsà xíngfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Method of Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva), one fascicle; the lower note states it is extracted from the *Shēngōngdé jīng* (Sūtra of Profound Merit), or that the characters "xíngfǎ" (method of practice) may be absent, and it is also called the *Púxián guān jīng* (Sūtra of the Contemplation of Samantabhadra).
The third appearance, according to Sēngyòu’s record, is found in the *Wǔmén chán* (Five-Gate Dhyāna).
*Jingyao fayong* (Essential Methods of the Sūtras), one fascicle; the second translation, identical in text to that produced by An Shigao, as recorded in the *Baochang lu* and the *Sengyou lu*.
*New Wuliangshou jing* (New Sūtra of Immeasurable Life), two fascicles;

the tenth translation, identical in text to the *Wuliangshou jing* of An Shigao and the "Immeasurable Life Assembly" (*Wuliangshou hui*) of the *Ratnakūṭa*, as recorded in the *Zhenji si lu*. *Yugajiangzhe* (The Householder Ugga).
*Suowen jing* (Sūtra on What Was Asked), one fascicle; the sixth translation, identical in text to the *Anxuan fajing jing* and the *Ratnakūṭa-uragasena-parivarta*, as seen in Li Kuò’s record.
*Buddha sheng daoli tian wei mu shuofa jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother), one fascicle;
the third translation, identical in text to the *Fahuo fo sheng daoli tian jing*, as seen in Li Kuò’s record.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life), one fascicle; the second translation is identical in text to that produced by Jñānagupta and Śīladharma, as recorded in the *Baochang lu*.
The *Dhyāna-guhyārtha Sūtra*, five fascicles—or perhaps omitting the word "sūtra"—also known as the *Dhyāna-dharmāvadāna*;
translated at Qihuan Temple in the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era, or in three fascicles, as recorded in the *Sengyou lu*. This is the third translation appearing here.
There is the *Canyao miji jing* (Secret Essentials of Dhyāna Sūtra) in five fascicles; its text is extremely disordered and cannot be circulated.
As described in the *Shanfan bulue* (Abridged Compendium of Monastic Rules), the above twelve works comprise seventeen fascicles.
Of these, the seven works on the five gates of dhyāna totaling seven fascicles are extant, while the five works on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* totaling ten fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmamitra—
translated into the Song language as Fashou—
was a native of Jibin.
At the age of six or seven, his spiritual intelligence was clear and upright.
Whenever he witnessed a Dharma ceremony, he would spontaneously leap for joy.
His parents cherished him and marveled at his nature, so they eventually allowed him to leave the household life.
In Kaśmīra, many sages and realized ones have appeared;
having repeatedly encountered enlightened masters,
they have extensively mastered the various scriptures and possess particularly profound mastery of the methods of dhyāna.
The essentials he attained were extremely subtle and profound;
as a person, he was deep and far-reaching, possessed of wisdom and understanding,
and his ritual procedures were detailed and orderly.
He was born with eyebrows joined together;
thus, he was known in the world as Chan Master Lianmei (Joined-Brow).
From his youth, he delighted in traveling to various regions, vowing to propagate the teachings.
Traveling through various countries, he eventually reached Kucha.
One day before his arrival, the king dreamed that a deity told him:
"A person of great merit and virtue shall enter the kingdom tomorrow."
"You should make offerings to him.
The following morning, he immediately issued an edict to the external offices:
"If any extraordinary person enters the borders, you must immediately dispatch a messenger to report it to me."
Before long, Maitreya arrived.
The king went out to the outskirts of the city to welcome him in person and invited him into the palace;
he then received the precepts from him.
He provided him with the four types of offerings until they were exhausted.
Because Śāriputra was peaceful yet capable of moving on, he did not become attached to gain and honor.
After several years, Śāriputra formed the intention to depart.
A deity again descended in a dream and said,
"A person of merit has abandoned the king and departed.
The king woke up in a state of startled alarm.
Soon thereafter, although his sovereign and ministers earnestly entreated him to remain, none could stop him.
He then crossed the shifting sands and proceeded to Dunhuang,
where he established a vihāra in the midst of the wilderness.
He planted a thousand peach trees and established a garden of one hundred mu;
its chambers, pavilions, ponds, and groves were exceedingly solemn and pure.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled again to Liangzhou.
He further renovated the halls and chambers within the old monastery at the former government office;
there, students gathered in great numbers and the practice of meditation flourished exceedingly.
He constantly desired to transmit the Dharma, as the region east of the Yangtze River was densely populated.
In the first year of the Yuanjia era, he traveled by stages until he reached Shu.
Shortly thereafter, he crossed the gorges and stayed in Jingzhou,
where he established a meditation hall at Changsha Temple.
With uplifted sincerity and profound compassion, he prayed for a relic;
after more than ten days, he was moved by a single one,
which struck against its container with a sound and emitted light that filled the room.

Among his disciples, both monastics and laypeople, there was none who did not redouble their vigor, each with a hundredfold resolve. After staying for a short while, he followed the river downstream to Jianye, where he initially resided at Zhongxing Temple.
In the evening, he rested at the Jetavana Monastery.
His reputation for the sound of the Way had long been renowned, and the entire city turned out to pay their respects.
From Empress Yuan of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, down to the crown princes and princesses, there was none who did not observe the fast.
From the Gui Palace, invitations for the precepts were issued;
from the inner chambers, envoys to inquire after his health arrived in succession every ten days.
This continued from the first year of the Yuanjia era, the Jiazi year, until the eighteenth year, the Xinsi year.
He translated twelve sections of scriptures, including the *Ākāśagarbha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
He constantly instructed his disciples in the path of dhyāna.
All who sought refuge with him traveled from as far as a thousand li.
The fourfold assembly, both far and near, all hailed him as the Great Chan Master.
Meng Yi, the Governor of Kuaiji, had deep faith in the True Dharma and took it upon himself to serve as the guardian of the Triple Gem.
He had long cherished a fondness for the flavor of Chan and possessed a profound sense of reverence.
Upon reaching the banks of the Zhejiang River, he requested to travel together with him,
and subsequently established a monastery on the mountain in Zan County.
In the eastern regions, the ancient customs had largely inclined toward sorcery and incantations;
however, through the transformation brought about by this wondrous edification, every household has returned to the orthodox path.
From west to east, there is none who does not submit with sincerity.
Later, he returned to Jianye and stayed at the Lower Dinglin Temple.
By nature, the Dhyāna Master was serene and tranquil, and he held a refined love for mountains and rivers;
he considered Mount Zhong, as a guardian peak, to be particularly beautiful, surpassing even Mount Song and Mount Hua.
He often lamented that the foundation and structure of the lower temple had not yet fully realized the site's scenic excellence.
Thereupon, he ascended a high point to survey the terrain and deliberate upon the mountain’s topography;
he cleared stones and felled trees to establish the upper temple.
The imperial halls and meditation chambers were solemn and profound;
they truly bore a faint resemblance to Vulture Peak and a vague likeness to the Jetavana Grove.
Thereupon, a multitude of those who had stilled their minds gathered from ten thousand li away.
Reciting the scriptures with solemnity and harmony, he transformed others by his mere presence.
From the Western Regions to the southern lands,
wherever he traveled, [he left his mark].
There was no one who did not establish assemblies for almsgiving (*dāna*) and expound the teachings.
When the First Dhyāna Master first departed from Kaśmīra,
the deity Kapiśa escorted him with protection.
He eventually reached Kucha.
On the way, he wished to turn back,
whereupon [the deity] manifested his form and took leave of the Dhyāna Master, saying:
"You possess the sovereign power of supernatural transformations and travel freely;
shall we not follow you together to the south?
Having finished speaking, he immediately withdrew his shadow so that it was no longer seen.
He subsequently traveled far to follow [the Master] to Yangdu.
Consequently, he had images of him painted upon the walls of the Upper Temple;
even until the present day, there are still reports of miraculous manifestations such as voices and shadows.
Through her purity and sincerity in seeking blessings, there were none of her prayers that were not fulfilled.
She passed away at Shangsi on the sixth day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era,
at the age of eighty-seven.
The fourfold assembly of monastics and laypeople followed him, wailing as they proceeded.
He was subsequently buried at Mount Zhong, in front of Songxi Temple.
The *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* consists of six fascicles; its initial title reads: "The Akṣayamati-parivarta from within the Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra."
Chapter Twenty-two: On the Meaning of the Inexhaustible. Also simply titled the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*, it is also known as the *Acchāma-sūtra*.
The fourth edition is identical to the *Acchāma* translated by Dharmarakṣa; this is seen in Li Kuò’s record.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* in one fascicle is a branch of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; this is seen in Chángfáng’s record. The *Vaipulya-vyūha-avivartya-sūtra*.

The *Cakrasūtra* (Wheel Sūtra) in four fascicles, the third [translation], or in six fascicles; alternatively, it is simply called the *Vaipulya-prabhāsvara-pariśuddha-sūtra* (Extensive and Pure Sūtra), or directly the *Avivartika-dharmacakra-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma).
It is identical in its original text to the *Dharmarakṣa-avaivartika-caryā-sūtra* and others, and was translated in the fourth year of the Yuanjia era.

It appears in the *Song-Qi-lu* (Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties) and the *Sengyou-lu* (Record of Sengyou). The *Caturmahārāja-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Four Heavenly Kings) in one fascicle appears in the *Seng...*.

The *Shūlù* (Catalogue of Scriptures) and the *Gāosēngzhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) record that the *Puyao jīng* (Lalitavistara-sūtra) in eight fascicles was the third translation; it also appears in six or four fascicles.

It is identical in its original text to the *Shǔ Puyao* (Lalitavistara from Shu), the *Zhú Fǎhù Puyao* (Lalitavistara by Dharmarakṣa), and the Tang translation of the *Fāngguǎng Zhuāngyán* (Vaipulya-vyūha).

This is seen in the *Sòng Qì lù* (Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties), the *Sēngyòu lù*, and the *Gāosēngzhuàn*. The *Jìngdù sānmèi jīng* (Nettippakaraṇa-sūtra) in one fascicle was the first translation.
The *Bodhisattva-vaipulya-śīla-sūtra* (Pusa yingluo benye jing) in two fascicles; second appearance, recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Sheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth) in five fascicles;
second appearance, identical in text to that translated by Dharmarakṣa. Changfang states it is seen in a separate catalogue.
The *Śubhavyūha-upāsaka-sūtra* (Shande youposai jing) in one fascicle; recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Anāgāmin-sūtra* (Ana han jing) in two fascicles; recorded in the *Changfang lu*.
The above record comprises ten sections totaling thirty-one fascicles: the first four sections, totaling twelve fascicles, are extant;
the latter six sections, totaling nineteen fascicles, are missing. *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra*.
The śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan was a native of Xiliangzhou.
He entered the monastic order in his early twenties and soon became renowned for his diligent application.
Wearing patched robes, he sat in meditation and sustained himself on vegetarian food for many years.
Desiring to study extensively under renowned masters and seek out the vast scriptures,
he eventually traveled throughout the Western Regions until he reached Kaśmīra.
He entered the Mahāmandala Vihāra and received instruction on the methods of dhyāna from the bhikṣu Buddhasena.
Having practiced for three years, his mastery surpassed that of ten.
Buddhayaśas first observed that his meditative contemplation was systematic and profound, and he held him in exceptional esteem.
Upon hearing this, the monastics and laypeople there sighed in admiration, saying:
"In the land of Qin, there is indeed a śramaṇa who seeks the Way. For the first time, they no longer looked down upon those of the Qin race, but began to receive foreigners with respect.
At that time, there was the bhikṣu Buddhabhadra,
who was also a master of dhyāna in that country;
Yan then invited him to return eastward, desiring to transmit the Dharma to the Middle Kingdom.
Bhadra, admiring his sincerity, eventually traveled east with him.
After more than a year had passed, they reached the interior of the pass;
there they remained together in Chang’an, constantly relying upon one another.
Shortly thereafter, Guṇabhadra was unjustly expelled by the monks of the Qin court.
Huiguan and the assembly who had come from the West dispersed and departed the Pass,
eventually resting at a monastery in Shandong.
He sat in meditation and recited the sutras, diligently cultivating his studies with great vigor.
In the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, when Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty launched a western campaign against Yao Hong,
he achieved a decisive victory and returned with his banners passing through Shandong.
At that time, Wang Hui, the Duke of Shixing, followed the imperial carriage on an excursion through the mountains and rivers until they reached the Yan Monastery.
There he saw three fellow monks sitting cross-legged on rope beds, their minds immersed in profound meditation.
Hui then snapped his fingers;
the three men opened their eyes,
but after a brief moment, they closed them again.
He would not engage him in conversation;
however, his mind was expanded by reverence for the man's extraordinary nature,
so he inquired about him from the local elders.
Everyone said that he had lived in seclusion for many years and had never once ventured out.
Hui then petitioned Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty to invite him back to the capital.
No one was willing to go.
After repeated requests, they finally arrived;
the two men then urged Baoyan to accompany them.
Huikai’s Way was vast and his integrity profound; he was deeply devoted to the rites of propriety and attended to them with great thoroughness.
Upon returning to the capital, he resided at Shixing Temple.
By nature, Yan was empty and tranquil, and his will was set on avoiding the clamor and dust of the world.
Huī then established another vihāra on the outskirts of the eastern suburb;
this was the Jīyuán Monastery (Zhìyuán Sī).
Yán subsequently returned to the Western Regions.
The various Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras that had been obtained had not yet been translated or transcribed.
Then, in the fourth year of the Yuanjia era (the Dingmao year),
he joined with the śramaṇa Baoyun.
He translated ten scriptures, including the Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra.
He resided at Yan Temple and did not accept private invitations, constantly supporting himself through almsrounds.
His spiritual transformation reached both the hidden and the manifest, so that all were moved to submission.
Yan Qing was pure and simple, possessing few desires;
he gave away whatever he received and traveled through various regions from his youth, remaining unattached to anything.
By nature humble and retiring, he did not present himself for public notice;
thus, although his virtuous deeds were many, none could be fully transmitted to the world.
Previously, before Yan had left the household life, [he was as follows].
Having previously received the five precepts, he had committed transgressions against them;
later, upon entering the Way and receiving full ordination,
he constantly doubted whether he had attained the precepts.
I have always lived in fear of this;
though I engaged in meditative contemplation for many years, I could not achieve self-realization.
Consequently, I once again crossed the sea and returned to India.
He consulted various wise and learned men and,
upon meeting an Arhat bhikṣu, related the matter in full to him; however,
the Arhat did not dare to reach a definitive judgment.
Thereupon, Yan entered meditative absorption and went to the Tuṣita Palace to consult Maitreya.
Maitreya replied, "You have obtained the precepts."
Yan Da was filled with great joy.
He then returned on foot;
when he reached Jibin, he passed away without illness.
At that time, he was seventy-eight years old.
In that country, ordinary people and sages each had their own designated places for cremation.
Although Yan’s observance of the precepts and his moral integrity were lofty and brilliant, [he was not permitted to burn his body there].
However, as the practice had not yet been verified,
they began moving the corpse toward the cemetery for ordinary monks,
but the corpse was so heavy that it would not budge.
When they turned toward the holy tomb, they felt a sense of lightness as if floating away.
The disciples Zhiyu and Zhiyuan, who had originally come from the West,
reported these auspicious omens and both returned to their foreign land.
Based on this, one may infer that Yanxin was a person who had attained the Way;
however, it remains unknown whether his realization was at the stage of fruition or the path, and to what degree its depth or shallowness lay.

Regarding the four works—*Tiaozu zhongsheng jing*, *Yiyin xian zhengfa jing* (also known as *Yiyin yan zhengfa jing*), *Shande boluomen wen Tiyuoduo jing*, and *Piluosanmei jing* in two fascicles—which appear respectively in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*: various catalogs such as those by Sengyou and others all marked them as doubtful. The *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalog) included them among the authentic scriptures. However, upon examining their wording, which is shallow and vulgar, and their principles, which are sparse and neglected, they have been placed in the category of "doubtful" to weed out the chaff. These four works comprise five fascicles in total.
The catalogs compiled by Sengchang and others all attribute these to the translation of Guṇabhadra.
However, I now consider the first three to have been produced separately and the last one to be suspicious and spurious.
Since this is intended as a record of authentic works, I have deleted them all.

The *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (佛本行經) in seven fascicles, also known as the *Buddhacarita-praśaṃsā* (佛本行讚), was produced at Mount Liuhé Mountain Monastery; some say it consists of five fascicles and is found in the catalogs of Sengyou, Baochang, and the *Neidian lu*. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states that the *Buddhacarita-praśaṃsā-sūtra* and the new *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* in two fascicles were produced at Daochang Monastery in the second year of the Yongchu era. One catalog records it as having been produced at Mount Liuhé Mountain Monastery. This ninth translation is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatī-parivarta*, and others, according to the catalogs of Daohui and Sengyou. The *Vimaladhyāna-samādhi-sūtra* (淨度三昧經) in two fascicles is the second production, appearing in the miscellaneous records of Zhu Daozu. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (付法藏經) in six fascicles is the first production, appearing in the records of Li Kuò. These four works comprise seventeen fascicles in total: the first work of seven fascicles currently exists, while the remaining three works totaling ten fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Baoyun) was a native of Liangzhou.
Having entered the monastic order in his youth, he was diligent and possessed both learning and virtuous conduct.
His character and temperament were firm and pure, such that he did not conform to the world.
Thus, in his youth, he was renowned for his integrity, rectitude, and pure conduct;
yet he sought the Dharma with such earnestness and sincerity that he forgot his own person to devote himself to the Way.
Vowing to personally behold sacred traces and extensively seek out the scriptural teachings,
he traveled far to the Western Regions at the beginning of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty,
traveling in succession with Faxian and Zhiyan.
Traversing the shifting sands and scaling the snowy peaks,
he endured hardships and difficulties without regarding them as arduous;
he thus journeyed through the various kingdoms of Tianzhu (India).
Having fully witnessed these spiritual wonders,
he then traversed the wilderness of the rākṣasas and heard the sound of celestial drums.
He paid homage at many sites associated with the traces of Śākyamuni.
While abroad in foreign lands, he studied Sanskrit scripts extensively;
he became thoroughly proficient in the phonology, orthography, and glossaries of all the various kingdoms of India.
Later, he returned to Chang’an,
where he followed the Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra to receive instruction.
He devoted himself to the study of the dhyāna methods with diligent and tireless effort.
When the Meditation Master was unjustly expelled by a monk from the Qin,
Huiyun also fled.
It was only upon meeting Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu that his expulsion was resolved.
Together they returned to Yangdu and settled at Daochang Temple.
Because Yunzhi’s resolve was firm and fierce, and he propagated the Way in a remote region,
there were none among the monastic community who did not open their hearts to consult him, receiving his teachings with reverence.
Initially, he worked together with Zhìyán to produce various sutras.
Once Zhìyán had passed away, Yún translated them alone.
During the Yuánjiā period, he translated four works, including the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*.
Yun held the Sanskrit manuscript in his hands and translated it orally;
as he was proficient in both Chinese and foreign languages, his phonology and terminology were truly correct.
All present were convinced and accepted the version finalized by Yun.
In the early period, the śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Guanzhong was skilled at proclaiming and translating;
during the reigns of the Fu and Yao dynasties, he brought forth numerous scriptures.
As for those refined in the Bactrian script (Sanskrit) in the region south of the Yangtze, none surpassed Fotudeng.
Thus, during the transition between the Jin and Song dynasties, he propagated the Dharma-treasury;
the śramaṇa Huiguan and others all befriended him and esteemed his virtue.
Daoyun’s nature was fond of what was profound and obscure.
He lived there to preserve his seclusion and tranquility,
eventually proceeding to the temple on Mount Liuhexiang; however,
the mountain was largely inhabited by uncivilized folk who were fond of banditry.
Yun preached the Dharma to instruct and guide them;
many reformed their evil ways and engaged in reverent service and offerings,
such that nine out of ten households did so.
Recently, when Daochang and Huiguan were approaching death,
they requested that Huiyun return to the capital to take overall charge of the monastic administration.
Reluctantly, Huiyun returned.
He resided at the site of enlightenment for about one year,
after which he returned to Liuhe.
He passed away at the mountain monastery in the twenty-sixth year of the Yuanjia era.
He was seventy-four years old.
His travels abroad are recorded in separate biographies.

The *Za apitan xin* (Miscellaneous Abhidharma-hṛdaya) in thirteen fascicles—third edition—is found in the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) and Sengyou’s catalog; it is also listed as fourteen fascicles. This one work in thirteen fascicles is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Iyebaluo (Ekapāla), translated as "Sovereign" (Zìzài) in the Song language,
was a native of the Western Regions.
Proficiently versed in the Tripiṭaka and clearly understanding the four Āgamas,
he traveled to Pengcheng in the year of Jǐngyīn (327 CE) during the Yuánjiā era,
serving as a preceptor to Wáng Zhōngdé of Tàiyuán, the Regional Inspector of Northern Xuzhou.
He translated the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vyākhyā*;
having reached the "Chapter on Investigation" (*Vīmaṃsā-varga*),
he ceased his work because the section on "conditions and obstructions" (*ālambana-pratighāta*) was not yet complete.
It was completed in ten fascicles,
with the Prefect personally receiving the dictation by pen.
In the eighth year, the *xinwei* year, he again requested Guṇabhadra to continue the translation.
The entire work consists of thirteen fascicles.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (菩薩善戒經) in nine fascicles—also known as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (菩薩地)—or in ten fascicles, was produced at the Jetavana Monastery (祇洹寺).

This is recorded in the two catalogs by Zhu Daozu and Sengyou, as well as in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and the catalog of Fa-chang and others, all of which state it is the *Śīla-sūtra*.
The scripture consists of twenty fascicles; it is further stated that the disciples produced two additional chapters to complete thirty fascicles, but this is not correct.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Pusa shanjie jing) in one fascicle, concerning the method for a bodhisattva’s reception of the precepts as questioned by Upāli, is recorded in the *Baoshang lu*.

According to Sengyou’s record, this [text] constitutes the first fascicle, which, when combined with the preceding nine fascicles, forms a total of ten fascicles. However, the version from the Northern Region...

It has been long since this was separated [from the canon] and cannot be reconciled with it. Furthermore, there is the *Nei jie jing* (Inner Precepts Sūtra) for Bodhisattvas in one fascicle, recorded by Fashang;
the *Upāsaka wu jie wei yi jing* (Sūtra on the Dignified Conduct of the Five Precepts for Lay Followers) in one fascicle, found in Baochang’s record;
the *Śrāmaṇera wei yi* (Dignified Conduct of Śrāmaṇeras) in one fascicle—also called the *Śrāmaṇera wei yi jing*—found in Changfang’s record; and the *Sifen biqiuni* (Four-Part Vinaya for Bhikṣuṇīs).
*Jie-mo-fa* (Karmavācanā-dharma), one fascicle. Sengyou states that it is also called the *Tánwúdé Jie-mo* (Sarvāstivāda Karmavācanā) or the *Zá Jie-mo* (Miscellaneous Karmavācanā).

It was translated at Qiyuan Temple in the eighth year of the Yuanjia era. It appears in Sengyou’s and Baochang’s catalogs as well as the *Gaoseng-zhuan* and other records; it is also simply referred to as the *Sìfēn Jie-mo*.
*Ūpāsaka-wǔjiè-xiāng-jīng* (Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts for Lay Disciples), one fascicle. Also known as the *Ūpāsaka-wǔ*... [text fragment]
*Jielü lùn* (Abridged Treatise on the Precepts), translated at Qihuan Monastery in the eighth year of the Yuanjia era; listed in Sengyou’s *Lù* and Baochang’s *Lù*, as well as the *Gāosēng zhuàn*.
*Lóngshù púsà wèi Chántuójiā wáng shuō fǎyào jì* (Verses on the Essentials of the Dharma Spoken by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna for King Śāntaka), one fascicle;
listed in the Tang *Jiùlù*. *Shànxìn èrshí’èr jiè* (Twenty-two Precepts of Good Faith), also titled *Líyù ōubāsè* (Upāsaka Free from Desire), one fascicle.

The *Upāsikā-dvāviṃśati-śīla-sūtra* (The Text on the Twenty-two Precepts of the Laywoman); it is also called the *Tri-śaraṇa-upāsaka-śīla*. Sengyou states that it consists of the Three Refuges and the twenty-two precepts of the layman (*upāsaka*). It is also referred to as the *Upāsaka-śīla*. These are found in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and Sengyou’s *Catalogue* (*Lu*). The *Jinglü fenyi ji* (Record of the Differentiation of Sūtras and Vinaya), one fascicle, is found in the *Changfang lu*. Thus, there are ten works in total.
The *Dharmapada-gāthā* (Verses on the Essentials of the Dharma) by Nāgārjuna, in eighteen fascicles, consisting of eight sections totaling sixteen fascicles, currently exists;
the *Śraddhā-prakaraṇa* (Treatise on Faith), in twenty-two fascicles, and the [text] in two fascicles below, which is missing from its original, are also extant.
The śramaṇa Guṇavarman—
translated into the Song language as "Armor of Merit"—
was originally of the kṣatriya caste.
For generations his family served as kings, and his domain was in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
His grandfather, Haribhadra—translated here as "Lion-Wise"—was exiled due to his upright and rigid character.
His father, Saṃghananda—translated here as "Joy of the Multitude"—consequently lived in seclusion among the mountains and marshes.
At the age of fourteen, Guṇavarman was already exceptionally perceptive and talented, possessing profound foresight.
He was magnanimous and broad-minded, honoring virtue and striving for goodness.
Once, his mother required some wild meat and ordered Guṇavarman to procure it for her.
Guṇavarman submitted this memorial:
"Among all classes of living beings, there are none that do not cherish life.
To take away another's life is not the act of a benevolent person."
The mother said in anger,
"Even if you should incur offense, I shall take your place. Later,
when Guṇavarman was boiling oil, he mistakenly poured it onto his finger.
The son said to his mother,
"Please endure this pain on my behalf.
The mother replied:
"The pain is in your own body; how could I possibly take its place for you?
Guṇavarman replied, "If I cannot even take the place of suffering before my very eyes, how much less so for the three miserable realms?"
The mother then realized her error and renounced killing for the rest of her life.
When she reached the age of eighteen, a physiognomist saw her and said,
"When you reach the age of thirty, you shall rule over a great kingdom and sit facing south as its sovereign."
If one does not delight in worldly glory, one shall attain the fruits of sainthood.
At the age of twenty, he left the household life and received the precepts;
he thoroughly mastered the nine divisions of the scriptures and was extensively learned in the four Āgamas.
He recited over one million words of the scriptures;
he profoundly mastered the categories of the Vinaya and entered subtly into the essentials of dhyāna.
At that time, he was titled the Dharma Master of the Tripiṭaka.
When he reached the age of thirty, the King of Kaśmīra passed away, leaving no heir to the throne.
The assembly deliberated and said:
"Guṇavarman is a scion of the royal house; moreover, he is talented, virtuous, and of great renown."
He requested that [the prince] be allowed to return to lay life so as to succeed to the throne;
several hundred ministers repeatedly and earnestly petitioned Guṇavarman, but he would not accept.
He then took leave of his teacher, went against the will of the multitude, and dwelt in the forest, drinking from mountain streams.
He traveled alone through mountains and fields, withdrawing from the human world.
Later, he arrived in the Kingdom of Siṃhala to observe the local conditions and propagate the teachings;
those who recognized the truth all declared that he had attained the first fruit of the path.
His dignified appearance moved all who beheld him, causing them to resolve to attain enlightenment.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Śrīvijaya.
One day before his arrival, the mother of the King of Śrīvijaya dreamed that a Daoist priest boarded a flying ship and entered the country.
At dawn the next day, Guṇavarman indeed arrived.
His mother received the five precepts from him with the reverence due to a holy one.
Thereupon, she exhorted the king, saying:
Through karmic conditions from past lives, we have become mother and son;
yet while I have received the precepts, you do not believe them.
I fear that the causes for future births will be forever severed, thereby terminating our present fruit.
The king, constrained by his mother’s command, immediately accepted the precepts at her behest.
As time passed, his cultivation deepened and his devotion gradually became more earnest.
Shortly thereafter, the troops of a neighboring state invaded the borders.
The King said to Guṇavarman,
"External enemies, relying on their strength, wish to invade and insult us.
If we were to engage them in battle, the number of those wounded and killed would surely be great."
"If you do not reject [this path], ruin will soon arrive.
Now, having taken refuge solely in the Venerable Master, I know not what plan to follow.
Guṇavarman said:
"Since these violent bandits are attacking one another, they ought to be resisted and repelled.
However, you should simply give rise to a mind of compassion and refrain from harboring thoughts of harm.
Your Majesty should personally lead the troops to confront them."
As soon as the banners and drums first clashed, the rebels retreated and dispersed.
King [Yuan] was struck by a stray arrow and wounded his foot;
Guṇavarman performed a consecration with water to wash it, and within two nights he was fully restored.
King Gongxin’s devotion gradually deepened, and he desired to leave the household life to cultivate the Way.
He therefore addressed his ministers, saying,
"I wish to personally take refuge in the Dharma-gate."
"You all should further select a wise sovereign.
The ministers all prostrated themselves and entreated him, saying,
"If Your Majesty abandons the kingdom, the subjects will have no one to rely upon."
Furthermore, our enemy nation is fierce and powerful, confronting us by relying on its natural barriers.
If we lose your gracious protection, where shall the common people find refuge?
Your Majesty’s heavenly compassion—how can you not take pity upon their lives?
The King, unable to bear the firm refusal, approached his ministers and requested three boons,
saying that if they were granted, he would remain to govern the kingdom.
His first boon was that all within the realm of his rule should likewise serve the Upādhyāya.
Second, he vowed to completely eliminate all killing within his realm.
Third, he vowed to distribute his accumulated wealth to relieve the poor and the sick.
The ministers were delighted and unanimously gave their respectful assent.
Thereupon, the entire kingdom followed suit and received the precepts.
Later, the king established a vihāra for Guṇavarman;
while personally leading the timber, he injured his toe.
Guṇavarman further treated him with incantations, and after a short while, he was restored to health.
The fame of his spiritual transformation spread far and wide;
hearing of his reputation, neighboring kingdoms all dispatched envoys to invite him.
At that time, the eminent and virtuous śramaṇas of the capital city of Yangdu, such as Huiguan and Huicong,
held his character and conduct in high esteem and desired to receive his instruction.
In the ninth month of the first year of the Yuanjia era, they personally petitioned Emperor Wen to request the invitation of Guṇavarman.
The Emperor immediately issued an edict to the Regional Inspector of Jiaozhou, ordering him to dispatch vessels to invite Guanding and the others.
He also sent the śramaṇas Fachang, Daochong, Daojun, and others to that region to entreat them to come.
He also sent letters to Guṇavarman and King Bhadravarman of Java, among others,
earnestly hoping that they would deign to visit the territory of the Song dynasty to propagate the Way of the Buddha.
Guṇavarman, believing that the holy transformation should be spread widely, did not hesitate to travel to distant lands.
Previously, he had followed the merchant Zhu Nanti on his ship intending to head for a small country;
however, encountering a favorable wind, they instead arrived at Guangzhou.
Thus, his surviving writings state:
Driven by the winds of karmic action, he was thus carried to the borders of Song;
this is what is meant by that.

When Emperor Wen learned that Guṇavarman had already arrived in Nanhai, he again issued an edict to the provincial and commandery authorities ordering them to provide the necessary provisions for his journey to the capital.
The route began at Shixing and took about a year to complete.
In Shixing there is Mount Huqiu;
its form is steep and precipitous, with peaks and ridges rising to great heights.
Guṇavarman remarked that it resembled Gṛdhrakūṭa,
and thus he renamed it Lingjue (Vulture Peak).
Outside the mountain monastery, he established a separate meditation hall.
The temple was several *li* away, yet the sound of the sounding-stone could not be heard;
whenever the mallet was struck, Guṇavarman had already arrived.
On other occasions, he would cause rain to fall that did not wet him.
Sometimes he walked upon mud without getting wet;
at that time, among the assembly of monastics and laypeople, there was none who did not feel solemn awe and increase their reverence.
The monastery contained a Baoyue Hall (Jewel Moon Hall).
Guṇavarman personally painted images of Rāhula and the scene of the Bodhisattva as a young Brahmin (Jotipāla) spreading his hair upon the path at the northern wall of the palace.
After they were completed, they emitted light every evening, which would only cease after a long time.
Cai Mozhi, the Governor of Shixing, held him in profound reverence and admiration.
Later, when Mozhi was about to die,
Guṇavarman went in person to visit him, preaching the Dharma to comfort him.
Later, his family members dreamed that Sengmao was in the temple expounding the Dharma with the assembly of monks;
this was truly due to the power of Guṇavarman’s transformative guidance.
Originally, this mountain had been plagued by many tiger disasters.
Ever since Guṇavarman resided there, he would travel by day and return at night;
occasionally, when he encountered a tiger, he would press its head with his staff, play with it, and depart.
Consequently, travelers on land and visitors by water came and went without obstruction.
Those who were converted by his profound virtue numbered seven or eight out of ten.
Guṇavarman once entered meditative absorption in a separate chamber for several days without emerging.
The monks of the monastery sent a śrāmaṇera to go and inquire after him.
He saw a white lion standing upon a pillar,
extending across the sky and filling it with blooming blue lotuses;
the śrāmaṇera was struck with terror and cried out loudly.
He went out in pursuit of the lion but saw nothing at all;
such were the many manifestations of his spiritual wonders, beyond compare.
Later, Emperor Wen again issued a decree to Fashen and others, earnestly requesting him once more.
He then traveled by boat downstream to the capital,
arriving at Jianye in the first month of the eighth year of the Yuanjia era.
Emperor Wen received him in audience, greeting him with earnest inquiries and consolation, and further remarked:
"I, your disciple, have always desired to observe the fasts and refrain from killing;
however, constrained by the necessity of sacrificing my body for the sake of worldly affairs, I have been unable to follow this aspiration.
Now that the Dharma Master has come from ten thousand li away to transform this land,"
"How will you instruct them?
Guṇavarman replied,
"The Way resides in the mind, not in external affairs."
The Dharma arises from oneself and not from others.
Furthermore, the practices cultivated by a sovereign and those of a commoner differ.
A commoner’s status is lowly and his reputation inferior; thus, his words and commands lack authority.
If one does not discipline oneself and subject the body to hardship, what purpose would such a life serve?
To an emperor, the four seas are home and the myriad people are children;
when he utters a single virtuous word, both men and women rejoice together.
When one virtuous administration is established, humans and spirits are brought into harmony.
When punishments do not cut short lives and labor does not exhaust strength,
it causes wind and rain to arrive at their proper times, cold and warmth to correspond with the seasons, the hundred grains to flourish, and mulberry and hemp to grow luxuriantly.
If one observes the fast in this manner, the merit of the fast is indeed great;
if one refrains from killing, the benefit is likewise vast.
Must one wait until half a day’s meal is omitted and the life of a single bird is spared before it can be considered a grand act of salvation?
The Emperor then leaned on his desk and sighed, saying:
"Ordinary people are deluded by distant principles,
while śramaṇas are hindered by proximate teachings."
Those who are deluded regarding the profound principle claim that the ultimate Way is but empty talk;
those who are mired in superficial teachings remain bound and attached to the written texts.
This is as the Dharma Master Baomo has stated:
Zhen was truly one who had attained awakening and clear insight;
he was fit to discourse upon the relationship between heaven and humanity.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Zhihuan Temple, where he was provided with abundant and generous offerings.
Dukes, kings, and eminent scholars all revered him.
Shortly thereafter, he began lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* at the monastery;
on the days of these sermons, the streets were filled with carriages and canopies.
As people watched him come and go, they followed one after another in continuous succession;
yet Guṇavarman’s spiritual treasury was naturally such that his wondrous eloquence was transcendent, surpassing even the heavens.
At times, he would employ a translator, yet his responses were so profound and intuitive that he seemed to grasp the meaning instantly.

Guṇavarman immediately translated ten works, including the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, at the Jetavana Monastery. Regarding the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, the catalogs of Sengchang and others all state it consists of ten fascicles;
the note below stating that his later disciples produced two additional chapters at Dinglin Temple to form thirty fascicles is incorrect.
At present, it exists in either nine fascicles or ten;
this must be a scribal error resulting from the addition of two characters.
Sengyou’s catalog records it as having only ten fascicles.
Thus, we know that other catalogs contain transcription errors.
Furthermore, according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*),
Huiyi of Jetavana requested the translation of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.
Initially, twenty-eight chapters were obtained;
later, a disciple produced one additional chapter, completing the thirty chapters.
To claim, as Sengfang and others recorded, that it was subsequently completed in thirty fascicles is a grave error.
Furthermore, the records of Sengchang and others state that Guṇavarman translated the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* in thirteen fascicles.
Now, since the ten fascicles were produced by Saṃghavarman, it is understood that Guṇavarman subsequently completed them to reach thirteen.
It is not meant that Guṇavarman translated it separately;
nor is it the case that it is recorded in both places.
Now, this has been deleted and included in the previous record.
The phrasing and meaning were both detailed and accurate, with no discrepancies between the Sanskrit and the Chinese translations.
At that time, the nuns Huìguǒ and Jìngyīn of Yǐngfú Monastery and others collectively requested Guṇavarman, saying:
"Six years ago, eight nuns from Siṃhala arrived at the capital and said: [and so forth].
Previously, the land of Song had never had bhikṣuṇīs, so how could they receive the precepts from the two assemblies?
Fearing that their precept-articles might be incomplete,
Guṇavarman said, "The Dharma of the precepts fundamentally originates within the great assembly of monks."
Even if one does not fulfill the preliminary requirements, there is no obstacle to obtaining the precepts,
as in the case of Mahāprajāpatī.
Furthermore, the nuns feared that their years [of seniority] were not yet complete and thus desired to receive the precepts once more.
Guṇavarman replied, "Excellent!
If you wish to increase the clarity [of the Dharma], I shall most gladly assist you.
However, the nuns of the Western Regions have not yet reached the required seniority, nor do they number ten."

Furthermore, she was instructed to learn the Song language; subsequently, at the request of a layman from the Western Regions, she invited foreign nuns to arrive so that their number would complete the required ten.
That summer, she observed the rains retreat at the Lower Dinglin Temple.
At that time, there were believers who gathered flowers to spread over the seats;
however, the flowers where Guṇavarman sat were even more vibrant in color.
The assembly all honored him with rites befitting a sage.
At the end of summer retreat, he returned to the Jetavana Monastery.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of that year, before his midday meal was finished, he rose first and returned to his chamber.
His disciple arrived later and found that he had already passed away.
At sixty-five years of age,
before his passing, he composed thirty-six lines of verses as a final testament,
in which he himself recounted the causes and conditions [of his life].
Having realized the second fruit,
he personally sealed it with his own hand and entrusted it to his disciple Āśvalāyana,
saying: "After my passing, you may present this text back to the monks of India."
He may also manifest this state to the monastic community.
After his passing, he was immediately assisted to sit upon a rope bed; his countenance showed no change, appearing as if he had entered meditative absorption.
More than a thousand people, both clergy and laity, flocked to see him.
They also smelled a pungent and intense fragrance.
Everyone saw an object resembling a dragon or snake, about one *pí* in length, which rose from the side of the corpse and soared straight up toward heaven; none could identify it.
Thereupon, in accordance with the foreign rites, he was cremated before the ordination platform in the Southern Grove.
The four assemblies gathered like scales, piling up fragrant wood into a pyre;
they drenched it with scented oil to consume his remains.
Flames of five colors rose up, their swirling vapors beautifying the sky.
At that time, the celestial landscape was clear and bright, while both monastics and laypeople sighed with grief.
Thereupon, they erected a white stupa at that very spot.
The bhikṣuṇīs who wished to receive the precepts again wept bitterly, their hopes severed and unable to restrain themselves.
When Guṇavarman first arrived in the Song dynasty,
Emperor Wen wished to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from him.
Before he had even had the opportunity to seek instruction,
he suddenly passed away;
thus his original intention remained unfulfilled.
My grief and regret grow ever deeper.

I have therefore ordered the assembly of monks to translate his posthumous writings; however, as these writings are already extant in circulation, I fear they would be too voluminous, and thus I shall stop here.
Regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā* in ten fascicles, the first fascicle states: "The Sarvāstivāda-vinayamātṛkā."
In the first month of the year Yi Hai, the twelfth year of the Jia-yuan era, [this work] was produced at Pingle Monastery in Moling;
it was completed on the twenty-second day of the ninth month. According to Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu* and Sengyou’s *Lu*, the *Za apitan xin lun* consists of eleven fascicles;
some omit the character "lun" (treatise), while others call it the *Za apitan jing*. Faxiang calls it the *Za apitan*.

The *Dharmaviśeṣa-vaibhāṣika* (or *Tang-pi-po-sha*), fourteen fascicles; the fourth translation, produced at Changgan Monastery in the ninth month of the Jiashu year, the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era, and completed after one year.
See the *Sengyou lu* and the *Preface to the Sūtras*. *Quanjian zhuwang yaoyi* (Verses Exhorting Various Kings to Generate Resolve), one fascicle;
composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; the second edition. See the *Sengyou lu* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

*Fenbie yebao lüe* (A Brief Compendium on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution), one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Dayong; also known as *Dayong pusa fenbie yebao lueji* (The Brief Compendium on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution by Bodhisattva Dayong).
Recorded in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*. *Qing shengseng yu wen* (Text for Inviting Holy Monks to Bathe), one fascicle.
Recorded in the *Sengyou lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*. The above five works comprise twenty-four fascicles; the first four works comprise twenty-three [fascicles].
The first volume currently exists; one volume is missing from the latter part.
[Compiled by] the Śramaṇa Saṃghavarman (translated into Chinese as Zhòngkǎi, "Armour of the Multitude").
He was also an Indian.
Having renounced worldly life in his youth,
he was pure and austere, possessing the virtue of the precepts.
He was clearly versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka and especially proficient in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era (the Guiyou year),
he traveled from Liusha and arrived at Jianye.
His presence was so majestic and solemn that both monastics and laypeople revered and marveled at him;
they all followed him as their master and served him,
calling him the Tripitaka Master.
In the first year of the Jingping era, Xu Sang, the Magistrate of Pinglu, donated his residence to establish a monastery,
which was consequently named Pinglu Temple.
Later, Daofang Huiquan invited Guṇavarman— whose spiritual conduct was perfectly complete— to reside at this temple.
They honored him with offerings to manifest his virtue.
Guṇavarman and Guan together raised a three-story stupa;
they practiced the Way and chanted sutras day and night without ceasing.
The monastic community gathered together as the influence of the Dharma spread.
At that time, the Tripitaka Master, who had a profound understanding of the categories of the precepts,
was about to administer the full ordination once again to the nun Huiguo and others of Yingfu Temple.
At that time, before the two assemblies were fully prepared,
the Tripitaka Master passed away.
Shortly thereafter, the Bhikṣuṇīs Tiexialuo and others from the Kingdom of Siṃhala arrived.
The assembly then collectively requested Guṇavarman to serve as their teacher to succeed the Tripitaka Master.
Huiyi of Jetavana Monastery was prominent in the capital of Yangdu, yet he was considered eccentric;
because his convictions differed from theirs, they did not associate with him.
Sengqin and Guṇavarman engaged in a debate that shifted back and forth;

however, Guṇavarman established his thesis and elucidated the principles of the Dharma with such clarity and conviction that Huiyi eventually turned from his rigid narrowness and submitted in humble admiration.
He then led his disciples to take up the teachings and receive the precepts;
several hundred monks and nuns received them.
Liu Yikang, the Prince of Pengcheng of the Song dynasty, held his monastic discipline and model in high esteem.
He extensively prepared vegetarian offerings for the fourfold assembly,
such that their abundance surpassed that of the capital city.
Recently, renowned and virtuous great monks such as Hui-guan and others [arrived].
Because Guṇavarman had an excellent understanding of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and had mastered it through recitation,
although the Tripiṭaka masters of former times had already translated it, they had not yet transcribed it; thus,
in the ninth month of the eleventh year, [he began the transcription].
At Changgan Temple,
he convened a group of scholars and requested that [the text] be translated once more;
Baoyun acted as the oral interpreter, while Guanzhi transcribed it by hand.
He studied and collated them with meticulous thoroughness, completing the work only after a full year.
He subsequently produced five more sections, including the *Mātṛkā*, totaling ten parts.
Guṇavarman was dedicated to traveling and teaching, never remaining in one place for long.
Having completed the task of transmitting the scriptures, he was about to return to his native land;
the assembly all entreated him,
yet none were able to detain him.
In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he returned to his native country on a merchant ship from the Western Regions;
the details of his final days are unknown.
*The Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-vipula-sūtra*, one scroll; the second translation, produced alongside the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* and other texts were translated together on the fourteenth day of the eighth month of the thirteenth year of the Yuanjia era at Danyang Commandery.
Baoyun acted as oral interpreter, Huiquan received the words by pen, and they were recorded by Daohui, Sengyou, Li Kuo, and others.
This is the fourth translation of the three-fascicle *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*, or alternatively, it consists of two fascicles and is titled the *Mañjuśrī-ratnakūṭa-prakāśana*.

The *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-bhūmi-pāramitā-nītārtha-sūtra* (or *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-nītārtha-sūtra*, also simply called the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*) is found in the Tripitaka as a single fascicle or two fascicles;
it was produced at Dong’an Temple. It corresponds to the final two chapters of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. Sengyou and Li Kuò [recorded] that it was seen by Daohui.

The *Fashang shangsi silu gaozhuan* (The Record of the High Transmissions of the Four Monastic Archives by Dharma Master Shàng) states that the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ratna* was produced in Jingzhou;
it was the second edition, translated at Daochang Temple in the twentieth year of the Yuánjiā era, with Huìguān serving as the scribe.
It is the same text as the *Ru laṅgā jīng* and the *Dàchéng rù lǎngqī jīng*. This is recorded in Sēngyòu’s *Jiàn dàohuì fǎ*.

The *Shangsheng lü gāosēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled by Imperial Decree) states that the *Púsà xíng fāngbiàn jìngjiè shéntōng biànhuà jīng* (Sūtra on the Supernatural Transformations and the Realm of Expedient Means in the Practice of Bodhisattvas) in three fascicles originated in Danyang Commandery.
Its initial appearance was identical to the *Dà sàzhé níqiánzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Great Sāṃkhya Nirgrantha), though some versions lack the character "jìngjiè" (realm).

It is also recorded in Li Kuò’s catalog as the *Lǎomǔ nǚ liùyīng jīng* (Sūtra of the Six Heroines of the Old Mother) in one fascicle, also known as the *Lǎomǔ jīng* (Sūtra of the Old Mother). Number [ ].
The third version is identical to the *Lao nüren jing* (Sūtra of the Old Woman) and others; Master Benfáng says he saw it in the *Bièlù* (Separate Record).
There is also a one-fascicle *Shēnrì'ér běnjīng* (Original Sūtra of Shenrì’ér), or as some say, the *Shēn’ér běn* (Original of Shen’ér);

this third version is identical to the *Yuèguāng tóngzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Youth Candraprabha), and Master Benfáng says he saw it in the *Bièlù*. The record states that "Shēndōu běn" is an error. Ānanda, Mūkha, and Nigrodha.
One fascicle; alternatively, it is said to be the sixth translation of the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, which is identical in text to the *Anantamukha-sūkṣma-rahasya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Fang states that he saw this in the *Bielu* (Separate Record). It is an error for Fang’s catalog to list the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* as a separate entry.
The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, four fascicles, was produced at Daochang Temple; it is recorded in the catalogs of Daohui and Sengyou.
The *Shangsheng lù gāosēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks by Shangsheng) states that the two-fascicle *Dàfǎgǔ jīng* (Mahābherīhāraka-sūtra) was produced at Xīn Temple in Jīngzhōu;
the four catalogs of Dōng'ān Temple—including those of Dào huì, Sēngyòu, Lǐ Kuò, and Fǎshàng—state that the one-fascicle *Dàyì jīng* (Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra) was produced there.
Fáng states that the one-fascicle *Shí'èr tóutuó jīng* (Dvādaśadhyāna-sūtra) is seen in the *Bié lù*; [the catalog of] Shùtíjiā [states the same].
One fascicle. Fang states that it is seen in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record). The *Wu shi juan Za ahan jing* (Fifty-fascicle Saṃyukta Āgama) was translated at Waguan Temple;
the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) states it appeared at Qiyuan Temple. It is also recorded in the *Song Qi lu* and the *Sengyou lu*.
