One fascicle of the *Yingwu jing* (Śuka Sūtra), also titled the *Dou tiao jing*, appears as the fourth [sūtra] in the *Zhong ahan* (Madhyama Āgama).
Regarding fourteen alternative translations, Fang states they are found in the *Bie lu* (Separate Record):
1. *Vimānasūtra*, one fascicle; translated from the fifty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyamāgama*. 2. *Caturmahāpuruṣaprasūti-sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated from the eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarikāgama*. 3. *Ekādaśasmṛtyupasthāna-tathāgatānusmṛti-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively...

The *Sūtra on Eleven Contemplations of the Tathāgata* (Yún shíyī sīwéi niàn rúlái jīng), translated by Fáng [Xuan], is recorded in the first section of the *Zēngyī Āhán* (Ekottarika Āgama), fascicle 48;

it is also noted in the *Bié lù* (Separate Record) as the *Āsūdá jīng* (Aśokadatta Sūtra) in one fascicle. The third version is identical in substance to the *Yùjié jīng* (Śrīmālādevī Sūtra) and others;
it is also noted in the *Bié lù*. The *Guòqù xiànzài yīnguǒ jīng* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect of Past and Present), four fascicles, was obtained at Xīn [Monastery] in Jīngzhōu.

The temple catalog records a sixth translation of the *Sūtra on the Origins of Practice* (*Xiuxing benqi jing*) and the *Sūtra on Auspicious Responses to the Origins of Practice* (*Ruixiang benqi jing*), both of which are identical to the *Jianshi* (Beginning of Arising) and the records of Li Kuò and Sengyǒu.
There is also one fascicle of the *Sūtra of Mahākāśyapa Saving the Poor Mother* (*Mohejiaye du pinmu jing*), which Fang says is found in the separate catalogs;

and one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Twelve Stages of Birth and Death* (*Shierpin shengsi jing*), which Fang says is found in the separate catalogs; and the *Sūtra of the Retribution of Sin and Merit* (*Zuifubaoying jing*).

One fascicle. Also titled *The Sūtra on the Retribution of Sin and Merit in the Revolving Five Paths*, also called *The Sūtra on the Revolving Five Paths*, and also called *The Sūtra on the Wheel of the Five Paths*.

Fáng states that he saw it in the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* without the character "lùn") in twelve fascicles, translated together with his disciple Buddhabhadra.
Its initial appearance corresponds to the *Prakaraṇapāda* in the Chinese (Táng) translation.

The *Zulun* (Foot Commentary) and the *Tongben Fanglu* (Record of the Same Texts) do not specify their source. There is one fascicle of the *Sipin Xuefa Jing* (Sūtra on the Fourfold Training Methods), sometimes omitting the word "sūtra.

Fang states that he saw it in the *Bielu* (Separate Record). There is also one fascicle of the *Bin-tou-lu Tu-lo-sha Wei You-ta-yen Wang Shuo Fa Jing* (Sūtra on Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja Preaching the Dharma for King Udayana), also called the *Bin-tou-lu Wei Wang Shuo Fa Jing*.
Fang states that he saw this in the *Bielu*, and the former [text] still exists today.

The *Xukongzang pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha) in one fascicle, translated later [during the Liu Song dynasty], is identical in text to the *Xukongzang jing* translated by Buddhayaśas under the Yao Qin;
the Fang catalogue notes that it is not found in the *Bielu*.

The *Wuliangyi jing* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Meanings) in one fascicle, the first translation, is identical in text to that produced by Dharmagatayaśas under the Xiao Qi; this is noted in the Li Kuò catalogue.

*Zhufa wuxing jing* (Sūtra on the Non-Activity of All Dharmas), one fascicle; the second translation, which is the same text as the two-fascicle version produced by Kumārajīva and the *Zhufa benwu jing* (Sūtra on the Original Non-existence of All Dharmas)—Fang states that he saw this in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalog).
*Xiao wuliangshou jing* (Smaller Sūtra of Immeasurable Life), one fascicle; sometimes without the word "smaller";
the second translation, which is the same text as Kumārajīva’s *Amituo* [Sūtra] and the Tang translation of the *Chengzan jingtu* (Praise of the Pure Land).
It was produced during the Xiaojian era; one name for it is *Amitābha-jian-dao*. Sengyou’s two catalogs and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* state that it was produced at Jingzhou.
It is an error to claim that the *Amitābha-sūtra* exists separately [from this].
One fascicle of the *Aṣṭamaṅgala-sūtra*; this is the third production. It is identical to Zhi Qian’s *Aṣṭamaṅgala-mantra* and Dharmarakṣa’s *Aṣṭasūrya-deva-mantra-sūtra*.
On the third day of the first month in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era, at the city of Jingzhou, I produced [this text] for Liu Yixuan,
the Minister of Works and Governor of Jingzhou, Prince of Nanqiao, completing it on the sixth day. It is seen that in the two catalogs by Sengyou and Baochang,

there is one fascicle of the *Anantapāramitā-dharmamukha-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Dharma-gate of Boundless Perfection), which is the second production, identical to that produced by Shengjian, as well as the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā*.
The *Bodhisattvapraśna-sūtra* (菩薩所問經) is recorded in the *Tongben fang* (同本房) as being found in the *Bie lu* (別錄);
the *Daridraputra-sūtra* (貧子須賴經), one fascicle, is the fourth translation, identical in text to those produced by Bo Yan, Zhi Qian, and others, according to the record of Li Kuò.
The *Pratyutpannabuddhastotrasūtra* (現在佛名經), three fascicles—also titled *Huafu xianzai fo ming* (華敷現在佛名)—is the second translation, identical to the *Chengyang zhufu gongde jing* (稱揚諸佛功德經).

The *De jing* (Sutra of Virtue) and others correspond to the original text. On the seventh day of the first month in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era, it was produced for Prince Nanyuan at Jingzhou;
this appears in the *Shixing lu* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*. The three-fascicle *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sutra of the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance) is the third production;
this appears in the *Li kuo lu*. The one-fascicle *Wuyouwang jing* (Sutra of King Aśoka) was translated at Xin Temple in Jingzhou; this appears in the *Wu lu*.
Furthermore, Sengyou’s catalogue lists the *Baoxing liuboluomi jing* (Sūtra on the Six Pāramitās of Past Conduct) in one fascicle; Fang says it is seen in a separate record under a different title.

The *Qichu sanguan jing* (Sūtra on the Three Contemplations in Seven Locations), or sometimes without the words "seven locations," is a variant translation of the *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama); Fang says it is seen in a separate record.
The *Zazang jing* (Sūtra of the Miscellaneous Basket) in one fascicle is the fourth [recension] that shares the same text as the *Guiwen mulian jing* (Sūtra of the Ghost Questioning Maudgalyāyana).
Fáng states that he saw in the *Bièlù* (Separate Record) the *Mùlián jiàng lóngwáng jīng* (Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana Subduing the Dragon King), one fascicle;

sometimes the character "Wáng" (King) is omitted, or it is called the *Jiànglóng jīng* (Sūtra of Subduing Dragons), or the *Jiànglóngwáng jīng* (Sūtra of Subduing the Dragon King). Its second appearance is the same text as the *Lóngwáng xiongdi jīng* (Sūtra of the Dragon King Brothers).

Fáng states that he saw in the *Bièlù*: the *Nánjīng* (Sūtra of Difficulties), one fascicle; one version calls it the *Yuènán jīng* (Sūtra of Overcoming Difficulties). Its third appearance is the same text as the [Sūtra of] Nièchéng.

The *Yuanyue nanjing* (Sūtra on Overcoming Difficulties) and others; Fang says he saw them in the *Bielu* (Separate Record). The *Shi liuershijian jing* (Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views), four fascicles;
Fang says he saw it in the *Bielu*. The *Youlu* (Record of You) says it is one fascicle. The *Qing bantebiqiu jing* (Sūtra Requested by the Bhikṣu Bhaṇḍuka), one fascicle;
sometimes written as Bhaṇḍika, also called Bhaṇṭika; Fang says he saw it in the *Bielu*. The *Shier toutuo jing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Dhūtas), one fascicle; Fang says [he saw it in the *Bielu*].
*Anaruddha-saptānusmṛti-sūtra*, one fascicle; Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu*. *Shibao-fa-san-tong-lüe-jing*, one fascicle;
Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu*. *Liuzhai-bajie-jing*, one fascicle;
Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu*. *Aranya-xichan-jing*, two fascicles; this second edition is identical to the *Zuochan-jing* translated by Kumārajīva.

The *Mèijīng* (Sutra on Obscurity) is the same text as that recorded in Li Kuò’s catalogue; the *Púsà hēyù jīng* (Bodhisattva Sutra on Rebuking Desire), one fascicle, is the second translation and is the same text as that translated by Kumārajīva—Fáng says he saw it in a separate catalogue;
the *Nàxiān jīng* (Nagasena Sutra), one fascicle, is the second translation and is the same text as the two-fascicle version—Fáng says he saw it in a separate catalogue;
the *Shí'èryóu jīng* (Sutra of the Twelve Wanderings), one fascicle, is the second translation—Fáng says.
In the *Jiùlù* (Old Catalogue), the first section on the "Five Phases of the Primary Meaning" (*Wǔxiàng lìjí yījuàn*) was produced at Dong'an Temple;
this is recorded in Sengyou’s *Lù* (Catalogue) and the *Gāosēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), which state it was produced at Xin Temple in Jingzhou.

The above fifty-two works comprise one hundred thirty-four fascicles. Under the entry for Piṇḍola, twenty-six works comprise one hundred fascicles; these are currently extant under the entry for Ākāśagarbha. II.
Sixteen sections, thirty-four fascicles; the original texts are missing.
Translated by the śramaṇa Guṇabhadra (in the language of Song, "Virtuous Merit").
He was a native of Central India.
Because he studied the Mahāyāna, he was known in the world as Mahāyāna.
He was originally of Brahmin descent.
In his youth, he studied the various treatises of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*);
there was nothing he did not master, from astronomy, literature, mathematics, and medicine to incantations and esoteric arts.
Later, upon encountering the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, he read it and was struck with sudden awakening.
He then deeply revered the Buddha-dharma.
Although his family had followed the ways of external paths for generations and strictly prohibited the presence of śramaṇas,
he abandoned his home and went into hiding to seek out a master from afar.
He immediately shaved his head, changed his attire, and devoted himself single-mindedly to his studies.
Upon receiving full ordination, he became widely learned in the Tripiṭaka.
By nature compassionate, harmonious, respectful, and compliant, he served his teacher with the utmost diligence.
Shortly thereafter, he took leave of his teacher of the Hīnayāna to advance in the study of the Mahāyāna.
His Mahāyāna teacher tested him by having him reach into a scripture chest;
he immediately retrieved the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
The Master rejoiced and sighed, saying,
"You have a profound karmic affinity for the Mahāyāna.
Thereupon, in his reading, recitation, and exposition of the teachings, none were able to challenge or oppose him.
He proceeded to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
He then presented a letter to his parents, urging them to return to the True Dharma, saying:
"If you persist solely in following non-Buddhist paths, then even if I were to return, it would be of no benefit."
"If you take refuge in the Triple Gem, we shall long meet again.
His father, moved by these sincere words, subsequently abandoned heterodoxy and followed the orthodox path.
As Bhadra proceeded forward, he reached the various kingdoms of Siṃhala, where he was provided with travel provisions and offerings at every stage.
Having already established a connection with the East,
he followed a merchant ship across the sea;
midway through the journey, the wind ceased.
The fresh water was exhausted once more,
and the entire crew on board were filled with anxiety and fear.
Guṇabhadra said:
If you can unite your hearts and join your strength to mind the Buddhas of the ten directions and invoke Avalokiteśvara, what could you not move?
Thereupon, they secretly recited the dharanis and sutras and performed repentance with utmost sincerity.
Suddenly, a favorable wind blew violently and thick clouds sent down rain, whereby the entire ship was saved.
Such was the power of his sincere resonance.
On the *yihai* day of the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at Guangzhou;
at that time, the Regional Inspector Che Lang submitted a memorial to inform Emperor Wen.
An envoy was dispatched to welcome him.
Once he arrived at the capital of Yang,
the Emperor issued an edict for the renowned monks Huìyán and Huìguān to meet him with honors at Xīntíng.
His countenance was clear and penetrating, and there was none who did not feel profound reverence;
though they communicated through a translator,
their joy was like that of meeting an old friend under a roadside canopy.
He first resided at Jetavana Monastery.
Shortly thereafter, Emperor Wen invited him and showed him the highest degree of reverence.
Yan Yanzhi of Langya, a man of versatile talent and profound learning, girded his belt and called at his door.
Thereupon, from the outskirts to the center of the capital of Song, carriages and canopies followed one after another.
The Grand General, Prince Yikang of Pengcheng,
and the Chancellor, Prince Yixuan of Nanqiao, [were present].
He served both masters as his teachers.
After some time, the assembly of monks collectively requested that he produce a translation of the sutra;
they gathered various monks specializing in doctrinal studies at Jetavana Monastery.
He translated the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
At Dong’an Temple, he produced the *Dharmaghoṣa Sūtra*.
Later, at Danyang Commandery, he translated the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
The assembly consisted of more than seven hundred people;
Baoyun transmitted and translated the text,
while Huiguan held the brush to record it.
Through their repeated discussions and inquiries, they excellently grasped the fundamental meaning [of the teachings].
Later, when Prince Qiao was stationed in Jingzhou,
he invited him to go with him and settled him at Xin Temple.
He further constructed temple halls and brought forth from the Xin Monastery various scriptures,

including the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, the *Past and Present Causes and Effects of King Aśoka*, the *Shorter Aparimitāyur-jñāna-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, the *Saṃtati-nirmocana-sūtra*, the *Pāramitā-samuccaya*, the *Nītārtha-pratyutpanna-buddha-nāma-sūtra*, the *Paramārtha-pañca-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, and the *Aṣṭamaṅgala-sūtra*.
Including those previously mentioned, there were fifty-two works in total,
most of which were transmitted by his disciple Fayong.
Prince Qiao wished to invite him to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and other scriptures.
Bhadra, however, reflected that she was not yet proficient in the Song language and felt deep shame and regret for many days.
She immediately performed prostrations and repentance morning and evening, praying for a divine response.
In a dream, a person dressed in white appeared before her, holding a sword and carrying a human head. He said:
"Why are you grieving?
Vatsa related the matter in full.
He replied:
Without excessive sorrow,
he immediately exchanged his head for that of the sword and placed the new head upon it.
He then spoke to it, commanding it to turn around, saying:
"Is there no pain?
He replied,
"There is no pain."
Suddenly, his mind and spirit became joyful;
when he rose the next morning, he was fully able to comprehend the meaning of the doctrines and understand the Song language.
Thereupon, he proceeded to give lectures.
The disciple Fayong served as the translator,
while Sengnian acted as the presiding lecturer (*dugang*).
Although this was conducted through a translator, there was profound mutual exchange of understanding regarding the profound mysteries.
Toward the end of the Yuanjia era,
Prince Xiao Ziliang of Qiao had frequent strange dreams.
Guṇabhadra said:
Calamity and disorder were about to break out within the capital;
before even a year had passed, two villains conspired in rebellion.
This occurred at the beginning of the Xiaojian era.
The Prince of Qiao harbored secret treasonous intentions.
Buddhabhadra’s countenance was grave and sorrowful, yet he had not yet spoken.
When the Prince of Qiao asked him the reason for this, [Buddhabhadra replied:]
Bhadra admonished him with such earnestness that he wept as he departed, saying,
"I have no hope at all;
I cannot bear to accompany you."
Because the Prince of Qiao was trusted by the public sentiment,
[Senglang] was coerced into accompanying him downstream.
At the defeat at Liangshan, the fire-traps were closing in from all sides.
The shore was so far away that it seemed impossible to reach;
he could do nothing but single-mindedly invoke Avalokiteśvara,
grasping a bamboo staff in his hand as he threw himself into the river.
The water reached his knees; as he probed the water with a staff, it was deep and the current swift.
He saw a young boy following behind him and pulled him back by the hand.
Looking at the boy, he said:
"How could you, a mere child, deliver me?
In a state of daze, he found himself having already walked some ten or more paces and had reached the shore.
He immediately took off his inner robe, intending to reward the youth; however, upon looking around, he could not find him.
His hair stood on end as he realized it was due to supernatural power. At that time, General Xuanmu was supervising the army at Liangshan.
Emperor Xiaowu (r. 453–464), whose personal name was Jun, issued an edict to the military command stating:
"Should any Mahāyāna [texts] be found, treat them with special care and dispatch them to the Imperial Palace by express messenger."
Shortly thereafter, he was found and sent to the capital on a boat.
Emperor Xiaowu immediately summoned him for an audience and questioned him in detail,
saying, "I have long looked forward to this, and only now do we meet."
Bhadra replied: "Since I have been defiled by wickedness and am destined to be reduced to ashes and dust, I now have the honor of being granted an audience;
I am deeply grateful for Your Majesty’s gracious inquiry."
They further accused him of being a rebel.
He replied,
"Those who have left the household life do not participate in military affairs."
However, Zhang Chang, Zong Lingxiu, and others were all coerced [into this].
What I, this poor monk, have clarified is simply that I did not anticipate meeting such a matter due to past karmic conditions.
Emperor Xiaowu said:
He had nothing to fear.
On that day, an imperial decree ordered him to reside in the Rear Hall, providing him with offerings of clothing and goods, as well as a carriage and attendants.
Previously, Guṇabhadra had resided in Jingzhou for ten years.
Whenever he corresponded with the Prince of Qiao, there was nothing that was not recorded.
Yet, upon the defeat of the army, when the documents were examined, there was not a single word concerning military affairs.
Emperor Xiaowu recognized his absolute integrity and treated him with even greater courtesy and esteem.
Later, during a casual conversation, he jokingly asked,
"Do you miss the Prime Minister?
He replied:
"Having received your patronage for ten years, how could I forget your virtue?
I now beg of Your Majesty:
I wish to burn incense for the Chancellor for three years."
The Emperor’s countenance moved with deep emotion;
he was moved by the righteousness [of the request] and granted it.
When Zhongxing Temple was completed, he issued an imperial decree ordering [the Master] to move his residence there.
He had three rooms opened for him.
Later, at a banquet in the Eastern Palace where the princes and dukes were all assembled,
an imperial decree was issued for Guṇabhadra to be presented.
At that time, his hair had not yet been cleansed, and his white head was brilliantly radiant.
Emperor Xiaowu gazed at him from afar and, turning to the Minister of the Interior,
Xie Zhuang, said, "Mahāyāna is brilliant, intelligent, and quick-witted."
I merely reflect that the time for my own old age has arrived;
let me test him with a question,
and he will surely understand the intent of my mind.
As he ascended the steps, Buddhabhadra greeted him and said, "The Mahāyāna does not fail to honor your intent in coming from afar; however, there is one thing remaining.
Thereupon, [the visitor] replied at once:
This poor monk has returned to the imperial capital from afar for nearly thirty years.
The Emperor’s gracious treatment fills me with boundless gratitude;
yet, at seventy years of age and beset by illness, death is my only remaining prospect.
The Emperor praised his quick wit and eloquence,
ordering him to sit near the imperial presence;
the entire court turned their eyes toward him.
Later, he established a monastery west of the Phoenix Tower within the borders of Moling.
Every time it reached midnight, there would be someone knocking on the door and calling out;
though they looked, no person was to be seen, and the assembly frequently suffered from nightmares and sleepwalking.
Bhadra burned incense and made this prayer:
"By your past karmic conditions, you dwell here;
I now establish a temple and practice the Way, performing rites of repentance for your constant sake."
If there were those who remained, they served as guardian deities for the temple;
if they could not reside there, each departed to dwell wherever they found peace.

Subsequently, more than ten monastics and laypeople alike dreamed on the same night that thousands of spirits were carrying their belongings away on their shoulders, whereupon the community of the temple was finally at peace.
In the seventh year of the Daming era, a severe drought occurred throughout the realm.
Although prayers were offered to the mountains and rivers for many months without result,
the Emperor then requested that he be granted the power to pray for rain, ensuring that it would surely produce a response.
"If it proves ineffective, there is no need for us to meet.
Badanta replied,
"I look up to the Triple Gem and Your Majesty’s celestial majesty, hoping that your grace will surely descend as rain."
Thinking that if nothing were obtained, he would not see [the deity] again,
he went immediately to the Fishing Platform at the Northern Lake.
There he burned incense and offered prayers, abstaining from food and drink.
He silently recited the sutras and secretly added secret mantras.
At the hour of *bhu* the following day, clouds rose from the northwest corner,
initially resembling a carriage canopy.
The sun hung low in the western sky like the mulberry and elm trees;
winds shook and clouds gathered,
and it rained continuously for several days.
At dawn the next morning, the high officials entered to offer congratulations.
By imperial decree, he was granted an audience and comforted with gifts that arrived in continuous succession.
Since his youth, Guṇabhadra had maintained a vegetarian diet throughout his entire life.
He constantly held an incense burner, never letting it leave his hand.
Whenever he ate, he would invariably share his food with the birds, which would gather around to take the food directly from his hands.
During the reign of Emperor Ming, his offerings and veneration became even more abundant.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Taishi era, he perceived that his physical condition was failing.
He then took his leave in advance of Emperor Ming and the high officials.
On the day of his death, he gazed out into the distance and said:
He beheld a divine flower and a sacred image;
at the hour of Youzhong (the fifth watch), he passed away.
He was seventy-five years of age. Emperor Ming mourned him deeply and provided lavish funeral offerings and gifts.
The high officials assembled for the funeral, providing full honors for both the glory and the sorrow.
The *Parnirvāṇa-sūtra* (or *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* without the character *pan*), one fascicle, was translated at Xin Temple in the first year of the Xiaojian era;

it appears in Daohui’s *Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties*. Now, upon examining the preceding and following passages of this single-fascicle *Nirvāṇa*, they do not belong to [the work of] Dharmabhadra.
What appears to be a humble translation by Dharmarakṣa and others has now been found in two fascicles and is provisionally appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin.

The *Śreṇika-bhikṣu-sūtra* (formerly titled *Śramaṇa-mānava-sūtra*) in one fascicle was translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The *Tripiṭaka-dharmācārya-svavṛtti-upamā* in one fascicle was not produced from a Sanskrit original;
therefore, it has also been deleted. The *Sūtra on the Selection of Future Evil Worlds* contains [accounts of] past practices of dānapāramitā.
The two aforementioned *Pāramitā* sūtras both derive from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The *Sūtra on Saving a Nation by Killing a Dragon* derives from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on the Three Causes and Conditions* derives from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. The *Sūtra on the Three Minor Kalpas* derives from the *Lokadhātu-vibhāga-sūtra*.

The *Sūtra on the Buddha Entering the Gate of Amṛta with Right Intention* derives from the *Mahādvādaśamukha-sūtra*. The *Āraṇya-sūtra* derives from the *Madhyama Āgama*. The *Śarabha-sūtra* [derives from the same].
The *Śāriputra-ādi-bhikṣu-kāyasaṃsākṣāt-kriyā-sūtra*, the *Nārada-sūtra* from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the *Muktā-patana-samudra-praveśa-sūtra*,
the *Mātula-mātula-sūtra*, the *Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Ṛṇa-go-bhūta-rāja-amātya-sūtra*— these six sūtras are all derived from the *Utpatti-sūtra*.
Also included are the *Catur-āhāra-sūtra* and the *Hīnayāna-saṃkṣipta-saṃgraha*, as well as the account of Ānanda witnessing music and dance.
The *Sūtra on Weeping at Impermanence*, the *Sūtra on the Buddha Going to Console Kāśyapa’s Illness*, the *Sūtra on the Buddha Commanding Ānanda to Visit the Householder Jyeṣṭha*,
and the *Sūtra of the Two Arrogant Men*; the *Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana’s Younger Brother Giving Alms and Expecting Immediate Retribution*—
these five preceding sūtras are all extracted from twenty-three sections, including the *Udānavarga* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
It consists of twenty-three fascicles.
It may be a separately produced excerpted scripture,
or it may not have been translated by Buddhabhadra.
Now, for the sake of an authentic record, I have deleted them all in their entirety.

The *Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva* (one fascicle), also titled the *Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara*, is the third [version] translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin and Daozhen; it is identical in its original text to that produced by [Dharmarakṣa]. This is seen in the catalogs of Wang Zong, Sengyou, Li Kuò, Fashang, and others, as well as in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, its manuscript currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Fayong,
whose Sanskrit name was Dharmodgata,
was originally surnamed Li.
He was a native of Huanglong Commandery in Youzhou.
From his youth, he served as a śrāmaṇera and practiced asceticism;
because he maintained the precepts and recited the sūtras, he was held in high esteem by his teacher.
I have heard that the monks Faxian and Baoyun personally traveled to the Buddha-lands;
moved by their example, they made a solemn vow to disregard their own lives.
Thus, at the beginning of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, they set forth.
He gathered twenty-five fellow śramaṇas, including Sengmeng and Tanlang,
and together they took with them banners, canopies, and various articles for making offerings;
setting out from the northern lands, they traveled far toward the West.
Upon first arriving in the kingdom of Henan, he continued westward through Haixi Commandery;
proceeding into the shifting sands, he reached Gaochang Commandery and passed through the various kingdoms of Kucha and Kashgar.
Previously, he ascended the Pamir Mountains and the Snow Mountains.
The mountain paths were perilous and treacherous, impassable for mules or horses;
the frozen ice rose high and steep, utterly devoid of grass or trees, and the mountains were thick with miasmic vapors.
Below lies a great river, deep and swift as an arrow.
A rope bridge has been constructed by fastening cables to the flanks of the eastern and western mountains;
it is so extremely wide that ten people must pass across it together.
Once they have reached the other shore, they raise smoke as a signal.
Those behind see the smoke and know that those ahead have already crossed, so they may advance further.
If they do not see smoke for a long time, they know that the rope has been blown away by a violent wind.
The person fell into a river;
after traveling for three days across the Pamir Mountains, he finally crossed it and ascended the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*),
where precipitous cliffs rose sheer with no place to set foot.
The stone walls were all covered with old arrow-holes,
facing one another at every point;
each person held four arrows.
First, they pulled down those below and climbed up by grasping the rungs above;
passing from one to another in succession, it took three days to reach level ground.
There, they waited for one another and counted their companions, finding that twelve people were missing.
He proceeded to the kingdom of Kaśmīra, where he paid homage to the Buddha’s almsbowl and stayed for over a year.
Having completed his studies of the Brāhmī script, he mastered the Sanskrit language.
There, he sought out and obtained a single Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.

Wujie was accompanied by thirteen other śramaṇas who traveled westward to the Sindhu River (here translated as "Lion’s Mouth"); following the river's course westward, they entered the kingdom of Yuezhi.
He paid homage to the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa* bone and beheld a white fly-whisk and a wooden boat.
Later, he arrived at Shiliu Monastery on the southern side of Mount Dantaka,
where more than three hundred resident monks practiced the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

Wujie then stayed at this monastery and received full ordination. The Indian śramaṇa Buddhatāra—translated as "Awakening Savior"—was said by the monastic community of that region to have already attained the fruits of the Path.
Wujie requested to serve as his upādhyāya,
and the Chinese śramaṇa Zhiding served as his ācārya.
He observed the three-month summer retreat at the monastery.
Day after day he traveled northward until he reached Central India.
In these vast and remote regions, he constantly carried rock honey as his provisions.
Of his eight companions, five died along the way; they traveled together, frequently encountering peril and hardship.
Wujie constantly focused his mind on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra that he carried with him.
As he was traveling through the wilderness of Śrāvastī, he encountered a herd of wild elephants.
Wujie invoked the name [of the Bodhisattva] and took refuge in him.
Immediately, a lion emerged from the forest, causing the elephant to flee in terror.
Later, while crossing the Ganges, he encountered a herd of wild oxen that came bellowing toward him, intending to harm him.
Wujie prostrated himself as before;
immediately, a large vulture flew down and the wild oxen scattered in alarm, whereby he was able to escape harm.
That his sincere heart could move such a response, enabling him to overcome danger and achieve deliverance, is all of this nature.
Later, he traveled by ship across the South Indian Ocean and reached Guangzhou;
the details of his travels and experiences are recorded in a separate biography.
At the end of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at the capital, Yangdu.
He personally translated one fascicle of the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*,
which is still transmitted in the world today.
His ultimate end is unknown.

The *Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Ascent to Tuṣita Heaven Sūtra*, one fascicle, also known as the *Maitreya’s Ascent Sūtra*, is recorded in the *Dàohuì* (Dao-hui) catalogue of the Song and Qi dynasties and in the *Sēngyòu* (Seng-you) catalogue.
The *Sēngyòu* catalogue states that it was first translated in Gaochang Commandery and later brought back [to China].
The *Jiàn Wáng Jīng* (Sūtra of King Mahādeva), one fascicle, was also initially titled the *Dàxiǎo Jiàn Wáng Jīng* (Great and Small Sūtras of King Mahādeva). It is identical to [the aforementioned].
The *Sūtra of King Prasenajit* and the *Sūtra of the Devaputra Prabhāsa* translated during the Tang dynasty share the same original text; this was noted by Fang in his *Separate Record*.

There is one fascicle of the *Secret Essentials for Treating the Illnesses of Dhyāna*, also known as the *Secret Methods for Treating the Illnesses of Dhyāna* (omitting the character "jing" [sūtra]) or the *Secret Sūtra for Treating Illnesses through the Essentials of Dhyāna*.
Some versions consist of two fascicles and state that it was extracted from the *Saṃyuktāgama*; it dates to the second month of the ninth year of the Xiaojian era.

On the eighth day of the month, at Zhuyuan Temple, he produced [the *Jingfàn wáng nièpán jīng*], completing it on the twenty-fifth day of that month; this is seen in the catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang.
It is one fascicle, sometimes titled with the character "bān" (passing away) added [as *Bānjìngfàn wáng nièpán jīng*]. This second production is the same text as that produced by Faju.
Fang says it is seen in a separate catalog. He also produced the *Jìn xué jīng* (Sutra on Encouraging Study), also called the *Quànjìn xué dào* (Encouraging the Study of the Path).

The second version of this sutra is the same text as those translated by Zhi Qian and others; Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu* (Separate Record). There is one fascicle of the *Baguanzhai jing* (Sutra on the Eight Precepts of Abstinence) with a different title;

Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu*. There is one fascicle of the *Wu fanfu jing* (Sutra on the Five Non-Reciprocities), also known as the *Wu fanfu dayi jing* (Sutra on the Great Meaning of the Five Reversals);
alternatively, the character "fu" (覆) is written as "fu" (附); Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu* as the *Fodasengda jing* (Sutra of the Great Assembly of Buddhas and Monks).
One fascicle: *The Sūtra of the Two Sons*, also known as the *Yejī jīng* (Skt. *Yaṣṭi-sūtra*), one fascicle; [Fáng says it is seen in a separate record].
*The Mēluowáng jīng* (Skt. *Mallarāja-sūtra*), one fascicle; [Fáng says it is seen in a separate record]. *The Módáguówáng jīng* (Skt. *Madrakarāja-sūtra*), one fascicle;
[Fáng says it is seen in a separate record, though some versions lack the word "king"]. *The Zhāntuōyuèguówáng jīng* (Skt. *Caṇḍavastirāja-sūtra*), one fascicle; [some versions lack the word "king"].
*Zi fáng yún jiàn bié lù* (Fangyun says he saw it in the *Bié lù*). *Wǔ kǒng bù shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Terrors of the World), one fascicle;

alternatively called *Wǔ kǒng bù jīng*. Fangyun says he saw it in the *Bié lù*. *Dì zǐ sǐ fù shēng jīng* (Sūtra on Disciples Who Die and Are Reborn), one fascicle; alternatively called *Sǐ wáng gèng shēng*. Fangyun says he saw it in the *Bié lù*.
*Jiāshè jìn jiè jīng* (Kāśyapa’s Sūtra on Prohibitions and Precepts), one fascicle; also named *Móhē bǐqiū jīng* (Mahābhikṣu Sūtra) and also named *Zhēn* (Truth).

The *Wei shamen jing* (Sūtra on the False Śramaṇa), fascicle 2; the *Pusa shi jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Vow), one fascicle—fascicle 5, which is the same text as the *Zhi jing* (Sūtra on [the Layman] Zhi) and others;
the *Zhongyin jing* (Sūtra on the Intermediate State), one fascicle;

and the *Guanshiyin guan jing* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara), one fascicle—were all previously translated at Gaochang Commandery. These were recorded in the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog).
He brought back [this text] and saw it recorded in Sengyou’s *Lu* (Catalogue) as the *Bosinidawang Sangmu Jing* (Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Mourning for His Mother), one fascicle;

some call it the *Bosinidawang Jing*. Sengyou says it is the *Boxie-ni Wang*; Fang says he saw it in the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue). It was translated from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Zengyi Ahan* (Ekottarika Āgama).
There is also the *Fomu Baninihuan Jing* (Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s Mother), one fascicle, which was [recovered] at Mount Zhong in the second year of the Xiaojian era.
The *Dà'ài dào bānnièhán jīng* (Mahāprajāpatī-parinirvāṇa-sūtra), one fascicle, was produced at Shàngsì in Dìnglín;
it is listed in Sēngyòu’s catalog as a variant translation of the fiftieth fascicle of the *Zēngyī āhán jīng*.

Also, the *Dìzǐ wèi Qíyù shù jīng* (Sūtra on Disciples’ Pride Narrated to Jīvaka), one fascicle—also titled *Dìzǐ wèi Qíyù shù mànjiè yǔ dìzǐ xìtàn jīng* (Sūtra on Disciples’ Pride, Precepts, and the Disciple’s Frolic)—is the fourth [variant] produced alongside the *Āhán jīng*.

*The Scripture on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Questioning the Buddha* (Nanwen shifo jixiong jing), one fascicle; the second translation, identical to that produced by Zhi Qian. Master Fang says he saw it in the *Bielu*.

*The Scripture on the Sounds and Pleasures of the Elder* (Zhangzhe yinyue jing), one fascicle; the second translation, identical to that produced by Dharmaratna. Master Fang says he saw it in the *Bielu*.

*The Scripture on the Chapters and Sentences of the Five Sufferings* (Wuku zhangju jing), one fascicle; the second translation, identical to that produced by Dharmaruci. Master Fang says he saw it in the *Bielu*.

*Fen hu dan wang jing* (The Sūtra of King Vatsa), one fascicle; the second edition is the same text as the *San mo jie jing* translated by Zhu Lüyan. Fang says it is seen in the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog).

*Di zi wen shi fo ji xiong jiong jing* (The Sūtra on Disciples Asking about the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha), one fascicle; Yu says it is the *Di zi wen shi fo ji xiong jiong jing*. Fang says it is seen in the *Bie lu*.
*Sheng si bian shi jing* (The Sūtra on the Transformation of Consciousness through Birth and Death), one fascicle; I now suspect this is from the Tripiṭaka.
Among these, I have seen various alternative titles for the *Zhengjing* (Correct Scripture):

the *Upāsaka-wujie-jing* (Sutra on the Five Precepts for Lay Followers) in one fascicle, also called the *Wuxiang-jing* (Sutra on the Five Characteristics), which is the second [text] produced and is the same as the *Wujiexiang-jing* (Sutra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts);

and the *Xianzhe-luyi-jing* (Sutra on the Venerable One’s Discipline) in one fascicle, also called the *Wei-yi* (Dignified Conduct). [Fang] states that he saw these in the *Bielu* (Separate Record). Altogether, there are twenty-eight sections.
Twenty-eight fascicles: *Kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra*, Part 1, fifteen sections, totaling fifteen fascicles; currently extant.
*Bodhisattva-pratijñā-sūtra*, Part 2, thirteen sections, totaling thirteen fascicles; missing texts.
The layman Juqu Jingsheng was the Anyang Marquis and a younger brother of Mengsun, the Prince of Hexi of Northern Liang.
After the Wei dynasty annexed Liang, he fled south to the Song.
He concealed his ambitions and humbled himself, refusing to involve himself in worldly affairs.
He frequently stayed at monasteries and temples, completing his life as a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).
Meng Yi, the Governor of Danyang, saw him and approved of him, requesting an audience with him.
After their first meeting, they held each other in profound esteem and affection;
he frequently prepared offerings and provided him with generous support.
According to the records of the capital, in the second year of the Xiaojian era (the year of Yiwu) of Emperor Xiaowu, [Sengyou] resided at Zhuyuan Temple in Yangdu and Dinglin Shangsi on Mount Zhong.
He translated twenty-eight works, including the *Maitreya’s Ascent to Heaven Sūtra*.
Having practiced these extensively over a long period, his hand was unimpeded when he took up the brush.
His reputation resounded throughout the capital; he lived apart from his wife and children and harbored no desire for honor or profit.
He composed himself as a fellow practitioner to propagate and expound the scriptures.
For this reason, both the clergy and the laity in Jianye revered and admired him.
At the end of the Daming era, he fell ill and passed away.

The *Pumingwang jing* (Sūtra of King Universal Radiance) and the *Fanyu Huang jing* (Sūtra of King Brahmā), these two sūtras both appear in the *Liudu ji jing* (Collection of the Six Pāramitās). The *Yibhikṣu jing* (Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Yī) and the *Upāsaka wufa jing* (Sūtra of the Five Dharmas of a Lay Disciple), these two sūtras both appear in the *Zhong ahan jing* (Madhyama Āgama). The *Qixin shi Ayishan jing* (Sūtra of the Layman Ayishan)—also called the *Ayishanchi fuzi jing* (Sūtra of Ayishanchi, Father and Son)—and the *Chusheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth), the *Wubai fanzhi jing* (Sūtra of the Five Hundred Brahmins), and the *Qunlu zhu* (Commentary on the Various Records) all raise doubts regarding them. Among these seven sūtras, including the *Pumingwang jing*, six are derivative works.
One source claims it is spurious;
however, as this is now being compiled as a veritable record, both [versions] have been deleted.
The *Yanluowang Wentiānshìzhě jīng* (Sūtra of the Five Divine Messengers of King Yama), also known as the *Tiéchéng Nílí jīng* (Sūtra of the Iron-City Niraya), is found in Zhǎngfáng’s collection.
Extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 12; an alternative translation of the *Gautamī-vyākaraṇa-phala-sūtra*, one fascicle.
Found in the catalogue of Sengchang’s collection (*Chángfáng lù*). *Jiāngzhězǐ liùguò chūjiā jīng* (Sūtra on the Six Times a Householder’s Son Left Home), one fascicle.
Extracted from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Ekottara Āgama*; an alternative translation found in the catalogue of Sengchang’s collection. *Bófùmō bān* (The Mother of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa).

*Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated from the fiftieth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; a variant translation seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Pīngōng Lǎogōng Jīng* (Sūtra of the Poor Old Man), one fascicle;
also called the *Pīnlǎo Jīng* (Sūtra of the Poor Old Man); the second [entry] appearing in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Xidi Gēngzhě Jīng* (Sūtra of the Lazy Plowman);
the old catalogs call it the *Xidi Gēng'ér Jīng* (Sūtra of the Lazy Plowman’s Son); seen in the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Qǐngbīn* (Inviting Guests).
*The Dharma of Tulu*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra*, seen in the Record of Changfang. *The Sūtra of the Good Son*, one fascicle;
also called *The Sūtra of Sixfold Prostrations from Different Sources*, seen in the Record of Changfang.

Translated from the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, it is an alternative translation of *The Sūtra on Various Bhikṣus After the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa*, one fascicle; also called *The Sūtra of the Malla Bhadra*. It says:
The *Za ahan jian changfang lu* (Record of the *Saṃyukta Āgama* as seen by Changfang) contains one fascicle of the *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Parables), as recorded in Changfang’s catalog.
The above ten works comprise ten fascicles. Among them, the first seven works totaling seven fascicles—beginning with the *Qing binzhoulu shang* (Invitation to Piṇḍola)—are extant;
the final three works totaling three fascicles are missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Huijian was a man of unknown origins.
In the first year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu, the Dingyou year, he...
At the Mṛgadāva Monastery, he translated ten sūtras, including the *Pañcadevaputrasūtra*.
The *Saddharmatattvasramaṇasūtra* is identical in wording to the *Kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra* produced at the capital;

it is simply an alternative title for that latter sūtra, though catalogers have erroneously attributed it to this one. The *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-sūtra* is also referred to as the *Abhiṣeka-mocana*.

*Chuguozui shengsi dedu jing* (Sūtra on Deliverance from Transgressions and Birth-and-Death); translated in the *Daguanding jing yulu zhu* (Record of the Great Consecration Sūtra with Commentary), it is classified as a doubtful sūtra.

It is not the *Shijia bi zui jing* (Sūtra on Śākyamuni’s Expiation of Sins). *Shashen ji jiaren jing* (Sūtra on Sacrificing One’s Body to Rescue Merchants); both of these two sūtras appear in the *Liudu ji* (Collection of the Six Pāramitās).

*Anan jian shuiguang rui jing* (Sūtra on Ānanda Seeing the Auspicious Omen of Water-Light); also known as the *Shuiguang jing* (Water-Light Sūtra). *Dacheng chao jing* (Abridged Mahāyāna Sūtra); *Shangren qiucain jing* (Sūtra on the Merchant Seeking Wealth).
The *Gautamī Sūtra* and the aforementioned two sūtras are all found in the *Madhyama Āgama*:

the *Sūtra on a Person of Śrāvastī Going Mad after the Death of a Son* and the *Sūtra on a Student with a Disturbed Mind*, also known as the *Sūtra on a Mother and Son Becoming a Bhikṣu and a Bhikṣuṇī with Disturbed Minds*.
The aforementioned two sūtras are also both found in the *Ekottara Āgama*: the *Sūtra on a Great Malla Leaving Home and Attaining the Way*, also known as [the same].
The Sūtra of the Malla Bhadra; the Sūtra of the Two Old Men and Women Who Saw the Buddha, Left Home, and Attained the Way (upper volume);
these two sūtras are both from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. The Sūtra of Ciñcā Mānavikā’s Slander of the Buddha; the Sūtra of Birth; the Sūtra of the One Who Secretly Became a Śramaṇa;
the Sūtra of the Hunter Who Abandoned His Home to Study the Way (upper volume); these two sūtras are both from the *Udānavarga*. The Sūtra of the Prayer for Blessings is recorded by [Dao]you.
The fifteen works, including the *Wei lu zhen wei sha men* (Pseudo Records of True Śramaṇas),
are all stated by the catalogs of Sengchang and others to have been produced by Huijian. However,
since most of them are apocryphal scriptures such as the *Biéshēng* (Separate Birth) sūtras, [they are not included here].
Therefore, they were deleted and no longer extant.

The *Bodhisattva Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra) in six fascicles—sometimes simply called the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* or in five fascicles—is the first translation; it is the same text as that produced by Guṇabhadra during the Sui dynasty and is a separate division of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*. It is recorded in the *Song Qi Lu* and the *Sengyou Lu*. The *Wuliangmen Po mo tuoluoni Jing* (Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī for Subduing Māras) in one fascicle—sometimes simply called the *Po mo tuoluoni Jing*—is the seventh translation; it is recorded in the *Sengyou Lu* and is the same text as Zhi Qian’s *Wuliangmen Weimi Chi Jing*. These two works, totaling seven fascicles, both have their original texts extant.
Shamen Gongdezhi was a native of the Western Regions.
His realization of the Way was vast, and his skillful guidance improved daily.
In the sixth year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu, the year of Renyin,
he traveled to Jingzhou and stayed at Chanfang Temple.
The śramaṇa Xuanchang requested that he translate two scriptures, including the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha).
Chang’s published commentaries on the texts were elegant in their phrasing and subtle in their meaning;
yet when he extended his hand, fragrant water flowed from his palm, a phenomenon that no one could fathom.
Later, he traveled to Chengdu and stayed at Dashi Temple.
This was the stupa of King Aśoka.
It contained images of the sixteen deities, such as Vajrapāṇi and Guhyapada, which he had fashioned with his own hands; these have been passed down to the present day.
They remained in Jingzhou for several years before their ultimate whereabouts became unknown.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-karmavācanā-bhikṣu-āvaśyaka* (Ten Recitation Karmavācanā for Bhikṣus’ Essential Use), one fascicle; also known as the *Lüyào Jīemó Fǎ* (Abridged Essential Karmavācanā Method). Fáng says it is in two fascicles, while Yòu says it is in one fascicle; it is recorded in Sēngyòu’s catalog. This single work in one fascicle currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Sengqu,
whose secular surname was Zhu, was a native of Wugu.
He left the household life as a disciple of Sengye.
Zongyue was particularly proficient in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* among all the various sūtras;
he was also well-versed in historical records and composed literary works with considerable elegance.
He first resided at Mount Huqiu in Wu.
Emperor Xiaowu admired his reputation and issued an imperial decree for him to go to Yangdu to serve as the *Sengzheng* (Chief Overseer of Monks) and delight the assembly.
He resided at Zhongxing Temple.
In the seventh year of the Daming era, the year of Gui Mao (463 CE), Huigui compiled one volume of the *Jiesong* (Karma-vācanā) of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

*The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Ten Recitations*, one fascicle; also called *The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Ten Recitations* or *The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāśīla of the Ten Recitations*. Recorded in the *Sengyou lu* and *Baoshang lu*. This one work in one fascicle exists today.
The śramaṇa Shi Faying was of the Su clan and a native of Dunhuang.
He left home at the age of thirteen to become a disciple of Faxiang.
He resided at Gongfu Temple in Liangzhou together with his fellow student Fali; both were renowned for their mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
After Ling had received the teachings and taken them to heart, his learning was such that he never needed to ask a question twice, as everything was recorded upon hearing it once.
He devoted himself to the meticulous study of the Vinaya-piṭaka and extensively perused the sūtras and śāstras.
Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at Jianye and resided at Xinting Temple.
Because his learning and scholarly achievements were both eminent, Emperor Xiaowu issued an imperial decree appointing him as the Sangharāja (Monastic Administrator) of the capital.
Later, he resigned from his office and returned to Duobao Monastery.
He frequently practiced meditative concentration in a secluded room and occasionally established a lecture series on the Vinaya.
Afterwards, he moved his residence to Changgan Monastery.
During the Taishi era of Emperor Ming Yi,
he compiled and produced one section of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-bhikṣuṇī-śīla*,
and also produced the *Karmavācanā* for circulation in his time.

*The Sūtra of Akṣayamati* in ten fascicles; the fifth translation, identical in substance to the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*, appearing in the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Āśvaghosa* in one fascicle; the fourth translation, identical in substance to the "Assembly on the Fearless Virtue" from the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, translated in the Tai-shi era at Guangzhou, appearing in the catalogs of Shi-xing, Bao-chang, and others. *The Sūtra of Samantabhadra’s Intention* in seven fascicles; appearing in the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. *The Sūtra of the Inconceivable Benevolence and Wisdom of the Tathāgata* in five fascicles; appearing in the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. *The Sūtra of the Jewel Summit* in five fascicles; appearing in the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. *The Sūtra of the Three Secret Dhāraṇīs* in one fascicle; the Song translation titled *The Sūtra of the Wise Man Using the Vinaya*; appearing in the catalogs of Shi-xing, Seng-you, Bao-chang, and others. The above six works comprise twenty-nine fascicles; the original texts for all of them are currently missing.
The śramaṇa Zhu Fajian was a native of India. His disposition was broad and simple,
and he dedicated himself to the task of opening and benefiting others.
During the Taishi era of Emperor Ming Yi, six scriptures including the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa* were translated at Guangzhou.

The *Ruru-bodhisattva-anuttara-viśuddha-piṇḍapāta-sūtra* in two fascicles—also titled the *Jue liao zhu fa ru huanhua sanmei jing*—was the second translation produced; it is identical in text to the version translated by Yan Fotiao of the Han dynasty and the portion by Mahāprajñānāgaśrī. This is recorded in the *Shixing lu*. This one work in two fascicles still exists today.
The śramaṇa Shi Xianggong,
also known as Shuogong,
translated one fascicle of the *Rushou pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī) while in Nanhai Commandery.
The *Qunlu* states directly that [this work] was not prominent during the Song dynasty and its title and date are unknown;
it is unclear which emperor’s reign it belongs to.

The *Fozang Dafangdeng Jing* (Buddha-Treasury Mahāvaipulya Sūtra), one fascicle—also titled *Wenming Xianjing* (Sūtra of the Manifestation of Inquiry)—is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Difficult Questions" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. It appears in the *Shixing Lu* and the *Fashang Lu*. The *Yingluo Benye Jing* (Sūtra of the Original Vows of the Garland), two fascicles—also known as the *Pusa Yingluo Jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Garland)—is the third edition to appear, as recorded in the *Shixing* and *Fashang* catalogs. These two works, totaling three fascicles, are currently missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Daoyan translated two works,
including the *Buddhapiṭaka Vaipulya Sūtra*, during the Song dynasty.
Various catalogs simply state they were produced during the Song period without specifying the imperial reign year.

*The Sutra of the Brahma Maiden Śirīṣā*, one fascicle; second appearance in the *Shixing lu*, the *Zhao lu*, and the *Fashang lu*. *The Sutra of Emptiness-Purity Samādhi*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sutra on the Response of the Emptiness-Purity Deva to Samādhi*; second appearance in the *Shixing lu*, the *Zhao lu*, and the *Fashang lu*. *The Sutra Encouraging the Pursuit of the Way*, one fascicle; also named *The Sutra of Encouragement*; appeared together with the Liang History as the third translation. These three works comprise three fascicles; their original texts are all missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Yong translated three sūtras,
including the *Vimaladattāparipṛcchā*, during the Song dynasty.
Although various catalogs state that he was active during the Song period, they do not specify the imperial reign year.
The *Ananda-sūtra* (also titled the *Ananda-pūrvāparānta-sūtra*) is found within the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*.
Although various catalogs state it was translated by Fajun, as it is a separately circulated excerpted scripture, it has been deleted and is no longer extant.
The *Śāntasvaravyākaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle, is also titled the *Tathāgatopadiṣṭaviśuddhi-sūtra*.
The *Tiaofu jing* (Sūtra on Taming) is the same text as the *Wenshu jinglü jing* (Mañjuśrī Sūtra on Pure Discipline) translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin;

it is the fourth appearance [of this text] according to the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*. The *Yue yingluo zhuangyan fangbian jing* (Sūtra on the Skillful Means of Adornment with Joyous Garlands), one fascicle—also known as the *Dacheng yingluo zhuangyan jing* (Mahāyāna Sūtra on Adornment with Garlands) or the *Zhuan nüshen pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva who Transforms the Female Body)—is the fourth appearance [of this text], identical to that of the Western Jin.
The *Dharmarakṣa-shun-quan-fangbian-jing* (Sūtra on Dharmarakṣa’s Accordance with Expedient Means) and its counterparts are recorded in the *Jixing lu* and Sengyou’s *Fashang lu*.
Of these two works in two fascicles, the former, the *Jiaojiaoyin jing*, is extant; the latter, the *Leyingluo jing*, is missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Fahaï translated two sūtras,
including the *Jiaotiyaoyin jing*, during the Song dynasty.
Various catalogues note that these were translated and brought forth during the Song period.
Since the year is not clearly stated, it is uncertain which emperor’s reign it belongs to.

*Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as *Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-daśa-kriyā-sūtra* or *Prāptajñāna-samādhi-sūtra*. This is a variant translation of the seventh fascicle of the *Mahā-candrapradīpa-sūtra*. It appears in the Zhao lu and the Fa shang lu. This one work, consisting of one fascicle, its manuscript is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Xian translated one fascicle of the Candrapradīpa-sūtra during the Song dynasty.
Various catalogues note that the year of its translation was not recorded during the Song period.
The emperor under whom this was produced is unknown.
One fascicle of an abridgment of the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya is recorded in the Baochang lu; this one work in one fascicle is missing.
[Compiled by] the śramaṇa Saṃghavarman.
He was a native of Siṃhala.
He translated one fascicle of an abridgment of the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya.
In the *Dazhou lu*, it is noted that the *Baochang lu* does not specify the imperial reign period.
The *Bǎochàng lù* (Record of Baochang) has not yet been located;
for now, it is provisionally included in the *Sòng lù* (Song Record) to provide a basis for its existence.

In the *Xījī shīyī zhūjīng* (New Collection of Lost-Translator Scriptures), there is one fascicle titled *Rúláizhìyìn jīng* (Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā Sūtra), also known as *Zhūfǎfǎshēn dì* (Chapter on the Dharma-body of All Buddhas).

The second version is the same as the *Lao mu jing* (Sūtra of the Old Mother) in one fascicle; the third version is the same as the *Lao nü ren jing* (Sūtra of the Old Woman) and others in one fascicle;
the *Fa mie jin jing* (Sūtra on the Extinction of the Dharma) in one fascicle; the *Shen shen da hui xiang jing* (Sūtra of the Profound Great Dedication) in one fascicle;

and the *Fo wei huang zhu yuan lao po luo men shuo xue jing* (Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha for the Old Brahmin of Huangzhuyuan on Training), which appears in the fourth division of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
*The Ten-Scroll Variant Translation of the Upāli-paṭisambhidā-sūtra*, one scroll; translated from the fifty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* (variant translations may lack the character "jiā").
*The Sūtra on Wrong Views*, one scroll; translated from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
*The One Hundred and One Karmavācanās of the Great Śramaṇa*, one scroll; also known as the *Karmavācanās of the Great Śramaṇa*.

*The Sutra on the Transformations of the Future Spoken by the Bhikṣu Kātyāyanīputra* from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *The Sutra of the Bhikṣu Kātyāyanīputra*; the latter portion is missing.

*The Sutra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*, one fascicle; the original text consisted of one hundred thousand [verses], but this is likely an error. *The Pure Sutra of the Avataṃsaka*, one fascicle. *The Sutra of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment*, one fascicle. Two versions were recorded by Sengyou.

It is further stated that there are separate editions; for now, we retain one version: *The Seven Buddhas Each Speaking a Gāthā*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Milk-King Tathāgata*, one fascicle (alternatively titled *The Sūtra Without the Milk-King*, which is currently suspected to be the same text as the *Sūtra of the Buddha Milk-Light*);

*The Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions Presently*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Past*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Names of One Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas*, one fascicle;

*The Sūtra of the Names of Five Hundred or Seven Hundred Buddhas*, one fascicle (alternatively titled *The Sūtra of Avalokiteśvara Attaining Buddhahood*, five hundred and seventy fascicles); and *The Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Causes and Conditions*, one fascicle.

One fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-praṇidhāna-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-dhyāna-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Maitreya-susvāhā-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Śāstṛ-paripṛcchā-buddha-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-śata-dvisahasra-praśna-sūtra*;
one fascicle of the *Dhṛtikāya-bodhisattva-sūtra* (also known as the *Dhṛtikāya-sūtra*); one fascicle of the *Bhadramukha-bodhisattva-dviśata-praśna-sūtra*;
one fascicle of the *Vajradharī-bodhisattvī-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Sumati-bodhisattva-sūtra*; one fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-tuṣita-deva-loka-antarābhava-avataraṇa-sūtra*. Bodhisattva...

*Xi xing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of Joy), one fascicle; *Pusa jing benye jing* (Sūtra on the Pure Original Karma of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa chuye jing* (Sūtra on the Initial Vocation of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa sishi jing* (Sūtra on the Four Matters of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle;

*Pusa shiliu yuan jing* (Sūtra on the Sixteen Vows of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa wushi dexing jing* (Sūtra on the Fifty Virtuous Deeds of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa jiaofa jing* (Sūtra on the Teachings of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa zhengxing jing* (Sūtra on the Right Practice of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle;

*Pusa churu zhuze jing* (Sūtra on the Various Rules for the Entrance and Exit of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa mu xingzi jing* (Sūtra on the Family Name and Surname of the Mother of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa jiaxing jing* (Sūtra on the Family Lineage of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Pusa biqiu jing* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣus who are Bodhisattvas), one fascicle. [Bodhisattva...]

*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; currently suspected that characters have been omitted from the original text. *The Sūtra of the Original Deeds of the Six-Tusked Elephant Bodhisattva*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Lion King*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Image*, one fascicle;

identical to the Sanskrit manuscript of the new translation, though it remains unclear whether they are the same or different. *The Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Sangha*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī-akṣi*, one fascicle;

currently suspected to be the same as the *Ānanda-akṣi-nirdeśa-sūtra*. *The Sūtra on Paying Homage to the Various Stūpas*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of Verses on the Prajñāpāramitā*, one fascicle. *Buddha*... [text fragment]

*Qingjing jie jing* (Sūtra of the Verses on Purity), one fascicle; *Taizi chu guo ershi jie* (Twenty Verses on the Prince’s Departure from the Country), one fascicle; *Fo shili jie* (Verses on the Ten Powers of the Buddha), one fascicle; *Shifang fo shenzhou* (Divine Incantation of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions), one fascicle;

*Sitiwang shenzhou* (Divine Incantation of the Four Heavenly Kings), one fascicle; *Shier yinyuan jielü shenzhou* (Divine Incantation of the Silk Thread of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination), one fascicle; *Moheshenzhou* (Great Divine Incantation), one fascicle; *Yishan shenzhou* (Divine Incantation for Moving Mountains), one fascicle;

*Jiangma shenzhou* (Divine Incantation for Subduing Māra), one fascicle; *Weide tuoluo shenzhou* (Divine Incantation of the Dhāraṇī of Majestic Virtue), one fascicle; *Benzuo chengzi cuohemo jie shenzhou* (Divine Incantation of the Knot of the Original Composition and the Erroneous Spell of the Demons), one fascicle; *Jiumojia she jing* (Sūtra of Kātyāyanīputra), one fascicle.

The *Jǔ yǔ tóngjiāshè jiě nán jīng* (Sūtra on Kāśyapa Unraveling Difficulties) shares the same original text as the seventh fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. According to the *Fājìng lù* (Record of the Dharma Scriptures), it is an alternative translation from the sixteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
There are also twenty fascicles of the *Chūyào jīng* (Sūtra of Essential Excerpts), seven fascicles of the *Xíngdào jīng* (Sūtra on Practicing the Path), and three fascicles of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

Sengyou states that these are likely incomplete versions of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. There are also two fascicles of the *Hóngdào jīng* (Sūtra on Spreading the Way) and one fascicle of the *Sìtiānwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Four Heavenly Kings). Sengyou notes that this latter text contains incantations resembling those used when spirits possess people. There is also one fascicle of the *Tiān āxūlún dòu jīng* (Sūtra on the Battle between Devas and Asuras). [There is also] the *Jīn...* [fascicle].

*The Scripture on the Woman of Form*, one fascicle; among the *Miscellaneous Parables*, Yu states it is a different edition. *The Scripture on Treating Demons and Ghosts Who Cause Unease*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Buddha’s Preaching the Precepts in the Kingdom of Campā*, one fascicle.

*The Scripture on the Buddha Preaching the Dharma at Mount Śrīkṣetra*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Buddha’s Three Poisons*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Seven Matters of the Buddha*, one fascicle.

*The Scripture on the Buddha Questioning Huǒfú*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Buddha’s Mental Activities*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Three Minds Arising Because of the Buddha*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Buddha’s Assemblies*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Original Conditions of the Seven Buddhas*, one fascicle. [End of] Explanatory Notes.

*The Sūtra of Kāśyapa’s Branch and Bowl*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Kāṣāya*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Kāṣāya*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Kāśyapa’s Explanation*, one fascicle;

*The Sūtra of Kāśyapa’s Causes and Conditions*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Śāriputra’s Inquiry into Administrative Duties*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Kāśyapa’s Sole Witness and Self-Vow*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Śāriputra’s Praise for the Ordination of Women*, one fascicle;

*The Sūtra of Śāriputra’s Rebirth in the Western Land*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Parinirvāṇa of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana*, one fascicle—this last is now suspected to be the "Śāriputra’s Parinirvāṇa" from within the *Sūtra of Births*.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of Maudgalyāyana*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Maudgalyāyana*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on Ānanda Witnessing a Transformation*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Nanda*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Seven Recollections of the Anāgāmin*, one fascicle;

*The Sūtra of the Arhat Puzi*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on Piṇḍola Taking the Alms Bowl*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Priyadarśana*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Kāyadṛṣṭika*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Dharmadinna*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Six Groups of Bhikṣus*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Vaśavartin*.

One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Bhikṣu Rājada* (or *Rājadatta*). One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Bhikṣu Huśrīma*. One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Bhikṣus of Future Eons and Profound Precepts*. One fascicle: *The Scripture on the Dharma Characteristics of Bhikṣus* (the character "xuan" [profound] here is likely an error).

One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Śākya Boy*. One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Venerable Vaccha’s Vinaya*. One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Two Śrāmaṇeras from Kaśmīra*. One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Śrāmaṇera’s Observance of the Precepts*.

One fascicle: *The Scripture of the Assembly of Upāsakas on the Sea Isle*. One fascicle: *The Scripture of Miscellaneous Matters of the Worthy One*. One fascicle: *The Scripture on the Disciple’s Cultivation and Study*.
*Disciple Xingze Meets Bandits While Carrying Sutras*, one fascicle; *Disciple’s Sutra on Diligence*, one fascicle; *Sutra on the Five Precepts Asked by Kātyāyanīputra*, one fascicle;

*Sutra of the Heavenly King Nārāyaṇa*, one fascicle; *Sutra of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa*, one fascicle; *Sutra of the Four Great Heavenly Kings*, one fascicle; *Sutra on the Lifespans of the Various Devas*, one fascicle; *Sutra on Māra Manifesting as a Buddha*, one fascicle;
*Sutra on the Demon King Admonishing Doubts and Testing [the Disciples]*, one fascicle; *Sutra of King Śuddhodana*, one fascicle; *Sutra on the Buddha’s Funeral for King Śuddhodana*, one fascicle.

*Juǎnxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Scroll), one fascicle; *Liùbèi āwéiyuèzhì jīng* (Sūtra on the Six Classes of Non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; *Qīzhòng jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Groups), one fascicle; *Qīliú jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Streams), one fascicle; *Qīsì jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Latent Tendencies), one fascicle; *Qībàirén héngsǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Classes of People Who Die Prematurely), one fascicle;

*Qīsui zuòshàn jīng* (Sūtra on Performing Good Deeds for Seven Years), one fascicle; *Bāfāng wànwù wúcháng jīng* (Sūtra on the Impermanence of All Things in the Eight Directions), one fascicle; *Bāshuāng jīng* (Sūtra on the Eight Pairs), one fascicle; *Jiǔjié jīng* (Sūtra on the Nine Ties), one fascicle.
One fascicle: *The Sūtra on the Nine Afflictions*. One fascicle: *The Sūtra on Contemplating the Body through the Nine Paths*. One fascicle: *The Sūtra on the Ten Divisions of the Saṃgha*.

*The Sūtra on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Simile of Goddess Puṇyavatī*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Simile of the Bhadrakalpa*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Simile of the Vajra*, one fascicle; and *The Treasury of Jewels*.

*Pí jīng* (Parable Sūtra), one fascicle; *Míngzhū pì jīng* (Parable of the Bright Pearl Sūtra), one fascicle; *Jùmù pì jīng* (Parable of the Heaped Wood Sūtra), one fascicle; *Sìdà pì jīng* (Parable of the Four Great Elements Sūtra), one fascicle;

*Wǔbù wēiyí suǒfú jīng* (Sūtra on the Robes Worn According to the Rituals of the Five Divisions), one fascicle—also called the *Wǔbù sēngfú jīng* (Sūtra on the Monastic Robes of the Five Divisions); according to the *Gāosēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), translated by Bái Fǎzǔ; *Jièjiè wén jīng* (Text on the Delimitation of Boundaries), one fascicle; *Shāmí líjiè jīng* (Sūtra on the Śrāmaṇera’s Departure from Precepts), one fascicle;

*Wǔjiè bàoyìng jīng* (Sūtra on the Retribution of the Five Precepts), one fascicle; *Liùzú āpítán* (Abhidharma of the Six Feet), one fascicle; *Zá pìyù jīng* (Miscellaneous Parable Sūtra), six fascicles—also called the *Zhūzá pìyù pìyù jīng* (Various Miscellaneous Parable Sūtra).

Sengyou states that there is another version with a different provenance, which is currently preserved; this *Zapiyujing* (Miscellaneous Parable Sūtra) in one fascicle contains eleven items in total. To the right, of the three hundred and seven works totaling three hundred and forty fascicles, only the first nine works comprising nine fascicles currently exist;
the remainder are all missing. These were all newly compiled by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou from among the various sūtras of unknown translators recorded in his catalog.
However, regarding Sengyou’s original catalog, those [missing works] were newly compiled by Sengyou himself.
In total, there were one thousand three hundred and six works comprising one thousand five hundred and seventy fascicles.
Now, upon detailed inspection, there remain nine hundred and ninety-nine works comprising one thousand two hundred and thirty fascicles.
Most of these are *pṛthagjanotpatti-sūtras* (sūtras concerning various rebirths),
or they are already recorded in the catalogs of lost translations by Changfang and others,
as well as being identified with their respective translators in the *Dai-lu* (Catalog of Successive Dynasties).
In addition to these, there are three hundred and seven works comprising three hundred and forty fascicles.
A thorough examination of the catalogs compiled by Hui Changfang and others reveals that none of these were ever recorded therein.
I have now newly collected them here, considering them to be lost sources.
However, in Sengyou’s Catalogue, it is merely stated that the translator is lost and no date is provided.
For now, I have appended it to the end of the Song-period catalogue so as to avoid the risk of omission.
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Volume Five, General Catalogue V;
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Volume Six,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu year.
Part Six: General Compendium of Various Scriptures, Upper Section Six.

During the Qi Dynasty of the Xiao clan, the capital was Jianye; it is also called Southern Qi. This period spans from the first year of the Jianyuan era of Emperor Gao (Jiwei) to the second year of the Zhongxing era of Emperor He (Renwu).
In total, seven reigns spanning twenty-four years elapsed.
Seven śramaṇas translated twelve works comprising thirty-three fascicles; among these, seven works totaling twenty-eight fascicles are extant, while five works totaling five fascicles are missing.

One fascicle of a scripture translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmagatayaśas of the Xiao Qi dynasty; two fascicles of scriptures and vinayas translated by the Śramaṇa Mahāyāna; eighteen fascicles of vinaya translated by the Śramaṇa Saṃghabhadra; two fascicles of scriptures translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmamati; six fascicles of collected scriptures translated by the Śramaṇa Guṇavidi; and two fascicles of scriptures translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanying. One fascicle of a scripture translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Fahua, titled the *Anantārthasūtra* (Wúliàngyì jīng), which is the second edition appearing in Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Sēnyòu lù*). This one work in one fascicle currently exists.
The śramaṇa Dharmagatayaśas (translated into Qi as Fashengcheng) was a native of Central India.
Awakening to the nature of things and abiding in the realm of feeling, he guided others toward benefit without ceasing.
In the third year of the Jianyuan era (the *xin-you* year), when Emperor Gao had established his reign,
he translated the *Anantārthasūtra* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings) in one fascicle at Chaoting Temple in Guangzhou.
The monk Hui-biao of Mount Wudang brought [this text] to the capital city of Yangdu in the third year of the Yongming era;
it was transcribed by the scribe Shan-li with his hand, while he orally interpreted the Qi pronunciation for the person receiving the transmission of the scripture.

Copied and circulated. One fascicle of the *Pañcajātaka-sūtra* (Five Birth Stories) is recorded in Sengyou’s Catalogue; Sengyou states that the number of fascicles is unknown, while Fazang states it is one fascicle. One fascicle of the *Tāpali-vinaya* (The Vinaya of Tāpali)—translated into Qi as the *Xiude-lü* (Vinaya of the Venerable Elders)—is recorded in Sengyou’s Catalogue; Sengyou states that the number of fascicles is unknown, while Fazang states it is one fascicle. These two works, totaling two fascicles, are both missing from the original collection.
The śramaṇa Mahāyāna was a native of the Western Regions.
He settled his mind upon the wondrous Way and resolved to propagate it far and wide.
During the Yongming era of Emperor Wu’s reign, [Guṇavarman] translated two works at Guangzhou, including the *Pañcāśat-jātaka-sūtra* (The Sutra of Five Hundred Birth Stories).

The *Sudarsana-vinaya-vibhāṣā* in eighteen fascicles—also known as the *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* or simply the *Sudarsana-vinaya*—was translated by Daohui during the Song and Qi dynasties. This single work, consisting of eighteen fascicles, is extant today. Its record appears in the *Song Qi Lu* and the *Sengyou Lu*.
The śramaṇa Saṃghabhadra, whose name means "Saṃgha-virtuous" (Zhòngxián) in the Qi language,
was a native of the Western Regions.
Embracing the Way with expansive freedom, his transformative kindness was inexhaustible.
According to the tradition passed down from master to disciple:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, once Upāli had completed the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka...
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of that very year, having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony,
he made offerings of incense and flowers to the Vinaya-piṭaka and placed a single dot before it.
It was thus year after year.
Upāli, desiring to enter parinirvāṇa, entrusted it to his disciple Dharmadatta.
Dharmadatta, desiring to enter parinirvāṇa, entrusted it to his disciple Śukra.
Śuklodana entrusted it to his disciple Siggava;
Siggava entrusted it to his disciple Moggaliputtatissa;
and Moggaliputtatissa entrusted it to his disciple Candavajji.

In this manner, the masters transmitted [the teachings] to one another until the present day; however, the name of the Tripiṭaka Master who brought the Vinaya Piṭaka to Guangzhou has not been recorded.
When he was about to board the ship, he turned back and departed.
He entrusted the Vinaya Piṭaka to his disciple Saṃghabhadra.
In the sixth year of Emperor Wu’s Yongming era, the year Wuchén (488 CE), Saṃghabhadra, together with the śramaṇa Senghui, [began the work] on the day Jǐsī (the 17th day of the fourth lunar month).
It was translated at Zhulin Monastery in Guangzhou and titled the *Śariputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (also known as the *Sajian Lü Piposha*).
This occurred because [the translators] were together in retreat during the summer rains.
In the seventh year of the Yongming era, the year of Jisi (489 CE), on the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the Gengwu year, he completed the *Prātimokṣa* ceremony.
Following the ritual methods of his former masters, he made offerings of incense and flowers to the Vinaya-piṭaka and then applied a single dot [to mark the completion].
When calculated by the year, this amounts to nine hundred and seventy-five points;
one point equals one year.
Zhao Baxiu encountered the ascetic Vinaya Master Hongdu at Mount Lu in the ninth year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty.
After this Buddha attained parinirvāṇa, the various sages completed their recording of the dates and years.
In the seventh year of the Yongming era, Boxiu asked Hongdu:
"Since the seventh year of Yongming onwards, why have you no longer seen any such markings?"
Hongdu replied, "From this point onward,
all [the characters] were personally inscribed by the hands of sages who had attained the Way.
I, a mere ordinary person, can do no more than receive, uphold, and revere them upon my head."
He did not dare to calculate it arbitrarily.
Based on this reckoning by Boxiu,
it reached the year of Guihai, the ninth year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty.
This totals one thousand twenty-eight years.
According to the calculations of Shi Boyu,
this reaches the year Gengwu, the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang.
The total duration amounts to one thousand two hundred and sixteen years.

If this were so, then the dates of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa would vary inconsistently between distant and near accounts, making them untenable for practice. Furthermore, the chronological records (*chàngjì*) regarding the Buddha-tooth shrine in Siṃhala as transmitted by Faxian differ entirely from these. As for the claim that Upāli, having completed the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka and finished the *Pravāraṇā* ceremony, personally applied a dot (*diǎn*) each year, and that this was thus handed down in succession until the present day—this may not be the case. Upon examining the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, it is clear that this was not compiled by Upāli; rather, it is an abridged commentary on the essential points of a specific school’s interpretation among the twenty sects that emerged after the division of the teachings. It is not the complete Vinaya itself. Even if one accepts that a dot was added at the end of each year following its compilation, the assertion that Upāli personally applied the dots cannot be taken as an authoritative guide.

The *Devadatta-parivarta*, the twelfth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in one fascicle, is now included at the beginning of the fifth fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The śramaṇa Fǎxiàn obtained a Sanskrit manuscript in the kingdom of Yutian (Khotan).
