According to the *Lù Dàohuì* (Record of Dàohuì) and the *Sēnyòu Lù* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), it was acquired in Gāochāng Commandery; it is unclear which source is correct. The *Guānshìyīn Chànhuǐ Chúzé Zhòujīng* (Sūtra of Avalokiteśvara’s Repentance and Mantra for Eradicating Sin), in one fascicle, was translated on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month in the eighth year of the Yongmíng era. This is recorded in the *Sēnyòu Lù* and the *Bǎochàng Lù*. The above two works comprise two fascicles. The *Devadatta-parivarta* currently exists, while the *Guānshìyīn Zhòujīng* (Avalokiteśvara Mantra Sūtra) is missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmamati, whose name in the Qi language means "Dharma-mind," was a man from the Western Regions.
His realization of the nature of things was profound, and he employed analogies according to the circumstances to enlighten others.
This was in the eighth year of Emperor Wu’s Yongming era, the Gengwu year.
The Śramaṇa Dharmakṣema translated two works, including the *Devadatta-parivarta*, at Waguan Temple in the capital of Yangdu.
At the time of these offerings, he served as the Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng).
He had first traveled to the Western Regions in the third year of the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty.
In the kingdom of Yutian, he obtained a Sanskrit manuscript of the sūtra as well as a tooth of the Buddha.
Protected by the deity Kapila, he returned to the Song dynasty.
When the sūtra arrived during the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, it was translated together with the śramaṇa Fayi.

The Buddha’s tooth relic was enshrined at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong. It is approximately three cun in length, with a circumference of the same measure; its color is yellowish-white. The tip of the tooth is slightly convex, resembling modern seal script, and it is warm, lustrous, and polished, much like jade or pearls. According to the *Nèi jīng* (Inner Sutra), the Buddha has four teeth: one in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one in the palace of the Dragon King, one in the Kingdom of Siṃhala, and one in the Kingdom of Udyāna. This is the tooth from the Kingdom of Udyāna. Later, it was suddenly lost, but subsequently appeared in the land of Tian (Tibet). When Xian Yuanyin requested its return, it was granted back to him.
In the first month of the third year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty,
several men suddenly appeared, all bearing weapons;
at the beginning of the night, they knocked on the door, claiming that a slave of the Prince of Linchuan had rebelled.
Someone informed him, saying, "It is upon the Buddha-tooth pavilion; please request that the pavilion be opened for inspection.
Following these words, the temple monks and the commander-in-chief proceeded to the front of the Buddha-tooth throne.
He opened the casket, took the tooth, and after performing three prostrations,
he placed the tooth in a silk handkerchief and departed for Mount Dong.
Later, he found it again and returned it to the forest of Anding.
When Emperor Wen of the Sui unified the Chen dynasty, he remained at Mount Zhong.
In the third year of the Renshou era, an imperial envoy ordered Prince Yu-zhang, Yang Jian,
to lead the entourage from Yangzhou to present Emperor Wen to the throne.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of that year, an imperial edict was issued to send [the tooth relic] to Dong Chan Ding Temple for veneration.
The miraculous manifestations of the Buddha’s tooth are fully detailed in Sengyou’s *Record of the Buddha’s Tooth*;
they shall not be elaborated upon here.
The Chan-ting Temple to its east is the present-day Ta-chuang-yen Temple.

*The Sūtra of Sudatta*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra of the Elder Sudatta*. Translated from the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*. Sengyou states it was translated in the second year of the Jianwu era. A different translation is recorded in the *Changfang lu* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. *The Sūtra of One Hundred Parables*, four fascicles; also called *The Sūtra of One Hundred Sentences of Similes*. Alternatively, five fascicles. Compiled by the Indian monk Saṃghasena. Translated on the tenth day of the ninth month in the tenth year of the Yongming era. Recorded in the catalog of Sengyou. Sengyou and others all state that the complete translation consists of ten fascicles, and these four fascicles contain a hundred matters, which is sufficient. *The Sūtra of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle. The fifth translation; it shares the same text as the *Sūtra under the Pei-tuo Tree* and others. Sengyou states it was translated in the second year of the Jianwu era. Recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Changfang lu*. Of the three sections totaling six fascicles mentioned above, the first two sections of five fascicles each are extant; the latter section of one fascicle is missing.
The śramaṇa Guṇavidi,
whose name in the Qi language means "Virtuous Progress," was a native of Central India.
In his youth, he followed the Way and served as a disciple of the Mahayana Dharma Master Saṃghasena from India.
Intelligent and possessing a powerful memory, he was diligent in recitation and study;
he had memorized more than one hundred thousand words of both Mahayana and Hinayana sutras.
He also studied the secular classics and was clearly versed in the principles of yin and yang.
His prognostications regarding seasonal omens were frequently verified by results;
consequently, his reputation for mastery of esoteric arts spread throughout the Western Regions.
At the beginning of the Jianyuan era, he came to the Jianghuai region and stayed at Vairāṭī Monastery.
Carrying his mendicant’s staff and followed by his disciples, his deportment was dignified and solemn;
from princes and dukes downward, they all vied with one another to pay him their respects.
Originally, Saṃghasena, in the kingdom of India,
excerpted essential parables from the twelve divisions of the Sūtrapiṭaka and compiled them into a single work containing one hundred items to instruct beginners.
Vidhi was able to recite all [the texts] by heart and was also well-versed in their meanings and principles.
In the ninth month of the autumn of the tenth year of Emperor Wu’s Yongming era (the *renshen* year), he translated them into the Qi language; this is the *Śatākavavadāna-sūtra*.
He further produced the *Sudatta-sūtra* and the *Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*.
From the Daming era of the Song dynasty onward, the translation of scriptures had almost ceased;
yet when he propagated the Jewel of the Dharma, everyone praised him.
Vidi was a person of broad magnanimity and great discernment.
He was skilled at guiding and inspiring others, and he diligently practiced the Way with such tireless devotion that he never slackened day or night.
Consequently, monastics from foreign lands gathered there from ten thousand li away.
The merchants of the South Sea all revered and served him together;
offerings and gifts came and went without ceasing throughout the year.
By nature, he had accumulated great merit and was rich in wealth and treasures.
Nevertheless, he had no private interests in the construction of these religious edifices.
On the banks of the Huai River in Jianye, he established Zhiguan Temple,
where multi-storied pavilions, tiered gates, and halls were magnificently adorned.
He nurtured disciples and propagated the teachings, his virtuous achievements being highly renowned. He passed away in the winter of the second year of the Zhongxing era.

One fascicle of the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*, the second translation, also titled *The Buddha Ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, or simply *The Māyā Sūtra*; alternatively in two fascicles, is found in the three catalogs of Wang Zongbao, Chang, Fashang, and others. Two fascicles of the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra* (Sutra on Unprecedented Causes and Conditions), including the preface by the novice Rāhula; also simply called the *Unprecedented Sūtra*, the second translation, is found in the Shixing Catalog. These two works, totaling three fascicles, all have their original texts extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Tanjing was a man of unknown origins.
During the Qi dynasty, he translated two works, including the *Māyā-sūtra*.
The *Qunlu* states directly that it was translated during the Qi dynasty;
since the specific year is not indicated, it remains unclear under which emperor it appeared.

One fascicle, titled *Fuzhong nǚ tīngjīng* (The Woman in the Womb Listens to the Sutra), is listed as the fifth translation and is identical in origin to the *Wúgòu xián nǚ jīng* (The Sutra of the Immaculate Virtuous Woman). The *Fánglù* (Catalogue of the Library) notes that this one work in one fascicle is missing from the extant collection.
The śramaṇa Shi Faha,
during the Yongyuan era of the deposed Emperor Baolian,
recited from within his belly a single fascicle of the *Nüting jing* (Sutra for Women to Listen To).
The various catalogs have been handed down in succession, all stating that these were "recited.
Although the underlying intent of this term "recited" remains unclear, I have listed them here in accordance with tradition.
Since there are earlier translations already extant, this avoids the risk of doubt or error.
Furthermore, the catalogs of Changfang, the Neidian,
and others state that during the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Daozheng of Jiangzhou revised and abridged one fascicle of the *Mile chengfo jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood).
This may not be the case.
This is as described in detail in the later *Dacheng lu* (Record of the Mahāyāna).
Furthermore, Fang and others further state that during the Qi dynasty,
the śramaṇa Fadu produced the one-fascicle *Huīhé jīng* (Ash River Sūtra) in the capital of Yangdu.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘跋律) in one fascicle:
it is now included as the *Kāpota-nadī-sūtra* (灰河經) within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Regarding this *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Sui Falu* (隋法錄) states:
The *Faduo* (Dharmapada) was forged to falsely claim the name of a canonical scripture; it is now abolished and shall not be established.
Fang and others further state that during the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Shi Fani translated the *Yiyi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaning of Benefit) in two fascicles.
This present scripture is that which the nun Sengfani recited from memory with her eyes closed at the end of the Qi dynasty and the beginning of the Liang dynasty;
the current version contains discrepancies in its phrasing and structure, making it unfit for circulation.
If one claims it emerged at the end of the Qi dynasty,
why was it not included in Sengyou’s catalog?
It is now compiled in the Section on Doubtful Works, as it does not exist in the Authentic Catalog.
Fang et al. further state:
"During the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Daobei produced five scriptures in five fascicles, including the *Jiushang jing* (Scripture on the Nine Wounds) and others;
all bibliographical records express doubt regarding them."
Now, the previous [dynasty] is established as the "Former Liang.

Regarding the Former Liang of the Xiao clan, which had its capital at Jianye: it is said to have lasted from the first year of the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu (Renwu) until the second year of the Taiping era of Emperor Jing (Dingchou).
In total, under four successive rulers, over a period of fifty-six years, eight individuals— both monastics and laypeople—
produced various sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographical records, as well as a newly compiled collection of sūtras of unknown translation.

In total, there are forty-six sections comprising two hundred and one scrolls; among these, forty sections totaling one hundred and ninety-one scrolls are extant, while six sections totaling ten scrolls are missing from their original texts.
The śramaṇa Śīla Saṃghavarman [compiled] three sections totaling thirty-nine scrolls from various catalogs;
the śramaṇa Mandaraka compiled three sections totaling eleven scrolls of sūtras; and the śramaṇa Saṃghavarman [translated] ten sections totaling thirty-two scrolls.

*Jinglun chuan* (Biographies of Śramaṇas in Sūtras and Śāstras) by the Śramaṇa Shi Baochang: two sections, fifty-four fascicles; *Jingji nichen zhuan* (Collected Biographies of Nuns in Sūtras) by the Śramaṇa Shi Minghui:
one section, one fascicle; *Nijie wangzi yueboshouna* (The Nuns’ Precepts: Prince Upasena) by [the Śramaṇa] Yuezhi: one section, one fascicle;
*Jing* (Sūtras) by the Śramaṇa Paramārtha: eleven sections, twenty-four fascicles; *Jinglun* (Sūtras and Śāstras) by the Śramaṇa Shi Hui... [text fragment].
The *Jiǎo* (皎) collection consists of one volume and fourteen fascicles; the *New Collection of Biographies of Monks* (*Sēngzhuàn xījì*) consists of fourteen works in twenty-five fascicles;

the various translated scriptures consist of fourteen works in twenty-five fascicles; and the *Śākyaputra-vamśa* (*Shìjiāpǔ*) consists of ten fascicles, compiled during the Qi dynasty. There is also a separate five-fascicle version, which differs in length from this [ten-fascicle] edition.
Fáng (房) states it has four fascicles, but this is likely an error, as seen in Sēngyòu’s catalogue and Chángfáng’s *Nèidiǎn*.

The *Denglu* (Equal Record) combined this with the *Qilu* (Qi Record), appending it according to the person to the *Liangchu sanzang ji ji* (Collected Records of the Tripitaka Translated during the Liang Dynasty) in fifteen fascicles.
Sengyou’s record himself states it was ten fascicles, yet fifteen fascicles are currently extant. The two records, the *Changfang* and the *Neidian*, state it was sixteen fascicles;

the *Sengyou*, *Changfang*, and *Neidian* records likewise were compiled during the Qi period. The *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) in fourteen fascicles was compiled by Sengyou and others.
The three catalogs all state that there were ten fascicles; however, fourteen fascicles are currently extant.
According to the catalogs of Sengyou, Baochang, the Neidian lu, and others, these three works comprise thirty-nine fascicles in total, and their manuscripts are all still present.
The śramaṇa Shi Sengyou was a monk of Jianchu Monastery in Yangdu.
His original surname was Yu,
and his ancestors were from Xiapi in Pengcheng.
His father had lived in Jianye for generations.
When Sengyou was several years old, he entered Jianchu Temple to pay his respects;
thereupon, he leaped for joy at the Way and refused to return home.
His parents, pitying his resolve, permitted him to enter the religious life.
He served the practitioner Sengfan as his teacher.
When he was fourteen years old, his family secretly sought a marriage for him.
Sengyou, knowing this, avoided him and went to Dinglin Temple to take refuge with Dharma Master Fada.
Fada was also one whose preceptual virtue was refined and strict, serving as a pillar for the Dharma gate;
Sengyou served his master with the utmost sincerity.
When he reached the age for full ordination, his conduct and resolve were firm and clear.
He first received instruction from the śramaṇa Faying;
since Faying was a renowned master of his time, he was the preeminent authority for the study of the Vinaya.
Fayou then exhausted his thoughts, drilling into and seeking out the teachings without ceasing from dusk until dawn.
He subsequently achieved great mastery in the Vinaya section, exerting himself to the point of surpassing the sages of old.
Emperor Wu (Yan) treated him with profound courtesy and high regard.
Regarding all monastic affairs involving doubt or hesitation, he issued imperial edicts for their examination and resolution.
When his age declined and he suffered from foot ailments, the Emperor issued an edict permitting him to enter the inner palace in a palanquin,
where he conferred the precepts upon the women of the six palaces.

He was held in such high esteem by [the rulers] as Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of Qi, Ziliang; Prince Hong of Linchuan and Prince Wei of Nanping of Liang; the Court Gentleman Yuan Ang of Chenjun; and Princess Yongkangding, the Noble Consort Ding, and others.
They together revered his precepts and models, exhausting all the respect due between teacher and disciple.
His followers, both monastics and laypeople, numbered more than ten thousand.
Sengyou was profoundly versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka and was also skilled in literary composition.
I have collected these records and compiled them into volumes,
so that those who seek and peruse them may achieve broad understanding with little effort.
This is truly the essential outline of the Dharma-gate and the fundamental source of the Śākya lineage.
From the end of the Xiao-Qi dynasty through the Liang period,
he compiled three works, including the *Śākyamuni-pūrvapraśasti* (*Shijia pu*).
Beyond these, there are the *Dharmārāma-saṃgraha*, the *World Record* (*Shijie ji*), and the *Biographies of Teachers and Disciples* (*Sizichuan*).
Because they were not included in the Tripiṭaka, they are omitted from this discussion;
these matters are fully elucidated in works such as the *Sanzang ji*.
Furthermore, there is the *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in two fascicles, or alternatively in one fascicle.
It is stated directly that the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, first translated by Saṃghavarman, is the same text as the "Mañjuśrī Section" of the seventh assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;

it is also included in the *Ratnakūṭa* as its forty-sixth assembly, according to the records of Li Kuò and the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*. It is the *Dharmadhātu-svabhāva-avikalpa-sūtra*.

The second fascicle, volume two, is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* as the eighth assembly; see Li Kuo’s *Shishi yaolan* (Essentials of the Real History) and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
The *Baoyun jing* (Sutra of the Jewel Cloud) in seven fascicles was first translated during the Chen dynasty by Subhūti as the *Mahāyāna-baoyun-jing*;
it is a different translation of the same text as the *Baoyu jing* (Sutra of the Jewel Rain) by Dharmaruci of the Tang dynasty, as seen in the *Dongyu lu* (Eastern Records).
The *Lü* (Record) and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), these three sections comprising eleven fascicles, all of which are extant.
The śramaṇa Mandarasena— “Mandarasena” being the Liang pronunciation for “Weak Sound” (*ruoshēng*)— ...
He was also known as Hongruo.
A native of the kingdom of Funan, his spiritual understanding was transcendent and awakened; he perceived both the hidden and the manifest realms with complete clarity.
Undaunted by the hardships of the journey, his resolve was set upon spreading the teachings.
Carrying a great collection of Sanskrit scriptures, he traveled from afar to present them as tribute.
In the second year of Emperor Wu’s Tianjian era, the year Guiwei, he arrived at the capital of Liang.
The Emperor issued an edict for Saṃghabhadra to collaborate on the translation,
whereupon three scriptures, including the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā*, were produced.
Although the work was carried out through translation, it was not yet proficient in the Liang language.
Therefore, the scriptural text produced here is mostly obscure and substantial.

This one fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Spoken by Mañjuśrī*, the second production, is the same text as that previously produced at Mandarava and the *Mañjuśrī-parivarta* section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*;
Master Fang says it is slightly superior to the former.

The two fascicles produced from the Mandala consist of: *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Ten Dharmas*, one fascicle—first translated during the Putong era, identical in text to the *Sūtra of the Ten Dharmas* produced by Jueding of the Northern Wei, also simply titled *The Sūtra of the Ten Dharmas*;
and *The Sūtra of the Adornment of Wisdom that Transcends the Realm of All Buddhas*, one fascicle—a second translation, identical to the [text] produced by Dharmaruci of the Northern Wei.
*The Sūtra on Entering the Buddha’s Realm*, same text as the *Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones*, one fascicle:
If a person hears the names of these eight Buddhas, they shall not be harmed by any demons, spirits, or obstacles. Fourth:

*The Sūtra of the Peacock King Spell*, two fascicles, also known as the *Spell of the Eight Yang Deities*, same text as the aforementioned *Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones*. Also called "Kong... [text fragment].
The *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the King of Sparrows*, the seventh translation, which is identical in text to the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra* translated by Yi Jing of the Tang dynasty;
as recorded in the *Baochang lu*, there is one fascicle of the *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. This dhāraṇī possesses great supernatural power;
if one can maintain it, eight yakṣa kings from the Snowy Mountains will constantly come to protect and guard them, fulfilling all their wishes according to their hearts' desire.
The ninth translation, which is identical to the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (Wuliangmen weimi chi jing) produced by Zhi Qian, corresponds to the original two-fascicle *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
It is also simply titled the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. It was translated at the Zhanyun Hall in the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era;
Yuan Tanyun received the oral transmission, and the śramaṇa Fayun of Guangzhai Temple and Xiangding verified the Bodhisattvapitaka.
*Sūtra*, one fascicle; *Vimuktimārga-śāstra* (*Jiětuōdào lùn*), twelve fascicles (also said to be thirteen fascicles), translated at the Zhanyún Hall in the fourteenth year of the Tiānjiān era;

*Aśokarāja-sūtra*, ten fascicles (sometimes titled with the character "Da" [Great]), the second translation, which shares the same source as the *Aśokarāja-zhuàn* by Ān Fǎqīn of the Western Jìn dynasty but is a different translation, completed on the twentieth day of the sixth month in the eleventh year of the Tiānjiān era.
Translated at the Shouguang Hall in the capital of Yangdu; as recorded in the Biànchàng lu (Record of Biànchàng), these comprise ten works in thirty-two fascicles.

The original texts for all of them are extant and are listed in the Chángfáng lu (Record of Zhìchángfáng) and the Xu gāosēng zhuàn (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks); however, the number of works and their titles are not fully enumerated here.
The śramaṇa Saṃghavarman— “Saṃgha” meaning “army” (in the Liáng language) and “varman” meaning “armor”—
is also called Saṃgyǎng.
He was a native of the kingdom of Funan.
From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and early on entered the stream of the Dharma.
Although he thoroughly investigated both the Sūtras and the Śāstras, he specialized in the Abhidharma.
The Śrāvakas gradually spread their fame across the South Sea;
after completing his studies, he extensively refined the Vinaya Piṭaka.
With courageous resolve, he surveyed the regions, delighting in honoring and promoting the transformation of others through the Dharma.
Having heard that the Dharma was flourishing in the state of Qi, he traveled by ship to the capital and resided at Zhengguan Temple.
He was a disciple of the Indian śramaṇa Guṇabhadra,
and subsequently studied the Vaipulya scriptures with Guṇabhadra under him with great diligence.
Before he had even reached maturity, he was already extensively learned and versatile;
he could understand the scripts and languages of several countries.
It was during this time that the Qi calendar fell into ruin and the Way of the Daoists declined.
Pure and serene in body and mind, he severed all external ties.
Thus, he dwelt in seclusion within his chamber, cultivating his fundamental nature and refining his spiritual practice.
When the Great Liang dynasty governed the realm, they sought out those with exceptional skills and abilities.
In the fifth year of the Tianjian era, he was summoned by imperial decree to engage in translation at five locations within the Liang capital:
the Shouguang Hall, the Hualin Garden, Zhengguan Temple, the Zhanyun Pavilion, and the Funan Pavilion.

From the *jǐng* year of the fifth year of the Tiānjiān era (506 CE) until the *gēngzǐ* year of the first year of the Pǔtōng era (520 CE), he translated ten scriptures, including the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*, for which the Sanskrit originals were all provided by Mandaraka.

The records of Sengchang and others further state that Dharmabodhi additionally produced a five-fascicle *Aśoka-avadāna*; however, this is incorrect, as the previously existing *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra* is itself its biography and should not be recorded twice. On the day the translations first commenced at the Shòuguāng Palace, Emperor Wŭ personally attended the Dharma seat and acted as the scribe to receive the text.
Thereupon, he entrusted the complete manuscript of the sutra to the translators and commanded the śramaṇas Baochang,
Huichao, Sengzhi, Fayun, Yuan Tanyun, and others to work together to transcribe and annotate it.
His elegant character and refined substance followed a proper sequence, ensuring that the tradition of translation did not decline.
The Son of Heaven received him with great courtesy and appointed him as a private monk of the imperial household.
The relevant authorities provided him with all necessary provisions, causing both the monastic and lay communities to change their perceptions of him.
Balu did not keep private wealth;
he established his residence at the monastery through the offerings and gifts he received.
He was treated with great honor by the Grand Marshal, Prince Hong of Linchuan.
In the fifth year of the Putong era, he passed away at Zhengguan Temple due to illness at the age of sixty-five.

His work, *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Diverse Features of Sūtras and Vinaya), consists of fifty fascicles; it was compiled by imperial decree in the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era. It is said that this included a table of contents making fifty-five fascicles in total, but now the table of contents is missing, leaving only the fifty fascicles. The table of contents merely compiles the titles of the chapters and appears to contain no other distinct matter. This is recorded in the *Bǎochàng lù* and the *Chángfáng lù*. The *Biqiūnì zhuàn* (Biographies of Bhikṣuṇīs) in four fascicles describes the conduct of nuns during the four dynasties of Jin, Song, Qi, and Liang; it has been newly included in the present record. These two works comprise fifty-four fascicles in total, and their original texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Baochang was a monk of Zhuangyan Temple in the capital of Liang.
His secular surname was Cen, and he was a native of Wu Commandery.
He was a preeminent disciple of the Vinaya Master Sengyou.
His vast learning and extensive knowledge were rarely equaled by his peers;
Emperor Wu held him in the highest esteem and veneration.
During the Tianjian era, he was repeatedly commanded by imperial decree to compile various works, all of which satisfied the Emperor’s wishes.
In the Jingshen year of the fifteenth year, he was again commanded to compile the *Jinglü yixiang* (A Collection of Extraordinary Phenomena from the Sutras and Vinaya) in one volume,
and he also separately compiled the *Nihuan zhuan* (Biographies of Nuns) in four volumes.
Within the *Fanglü* (Records of the Monasteries), there are further seven works, such as the *Ming seng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks);
because they were not included in the canon, they are omitted here and not discussed.
The remainder are all fully contained in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
The *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra* in Five Sections, one fascicle; also known as the *Mīśāsaka Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, according to the *Bǎochàng lù*. This one work in one fascicle is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Minghui was a monk at Jianchu Monastery in the capital of the Liang dynasty.
He was rigorous and austere in his observance of the precepts and studied the Mahīśāsaka school.
During the Song dynasty, Huiguo translated the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya with Jue-shou;
however, it only produced the *Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra* and lacked the *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla*.
Consequently, in the third year of the Putong era of Emperor Wu, the Renyin year, he...

Within the *Mahāvinaya*, one fascicle of the Bhikṣuṇī-śīla was excerpted; this is precisely what is practiced today. The compiler states: "Upon examining these precepts, following the *saiksa-dharmas* (rules of training), there is no text for the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmāḥ saṃgha-rajanāḥ*).

Although the original text is brief, according to the meaning, it ought to be inserted here. How could it be that when a dispute arises among the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha and is not extinguished, [the rules] are absent? The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (祇律) clearly states that they are identical to those of the monks. Thus, the fortieth fascicle of that Vinaya says: 'Among the *saiksa-dharmas*, with the exception of [the rules regarding] trampling grass and water, the seven methods for settling disputes and the *anuvartana-dharmas* (rules of conformity) are all the same as those of the bhikṣus. Therefore, the Master's failure to insert them is illogical and contrary to principle."

The *Mahāyāna-śikhara-rāja-sūtra* in one fascicle, also known as the *Vimalakīrti-putra-sūtra*, is the same text as the *Vaipulya-śikhara-rāja* translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Western Jin dynasty and the *Sudhana-kumāra-sūtra* translated by Guṇabhadra; it is the third appearance [of this text] and is recorded in the *Chángfáng-lù* and the *Xù gāosēng-zhuàn*. This one work in one fascicle currently exists.
Prince Candraprabha was the son of the King of Ujjayinī in Central India.

This country of Ujjayinī is sometimes said to be in Southern India and sometimes said to be in Western India; it has not yet been definitively settled. Alternatively, this country may be situated at the southwestern corner of Central India, bordering the west and near the south; thus, the various traditions are inconsistent and indeterminate.
Born with innate wisdom, he was brilliant and possessed a profound understanding of subtle mysteries.
He specialized in the study of Buddhist scriptures and excelled particularly in their philosophical principles.
He had a thorough mastery of phonology and was also skilled in local dialects.
Previously, during the Xinghe era of the Eastern Wei, he translated three sections of scriptures.
During the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, he traveled from the Wei to the court of Emperor Wu of Liang and was invited to remain;
by imperial decree, he was appointed to oversee all foreign diplomatic missions.

I translated one fascicle of the *Cūḍāmaṇi-sūtra* and seven (or six) fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, consisting of twenty-two chapters. In the first year of the Chengsheng era, at Zhengguan Temple and at the residence of Yang Xiong, I produced this version.

Previously, during the Liang dynasty, Dharmakṣema had produced a four-fascicle version containing eighteen chapters; Paramārtha later produced four additional chapters to supplement it, making twenty-two chapters in total and forming seven fascicles. This version is currently included in the *Shanfan yulu*.

The above is based on two fascicles of a sutra translated at the request of Liu Wéntuó, the Interior Secretary of Nánkāng in Pínggù County, on the eighth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Shàotài era (Dīngchū, 522 CE).

This is recorded in the postscript to the extant sutra. Fǎng states that the version produced during the Chén dynasty is incorrect; furthermore, none of the various chronological records contain a third year of the Shàotài era.

As for the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* in one fascicle, which contains the "Verses on What Exists and What Does Not Exist" (*yǒu jīn wú gē*), Fǎng states it was produced in the fourth year of the Tàiqīng era. However, upon examining the various chronological records, the Tàiqīng era did not reach a fourth year; all accounts below this point are identical.

The *Nirnaya-samgraha-śāstra* (決定藏論) in three fascicles contains characters from the Liang dynasty; examining its phrasing and sentences, it was produced by Paramārtha. The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (大乘起信論) in one fascicle, first translated, is the same text as that later produced by Śikṣānanda of the Tang.
It was produced on the tenth day of the ninth month of the second year of the Chengsheng era (the Guiyou year), at Jianxing Temple in Shixing Commandery, Hengzhou.

Upasena and others acted as interpreters, while the śramaṇa Zhikai and others took up the pen [to record the translation], and he also composed the preface; this may be seen in the preface to the treatise. The *Yathābhūta-śāstra* (如實論) in one fascicle has the following title at its beginning:

The *Yúshí lùn* (Treatise on Reality), Chapter on Refutation through Counter-Interrogation. Fáng says it was brought out in the fourth year of the Tàiqīng era; the *Rénwáng bōrě jīng* (Benevolent Kings Prajñā Sūtra), one fascicle, translated at Bǎotián Monastery in Yùzhāng in the third year of the Chéngshèng era.

This third translation is identical in text to that produced by Dharmarakṣa and others during the Western Jìn dynasty. The *Mílè xiàshēng jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born), one fascicle, translated at Bǎotián Monastery in Yùzhāng in the third year of the Chéngshèng era.

This fifth translation is identical in text to that produced by Kumārajīva and others. The *Shíqī dì lùn* (Treatise on the Seventeen Stages), five fascicles, is identical to the *Yúqié shīdì lùn* (Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra) translated during the Táng dynasty.

The original translation comprised five fascicles, but it was interrupted due to the onset of difficulties; this is recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks). In the fourth year of the Taiqing era, at the residence of Lu Yuanzhe, the Magistrate of Fuchun, he translated one fascicle of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* for twenty virtuous śramaṇas, including Baoqiong.
[Seng]fang states that it was produced in the fourth year of the Taiqing era. He also translated one fascicle of the *Traikālyaparīkṣā-śāstra* in the fourth year of the Taiqing era.
Both of these are found in the catalogs of the Inner Canon by Daochang and others.
The śramaṇa Paramārtha— translated into the Liang language as Zhendi—
or alternatively known as Julanata.
This is called "Intimate Reliance" (*Pratyāśraya*); both are Sanskrit names.
He was originally a native of Ujjayinī in Western India.
He was of the Brahmin caste;
his conduct was clear and bright, his character serene and solemn,
and his spirit was so refined and noble that he appeared naturally remote and transcendent.
There was no part of the vast sections of the Tripitaka that he did not contemplate;
his artistic talents and extraordinary skills were particularly refined and polished.
Although he followed the profound principles of Buddhism, he became renowned for his mastery of the Way.
Having traveled far across arduous passes, undaunted by either level ground or steep terrain,
he journeyed through various kingdoms before finally settling in Central India.
During the Datong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, he was summoned by imperial decree by Zhang Fan and others from the Office of Attendants.

He escorted the envoys from Funan back to their own country and subsequently dispatched an embassy to the kingdom of Magadha in Central India to invite a virtuous Tripiṭaka master and to seek Mahāyāna treatises, the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*, and other scriptures.
Paramārtha’s reputation for propagating the teachings had long been heard afar, and his ritual conduct was revered by sages and worthies.
He sought out renowned masters to bring benefit to the common people.
Consequently, that kingdom humbled itself before Paramārtha and respectfully received the imperial decree, providing him with the necessary scriptures and treatises.
Having long cherished this aspiration in my heart, I was filled with joy upon hearing the command.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the twelfth year of the Datong era, I arrived at the South Sea;
traveling along perilous and vast waters, I remained there for two consecutive springs.
In the intercalary eighth month of the second year of the Taicheng era, [the image] first arrived at the capital.
Emperor Wu personally offered his respects and enshrined it in Baoyun Hall, making offerings with utmost sincerity.
The Emperor desired to transmit the teachings of the translated scriptures, not envying the era of Qin;
he produced new texts that surpassed those of the Qi dynasty.
However, as the Way declined at the end of the Liang period and the Hu rebels surged in their arrogance, the Dharma collapsed under the circumstances of the times.
Failing to achieve his purpose in proclaiming [the teachings], he entered the Eastern Land (China).
He further went to Fuchun, where he requested the Magistrate Lu Yuanzhe to establish a place for him to seek instruction and undertake the work of translation.
He invited more than twenty eminent śramaṇas, including Baoqiong and others, to join him.

He had just finished translating five fascicles of the *Shiqi di lun* (Treatise on the Seventeen Stages) when the national crisis failed to subside; thus, he remained in seclusion, relying on the *Tongzhuan*.
During the Dabao era, he was invited back to the imperial court by Hou Jing to receive offerings there.
At that time, military conflict and famine followed one another, and the Dharma was nearly on the verge of collapse.
It was only when Emperor Yuan ascended the throne and the realm became peaceful and pure that [the Master] finally settled at Zhengguan Temple in Jinling.
Together with Chan Master Yuwuan and some twenty others, he translated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
In the second month of the third year, he returned to Yuzhang,
and subsequently traveled to Xinwu and Shixing.
He subsequently followed Xiao Taibao across the mountain passes to Nankang,
where he translated scriptures according to the circumstances of each place, living a life of restless wandering without a fixed abode.
In total, he verified eleven works of sutras and śāstras produced during the Liang dynasty.
At the end of the Liang dynasty, he entered the Chen dynasty and again produced sūtras and śāstras as described below.
The *Chángfáng nèidiǎn lù* and other catalogs list eighteen treatises in one fascicle, also attributed to Tí.
Now, upon examining the wording, this is not a literal translation.
Since it is identical in substance to the original text of the school’s tenets (*nikāyābhyupagama*), it is inappropriate to reproduce it again;
therefore, I have deleted it here, as described in the separate record.
Furthermore, there are six works totaling twenty-six fascicles, including the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra-śāstra* and others;

these were all composed by Paramārtha and have likewise been omitted [from this collection]. The *Chángfáng nèidiǎn lù* and other catalogs further state that in the fifteenth year of the Tiānjiān era, Mù Dàoxián presented one fascicle of the *Ullambana-sūtra*, which simply states "presented to the Emperor" without clarifying the specific details; thus, it has been included in the *Yílù* (Record of Doubtful Works) and is not recorded here among the deleted texts.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) consists of fourteen volumes: one volume for the preface and catalog, and thirteen volumes for the biographies, totaling fourteen. It was compiled in the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era. It is recorded in the two catalogs of the Inner Canon by Sengchang and Faxiang. This single work comprises fourteen volumes, and its manuscript is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Huijiao,
whose clan and lineage are unknown,
was a native of Shangyu in Kuaiji.
His learning encompassed both internal and external traditions, and he was extensively trained in the sutras and vinaya.
Residing at Jiaxiang Temple, he propagated the Dharma during the spring and summer and engaged in composition during the autumn and winter.
He authored commentaries on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
Furthermore, because the biographies of eminent monks compiled by Master Chang were largely verbose and redundant,
he subsequently established a precedent and composed the *Guangzhao gāosēng zhuàn* (Extended Biographies of Eminent Monks) in one volume.
It begins with the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty and concludes with the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty.
In total, there were four hundred and fifty-three years and two hundred and fifty-seven individuals;
additionally, there were two hundred and thirty-nine persons mentioned incidentally in the appended records.
In total, there were four hundred and ninety-six individuals.
Their virtues and achievements were categorized into ten major classes.
The preface briefly states:
Previous authors, perhaps finding the account too voluminous, have excised certain details;
consequently, many of the extraordinary traces of his transcendent conduct have been omitted or abridged.
They claim that as a renunciant, he remained among the state’s guests and honored by kings.
One should not be haughty and distant, loftily transcending all alone.
To seek to decline honor and abandon affection was originally intended to encourage the world by setting an example of virtue.
If this were not discussed, what would there be to record?
Furthermore, it is said:
"The compilations of previous eras mostly refer to them as 'famous monks' (ming-seng).
I venture to suggest that there is a distinction between being 'famous' and being 'exalted' (gao), much like the difference between superiority and inferiority."
As for those whose true practice conceals their brilliance, they are lofty yet remain unnamed;
those with meager virtue who happen upon their time gain fame yet lack loftiness.
Fame without loftiness is fundamentally not worth recording.
Since "Gao" (High) was used instead of specific names for the sake of completeness, I have now recorded them;
thus, I have omitted those names and phonetic transcriptions, substituting them with the character "Gao.
I have carefully examined the principles of this biography and its literary style, which is characterized by refined and elegant diction.
Truly, this may be transmitted as something imperishable, serving forever as a mirror for guidance.
The *New Collection of Lost Translations of Various Scriptures* contains one fascicle of the *Mārīcī-devī Sūtra*, also known as the *Minor Mārīcī-devī Sūtra*;
it is a partial variant translation of the *Mārīcī-devī Sūtra* found at the beginning of the tenth fascicle of the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha Sūtra*.
*The Scripture of the Six-Syllable Divine Mantra King*, one fascicle; the second edition is identical in substance to the *Scripture of the Six-Syllable Mantra King*.
*The Scripture of the Questions of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva to the Buddha*, one fascicle;

it is also called the *Scripture of the Seven-Buddha Dhāraṇī Mantra of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva* and the *Scripture of the Divine Mantras of the Seven Buddhas*. Its initial edition is identical in substance to the *Tathāgata-upāya* translated during the Sui dynasty.
The *Śūramgama-mantra-sūtra* (same text as the *Sūtra of the Names of Three Thousand Buddhas of the Three Kalpas*, three fascicles):
the first fascicle, *Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Past Adornment Kalpa*; the middle fascicle, *Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Present Auspicious Kalpa*;

and the final fascicle, *Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Future Constellation Kalpa*. According to the *Chángfáng Rùzànglù*, these were originally three separate texts which have now been combined.

One fascicle of the *Mūlamandala-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (or without the word "sūtra"), or one fascicle of the *Āṭavaka-mahāyakṣasenāpati-buddhotaraṇī-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, also simply called the *Āṭavaka-dhāraṇī-sūtra*;
one fascicle of the *Amitābha-dundubhisvararāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra*; and the *Mahāsamantabhadra-dhāraṇī*.
*Sūtra*, one fascicle; *Mahā-saptaratna-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Ṣaḍakṣara-mahādhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Gṛhapati-duhitṛ-āntaśikṣā-siṃhanāda-nītārtha-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Bodhisattva-pañcadharma-pratideśanā-vinaya*, one fascicle—also titled *Bodhisattva-pañcadharma-pratideśanā-sūtra*; and *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*, ten fascicles.
*Mahāyāna-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. It was seen in the catalog of the Mahāyāna Temple during the Chen dynasty;
its initial appearance is identical to the *Mahāyāna-pañcaskandha-śāstra* translated in the Tang dynasty. This treatise is missing [the right portion].

Of the fourteen works and twenty-five fascicles listed above, with the exception of the *Pañcaskandhaka*, all have been included in the *Lushan lüeyi lu* (Record of Lost Translations from the Library of the Canon).
The middle section is missing and not included.
Examining its phrasing, it is not from a remote era;
therefore, it has been compiled as belonging to the late Liang period, though it is said that the source for the Liang dynasty is lost.
The Later Wei, the Yuan clan of the Wei, initially established their capital at Heng’an.

After migrating south to Luoyang, they subsequently moved to Ye; this period is also called the Later Wei. It began from the first year of Huangshi of Emperor Daowu (the Bingshen year), which corresponds to the twenty-first year of Taiyuan of the Eastern Jin, and ended in the eighth year of Wuding of Emperor Xiaojing of the Eastern Wei (the Gengwu year).

In total, there were thirteen emperors over a period of one hundred and fifty-five years. Five emperors resided at Heng’an; until the eighteenth year of the Tahe era of Emperor Xiaowen, seven emperors resided at Luoyang; and one sovereign resided at Ye. There were twelve individuals, both monastics and laypeople, [who served as translators].

The translated sūtras, śāstras, biographies, and so forth, total eighty-three works comprising two hundred and seventy-four fascicles; among these, seventy-three works totaling two hundred and fifty-five fascicles are extant, while ten works totaling nineteen fascicles are missing.
One collection in thirteen fascicles by the Northern Wei śramaṇa Shi Huijue; three collections in seven fascicles of sūtras and biographies by the śramaṇa Shi Tanyao;
five collections in nineteen fascicles of sūtras, śāstras, and biographies by the śramaṇa Jikaya;
three collections in eight fascicles of sūtras by the śramaṇa Dharmaruci; and one collection in one [fascicle] by the śramaṇa Shi Fachang.
The *Sūtra on the Scroll*, translated by the śramaṇa Ratnamati: three works in nine fascicles. The śramaṇa Bodhiruci:
thirty works in one hundred and one fascicles, comprising both sūtras and śāstras. The śramaṇa Buddhasanta:
ten works in eleven fascicles, comprising both sūtras and śāstras. The brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci: eighteen works in ninety-two fascicles.
The *Sūtra*, *Vinaya*, and *Śāstra* of Prince Śubhakarṣa: three sections totaling seven fascicles; the *Śāstras* of the śramaṇa Vimokṣaprajña:
five sections totaling five fascicles; the *Śāstra* of the śramaṇa Dharmaprajña: one section totaling one fascicle;

and the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Kṣudrakapiṭaka-sūtra*) in thirteen, fifteen, sixteen, or seventeen fascicles, also known as the *Sūtra of the Causes and Conditions of the Wise and the Foolish*.
The *Jingjian dao hui* (Wisdom of Seeing the Path), recorded in the Song Qi Lu and the Sengyou Lu, consists of one volume in thirteen fascicles;
its manuscript currently exists.
[Compiled by] the śramaṇa Shi Huijiao.
One source says his name was Tanyue.
Daoyou states that Tanyue was a native of Liangzhou;
he was as tall as a wall reaching the clouds, and his spirit and character were clear and enlightened.
His precepts were pure and his wisdom was so penetrating that he could discern the subtle; in the Kingdom of Khotan, he obtained the Sanskrit manuscripts of the scriptures.
This occurred in the sixth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of Emperor Taiwu, the year of Yiyou (485 CE).
Returning from Khotan to the kingdom of Gaochang, he translated the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) in one fascicle together with the śramaṇa Wèidé.
He consulted Jingmài’s *Jīngtú*, which cites the record by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sēngyòu concerning the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*. It states:
There were eight monks in total from Hexi, including the śramaṇas Shi Tanjue and Wei-de,
who resolved to travel abroad to seek out the scriptures.
At a great monastery in Khotan, they encountered the Pañcavārṣika assembly.
Pañcavārṣika is translated in the Han language as "the five-year assembly of the entire great community.
The various scholars of the Tripiṭaka each propagate the jewel of the Dharma, preaching the sūtras and expounding the vinaya, instructing according to [karmic] actions.
The eight monks, including Foju, were permitted to divide the work according to their respective capacities;
thereupon, they vied with one another in practicing the Hu (foreign) sounds and analyzing them through Han (Chinese) meanings.
Having reflected deeply upon and mastered the various texts he had heard while translating,
he returned to Gaochang and compiled them into a single work.
Subsequently, he crossed the shifting sands and brought [the scriptures] to Liangzhou.
At that time, the śramaṇa Shi Huilang was a preeminent master of Hexi;
his spiritual practice was profound and vast.
The Vaipulya dhāraṇīs take this sūtra as their source, for its origins lie in parables;
what these parables clarify encompasses both the good and the evil.
The distinction between the worthy and the foolish is simply the inversion of good and evil.
Since previous generations have already transmitted many parables through the scriptures,
this work was titled *The Worthy and the Foolish* (*Xiányú*) based on these events.

The *Daji-yi shenzhou jing* (Sūtra of the Great Auspicious Meaning Divine Spells), in two fascicles or four fascicles, is recorded in the *Fashang lu*. The *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance), in one fascicle, is the fourth appearance [of this title], recorded in the *Zhu Daozu lu* and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*. The *Fufa zang zhuan* (Tradition of the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury), in four fascicles, is the second appearance, recorded in the *Bodhiruci lu* and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*. Of these three works totaling seven fascicles, the *Jiyi zhujing* (Spells Sūtra of Auspicious Meaning) in one part of two fascicles is extant; however, the *Jingdu jing* and other works, totaling two parts in five fascicles, are missing.
The śramaṇa Shi Tanyao was a man of unknown origins.
Having left home at a young age, his conduct was firm and upright, and his character was refined and austere.
During the Heping era of the Wei dynasty, he resided at Beitaishan.
As the Director of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuantong),
he harmonized and gathered the monastic community, skillfully winning their hearts.
He resided at Tongle Temple in the Heng’an Grottoes,
which was constructed by the Wei Emperor.
Located thirty *li* northwest of Heng’an, he carved the temple into the stone cliffs on the northern face of Mount Wuzhou and established the Buddhist monastery there.
It is named Lingyan.
Its largest grottoes are over twenty zhang in height and can accommodate approximately three thousand people;
their facades are individually carved with images that exhaust every refinement of artistry and beauty.
The niches vary in shape and appearance, striking awe into both humans and spirits.
Arranged side by side like the teeth of a comb, they extend for over thirty li.
At the eastern end, a monastic temple constantly provides sustenance for a thousand monks.
The inscriptions on the stelae still exist, though their full details have not yet been exhaustively set forth.
Previously, in the seventh year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of Emperor Taiwu,
the Minister of Education Cui Hao was a sycophant of depraved character and shallow rhetoric.
He caused Emperor Taiwu to honor and revere the Daoist Kou Qianzhi, who was appointed as the Celestial Master.
[The Emperor] held the Elder of the Lao family (Laozi) in high esteem while harming the followers of Śākyamuni and burning down monasteries and stupas.
It was not until the Gengyin year that Emperor Taiwu contracted a malignant illness, at which point he finally attained awakening.
Furthermore, the Chan Master Bazu came to provide him with spiritual exhortation.
Feeling remorse and shame, he immediately executed Cui Hao,
burying him in the marketplace and using his mouth as a latrine to defile him before the public.
In the year of Renchen, Emperor Taizu died,
and his grandson Wencheng ascended the throne;
he immediately established stupas and monasteries and sought out the Buddhist scriptures.
After the Dharma had been destroyed for seven years, the Three Jewels were restored.
Yao Xun lamented the former decline and destruction while rejoicing in their renewed presence.
In the third year of the Pinghe era (the Renyin year), he gathered a community of virtuous monks at the North Terrace Grottoes.
He translated three scriptures, including the *Śrī-artha-sūtra*, together with the Indian śramaṇa Ji-yi and others.
His intention was that these might circulate so as not to be lost to future worthies.
This one fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra* is the fifth edition, produced alongside Kumārajīva’s *Bodhisattvabhūmi-alaṃkāra*.

The *Heart Sūtra* and others share the same original text; this is seen in the *Shixing lu* (Record of the Beginning of Flourishing) and the *Daohui Songqi lu* (Record of Daohui on the Song and Qi Dynasties).

It is stated that the *Jingyang zhufu gongde jing* (Sūtra Praising the Merits of All Buddhas) in three fascicles—also titled the *Jizhufuhua jing* (Sūtra of the Flower Collection of All Buddhas), also simply called the *Jihua jing* (Sūtra of the Flower Collection), alternatively titled the *Xianzai fuming jing* (Sūtra of the Names of Present Buddhas)—in either four fascicles, is a third translation that shares the same original text as those produced by Kumārajīva and others;
this is seen in the *Daming sanzang fashu* (Great Ming Catalogue of the Tripitaka).
The *Huìsòngqílù* (Record of the Song and Qi Dynasties) lists the *Fāngbiànxīnlùn* (Treatise on the Mind of Expedient Means) in one or two fascicles, comprising four chapters;

its second appearance is identical in text to that translated by Juéxián during the Eastern Jin. The *Jiàndàohuì Sòngqílù* and the *Sēngyòulù* (Monk Yòu’s Record) list the *Fùfǎzàng yīnyuánchuán* (Tradition of the Causes and Conditions of the Transmission of the Dharma) in six fascicles—though some versions omit the characters "yīnyuán" (causes and conditions)—also known as the *Fùfǎzàng jīng* (Scripture of the Transmission of the Dharma), in four fascicles.

Some say that the two-fascicle [version] was translated by Daohui during the Song and Qi dynasties; it shares the same source as the version translated by Zhiyan of the Song and Tan Yao of the Wei, as recorded in the *Sòngqí lù* (Record of the Song and Qi Dynasties).

It is also listed in Sengyou’s catalog. Regarding the eight-fascicle *Zá bǎozàng jīng* (Treasury of Miscellaneous Jewels), its catalog states it originally consisted of thirteen fascicles, though this remains uncertain;
currently, only eight fascicles are extant. These are found in Daohui’s *Sòngqí lù* and Sengyou’s catalog. The above constitutes five works.
The nineteen fascicles are all extant.
The śramaṇa Jikaya (translated in Wei as "What Matter?").
He was a man from the Western Regions.
He traveled to convert and transform others, making it his heart's purpose to guide sentient beings.
In the second year of the Yanxing era of Emperor Xiaowen, the Renzi year (472 CE),...

For the purpose of translating five sections of scriptures, including the *Da fang guang shi di jing* (Avataṃsaka-sūtra Daśabhūmika), the Śramaṇa Tanyao served as the Chief Administrator of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuantong);
Liu Xiaobiao acted as the scribe.

The *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* in five fascicles was translated in the first year of the Zhengshi era. The *Avataṃsaka-parivarta-sūtra*, namely the *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāra-sūtra* in two fascicles—also titled the *Tathāgata-avatāra-sarvabuddhaviṣaya-sūtra*—was translated at the Baima Monastery in the second year of the Jingming era; this first translation is identical to the *Sarvabuddhaviṣayajñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra* by Saṃghavarman of the Liang dynasty. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* in one fascicle was initially translated by Gautama Dharmakṣema with the same original text as that produced in the fourth year of the Zhengshi era. According to Fashang’s catalogue, Bodhiruci later re-examined it. Of these three works totaling eight fascicles, the first two totaling seven fascicles are extant, while the latter work, one fascicle, is missing.
The śramaṇa Dharmaruci;
in Wei it is translated as Fāxī (Dharma-Desire),
and also as Fālè (Dharma-Joy).
A man from South India who left his home to enter the monastic path, he became particularly renowned for his transmission of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Devoted to the propagation of the Way, he was moved by the resonance of external conditions.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanwu, he traveled to Luoyang to propagate the Dharma.
From the second year of the Jingming era (Xinsi) until the fourth year of the Zhengshi era (Dinghai),
he translated three scriptures, including the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, for Emperor Xuanwu.
Śramaṇa Dàobǎo recorded it in writing.
It is seen in the catalogues of Fǎláng and others.

*The Scripture on the Elder’s Son Biànyì*, one fascicle; also called *The Scripture on the Questions of the Elder’s Son Biànyì*, or simply *The Scripture of the Elder Biànyì*. It is found in the catalogue of Fǎshàng. This one work, in one fascicle, its manuscript currently exists.

The śramaṇa Shi Fanchang was a person of unknown origins. During the reign of Emperor Xuanwu, he also translated the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra of the Meaning of Discernment) in one fascicle at Luoyang; the compiler records:

"I have carefully consulted the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and other records, all of which state that during the Jin dynasty, Dao’an, after several years of monastic life, requested a scripture from his teacher. The teacher first gave him one scroll of the *Bianyi jing*, consisting of approximately five thousand words, which Dao’an recited from memory upon a single reading. Furthermore, since Master Dao’an’s record of lost translations also includes this title, it follows that the *Bianyi* had already been circulating in the world during the Eastern Jin. How is it that it is only said to have been produced by Fanchang during the reign of Emperor Xuanwu of the Wei?"
*The Treatise on the Lotus Sutra*, one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; also known as *The Treatise on the Lotus Sutra*.
Transcribed by the Palace Attendant Cui Guang, Senglang, and others. Recorded in the *Changfang Lu*.
Its initial appearance was largely identical to the translation by Bodhiruci, with only minor differences. It is titled *The Upadeśa of the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma*, concluding here.

The *Ratnagotravibhāga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Jewel Nature of the One Vehicle) in four fascicles—also known as the *Saptayāna-viśeṣa-uttara-śāstra*—exists in versions of either three or five fascicles.
It was produced at the residence of Zhao Xin; see the second entry in the *Baoshang lu*.

This second translation is identical in text to that produced by Bodhiruci. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* in four fascicles is the second [translation] produced alongside that of Bodhiruci. Great... [text fragment].
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Jewel Heap Sutra) is recorded as being of the same text in Baochang’s Catalogue; these three works comprise nine fascicles in total.
Of these, the first two works consist of five fascicles and are extant, while the third work consists of four fascicles and is missing.
The śramaṇa Ratnamati, also called Bodhi;
in the Wei language, this means "Precious Intention."
A native of Central India,
he was of profound learning and erudition, well-versed in both principle and practice.
He could recite one hundred million verses from the texts of the Tripiṭaka.
The gāthā consists of thirty-two characters;
it clearly elucidates the intent of meditative contemplation and emphasizes the practice of wandering to transform others.
In the fifth year of the Zhengshi era of Emperor Xuanwu, the wuzi year, he first arrived at the capital of Luoyang.
He then translated three works, including the *Dharmapada-śāstra*,
with the śramaṇa Senglang, Jueyi, and the Palace Attendant Cui Guang serving as scribes.
On the day of the translation, this took place in the Inner Hall of Luoyang.
The version transmitted by Bodhiruci was assisted by Ratnaśānti; subsequently,
these three virtuous masters followed the rumors.
The various masters of transmission practiced in isolation and did not consult one another.
The Emperor, noting the flourishing state of the propagation of the Dharma, briefly outlined the details and issued an imperial decree to the three locations.
Once each had completed their translations, they were then compared and collated.
In the interim, there were omissions and variations, leading to differences in the phrasing and intent at times; later generations combined these to form a complete collection.
This is why works such as the *Ratnakūṭa-śāstra*, the *Ratnagotra-śāstra*, and others each exist in two versions, as seen in the records of Baochang and others.
At first, the śramaṇa Baoyi was distinguished for his profound spiritual principles;
he mastered the Wei translations and exhausted every subtle nuance of their meaning.
The Emperor frequently commanded him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
As he was expounding and elucidating the essential meanings, insights frequently emerged.
One day, while he was seated upon his high throne,
there suddenly appeared a man holding a ceremonial tablet and bearing a name-plate, with the appearance of a high official.
He said, "I have come by the command of the Lord of Devas to invite the Dharma Master to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
[The Master] replied, "The meaning is this:
this current dharma assembly has not yet concluded."
Once you have finished reciting the scripture, you shall comply with my subsequent instructions.

Although the ritual requirements for the Dharma service cannot be established by you alone, the *dougong*, the incense-burner attendant, the *weina*, and the *fanbai* chanters all likewise require them; therefore, please request that they be settled.
The messenger immediately acted according to the request.
When he saw that the monks were preaching and the religious service was about to conclude, he further saw the former messenger say:
"I have come down by the command of the Lord of Devas to welcome you."
Daoyi then smiled with a serene and joyful countenance, bidding farewell to the assembly.
Suddenly, he passed away upon his Dharma seat;
four monks, including the *dougong*, likewise died at the same time.
Whatever was heard or seen therein was praised as unprecedented.
Regarding the *Viyāsaparipṛcchā-sūtra* in two fascicles, the catalogs of Sengchang and others all state that it was translated by Baoyi at Luoyang;

however, according to the preface to the sūtra itself, it was actually translated by Gautama Dharmapriya at the capital of Ye in the fourth year of the Heping era, and has now been reclassified accordingly.

In the *Jiǔtán lù* (Record of Gautama), it is noted regarding the twelve-fascicle *Shìdì jīnglùn* (Treatise on the Ten Stages Sūtra) that when the treatise was first translated, the Chinese language had not yet been mastered;

thus, the term *bhājanaloka* (the receptacle world) was rendered as "the world of cups. Later, while entering the palace for a vegetarian feast, [the translator] saw several venerable elders requesting vessels from their disciples.
He then presented them with his entire bowl and bag. Thereupon, he realized that "vessel" (*qì*) was a general term and subsequently changed the translation to "receptacle world" (*qìshìjiān*).
Regarding this *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the catalogs of Changfang and others record it as having been translated at both places—by Ratnamati and Bodhiruci.
However, according to Cui Guang’s preface to the treatise, it states that Bodhiruci and Ratnamati were together in the palace hall in Luoyang;

the two men translated it together while Buddhabhadra acted as an interpreter, and the Emperor personally received the text by pen. Since these two records each exist, the matter is likely not yet settled.
Now, these are combined into a single volume within the Record of Bodhiruci: *The Incense Formula of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna*, one fascicle, containing fifty methods in total.
Since these do not belong to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, they are not recorded here; the three sections mentioned above are all now deleted.
*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated in the second year of the Yongping era at the residence of Duke Hu Xiangguo.

This is the second translation; Senglang acted as the scribe. It is identical in text to the "Vajracchedikā" section of the ninth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from the Qin dynasty translated by Kumārajīva.
[This was recorded] in the catalog of Fashang. Also included: *The Sūtra on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva*, one fascicle.
Scroll Two. This text shares the same original source as the *Mahāyāna Vaipulya Essential Wisdom Sūtra* (Dacheng Fangdeng Yaohui Jing) and was translated at the residence of Zhao Xin.

Jueyi acted as the scribe. It is now included within the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* as the forty-first assembly, with its title changed to the "Assembly on the Eight Dharmas Questioned by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
The *Sūtra of the Questions of the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin* in six scrolls was translated in Luoyang in the first year of the Shenggui era.

The translation by Yang is the third edition; it is identical in content but differs in its production from the translations by Dharmarakṣa, Sīmhamati, and Kumārajīva, as seen in the *Fashang lu* and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*.
The five-fascicle *Śālistambasūtra* (Shenmi jietuo jing) was first translated in its entirety in the third year of the Yanchang era at Luoyang;
the scribe for the transcription was the monk Bian. It corresponds to the *Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra* translated during the Tang dynasty.

The *Xiāngxù jiètuō jié jīng* (Sūtra on the Succession of Liberation Chapters) and others are all the same text as seen in Fǎshàng’s record and the *Xu gāosēng zhuàn* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
The ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, translated in the second year of the Yánchāng era, is the third translation;

it is the same text as the four-fascicle *Laṅkā* by Guǒdéxián of the Song dynasty, as well as the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* translated during the Táng dynasty, and so forth—[all attributed to] Sēnglǎng and Dàozhàn.
The scribe noted that the *Mahāsāṃghika-satyaka-nirgrantha-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (also known as the *Bodhisattva-viṣaya-vega-dharmamukha-sūtra*) consists of ten fascicles—
sometimes with the characters "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) and "nothing said" (*anabhilāpya*) added— or seven or eight fascicles;
it was translated at the residence of the Prince of Runan, Governor of Sizhou, in Luoyang during the first year of the Zhengguang era.

The second translation, the *Wuzi baoxie jing* (Sutra of the Jewel Casket Without Letters), one fascicle, is identical in origin to the *Shentong bianhua jing* (Sutra of Supernatural Powers and Transformations) and was first produced with Senglang as the scribe.
It is also identical in origin to the Tang translation of the *Dacheng liwenzi jing* (Mahāyāna Sutra on Transcending Words).

The *Jiaye shanding jing* (Sutra of the Summit of Gayā), one fascicle—also known as the *Jiayeding jing* (Sutra of the Peak of Gayā)—is a second production identical to Kumārajīva’s *Wenshu wen puti jing* (Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into Bodhi).

*Jīng děngtóngběn bàfójīng* (Sūtra Corresponding to the Original *Buddhabhāṣita-sūtra*), one fascicle; second edition, identical to the *Xuǐjìnduǎngchí jīng* translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
*Dàfāngděng xiūdúluówáng jīng* (Sūtra of the King of Mahāvaipulya Sūtras), one fascicle; first edition, identical to the *Juédingzhuǎnyǒu jīng*.
*Móshǒulí xúnxíng jīng* (Mañjuśrī’s Perambulation Sūtra), one fascicle; first edition, identical to the [text] translated by Jñānagupta of the Sui.

*Śuśrīcarita-sūtra*, one fascicle; same text as the *Samyaksaṃbuddhacittotpāda-pen-shou* (Oral Transmission of the Buddha’s Words by Samyaksaṃbuddha), first translated during the Zhou dynasty by Ju-duo, with Seng-lang serving as the scribe.
*Buddhanāma-sūtra*, twelve fascicles (alternatively said to be thirteen fascicles, or divided into twenty fascicles);
translated in the Zhengguang era at the residence of the Hu State Councilor. Recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
The *Saṃgha-dharmasaṃgraha-sūtra* (or *Saṃgha-dharmasaṃgraha-piṭaka-sūtra*), in six, seven, or eight fascicles, was translated at Luoyang in the fourth year of the Yanchang era;
it was transcribed by Senglang, as recorded in the *Fashang lu* and the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The *Dhāraṇī for Protecting All Children*, also titled the *Dhāraṇī Requested for Sons and Daughters for Protecting All Children*, in one fascicle, [translated by] Chama.

*The Sūtra on the Prophecy of Vajra* (Bādi shòujì jīng), one fascicle; translated in Luoyang during the Zhengguang era. *The Sūtra on Neither Increasing nor Decreasing* (Bùzēngbùjiǎn jīng), one fascicle;
translated in Luoyang during the Zhengguang era. According to the *Record of Seven Sheets*, the version in two fascicles is an error.

*Treatise on the Ten Stages Sūtra* (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*), twelve or fifteen fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu as a commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*; translated in the first year of the Yongping era.
In the fourth month, at the Ziting (Purple Pavilion) in the Taiji (Grand Pole) Palace, the Emperor personally received the oral transmission and dictated the translation.
It was subsequently completed by the śramaṇa Sengbian and others. Upon reaching the end of the treatise, it was finished at the beginning of summer in the fourth year.
As seen in the preface by Cui Guang, the *Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra-śāstra* consists of five, six, seven, or ten fascicles; it is a commentary on the *Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra*, namely the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The forty-first assembly, the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* in four fascicles, translated at the residence of Zhao Xin in Luoyang;
this is the first translation, identical in text to that produced by Baoyi.

It provides an exposition on the single-fascicle *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, which is the forty-third assembly of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the "Assembly of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha," and is the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
*The Sūtra and Treatise in Three Volumes*, composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated at the residence of the Marquis of Hu in the second year of the Yongping era, with Senglang acting as scribe.
This is the first translation, identical in text to the *Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* produced by Yi Jing of the Tang dynasty.
*The Treatise on the Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra* in two volumes; also known as the *Gayāśīrṣa*.
The *Sūtra-śāstra* composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu was translated at Yecheng (Yecheng) in the second year of the Tianping era at Yinzhou Temple;

Sengbian and Daozhan acted as scribes. It consists of two fascicles, titled *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Youbotishe* (*Upadeśa on the Lotus Sūtra*), or alternatively one fascicle with a preface composed by Tanlin.
This second edition is identical to the previous version by Baoyi.
Regarding the translations produced during the same period as the *Benmo* (Original Beginning), there is a preface of homage.

This refers to the four-fascicle (or three-fascicle) *Śūraṅgamasamādhisūtra-śāstra* by Vasubandhu, which was translated at the residence of Yuan Tiao Tang in Luoyang during the first year of the Putai era.
Sengbian and Senglang acted as scribes. The record states it was ten fascicles, which is likely an error; this is not seen in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
*Commentary on the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle; titled *Upadeśa on the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life: Verses on the Vow for Rebirth*, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated at Yongning Monastery in Luoyang in the second year of the Yong’an era, with Sengbian acting as scribe.
*Treatise on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle; composed by the Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati. *Treatise on the Hundred Syllables*, one fascicle; composed by Āryadeva.
*The Bodhisattva’s Treatise on Refuting the Four Schools of Heterodoxies and the Lesser Vehicle*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Deva.
*The Bodhisattva Deva’s Treatise on Refuting the Nirvāṇa of Heterodoxies and the Lesser Vehicle*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Deva. *The Ratnagotravibhāga-śāstra*, four fascicles (or five);
the original edition was identical to that produced by Baoyi. All of the above are recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù* and the *Nèidiǎn*.
The above records thirty works in one hundred and one fascicles; the first twenty-nine works are extant, while the latter work, the *Ratnagotravibhāga-śāstra*, is missing.
[Compiled by] the Śramaṇa Bodhiruci.
Weiyan Daoxi was a native of North India.
He was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and had attained profound mastery of dhāraṇī.
His resolve was to propagate the Dharma so that it might spread widely to all who hear and see it;
he thus traveled by night, carrying his teachings, and journeyed far to the left of the Pamir Mountains.
In the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty, he arrived at the Eastern Capital.
Emperor Xuanwu issued an edict expressing his earnest concern and respect for his labor;
subsequently, he appointed him to the Yongning Great Monastery, where provisions were most abundant,
and seven hundred Indian monks were all provided with full support.
By imperial decree, Paramārtha was appointed as the preeminent master for translating the scriptures.
That monastery had originally been established by Empress Dowager Hu in the first year of the Xiping era (516 CE) during the reign of Emperor Xiaoming.
It is located to the east of the imperial road south of the Chāṅhè Gate in front of the palace.
In its center stands a nine-story pagoda constructed of wood,
rising to a height of over ninety zhang.
Above it stood a golden finial ten zhang high;
rising a thousand chi from the ground, it could be seen from a distance of one hundred li from the terrace.
On the day the foundation was first laid, they excavated down to the Yellow Springs and obtained thirty-two golden images.
The Empress Dowager regarded this as an auspicious omen and a sign of the faithful transmission of the Dharma.
Consequently, she adorned it with exquisite craftsmanship and the most magnificent ornaments of the age.
Atop the stupa’s pinnacle, she placed a golden jeweled vase with a capacity of twenty-five hu.
The dew-receiving golden basin has eleven tiers;
iron chains extend from its corners.
Both the basins and the chains are adorned with golden bells, each as large as a stone jar.
On each of the nine tiers, large bells were suspended from every corner;
in total, there were one hundred and thirty such bells.
The four sides of the stupa consisted of nine bays, with six windows and three doors.
All the doors and panels were lacquered vermilion and hung with various golden bells;
there were five thousand four hundred such pieces in total.
Furthermore, golden bells and door-knobs were affixed.
The Buddha-work is exquisite and refined, exhausting the skill of masonry and carpentry;
its embroidered decorations and gilded ornaments startle both the eyes and the mind.
Through the long nights, a lofty breeze causes the bells and chimes to resonate in harmony.
The resonant sounds of its bells could be heard for more than ten li.
To the north was the main hall, modeled after the Taiji Hall;
within it, various statues were adorned with gold, jade, pearls, and embroidery.
His craftsmanship was exquisite and unparalleled in his time.
The monastic quarters extended for more than a thousand rooms,
while towers and pavilions were scattered like stars, rising in错落 (chaotic yet harmonious) succession.
It was adorned with vermilion and purple, and decorated with cinnabar and azure.
Cypresses, deodar pines, *zheng* pines, and junipers grew there, with various plants clustered together.
The surrounding walls were entirely covered with glazed tiles.
To the due south, the three-gated tower opens onto three paths and has three stories;
rising more than two hundred feet from the ground,
it is as magnificent and resplendent as the Gate of Heaven.
Flanking the gates stood four powerful warriors and four lions,
adorned with gold and jade, their magnificent splendor resplendent;
both the eastern and western gates were similarly decorated.
The only differences were that the pavilion had two stories and the north gate provided a passageway, which was merely a path;
furthermore, outside its four gates, green poplars were planted and it was spanned by emerald waters.
Travelers in the capital frequently sought shelter beneath it;
the road was cut off from flying dust,
not by the moisture of drifting clouds.
A pure breeze brings coolness;
it does not depend on the blossoming of the *saṃharṣaṇī* flower.
Thereupon, he commanded Chang Jing, the Secretariat Drafter, to compose the inscription for the temple stele.
Therefore, it is said that among the jeweled palaces of Mount Sumeru and the pure abodes of Tuṣita, none surpass this;
all the scriptures and images offered from foreign lands were kept in this temple.
When the temple was first completed...
Emperor Ming and the Empress Dowager ascended the stupa together and viewed the palace from above as clearly as if it were in the palm of their hands.
From below, they looked down upon the clouds and rain, while above, the sky was clear and bright.
Because they had witnessed the affairs within the palace, the Emperor prohibited people from ascending it.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa from the Western Regions named Bodhidharma,
a native of the country of Persia,
who had traveled across the Western Regions to visit the capital of Luoyang.
He saw golden trays dazzling like the sun, their light illuminating the heights beyond the clouds; precious bells, catching the breeze, emitted sounds as if from beyond the heavens.
His chanting and praises were such that they seemed the work of divine artistry.
He himself claimed to be one hundred and fifty years of age.
I have traveled through various countries, visiting them all without exception;
yet a monastery as exquisite as this one, with its hermitages, is nowhere to be found in Jambudvīpa.
Even throughout the entire realm of the Buddha, there is nothing to compare with it.
Day after day, he chanted "Namu" with palms joined.
