In the second year of the Xiaochang era, a great wind arose that blew off roofs and uprooted trees;
the precious vase atop the stupa was carried by the wind and fell to the ground at a depth of more than one zhang.
He further ordered artisans to replace them with new ones.
In the second month of the third year of the Yongxi era, the temple was struck by lightning from heaven.
The Emperor ascended the Lingyun Terrace to observe the fire.
He dispatched Prince Baoru of Nanyang, along with Changsun Zhi, the Director of the Secretariat, leading one thousand feathered-guards (yulin) to come to their rescue.
At that moment, thunder and rain obscured the heavens in darkness, while sleet and snow fell in torrents.
On the eighth day, at dawn, a fire broke out;
two men, unable to bear being consumed by the flames, threw themselves into the fire and died.
The flames continued to burn for another three months.
After the foundation pillar was erected for one year, a lingering scent of smoke still remained.
In the fifth month of that year, a person arrived from Donglai Commandery and reported that he had seen the stupa in the midst of the sea, its radiance solemn and majestic.
They all witnessed this phenomenon together;
suddenly, clouds and mist arose in confusion, and he vanished from their sight.
In the seventh month, Prince Pingyang was seized by the court attendant Yan Sichun and fled westward to Chang’an.
In the tenth month, the capital was moved from Luoyang to Zhangye.
Prior to this, Ratnamati had been commissioned by imperial decree to begin the initial translation of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*.
At its outset, Emperor Xuanwu personally acted as the scribe for the oral transmission of the text.
Thereafter, he entrusted the entire treatise to the śramaṇas Sengbian and others;
the Buddha-dharma flourished, and eminent talents gathered in abundance,
diligently transmitting it from one to another with tireless devotion.
From the first year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xuanwu of Luoyang, which was the *wuzi* year,
until the second year of the Tianping era of Emperor Xiaojing at the capital of Ye, which was the *yimao* year, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha resided there.
For nearly thirty years, he translated in succession a total of thirty works,
including scriptures such as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and treatises such as the *Daśabhūmika Śāstra*.
The Emperor further commanded the lay devotee Li Kuò to compile a catalogue of these various scriptures.
Kuo’s learning encompassed both the profound and the fundamental; he mastered the sutras and śāstras and possessed refined models for his own practice.
Thus, his record states:
"Within the quarters of the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra..."
The Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras and śāstras amount to ten thousand fascicles;
the newly translated texts and the transcribed original manuscripts fill an entire room.
Nevertheless, his wisdom and understanding are nearly equal to those of Ratnamati.
He possessed spiritual insight and keen intelligence, was thoroughly proficient in local dialects, and was also skilled in incantations; thus, there was no one who could rival him.
Once, while he sat at the mouth of a well with his ritual pitcher inside the empty shaft, his disciples had not yet arrived and there was no one to draw water for him.
Bodhiruci then took up a willow staff and gestured toward the well;
while silently reciting mantras for only a few repetitions,
the spring water surged upward until it reached the rim of the well.
He immediately took some from his bowl and used it to wash himself;
the monks standing nearby witnessed this entirely but could not fathom its spiritual power,
and they all marveled together, saying, "This is a great sage!"
Buddhayaśas said,
"Do not praise this recklessly;
such ritual methods are practiced commonly by foreigners."
In this region, it is not customary to refer to [these] as "sacred";
fearing they might confuse the world, they have been kept secret and are not commonly practiced.
*The Sūtra of the Questions of King Vikrīḍita* in two fascicles; *The Sūtra of the Seal of Entering the Indeterminate* in one fascicle; *The High King of All Dharmas*.
*Ekottarikāgama-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Paramārthadharmavijaya-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Madhyamaka-anupūrva-śāstra*, two fascicles.

The above five works, totaling seven fascicles, were all recorded in the catalogs of the Chángfáng and others as translations by Bodhiruci. However, upon examining the prefaces and colophons of these scriptures, it is stated that they were translated by Gautama Ruci, not Bodhiruci.
They are therefore now moved to the catalog of Gautama. [Recorded in the section on] Treasures (*Bǎo*).

*Upāyakauśalya-sūtra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sūtra of the Four Dharmas of the Crested Bodhisattva), one fascicle; *Tri-samaya-sūtra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sūtra of the Threefold Endowment), one fascicle;

*Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sūtra of Turning the Wheel of Dharma), one fascicle. These three works, totaling three fascicles, were previously attributed by Dao’an and others to Bodhiruci.

However, according to the prefaces and records, they were actually translated by Vimalākṣa; therefore, these three treatises have now been moved to that [Vimalākṣa] catalog among the various sūtras and śāstras.
The Catalogue, one fascicle: this was compiled by Bodhiruci and is not a separate translation from a Sanskrit original;
it is no longer extant today, as it is not recorded within the current catalogue. The *Bodhisattvaviṣayavikrīḍita-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, ten fascicles:
the Baochang lu states it was translated by Bodhiruci; however, as this is merely another name for the *Satyaka-irreṇyaputra-sūtra*, it is not included here.
*The Sūtra on the Ten Dharmas*, one fascicle. Translated at the capital of Ye in the second year of the Yuangxiang era;

this second translation is the same text as that produced by Saṃghavarman of the Liang dynasty. It is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection as the ninth assembly, titled the "Assembly on the Ten Mahāyāna Dharmas.
*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Abhayamati*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra of the Girl Abhayamati*. Translated during the Yuan... [period].
The *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated at the capital of Ye in the second year of the Xiang era;
this fifth translation shares the same text as the *Āśutara-sūtra* and others, and is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* as the thirty-second assembly. Transcribed by Tanlin.
The *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated at Luoyang in the sixth year of the Zhengguang era; this first translation corresponds to the *Sūryaprabhā-paripṛcchā-vaipulya-siṃha-sūtra*.
*Hǒu jīng tóngběn yínsè nǚ jīng* (The Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman, Same Text as the *Hǒu jīng*), one fascicle. Translated at Yedu in the second year of the Yuánxiàng era.
Second translation; same text as the *Xījìn fǎjù shìshén sānzhuǎn jīng*. *Zhènggōngjìng jīng* (Sūtra on Right Reverence), one fascicle.

Also known as the *Wéidé tuóluóní zhōngshuō jīng* (Sūtra Spoken within the *Vīrya-dhāraṇī*) or the *Zhèngfǎ gōngjìng jīng* (Sūtra on Reverence for the True Dharma). Translated in the second year of the Yuánxiàng era.

The first translation produced at the capital of Ye was the *Zhuanyou jing* (Sūtra on Turning the Wheel), one fascicle, which shares the same source as the *Shan jing* (Sūtra of Good Respect) translated by Śīladharma Jñānagupta during the Sui dynasty;
it was translated at the capital of Ye in the second year of the Yuangxiang era.
The second translation produced was the *Ānandamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, which shares the same source as the *Fangdeng xuduoluo jing* (Vaipulya Sūtra) translated by Bodhiruci.
Scroll Eight. Translated together with the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (also known as the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*) by Zhi Qian;
same original text as the one-scroll *Vajra-agrya-rasa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, translated at Luoyang in the sixth year of the Zhengguang era. First translation;
same original text as the *Vajra-maṇḍala-sūtra* by Xuanzhuang (Kūtadanta) of the Sui dynasty. Two scrolls of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, translated at Luoyang in the first year of the Putai era.

The *Asaṃkhyeya-kṛta-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* in one fascicle, translated by Yangchou together with Chen Zhendi and Tang Xuanzang from the same source as the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, was produced at Ye-du in the second year of the Yuanyang era; this second translation shares the same source as that produced by Buddhabhadra and others.
These ten works above are all recorded in the Sui dynasty’s *Fei Changfang lu* and the Tang dynasty’s *Neidian lu*.
The above consists of ten sections totaling eleven fascicles; the first nine sections comprising ten fascicles are extant, while the final section of one fascicle is missing.
Translated by the śramaṇa Buddhayaśas.
Known in Wei as Jueding (Jñānasiddhi),
he was a native of Northern India.
Possessing divine insight and keen intelligence, he was extensively learned in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings.
He was particularly skilled in local dialects and especially adept at the arts.
He arrived during the sixth year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming (the year of Yisi) and remained until the second year of the Yuanxiang era of Emperor Xiaojing (the year of Jiwu).
At Baima Monastery in Luoyang and Jinhua Monastery in the capital city of Ye,
he translated ten works, including the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra*, totaling ten fascicles.
The śramaṇa Tánlín and others acted as scribes for the oral transmission.
*The Sutra of the Girl Vimaladattā*, one fascicle; alternatively, without the character "wu" (no), also titled *The Dharma-Gate of Eloquence in Discourse*.
Translated at the capital of Ye in the third year of the Xinghe era. This third translation is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa: The Assembly of Vimaladattā* and the *Dharmapāla:
The Sutra of Vimaladattā*; it is recorded in the *Changfang Lu*. [3] *The Sutra of the Questions of the Devaputra Susīma*.
In the third year of the Xinghe era, it was translated at Jinhua Temple in Ye City with Tanlin serving as the scribe.

This fifth translation consists of either four or five fascicles; it is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the *Susthitamati-paripṛcchā*, and the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra*, according to the Changfang Lu.
The two-fascicle *Vaiśravaṇa-paripṛcchā-sūtra* was first translated alongside the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* and the *Vistara-ṛṣi*.

On the seventh day of the seventh month in the fourth year of the Xinghe era, the translation was completed at the residence of the Duke Gao, Minister of the Secretariat and General of the Same Rank, over a period of thirty days.
The śramaṇa Tánlín acted as the scribe. This preface to the *Qǐfēnxùnwángwèn jīng* (Sūtra on the Questions of King Vighuṣṭa) in two fascicles is the second translation;
it is the same text as Kāśyapa Mātanga’s *Zìzàiwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Sovereign King). [The translation was finalized] on the seventh day of the seventh month in the fourth year of the Xinghe era.
On the thirtieth day of the month, at the residence of the Duke Gao, Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, I submitted the following:
the *Jianjing qianxu ji* (Preface and Record of the Newly Translated Scriptures) by the śramaṇa Tanlin, who acted as the scribe;

the *Rujing buru dingyin jing* (Sūtra on Entering and Not Entering the Seal of Concentration), one fascicle, which was first produced on the tenth day of the ninth month of the fourth year of the Xinghe era, sharing the same original text as the *Rujing budingyin jing* (Sūtra on Entering and Not Entering the Seal of Concentration) translated by Yi Jing of the Tang.
On the ninth day, at the residence of the Minister of State, the Grand Master (Yitong) Duke Gao, the śramaṇa Tánlín acted as scribe for the translation.

Recorded in the preface to the *Jièyīqièfǎ Gāowáng Jīng* (Sūtra of the High King of All Dharmas), one fascicle; also known as the *Jièyīqièfǎ Yìwáng Jīng* (Sūtra of the King of the Meaning of All Dharmas).

This third edition is identical in substance to the *Zhūfǎ Yǒngwáng Jīng* (Sūtra of the Heroic King of All Dharmas) and others. Translated on the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Xinghe era.
Translated by the Bhikṣu Daoyi at Dingchang Temple in the residence of Minister of Works Dou; received by the pen of the Śramaṇa Tanyin. Recorded in the Preface to the Sūtra:
The *Dharmasamuccaya-sūtra*, one fascicle. Its initial translation was the same text as the *Mahātejo’rcis-ṛṣi-sūtra*.
Translated on the first day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Xinghe era at the residence of the Duke Gao, the Grand Marshal and Minister of the Secretariat. Śramaṇa [Daoyi].
The *Suvarṇavarṇa-rāja-sūtra* (Golden-Winged King Sūtra), one fascicle; transcribed by the śramaṇa Tánlín under imperial command at Jīnhuá Temple in the fourth year of the Xìnghé era.
This second edition is identical to that produced by Dharmaruci; see the Chángfáng Lù.
The *Buddhanāma-aṣṭaka-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Names of Eight Buddhas), one fascicle; also called the *Āṣṭabuddhanāma-sūtra*; [produced in] the Xìnghé era.

In the fourth year [of the Taihe era], at Jinhua Temple, the śramaṇa Tánlín acted as scribe for the transcription of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra-anuvyākhyāna* (Shùnzhōng lùn) in two fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
it was translated on the tenth day of the eighth month of the first year of the Wǔdìng era at the residence of the Duke Gāo, Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Marshal.
This is recorded in the preface to the sutra found in the *Chángfáng lù*. First, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wéishí lùn).
*Roll One: Refuting Form and Mind*, also known as *The Treatise on Consciousness-Only Without Objects*. Translated at Jinhua Temple by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;

the first translation. It is identical in text to Paramārtha’s *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* of the Chen Dynasty and the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* translated during the Tang Dynasty, according to the *Chángfáng Lù*. *Ekaslokika-śāstra*, one roll, composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
*Zao zai Jinhuasi chujian changfang lu* (Record of Works Compiled by Changfang at Jinhua Temple). The record states: *Iqiyishuluo jian lun* (*Īśvarakṛṣṇa-śāstra*), one fascicle;

*Zhengfa nianchu jing* (*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*), seventy fascicles, translated in the first year of the Xinghe era at the residence of Gao Cheng, the Grand Chancellor in Ye City, with Tanlin and Sengfang serving as scribes—seen in the *Changfang lu*;
*Wugou youpoyi wen jing* (*Vimalā-upāsikā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*), one fascicle.
In the fourth year of the Xinghe era, the *Jiětuō jièběn* (Sūtra on the Code of Liberation) in one fascicle was produced from the Kāśyapīya school;
it appeared during the Wuding era, in the first year, at the capital of Ye, at the request of Gao Cheng, the Palace Attendant and Chief Minister of the Secretariat.

It is recorded in the catalogue of Daochang that Sengfang transcribed the text and composed the preface, which is also found in Daochang’s record. Furthermore, the *Púsà sìfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Four Dharmas of a Bodhisattva) in one fascicle [was translated by] Jin.
At Huasi Temple, Tanlin and Li Xi-yi and others transcribed [the text] for Gao Zhongmi; this is recorded in the Chángfáng-lù.
*Bǎoyì-māo'ér-jīng* (The Scripture of the Cat of Bao-yi), one fascicle, was produced at Jinhua Temple for Gao Zhongmi; this is recorded in the Chángfáng-lù.

*Dúzi-dàorén-wèn-lùn* (The Treatise on the Questions of the Vatsiputriya Ascetic), one fascicle, was produced at Jinhua Temple for Gao Zhongmi, with Li Xi-yi serving as scribe. The above comprises ten items.
Eight divisions, ninety-two fascicles: *Śīla-vinaya-vimukti* (upper), fifteen divisions, eighty-nine fascicles;
*Bodhisattva-caturdharma-sūtra* (lower), three divisions, three fascicles; missing texts.
The Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci— translated into Wei as Zhīxī (Wisdom-Longing)—
was of the lineage of Jingzhì from the city of Vārāṇasī in Central India.
Having studied the Buddha-dharma in his youth, he was profoundly proficient in the essential meanings of the scriptures.
His spiritual insight was extraordinary, and he possessed a keen understanding of local dialects.
In the first year of the Xiping era of Emperor Xiaoming, he traveled to and resided in Luoyang.
Later, when the capital was moved to Ye, he also relocated with the times.
From the first year of the Yuangxiang era of Emperor Xiaojing (Wu-ma) to the first year of the Wuding era (Gui-hai),
he resided within the Jinhua and Changding temples in the city of Ye, as well as in the residence of the Duke Gao, the Minister of State and Grand Marshal.
He translated eighteen sections of scriptures, including the *Vimalā-dārikā-sūtra*.
The śramaṇas Sengfang and Tanyin, along with the layman Li Xi-yi and others, acted as scribes.
One fascicle of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* was also translated.

The *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* (Treatise on the Accomplishment of Karma) in one fascicle; regarding these two treatises above, the catalogs of the Chángfáng and others all state they were translated by Gautama Prajñāruci. Now, examining the preface to the original translation of the sutra, it states that it was translated by Vimalamitra. I shall now rely on the record in the sutra as being correct. Furthermore, the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:
During the Wei dynasty, there were the śramaṇas Bodhiruci and Prajñāruci,
who produced translations of the scriptures at different times; yet,
in the various catalogs and transcriptions, these works were for the most part treated with negligence and oversimplification.
In each case, the character "shang" (上) has been omitted, leaving only "Liu-zhi.
It is not known which Liu-zhi this refers to;
even now, as the various catalogs of translations overlap, it is difficult to establish a definitive identification.
I have now searched for and recorded the authentic records as noted above; those yet to be found shall await future scholars.

The *Mahākāśyapa-sūtra* in two fascicles—also called the *Mahākāśyapa-sūtra*, or sometimes omitting the character "Da" (Great)—was translated in the third year of the Xinghe era at the residence of Gongsun Teng, the General of the Chariots and Cavalry, Vice President of the Secretariat, and Duke of Neishizhong. This is seen in the preface of the sutra and is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* as the twenty-third assembly. The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* in four fascicles was translated in the first year of the Yuanxiang era at the residence of Gongsun Teng, the Duke of Neishizhong; it is recorded in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*. The *King Bimbisāra Asks the Buddha about Offerings Sūtra* in one fascicle appeared in the third year of the Xinghe era; it is an alternative translation of the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Of these three works totaling seven fascicles, the first two consist of six fascicles which are extant, while the latter one consists of one fascicle which is missing.
Prince Candraprabha— translated into Wei as Gāokōng (High Void)—
was a prince from the kingdom of Ujjayinī in Central India.
From the first year of the Yuangxiang era of Emperor Xiaojing (Wu-wu) until the third year of the Xinghe era (Xin-you),
he translated three sections of the scriptures of Kāśyapa and others at the residence of the Duke of Sigu, Gongsun Teng, in the capital city of Ye.
The śramaṇa Sengfang transcribed [the text].
Śūna traveled from the Wei dynasty to the Liang,
and during the Chen dynasty, he further translated various sūtras.
As described elsewhere:
*The Commentary on the Sūtra of the Four Dharmas of the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin*, one fascicle, titled *Ratnaśikhī-sūtra-caturdharma-upadeśa*, composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya (Sthiramati).
On the first day of the ninth month of the third year of the Xinghe era, it was [presented] at Jinhua Temple for the Emperor.
Translated by the Court Historian Gao Zhongmi; recorded by the Śramaṇa Tanlin.
Preface to the *Sūtra on the Threefold Endowment*, Volume One, titled *Upadeśa on the Sūtra of the Threefold Endowment*, composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya (Asaṅga’s brother).
On the thirteenth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Xinghe era, at Jinhua Temple, for the sake of the General of the Flying Cavalry Gao... [text fragment].
Translated by Zhongmi; orally received by the śramaṇa Tanlin. Preface to the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Titled: *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra-upadeśa*. Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya (Asaṅga’s brother).
On the eleventh day of the eighth month in the third year of the Xinghe era, at Jinhua Temple, for Gaofu Yitongsī Gao Zhong [Xiao], of Bohai.

*The Treatise on the Accomplishment of Karma* (Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa), one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Śramaṇa Mi (Mitra) with the Śramaṇa Tanlin serving as scribe.
This preface to the scripture records that it was first produced as the same text as the *Mahāyāna-karmasiddhi-śāstra* translated during the Tang dynasty.
On the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month in the third year of the Xinghe era, it was translated for Gao Zhongmi at Jinhua Temple, with the Śramaṇa Tanlin acting as scribe.
*The Preface and Record of the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Vigrahavyāvartanī-śāstra*, one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.

Translated on the twentieth day of the third month in the third year of the Xinghe era at Jinhua Temple by Gao Zhongmi of Bohai, General of the Household, Grand Commandant, Acting Minister of State, and Censor-in-Chief;
received by the śramaṇa Tanlin. [Preface to the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*]... [End of] Preface to the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
Preface: The five sections comprising five fascicles of the above-mentioned works are extant.
The śramaṇa Vimalākṣa was a native of Ujjayinī in North India.
He was of the Kṣatriya royal lineage, a descendant of the Śākyas.
Long ago, when King Virūḍhaka destroyed the city of Kapilavastu and slaughtered the remaining members of the Śākya clan,
there were four Śākya youths at that time.

Enraged by their harassment, he did not consider breaking his precepts; he went outside to repel the army, but being driven into exile, he eventually returned to his own country. However, the city would not accept him.
He declared:
"For the sake of the seed of the Dharma, I swear I shall not serve as a teacher."
"One who retreats from that army is not of my clan.
Having been cast out and forced to flee to distant lands,
he was originally a descendant of the sages whom we all vied to honor and establish as our leader."
The four Śibi and Cīra kings each ruled over their own kingdoms;
the present-day kings of Udyāna, Bamiyan, and other regions are all their descendants,
whose lineage has been passed down to this day without interruption.
Dharma Master Zhixian was of this royal lineage;
he was profoundly versed in the Tripiṭaka and especially skilled in the Abhidharma.
He traveled through the territory of Wei together with Gautama Liuqi.
Taking Guṇabhadra as his honored teacher, he served him with devotion;
then, in the third year of the Xinghe era (the *xin-you* year) of Emperor Xiaojing’s reign,
at Jinhua Temple within the city of Ye.
Translated together by Gautama Liu-zhi, with the śramaṇa Tan-lin acting as scribe;

for these five works, including the *Ratnacūḍa-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, the General of the Household, Grand Marshal, Minister of the Interior, and Censor-in-Chief, Gao Zhong-mi of Bohai, served as the patron (*dānapati*) and requested their recitation and offerings.
I have also seen the preface and record of the sutra.
Therein it is said that Dharma Master Zhixian traveled abroad to propagate the teachings,
crossing over desert wastes and perilous terrain with the sole intent of benefiting sentient beings.
I have already opened the volumes of the various schools from the Sanskrit originals;
however, as my own insight is shallow and narrow, my examination has not been exhaustive.
Of the five scriptures I have observed, the items described are as follows.
If those of later generations should happen to encounter this, I hope they will continue to supplement it.
Would it not be excellent if the Dharma-gate were thus rendered free from error?
From the Wei to the Tang dynasties, there have been numerous transmissions and records.
Dharma Master Zhixian has not yet been included in the records;
his fame for propagating the Dharma is unestablished,
and the traces of his noble conduct have not been manifested.
How tragic! How sorrowful! How deeply lamentable it is!

The *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*—composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; a brief commentary on the Great Sūtra, first appearing in the *Neidian lu*. This single work in one fascicle currently exists.
The śramaṇa Dharmabodhi— here translated as "Dharma-Awakening"—
is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog) as having translated the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*.
Although it does not mention the imperial dynasties, it is compiled at the end of the Wei period.

Now, this [text] likewise follows that precedent by being appended here. Furthermore, there is a *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* in three fascicles, also titled as translated by Dharmaprabhāsa; however, upon examining the text, it appears to be an exposition of the aforementioned treatise, leading some to suspect it may have been fabricated by that person.

The Gao Qi dynasty was ruled by the Gao clan with its capital at Ye; it is also referred to as the Northern Qi. It began from the first year of the Tianbao era of Emperor Wenxuan, the *gengwu* year, and ended with Gao Heng’s reign, which lacked a posthumous title, until the first year of the Chengguang era, the *dingyou* year.
In total, under six successive rulers, for a period of twenty-eight years,
two individuals— one a monk and one a layperson—
produced eight works, comprising fifty-two fascicles, consisting of both sutras and śāstras.
The Śramaṇa Narendrayaśas of the Gao Qi translated seven works totaling fifty-one fascicles; the layman Wan Tianyi translated one work of one fascicle.

The *Bodhisattvadarśanaratnasamādhi-sūtra* consists of sixteen fascicles (or fourteen fascicles) and was produced at T'ien-p'ing Temple in the fourth year of the T'ien-t'ung era; it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa*, as its sixteenth section.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-candragarbha-sūtra* in ten fascicles is titled the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra, Candragarbha-parivarta*;
it is also found in twelve or fifteen fascicles, or simply as the *Candragarbha-sūtra*. In the second year of the Tiāntóng era, it was produced at Tiānpíng Monastery.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sumerugarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles has the internal title: "The Mahāyāna Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra, Sumerugarbha-parivarta, Part One."
Fifteen [scrolls], or simply titled the *Sumeru-kośa Sūtra*. In the ninth year of Tenpō, it was produced at Tennyō-ji Temple.
The *Daizhou lu* states that the *Nirvāṇa-vibhāga-candraprabha-samādhi Sūtra*, in eleven or ten scrolls, was produced at Tennyō-ji Temple in the eighth year of Tenpō.
*Śīdīpa-dāna-guṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Dīpa-prajvālana-sūtra*. Translated at Tientianping Temple in the ninth year of the Tianbao era.
*Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, six fascicles; composed by the Venerable Upaśānta.

[The text] sometimes consists of seven fascicles, sometimes lacks the word "sūtra," sometimes lacks the name "Dharmottara," sometimes includes the term "alternate translation," or states "Dharmottara Abhi-... [The text is fragmentary].
The *Abhidharma-śāstra* was translated at T'ien-p'ing Temple in the second year of the Ch'ing-ch'ing era;
it is recorded in the catalog of Fa-ch'ang. The seven sections comprising fifty-one fascicles are all extant.
[Translated by] the Śramaṇa Narendrayaśas.
"Qi" (齊) is a respectful term of address.
He was a native of Uḍḍiyāna in North India;

the correct phonetic transcription should be *Uḍḍayana* (the character for *ya* being pronounced as *chí*, with the second tone). Master Xuanzang says that "Uḍḍayana" translates into Chinese as "Garden" (*yuàn*), referring to what was formerly the pleasure gardens of a Cakravartin king.
The king shared the same clan as the Buddha;

he was also surnamed Śākya and belonged to the Kṣatriya caste—known in Chinese as *chíyún*, meaning "lord of the land"—a title derived from the fact that in the beginning of the kalpa, he was first appointed as the distributor of land, and thus received this name. He is the one currently known as the King. At the age of seventeen, he resolved to leave the household life and become a renunciant.
He soon encountered a renowned master and heard the complete teachings of the True Dharma.
At the age of twenty-one, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Hearing from various senior elders about the wondrous traces of the Buddha’s life, he was deeply moved.
Some said that in a certain country there were alms bowls, and in another country there were robes, cranial bones, and teeth; their miraculous manifestations were manifold.
Consequently, they conceived the aspiration to behold and venerate them.
Since one must understand the characteristics of the Vinaya at the very outset of receiving the precepts, [he studied it].
Having completed five years of summer retreats, he set out on his travels to distant lands.
Thus, there are the traces of the Celestial Ladder and the Stone Terrace,
as well as the regions of the Dragon Temple and the Jewel Stupa.
He traveled extensively throughout various kingdoms, personally paying homage to them all without exception.
He once resided at Zhuyuan Monastery for ten years;
traversing many monasteries, he frequently encountered men of eminent virtue.
There was an elder who, possessing profound insight into the capacities of others,
said to Śreṇika:
"If you can practice in tranquility, you shall surely attain the fruits of sainthood."
I fear that as you wander about, you will ultimately achieve nothing.
Although you heard [the teachings] on that day, your mind failed to grasp them;
if you only reflect on this later, what regret can avail?
Yaśas turned his back on the Snow Mountains to the north and traveled as far as Siṃhala to the south;
having surveyed the sacred sites, he returned to his former abode,
where he beheld the King of Uḍḍiyāna, a true Mahāsattva.
Among what I have personally witnessed and experienced, few can be compared to this.
Allow me to briefly describe it:
he governs the people through principle, and the people love him as if he were their own kin.
During the fifth watch of the night, he first pays homage to the Triple Gem,
making offerings with incense, flowers, and music with utmost sincerity;
only after the sun rises does he ascend the throne to attend to the myriad affairs of state.
Next, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), the image was bathed with scented water.
Within the palace, a vegetarian feast for one hundred monks was regularly prepared,
which the King and his consort personally served by hand.
After the midday meal, he practiced various martial arts to aid digestion.
As the sun was about to set, he transcribed ten lines of scripture and engaged in discussions on the meaning of the Dharma with virtuous monks.
Furthermore, he deliberated on matters of governance with his ministers;
at night, he would enter the Buddha hall to offer lamps and candles,
performing prostrations and reciting scriptures according to his established routine.
Having completed his regular duties, he would then return to quietude;
for over thirty years, he never ceased this practice.
The King had one hundred sons, all of whom harbored sincerity and filial piety in their hearts.
The remaining descendants of the Śākya clan have migrated to this country;
however, as their monasteries were situated along hills and ridges, they were consumed by wildfires.
Consequently, each person sent word to others, seeking refuge and lodging throughout the distant regions.
Six men traveled together as companions to convert those in the north of the Snowy Mountains.
Upon reaching a steep summit, they saw two paths:
a human path that was desolate and perilous, and a ghost path that was advantageous and passable.
Travelers whose minds are deluded often seek the path of ghosts;
as they gradually enter its realm, they encounter slaughter and harm.
Long ago, there was a holy king.
At the head of the road, he fashioned a stone image of King Vaiśravaṇa pointing out the path for humans.
One of his fellow monks mistakenly entered the path of ghosts;
Yaśas, having realized this, recited the Avalokiteśvara Dharani from memory.
When he reached the hundred paces, he was overtaken and had already been harmed by a ghost;
relying on the power of his incantations, he managed to escape this calamity and continued forward.
Again he encountered mountain bandits, but by single-mindedly reciting his previous incantation, he was protected by its spiritual efficacy.
When bandits came to attack him, he could not even see them face-to-face.
Following the road toward the east, he reached the kingdom of Rouran;
encountering the turmoil of the Turks, the western route was blocked, and his hope of returning home was severed.
He then followed the river's course northward until he reached the vicinity of the Ni-hai (Jaxartes) Sea;
this was more than seven thousand li south of the Turks.
Since he could no longer find safety there, he fled far away to the borders of the Qi state.
In the seventh year of the Tenpō era, he arrived at the capital of Ye.
Emperor Wenxuan Yang treated him with exceptional courtesy, distinguishing him far beyond the common rank.
At that time, Guṇabhadra was forty years of age.
Gukǐng was esteemed for his heroic elegance, yet he was criticized by public opinion.
Consequently, Wenxuan treated him with great honor and appointed him as a Tripiṭaka Master at Tiānpíng Monastery to translate scriptures.
Within the palace were more than one thousand fascicles of Sanskrit manuscripts;
by imperial decree, these were sent to the temple and placed in the upper chambers,
where a ritual arena was established and offerings of the most exquisite and rare treasures were made.
A separate kitchen and storehouse were established to manifest his veneration.
The temple was constructed from the eighth year of the Tianbao era of Emperor Wenxuan (dingchou) until the fourth year of the Tiantong era of Emperor Wai (wushi), who received no posthumous title.
At T'ien-p'ing Temple in the city of Ye, he translated seven scriptures, including the *Bodhisattvadarśanavastu-sūtra*,
under the supervision of more than twenty individuals, headed by the Śramaṇa Fa-shang, the Great Steward (Datu) of the Office for Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuan), as per imperial decree.

Translated by the Chief Monk of the Office of the Imperial Monastery, Gautama Prajñāruci’s eldest son, the Śramaṇa Dharmajñāna (whose name means "Dharma-Wisdom" in the language of Qi), together with the lay devotee Wàn Tiānyì, who acted as the oral interpreter.
During the period of fasting, Śīla caused the True Dharma to flourish greatly and widely inspired the minds of the multitude.
Emperor Wenxuan, who held the Dharma in high esteem, personally prostrated before the Sanskrit manuscripts.
Turning to his ministers, he said:
"Since this is the great foundation of the Triple Gem, I pay it particular reverence;
such is the sincerity with which I offer my faith.
Whenever Yaśas had leisure from his work of proclaiming and translating the scriptures, he would recite divine mantras.
He provided secret aid in the darkness and manifest assistance in the light, performing many meritorious deeds.
Before long, he was appointed as the Metropolitan Superintendent of the Office of the Orthodox Mysteries (Zhaoxuan Du), and soon thereafter promoted to Grand Master (Tong).
The stipends and provisions he received were not used solely for his own support.
He delighted in giving rise to loving-kindness and compassion, joyfully undertaking meritorious deeds.
He provided offerings for the Sangha and bestowed alms upon the poor and destitute;
he brought relief to all prisoners and those confined in cages.
In the bustling marketplace, he constructed many public wells for the benefit of others,
personally filtering the water to provide it to sentient beings.
Furthermore, he established three monasteries on the western mountains of Ji County.
The scenery of Mount Jike is most beautiful, with its springs and adjacent valleys.
Furthermore, it maintains separate quarters for men and women afflicted by chronic illnesses,
providing them with the four requisites and ensuring they receive all necessary provisions.

Furthermore, he went to the guest quarters of the Turks and exhorted them to observe the six fast days, to refrain from eating sheep, to practice the release of living beings, and to adopt a vegetarian diet.
On another occasion, he fell ill and was unable to rise for a hundred days;
the Emperor and Empress personally came to inquire after his health.
Yaśas sighed and said,
"I was originally but a stranger whose virtue was not yet eminent;
that you have deigned to descend from your carriage to honor me is solely because of the gravity of the Dharma."
Internally reflecting on his own mind, he was overcome by a mixture of shame and trepidation.
Later, during the Sui dynasty, Yaśas translated various scriptures once again;
these are fully recorded in the Sui Catalogue, as detailed therein.

The *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-bodhisattva-paripṛcchita-sarvadharmāpramāṇamukha-praveśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle; the third edition, identical in text to the *Anantakoṭi-dharmamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and others, also simply titled the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-bodhisattva-paripṛcchita-sūtra* or the *Apramāṇamukha-praveśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. This one work in one fascicle is extant.
The layman Wan Tianyi was originally surnamed Tuoba and was a native of Yunzhong in Beida.
During the Wei dynasty, they were divided into ten clans and thus became the Wan-mo (Wan-qi) clan.
Because their ancestors had resided in Luoyang for generations, they were also known as people of Henan.
Later, they were simply called the Wan clan.
In his youth, he had briefly left the household life to study under a Brahmin;
he was intelligent and possessed great willpower,
being proficient in Sanskrit script and language while also being skilled in incantations.
Consequently, he was summoned and permitted to join the ranks of those engaged in translation.
During the Zhanyang River-Clearance era of Emperor Wucheng’s reign,
he personally translated at the capital of Ye one fascicle of the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
Seen in the *Chángfáng lù*.
*Kāiyuán shìjiào lù*, fascicle six;
*Kāiyuán shìjiào lù*, fascicle seven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Xichongfu Monastery in the Gengwu year (670 CE).
Part Seven: General Compendium of the Records of All Scriptures, Volume One, Part Seven.

During the Zhou Dynasty, the Yuwen clan, with its capital at Chang’an, followed the first year of Emperor Min, the Dingchou year (517 CE), which, following ancient precedent, lacked a specific title and was simply called the "first year," continuing until the first year of Emperor Jing’s Dading era, the Xinchou year (569 CE).
In total, over the course of twenty-five years during the reigns of the Five Emperors,
four śramaṇas produced fourteen works comprising twenty-nine fascicles; of these, six works totaling eleven fascicles are extant, while eight works totaling eighteen fascicles are missing.

One work in one fascicle by the Zhou-period śramaṇa Raṅgnavardhana; six works in fifteen fascicles by the śramaṇa Jñāyasa; three works in eight fascicles by the śramaṇa Yaśakūṭa; four works in five fascicles by the śramaṇa Jñānakūṭa; and one fascicle combining the *Pañcavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Sciences), consisting of: 1. Phonetics (*Śabda-vidyā*), 2. Medical Formulas (*Cikitsā-vidyā*), 3. Arts and Crafts (*Śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), 4. Incantations (*Vidyā-mantra-vidyā*), and 5. Seals and Talismans (*Mudrā-mudrā-vidyā*). These are recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The aforementioned one work in one fascicle is currently missing.
The śramaṇa Rāṇabhadra— translated in the language of Zhou as Zhixian (Wise and Virtuous)—
was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra.
Although he was well-versed in the Tripitaka, he specialized particularly in the Vinaya section.
In the second year of the Mingdi era (the Wuyin year),
at Bogasi Temple in the Old City of Chang’an, he translated the *Pañcavidyāśāstra* (Treatise on the Five Sciences) in one fascicle together with Śayanāśas.
Translated by Yaśagupta, Jñānagupta, and others, with the śramaṇa Zhixian acting as scribe.

Furthermore, the catalogues of Sengchang and others state that in the fourth year of the Tiānhé era (the *jǐchǒu* year) during the reign of Emperor Wŭ of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the śramaṇa Dharmaruci from the country of Mūla—translated as Fǎxī in the language of Zhou—translated the *Báluómén Tiānwén* (Brahmanical Astronomy) in twenty fascicles under the supervision of the Grand Chancellor, Duke of Jìndàng, Wén Hù. These are not included here because they do not belong to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
The *Mahāyāna-saṃbhoga-samatā-sūtra* (Dacheng tongxing jing), two fascicles; also titled the *Sarvabuddhacaryā-praveśajñāna-vairocana-garbha-nirdeśa-sūtra*, or the *Buddha-daśabhūmi-sūtra*.
Translated in the fifth year of the Tianghe era [629 CE]. The initial protocol was the same as that for the Marquis of Chengyang, Xiao Ji, who served as the scribe.
Its original text upon first appearance was identical to the *Mahāyāna-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* translated by Wuxing during the Tang dynasty.
*Yun qing yu jing* (Clouds Entreat Rain Sūtra), one fascicle. The internal title reads "The Sixty-fourth Chapter: The Great Cloud Entreaty for Rain" (*Dà yún qǐng yǔ pǐn*).
Fang [Guangchang] states that calling it "Chapter One" is incorrect. It was translated in the fifth year of the Tiānhé era; the śramaṇa Yuánmíng acted as scribe.

Its initial publication shares the same source text as the *Dà yún lún qǐng yǔ jīng* (Great Cloud Wheel Entreaty for Rain Sūtra) and the *Dà fāngděng dà yún qǐng yǔ jīng* (Mahāvaipulya Great Cloud Entreaty for Rain Sūtra), both belonging to the *Ratnakūṭa*.
*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Devaputra Samādhi-mati* (定意天子所問經), three fascicles; translated in the sixth year of the Tianhe era, with the śramaṇa Daoluo (道璉) acting as scribe.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Devaputra Samādhi-mati*, five fascicles; translated in the sixth year of the Tianhe era, with the śramaṇa Yuanming (圓明) acting as scribe. [These were] excerpted from the *Mahāsannipāta*.

It is currently suspected that this is the same text as the *Sūtra on the Well-Abiding Mind* (善住意經). *The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Wisdom of the Tathāgata* (入如來智不思議經), three fascicles; recorded in the *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures* (*Fanying tu*).
The second [version] is the same text as the *Dù zhū fó jìngjiè zhìguāng yán jīng* (Sutra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom of the Realm of All Buddhas), translated in the first year of Jiande;
the *Fóding zhòu jīng bìng gōngnéng* (Buddhōṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī Sutra with its Efficacy), one fascicle, translated in the fourth year of Baoding, with the scholar Bǎo Yǒng serving as scribe.
These five works are recorded in the Chángfáng Lù. Thus, there are six works totaling fifteen fascicles, including the two aforementioned sections of the *Qǐngyǔ jīng* (Sutra on Invoking Rain).
Three fascicles of the extant *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, comprising four sections totaling twelve fascicles, are missing.
Translated by the śramaṇa Jñānayaśas,
whose name means "Renowned in the Treasury" in the language of Zhou.
He was also known by the name Śaṅghabhūti.
A native of Magadha in Central India,
he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of seated meditation, reaching the ultimate mastery of the discipline of concentration.
Together with his two disciples, Yaśagupta and Jñānagupta,
[he arrived] from the fourth year of the Baoding era of Emperor Wu (Jia-shen) until the first year of the Jiande era (Ren-chen).
For the Grand Chancellor, Duke Tang of Jin, Yuwen Hu,
at the Temple of the Four Heavenly Kings in the Old City of Chang’an,
he translated six works, including the Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-sūtra.
Guo Ping of Gui was appointed as the General Supervisor (Dianjian) for the Pacification of Gao, with the rank of Duke (Gonghou) and the title of Fu Shou.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (Expanded Version on the Great Measure of Life and the Dharani of Great Eloquence), five fascicles, translated at Guisheng Monastery with Zhixian serving as scribe. These five fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* are not the current translation; rather, they are an extension of the two chapters on the "Measure of Life" and "Great Eloquence" from the four-fascicle version by Dharmakṣema, which are now contained within the *Shanfan Yuzhu Jinguangming Jing*. The *Ekadaśamukha Avalokiteśvara Deva-mantra Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated at Sītānātha Monastery with Shangyi, Duke of Tongyang, Xiao Ji, serving as scribe. Its initial publication was identical in text to the Tang translation of the *Ekadaśamukha Deva-mantra-hṛdaya Sūtra*. The *Sudatta-nidāna-śāstra*, two fascicles, translated at Sītānātha Monastery with the śramaṇa Yuanming serving as scribe. Both [the preceding and this work] are recorded in the *Changfang Lu*. Of the three sections totaling eight fascicles mentioned above, the first two sections comprising six fascicles are extant, while the final section of two fascicles is missing.
The śramaṇa Yaśogupta,
whose name in the language of Zhou means "Renowned Treasury," was a native of the country of Udyāna.
Together with his junior fellow student Śīlāditya (Jnanagupta),
during the reign of Emperor Wu, he served as Grand Chancellor under Yuwen Hu at the Four Heavenly Kings Temple and the Return to Sagelyness Temple.

In the *Jingmai jingtu* (Catalogue of Scriptures by Jingmai), there is also a one-fascicle *Dayun qingyu jing* (Sūtra on Requesting Rain from the Great Cloud), which is also said to have been translated by Baoyi. Now, this scripture is identical to the one previously co-translated with Jñānayaśas; it is incorrect for these two versions to exist separately in both places, as their existence there is an error.

*The Lotus Sutra, Chapter on the Universal Gate: Verses for Repeated Recitation*, one fascicle; translated at Longyuan Temple in Yizhou, now included in the eighth fascicle. *Sutra of Various Miscellaneous Dhāraṇīs of the Universal Gate*, one fascicle (or without the word "sutra"); contains twenty-three dhāraṇīs in total; translated at Longyuan Temple in Yizhou. *Sutra of the Buddha’s Words*, one fascicle; a second edition identical in text to that translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei; translated at Longyuan Temple in Yizhou. *Sutra of the Questions of the Golden-Colored Rishi*, two fascicles; translated at the Four Heavenly Kings Temple in the Old City of Chang’an; received by Xiao Ji as scribe. The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* (Six-Scroll Sūtra on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution), one scroll, translated in the third month of the second year of the Kaihuang era.
The Record Office states that this is the second edition, which is largely identical to but slightly different from the *Pāpakarmavipāka-sūtra*; however, it is entirely distinct [from that].
This is recorded in the Changfang lu and the Xu gaoseng zhuan. This one work, consisting of one scroll, is currently extant.
The upāsaka Dharmajñāna— translated into the Sui language as "Dharma-wisdom"—
was of the Gautama clan.
He was the eldest son of Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei dynasty.
He was originally a native of Vārāṇasī in Central India and belonged to the Brahmin caste.
He settled in the eastern region and eventually adopted the customs of the local people.
Father and son inherited the ancestral tradition of translating scriptures.
Toward the end of the Northern Qi dynasty, he served as the Director of the Office of Buddhist Propagation (Zhaoxuan Du).
Once the state of Qi had been pacified, the Buddhist Dharma was likewise destroyed.
Zhi, by virtue of his monastic office,
was transferred to a secular post and was appointed by imperial decree as the Governor of Yangchuan Commandery in Yangzhou.

When the Sui dynasty received the abdication from the Zhou, the Sanskrit manuscripts arrived immediately; the Emperor issued an edict summoning Paramārtha to return and take charge of the translations.
Since Paramārtha was already proficient in both the Sui and Sanskrit languages, he could translate directly from the original texts without the need for an intermediary to transmit them.
In the second year of the Kaihuang era, the year of Renyin,
he translated one fascicle of the *Karmavibhāga-sūtra*.
The śramaṇa Shi Zhixuan of Chengdu served as the scribe for the oral transmission.
Regarding the literary style, the arrangement, and the doctrinal substance:

the preface composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Yancong of Zhao County, as well as the records of Changfang and others, all state that the *Karmavibhanga-sūtra* was translated at Xingshan Monastery; however, this is not correct. This sūtra was translated during the late spring of the second year [of the reign], while the imperial decree to move to Daxing Monastery occurred only in the late summer. Thus, it is clear that the claim that it was translated at Xingshan Monastery is an error.

*Mahāyāna Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle (sometimes without the word "Mahāyāna"). Translated in the seventh month of the second year of the Kaihuang era; this second translation is the same text as the *Ji zhū fāngděng xué jīng* by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin, as noted in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Sūtra of the Elephant Head Vihāra*, one fascicle. Translated in the second month of the second year of the Kaihuang era; this third translation is the same text as the *Wénshū wèn pútí jīng* by Kumārajīva, as noted in the *Chángfáng lù*. The above two works comprise two fascicles, and their manuscripts are both extant.
The śramaṇa Vinītadeva, whose name means "Extinction of Joy" in the Sui language,
was a native of Ujjayinī in North India.
Traveling from no less than five hundred *yojanas* away, he struck his mendicant’s staff and toured the regions to witness the flourishing of the teachings.
Upon his arrival, he was summoned to enter the palace and translate scriptures.
This was in the second year of Emperor Wen’s Kaihuang era, the *Ren-yin* year.
He translated two sections of scriptures, including the Vaipulya and the Dhāraṇī.
Li Daobao, an attendant, and Tanpi, the younger son of Prajñāruci, acted as interpreters.
The śramaṇa Shi Fazuan of Chang’an received the oral transmission and rendered it into the Sui language.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Yancong collated and compared both the text and its meaning, and composed a preface for all of them; the records of Changfang and others also state that this was produced at Xingshan Temple, but this too is not so, as the errors have been described above.
The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra: The Division on the Sun-Treasury (Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra-sūryagarbha-parivarta), in ten fascicles, or twelve fascicles, or fifteen fascicles.
The title reads: *Mahāyāna Mahāvaipulya Sūryagarbha-vibhāga Sūtra*. This is the same text as the *Mahāsannipāta Sūryaguhya-vibhāga*. It is the fourth translation.

Begun on the fifth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Kaihuang era and completed on the second day of the second month in the fifth year. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhixuan at the cost of Chang.
The *Mahāmegha-parivarta-varṣa-prārthana-sūtra* in two fascicles was transcribed by Fang et al. It was translated in the first month of the fifth year of the Kaihuang era;
the śramaṇa Huixian transcribed it. This is the sixty-fourth chapter of the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the second translation.
It is identical to the *Mahāmegha-varṣa-prārthana-sūtra* translated by Jñānayaśas during the Zhou dynasty, as well as the *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-varṣa-prārthana-sūtra* and others.
The Mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya Sūtra, two fascicles; also known as the Mañjuśrī-ṛddhibala Sūtra, and also known as the Śrī-golden-light-virtuous-daughter Sūtra.
Translated in the first month of the third year of the Kaihuang era. This third translation is the same text as the Dharmarakṣa translation of the Mahāpariśuddha-dharmaparyāya Sūtra.
Transcribed by the śramaṇa Zhixuan under the supervision of the Elder Dehu.
Sūtra in two fascicles, also known as the *Śrīgupta-gṛhapati-sūtra*. Translated in the sixth month of the third year of the Kaihuang era; received by the scribe-monk Sengkun.
This is the fourth translation, which is identical in text to the *Dharmarakṣa-yuèguāng-tóngzǐ-jīng* and others. *Bǎifó-míngjīng* (Sūtra of the Names of One Hundred Buddhas) in one fascicle.
Translated in the twelfth month of the second year of the Kaihuang era; received by the scribe-monk Huìxiàn. This is the [fifth]...

The *Chuli zhuangyan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Adornment of the Arising of Power), two fascicles; translated in the tenth month of the fifth year of the Kaihuang era, with Fei Changfang acting as scribe.
The *Lianhuamian jing* (Sūtra of the Lotus Face), two fascicles; translated in the third month of the fourth year of the Kaihuang era, with the śramaṇa Huixian acting as scribe.
The *Jiangunü jing* (Sūtra of the Firm Woman), one fascicle; translated in the twelfth month of the second year of the Kaihuang era, with the śramaṇa Huixian acting as scribe.
The *Śrī-āryāvalokiteśvara-vimokṣa-sūtra* (also known as the *Liaofu nüshang*) and the eight sections [of the *Aṣṭabuddhaka-sūtra*] are all listed in Changfang’s catalog.
These eight sections comprise twenty-three fascicles, and their original texts are all extant. Translated by the śramaṇa Narendrayaśas.
"Sui" is a respectful title.
He was a native of Ujjayinī in North India.
Previously, during the Qi dynasty, he served as the Administrator of the Court of Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuantong).
Together with the śramaṇa Fazhi of the Zhaoxuan Monastery, he translated seven works of the sūtras,
all of which are recorded in the Qi Records.
Toward the end of the Jiande era, Emperor Wu of Zhou conquered Qi.
When Buddhism and the state were simultaneously extinguished,
Guṇayśas outwardly assumed the garb of a layman while inwardly donned the three robes;
he fled from place to place, east and west, finding no time for rest.
When the five aggregates were worn down and distressed, with nowhere to turn for refuge,
he reduced his own food to give to those starving in the ditches and ravines;
to the elderly and the infirm, he provided aid and benefit according to their needs.
Although his resources were meager and he persisted in acting despite being dissuaded from his advice,
his spirit remained robust and his exhortations tireless.
Thus, he endured hardships and obstacles for as many as four years.
When the Sui dynasty governed the realm, the Three Jewels were restored;
at the beginning of the Kaihuang era, the Sanskrit scriptures responded from afar.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued requesting that he come to propagate and translate them.
In the seventh month of the second year, his disciples, including Daomi and others,
escorted him to the capital, where he resided at Daxingshan Temple.
In the late winter of that same year, they began the preliminary work on the translation.

An imperial edict was issued for more than thirty individuals, including the Śramaṇa Tanyan, Chief Administrator of the Zhaoxuan Monastery, to collaborate on the translation and transmission [of the texts].
The Sovereign’s inquiries were frequent and his offerings most generous.
Although he was advanced in years, his practice became increasingly diligent.
Having relied upon the Śāriputra-dhāraṇī and fully practiced its cultivation,
he attained a visionary realm in a dream, realizing that he would himself become a Buddha.
Such auspicious signs occurred in profusion, and examples like this were not limited to a single instance.
Later, he moved to Guangji Temple; because Emperor Yang had named it Guang, it was changed to Hongji, and now, to avoid the imperial taboo, it is called Chongji.
He served as the chief prelate for foreign monks, caring for travelers and winning their hearts through his skillful management.
Suddenly, on one occasion, he said to his disciples:
"I am old and my strength is failing; I shall not remain long in this world.
While I am still clear-headed, I exhort you, my followers."
"The Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter; you should diligently practice and study it.
A human body is difficult to obtain; be careful not to let it pass in vain.
Having finished speaking, he lay upon his pillow and passed away suddenly.
When the hundred years were complete,
it was on the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month in the ninth year of the Kaihuang era.
Previously, Guṇavīrya had met a master of physiognomy who said:
He would surely have reached a hundred years of age and attained the rank of an immortal.
That he ended his life at middle age has proven his words true;
yet, the principle of ascending to immortality remains difficult to fathom.
However, his physical appearance was extraordinary and marvelous:
his crown was like a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa),
and his ears were long and upright.
His eyes were perfectly centered,
possessing an extraordinary quality that distinguished him from his peers as a truly exceptional mark;
he was certainly a man of profound virtue who transmitted the Dharma.
When the Master of the Dharma passed away, both monastics and laypeople were filled with grief and alarm;
the task of propagating and upholding the teachings was on the verge of falling into decline.
In total, he translated eight sections of sutras during the Sui dynasty.
These are the *Mahāsannipāta-ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-mahāmegha-cakravarti-mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya* and other such sutras.
They were [translated] by the śramaṇas Sengchen and Mingfen, the courtier Li Daobao, and the scholar Tampi, among others.
Four individuals, both monastics and laypeople, took turns orally transmitting the words.
They were transcribed by the śramaṇas Zhixuan, Daosui, Huixian, and Sengkun, as well as by the Court Gentleman Yu Zhi and the scholar Fei Changfang.
The Śramaṇa Tanyan, Chief Administrator of the Zhaoxuan Office, and Lingzang, Head of Daxingshan Monastery in the Zhaoxuan Capital,
along with more than twenty other virtuous monks, supervised the proceedings from beginning to end.
By the winter of the fifth year, the examination and refinement were all completed.
The śramaṇa Yancong composed the preface.
He followed Guṇabhadra on his travels for approximately forty years,
visiting over fifty countries.
The territory spans one hundred and fifty thousand *li*.
Auspicious omens, numinous traces, eminent temples, and high monks; swift waters, deep forests, mountain deities, and sea creatures—all without exception pay him homage.
Since these matters are so extensive and pervasive, I have not yet had the leisure to describe them in detail.
The śramaṇa Yancong composed a biography for him, which has circulated widely in the world.
The *Bodhisattva-rakṣā-kuśala-sūtra* in two fascicles is listed in the *Neidian lu*; it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, as its eighteenth [chapter].

The *Huìyí shí jīng* (Sūtra on the Transference of Consciousness), two fascicles, is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* as the thirty-ninth assembly, with its title changed to the "Assembly of the Elder Bhadrapāla.
Its initial publication was identical to the *Xiǎnshí jīng* (Sūtra on Manifesting Consciousness) translated during the Tang dynasty.

It was issued in the tenth month of the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the twelfth month. The scholar Fèi Chángfáng acted as the scribe; this is recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. It was revealed by Fájue Jìng.
The *Heart Sūtra* (Cixin jing), two fascicles; first translated, it is the same text as the *Assembly on Generating Superior Aspiration* from the *Ratnakūṭa*.
Translated in the ninth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era; recorded in the tenth month by the śramaṇas Sengkun and others as pen-receivers (*bishou*).

See the *Changfang lu*. The *Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva Sūtra* (Xukong ying pusa jing), two fascicles; the fourteenth section of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, translated fourth. It is the same text as the *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* (Xukong zang jing).
The *Ākāśagarbha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and others were translated from the same original texts during the first month of the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the third month.
The śramaṇa Sengtan acted as scribe, and Yancong composed the preface; this is recorded in the *Changfang lu*.

The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-bhadrapāla-sūtra* consists of five or six fascicles; its title is also given as the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* of the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, and it is so called as well.
The *Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-sūtra*, seventh translation; identical in text to the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*.
Translated in the twelfth month of the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the second month of the fifteenth year. Scribe: Śramaṇa Mingfen and others.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-dṛṣṭāntarāja-sūtra* in two fascicles (sometimes lacking the word "Mahāsaṃnipāta"); this is a separate chapter from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*. Translated in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era.
In the fifth month of the fifth year, it was translated and completed in the sixth month. It was transcribed by the śramaṇa Daomi and others.
Together with the previously mentioned *Sūtra of the Protector of the Dharma*, both are recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*.

The *Buddhāvatamsaka-tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāra-sūtra* in two fascicles is the third translation; it is the same text as the *Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokalaṃkāra-sūtra*, as seen in the *Neidiàn*.
*Lu sì tóngzi sānmèi jīng* (Record of the Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Four Boys), three fascicles; alternatively titled simply *Sì tóngzi jīng* (Sūtra of the Four Boys).

Second edition, same text as the *Fǎhù* translation of the *Fāngděng níhuán* (Vaipulya Nirvāṇa). Translated in the fifth month of the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the seventh month.
Transcribed by the śramaṇa Sēnghuī; recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. *Miàofǎ liánhuá jīng Tiānpǐn* (The Lotus Sūtra with Added Chapters), seven fascicles, or eight.
Volume Twenty-seven. The *Sūtra of the Precious Stūpa* and the *Sūtra of Devadatta’s Succession* are combined into one, thus making twenty-seven [volumes].
In the first year of the Renshou era, at the request of the śramaṇa Shangxing of Puyao Monastery, the two Dharma Masters Kumārajīva and Dharmagupta re-examined the Sanskrit manuscripts;
those portions missing were supplemented. This includes the preface to the sūtra and the second volume of the *Sūtra of the Good-Thought Boy*, which is the fourth [text] produced.
The *Mahāvaipulya-uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra* are identical texts;

translated from July to September of the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, with the scholar Fei Changfang serving as scribe and the śramaṇa Yancong composing the preface (as recorded in Changfang’s catalogue).
Also: the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, one fascicle, containing the "Rajata-pati-dhāraṇī-parivarta" and the "Parīndanā-parivarta. Tán.
The four-fascicle version translated by Wu Chen, the seven-fascicle version by Paramārtha, and the five-fascicle version by Jñānagupta during the Zhou dynasty all lacked these two chapters;

however, as they were found in the Sanskrit original, they were added back. According to the *Chángfáng Lù*, seventeen years later, the śramaṇa Bǎoguì combined the earlier and later translations into eight fascicles;
therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-varṣa-prārthanā-sūtra* is no longer preserved separately.
The title within the first fascicle states: *Mahāvaipulya Mahāmegha Sūtra*, Chapter Sixty-four, "Invoking Rain," the third translation;
it is identical in substance to the *Mahāmegha-avarṣaṇa* and the *Mahāmegha-cakra-avarṣaṇa* sūtras, though differing in translation, as recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
The two-fascicle *Sarvadharmābhāvasvabhāva Sūtra* is the third translation, identical in substance to the *Sarvadharmāpracāra Sūtra* and others.
The same original text as the *Mahātejo’rciḥ-prabhāsa-ṛṣi-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (一卷), translated between the sixth month and the seventh month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era;
transcribed by the scholars Liu Peng and others, according to the Changfang lu.

The second translation, which shares the same original text as the *Prathama-artha-dharmavijaya-sūtra*, was translated between the first month and the second month of the sixth year of the Kaihuang era; [transcribed by] the śramaṇa Dao...

The profound text was transcribed by the śramaṇa Yancong, who composed the preface; it is recorded in the Changfang lu as one fascicle of the *Dharmadhātusvabhāva-sūtra* (or, in some versions, without the word "svabhāva").
This second translation is identical in origin to the *Ratnakūṭasamādhi-mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-dharmakāya-sūtra*.
It was produced beginning on the seventh day of the seventh month in the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era and completed on the eighth month. The śramaṇa Daomi and others were the scribes.

In the *Chángfáng lù*, it is recorded that there is one fascicle of the *Xīyǒu xīyǒu jiàoliàng gōngdé jīng* (The Sutra on the Rare and Wondrous Measurement of Merit), also known as the *Xīyǒu jiàoliàng gōngdé jīng*.
It was first produced and is identical in substance to the *Zuībǐ bēijīng* translated during the Tang dynasty.
It appeared in the sixth month of the sixth year of the Kaihuang era; the śramaṇa Sengtan took dictation, and the śramaṇa Yancong composed the preface. This is seen in the *Chángfáng lù*.
*Lu shan jing* (Record of Good Reverence), one fascicle; also titled *Shan gongjing jing* (Sūtra on Good Reverence) or *Shan gongjing shi jing* (Sūtra on Good Reverence for Teachers).
Second edition, same text as the *Zheng gongjing jing*. Translated in the seventh month of the sixth year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the eighth month.
Scribe: Śramaṇa Sengtán et al.; preface composed by Yànzōng. Recorded in the Chángfáng Lù. *Wénshūshīlì xíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Deeds of Mañjuśrī).
One fascicle; the second emergence, identical in text to the *Mañjuśrī-caryā-saṃyukta-sūtra*. Translated in the third month of the sixth year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the fourth month.
Transcribed by the śramaṇa Sengtan; the śramaṇa Yancong composed the preface. Recorded in the *Chángfáng-lù* (Catalogue of Dharma-hall).
One fascicle of the *Aṣṭabuddhanāma-sūtra*; the fifth emergence, identical in text to the *Aṣṭamaṅgalaka-mantra-sūtra* and the *Aṣṭasūrya-mantra-sūtra*.
Identical to the original, this was produced beginning in the fifth month of the sixth year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the sixth month.
The śramaṇa Daosui and others acted as scribes, and Yancong composed the preface; it is recorded in the Changfang lu.

*The Sūtra of the Mantra of Amoghapāśa*, one fascicle, also titled *The Heart-Mantra of Avalokiteśvara of Amoghapāśa*. Its initial translation is identical to the Tang dynasty translation of the *Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-mantra*.

The *Jīngděngběn* (Scripture Corresponding to the Original) was produced beginning in the fourth month and completed in the fifth month of the seventh year of the Kaihuang era. The monk Tán and others served as scribes, and Yànzōng composed the preface;

this is recorded in the *Chángfáng Lù*. The *Shí’èr Fómíng Shénzhòu Jīng* (Sūtra of the Divine Mantras of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas), one fascicle, is titled *Shí’èr Fómíng Shénzhòu Jiàoliàng Gōngdé Chúzhàng Mièzuì Jīng* (Sūtra of the Divine Mantras of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas for Measuring Merit, Removing Obstacles, and Extinguishing Transgressions).
Its initial translation is identical to the Tang dynasty translation of the *Chēngzàn Rúlái Gōngdé Měihǎo Jīng* (Sūtra of the Praise of the Merit and Sublime Virtues of the Tathāgata).
The *Lai-gongde shenzhou jing* (Sutra of the Divine Incantation of Coming Merit), same text as [the preceding], was produced in the fifth month of the seventh year of the Kaihuang era;

it was completed that same month, with Sengkun and others taking dictation, and Yancong providing the preface. This is recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Yixiang chusheng pusa jing* (Sutra on the Single-minded Birth of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle, is the tenth translation;

it is the same text as the *Wuliangmen weimi chi jing* (Sutra of the Immeasurable Gate of the Subtle and Secret Retention) and others, produced in the eleventh month of the fifth year of the Kaihuang era.
Completed in the twelfth month. Transcribed by the śramaṇas Saṃghatana and others; the preface was composed by the śramaṇa Yancong. Recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.
*The Vajrapadadhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle. Second translation; identical to the *Vajrarasottamadhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Translated in the sixth month of the seventh year of the Kaihuang era; completed in the eighth month. Transcribed by the śramaṇa Saṃghuṇa and others.
The *Rulai fangbian shanqiao zhou jing* (Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Skillful Means and Expedient Dhāraṇī), one fascicle;

the second translation, identical in text to the *Xukongzang pusa wen fo jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha to the Buddha). Translated in the first month of the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the second month.
Recorded by the śramaṇas Sengtan and others; the preface was composed by the śramaṇa Yancong. This is recorded in the Changfang lu.
In the *Chángfáng lù*, there is one fascicle of the *Dōngfāng zuìshèng dēngwáng rúlái jīng* (Sūtra of the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King of the East), titled:
"The Sūtra Sent by the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King of the East, Dispatching Two Bodhisattvas to Deliver a Dhāraṇī to Assist Śākyamuni Tathāgata in Protecting and Sustaining the World.

This is the fourth [text] produced; it is identical in substance to the *Chíjù shénzhòu jīng* (Sūtra of the Divine Dhāraṇī of Holding Phrases) and others, as seen in the *Nèidiǎn lù* (Record of Inner Scriptures) under the entry for the *Dàfǎjù* (Great Dharma Torch).
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, twenty fascicles. Translated from April to June of the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era (604 CE).
Recorded by the śramaṇa Daosui and others; listed in the Chángfáng Record. *The Mahātejas Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, twenty fascicles.
Translated from July of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era to December of the sixteenth year (615–616 CE). Recorded by the śramaṇa Seng... [text ends].

According to the *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Hui-chángfáng), the *Wǔqiānwǔbǎifó míng jīng* (Sūtra of the Names of Five Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas) in eight fascicles was transcribed by pen-receivers including Kūn et al.;
it began in the eighth month of the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era and was completed in the ninth month of the fourteenth year.

Transcribed by pen-receivers including the śramaṇa Sēngtán et al., the *Guānchá zhūfǎ xíng jīng* (Sūtra on Observing the Practice of All Dharmas) in four fascicles [was completed] on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era.

The *Nirmita-bodhisattva-sūtra* in four fascicles was translated on the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month; it was transcribed by the Academician Fei Changfang and others, as recorded in the *Changfang lu*.
The *Candrottarā-dārikā-sūtra* in two fascicles was translated in the fourth month of the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the sixth month;
it was transcribed by the Academician Liu Ping and the Śramaṇa Yancong.

The preface states that the *Bodhicittotpādana-sūtra* (一卷) was produced in the tenth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era, completed in that same month, with Xuéshì Liú Péng and others taking dictation; this is recorded in Zhǎngfáng’s catalogue.
The *Sārthavāha-devaputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (一卷), or alternatively titled *Anuparipṛcchā*, was produced in the eighth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era and finished in the ninth month.

The transcription was completed by the Academician Fei Changfang and others; it is recorded in Changfang’s catalogue as *The Sūtra of the Supreme King of All Dharmas*, one fascicle, translated in the fifth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era and finished in the seventh month; the transcription was completed by the śramaṇa Mingfen and others;

it is recorded in Changfang’s catalogue as *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Three Aggregates of Repentance*, one fascicle, as noted in the *Neidian lu*; and the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of the World), ten [fascicles].
Fifth Fascicle. This is a variant translation of the *Lokānuvartana-sūtra* from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

As seen on the title page of this scripture, it was jointly newly translated by the two Dharma Masters Guṇabhadra and Jñānagupta. It was incorporated into the sixty-fascicle *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*.
It was begun in the seventh month of the seventh year of the Kaihuang era and completed in the second month of the eleventh year. Translated by the Śramaṇa Sengtan and the Academician Fei Changfang.
Recorded by Liu Peng and others; the preface was composed by the śramaṇa Yancong. It is listed in the Changfang lu.

*The Scripture on the Questions of the Devaputra Susīma*, four fascicles. The sixth translation; it is the same text as the *Ruhuan sanmei jing* (Sūtra of the Illusion-like Samādhi) and the *Baoji shanzhuyi hui* (Assembly on the Precious Accumulation of the Well-Abiding Mind).
Translated in the fourth month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era. Recorded by the śramaṇa Daosui and others.

*The Scripture on the Buddhas’ Protective Recollection*, ten fascicles, translated by Zhu Fahu; recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. Translated in the tenth month of the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, completed in the twelfth month;
transcribed by the śramaṇa Sengtan and others. [Recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*. The above thirty-nine works comprise one hundred and ninety-two fascicles.
The *Bénxíng jí* (Collection of Past Deeds), upper volume, thirty-seven works comprising one hundred and seventy-eight fascicles, as recorded in the *Chángfáng lù*.
The fourteen fascicles of the two sections following the *Ārya-suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā* are missing.
[Translated by] the śramaṇa Jñānagupta (translated as Zhìdé in the Sui).
The original pronunciation of *Uttarakuru* is *Indrasaṭhana*,
which is translated here as "Abode of the Lord.
This is because it is protected by Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
The term "Xiandu" (賢豆) is merely a corrupted abbreviation of that country's name.
"Shendu" (身毒) and "Tianzhu" (天竺) are likewise corrupted appellations used here in this region;
however, the people of that land refer to it collectively as simply "Śāli" (聖豆, *śāli*).
These are summarized as the five directions.
The *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* states:
"The correct pronunciation is *Indu*; *Indu* [refers to]..."
Translated into Chinese as "Moon" (yue) during the Tang dynasty, the moon has many names;
this is one such appellation. It refers to how all sentient beings revolve in saṃsāra without ceasing.
In the long night of ignorance, there is no one to oversee the dawn;
it is as if the bright sun has already set. Once the sun is hidden, the night lamp must follow;
yet though the light of the stars may shine, how can it compare to the brilliance of the full moon?
If we follow this reasoning and draw an analogy from the moon, it is because the sages and worthies have successively followed in their tracks to guide the common people and manage all things,
just as the moon shines upon us.
For this reason, it is called India.
In India, the castes and clans are divided into distinct groups;
however, the Brahmins are particularly pure and noble.
Following their elegant designation, this has become established as custom, such that no distinction of boundaries is spoken of.

He was generally known as a Brahmin from the kingdom of Gandhāra (which the Sui dynasty called the "Fragrant Practice" Kingdom). He resided in the city of Puruṣapura (which the Sui dynasty called "City of Men"), and belonged to the Kṣatriya caste.

His surname was *Kambu* (the "bu" pronounced as *fan*; in the Sui language, it means "neck"), which signifies a neck like that of a peacock; this was considered a noble clan in that country. His father’s name was *Vajrasāra* (in the Sui language, it means "adamantine firmness").
In his youth he harbored far-reaching capacity, and in his maturity he established a pure model; holding the position of Grand Chancellor, he managed the affairs of state with systematic order.
Among the five brothers of the Kue-ch'o clan, he was the youngest, yet having planted the roots of virtue in past lives, he had early awakened the aspiration for the Way.
While still in the prime of youth, he sought renunciation;
his parents, recognizing the sincerity of his resolve, supported him.
He immediately entered the Mahāvana Monastery and was thereby granted ordination.

Regarding *upādhyāya*, translated in the Sui period as "Constantly Near" (*chángjìn*), those who receive and maintain [the precepts] from him are what is currently called a *heshang*; this is a corrupted abbreviation of the Yutian (Khotan) pronunciation. Master Xuanzang says that the correct Central Indian pronunciation is *upādhyāya*, which in the Tang language means "Personal Teacher" (*qīnjiào*); it is also termed *śaikṣa*, meaning "One Who Relies on Learning. As for *kṣāntivādin*, translated in the Sui period as "Superior Name," it refers to one who exclusively practices seated meditation and has profoundly mastered the work of meditative concentration.

The term *ācārya*—translated into the Sui language as "transmitter" (*chuanshou*) or "correct practice" (*zhengxing*)—refers to what is known as an *ācārya*. It is also a phonetic abbreviation of the local dialect of that country. Master Xuanzang states that *ācārya* in the Tang language means "model" (*guifan*) or "instruction" (*jiaoshou*). His name was *Śrīñānabhadra*, translated into the Sui language as "Wise and Virtuous" (*zhixian*), one who was universally proficient in the three studies and especially clear in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Since his ordination, Jñānagupta had been devoted to filial piety and sincerity;
after many years of instruction, his understanding of the ultimate goal reached full realization.
Nevertheless, he felt that the sacred sites and miraculous traces of the Holy Land of India still remained to be visited.
He then followed his original teacher, serving him with complete devotion.
At the age of twenty-seven, he received the full precepts after three summer retreats.
Master and disciple then resolved together to travel abroad to propagate the Dharma.
Initially, there were ten men who made a pact to travel abroad.
On their route, they stayed for many years in the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
The king earnestly invited their teacher to serve as the Dharma Master, providing extensive benefit and assistance.
As he was traveling on his inspection tour,
