he crossed the western foot of the Great Snow Mountains;
it was truly the most extreme height of a natural precipice.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Yantaka,
he found that the land was vast and sparsely populated;
there was no one to provide the food and drink he required.
Kūṭa then renounced his full ordination and served him with all his might;
after passing through several periods of hardship, he was fortunately spared from calamities through the protection of the numinous spirits.
He subsequently traveled through the kingdoms of Kharbandha, Khotan, and others.
He encountered summer rains and cold snow several times, which caused him to halt for short periods.
Since there was no place for him to propagate the teachings, he did not remain in any one location for long.
He then reached the kingdom of Tuyuhun and gradually proceeded toward Shanzhou.
At that time, it was the first year of the Later Yuan era of the Western Wei dynasty.
Although he had passed through hardships and perils, his resolve grew ever more fierce and determined;
three years had already elapsed since he first set out on his journey across mountains and rivers.
Of the ten companions, only four remained.
In the first year of the Wucheng era of Emperor Zhou Ming, they arrived in Chang’an and stayed at Caotang Temple.
Having traveled and taught throughout the land, the master and his disciples had fulfilled their original intention.
He ascended the pure altar once more to receive the full precepts;
his devotion to the Way was even more profound than it had been before.
Having settled in the capital, he gradually became proficient in the Sui language.
His fame spread somewhat afar and he was held in esteem by his contemporaries.
By imperial decree, he was invited into the rear garden to discuss the Buddha-dharma together;
exceptional honors and special provisions were provided throughout the inner palace.
Desiring to propagate the Dharma, he had no means by which to manifest his aspirations; thus, with full sincerity, he submitted a petition to the Emperor.
He was immediately granted a special edict permitting him to establish the Four Heavenly Kings Temple (Sìtiānwáng Sì) for his residence.
From that time forward, he began to revise newly translated scriptures and to supplement those previously missing.
Since it was not merely a matter of being loosely bound under broad favor,
when Prince Xiao of Qiao, Yuwen Jian, was stationed in Shu, he again invited him to go there with him.
For three years, he constantly served as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu) of Yizhou, residing at Longyuan Temple.
During the Jian-de era, the fortunes declined and the teachings of the Image Period were not propagated;
the five groups of monastics for a time donned the same secular clothing as the laity.
Emperor Wu then issued an edict summoning them to the imperial capital.
The Emperor repeatedly conferred upon him ranks and emoluments, pressuring him to adopt the rites of Confucianism;
yet he maintained his integrity with resolute firmness, remaining fearless even unto death.
The Emperor, moved by his steadfast sincerity, pitied him and allowed him to return home.
The route departed from north of Ganzhou via the Turks.
There, he encountered Zhongmian Taba Kaghan, who earnestly requested that he remain;
consequently, they engaged in a dialogue back and forth as follows:
In the Zhou dynasty, there was decline and ruin, leading to armies being sent out and returning in toil;
here, there is neither decay nor rise, so you may dwell at ease.
All provisions and offerings shall be made to your heart's content.
Consequently, [the transmission] was suspended for more than ten years.
After the Ācārya Zhixian returned to the West and passed away,
before long, the Upādhyāya also entered nirvāṇa.
A solitary figure dwelling alone, he knew not where to find peace.
Relying on the fact that the ruler and people of the Northern Di had extensively propagated merit and benefit,
he thus drifted as a sojourner, benefiting all beings according to the circumstances of each place.
There were ten men— Sengbao Xian, Daosui, Zhizhou, Sengwei, Fabao, Sengtian, Zhi Zhao, Senglü, and others from Qi—
who in the sixth year of the Wuping era formed a pact to travel together to the Western Regions to seek Buddhist scriptures.
After traveling back and forth for seven years, he was about to return to the East.
Having obtained two hundred and sixty volumes of Sanskrit texts,
he was returning to the land of the Turks when he heard that the Zhou had extinguished the Qi dynasty and had simultaneously destroyed the Buddha-dharma.
If he had retreated, he could not advance, having nowhere to turn; lingering there,
he eventually encountered one of supreme virtue—
like a thirsty man finding a drink, or as one in darkness meeting with light.
Because he lived with me, we studied the Way together and took pleasure in one another's company.
We continued to examine the new scriptures he had brought;
when I requested that their titles be translated, I compared them with the old catalogues and found them increasingly ingenious and distinct from those of previous scholars.
Within the Vinaya and other teachings, each person’s inner sincerity brings private joy;
having obtained the Treasure and encountered the Master, our practice shall not be in vain.
We vow together to burn incense and pledge to jointly propagate this accord.
When the Sui dynasty received the abdication of the throne, the Buddha-dharma flourished.
Xian and others brought the scriptures ahead of time to respond to this destiny,
arriving at the end of winter in the first year of the Kaihuang era.
An imperial decree was issued to the relevant authorities to seek out persons capable of translating it.
In the second month of spring in the second year, the work began to be transmitted and narrated.
In the last month of summer, an edict was issued, stating:
During the five relocations of the Yin dynasty, there was fear that the people would all perish.
This suggests that one’s longevity or brevity of life is determined by the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the soil.
Planning for the new while abandoning the old is like a farmer looking forward to autumn.
The mountains and rivers of Longshou are magnificent and beautiful, with flourishing vegetation and abundant flora;
it is well-suited as a foundation for establishing a capital and setting up the cauldron of state,
ensuring that the eternal enterprise remains secure and inexhaustible.
The territory established here was called Daixing City,
and the palace was called Daixing Palace.
The gate was called Daxing Gate;
the county was called Daxing County;
and the names of the gardens and ponds were all likewise the same.
The temple was named Daxingshan.
It was within this temple that the fundamental texts of the Dharma were transmitted and conferred.
At that time, Kumārajīva was still residing among the Northern Di tribes.
In the fourth year of the Kaihuang era, more than thirty śramaṇas, including Tanyan of Daxingshan Monastery,
felt that as they were personally engaged in translation, the phonology and meaning were inconsistent and erroneous.
Hearing that Guṇabhadra was in the north, they submitted a petition to request his return to the capital.
The Emperor then issued a separate edict to summon him back.
Having returned to the West, Kumārajīva had been beset by delays for ten years;
he reflected deeply upon how, in this enlightened age, he had once again encountered the Triple Gem.
Suddenly, I was honored by your visit from afar; I rejoiced at the prospect of our meeting.
I immediately accompanied the envoy back into the country.
At that time, Emperor Wen was on a tour of inspection in Luoyang, and I paid my respects to him there.
The Son of Heaven was greatly pleased and repeatedly bestowed inquiries upon him.
Before he had yet returned to the imperial capital, an edict was issued to have him expound and translate [the scriptures].
The newly arrived Sanskrit manuscripts were numerous across many sections.
Whether it be the Sūtras or the Śāstras, whether internal or external,
all those translated and transmitted were necessarily presided over by Jñānagupta.
Everyone agreed that Jñānagupta was proficient in the scripts of foreign lands and well-versed in the customs of distant peoples.
Thus, he was able to expound and debate with spontaneous ease without the need for formal transmission;
he mastered the gates of principle, perfected the phrasing, and established the structure of the words.
Once the meaning of the text was roughly settled, the critical edition was completed.
The scribes did not expend their efforts;
let me now compare this with the works of former masters and continue the tradition.
In the fifth year, an imperial edict was issued to Jñānagupta.
Together with the Brahmin śramaṇa Yanajie (Yaśas),
Kaifu Gao Gong,
and his son, the Commandant Tian Nu.
He commissioned six individuals, both monastics and laypeople— including Huiren and the Brahmin Viśada—
to work within the Inner History and the Inner Office on the translation of ancient Indic manuscripts and Kharoṣṭhī documents.
At that time, at Guangji Monastery, only Yaśas alone was translating the scriptures.
By imperial decree, Ratnarakṣita was additionally commissioned to assist in the translation work.
Thus, they worked back and forth between the two locations until the twelfth year.
When the translation was completed, totaling more than two hundred fascicles, it was presented [to the Emperor].
At that time, Guṇabhadra had already passed away;
consequently, an imperial decree was issued appointing Paramārtha (Jueduo) as the sole director of the translation bureau.
The Dharma seat was moved to Daxingshan Temple.
Furthermore, the Brahman śramaṇa Dharmagupta was summoned,
and an imperial edict was issued for Gao Tiannu and Gao Heren, brothers, to jointly transmit the Sanskrit language.
Furthermore, ten more eminent śramaṇas were added to the assembly: Sengxiu, Facan, Fajing, Huizang, Hongzun, Huiyuan, Fazuan, Senghui, Mingmu, and Tanqian.
The Director of Translation presided over the work and determined the fundamental principles.
The śramaṇas Mingmu and Yancong re-examined the Sanskrit manuscript against the original, conducting a thorough verification and refining the phrasing and meaning.
This was previously transmitted by Kumārajīva.
More than two thousand li to the southeast of Wutian lies the kingdom of Cakuka.
Its king possesses pure faith and deeply reveres the Mahāyāna;
within his palace he personally maintains the three great sūtras: the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Mahāsannipāta, and the Avataṃsaka.
It comprised one hundred thousand verses.
The king personally received and maintained it, keeping the locks and keys himself;
whenever he recited it, he would open [the treasury] and make offerings of incense and flowers.
Furthermore, within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
various adornments were displayed to entice the minor kings to enter and pay their respects.
Twenty-odd *li* to the southeast of this country, there is a mountain that is extremely precipitous and perilous.

In a deep and pure grotto there were twelve sections in total, including the *Mahāsannipāta*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, *Ratnakūṭa*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Vaiśālīprajñapti*, *Śāriputrābhidharma*, *Puṣpasaṃcaya*, the two *Dhāraṇīs*, the *Duḥśārasaṃgraha*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the eight sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*.
It consists of one hundred thousand verses.
According to the laws of the kingdom, it has been handed down through tradition and is strictly guarded and protected.
Furthermore, there are three arhats who have entered the samādhi of cessation, dwelling in meditative stillness within a cave.
Every half-month, the monks would go to the mountain to shave his head;
this was a practice that served as a reliance for those who had taken up the life of a renunciant.
Guṇabhadra’s spiritual nature was pure and profound, and his mind and will were firm and upright.
He cherished virtue without weariness and sought the Dharma without indolence.
He was widely learned in the Tripiṭaka and profoundly investigated the True Doctrine;
he studied all five sciences and was equally proficient in worldly treatises.
Through walking meditation, he attained the path to the site of enlightenment;
through dharanis, he mastered the principles of divine mantras.
Wearing the three robes and eating but one meal a day, he remained steadfast in his sincerity until the end.
His benevolence and compassion were vast and his inducement of others was not dependent on being exhorted.
He diligently recited Buddhist scriptures, becoming even more earnest in his old age;
he possessed a powerful memory of antiquity, reaching ever deeper understanding as time passed.
Scholars and commoners alike revered him, and both monastics and laypeople venerated him with deep respect.
Prince Teng of the Sui dynasty looked up to his moral example and followed him as his teacher.
However, due to certain affairs involving worldly defilements, he was exiled to Dongyue.
Furthermore, his reputation spread widely throughout the regions of Wuyue and Min;
by saving both body and mind, he brought immense benefit to many.
In the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era, he passed away.

At the age of seventy-eight, in accordance with the *Addendum to the Preface of the Lotus Sūtra*, the two Dharma Masters Jñānagupta and Dharmagupta re-examined the Sanskrit manuscript at Daxingshan Temple during the first year of the Renshou era (the Xinyou year). They translated what was missing and supplemented the text.
Since this *Supplementary Version* was produced during the first year of the Renshou era, it cannot have been composed at the time of his death in the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era.
Furthermore, the *Neidian lu* states that toward the end of the Renshou era, Kumārajīva was exiled to Dongyue due to other circumstances.
The *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Xu gaoseng zhuan) states that he passed away in the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era.
Since both the biography and the record were compiled by Xuánzàng himself, why do they contradict one another?
From the time Kumārajīva arrived in the eastern capital from the western regions, he traveled through various places, translating and transmitting the scriptures.
From the fifth year of the Kaihuang era until the end of the Renshou era, he produced scriptures such as the *Huguo jing* (Sūtra on Protecting the State),
totaling thirty-nine works comprising one hundred and ninety-two fascicles;
all of these comprehensively encompass the refinement of the principles of the teachings, which are perfectly integrated and penetrating.

The *Mingwen yi jie* (Collection on the Meaning of the Translations) circulated widely throughout the world. Examining the two catalogs of the Sui and Tang dynasties, the following six internal scriptures are recorded as translations by Kumārajīva:

the *Huguo pusa jing*, the *Fohuayan ruru lai de zhi jing*, the *Dafangdeng dayun qingyu jing*, the *Dongfang zuisheng dengwang rulai jing*, the *Wusuoyou pusa jing*, and the *Dasheng sanju chanhui jing*. Regarding the three scriptures—the *Daji piyuyang jing*, the *Yishi jing*, and the *Faju tuoluoni jing*—the *Jingmai jingtu* (Catalogue of Scriptures by Jingmai) attributes them to Dharmagupta. However, this is an error, as both the records of Kumārajīva and Dharmagupta include these titles; they should properly be attributed to Kumārajīva. Therefore, I have included them here according to Kumārajīva’s record and removed them from Dharmagupta’s record.

The *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Sutras) in seven fascicles was compiled by order of the Emperor at the Translation Office of Xingshan Monastery on the tenth day of the fifth month of the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era; it was completed on the fourteenth day of the seventh month. It consists of a separate catalogue in six fascicles and a general catalogue in one fascicle, totaling seven. This is recorded in the *Changfang lu*. The *Zhongjing mulu* in five fascicles was compiled by order of the Emperor in the second year of the Renshou era, with the śramaṇas and scholars of the Translation Office at Xingshan Monastery. This is recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*. These two works comprise twelve fascicles in total, and their original texts are extant.
The śramaṇas Śikṣānanda (Shi Fa-jing) and others were all eminent *bhadanta*s for translating scriptures at Daxingshan Monastery.
This was in the Jiayin year, the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era.
Emperor Wen issued an edict to compile a catalog of all the scriptures.
Twenty great virtuous ones, including Fajing, compiled and completed it.
It provides a general outline of the framework and is organized into nine sections.
The classification of categories consists of forty-two divisions.
In total, there are two thousand two hundred and fifty-seven fascicles comprising five thousand three hundred and ten volumes.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Mingmu of Yanghua Monastery.
The regions were divided into sections and their interconnections traced;
the śramaṇa Yancong of Riyen Monastery meticulously compiled and collated them,
examining both similarities and differences.
I consulted the *Chángfáng lù*. Furthermore,
in the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities,
requesting that the virtuous masters (*dàdé*) of Xingshan Monastery, along with the śramaṇas and scholars engaged in translating scriptures, [be assembled].
Having examined the treasury of the Dharma and meticulously determined the catalog of the scriptures, they have classified them according to their types into five general divisions.
The first division consists of single-text translations; the second, re-translations.
The second is the section on distinct origins;
the third is the collection of biographies of worthies and sages;
the fourth is the section on doubtful and spurious works.
The fifth category consists of those missing from the canon.
Altogether, there are two thousand one hundred and nine works in five thousand fifty-eight fascicles.
These are separately identified as suspicious or spurious and need not be transcribed.
The three sections outside [the main body] were included in the *Zangjian jilu* (Catalogue of Works Seen in the Canon),
all of which were compiled, organized, and finalized by the śramaṇa Yancong.
I consulted the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).

It records that the eight-fascicle *Jin guangming jing* (Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra) in twenty-four chapters was compiled in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era; this corresponds to the fourth version. According to the *Changfang lu* (Catalogue of Changfang), the preface was composed by the śramaṇa Yancong. This one work in eight fascicles is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda Baogui,
a monk of Daxingshan Monastery,
in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era (the Ding-si year), compiled a single edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra.
Gui was the spiritual disciple of Dao’an, the master of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* during the Zhou dynasty.

While perusing various scriptures, he observed that in the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Zhi Min-du had combined the works of two Zhis, two Zhus, and one Bai—five masters in total—into a single version of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, consisting of eight fascicles. Now, according to the *Fajing lu* and the *Hejing ji*, four versions have been synthesized; this edition lacks the Bai and Yan recensions. Furthermore, he combined the works of one Zhi and two Zhus—three masters in total—into a single version of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, consisting of five fascicles.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Sengjù combined four different editions into sixty fascicles;
in these compiled scriptures, both the text and the meaning are complete and precise.
Since these are the surviving traces left by former sages, they should be preserved.
The Master Gui subsequently relied upon this as his standard.

Thus, the *Liangshifa feng* (The Abundance of the Liang Dynasty’s Dharma) in four fascicles and eighteen chapters was expanded by the Zhou dynasty into five fascicles by dividing the "Chapter on the Vast Capacity of Life" (*Zhòulìng shòuliàng pǐn*) and the "Chapter on Great Eloquence" (*Dàbiàn pǐn*). During the Liang dynasty, Paramārtha further produced four additional chapters—namely, the "Chapter on the Distinction of the Three Bodies" (*Sānshēn fēnbié pǐn*), the "Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions" (*Yèzhàng miè pǐn*), the "Chapter on the Most Pure Ground of Dhāraṇī" (*Duōluóní zuìjìngdì pǐn*), and the "Chapter on Fulfilling Vows Based on Emptiness" (*Yīkōng mǎnyuàn pǐn*)—which, when added to the previous eighteen, totaled twenty-four chapters and seven fascicles. During the Sui dynasty, Zhìdé further produced the "Chapter on the Dhāraṇī of the Silver Lord" (*Yínzhǔ duōluóní pǐn*) and the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Zhūlèi pǐn*). These were the chapters produced at various times.
It consists of twenty-four chapters divided into eight fascicles.
The śramaṇa Yancong carefully re-examined and verified the chapters and sections until they were complete;
it was from this point that the title "King of Sūtras" (Jingwang) was first applied to this text.
The meaning is profound and subtle, and I pray that it may be protected and upheld by both the hidden and the manifest.

Furthermore, the *Chángfáng lù* states that the śramaṇa Sengjiu of Zhaoti Monastery compiled the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* into sixty fascicles during the sixth year of the Kaihuang era. Now, upon examining the sūtra compiled by Jiù, it is difficult to rely upon as it contains discrepancies, as described in detail in the *Dàchéng lù* and the *Shānfán lù*. Therefore, in this present catalog, I have retained its separate version while deleting those that were incorporated into the combined edition.

The *Zhan cha shan e ye bao jing* (Sūtra on the Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karmic Actions), two fascicles; it is said to have been extracted from the *Liu gen ju jing* (Sūtra on the Collection of the Six Sense Faculties), also called the *Dacheng shimu yi jing* (Mahāyāna Sūtra on the True Meaning), also named the *Dizang pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha), and also simply called the *Zhan cha jing* (Sūtra of Divination). This one work in two fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Bodhideng was a man from foreign lands;
it is unknown in what era he translated one fascicle of the *Yiqiancha jing* (Sūtra on the Divination of Karma).
The *Chángfáng lù* states:
"Although this scripture cannot be found among the cataloged records,
the title at the beginning of the scripture reads:"
The *Bodhicaryāvatāra* was translated by Wai-guo (Foreigner).
It appears to have appeared in recent times;
currently, it is copied and circulated within all the various Tripitakas.
Now, there was a monk in Guangzhou who practiced the *stūpa-kṣānti* (pagoda-penance) method.
He made two slips of paper out of leather;
on one he wrote the character for "good" (*śubha*), and on the other he wrote the character for "evil" (*aśubha*).
He had people cast [the divination sticks] into them;
those who obtained the auspicious were considered good, while those who obtained the inauspicious were considered not good.
Furthermore, he practiced the method of self-prostration to extinguish his transgressions.
There was also a lay practitioner in Qingzhou who practiced this same method.
In the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, someone reported to the local authorities in Guangzhou that he was a sorcerer.
The authorities then conducted an investigation.
That person cited evidence, stating:
"The method for repentance at the stupa is based on the *Zhancha jing* (Sūtra on Divination),
while the method of self-prostration is based on various sūtras."
He prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground like a collapsing great mountain.
Guo Yi, the Commandant of Guangzhou, came to the capital and presented a formal petition to Qizhou for submission to the throne.
An imperial edict was issued stating that he did not believe in the principles of the *Zhancha jing* (The Scripture on Divination).
The Palace Secretary and Gentleman-in-Waiting Li Yuancao, together with Guo Yi, went to Baochang Temple to consult various virtuous elders.
The śramaṇa Fajing and others replied,
"The catalog of the *Zhancha jing* contains neither its name nor the place of its translation."
"The method for repentance at the stupa differs from that of the various scriptures and cannot be followed in practice.
The Imperial Decree states:
'All such [practices] need not be circulated.'"
Now, I say this is not so.
How can one refuse to acknowledge those of broad vision simply because one peers through the narrow tube of one's own perspective?
Within the eighty thousand gates of the Dharma, the principles are manifold.
Were it not for that which was proclaimed from the Golden Mouth, how could such profound principles be revealed?
In the first year of the Tiace Wansui era of the Great Tang Empress,
an imperial edict was issued to the śramaṇa Mingquan and others of the Fo-shou-ji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
The cataloging and determination of all scriptures for inclusion in the orthodox canon is hereby completed.
May future readers be free from confusion.

The *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era) in fifteen fascicles was presented to the Inner Court on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era; its internal title reads *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Chronicle of the Three Jewels Through Successive Dynasties). This single work in fifteen fascicles is currently extant, as seen in the *Neidian Lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) and the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Fei Changfang, the scholar-translator of scriptures,
was a native of Chengdu.
Changfang originally entered the monastic order.
When the Zhou dynasty abolished the monastic order,
and the Sui dynasty rose again to restore it, [he] continued to practice as a layperson (*baiyi*).
At that time, he participated in the transmission of the teachings, receiving and transcribing the terminology and meanings.
Since the various records of successive dynasties mostly compiled only the scriptures while accounts of the Buddha and the Sangha were scarce, I have composed this *History of the Three Jewels*,
beginning from the reigns of Kings Zhuang of Zhou and Lu up to the final year of the Kaihuang era.
The *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era) lists the *Jiazi* [year] at the head and arranges various scriptures alongside it,
with the dates of their translation appended to the comprehensive compilation.
Having completed the compilation, it was presented for imperial review and issued by edict for implementation.
Its preface states in brief:
"That which has now been compiled is modeled roughly upon three scriptures to serve as a guide, thereby manifesting these Three Jewels."
The auspicious signs of the Buddha’s birth followed the night illumination of Zhou,
and the portents of the time of the Sūtra’s transmission were received during the nocturnal dream of Han; thus,
the Sangha became the foundational beginning, the ramparts, and the main beams [of the Dharma].
The brilliance of his assistance was as lofty as the clarity of wisdom.

Furthermore, he extensively consulted dozens of sources, including biographies of recluses, chronological records of dynasties, canonical texts, Sengyou’s *Collection of Records*, and various historical monographs.
Gathering those fallen fragments of jade-green, he composed this chronicle;
fanning the winds of a thousand years for the sake of a hundred kings,
all together uphold the light of the torch of wisdom.
When the light shines, the darkness is dispelled;
it spreads the moisture of the transmitted Dharma-stream to nourish the parched world,
and elucidates our Imperial Way to guide its initial unfolding.
In the past, at the beginning of the councils, it was uniformly stated that [the scriptures] originated in a certain kingdom or city.
Now, regarding the merit of this current compilation and translation, it is necessary to follow the respective eras.
Therefore, the structure of this catalog generally cites the dynastic titles as the "Catalogs of the Han, Wei, Wu, and Great Sui."
Those translations whose translators are lost or which are suspected of being apocryphal are annotated according to their traditional designations. The scriptures are arranged chronologically by era;
where there are duplicate listings, they are still categorized according to their respective periods.

In total, including both Chinese and foreigners, monastics and laypeople, as well as those of the Way and the secular, there were one hundred and ninety-seven persons who produced two thousand one hundred and forty-six works in six thousand two hundred and thirty-five fascicles, comprising the sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographies.
Categorized by their positions, they comprise fifteen fascicles:
one fascicle for the general catalog and two fascicles for the collection of scriptures.
The *Sanjuan di* (Three-Scroll Record) and the *Jiuduan dailu* (Nine-Scroll Successive Record).
The *Dailu* compiles and examines the relative quantities of sutras translated during successive reigns.

Emperor [Wu] was able to discern the vast distance between the Buddha’s presence and his passing, and he entered the Tripiṭaka with specialized knowledge regarding the shallowness and depth of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, and so forth.
*The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on the Questions of the Devaputra Susthitamati*, four fascicles, the seventh translation; together with the *Sūtra on the Illusion-like Samādhi*...
The *Mèi* (Dhyāna) Sūtra and the *Śrī-saṃghāṭa-sūtra* (or *Ārya-bhadra-śrī-vihāra-sūtra*) share the same root text as found in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue);

they are now compiled into the thirty-sixth assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*. The ten-fascicle *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Bodhisattva Buddhanusmṛti Samādhi Sūtra* is a second edition that shares the same root text as the *Bodhisattva Buddhanusmṛti Samādhi Sūtra* translated by Guṇadharman during the Song dynasty; it is a separate version of the *Mahāsannipāta*.

The *Pifen jian neidian lu* (Record of the Internal Scriptures Classified by Sections) notes that the *Yuan sheng chu sheng fen fa ben jing* (Sūtra on the Fundamental Dharma of the Primary Stages of Dependent Origination), in two fascicles, was first produced and is the same text as the *Fenbie yuanqi jing* (Sūtra on the Analysis of Dependent Origination) translated during the Tang dynasty;
it is also simply called the *Yuan sheng jing* (Sūtra on Dependent Origination).

According to the preface of this scripture, its production began in the tenth month of the twelfth year of the Daye era and concluded, including the commentary, in the ninth month of the thirteenth year. (Source: *Yao*).

*The Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Medicine Master Tathāgata*, one fascicle. This second edition is identical in text to the twelfth fascicle of the *Guǎngdìng jīng* (Consecration Sūtra) and the Tang translation of the *Yàoshī běnyuàn gōngdé jīng* (Sūtra on the Meritorious Virtues of the Original Vows of the Medicine Master). It is recorded in the *Nèidiǎnlù* (Record of Inner Scriptures).
Translated at the Fānjīngguǎn (Translation Hall) on the eighth day of the twelfth month in the eleventh year of the Dàyè era. The preface was composed by the śramaṇa Xíngjǔ. [End of] *Jīngāngbān*.

Regarding the two-fascicle version composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, it is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Provisions for Enlightenment) in six fascicles, based on the original text of the Venerable Nāgārjuna and explained by the Bhikṣu Īśvara; this is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

Furthermore, the ten-fascicle *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Compendium of the Great Vehicle), the second edition, is identical in its original text to the translation by Paramārtha and the translation by Vasubandhu (the *She dasheng lun* [Compendium of the Mahāyāna] by Vasubandhu) produced during the Tang dynasty.

The *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhanganirdeśa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Exposition of the Analysis of Dependent Origination), one fascicle, composed by the Venerable Ullangha; it appeared simultaneously with the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
This is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue). The *Qishi yinben jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World), ten fascicles, is the sixth [translation] produced.

It is of the same textual basis as the fourth division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Ji shijie jing* (Sūtra on the Record of the World), as well as the *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātu Sūtra), and so forth. It is also a direct [translation].
The *Cloud-Arising World Sutra* (Yun qishi jing) is recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The above nine works comprise forty-six fascicles, all of whose texts are extant.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmagupta (translated into Chinese as Fami), of the Sui dynasty.
He is also called Dharmakara.

He was originally a native of the country of Lāḍha in South India; it is incorrect for the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures) and the *Fanjing tu* (Diagram of Scripture Translation) to state that he was a native of Udyāna in North India. He was of the Kṣatriya caste.
His family name was Bhṛgu (translated in the Sui period as "Tiger Clan"). He had four younger brothers and was the eldest son.
His parents were so deeply attached to him that they would not permit him to leave the household life.
However, because he was deeply devoted to the Dharma and harbored a profound aspiration to leave secular life, at the age of twenty-three he went to the city of Kaṇauj (Sui:

*Erchū*) in the region of Central India, located within the territory of Kōmudi (Sui: *Huánghuásè*). There he entered the Saṃghārāma (Sui: *Zhòngyuán*; the older term "sēngqiálán" is an abbreviation and corruption).
It was only at this monastery that Gupta was able to have her hair shaved;
she changed her name to Dharmamitra and did not receive full ordination until she was twenty-five years old.
The name of the upādhyāya was Buddhagupta, which in the Sui language means "Awakened Secret";
the name of the ācārya was Guṇadatta, which in the Sui language means "Virtue-Giver"; and there was another ācārya named Samantaprabha.
He was able to recite and expound upon the sūtras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

He practiced the piṇḍapāta dharma—what was formerly called *fenwei*, a corruption and abbreviation of that term—and entered *dhyāna* (translated in the Sui period as "contemplative cultivation," whereas the former term *chan-na* and the term *chih-ha-na* are both erroneous and deviant).
He constantly entered this contemplation as his regular practice.
After Guptā had received full ordination,
she remained [with him] for another three years.
He studied under his master,
gaining a slight glimpse through the door and window into what the master had attained.
Later, Master Puzhao was invited by the King of the Taka kingdom.
He followed his teacher to that place and stayed for one year; when the teacher returned to his own country,
Guptā remained for another four years,
residing at Devabhīṣaṇa (translated in the Sui language as "Sky-Wanderer").

"Tiān" (Heaven) refers to the king, and "yóu" (wandering) refers to the monastic quarters; because the king established himself therein, it is called Tiānyóu. Formerly, the term "sì" (temple) was used as a substitute for this.
"Sì" is a name for a public office or court in this land, referring to what are known as the "sī" (bureau) or the "tíng" (court).
Furthermore, it is said that "Zhao-ti" (Jātī) is also a corruption and abbreviation.
According to the conventional interpretation of the characters:
"zhao" (招) means to summon or attract.
"Tiwei" (提謂) and "Tixie" (提携) are both colloquial expressions;
these are merely Western (foreign) words.
The correct pronunciation is *Cātudīṣa*,
which means "the four directions.
This refers to a location where the Saṃgha from the four directions relies for their residence.
Thereupon, as he traveled through various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna countries and monasteries, what he heard and saw increased manifold.

Merchants from the northern routes frequently visited those lands, and from afar it was reported that there existed a great kingdom called *Dazhina* (Great China), formerly known as *Zhendan* or *Zhandan*. These names were neither phonetically accurate nor translatable in meaning; they were understood merely as general designations for this land of China. Although these accounts had been transmitted at first, they were not fully believed or accepted, and no thought arose to travel there.
However, as his resolve was set upon traveling abroad and his mind was free from worldly attachments,
he eventually departed for the kingdom of Kāpiśī accompanied by six companions;
they remained there, staying at the royal monastery.
Guptā then stayed with her four companions in the capital city for two years,
visiting all the monasteries to thoroughly observe their studies;
yet her desire to travel afar remained unappeased.
That country is a meeting point for the northern route, situated on the northern slope of the Snow Mountains.
Caravans from all quarters converge upon its borders.
Furthermore, among the merchants, he heard that in the great kingdom of China, the Three Jewels were flourishing.
My companions and I have come here with single-minded devotion;
we do not merely wish to observe its customs and transformations,
but aspire to benefit all beings and propagate the scriptures.
He then crossed the western foot of the Snow Mountains and traveled through the kingdoms of Bāhlika, Śatadrū, and Dharmasīkṣita;
in all these kingdoms, he did not remain for long.
He gained sufficient knowledge of the local customs and the rituals of the various monasteries.
He then proceeded to the kingdom of Kharapandha, where he stayed for one year,
yet did not extensively guide or convert others.
They then arrived at the kingdom of Kashgar;
one of their companions returned to his native city,
while the remaining three stayed at the Royal Monastery.
It was built by King Śāla.
He stayed there for two years and lectured on the *Vigrahavyāvartanī* (The Refutation of Objections) in two thousand stanzas for the local monks.
The purport of his teachings was clear; he extensively refuted non-Buddhist doctrines.
Furthermore, he lectured on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (The Treatise on Reality), which consists of two thousand verses, analyzing its literary structure and principles.
This was indeed the method for debating worldly doctrines.
Furthermore, he stayed at Wang Temple in the kingdom of Kucha for another two years,
where he continued to lecture on and explain the aforementioned treatises for the local monks.
The king was devoted to the Mahāyāna and had been greatly enlightened; with a heart intent on retaining him and inviting him to stay, he visited [the monk] morning and evening.
Guptā, however, fixed her mind on the Eastern Lands and had no intention of remaining there in concealment.
He secretly took a monk along as they traveled by stages until they reached the kingdom of Ujjayinī.
There, at the Araṇya Monastery, he lectured on the aforementioned treatises for another two years.
Gradually proceeding to Gaochang, he visited various monasteries;
the monks of that country were mostly learned in the Chinese language.
Although he stayed for two years, he was unable to propagate [the Dharma] or expound upon it.
He then proceeded to Yiwu, where he stayed for one year.
Encountering difficulties, he sought refuge in the southwest;
however, the road consisted entirely of sand and gravel, with both water and grass utterly lacking.
The companions looked at one another, their lives at a loss for refuge;
they therefore temporarily set aside the scriptures and treatises they were carrying by the side of the road,
crossing the mountains in search of water in hopes of sustaining themselves.
His petitions being unfulfilled, his exhaustion and distress increased;
he devoted himself solely to reciting the mantra of Avalokiteśvara,
when suddenly it began to rain at night.
His body and mind filled with joy, he immediately returned to his original path;
looking around in bewilderment, he realized he had lost his way and hesitated between advancing and retreating.
He then simply continued forward until he eventually reached Guazhou.
Only then did he realize that the path to the northern route had been taken by detours.
Guptā, having long yearned for the Great Kingdom, had traveled on foot for many years.
When her initial companions either remained behind or passed away, she was left alone with but a single shadow; thus she arrived at this magnificent place.
Reflecting quietly upon these matters, my emotions were a mixture of sorrow and joy.
Shortly thereafter, by imperial decree, I was invited to enter the capital,
where I was accommodated in a renowned temple and provided with abundant supplies.
This was precisely the tenth month of winter in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era. Not long after his arrival, he had mastered the Chinese language in its essentials.
Furthermore, by imperial decree, he was commissioned to engage in the translation of scriptures;
he moved his residence to Xingshan Monastery, where he compared the Indic manuscripts with the Chinese translations, ensuring they were accurate and correct in great abundance.
The Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna treatises you have recited are all profoundly essential;
as for their exposition and elucidation, they extensively propagate subtle and profound principles.
Those of us here who have long studied them have frequently sent forth their accumulated doubts.
Yet, he established himself through compassion and forbearance, and cultivated gentleness as his nature.
His mind did not stray outside the Way, and his conduct preceded his words.
He cautioned that the ground should be level and tranquil.
The water of wisdom is profound and pure;
the Sūtras penetrate the source of characters, exhausting both sound and meaning.
Furthermore, his majestic appearance is dignified and correct, while his diligent discipline is lofty and stern.
He recited [the scriptures] with resonant voices throughout the day and night;
his discourse on the Dharma was proficient in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist traditions.
Furthermore, by nature he preferred a simple and secluded life, distancing himself from worldly affairs.
He diminished his desires and ceased all seeking;
he never grew weary of instructing others, regarding their benefit as exceeding his own.
He never showed a countenance of displeasure toward those of low station, nor did he harbor contempt for those of humble sort.
Consequently, those who had not yet beheld him were drawn by his reputation, and those who visited him for even a brief moment felt profound reverence.
Standing at the forefront of translators, he focused solely on the faithful transmission [of the teachings].
In all matters of detail or omission, he strove to preserve the essential framework.
Emperor Yang established his capital in the Eastern Metropolis (Luoyang) and treated [the Sangha] with profound reverence and generosity;
regarding the Buddha-dharma, he further increased its veneration and promotion.
He subsequently issued an edict to establish a Translation Hall within the Shangling Garden on the southern bank of the Luo River.
He summoned those of outstanding talent to perpetually uphold the transmission of the Dharma.
Immediately, he issued an edict to summon Dharmagupta and all the scholars, who assembled together.
They were provided with the four types of offerings, and their sustenance was maintained as usual.
Consequently, the translators did not let their work fall into neglect, and the transcribed scrolls remained uninterrupted.
However, during the Sui dynasty, when the imperial authority collapsed and smoke rose from the military encampments,
the production of new Sanskrit scriptures was suddenly severed.
Gupta, having accumulated profound understanding, was consequently unable to continue his extensive exposition.
Beginning during the Kaihuang era, when he arrived at the capital,
he immediately joined with Kumārajīva to participate in the transmission and translation of the scriptures.
At that time, Ratnamati controlled the authority and was held in the highest esteem for his transmission of the Sanskrit texts into the Sui language;
he was universally praised for his profound meanings, such that there were none who did not turn to him to resolve their doubts.
Yet his demeanor was profoundly transcendent, remaining untainted by the ways of the world;
thus, in his reputation as a translator, he practiced self-effacement and the exaltation of others.
Toward the end of the Renshou era, Xuanzang was exiled to Dongyue due to certain other circumstances.
Gupta took this opportunity to specialize in translation.
From the beginning of the Daye era until its final year,
she translated nine sections of scriptures, including the *Mahāvaipulya-suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
The phrasing and meaning were both lucid and pure, with the elegant and the plain clearly unfolding.
The śramaṇas Yancong, Mingze, Xingju, and others served as scribes.
He passed away at Luoxui in the second year of the Wude era of the Great Tang.
The śramaṇa Yancong composed a biography for him.
Initially, Guṇabhadra translated one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and fifteen fascicles of the *Sarvārthasiddhi-sūtra*.
It had not yet reached the stage of being collated and verified when it encountered the fall of the spurious [Later] Zheng dynasty and fell into disuse, leaving no time for its revision.
The current fascicles are preserved in the capital;

they mostly clarify matters such as the eight signs [of the Bodhisattva’s birth]. Now, the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* in twelve fascicles translated by Tripitaka Master Fazu from the Great Tang also clarifies the eight signs and so forth within it, and its Sanskrit original appears to be the same as that of this *Pulè jīng*.
*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Volume Seven, General Catalogue Part Seven;
*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Volume Eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu year.
Part Eight: General Compendium of Various Scriptures, Upper Section, Part Eight.
The Great Tang Dynasty, the Li clan, with its capital at Chang’an. From the first year of the Wǔdé era of Gāozǔ Shényáo Huángdì, the year being Wùyǐn.
Reaching the year of Gengwu, the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Kaishen Yuwen (Xuanzong),
including the period of Empress Wu’s reign, a total of one hundred and thirteen years had passed.
There have already been thirty-seven individuals, both monastics and laypeople, who served as translators.

The total number of scriptures, vinayas, śāstras, biographies, and records produced by them amounts to three hundred and one works in two thousand one hundred and seventy fascicles; of these, two hundred and eighty-one works in two thousand one hundred and forty-three fascicles are currently extant, while ten works in twenty-seven fascicles remain unlocated despite efforts to find their original manuscripts.
The Śramaṇa Paramārtha (Bālāditya) of the Great Tang [translated] three treatises in thirty-eight fascicles;
the Śramaṇa Shi Falin [compiled] one treatise in ten fascicles;

the Śramaṇa Shi Xuanzang [translated] seventy-six works in one thousand three hundred and forty-seven fascicles, comprising sūtras, vinaya, śāstras, records, and biographies; and the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan [compiled] eight [works].
*Fubian* (Classified Sections), 81 fascicles; *Pulü zhuanji* (Collection of Biographies and Catalogues), by the śramaṇa Shi Xuanying, 25 fascicles;
*Jing yinyi* (Phonetic Meanings of the Scriptures), by the śramaṇa Shi Jingmai, 4 fascicles; *Tujì* (Illustrated Records), by the śramaṇa Shi Zhitong, 4 works totaling 5 fascicles;
*Jing* (Scriptures), by the śramaṇa Gāvadharma, 1 work totaling 1 fascicle; *Jing*, by the śramaṇa Ajita... [text ends].
One collection consisting of twelve fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Shi Xuanwen; one collection consisting of twenty fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Shi Yanzong;
one collection consisting of six fascicles of compiled discussions by the śramaṇa Nadi; three collections consisting of three fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Yanajñabhadra;
and one collection consisting of two fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Divākara; [and] ten [fascicles].
One collection of thirty-four fascicles consisting of sutras and śāstras by the lay devotee Du Xingyi;
one collection of one fascicle consisting of a sutra by the śramaṇa Shi Fuli; one collection of two fascicles consisting of a compendium of treatises by the śramaṇa Shi Huili;
four collections totaling eight fascicles consisting of biographical compilations by the śramaṇa Shi Huaisu; and [one collection] of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and *Karmavācanā* by the śramaṇa Buddhata.
One fascicle of the *Tārā* section; one fascicle of the scripture by the śramaṇa Buddhāpāli;
six treatises totaling seven fascicles by the śramaṇa Divākara-prajñā;
one fascicle of hymns by the śramaṇa Śrī-huizhi; fifteen fascicles of the catalog by the śramaṇa Śikṣānanda.
Nineteen works totaling one hundred and seven fascicles: the *Brahman Li Wuchan* (one work, one fascicle);
the *Śramaṇa Mito-shan* (one work, one fascicle); the *Śramaṇa Shi Xuanyi* (one work, three fascicles); the *Collection of Treatises*;
and the *Śramaṇa Anshengna* (seven works, nine fascicles); the *Śramaṇa Shi Yijing* (sixty-one [works]).
Section 239: One hundred and eleven fascicles of sutras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographies;
fifty-three works by the śramaṇa Bodhiruci totaling one hundred and eleven fascicles of sutras and śāstras; one work in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Shi Ai;
one work in two fascicles on *karmavācanā* by the śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan; and six fascicles of phonetic glosses for sutras by the śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan.
The *Collected Sūtras* by the śramaṇa Vajrabodhi: four works totaling seven fascicles; the sūtra by the śramaṇa Shi Huaidi: one work totaling ten fascicles;
the sūtras by the śramaṇa Śubhakarasiṃha: four works totaling fourteen fascicles; the sūtras by the śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng:
five works totaling twenty-five fascicles; and the catalog of repentance rituals and others, including the *Ratnaketudhāraṇī*.
This scripture consists of ten fascicles, or eight fascicles according to the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue).
It was produced at Xingshan Monastery in the third month of the third year of the Zhenguan era and completed in the fourth month of the fourth year. The śramaṇa Falin composed the preface.

The Buddha preached this scripture again within the Great Assembly (*Mahāsaṃnipāta*), specifically as the "Jewel Banner Chapter" (*Ratnaketu-parivarta*); thus, it is not a re-translation [of a separate text]. The *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* provides a commentary on fifteen [fascicles].
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, thirteen fascicles (or fifteen fascicles), composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga. Translated by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and Bodhisattva Maitreya-vyākaraṇa (Jian-nei-dian-lu).
Produced at Shengguang Temple from the sixth month of the fourth year of the Zhenguan era until the seventeenth day of the tenth month of the sixth year.
The preface was composed by the Śramaṇa Huize.

According to the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures), in the summer of the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, this work was translated at Shengguang Temple simultaneously with the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*.
The project was completed in the spring of the seventh year, and by imperial decree, Li Baiyao, Right Attendant to the Crown Prince, composed the preface.
These three sections comprise thirty-eight fascicles, and their original texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Prabhākaramitra; in the language of Tang,
this means "one who makes clear" (zuò míng) and "knowledgeable friend" (zhī shí),
abbreviated as "friend" (péng yǒu).
Alternatively, one source says his name was Prajñā;
in the language of Tang, this means "Light-Wisdom.
He was a native of Central India.

In the sixth month, my appointment was transferred once more, as circumstances remained unsettled.

In the ninth year of the Wude era, Prince Gaoping went on a mission to the foreign tribes and met with him there.
Having received this moral influence, he was about to prepare for his return to the East,

The King immediately reported this to the throne, and an imperial edict was issued to summon him.
He then arrived together with Gaoping to pay his respects to the Emperor.
On the twentieth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Zhenguan era, the year of Dinghai, he reached the capital and was ordered by imperial decree to reside at Xingshan Monastery.
Among the eminent and accomplished members of the Śākya school, there are none who have not engaged in such cultivation and construction.
Regarding those points in the transmitted teachings from antiquity whose phrasing and intent were not yet fully understood,
they all entrusted themselves to the fundamental lineages and synthesized their similarities and differences.

He then submitted a memorial to inform the Emperor, seeking an audience to present his inner insights.
Having personally transmitted the principles of the Dharma without error, you have offered a fitting response.

Furthermore, the five monks who accompanied you shall receive enhanced provisions and supplies.
He repeatedly offered words of comfort and received him with exceptional courtesy.
In the third month of the third year, the Emperor realized that all conditioned existences are not true happiness and that both self and phenomena are empty;
he reflected that among all essential truths, none surpasses the Buddhist scriptures.
Since the circulation [of the scriptures] has reached its ultimate extent, why should there still be a need for further translation?

An edict was issued to the relevant authorities to search for those of profound virtue who were well-versed in the Three Teachings and fully proficient in the ten disciplines; nineteen such individuals were identified.
At Daxingshan Monastery, the work of translation was first inaugurated.
The śramaṇas Xuánmó and Saṃgha served as translators,
while the Tripiṭaka master’s fellow student, the Vinaya Master Jñānagupta, acted as the proofreader and co-translator.
The śramaṇas Falin, Huiming, Huize, Huijing, and others took up their pens;
respectfully receiving his instructions, they meticulously reviewed and refined the work,
carefully verifying terminology and meanings to produce a text that fully conveys the intended sense.
The śramaṇas Huìshèng, Fácháng, Huìlǎng, Tánzàng, Zhìjiě, Zhìshǒu, Sēngbiàn, Sēngzhēn, Dàoyuè, Língjiā, Wénshùn, and others served as proofreaders and commentators on the meaning.

Furthermore, by imperial decree, Fang Xuánlíng (Duke of Xíng, Minister of the Left and Grand Marshal), Dú Zhènglún (Court Gentleman Attendant and Director of the Heir Apparent’s Office), and Lǐ Xiàogōng (Prince of Zhàoqùn and Minister of Rites) were commissioned to assist in the collation and final determination of the text.
The Right Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Minister of the Court of Imperial Treasury, and Marquis of Lanling, Xiao Jing, was in overall charge of supervision.
The various offices provided the four requisites in abundance and splendor.
By the fourth month of the fourth year, the translation of the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* was completed.
Later, they moved to Shenguang Temple and also translated the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*.
By the spring of the seventh year, the collation was complete and the transcription was finished.
The relevant authorities read them through in detail and then submitted a memorial to the throne.
An imperial edict was issued for ten copies of each to be transcribed and distributed throughout the realm;
furthermore, one hundred rolls of fine silk were bestowed [upon the translators],
while other monks who had received the translations were granted varying amounts of ceremonial silk bundles.
"Vappa, your intention lies solely in the transmission of the Dharma; you have no other concerns.
Yet those of this age do not inquire [into this], or they may give rise to dissenting opinions, saying:"
Some, seeking the fortune of contemporary fame, rush after it;
thus they accumulate reputations and neglect the lecturing on sūtras and śāstras.
This is not yet the way of one who widely propagates the Dharma.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Lingjia,
who was preeminent among his peers and possessed a subtle mastery of the opportune moment.
He fully explained the facts of the matter to the supervising official, saying:
Having traveled far to the Eastern Continent, my sentiments have diverged from the pursuit of fame and profit.
I wish to cause the Way to flow for a thousand years and its renown to resound through antiquity.
Formerly, during the two dynasties of Fu and Yao, there were three thousand scholars who translated the scriptures.
Currently, there are no more than twenty translators in the Great Tang;
their intention lies in manifesting the enlightened virtues so that others may equally realize and believe them, rather than merely engaging in empty discourse.
Thus, future generations will reverently uphold these teachings without any doubt, just as they do today.
The wise all concurred in this opinion, and consequently [the proposal] was not carried out.
At that time, the Crown Prince fell ill, and despite various treatments, there was no effect.
An edict was issued summoning Zhiyi (Pō) to enter the palace for more than one hundred days.
When the Emperor questioned him in person, his responses were such that they did not fall short of the Imperial will.
As his illness gradually abated, he took his leave and departed from the temple,
whereupon the Emperor bestowed upon him sixty segments of silk and brocade, as well as ten sets of seasonal garments.
Faxie vowed to propagate the Dharma and transform others, undaunted by hardships and dangers;
he traveled far across the Indus River to come to China,
traversing a route of more than forty thousand *li*.
I personally brought the Sanskrit manuscripts with the hope that they might all be translated;
yet, it was not said that the eminent scholars would fail to carry out the imperial decree.
My great ambition has thus collapsed, and my refined aspirations remain unvoiced.
Consequently, he fell ill and knew for himself that he would not recover.
He distributed his clothing and possessions to cultivate various pure deeds;

An imperial edict was issued granting him special permission [to pass away]. Shortly thereafter,
he passed away at Shengguang Temple at the age of sixty-nine.
The Crown Prince issued an order for twenty men to carry the corpse on a litter and escort it to the mountain site.
Once the cremation was completed, [the proceedings concluded].
The śramaṇa Xuánmú collected the remaining remains and erected a stūpa for them at Shèngguāng Temple,
to the east of the stūpa of the Dharma Master Chénfǎ;
this was on the sixth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Zhēnguān era.
All sentient beings lament together:
the Wheel of Dharma has ceased its course,
and the multitudes of living beings are left without a guide.

How truly lamentable! The *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) states: "At this time, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* in its Sanskrit original was about to be widely disseminated to guide future generations; yet, it is regrettable that because the methods for translating and refining it according to the Chinese style were not fully established, these Sanskrit treasures could not be distributed. Thus, the fact that three sections were completed over ten years of translation is deeply pitiable. Now, upon examining the dates in the prefaces, the translation began in the third month of the third year and was finished in the spring of the seventh year. However, the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) states it was completed in the sixth year. Both the *Zhuan* (Biographies) and the *Lu* (Catalogues) record the years of the Xuanhua era, and thus they contradict each other.

The *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Refuting the Erroneous) in two fascicles, or one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct) in eight fascicles; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. These two works, totaling ten fascicles, are extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Falin was surnamed Chen and was a native of Yingchuan.
His distant ancestor followed an official post and resided in Xiangyang.
Having left home to become a monk at a young age, he traveled extensively, hunting for knowledge across both Confucianism and Buddhism, and thoroughly mastered their terminology and meanings.
He sought the Way from masters throughout Jinling, Chu, and Ying.
From the groves of literary talent, there was nothing he did not explore and master;
yet his intent remained fixed on the essential framework, eschewing superficial ornamentation.
He dwelt in the wilds, subsisting on forest fruits among the mountains such as Qingxi.
By day he received instruction in the Buddhist scriptures;
by night he recited and examined secular classics.
Thus, regarding the internal and external teachings, their essential meanings, and the remaining texts of both the warp and the woof, [he was thoroughly proficient].
When the refined assembly gathers, they all indulge their inclinations;
yet his style is leisurely and elegant, concealing his virtue and remaining hidden in form.
When his spirit rises and his brilliance flies forth, he then unfolds his divine strategies.
At the end of the Sui dynasty, he entered Guanzhong during a period of chaos to observe the transformation of the times.
Wandering through the region of the Eight Rivers and pausing his steps throughout the Three Qin,
he frequently reflected upon how the traditions of Huaili and the Daoist immortals alternately presented their respective names and realities.
In the past, while I was in Jingchu, I had already grasped the general outline of its literature;

This was because I had not conformed my outward form and dress to that [region], nor had I integrated myself with their fundamental sentiments.
Only then could he embody the teachings of that master and bring this turmoil to rest;

Senglin was well-versed in the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi, and his speech was consistently refined and extraordinary.

Consequently, whenever there were texts or compositions he wished to prohibit, they would consult Senglin together to determine the final decision.
Consequently, the teachings of the Śākya lineage were fully restored and extensively unfolded by Master Li;

With books in hand, they await the light of wisdom; in their restless pursuit, they seek the Way.

Since the collapse of the Emperor’s reign and the ultimate convergence of all things within the teachings of the Name (mingjiao), it is clear that even the clamor of Zheng and Wei music can be easily corrected and regulated.
He then resided at Jifa Temple in the capital.

I request that the heretical teachings of Hufo be returned to India.

Emperor Wu tolerated his petty sophistry, and even his court ministers were unable to oppose him.

Wherein lies benefit? Wherein lies gain?
Wherein lie loss and gain?
I pray you move [the mind] toward that which is wondrous and appropriate.
Fenji was indignant; Fu Ci listened from the side for the imperial decree.
Upon receiving this inquiry, he stepped forward and replied, saying:
"As I, Lin, have heard..."
The Ultimate Way transcends words;
how could the nine schools of thought ever discern it?
The Dharma-body is formless.
It is not that which is expounded by the Ten Wings;
rather, the four realms of existence are vast and boundless, drifting and sinking in the ocean of desire,
while the beings of the three worlds are teeming and agitated, tumbling down the mountains of heterodoxy.
The sons are deluded and burn themselves;
the ordinary people are submerged and do not emerge.
For their sake, the Great Sage appears in the world.
It is for this reason that the Perfected One descended in spirit,
thereby opening the gate of liberation and demonstrating the path of peace and security.
Thus, among them, those of the celestial king lineage renounced worldly affection to leave the household life;
so too did the noble youth of the Eastern Lands.
Disgusted with worldly glory and splendor, they enter the Way;
they vow to transcend the two kinds of birth-and-death and resolve to seek the one wondrous Nirvana.
To propagate goodness in order to repay the four debts of gratitude,
and to establish virtue in order to provide sustenance for the three realms of existence— this is its benefit.
They alter their physical appearance to fulfill their resolve; thus,
they discard their beards and fine hair for the sake of beauty,
and change their worldly customs to accord with the Way.
Therefore, they discard the ornate robes of ruler and subject;
though their outward form lacks the service of attending to parents,
they inwardly harbor filial piety.
Though his ritual duties were neglected toward his lord,
his heart remained mindful of that kindness;
his grace extended to both enemies and kin, thereby achieving the highest harmony.
When blessings permeate both the hidden and the manifest, how could minor transgressions be restricted?
For those of superior wisdom,
acting in accordance with the Buddha’s words brings benefit.
Those of the lowest and common sort cause harm because they impair the holy teachings;
yet by punishing evil, those who have overstepped the bounds will naturally reform themselves.
Advancing toward the good leads to universal resonance and transformation;
this is the general outline.
As for what the Mr. Fu submitted:
Since the authorities had not yet implemented [the decree],
Yi then made numerous copies of his memorial and circulated them openly throughout both distant and near regions.
Throughout the capital’s wards and neighborhoods,
everyone spread the mockery of "Bald Ding";
it became a subject of intense discussion at wine banquets.
The rumors of barbarian ghosts were silenced by bold words;
the Buddha-sun, though obscured, was no longer dim,
and the monks and nuns, though obstructed, were left without power.
At that time, there were not a few among the monastics and laypeople who possessed the capacity for critical evaluation and could compose treatises with the slightest movement of their pens.
Each of them distanced themselves from the principles of the Buddha, citing the Sanskrit texts at length,
and providing detailed demonstrations of karmic conditions while extensively expounding upon what was heterodox and what was orthodox.
But all these are merely what Yi has discarded.
How can one cite what he has discarded as proof for establishing [one's own position]?
Though it is called "refuting the heterodox," in the end it is simply the heterodox being refuted.
Lín’s temperament and disposition were profound and subtle, awakening alone amidst a thousand years;
his capacity and scope were divinely bestowed, possessing vast understanding and innate wisdom.
He beheld that the creator leaves no trace of effort.
Trusting that there was a basis for the provisional teachings,
he then composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Refuting Deviant Doctrines) in two fascicles,
modeled after the style of Fu Yi’s writings.
It consists of more than thirty sheets.
Since Senglin compiled and refined this work, it has surpassed all other compositions;
no worthy man remains hidden in the countryside, and no scholar is left out from the court.
A copy was preserved in my family collection, which I have recited from memory;
it is the quintessence of all abridgments and the crown of literary compositions.
Thus, his excellent reputation spread far and wide, and through this, the obscured mind was opened;
how sublime! Furthermore, Lin [Senglin] considered that when the initial fascicles of the treatise were first produced, his intention was to propagate and disseminate it.

Had he not extensively revealed his inner sentiments, even menial servants would not have found his Way worthy of their dust. Thus, he submitted a memorial to the Crown Prince, the various princes, and the dukes, marquises, and earls;
in all cases, the principles of his writing were magnificently pervasive, and the multitude praised his profound erudition.
Consequently, Yu Yi submitted his memorial based on this, leading to the Emperor’s change of heart;
thus, the Buddhist community was once again restored to prominence,
and Senglin was truly responsible for this achievement.
Yu Shinan, the Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Eastern Palace,
composed a detailed commentary on this treatise and wrote its preface.
Yet the Fu family was dissatisfied with this outcome;
they again secretly plotted and instigated the Yellow Turbans to serve as their faction.
The Daoist Li Zhongqing submitted the "Treatise on the Ten Differences and Nine Delusions," and the Daoist Liu Jinxi submitted the "Treatise on Manifesting Orthodoxy";
both disparaged the Buddha and the sages, casting defilement upon the Buddhist school.
Deluding the living beings and flaunting his influence throughout the court and the realm,
he mixed the fragrant with the putrid, which caused suspicion among the people of the time.
In the spring of the ninth year of Wude, an imperial edict was issued to establish three monasteries in the capital, with only one thousand monks permitted to reside therein.
All others were released to return to their native villages;
once the stern edict was issued, no one dared utter a word of protest.
The fivefold assembly wailed in grief at the Gaotang Street.
The four classes of people looked on with sighs in the cities and towns.
At that time, both monastics and laypeople were bewildered, having no place to cast their bodies.
Fortunately, because an Emperor emerged from the eastern region, the miasmic vapors were cleared away.
Having submitted this memorial and briefly investigated the essential principles of the school,
he immediately petitioned for a general amnesty and returned to his divine abode;
thus, the Buddha-sun shone once more brightly during the Tang era.
Furthermore, it is due to Lin.
Having repeatedly encountered periods of demotion and promotion, Lin vowed to maintain his integrity.
Though the Way was thwarted by worldly sentiments, he relied on his meager learning as a resource.
He then explored the classics and extracted their profound mysteries,
composing the *Vādanyāya-śāstra* (Discourse on the Determination of Truth) in eight fascicles.
Chen Ziliang of Yingchuan annotated it and composed a preface.
A man of fine letters who was preeminent among his peers, he was looked up to and revered by the multitude of scholars.
When he exhorted others to achieve success, they followed him like clouds.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era.
Emperor Wen abandoned the old palace of Dàhé on Mount Zhōngnán and established Longtián Monastery there; Senglin,
by nature delighting in seclusion and tranquility, went to reside there.
Highly esteemed by all, he was appointed to the administrative duties of the monastery.
Dressed in mountain robes, he lived with ease among the forests and fields, chanting and singing.
For three years, he assisted the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra in translating the Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra, the Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra, and other treatises.
He summoned Senglin to take up the brush to receive his instructions and to verify the meanings of the names.
In the winter of the thirteenth year, there was one Qin Shiying,
who wore the yellow turban and sought honor by employing occult arts.
He subsequently evaluated the talents of the Crown Prince.

Having long harbored a hatred for the Śākya clan, he secretly presented Lin’s treatise, claiming it slandered the Imperial House and that its author deserved the punishment of deceiving the Sovereign.
The Emperor was incensed and issued an edict to purge the monks and nuns.
Seeing that there was a group of associates, [the authorities] decided they should rely on the Bequeathed Teachings;
they subsequently sought out Senglin’s person to interrogate him according to the Dharma.
Senglin gripped his bowl and exerted himself with vigor, refusing to wait for further summons.
He went alone to the public court, disregarding his own life to uphold the principle;
he was consequently bound in fetters,
and an imperial edict was issued to interrogate him, saying:
In the confederate alliances of the Zhou, those of different surnames were placed last;
this honoring of ancestors and valuing of kinship truly originated from antiquity.
Why do you pursue their shortcomings, waver between two extremes, and extensively cite arguments based on superficial resemblance?
They have set forth numerous insolent metaphors;
they have desecrated my ancestors and reviled my forebears.
"In such a case, the crime of pressuring the sovereign would be unpardonable.
Senglin replied,
"King Wen was a Great Sage and the Duke of Zhou were Great Worthies."
In honoring the distant past and being cautious in concluding funeral rites, the vast heavens offer no response;
yet the ultimate reach of filial piety and fraternal duty penetrates even to the divine spirits.
Although the House of Zhou was the ancestral dynasty, in principle one should not strive for precedence.
Why is this? The August Heaven has no partiality; it ultimately depends upon the support of virtue.
The ancients sided with principle rather than with kinship.
He does not place himself first nor does he place himself last.
Though a relative may have committed a crime, they must be punished;
though a distant person may have performed a service, they must be rewarded.
Because rewards and punishments accord with principle, the world is peaceful and harmonious.
Laozi practiced and taught the Way as his primary tenet, and his virtuous instruction was extended to the common people.
By extending his own self to others and manifesting humble radiance, his benevolent influence permeated the four seas.
It is further said:
"My teacher is named Buddha.
'Buddha' means one who awakens all people."
The Ancient Sovereign of Gandhāra ascended to the West and passed away;
yet the origins and end of the Laoist teaching may still be traced.
He personally bestowed the *Zhongjing* (Central Scripture) upon me, instructing his disciples, saying: [text continues].
"My Master was skilled at entering nirvana; he endures eternally in an unceasing continuity. I am now departing.
As for the slanders regarding the extinction of Laozi’s Master currently propagated by Liu and Li, no one in the world is able to know [the truth]."
This *Discourse on the Rectification of Deviations* consists of eight fascicles.
It briefly addresses more than sixty points raised by Daoist practitioners,
demonstrating through historical records and prior authorities that their claims are indeed false.
He slandered and defamed the state and its people.
Thereafter, more than twenty officials were summoned for interrogation;
all of them submitted formal reports based on Senglin’s testimony and presented them to the throne.
The Imperial Edict stated:
"In the 'Chapter on the Reciprocal Retribution of Faith and Slander' within your composed *Bianzheng lun*, you wrote:
'Those who mindfully contemplate Avalokiteśvara will not be harmed even when facing the blade.'"
Furthermore, grant him a seven-day reprieve so that he may reflect upon himself;
let us test whether, when the execution is finally carried out, he can remain free from injury.
Lin was bound externally by shackles and fetters while internally pressed by the approaching date of his execution.
With fire and water mingling within my breast, I have no way to voice my lamentations or look upward for succor.

Therefore, based on the scriptures and teachings I have heard since birth, as well as the names of the Three Holy Ones which I have engraved and recited within the depths of my heart, I pray that they will manifest a clear response.
When the term of his confinement had expired, his spirit suddenly became bold and soaring, his mind expansive and unrestrained.
Joy and celebration followed one after another, and he momentarily forgot the fear of death as he stood waiting for the interrogation.
In a brief moment, the imperial decree arrived, saying:
Now that the period for pardon has expired and I am about to face execution,
what do you think? Do you have a spirit within you?
Lín took up his brush and replied:
"Since the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, the four seas have been in turmoil,
pestilence has spread, and the clash of arms has raged."
They raise armies to strike one another, each monopolizing military power.
Ministers are sycophantic and their sovereigns are negligent, failing to govern with rectitude.
They block the royal road and stubbornly cling to a single corner.
Since the imperial kings have conducted punitive expeditions to bring peace to the lands and seas,
this has truly been through the power of Avalokiteśvara and entirely by virtue of the grace of Śrīmālā.
Matching their virtue and following in their footsteps, they were equal to the highest sages;
they rescued those facing untimely deaths within the imperial court and spared those condemned by licentious punishments in the marketplace.
For seven days now, Ling has not been mindful of Avalokiteśvara, but has only been mindful of Your Majesty.
An imperial edict was issued ordering the Secretariat Drafter Wei Zong to inquire with Ling:
"There is a decree commanding you to be mindful of Avalokiteśvara."
"For what reason do you not mention [yourself] but say only that you contemplate His Majesty?
Ling replied,
"I humbly receive the holy discernment of Avalokiteśvara, who observes my defiled form within the six realms."
From the heavens above to the earth below, all serve as models and teachers.
Thus, the Great Tang reigns over the four seas, while the nine barbarian tribes submit to their duties;
throughout the eight quarters, punishments are clear and just, for the ruler is sagacious and the ministers are worthy, ensuring no injustice or excess.
Now Your Majesty nurtures all beings like children, as described in the sutras; thus, You are indeed Avalokiteśvara.
Since Your spiritual discernment accords with this reality, we contemplate only Your Majesty.
Furthermore, that which Senglin has composed, the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct), is comparable to the annals and histories.
Should there be even a single phrase that deviates from the truth, let it be subject to the axe and the halberd.
If Your Majesty follows what is loyal and correct, [then this work shall stand].

yet if Your Majesty were to unjustly execute the innocent,
Lin would suffer the pain of seeing corpses lying prostrate.
He reported the matter in full to the throne,
