By imperial decree, he was transferred to a Buddhist monastery in the Yibu region.
He traveled to Bodhi Temple at Bailao Pass,
where he passed away due to illness.

The poetry, rhapsodies, petitions, hymns, epigraphs, memorials, eulogies, and treatises on the Mahāyāna teachings, along with various commentaries, records, and biographies, authored by Lin, comprise more than thirty volumes in total.
His refined style was like the resonance of metal and stone, while his literary thought was as richly patterned as brocade;
his elegant and flowing compositions blazed forth with increasing solemnity.

Furthermore, he excelled at responding to circumstances to provide guidance, employing terminology that accorded with the musical scales of *gong* and *shang*, while his meanings conformed to the profound scriptures.
In the end, Qin Ying was executed for his madness and wickedness, and both the public and the private sphere marveled at his death.
Later, Liu, Li, and the family of Fu followed him in conversion and departed;
thus, regarding their remaining writings and past deeds:
This may serve as a secure bolt for ten thousand generations.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in six hundred fascicles, as recorded in the *Fanjing tu*, was spoken by the Buddha in sixteen assemblies across four locations;
it was translated on the first day of the first month in the fifth year of the Xianqing era at the Yuhua Hall of the Yuhua Palace Monastery.

On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Longshuo era, the śramaṇas Dashengguang, Dashengqin, Jia Shang, and others transcribed one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

It is recorded in the fourth volume of the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as being identical in text to the version translated by Kumārajīva and others during the Yao Qin dynasty. This was produced in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era.
On the first day of the tenth month at the Hongfa Terrace of Yuhua Palace in Yijun County, Fangzhou, one fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* was translated;
Du Xingyi, an official of the Zhongshu Sheng, acted as the scribe. This is recorded in the second volume of the *Neidian lu*.
It was produced alongside the *Mahāprajñā-pāramitā-vidyā-mantra-sūtra* and others, and dates to the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era.

On the twenty-fourth day of the fifth month, at the Cuimigong Palace on Mount Zhongnan, the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in twenty fascicles was translated, with the śramaṇa Zhiren serving as scribe.
This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*; it is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa*, as the twelfth assembly.
On the second day of the fifth month of the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, [the translation] was completed at the Translation Hall of Hongfusi Temple in the Western Capital.

The translation was completed on the second day of the ninth month. The śramaṇa Zhizheng served as the scribe, and Daoxuan verified the text. *The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Daśacakrakṣitigarbha Sūtra*, ten fascicles;

listed in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue). This is the thirteenth part of the *Mahāsannipāta*, sharing the same original text as the earlier *Fangguang Dashilun Jing* (Broad and Extensive Daśacakrakṣitigarbha Sūtra).
On the twenty-third day of the first month of the second year of the Yonghui era, at the Western Capital.
The translation at the Translation Hall of Da Ci’en Monastery was completed on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month.
The *Sūtra on the Manifestation of the Merits of Boundless Buddha-lands* (one fascicle), received by the śramaṇa Damingguang and others as scribe, is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

It is an alternative translation of the "Life Span" chapter (*Āyuḥparyanta-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of the fifth year of the Yonghui era, at Da Ci’en...
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dashengyun at the Translation Hall of Ensi Monastery; orally received by Shuowugoucheng. Six fascicles.
Recorded in the Neidian lu as the seventh translation. This version is identical in text to Kumārajīva’s *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.

Translated at the Translation Hall of Daci'en Monastery on the eighth day of the second month of the first year of the Yonghui era, completed on the first day of the eighth month. Recorded by the Śramaṇa.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in five fascicles was transcribed by pen by Dàchén Guāng; it is recorded in the *Nèidiǎn lù*.
This is the second complete translation, which is identical in text to the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the *Ratnaśikhara*, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, and the *Saṃdhivyākaraṇa*.
It was translated at Hongfu Monastery from the eighteenth day of the fifth month to the thirteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era. Recorded by Sà.
*The Sūtra on the Analysis of the Initial Arising of Conditions*, in two fascicles, transcribed by the pen of Damengguang.
Recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as the second edition, this is the same text as the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* translated by Guṇabhadra during the Sui dynasty.
Translated at the Translation Hall of Daci'en Monastery on the third day of the second month of the first year of the Yonghui era; completed on the eighth day. Transcribed by the śramaṇa Damengxun.
*The Scripture on the Merit of the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha*, one fascicle. Recorded in the second volume of the *Neidian lu*.

This edition is identical to that translated by Dharmagupta and others during the Sui dynasty. Translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery on the fifth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yonghui era.
Scribe and recipient: the śramaṇa Huili. [Endorsed by] Chengzan Jingtu Foshi.
*Shou jing* (Receiving the Sūtra), one fascicle; listed in the third volume of the *Neidian lu*. Its appearance is identical to the *Amitābha Sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva.
Translated on the first day of the first month of the first year of the Yonghui era at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery.

Sramana Dashengguang received it in writing. *Shenxiyou jing* (The Very Rare Sūtra), one fascicle; listed in the third volume of the *Neidian lu*. Its appearance is identical to the [unspecified] sūtra.

There was once a scripture, the *Anupamā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Peerless), one fascicle, translated on the eighteenth day of the fifth month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at the Cuiwei Palace on Mount Zhongnan;
the śramaṇa Dacheng Qin acted as the scribe for the oral transmission.

It is recorded in the second volume of the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as being the same text as the *Āścaryādbhuta-guṇa-parivarta-sūtra* (Sutra on the Measurement of Merit through Rare and Wondrous Deeds) translated during the Sui dynasty. [End of entry for] the second year of the Zhenguan era.
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the thirteenth year, at the Translation Hall of Da Ci’en Monastery, the *Sūtra on Praising the Merit of the Mahāyāna* (one fascicle) was translated;
the śramaṇa Dàchéngguāng served as the scribe. It is recorded in the *Nèidiǎnlù*.

Its initial publication was the same text as the *Sūtra on Determining Karmic Obstructions*. On the fifth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of the Yǒnghuī era, [the text] was [revised] at Da Ci’en Monastery.
One fascicle of the *Tathāgata-śāsanopadeśa-rājasena-sūtra*, translated by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-prabhāsa at the Translation Institute; received in writing by [the scribe].
Recorded in the second volume of the *Neidian lu*. This translation was produced alongside the *Rājapraśnīya-sūtra* and others.

Translated on the sixth day of the second month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at the Translation Institute of the Great Ci’en Monastery. Recorded in writing by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-prabhāsa.

*The Sūtra on the Noble Path Conditioned by Feeling*, one fascicle. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue), section six. This text is identical to the *Sūtra Spoken under the Pāṭala Tree*.
Translated on the first day of the first month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at the Ziwai Hall within the Northern Gate of the Western Capital, at the Right Hongfa Court.

Transcribed by the śramaṇa Damingguang. [The text continues with: *Amoghapāśa...* [Note: The provided source text appears to be a bibliographic record for a Buddhist scripture, including its title, catalog reference, date, location, and the names of the translators and scribes.]

*The Dhāraṇī Heart Sūtra*, one fascicle. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures), second edition; identical in text to the version translated by Kuṃārājīva and others during the Sui dynasty.
Translated on the nineteenth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Xianqing era at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery.
Sramana Dashengguang received the text in writing. *The Eleven-Faced Divine Dhāraṇī Heart Sūtra*, one fascicle. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

The second version, translated by Zhou Yashe, Jueduo, and others from the same original text, was translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery on the twenty-eighth day of the third month in the first year of the Xianqing era.
Śramaṇa Xuánzé acted as the scribe. It consists of one fascicle containing five dhāraṇī sūtras, as recorded in the *Fanying tu*.
It was translated on the first day of the first month in the first year of the Līndé era at the Yuhua Monastery.
*The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Arm-Seal of the Victorious Banner*, one fascicle, translated at the Yu Hua Hall by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-prabhāsa, with the scribe being Śramaṇa Mahāyāna.
Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. First issued as having the same text as the *Dhāraṇī of the Arm-Seal of the Wondrous Banner*.
Translated on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month of the fifth year of the Yonghui era at the Translation Institute of Da Ci’en Temple. Śramaṇa Mahāyāna.
*Yunbishou zhufuxin tuoluoni jing* (The Scripture on the Heart Dhāraṇī of All Buddhas Received by Yunbi), one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

Translated at the Translation Hall of Da Cien Monastery on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month of the first year of the Yonghui era. Received by brush from the recitation by the śramaṇa Dashengyun.

*Bajidu kunnan tuoluoni jing* (The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī for Deliverance from Suffering and Calamity), one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. [Translated] in the fifth year of the Yonghui era.
On the tenth day of the ninth month, at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery, the *Aṣṭanāma-samantaguhyadhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle was translated;
the śramaṇa Damoqing received it by dictation. It is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month of the fifth year of the Yonghui era, at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery, [the same work] was translated; the śramaṇa Damoyun received it by dictation.

*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra on Upholding the World*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Translated at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery on the tenth day of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Yonghui era.
Śramaṇa Shencha received the oral dictation and took down the pen. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Six Gates*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
Translated at Hongfu Monastery on the fourteenth day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
*The Scripture on the Buddha-Bhūmi*, one fascicle; translated at the Translation Hall of the Monastery by the śramaṇa Bianji as scribe; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
Translated at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era;
the śramaṇa Bianji served as the scribe. *The Scripture on the Merit Arising from Receiving and Upholding the Names of the Seven Buddhas*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
Recorded on the ninth day of the first month in the second year of the Yonghui era:

one fascicle of the *Buddha-nirvāṇa-samaya-dharmasthiti-sūtra*, translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery with the śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha serving as scribe; noted in the *Fanying tu* (Catalogue of Translations).
Recorded on the fourth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Yonghui era: translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna...
*The Scripture on the Samādhi of Silent Illumination and Divine Transformation*, one fascicle;

transcribed by the śramaṇa Dàchéngguāng at the Yuànhuá Hall of Yuànhuá Monastery on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Lóngshuó era (663 CE); recorded in the *Fàn-jīng-tú*.
*The Bodhisattva Precepts Manual*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Nèi-diǎn-lù* as the third translation produced. *The Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, [translated]; recorded in the *Nèi-diǎn-lù*.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, translated by Dharmakṣema and others from the same original text as the version produced during the Zhenguan era,
was translated on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of Zhenguan at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
The *Mahāyāna-prabhāsa-pen-shou-pusa-jie-jiemo-wen* (One Scroll) is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as having been extracted from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*’s *Maulī Bhūmi*.

The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* in seven fascicles, composed by the Bodhisattvas Asvabhāva and others, was translated on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery; the śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha received it in writing.
This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*. On the third day of the tenth month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, at [the Great Ci’en Monastery]...
The translation at the Sutra Translation Hall of Cien Monastery was completed on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in one hundred fascicles, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, was transcribed by the Śramaṇa Dàchéngguāng; this is recorded in the *Nèidiàn lù*.
It was translated at the Sutra Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, up until the second [fascicle].

On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the twelfth year, the bhikṣus Linghui, Langyi, and others took up their pens to transcribe the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings) in twenty fascicles.
Recorded in the Inner Canon Catalogues as composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga,

it was translated at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the first day of the tenth month of the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, and completed on the fifteenth day of the first month of the twentieth year.
One fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*, transcribed by the śramaṇas Zhizheng and others;

recorded in the *Fanying tu* (Catalogue of Translated Scriptures) as composed by Bodhisattvas such as Jin-sheng-zi and others, translated on the first day of the second month of the first year of the Yonghui era at the Fanying Yuan of Da Ci’en Temple, with the śramaṇa Dashenghui acting as scribe.
One fascicle of the *Xianyang shengjiao lun song* (Verses of the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra*).

The *Rājadharmaviniścaya-śāstra* in one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, was translated at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the tenth day of the sixth month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era;
the śramaṇa Bianji received the oral transmission. [This is] seen in the *Neidian lu*.
The [text] composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya... on the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era at... [is seen in the *Neidian lu*].
The *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra* in seven fascicles was translated at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery by the śramaṇa [Xuanzang].
Śramaṇa Dashenglin acted as the scribe. It was composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.

According to the *Neidian lu*, it was translated at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery on the sixteenth day of the first month of the third year of the Yonghui era, and completed on the twenty-eighth day of the third month.
The *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* in sixteen fascicles was transcribed by the śramaṇas Dasheng Guang, Dasheng Yun, and others. It is recorded in the *Neidian Lu*.

Compiled by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati, it was translated at the Fanying Yuan of Hongfu Monastery on the seventeenth day of the first month in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, and completed on the twenty-ninth day of the third month of that same year. Recorded by Sha.

*The Root Text of the Hundred Verses on the Great Vehicle* (Mahāyāna-śata-śāstra-mūla), one fascicle; recorded by pen by Men Xuaze and others. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Composed by Āryadeva Bodhisattva.
Translated at the Translation Hall of Da Cien Monastery on the tenth day of the sixth month of the first year of the Yonghui era.
Pen-receiver: Śramaṇa Dasheng Chen. *The Commentary on the Hundred Verses on the Great Vehicle* (Mahāyāna-śata-śāstra-vyākhyā), ten fascicles; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Composed by Dharmapāla.

The Bodhisattva Śīla translated this at the Scripture Translation Hall of the Great Ci'en Monastery on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the first year of the Yonghui era, completing it on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month. The śramaṇa Jingming and others acted as scribes.

This is the third edition of the three fascicles of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Summary of the Great Vehicle), originally composed by the Bodhisattva Asaṅga; it was previously recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) and was produced during the second year of the Zhenguan era.
On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the twelfth year, at the Hongfa Monastery to the west of the Ziwai Hall in the Northern Palace, the translation began;
it was completed at Ci’en Monastery on the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the twenty-third year. Dacheng Wei acted as the scribe and received the oral transmission.
This ten-fascicle *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Vasubandhu is recorded in the third volume of the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as having been produced during the Chen dynasty.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* by Asvabhāva, ten fascicles, translated from the same manuscript as that produced by Dharmagupta during the Sui dynasty.

It was translated at the Hongfa Court of the Northern Gate on the eighth day of the twelfth month of the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, and completed at Cien Monastery on the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the twenty-third year.
Mahāyāna Wei and others acted as scribes. This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*. True.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* in one fascicle was translated by Śramaṇa Mahāyāna Wei and Mahāyāna Lin, with others acting as scribes,

beginning on the first day of the third month in the twenty-first year at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery and concluding on the seventeenth day of the sixth month in the twenty-third year at the Translation Hall of Da Ci’en Monastery. This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
Translated by Bodhisattva Paramārtha on the first day of the fifth month of the first year of the Longshuo era at the Jiashou Hall of Yuhua Monastery;
the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* in three fascicles was transcribed by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna Ji. [This is] recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
this second edition is identical in text to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*. [Recorded on] the tenth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Longshuo era.
On the [first] day, at the Jiashou Hall of Yuhua Monastery, the translation was completed on the thirtieth day.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahakarmasiddhi-śāstra* (One Scroll), composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, was transcribed by the Śramaṇa Mahāyāna Ji as the oral reception (*pi-shou*). This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
This second edition is identical in text to the *Karmasiddhi-śāstra*. It was produced on the fifth day of the ninth month of the first year of the Yonghui era at the Great Ci'en Monastery.

One fascicle of the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Gateway to Logic), translated at the Translation Institute of the Monastery by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-prabha, with the scribe receiving the dictation;
recorded in the *Neidian lu*. Composed by the Bodhisattva Śrīlāta. This initial translation is identical in text to that produced by Yijing.
On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, it was translated at the Ci’en Monastery.

One fascicle of the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering Logic), translated at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the sixth day of the eighth month in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin; the śramaṇa Zhiren acted as scribe.

Recorded in the Neidian lu. One fascicle of the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only), seen in the [Fanyi] lu. Translated at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the sixth day of the eighth month in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin; the śramaṇa Zhiren acted as scribe. Recorded in the Fanyi lu.
The Sūtra-śāstra composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; the third edition, which is identical in text to that produced by Zhi Shi of the Northern Wei and Paramārtha of the Chen dynasties.
Translated on the first day of the sixth month in the first year of the Longshuo era at the Qingfu Hall of Yuhua Monastery.
Recorded by dictation by the Śramaṇa Dasheng Ji. *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* in one fascicle. Listed in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) as the work of Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Compiled on the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery;
transcribed by the śramaṇa Dashengguang. *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), ten fascicles. Recorded in the Neidian lu as being composed by Bodhisattvas such as Dharmapāla and others.
Translated on the intercalary tenth month in the fourth year of the Xianqing era at the Yunguang Hall of Yuhua Monastery. Transcribed by the śramaṇa... [text fragment ends].
The *Mahāyāna-tattva-viniścaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Establishment of the Mahāyāna) in two fascicles, transcribed by Men Dachengji; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

Composed by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka; translated at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery on the eighth day of the ninth month of the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, completed on the thirteenth day.
Transcribed by the Śramaṇa Dachenghui. The *Mahāyāna-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Aggregates of the Mahāyāna) in one fascicle.

The *Ālambanaparīkṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Examination of Objects of Perception), one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; the second edition, identical in text to the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*.
Translated at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery on the twenty-fourth day of the second month in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era.
Scribe: the śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha and others. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue). Composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga.
The *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-vidyāmukha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna), one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;

translated at the Liri Palace within the Eastern Capital’s Great Inner Precincts on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Xianqing era, with Śramaṇa Dachengguang acting as scribe.
This is recorded in the Neidian lu. Composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva during the Zhenguan era.
On the seventeenth day of the eleventh month in the twenty-second year, at the Hongfa Monastery in the Northern Gate, the *Nidāna-sūtra* (Yuanqi jing), one fascicle, was translated;
the śramaṇa Xuanzhong acted as scribe. This is recorded in the *Fanying tu*.

It was also translated on the ninth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Longshuo era at the Bagui Pavilion in Yuhua Monastery, appearing as a variant translation in the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
The *Benshi jing* (Sūtra on Past Events) in seven fascicles, with the śramaṇa Shenjiao serving as scribe; recorded in the *Neidian lu*.

Translated at the Translation Hall of Daci’en Monastery on the tenth day of the ninth month of the first year of the Yonghui era, completed on the eighth day of the eleventh month, with the śramaṇas Jingmai, Shenfang, and others serving as scribes.
The *Tianqingshou wenjing* (Sūtra of Questions from Heaven) in one fascicle, recorded in the *Neidian lu*. [Translated] during the Zhenguan era.

On the twentieth day of the third month in the twenty-second year [of the Zhenguan era], at the Translation Hall of Hongfu Monastery, the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* in twenty fascicles was translated;
the śramaṇa Bianji acted as the scribe. This is recorded in the *Neidian lu*.
It was composed by Kātyāyanīputra and is the second translation, which shares the same original text as the former *Aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*. [This occurred] in the second year of the Xianqing era.
On the twenty-sixth day of the [eighth] month, the translation was begun at the Sunhyeon-gak Hall within the Great Palace in the Western Capital;
it was completed on the seventh day of the fifth month of the fifth year at Yuhwa Temple. The śramaṇa Hyonjeok and others acted as scribes.

The *Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra* in twelve fascicles, composed by Mahakausthila, is recorded in the *Neidian lu*; its translation began on the second day of the seventh month of the fourth year of Xianqing.
On the seventeenth day, at the Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery, the translation was completed on the fourteenth day of the ninth month.
The *Abhidharma-samgīti-paryāya-śāstra* in twenty fascicles was transcribed by the śramaṇa Mahāyāna-guṇaprabha and others.
It is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog) that Śāriputra spoke this on the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month in the fifth year of the Xianqing era at the Jade [Palace].
Translated at the Myeongyeokjeon Hall of Hwasa Temple; completed on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Longshuo era.

The *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*), sixteen fascicles, composed by Devaśarman, was recorded by the śramaṇas Hongyan and others as the scribe on the fifteenth day of the first month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era. [This is] seen in the *Neidian lu*.
Translated at the Hongfa Monastery of the Northern Gate; completed on the eighth day of the eighth month at Ci'en Monastery.
The *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* in eighteen fascicles was orally received by the śramaṇa Damodara and others, with Śramaṇa Mahāyānaprabha and others serving as scribes.

It is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue) that this second translation, produced by Vasumitra, is the same text as the *Saṃgītiparyāya-abhidharma*. [Dated] the fifth year of the Xianqing era.

His original name was Hui.

His father, Huīyīng, was pure and possessed refined integrity; he mastered the classical arts at an early age.
He stood eight chi tall, with beautiful eyebrows and clear eyes.

This was during the Daye era;
those who discerned the signs believed it would mark the end of his life.
This was due to the timing of his reclusion.
He had four sons, of whom Xuanzang was the youngest.
From childhood, he possessed exceptional virtues and was exceptionally intelligent, standing apart from his peers.
At the age of eight, while his father sat by a desk and orally transmitted the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) to him, they reached the passage concerning Zengzi leaving his seat.
Suddenly, [the boy] straightened his robes and rose, asking for the reason.
His father replied:
When Zengzi heard his teacher’s command, he still rose from his seat to show deference;
how much more so should I now, receiving my father’s compassionate instruction, remain seated at ease?
My father was greatly pleased, knowing that I would surely achieve success.
He summoned the master of the ancestral temple and spoke with him.
They all congratulated him, saying,
"This is your 'Yangwu' [a rare and auspicious bird], O Lord."
His precocity was such as this.
Thereafter, he thoroughly mastered the profound depths of the scriptures.
His elder brother, Changjie, had previously left the household life and resided at Jingtu Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
Because I, Xuanzang, had suffered extreme hardship in my youth, he took me under his wing and nurtured me;
daily he taught me the essential principles of the scriptures, while also supplementing my studies with skillful treatises.
At the age of eleven, I could recite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Dongdu Hengdu was already ranked among his peers;
from then on, he stood out as exceptionally upright and did not conform to the crowd.
He recited the texts aloud and followed them with his eyes, leaving no gaps in his mastery.
Seeing the śrāmaṇeras engaged in boisterous conversation and playful antics,
Xuanzang said to them,
"Does the Sūtra not say?"
Now, one who has left the household life practices the unconditioned Dharma;
how could they continue to engage constantly in childish play?
It may be said that such a person merely wastes a hundred years of their life.
At that time, there was Dharma Master Jing at the monastery who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
[The master] took up the volume and internalized its teachings, eventually forgetting both sleep and food.
He also studied Master Yan’s exposition of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.

At that time, he was thirteen years old.
Subsequently, the Sui dynasty lost its rule, and the world fell into turmoil.
The brothers accompanied one another to the capital city and resided at Zhuangyan Temple.

Consequently, he followed his elder brother through the Ziwu Valley into Hanchuan.

he further listened to the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*, and the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*.
Cherishing every moment, he applied himself with diligent energy and without slackening.
Having thoroughly studied and mastered the various schools over a period of two or three years,

During the summer retreat, I studied the fundamental principles of the five categories and seven groups of the Vinaya;

Xuanzang then reflected to himself:
In learning, what is prized is enduring far-reaching application; in principle, what is valued is broad comprehension.

He studied the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* under Dharma Master Jue;
he mastered its essential principles after a single reading, committing them to memory as soon as they passed before his eyes.
Even those of long-standing learning and advanced age could not surpass him.
As for those who probe the profound and reach the distant, who open up the subtle and reveal what was hidden—
attaining solitary enlightenment regarding the deep mysteries where the masses have not yet arrived— this is certainly not a matter of a single principle.
At that time, there were in Chang’an two Dharma Masters named Chang and Bian.
He served as a master of the Dharma in the capital.
Xuanzang further consulted and received instruction from him;

The two virtuous men both sighed with deep admiration and said to Xuanzang,

"The sun of wisdom shall shine forth once more through your person.
It is my regret that we, being old and decrepit, fear we shall not live to see it.
From then on, his disciples changed their perception of him, and his fame filled the capital.

He then reflected further, saying:
I have traveled extensively through Wu and Shu, reaching as far as Zhao and Wei, and finally arriving at Zhou and Qin.
Wherever I have attended lecture assemblies, I have always been among those who have ascended the platform; thus, my words are already widely distributed.
Although I now harbor thoughts within my breast that remain unspoken, there is no place for me to provide a commentary or interpretation upon the essential texts.
If one does not treat life lightly and is willing to sacrifice one's own existence in a vow to travel to Huaxu,
how could one fully behold the perfected words and thereby communicate with divine understanding?
Only by once beholding the clear Dharma and the true texts of definitive meaning can this be achieved.
If one intends to return to Donghua to propagate the sacred transformation,
how could the eminent and sublime sages of former times have left their doubts unresolved with Maitreya?
And how could the sharp-witted disciples of later generations cease their contemplation of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*?
Thereupon, he resolutely presented himself alone at the palace gate to submit a memorial,
but the officials would not admit him.
He halted his journey at the capital and traveled extensively among the various foreign tribes, studying their scripts and languages everywhere.
He practiced walking and sitting meditation and sought instruction for several days until he attained mastery.
He sat on a side mat facing west, contemplating and awaiting the opportune moment for the teaching.
It happened that in the third year of the Zhenguan era, a period of frost and famine occurred.
He issued an edict for both monastics and laypeople to depart in four directions according to their resources;
taking advantage of this opportunity, he traveled directly to Guzang and gradually reached Dunhuang,
journeying through the Tianse Pass with provisions for the road while traveling alone like a solitary shadow.
Looking ahead, all was vast and serene; I saw only level sands with no human paths at all.
In a state of anxious uncertainty, I surrendered my fate to the workings of karma and pressed on.
Through gradual and persistent travel, I reached the borders of Gaochang.
King Muku Wentai received news of the Buddha and treated him with exceptional courtesy and hospitality, requesting that he remain to propagate the Dharma.
Xuanzang, however, expressed his sincerity and earnest resolve, and was finally permitted to travel westward.
The king bestowed upon him generous gifts to serve as provisions for his journey.
He further commanded the Palace Attendant Shi Huan to carry five hundred rolls of silk and two wagons of fruit,
and to deliver twenty-four letters addressed to the Yehe Khan.
It traversed twenty-four countries, including Kucha and others.
For each letter sent, one bolt of fine silk was attached as a credential,
thirty horses were provided, and twenty-five laborers were assigned.
He was escorted to the headquarters of the Tujue Yehu Khan;
since more than sixty kingdoms north of the Great Snow Mountains were all under his jurisdiction,
he sent Da as a special envoy to clear the way for Xuanzang.
The Khan then issued an edict to the various states under his jurisdiction,
ordering them to provide supplies and transport; thus,
by successive relay, [the items] eventually reached the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
These were all due to the power of the Qūqū King of Gaochang and the Yehe Kagan.
Xuanzang traveled extensively throughout the Five Indias, studying under various eminent masters.
As for such works as the treatises on the five sciences and four Āgamas,
the rafters of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon,
and the sounds of the seven cases and eight inflections;
Regarding the phrases concerning the three types of sounds and the six methods of grammatical analysis,
he exhausted their subtleties and thoroughly investigated their mysteries.
Initially, at Nālandā Monastery, there were the virtuous masters Siṃhaprabha and others.
He established the tenets of the *Madhyamaka-śata-śāstra* to refute the doctrines of the Yogācāra school and others.
Xuanzang said,

It is only that scholars have differing orientations; therefore,

Previously, there was a consecration master from South India named Prajñāgupta,

The various masters all said:

These three treatises are profound and abstruse repositories of meaning;

Thus it is known that the influence of his teachings was illustrious and his virtuous conduct was lofty and brilliant.

scholars from India all looked up to his magnificent virtue,

Since this elephant, the national treasure, is now granted as a gift, it demonstrates the ultimate limit of his faith."

As for that elephant, its form was round and massive; it stood about thirteen feet high and was approximately twenty feet long.

Turning north from the kingdom, Xuanzang exited the borders of India; his travels through various countries, his veneration of sacred sites, and his experiences of spiritual responses are fully detailed in the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*, the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, and the *Biography of Dharma Master Xuanzang*. These works collectively manifest these matters in their entirety.
I, Xuanzang, obtained one hundred and fifty grains of the Tathāgata’s bodily relics in the Western Regions,

One gilt-bronze Buddha image, including its halo and pedestal, three feet three inches in height, modeled after the image from the Dragon Cave on Mount Prāgbodhi in the kingdom of Magadha.
One [image] modeled after the representation of the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

Two hundred and twenty-four Mahāyāna sūtras;

At that time, the Emperor’s carriage was traveling to Luoyang;

During this entire period, his reputation grew ever loftier, remaining a peerless example throughout all antiquity.
He had an audience with the Emperor at the Luoyang Palace, meeting him in the Yiluan Hall.

From the hour of the Rabbit (卯) until the hour of the Bird (酉), he did not perceive the passage of time, which continued until the sounding of the drum signaling the end of the session.
The Emperor immediately took up arms and set out to question the rebels in Liaodong.

The Emperor said:
The Dharma Master [Yijing] said: "Your Honors possess both Chinese and Sanskrit learning; your command of language and principles is thorough and敏捷 (agile).

"How could one with such limited ability presume to participate in the affairs of court?

Neither arrogant nor sycophantic, he acted and withdrew according to the times;
his expositions were profound and subtle, and his dialectic resolved all doubts.
He was truly a preeminent sage of this age.
He was truly a Dharma general of the Śramaṇa school.
Moreover, his initial entry into the teachings was exceptional compared to ordinary people;
he made the study and contemplation of sūtras and śāstras his constant practice.
Having traveled extensively throughout the Eastern lands and drawn from the teachings of various masters,
he laid bare his innermost thoughts and exhausted their essential meanings;
there was none among them who did not prostrate themselves in the forest retreats, thereby renewing the seat of learning.
He was thus able to travel tens of thousands of *li* to seek the supreme Dharma,
vowing that he would sacrifice his very body and life to meet with it as his ultimate goal.
Setting out from Zhangye, his route passed through Longsha.
Though his body and mind were nearly exhausted by the hardships and perils along the way,
upon reaching Gaochang, he was twice as radiant as when he had set out.
His royal ancestors sent envoys to escort him, providing a full ceremonial reception for his sacred remains.
He traveled through the Iron Gate and the Stone Gate;
personally traversing the Sha Ling and Xue Ling passes,
he braved celestial perils with a resolve that grew ever more resolute.
Though he encountered fierce bandits, his spirit became even more resolute and courageous;
furthermore, having returned to receive instruction from a true teacher and inherited the lineage of Śīlabhadra,
his principles were expressed through his words and his meanings did not require repeated teaching.
Having extensively heard various heterodox doctrines and harboring them within his breast,
he caused his fellow monks to incline their hearts toward him and not reject his teachings.
Furthermore, it was because the treatise *Awakening of Faith* emerged from Ma-ming (Aśvaghoṣa).
The monks of India sought to preserve its original source;
Xuanzang then translated it from Chinese into Sanskrit to disseminate it throughout the Five Indias.
Thus, the conditions for the propagation of the Dharma were mutually supported across both the East and the West.
Furthermore, Xihu (Yijing) was deeply devoted to the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*).
Xuanzang then humbly requested clarification; as he was instructed, he understood immediately.

Consequently, he underwent seven transformations of his physical appearance, manifesting various extraordinary traces, and three times he traversed extensive treatises to expand the breadth of his mind.

Consequently, he obtained the support of three thousand learned monks from the Wuya (No-Weary) Monastery, all of whom were known as "satchels of wisdom" and served as his protective ramparts and moats.
Upon beholding his countenance and hearing his discourse,
they all snapped their fingers in admiration, exclaiming, "What a man this is!"
As he traveled through the one hundred and thirty kingdoms beyond the Great Wall and across the Eastern Sea,
among both monastics and laypeople, as well as those of heterodox and orthodox views who heard his name,
there were none who did not look up to his virtue for refuge and further revere and deepen their faith.
This shall bring increased glory to our family and state;
as we extend our dominion far and wide, the annual offerings presented [to the Emperor] shall all be the achievement of Xuanzang.
Were it not for those endowed with innate brilliance by Heaven and granted sagehood through birthright,
how could they have sustained this grand legacy and guided others to the traces of the past?
Among the successive monastic biographies, those who traveled to India—
Beginning with Faxian and Fayong and ending with Daosui and Daosheng,
there were seventeen successive journeys to the Middle Kingdom.

Speaking generally of their mastery of both Chinese and Sanskrit, their exquisite command of literary expression, their guidance in propagating the national tradition, and their ability to enlighten others regarding the heterodox and the orthodox, none surpassed these Dharma Masters.
I regret that the Sūtra-piṭaka has not been translated in its entirety; the number [of remaining texts] is still vast.
His years were not yet advanced, so he would have been fully capable of producing them.
That impermanence has suddenly overtaken him—how lamentable!
The preface to the *Sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemó* (One Fascicle), titled *Tánwúdé bù sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemó*,
is recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The *Shìjiāshì lüèpǔ* (One Fascicle)— or, as seen in the *Neidian lu*, without the character "lüè" (abbreviated)—
was compiled at Ximing Monastery on the eighteenth day of the ninth month of the second year of the Lín dé era.
*Ji shijia fangzhi* (A Record of the Regions of Śākya), two fascicles; listed in the *Neidian lu*; compiled in the first year of the Yonghui era.
*Dada neidian lu* (Record of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang), ten fascicles; listed in the *Neidian lu*; compiled at Ximing Temple in the first year of the Linde era.

*Gujin fodao lunheng* (A Balanced Discussion of Buddhism and Daoism Past and Present), four fascicles; listed in the *Neidian lu*; the first three fascicles were compiled at Ximing Temple in the first year of the Longshuo era.
Compiled in the fourth fascicle; alternatively, compiled in the first year of the Linde era, or in two fascicles.

The *Dongxia Sanbao Gantong Lu* (Record of the Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem in the Land of the Eastern Xia) in three fascicles is also titled *Ji Shenzhou Sanbao Gantong Lu* (Collected Record of the Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem in the Divine Land); it is recorded in the *Neidian Lu*.

In the sixth month of summer in the first year of the Linde era, at the Qingguan Vihāra, he compiled the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) in thirty fascicles; this is recorded in the *Neidian Lu*. Extensive.

The *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism) in thirty fascicles is recorded in the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog). The aforementioned eight works totaling eighty-one fascicles all have their original texts extant.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan.
His secular surname was Qian;
he was a native of Wuxing and a descendant of Pengzu.
From his youth, Xuān sought out the characteristics of the teachings and longed to seek a master.
From east to west of Guān and from north to south of Hé,
he traveled in pursuit of virtuous friends, undaunted by any hardship or toil.
Externally, he studied the nine currents of learning; internally, he refined the three branches of study.
The fragrance of his precepts was pure and fragrant, and the water of his meditative concentration was clear and rippling.
He guarded the city of the Dharma and continued his literary compositions without ceasing.
He was particularly skilled in the Vinaya Piṭaka, frequently revising and supplementing its ritual manuals while constantly residing on Mount Zhongnan to fortify his resolve.
All that he composed and edited was put into practice during his era;
the essentials of his protection of the Dharma are recorded in this collection.
Other distinct ritual manuals were contained within the internal scriptures;
it was only at the end of the Zhenguan era that they were compiled and edited, resulting in eight works,
including the *Sifen shanbu jieben* (The Four-Part Code of Monastic Discipline with Additions and Subtractions).
Within the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog), there is further a sequel to the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) in ten fascicles;
as the original has not yet been obtained, it is missing.
The *Yiqiejing yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of All Scriptures) in twenty-five fascicles is listed in the *Neidian lu*; this one work in twenty-five fascicles currently exists.
The śramaṇa Shi Xuanying was a śramaṇa-translator at the Great Ci’en Monastery.
Widely learned and possessing a powerful memory, he mirrored the grand standards of the literary groves.
He exhaustively investigated the fundamental and branch lineages and the interrelated structures across antiquity and the present;
thus, he was able to collate their origins and trace their currents, scrutinize their historical eras,
and eliminate the crude simplicity of archaic texts.
It pares away the superficiality and clutter of decadence;
it awakens the common understanding through manifest teaching;
and it elevates excellence by selecting and condensing the essential.
Truly, he may be called a grand map for written characters and a mirror for speech and sound.

Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, by imperial decree he was summoned to participate in the transmission [of the teachings], synthesizing the warp and woof of the scriptures and consulted to produce the definitive record.
In the course of translating, I have consulted and excerpted from the Tripiṭaka to compile this *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings).
I have provided annotated glosses and interpretations,
citing a multitude of texts so that the evidence may be exceptionally clear and readily understood.
In the past, the śramaṇa Shi Daohui of the Northern Qi dynasty produced phonetic glosses for all the sūtras;
he followed the direct pronunciation of the characters without ever looking back to the underlying principles,
thereby causing the loss of doctrinal meaning and truly leading people astray in their guidance of the world.
That which ought to be done is entirely distinct from the common run;
in investigating the fundamental sources, one must strive for factual accuracy,
thereby establishing a model for ten thousand generations.
It was also a rare opportunity for an audience with the Emperor.
Alas, I had only just finished the composition when,
before I could revise it for errors, he passed away.
What a pity!
The *Jin gu yijing tuji* (Record of the Illustrations of the Translation of Scriptures Throughout Past and Present) in four fascicles: this one work in four fascicles is extant.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Jingmai.
He was a native of Jianzhou.
Renowned for his extensive learning,
he assisted the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang in translating various scriptures.
He was summoned to serve as a Great Virtuous One for the compilation of texts.
Later, in the Sutra Translation Hall of the Great Ci’en Monastery,
there were murals depicting the monastics and laypeople who had transmitted and translated the scriptures since ancient times.
Jingmai thereupon compiled and organized these matters,
composing a *Tujì* (Illustrated Record) and inscribing it upon the wall; however,
he merely abridged Fei Changfang’s record and continued it down to the present dynasty.

The details regarding the translation of these scriptures are recorded directly here, with nothing further to note. 1. *Qīānqiānbì Guānshìyīn Púsà Tuóluóní Shénzhòu Jīng* (The Scripture on the Divine Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Thousand-Eyed, Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva), in two fascicles—or one fascicle.

Translated during the Zhenguan era at the Neiyì (Inner Translation Office). It shares the same text as the *Qiānqiānshǒushēn Jīng* translated by Divākara in the Tang dynasty. A preface was composed by the śramaṇa Bolun. 2. *Qiānzhuǎn Tuóluóní Guānshìyīn Púsà Zhòu Jīng* (The Scripture on the Thousand-Turn Dhāraṇī Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva), in one fascicle—or without the word "scripture" (*jīng*). Translated in the fourth year of the Yonghui era at Zongchisi Monastery. 3. *Guānzìzài Púsà Suíxīn Zhòu Jīng* (The Scripture on the随心 [Suíxīn] Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva), also known as the *Duōlí Xīnjīng* (Tārā-hṛdaya Sūtra). Translated in the fourth year of the Yonghui era at Zongchisi Monastery. 4. *Qīngjìng Guānshìyīn Pǔxián Tuóluóní Jīng* (The Scripture on the Pure Avalokiteśvara Samantabhadra Dhāraṇī). Translated in the fourth year of the Yonghui era at Zongchisi Monastery. These four works comprise five fascicles; their original texts are all extant, according to the *Dàzhōu Lù* (Catalogue of the Great Zhou).
The śramaṇa Shi Zhitong was pure and austere in his observance of the Vinaya, while being equally proficient in the sūtras and śāstras;
he paid particular attention to the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Tong entered the monastic order during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.
He resided at Dazongchi Monastery in the capital and harbored the aspiration to travel abroad.
He subsequently studied the Sanskrit script and language at the Translation Hall in the capital of Luoyang,
quickly mastering their profound subtleties.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk from North India.
He presented a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Qianbi Qianyanshou Guanzizai Pusa Jing* (The Sūtra of the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) for imperial submission.
Emperor Wen issued an edict for Daotong to translate it in collaboration with the Indian monk,
resulting in a two-fascicle work.

Later, in the fourth year of the Yonghui era of the Heavenly Emperor, the Gui-chou year (653 CE), he further produced three sūtras at Zongchi Temple, including the *Qianshou Qianyan Guanshiyin Pusa Guangda Yuanman Wuai Dabeixin Tuo-lu-ni Jing* (The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Great Compassionate Heart of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) in one fascicle. This single work, consisting of one fascicle, still exists today.
The śramaṇa Gaovandarma— translated into Chinese as Zūnfǎ (Venerable Dharma)—
was a native of Western India.
He translated one fascicle of the *Qianshou Qianyan Dabeixin Jing* (The Sūtra of the Great Compassionate Heart of a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes).
However, the title of the sūtra states it was translated by Gāvadharma of Western India, without specifying the date.
Judging from its origins and characteristics, it appears to be a recent translation produced during the Imperial Dynasty.
However, as those who transmit the Dharma appear to benefit others according to conditions,
and as the translated scriptures are circulated further to other regions,
and since the imperial reign titles are not recorded therein, it is impossible to know whether [the dates] are recent or distant.
Shengqin asked a Brahman monk about it, who replied that there was a Sanskrit manuscript.
Since it was not erroneous, he included it in this record.
According to the preface to the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Sutra), it also states that Zhizong and others produced it together.

The *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha-sūtra*, twelve fascicles, listed in the *Da Zhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue). Translated at Huiri Monastery on the fourteenth day of the third month in the fourth year of the Yonghui era; completed on the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the fifth year. Received by brush from the śramaṇa Xuankai. This one work in twelve fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Ajitaghosa (translated into Chinese as Wujige [無極高]) was a native of Central India.
His learning exhausted the full range of the written word and his conduct was as pure as a perfect pearl;
he was refined in the five sciences and possessed a subtle mastery of the Tripitaka.
Furthermore, this Great Being, in benefiting sentient beings, showed no stinginess regarding his native land.
Determined to propagate the teachings of the Buddha, he feared no hardship or peril;
thus he crossed the Snowy Mountains to the west and traversed the Desert River to the east.
Having endured many trials and tribulations, he finally arrived at the Imperial Palace.
In the first month of the third year of the Yonghui era (the Renzi year),
Xuanzang arrived in Chang’an bringing numerous Sanskrit manuscripts;
by imperial decree, they were to be housed at Cien Monastery.
The śramaṇas Daśamahāyāna Zōng and sixteen others,
along with the Dukes Ying and Ē and twelve others,
requested Master Hǎo to reside at the Stūpa Courtyard of Huìrì Temple.
He constructed a maṇḍala for the universal assembly of dhāraṇīs;
all that was required for the maṇḍala were prepared and provided.
On the day the rite was completed, spiritual wonders descended repeatedly.
The monastics and laypeople of the capital all marveled at such a rare encounter.
Consequently, the śramaṇas Xuankai and others earnestly requested that he translate the original text of this Dharma.
Later, from the fourth year (Gui-chou) to the fifth year (Jia-yin), he worked at Huiri Monastery.
An abridged translation of the essential points from the *Vajramahāmaṇḍala-sūtra*,
compiled in twelve fascicles.
Transcribed by the śramaṇas Xuankai and others.
At that time, the monks Ānanda-vinaya-ācārya and Kāśyapa-ācārya from the Mahābodhi Temple in Central India were translating the *Dharmatārā-dharma* at their monastery during their walking meditation.
Because it was compiled within the tenth fascicle of the *Saṃyuktāgama*, it does not exist as a separate work.

The *Zhu jing yao ji* (Essential Collection of Various Scriptures) in twenty fascicles was compiled at Ximing Monastery during the Xianqing era; this one section in twenty fascicles is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Xuanwen,
whose original name was Shidao,
possessed a high reputation for his studies in the Vinaya and was held in deep esteem by his predecessors.
He devoted himself to the task of compiling and editing, while also transcribing commentaries and providing annotated exegeses on various scriptures.
Upon the founding of Ximing Monastery, he was summoned as a Mahādeba (Great Virtuous One).
During the Xianqing era, he recited the entirety of the Buddhist canon.
He compiled the essential matters from various sources into a single volume titled *Compendium of Essential Passages from the Various Scriptures* (*Zhujing yaoji*).
The remainder is recorded as it appears in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Classics).
The *Ji shamen buyai suyi* (Collection of Discourses on the Reason Why Śramaṇas Do Not Bow to Laypeople), six fascicles; recorded in the *Neidian lu*. This one work in six fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Yanzong was of comprehensive and acute intelligence, possessing a broad understanding of the various scriptures.
He was skilled at composing elegant prose and excelled particularly in scholarly writing.
In the second year of the Longshuo era (Renxu), during the reign of the Heavenly Emperor, an imperial edict was issued ordering that subjects should prostrate before their sovereigns and parents.
Fearing that this might harm the national transformation, the various ministries were commanded to deliberate on the matter extensively.
At that time, the śramaṇa Daoxuan and others collectively submitted a memorial to inform the imperial court.
After deliberation by various officials, the matter was presented to the authorities;
His Majesty personally reviewed it and issued an edict to abolish [the practice].
Fearing that future generations might lack knowledge of these matters,
I have compiled these events along with accounts from previous dynasties and the dialogues of former sages,
titling this work *A Collection of Discourses on Why Sramaṇas Do Not Prostrate to the Laity*.
He transmitted this to future generations to serve as an eternal model;
thus the dharma-city was fortified and the profound tradition did not decline.
Furthermore, he compiled the *Record of Temples in the Capital of the Great Tang*.
*Jingxing yidai*.
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Volume Eight, General Catalogue Part Eight;
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Volume Nine.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Xichongfu Monastery in the Gengwu year (679 CE), Part Nine: The Supplement to the *Dafangdeng Dajianjing Chuanji* (Great Tang Records of Translated Sutras), Volume Nine, Section on the Compendium of Various Scriptures. Supplement to the *Dafangdeng Dajianjing Chuanji*: 1 scroll of the *Sīzhūngyānwáng Púsà Qǐwèn Jīng* (Sutra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍitarāja), also known as the *Bāmántuólúó Jīng*.

Translated at Cien Monastery in the third year of the Longshuo era (663 CE). Recorded in the *Dazhou Lu*. 1 scroll of the *Lìgòuhuì Púsà Suowèn Lǐfǎ Fǎjīng* (Sutra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Vimalamati on the Rites for Worshipping the Buddha). Translated at Cien Monastery in the third year of the Longshuo era (663 CE). Recorded in the *Dazhou Lu*. 1 scroll of the *Āzhànàzhì Jīng* (Aṭānāṭiya Sūtra). Translated at Cien Monastery in the third year of the Longshuo era (663 CE). Recorded in the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks). The above three works comprise three scrolls in total; the first two works comprise two scrolls and are currently extant, while the latter work comprises one scroll, the original manuscript of which is missing.
The śramaṇa Nādi; in the language of Tang, he is called Fusheng (Born of Blessings).
According to the full Sanskrit term, he is called Pūrṇovāya.
Because his words were so numerous and prolix, this account is merely an abbreviated and phonetic rendering as "Nadi.
He was originally a native of Central India;
he entered the monastic order in his youth and was known as Master Kaiwu (Kai-ku).
His aspirations were grand and far-reaching, and he cherished the propagation of the Way as his primary concern.
He traveled extensively through various regions, devoted primarily to enlightening sentient beings;
moreover, he was highly proficient in phonology and grammar, mastering all systems of linguistic interpretation.
Dàxià was summoned to serve as a literary scholar,
comparable to the authors of the Lántái Academy in this land.
By nature, he was broadly affectionate, possessed a keen curiosity, and held refined ideals.
Having heard that there were those who attained realization there, he did not disdain the distant barbarian lands.
He once traveled to the Kingdom of Siṃhala,
and further proceeded southeast to Mount Laṅkā.
Having traveled afar to propagate the teachings according to conditions among the various kingdoms of the South Sea,
he encountered the flourishing transmission of Mahāyāna Buddhism in the Eastern Land of China (Zhina), which was most prosperous on Jambudvīpa and renowned as supreme.
He then collected over five hundred scrolls of Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras from both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions, totaling more than one thousand five hundred fascicles.
In the sixth year of the Yonghui era of the Heavenly Emperor, it first arrived at the capital.
An imperial edict was issued ordering that it be housed at Ci'en Monastery and provided for by the relevant authorities.
At that time, Dharma Master Xuanzang was engaged in translation work there.
His fame and brilliance rose majestically, yet there was no way for them to be fully manifested; he remained suppressed and desolate, as difficult as it would be for Vimalakīrti to respond.
Since Nāgārjuna had not been invited to lead him, there was no means for him to propagate his teachings on his own.
In the first year of the Xianqing era, by imperial decree, he was sent to the various kingdoms of Kunlun to collect rare medicinal herbs.
Having arrived at the various kingdoms of the South Sea, the local kings paid him their respects;
he established separate monasteries for them, ordaining people and transmitting the Dharma.
The breadth of his propagation of the teachings was twice as great as it had been previously.
Having previously received an imperial decree to go and manage affairs, he was required to return and report his findings.
Intending to further investigate and study the Sanskrit manuscripts at Cien Monastery,
he returned to his former temple in the third year of the Longshuo era.
The various scriptures he had brought were all intended by Xuanzang to be taken north;
he wished to translate them, but lacked any supporting materials.
He translated only three works, including the *Aṣṭamaṇḍala-sūtra*.
The Essential Summary of the *Abhidharmakośa* is to be constantly practiced and studied.
Translated by the śramaṇa Huize of Chanlin Monastery;
edited and with a preface composed by the śramaṇa Daoxuan of Fengde Monastery.
That year, those in the kingdom of Chenla in the South Sea who had been converted by Natisūtra were filled with boundless reverence and longed to see him.
They led one another by mutual invitation on a pretext of a distant journey, saying:
"Our country possesses excellent medicine; you alone, O Dṛḍha, are capable of identifying it. We request that you go yourself to gather it."
An imperial edict was issued permitting his travel back and forth,
yet this had never occurred before.
He extensively inquired of travelers from Da Xia (Bactria), who said:
The Tripitaka Master Nadi was a disciple of Nāgārjuna;
his understanding of the signless (animitta) was contrary to that of Xuanzang.
A monk from Western India said:
After the Great Master’s passing, this man was the foremost;
he profoundly understood the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and was well-versed in skillful means (*upāya*).
He was learned in the Vinaya of the five schools of the Hīnayāna as well as the four Vedas of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
There was nothing he did not penetrate to its very source and bottom; his mastery of words and meanings was thorough and luminous.
His expressions were as linked like pearls, and his principles soared like clouds.
He composed approximately forty volumes of the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-artha-śāstra*.
As the task of translating this was left unfinished, it has consequently been lost.
Indeed, sighs over the discovery of the *Lunyu* have occurred throughout the ages;
how difficult it is to truly know another!
A thousand years rarely witness such an encounter; Nadi, having traveled from afar with the Way, arrived here.
Having cast himself into the northern abyss, he had nothing left to wait for;
thus, he was poisoned three times and twice conscripted for labor in the south.
Having traversed tens of thousands of miles over treacherous terrain and repeatedly endured the miasma of pestilence, he surrendered his life to fate; yet such a man still remains.
Alas! How lamentable!

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, later translation, "Section on the Cremation" (also titled "Section on the Jhāpana," or "Later Section"), in two fascicles; the preface was composed by the śramaṇa Huili and is recorded in the *Da Zhou Lu*. This one work in two fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Yanabadra— translated into Chinese as Zhixian (Wisdom-Worthy)—
was a native of the kingdom of Po-ling, also called He-ling, in the South Sea.
He was well-versed in the Tripitaka.
Formerly, during the Linde era, the śramaṇa Huining of Chengdu in Yizhou traveled to India to visit and pay homage to the sacred sites.
The merchant ship sailed westward and passed through the country of Pāṇḍu;
there, he and Zhixian translated the latter two fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
which were then sent to Jiaozhou.
Huìníng compared this to the case of India;
later, at the beginning of the Yífēng era, Liáng Nándí, the Governor of Jiāozhōu,
dispatched an envoy who brought scriptures into the capital.
In the third year, the Wuyin year (658 CE), the śramaṇa Linghui of Da Cien Monastery requested at Dong'an that this be put into practice.
This second edition of the *Mahāyāna-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-sūtra* in two fascicles is the same text as the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the Chapter on the Householder Bhadrapāla.

According to the *Dazhou lu* (Catalogue of the Dazhou Era), in the first year of the Yonglong era, one fascicle of the "Continuation of the Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter" (*Fuxu rufajie pin*) of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* was translated at Dongtaiyuan Temple in the Eastern Capital;
some versions omit the character "xu" (continuation). This supplements the missing text of the previous *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
According to the *Dazhou lu*, in the first year of the Chuigong era, the *Vaipulya* [sūtra] was translated at Guining Yuan in Xitaiyuan Temple.
The Mahāvyūha-sūtra, twelve fascicles; also known as the *Abhijñāvikrīḍita*. This fourth edition is identical in substance to the *Lalitavistara* translated by Dharmarakṣa and other texts.
According to the *Dazhou lu*, it was completed on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the second year of the Yongchun era at the Guining Yuan of the West Taiyuan Temple.
Transcribed by the śramaṇa Fuli as the oral reception (*śrutidhara*), this is a seal of realization for the Mahāyāna sūtra.
The second fascicle is also titled *The Vairocana-garbha Entering the Realm of Wisdom of All Buddhas*, the second translation, which shares the same original text as the *Mahāyāna-saṃbhava-sūtra*;
it was translated at Dongtaiyuan Temple in the first year of the Yonglong era according to the *Dazhou Catalogue*.
The third translation is the one-fascicle *Mahāyāna-akṣara-vigata-samantaprabhāsa-garbha-sūtra*, which shares the same original text as the [translation by] Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei.

The *Anakṣara-ratnakoṭi-sūtra* translated by Bodhiruci and others, which corresponds to the same original text as seen in the *Dazhou Catalogue*, was translated at the Guining Court of the West Taiyuan Temple in the second year of the Yongchun era (683 CE).

This is the fourth translation of the *Mahāyāna-vairocana-prabhāsa-garbha-anakṣara-dharmamukha-sūtra* in one fascicle; it is identical to the previously mentioned *Vimukti-akṣara-sūtra* and was re-translated by Rizi.
*Mahāvaipulya Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, one fascicle; second edition, identical in text to the *Tathāgata-Siṃhanāda Sūtra*.
Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*; translated at Dong Taishan Temple in the first year of Yonglong.
*Mahāyāna Śatapuṇyalakṣaṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle; first edition. Recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*; translated at Xi Taishan Temple in the second year of Yongchun. During the Guining period.
*Mahāyāna-śatapuṇya-vyūha-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; the second translation, which is the same text as the preceding *Śatapuṇya-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*.
Re-translated by Rìzhào. *Mahāyāna-caturdharma-sūtra*, one fascicle; the first translation, recorded in the *Dàzhōu Lù*.
Translated at Dōng-Tàiyuán Temple in the first year of the Yǒnglóng era. *Bodhisattva-pratipatti-caturdharma-sūtra*, one fascicle.
Volume [X]: Translated at Hongfu Monastery in the capital during the first month of the second year of the Yonglong era; the preface was composed by the Śramaṇa Yancong.
This second edition shares the same source text as the previous *Mahāyāna-caturdharma-sūtra*.
The *Saptakoṭi-buddha-mahācitta-tāraṇī-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, was initially translated with the same source text as that produced by Vajrabodhi; see the *Dai* (Great) [Catalogue].
Recorded as translated at the Guining Hall of Xitaiyuan Temple in the first year of the Chuigong era of the Zhou dynasty;
this second edition is the same text as that produced by Du Yi and others.

On the twenty-second day of the fifth month of the first year of the Yongchun era, it was translated together with the śramaṇa Yancong at Hongfu Temple in the capital; Yancong also composed the preface.
*The Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Most Victorious Uṣṇīṣa for Purifying Karmic Obstructions*, one fascicle. This fourth edition is identical in substance to the preceding sūtra.
When Zhìrào was about to return to his country from the Eastern Capital, he retranslated it together with the śramaṇa Huìzhì.

It contains two sections: the "Prior Conditions" and the "Subsequent Dharma," both of which are extensive. Also included are the *Mahāyāna-Ghanavyūha-sūtra* in three fascicles, as recorded in the *Dàzhōu Lù*. Created.
*Stūpa-guṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Dazhou lu*; translated at Dongtaiyuan Temple in the first year of the Yonglong era.
*Koṭī-viṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-bhāṣya-nāma-tattvārtha-pariccheda*, two fascicles;
composed by Bodhisattva Guṇadatta (also known as the *Guṇadatta-śāstra*); recorded in the *Dazhou lu*; [translated] in the ninth month of the second year of the Yongchun era.
On the fifteenth day [of the month], at the Guining Yuan (Retreat Court) of the West Taiyuan Temple, one fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-vistara-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* was translated.
Composed by Bodhisattva Sthiramati; some versions omit the character "vistara" (extensive), as seen in the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue).
Translated on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Chuigong era. The above consists of eighteen sections and thirty-four [fascicles].
The original texts of these fascicles are all extant.
The śramaṇa Divākara— translated into Chinese as Rìzhào (Sunlight)— [translated them].
A native of Central India,
he had a profound mastery of the Eight Scriptural Collections (aṣṭapiṭaka) and a broad understanding of the Four Āgamas.
His observance of the precepts was pure and lofty, and his scholarly accomplishments were abundant and excellent.
He was particularly skilled in incantations and thoroughly mastered the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*).
With the aim of benefiting sentient beings, he traveled to this country.
He arrived during the initial years of the Tianhuang Yifeng era and remained until the final years of the Tiānhòu Chuigong era.

Regarding the two capitals, there were the West Taiyuan Temple and the East Taiyuan Temple; the West Taiyuan Temple is the present-day West Chongfu Temple, and the East Taiyuan Temple is the present-day Da Fuxian Temple.
Furthermore, at Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital, he translated eighteen works, including the *Mahāyāna-vijñapti-mātra-siddhi-sūtra*.
The śramaṇa Candraprabhadeva served as the oral interpreter,
and the śramaṇa Huizhi verified the Sanskrit terminology.
By imperial decree, ten men of renowned virtue were summoned to assist in his propagation of the Dharma:
the śramaṇas Daocheng, Bocen, Jia Shang, Yuan Ce, Lingbian, Mingxun, Huaidu, and others, who served as witnesses to the meaning of the teachings.
The śramaṇas Sīxuán, Fúlì, and others compiled the text and recorded it with the brush.
Empress Wu personally composed the preface with her sagacious pen and placed it at the head of the work.
Thus, the teachings of the Buddha were glorified and transmitted for eternity.

*The Scripture of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle. Originally translated together with [the version by] Rìzhào and others; same text. Translated on the fifth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Yífēng era. This work consists of one part and one fascicle; the manuscript is extant.
The lay devotee Du Xingyi was a native of Jingzhao. During the Yifeng era,
he served as the Acting Director of the Dianke Bureau of the Honglu Si, holding the rank of Chao-san-lang.
Zhiyi was proficient in the languages of various foreign regions and possessed literary elegance;
he had also mastered the subtleties of Indian speech and script.
At that time, there was a monk from the kingdom of Kaśmīra named Buddhapāli.
Carrying a fascicle of Sanskrit scriptures, he went to the palace to present them as an offering.
The Emperor issued an edict ordering Huikai to translate them;
the work was titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī*.
Certified and translated by General Ningyuan Dupo and the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India, Śīlabhadra,
in the first month of the fourth year of the Yifeng era.
In this translation by Du [Shunzhi], instances of temple names and national imperial names were all concealed and avoided; thus,
"World-Honored One" (世尊) was rendered as "Holy Honored One" (聖尊),
and "world" (世界) was rendered as "realm of beings" (生界).
"Mahāsena" means "Great Host.
"Jiūzhì" (救治) means "to rescue and eliminate [suffering].
Translation completed; respectfully presented.
After the Emperor had finished reading it, he looked at Fayi and said, "Since these are the words of a sage,
there is no need to avoid taboo characters.
Du Shi received the imperial decree, but because he was currently dealing with a personal matter, he set the matter aside.
In the brief interval that passed, Master Du passed away.
Before there was time to revise his translation, it was put into circulation.
Later, Tripitaka Master Prajñācakra received an imperial decree to translate it once again.
It is titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-sitatapatrā-aparājitā-dhāraṇī*.
The record of the Great Zhou states that it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman; this is an error.

*Shimen bianhuo lun* (Treatise on Dispelling Delusions through Ten Gates), two fascicles; *Dawaitaiwenxue quanwuer shidian jiyi* (Answers to Prince Wenxue Quanwu’s Questions Regarding Doubts Concerning the Buddhist Scriptures), perhaps three fascicles. This one work in two fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Fuli was a native of Jingzhao;
his secular surname was Huangfu.
He entered the monastic life at an early age and resided at Xingshan Monastery.
By nature he was serene and aloof, possessing few worldly desires;
he directed his mind toward the inner scriptures while also extensively studying the profound teachings of both Buddhism and Confucianism.
He was particularly skilled in poetic composition and excelled at writing;
both commoners and renowned scholars alike admired and looked up to him.
Among them were the Tripitaka masters Śīlabhadra and Śikṣānanda.
He translated such scriptures as the *Mahāvyūha* and the *Avataṃsaka*.
By imperial decree, he was summoned along with Li to collaborate on the translations;
it was truly this man who was responsible for composing the prose and determining the meanings.
In the second year of Emperor Jōkō, the year of Xin-si (741 CE),

because the Imperial Prince’s Literary Secretary Gwan Muni had composed ten points of inquiry regarding doubts concerning the Buddhist scriptures, [the Emperor] utilized them to question the ritualists and requested that their lingering uncertainties be resolved.
He then composed a response to it in two fascicles,
titled the *Shimen bianhuo lun* (Treatise on the Ten Gates for Discerning Delusions).
Within it, the host and guest engage in dialogue, analyzing points and resolving doubts.
The phrasing issues forth from the treasury of wisdom, while the meaning resides beyond the mind.
To whom else but him could such a response belong?
It may truly be said that Nāgārjuna has been reborn and Aśvaghoṣa has appeared once more.
Upon seeing this treatise, Literary Officer Quan’s many doubts were instantly dispelled;
he received it with reverence and began to practice it accordingly.
Although this was but a single response given at that time, it was of great significance.
This truly serves as a mirror for ten thousand generations.
The Dharma Master also possessed a collection of literary works that circulated during his time.
*The Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, ten fascicles: this one work in ten fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Hui-li,
whose original name was Zi-li,
had his name changed to Hui-li by the Emperor.
Her secular surname was Zhao,
and she was a native of Tianshui.
Her distant ancestors had migrated to Xingping due to official postings.
Therefore, what was formerly called Bīn has now been changed to Bīn-rén.
His grandfather and father both enjoyed high reputations;
he himself was the third son of Yì, who served as the Secretariat Drafter (Bìshū láng) during the Sui dynasty.
From birth, he was precocious and possessed the aspiration to renounce worldly life.
At the age of fifteen, in the third year of the Zhenguan era, he left home to become a monk at Zhaoren Temple in Bingzhou;
this temple was the very battlefield where Xue Ju had been defeated.
Established in his studies with keen talent and refined spirit, his path was far-reaching.
He emulated the lofty character of Lin Yuan and possessed the discernment and capacity of Zhao Rong.
His reputation spread far and wide, leading to an imperial decree summoning him to serve as a Great Virtuous Master for the translation of scriptures at Da Cien Monastery.
Next, he was appointed as the General Steward (Du Weina) of Ximing Monastery;
later, he was granted the position of Abbot of Taiyuan Monastery.
In both cases, imperial edicts were issued by the throne to appoint him to these monastic offices.
During the reigns of successive Emperors, he was frequently summoned to the inner palace to engage in debates with Daoist priests;
in all instances, his arguments satisfied the Emperor’s wishes.
These matters are recorded in a separate biography.
Considering that Master Xuanzang had traveled to India to seek the scriptures,
yet there was no record of his journey and such accounts were rarely heard in later generations,
[Daoshi] subsequently composed the *Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Ci'en*.
It was left unfinished when he passed away.
Later, the śramaṇa Yancong of Hongfu Monastery continued and completed it,
totaling ten fascicles.
Therefore, the initial title reads: *Śramaṇa Huìlì’s Original Commentary, Annotated by Yànzōng*.

One fascicle of the *Sifen Bǐqiū Jìběn* (Sifen Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra), titled *Sifen Jìběn with Preface*, was compiled by the Śramaṇa Huáisù of Xitāiyuán Temple.
