One fascicle of the *Sifen Bǐqūní Jìběn* (Sifen Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra) has the character "Ní" (Bhikṣuṇī) added [to the title]; the rest is identical to the preceding. Three fascicles of the *Sifen Sēng Jiémó* (Sifen Monastic Karma), titled *Jiémó, Fascicle Upper, with Preface*, were excerpted from the *Sifen Lǜ* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) and compiled by the Śramaṇa Huáisù of Xitāiyuán Temple. Three fascicles of the *Sifen Ní Jiémó* (Sifen Bhikṣuṇī Karma) have the character "Ní" added [to the title]; the rest is identical to the preceding. These four works comprise eight fascicles, all of which are extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Huaisu,
whose secular surname was Fan,
was a native of Jingzhao.
An hereditary crown prince,
he entered the monastic order in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era as a disciple of Master Xuanzang.
By nature intelligent and quick-witted, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of the sutras and śāstras.
After receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the Vinaya;
following the master Cheng Dao under whom he studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
he became a preeminent authority before long.
He first resided at Hongji and later stayed at Taiyuan.
Disciples flocked to him like clouds, and his teaching never ceased.
[He observed that] many of the works compiled by previous masters did not rely on the original texts, but instead followed their own private views, arbitrarily adding or subtracting content.
He then searched through the Vinaya-piṭaka and extracted the *Śīlacitta-karman*.
He took only those passages that were established texts, avoiding any arbitrary fabrication.
It can truly be said that he succeeded to the excellence of Kāśyapa and followed in the footsteps of Upāli.

Furthermore, he separately compiled the *Ji-fen-ji-chao* (Notes on the Record of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) in fifty-odd fascicles, along with commentaries and sub-commentaries on the sutras and śāstras, which are still in circulation today.

The *Dafangguang yuanjue xiduoluo liao yi jing* (The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment of the Great Vaipulya, Explaining the Definitive Meaning), one fascicle: this single work in one fascicle is extant.
The śramaṇa Buddhataḷa— translated into Chinese as Juejiu (Awakening Savior)—
was a native of Jibin in North India.
At the Baima Monastery in the Eastern Capital, he translated one fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-uttarārtha-bodhimaṇḍa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Perfectly Realized Meaning of Bodhi).
This sūtra was recently produced, and its exact date of translation is uncertain;
however, with the intention of propagating the Way, he strove to distinguish between the authentic and the fraudulent.
Since this authentic exposition is unerring, why should it depend on the precise knowledge of its year and month?

The *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, the third edition produced by Du Yi and others, is identical to the version found in the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue) and the preface to the scripture. This one work, in one fascicle, is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Buddhapālita—
translated into Chinese as Juéhù (Juehu)—
was a native of Jibin in North India.
Forsaking his own body to follow the Way, he traveled extensively to visit sacred sites.
Having heard that Mañjuśrī resided on Mount Qingliang,
he journeyed far across the shifting sands to pay his respects in person.
In the first year of the Yifeng era of the Heavenly Emperor (the Bingzi year),
he took up his monk’s staff at Mount Wutai and performed prostrations with utmost sincerity;
weeping with tears falling like rain, he gazed longingly for the sacred countenance.
Suddenly, an old man emerged from the mountains and, speaking in the language of a Brahmin, said to Pāli:
"Master, your sincerity and deep compassion are so profound; what is it that you seek?"
Pālitā replied,
"I have heard that the Great Being Mañjuśrī is dwelling in seclusion on this mountain;
I have come from India wishing to seek him out for veneration."
The old man said,
"Master, did you bring the *Buddhapiṭaka-uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* from that country?
The sentient beings of this land commit many transgressions."
Even among those who have left the household life, there are many who commit transgressions.
This secret method for removing sins through the Buddha-ūṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī—
if you do not bring the scripture, what benefit will it be to come here in vain?
"Even if you were to see Mañjuśrī, how could you necessarily recognize him?
You should return to the Western Land to retrieve that sūtra and circulate it here in this land;
this would be to universally honor all the sages and extensively benefit all living beings."
"To rescue those in the dark realms and repay the kindness of the Buddhas,
you, Master, have brought these scriptures here.
I, your disciple, shall now show you the location where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī resides."
Having heard these words, Pāli was overcome with such joy that he could not contain himself;
he then checked his weeping and prostrated once more toward the mountain.
In the brief moment it took him to raise his head, the old man had suddenly vanished.
Pāri was filled with even greater astonishment and redoubled his devotion;
he returned to his own country, obtained the sūtra,
and upon reaching the imperial capital, sought an audience with the Emperor.
The officials prepared a formal report and presented it to the Emperor.
The Emperor, appreciating their sincere devotion, esteemed this esoteric scripture and subsequently issued an edict for Du Xingyi,
the Director of Guest Reception at the Court of State Ceremonial, and the Tripitaka Master from Japan to translate it together within the palace.
Upon completing the translation, thirty bolts of silk were offered as a dedication.
The scripture was then kept within [the palace].
Pāli then wept and submitted this memorial:
He cast aside his own life, setting his will solely upon benefiting others;
it was his sincere hope that this [text] might be circulated and spread.
The Emperor, moved by his single-minded devotion, [granted his request].
He then left behind the translated scriptures and returned the Sanskrit originals to him, so that they might be circulated as he saw fit.
Pāli was overjoyed at having obtained the scriptures;
he traveled to Ximing Monastery to seek out a monk skilled in the Sanskrit language, Shunzheng, and submitted a memorial requesting that they translate them together.
The Emperor granted his request;
he then, together with the great virtuous ones, translated it alongside Zhen,
and it was titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī*.
Compared with the version previously translated by Prefect Du,
the phonology and scriptural text of this mantra are largely identical with minor differences.
Having fulfilled his aspirations, Poli took the Sanskrit manuscript of the sutra and entered Mount Wutai.
He has not emerged since then, and no one knows where he has gone.
Compared with various other translations, this one is the most widely disseminated;
according to its preface, it states that in the second year of the Yongchun era, it was brought back to the Western Capital.
A formal memorial was submitted for imperial review.
In that same year, he retranslated it together with Shunzhen;
it was titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.

Now, upon examining these accounts, the dates differ slightly: the translation by Du Ling was on the fifth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Yifeng era, while the re-translation by Rizhao was on the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Yongchun era.
Since it is stated that he only reached the borders of the Tang in the second year of the Yongchun era,
from where did he obtain the previous two versions?
Furthermore, by the second year of Yongchun, the Heavenly Emperor had already moved his court to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
How can it be said that this was translated in the capital?
Furthermore, its preface was composed by someone after the Yongchang era;
yet, it recounts earlier events, resulting in discrepancies.
Regarding this translation by Bo-li, its chronological order cannot be definitively established.

One fascicle (or two fascicles) of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, titled "The Chapter on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha," consisting of twelve sheets, was translated at Dongsi in Weiguo in the first year of Yongchang;
it is recorded in the *Dazhou lu* as having been produced both early and later.

The *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra* (Sutra on the Inconceivable State), translated by Śikṣānanda, which is the same text as the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, one fascicle, "Chapter on the Cultivation of Loving-kindness," translated at the Eastern Temple of the Great Zhou in the second year of the Tiangshou era; recorded in the *Da Zhou lu*.

The *Mahāyāna-pratimā-lakṣaṇa-guṇa-sūtra* (Sutra on the Merit of Making Images of the Mahāyāna), two fascicles, or one fascicle, translated at the Eastern Temple of the Great Zhou in the second year of the Tiangshou era.
The temple cataloguer notes that the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra of the Wisdom Torch* (Zhìjù tuóluóní jīng), one fascicle, was translated at the Eastern Temple of the Great Zhou in the second year of Tiānshòu;

it appears in the Great Zhou Catalogue. The temple cataloguer notes that the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra of the Assembly of All Buddhas* (Zhūfó jíhuì tuóluóní jīng), one fascicle, was translated at the Eastern Temple of the Great Zhou in the second year of Tiānshòu;
it appears in the Great Zhou Catalogue. The temple cataloguer notes the *Mahāyāna Treatise on the Non-differentiation of the Dharmadhātu* (Dàshèng fǎjiè wúchābié lùn).
One fascicle. Translated on the fourteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of Tiānshòu at Dàzhōu Dōngsì.
Recorded in the Dàzhōu Catalogue. The aforementioned six sections comprising seven fascicles are all extant.
The śramaṇa Divākara-prajñā,
also called Divākara-jñāna; in the Tang language,
this means "Heavenly Wisdom."
He was a native of Khotan whose learning encompassed both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and whose wisdom spanned both the ultimate and conventional truths.
He was thoroughly proficient in both the arts of incantation and the gates of dhyāna.
In the first year of the Yongchang era of Empress Wu, she arrived here.
In that same year, she had an audience with the Emperor in Luoyang.
By imperial decree, the temple was renamed the Eastern Monastery of the Great Zhou (Dazhou Dongsi) behind the Eastern Monastery of the Wei Kingdom, where he translated scriptures.
From the first year of Yongchang (Jichou) to the second year of Tianshou (Xinmao),
a total of six sections of sutras and treatises were produced,
with the śramaṇas Zhantuo and Huizhi serving as the translators.
The śramaṇa Yicheng served as the scribe;
the śramaṇas Fuli and others compiled the text;
and the śramaṇas Degan, Huiyan, Faming, Hongjing, and others verified the meaning.
*Praise for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; listed in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. This single work, consisting of one fascicle, is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Huizhi’s father was a man from India.
He was of the Brahmin caste.
Having traveled here on a mission, he gave rise to wisdom.
From his youth, he was diligent and possessed the aspiration to transcend the secular world.
During the reign of the Emperor, because he was an elderly Brahmin monk,
he was granted imperial permission to become a disciple.
Since his origins were Indian, he was well-versed in the scripts and languages of India.
Furthermore, having been born in the land of Tang,
he had thoroughly mastered the spoken language of this territory. All translations by the Tripiṭaka masters Divākara, Ratnacinta,
and others were conducted with Zhi summoned to serve as a witness and to facilitate the linguistic transference.
In the second year of the Changshou era (the Guisi year),
the Master Zhi personally translated one fascicle of the *Praise of Avalokiteśvara* at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
The *Dazhou kan ding zhong jing mulu* (Great Zhou Catalogue of Determined Scriptures) in fifteen fascicles: this one work in fifteen fascicles is extant.
It was compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Mingquan, a monk of Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
He was particularly proficient in the Vinaya and was also well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras.
In the first year of the Tiāncè Wànsuì era (the year of Yīmèi), by imperial decree, he was tasked with compiling and determining the catalog of the scriptures;
Xuànquán took charge of recording the titles from beginning to end and arranging them in their proper sequence.
I participated together with more than twenty virtuous masters (bhadanta) who were translating the scriptures in jointly revising and determining the text.
Although it was said that the revisions had eliminated much of the redundancy and corruption,
even as it circulated, it was truly difficult to rely upon as an authoritative standard.
There are discrepancies therein as described elsewhere.
This second edition of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* in eighty fascicles, translated by Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin dynasty from the same original manuscript,
was produced on the fourteenth day of the third month of the first year of Zhengsheng at Dabiankong Temple within the Imperial Palace in the Eastern Capital.
The Empress Dowager personally supervised the editorial revisions. On the eighth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Shengli era, the work was completed at Foshouji Monastery.
The *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-sūtra* in three fascicles was translated at Qingchan Monastery;
this is the third translation, which shares the same text as the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-sūtra*, and is now included in the *Ratnakūṭa* collection as the fifteenth assembly.
*The Great Vaipulya Sūtra on Entering the Inconceivable Wisdom and Virtue of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle; translated at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
This is the fourth translation, which is identical in text to the *Sūtra of the Radiant Adornment of the Wisdom that Transcends the Realms of All Buddhas*.
*The Great Vaipulya Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle; the second translation, which is identical in text to the [translation by] Tiyun Banna (Dharmabhadra).
The *Sūtra Spoken by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva on the Vast and Great Extent* in one fascicle, and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in seven fascicles,
the fourth translation produced together with Gongde Xian and others of the Song dynasty, were both based on the same original text.
They were first issued at the Sanyang Palace in the Eastern Capital on the fifth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Jiushi era, and subsequently reached Chang’an.
On the fifth day of the first month of the fourth year, the transcription was completed:
one fascicle of the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-guhyakoṣa-mantra-sūtra*, which is the same text as that first translated by Baosiwei and others;
one fascicle of the *Subāhu-mudrā-dhvaja-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, which is the second translation and the same text as the *Jaya-dhvaja-bāhu-mudrā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*; and [one fascicle of] the *Śatasahasrikā*.
*The Seal Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; *The Divine Mantra Dhāraṇī Sūtra for Saving the Face-Burning Hungry Ghosts*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra on the Merit of Circumambulating the Buddha Stūpa*, one fascicle (also titled *The Sūtra on the Merit of Circumambulating the Stūpa*);

*The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Four Dharmas*, one fascicle—although the titles of these are identical to those produced by the Tripiṭaka Master Faliu of the Sun Dynasty, their textual substance is entirely different. (10)
*Sūtra on the Paths of Wholesome Action*, one fascicle; *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, two fascicles (the second edition is the same text as that translated by Paramārtha);
*Sūtra of the Great Perfection of Wisdom According to the Mind*, one fascicle; *Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya on Non-arising and Non-ceasing*, one fascicle;
*Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle; *Dhāraṇī of the Stainless Pure Light*.
*Āṭānāṭīya Sūtra*, one fascicle (the initial translation is the same text as that translated by [Kumārajīva] for the *Amitābha Sūtra*). *Bodhisattva-prabhava-caturdharma Sūtra*, one fascicle.
The above nineteen works comprise one hundred and seven fascicles. [Works listed under] the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra*:
fourteen works comprising one hundred and two fascicles, currently extant. [Works listed] below the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*: five works comprising five fascicles, missing.
The original [text] was translated by the śramaṇa Śikṣānanda,
who in the language of Tang means "Delighting in Learning."
A native of Khotan,
his wisdom was vast and expansive, and he took the benefit of sentient beings as his primary concern.
He was proficient in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, as well as the treatises of non-Buddhist schools.
Empress Wu, who illuminated the sun of the Buddha and revered the Mahāyāna,
heard from afar that the Sanskrit original of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* existed in Khotan;
as the existing Chinese translations were incomplete in their assembly of chapters, she dispatched envoys to seek it out.
He also invited the translator Śikṣānanda to arrive at the imperial palace along with the scripture;
thus, in the first year of the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu (the year of Yiwei),
they translated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Dabiankong Monastery within the Great Inner Palace of the Eastern Capital.
The Empress Dowager personally attended the Dharma seat to illuminate the preface with her own hand,
using her immortal brush to inscribe the title of this sublime work.
The Śramaṇa Bodhiruci from South India and the Śramaṇa Yijing together proclaimed the Sanskrit original.
Later, the śramaṇas Fuli, Fazang,
and others translated it at Fo-shou-ji Temple;
the work was completed in the second year of the Shengli era (Jihai).
Furthermore, in the first year of the Jiushi era (the Gengzi year),
he translated the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* within the Sanyang Palace. Additionally,
at Qingchan Temple in the Western Capital and Shouji Temple in the Eastern Capital, he translated the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-sūtra* and other scriptures.
In total, nineteen works were translated from beginning to end.
The śramaṇas Polun and Xuangui and others took dictation,
while the śramaṇa Fuli and others composed the literary style.
The śramaṇas Fabao, Hongjing, and others verified the meaning of the text.
Jia Yingfu, Court Attendant of the Crown Prince, served as supervisor.
In the fourth year of the Chang’an era, Śikṣānanda requested leave to return home to visit his aged mother.
The memorial was submitted once more and was subsequently granted permission.
An imperial edict ordered the Censor Huo Siguang to escort [the relics] to Khotan.
Later, when Emperor He ascended the throne, he caused the sun of the Buddha’s teachings to shine with renewed brilliance.
By imperial decree, he was summoned once more and arrived at the imperial capital;
in the second year of the Jinglong era, he reached this land.
The Emperor, humbling his status as the sovereign of ten thousand chariots, personally went outside the Kaiyuan Gate to welcome him.
The monastics of the capital prepared various banners and streamers to escort him along the road;
furthermore, they adorned a blue elephant for him to ride into the city.
By imperial decree, he was installed at the Great Jianfu Monastery.
Before he had time to complete his translations, he fell ill and remained bedridden until his final moments.
On the twelfth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Jingyun era,
he passed away at Dajianfu Monastery, lying on his right side with his feet crossed.
He was fifty-nine years of age.
The monastic community choked with sobs, lamenting that the pillar of the Dharma had so suddenly collapsed;
the lay followers wailed in grief, regretting that all living beings had lost their guide.
An imperial edict was issued permitting burial according to foreign customs.
On the twelfth day of the eleventh month,
his remains were cremated outside the Kaiyuan Gate at the site of the ancient Lamp-Pillar.
When the fuel was exhausted and the fire extinguished, his tongue remained intact;
this was a magnificent omen of the propagation of the Dharma.
On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month, it reached [the capital].
The disciple of this country, Beizhi, acting as an imperial envoy,
sent back his remains and this miraculous tongue to Khotan, where a stupa was erected for their veneration.
Later, people erected a seven-story stupa at the site where the body was cremated.

The *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (one fascicle), also known as the *Samantamukha*, consists of sixteen chapters; this is a Sanskrit manuscript with a preface composed by the śramaṇa Bolun. This second edition is the same text as the three-fascicle version translated by Baosiwei. This one work, comprising one fascicle, is currently extant.
The Brahmin Li Wuchan was a native of Lampāka in North India.
He possessed keen intelligence and vast learning,
being thoroughly versed in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings.
He was thoroughly proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit without impediment.
When the Tripiṭaka masters Ān-chen-na (Anśena), Bodhiruci,
and others translated various scriptures, they did so without any words of flattery or exaggeration.
In the third month of the gengzi year, the third year of the Shengli era during the reign of Empress Wu,
there was a monk from the kingdom of Silla named Mingxiao who,
having observed the transformation of the Tang, was about to return home.
Having previously devoted his attention to the gateway of dhāraṇī,
he then earnestly and persistently requested that this mantra be translated,
so that those in the remote frontiers might likewise hear this secret teaching.
He then proceeded to the Sutra Translation Hall of the Fo-shou-ji Temple to translate one fascicle of the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
with the śramaṇa Bolun acting as the scribe and recipient of the oral transmission.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Jiushi era, he took the translated scripture and re-examined the Sanskrit original in Kaśmīra before finally transcribing it for circulation.
*The Sutra of the Vimalaprabhāsa-mahādhāraṇī*, one fascicle; this second edition is the same text as the *Vimalaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī* by Śikṣānanda. This single work in one fascicle currently exists.
The śramaṇa Mito-shan (彌陀山),
whose name in the language of Tang is Jiyou (寂友),
was a native of the country of Tukhāra.
Having left home at a young age, he traveled throughout India, studying the sūtras and śāstras extensively;
he was most proficient in the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Resolving to propagate the Semblance Dharma, he had no regard for his own native land.
Carrying his staff and almsbowl, he traveled on foot until he arrived at the Imperial Palace.
During the reign of Empress Wu, he collaborated with Śikṣānanda to translate the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* (Mahāyāna-avatāra-sūtra).

Later, during the final years of Empress Wu’s reign, he translated the *Amoghapāśa-vimala-prabhā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle together with the śramaṇa Fazang and others. Upon completing the translation,
he presented it within the palace, took leave of the Emperor, and returned to his home country.
The Empress Dowager bestowed generous gifts upon him, and he returned to his own country.
*Zhengzhenglun* (Discourse on Rectifying the True), three fascicles; this one work in three fascicles is extant.
[Compiled by] the śramaṇa Shi Xuanyi.
His secular surname was Du and his name was You.
Previously, he had been a Daoist priest serving as the abbot of Dahuangdaoguan in the Eastern Capital.
He roamed his mind through the seven classics and excelled in the three mysteries;
among the Yellow School’s teachings, this served as the guiding principle.
Empress Wu revered the Great Dharma and extensively propagated the Buddhist tradition.
The man subsequently turned his heart toward the Dharma and requested ordination.
An imperial edict granted him permission to enter the monastic order, and he resided at Fo-shou-ji Monastery.
Later, he served as the monastery’s administrative head and also participated in the work of translation.
Having thoroughly understood the emptiness and absurdity of their school and recognizing that the True Teaching is worthy of reliance,
he subsequently composed the *Jianzheng lun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct) in one fascicle to expose their falsehoods;
its dialogues between host and guest are exceedingly concise and essential.

The *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-īśvararāja-sūtra* in three fascicles, also titled the *Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-mantra-rāja-sūtra*, translated at the Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital in the seventh month of the second year of the Changshou era. Transcribed by the śramaṇa Degan.
This initial edition is the same text as the one-fascicle version produced by Li Wuchan; it concerns the merit of bathing the Buddha image.
One fascicle. Translated on the twenty-second day of the first month in the first year of the Shénlóng era at Dàfúxiān Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
Li Wúchǎn, a Brāhmaṇa, served as the oral translator. This initial translation was collated with the later version produced by Yìjìng.
*Jiǔshù Gōngdé Jīng* (Sūtra on the Merits of Rosaries), one fascicle. Translated on the twenty-third day of the first month in the first year of the Shénlóng era at [Dàfúxiān Monastery].

*The Sūtra of the Wish-Fulfilling Maṇi Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle: translated at Fuxian Temple by Li Wuchan as the initial version, identical to the later edition produced by Yi Jing;
second edition, identical to the version produced by Śikṣānanda and others. *The Mañjuśrī-mūla-ekākṣara-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one [fascicle].
One fascicle. Translated at Tiangong Monastery in the second year of the Chang’an era [702 CE] by the śramaṇa Huizhi and others, who verified the Sanskrit text;

the Brahmin Li Wuchan translated the oral glosses, and Li Wu’ai of the Zhongshu Sheng recorded the text in writing. This initial translation is identical in its original source to the later version produced by Yi Jing.
*The Great Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Single-Syllable Heart-Mantra for the Age of Dharma’s Decline*, one fascicle. Translated during the Shenlong era [705–707 CE].

In the first year [of the Longshou era], at Dafuxian Monastery, Li Wuchan served as the oral translator for the *Suqiu jide da zizai tuoluoni shenzhou jing* (One Scroll), also known as the *Suo dejian*; it is recorded in the *Dazhou lu*.
In the second year of the Longshou era, at Tiangong Monastery in the Eastern Capital, the Kapiśa śramaṇa Śrīnanda and others verified the Sanskrit text.
Li Wuchan translated the oral explanations; Li Wunai received them in writing. The texts for these seven sections in nine fascicles are all extant.
The śramaṇa A-ni-zhen-na—translated into Chinese as Baosiwei (Ratnamati)—[compiled them].
He was a native of Kaśmīra in North India,
of the Kṣatriya caste,
and a scion of that king’s noble lineage.
Having left home at a young age, he took the practice of meditation and recitation as his vocation.
After receiving full ordination, he specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka;
furthermore, his wisdom and understanding surpassed his peers, and his learning encompassed both the ultimate and conventional truths.
He was exceptionally skilled in the arts of *qianwen* and incantations, reaching their very essence.
Furthermore, with conversion and guidance as his primary concern, he felt no attachment to his native land.
In the second year of the Changshou era of Empress Wu (the Gui-si year), he arrived at the capital of Luoyang.
An imperial edict ordered that it be enshrined at Tiangong Monastery.
This was from the second year of the Changshou era of Empress Wu (Gui-si) until the second year of the Shenglong era of Emperor Zhongzong (Bing-wu).
In the Shouji Temple, Tiangong Temple, Fuxian Temple,
and other monasteries, he translated seven works, including the *Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Later, in the fourth month of the Renzi year, the first year of Emperor Ruizong’s Taicheng era, he arrived [at court].
The Palace Attendant for Washing Horses, Zhang Qixian, and others transcribed the text and presented it to the Inner Court.
In the sixth month of the first year of the Yanyang era,

an imperial decree was issued ordering the Minister of Rites, the Duke of Jin Xue Ji, the Right Attendant-in-Ordinary, Marquis of Gaoping Xu Yanbo, and others to examine and finalize the contents for implementation.
From the second year of the Shenlong era onward, the Tripitaka Master no longer translated scriptures;
he devoted himself solely to diligent prostrations, recitations, and the cultivation of various meritorious deeds.
Every morning, he would grind incense into water to bathe the Buddha images before partaking of food and drink.
From beginning to end, this was his constant practice.
Beyond his robes and alms bowl, he gave away whatever he obtained as soon as he acquired it.
Later, at Longmen Mountain, he requested that a monastery be established there.
Manufactured according to foreign styles, they were called "Indic" (Tianzhu).
Together with his disciples, he resided in this monastery;
moved by their sincere devotion, those who joined them became truly numerous.
He lived for over a hundred years and passed away at the monastery in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era.
His ten-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* was the fifth translation, corresponding to the four-fascicle version by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang dynasty.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, etc., translated at Ximing Monastery on the fourth day of the tenth month in the third year of Chang’an;
the śramaṇa Bolun Hui served as the scribe and received the text.

One fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the fifth translation, produced together with those by Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin, Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei, Paramārtha of the Chen, and others.
Translated on the fourth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Yongchang era at Ximing Monastery:
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha to Nanda on Leaving Home and Entering the Womb*, two fascicles.
Translated in the fourth year of the Jinglong era at Dayanfu Monastery from the eleventh and twelfth fascicles of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*; now included in the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The Fourteenth Assembly, renamed the *Womb-Treasury Assembly*, titled *The Scripture on Entering the Samādhi of the Fixed and the Unfixed Seal*, one fascicle;
the second edition, identical in text to the *Scripture on the Non-Certain Entry into the Samādhi of the Seal* translated by Gautama Dharmaruci of the Northern Wei.
Completed on the fifth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Jiushi era. [The following is] the *Seven Buddhas’ Original Vows of Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha*.

The *Gongde jing* (Sūtra on Merit), two fascicles; the fourth translation, which is the same text as that produced by Dharmagupta and others during the Sui dynasty, differing only in its degree of elaboration or brevity.

It was translated in the summer of the third year of the Shenlong era at the Foguang Hall within the Imperial Palace. At that time, the Emperor personally presided over the dharma assembly and received the text by hand with his own brush.
The *Mile xiasheng chengfo jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born as a Buddha), one fascicle; the sixth translation, [which is the same text as] that by Kumārajīva... [and others].

The *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching of the Dharma for King Śrīprabha* (one fascicle), translated at the Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital on the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the first year of the Dazú era;

this third edition is identical in its original text to the earlier *Sūtra on Admonishing the King* and the Tang translation of the *Sūtra of King Śrīsena*, both produced in the seventh month of the first year of the Shénlóng era.

On the fifteenth day [of the fourth month], at the Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital, the *Yuxiang Gongde Jing* (Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Image) in one fascicle was translated by the śramaṇa Xuansu, who acted as scribe;
this second edition is identical in text to that produced by Baosiwei.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth month of the Jinglong era (710 CE), the *Shuzhu Gongde Jing* (Sūtra on the Merit of the Rosary) in one fascicle was translated at the Translation Hall of the Dajianfu Monastery.

The second edition, which shares the same original text as that produced by Ratnabhadra, was translated at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery on the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Jinglong era;
it consists of one fascicle of the *Ārya-avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-cintāmaṇi-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
The third edition, which shares the same original text as those produced by Śikṣānanda, Ratnabhadra, and others, is likewise included herein.
In the fourth year of the Jinglong era, at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery, one fascicle of the *Ekākṣara-vidyārāja-sūtra* from the *Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-mantra-piṭaka* was translated;
this second edition is identical in text to that produced by Baosiwei.
On the fourth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Chang’an era, the *Tathāgata-guṇa-varṇana-devatā-sūtra* was translated at Ximing Monastery.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; the second edition, identical in text to the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas* translated during the Sui dynasty.
Translated on the twenty-third day of the intercalary sixth month in the second year of the Jingyun era at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery.
Recorded by brush by the śramaṇas Xuansan, Zhiji, and others. *The Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī Sūtra*, three fascicles; the eighth edition, identical in text to...
The *Buddhottama-śikhara-uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by Saṃghavarman and others during the Shenlong era (705 CE) at the Inner Court of the Eastern Capital;
this is the fifth translation, identical to the version produced by Du Xingyi,
Rizhao, Puli, and others, translated at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery in the Jinglong era (710 CE).

*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of King Adornment*, one fascicle; translated on the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the first year of the Dazú era at Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Incense King Bodhisattva*, one fascicle;
translated in the first year of the Shénlóng era at Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital. *The Sūtra of the King Adorned with All Merits*, one [fascicle].

One fascicle of the *Rājan-mantra for Eradicating Karmic Obstructions*, translated on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Jiǎlóng era at Dàfúxiān Monastery in the Eastern Capital;
recorded by the śramaṇa Xuānsàn as scribe. One fascicle of the *Sujāta-sūtra*, translated in the fourth year of the Jǐnglóng era at the Sūtra Translation Institute of Dàjiànfú Monastery.
On the twenty-third day of the ninth month in the first year of the Dàzú era...
On the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the first year of the Dazú era, at the Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital, he translated the *Mahāyāna-saṃsāra-bhava-sūtra* in one fascicle.

On the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the first year of the Dazú era, at the Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital, he translated the *Suvarṇavarṇa-rāja-nidāna-sūtra* in one fascicle. At the Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital... [text repeats].
*The Sūtra on the Seal of the Dharma Spoken by the Buddha to the Nāga King Sāgara*, one fascicle.
Translated at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery on the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the second year of the Jingyun era. Received by the śramaṇas Xuansan, Zhiji, and others.
*The Verses on the Treatise of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra that Can Sever [Delusion]*, one fascicle. By Asaṅga Bodhisattva.
In the second year of the Jingyun era, at the Translation Institute of Dajianfu Monastery,

the *Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in three fascicles— composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga in verse and explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu— was translated by Śramaṇa Xuanzang, with Zhiji and others serving as scribes.
This was undertaken in the second year of the Jingyun era at the Translation Institute of Dajianfu Monastery.
The *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Gateway to Right Reasoning), one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Śrīlāta;
translated at the Translation Hall of Da Jianfu Monastery in the second year of the Jingyun era by the śramaṇas Xuansan, Zhiji, and others, with Xuansan and Zhiji serving as scribes.
This second edition is identical in text to that translated by Dharma Master Xuanzang. Completed at the Chengyou... [text ends].

*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), five fascicles; also known as the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā-bhāṣya*. Composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla.
Translated at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery on the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Jinglong era. Scribe: Śramaṇas Xuansu, Zhiji, and others.
*Ālambanaparīkṣā-vyākhyāna* (Commentary on the Examination of Objects of Cognition), one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla. Translated in the [Jinglong] era.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Longshuo era, at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery, the *Pāṇipraharaṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on Striking with the Palm), one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga, was translated;
Śramaṇas Xuansu, Zhiji, and others acted as scribes. This second edition shares the same text as the *Vigraha-vyāvartanī*.
It was taken [for translation] on the fourteenth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Chang’an era at Ximing Monastery.

*Prajñapti-śāstra* (Treatise on Designations), one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Dignāga. Translated on the fourth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Chang’an era at Ximing Monastery;
received by the śramaṇa Huìbiǎo as scribe. *Sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-parīkṣā-kārikā* (Verses on the Examination of Universal Characteristics), one fascicle.
Composed by Bodhisattva Dignāga. Translated in the second year of the Jǐngyún era at the Translation Hall of Dà Jiànfú Monastery by the śramaṇas Zhìjī and others.

*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-kārikā* (Verses on the Stages of Yoga Practice), one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated at the Translation Institute of Dajianfu Monastery in the second year of the Jingyun era;
scribes included the śramaṇa Xuansan and others. *Danda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hand-staff), one fascicle; composed by the Venerable Śākyaprabha;
translated at the Translation Institute of Dajianfu Monastery in the second year of the Jingyun era; [scribes included] the śramaṇa... [text ends].

*The Treatise on the Practice of Concentration Based on the Six Gates of Instruction*, one fascicle; transcribed by Xuansan and others. Originally composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga and commented upon by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated at Ximing Monastery on the fourth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Chang’an era.

*The Sūtra on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates*, one fascicle; extracted from the second fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; a different translation made in the fourth year of the Jinglong era at Dà... [Monastery].
*The Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma*, one fascicle; translated at the Translation Hall of Jianfu Monastery by the śramaṇa Zhiji and others as scribe.

Extracted from the fifteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. Translated in the fourth year of the Jinglong era at the Translation Hall of the Great Jianfu Monastery, with the śramaṇa Xuansan and others as scribes.
*The Sūtra on Impermanence*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra on the Three [Turnings]*.
Translated on the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the first year of the Dazhu era at Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital:

*The Sūtra of the Eight Unfavourable and Favourable Conditions*, one fascicle. Translated on the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the first year of the Dazhu era at Dafuxian Monastery in the Eastern Capital:
*The Sūtra of the Questions of the Brahmacārin Dīrghanakha*, one fascicle. [Translated] in the tenth month of the Jiushi era...
On the twenty-third day of the second month, at Dàfúxiān Monastery in the Eastern Capital, one fascicle of the *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra* was translated.
On the twenty-third day of the intercalary sixth month in the second year of the Jǐngyún era, at the Translation Hall of Dàjiànfú Monastery,
one fascicle of the *Saṃkṣiptopadeśa-sūtra* was translated, with the śramaṇa Xuānsǎn and others acting as scribes.

One fascicle of the *Liao zhí bìng jīng* (Sutra on the Treatment of Hemorrhoids), also known as the *Zhǐ lòu [jīng]*, translated at the Translation Hall of the Monastery by the śramaṇa Zhìjī and others, with scribes including the śramaṇa Xuānsǎn;
translated at the Translation Hall of Dà Jiànfú Monastery in the fourth year of the Jǐnglóng era.
Fifty fascicles of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, translated in the tenth month of the third year of the Cháng'ān era.
On the fourth day of the month, at Ximing Monastery, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* in twenty fascicles was translated;

the śramaṇa Bolun Huiyao and others served as scribes. In the fourth year of the Jinglong era, at the Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* in forty fascicles was translated.
In the fourth year of the Jinglong era, translated at the Sūtra Translation Hall of Dajianfu Monastery:
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-nidāna-mātṛkā*, ten fascicles (or eight fascicles). On the fourth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Chang’an era, translated at Ximing Monastery:
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃvara-sūtra*, one fascicle. [Both dated] the fourth year of the Jinglong era.
One fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra* was translated at the Translation Institute of Dajianfu Monastery in the fourth year of the Jinglong era.

Ten fascicles of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karmavācanā* were translated at the Translation Institute of Dajianfu Monastery on the fourth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Chang’an era at Ximing [Monastery].
The *Vinaya-kārikā* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, five fascicles, composed by the Venerable Viśākha;

The Śramaṇa Shi Yi-jing was a native of Qizhou.
His secular surname was Zhang and his courtesy name was Wénmíng.
Having renounced worldly glory and cast off finery at the age of seven,
he subsequently sought out renowned masters and extensively explored a vast array of scriptures.
He was thoroughly versed in both internal and external teachings and possessed universal knowledge of the past and present.
At the age of fifteen, he resolved to travel to the Western Regions,
admiring the noble conduct of Faxian.
He admired the lofty character of Xuanzang;
moreover, he was diligent without wasting a moment, never setting down his scrolls.
Having received full ordination in his early twenties, he redoubled his efforts, remaining steadfast and resolute.
In the second year of the Xianheng era, at the age of thirty-seven, he finally realized his long-held aspiration.
He traveled to Guangzhou and first formed a vow with like-minded companions until their number reached ten;
however, by the time they boarded the ship, all but a few had withdrawn and desisted.
With his pure and steadfast mind burning ever more intensely, he set out alone.
Having endured countless hardships, he gradually reached India.
In every land he visited, he thoroughly mastered their languages and dialects.
Whenever he encountered kings or ministers, all received his profound respect.
He personally ascended both Vulture Peak and Cock’s Foot Mountain,
and traveled throughout both the Jetavana Grove and the Deer Park.
He rested at Nālandā and paid homage to the Bodhi tree;
having studied both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna under various masters and experts,
he completed his tasks and returned to his native village.
In all, he traveled through more than thirty countries,
spending over twenty years journeying back and forth to seek the Way.
In the second month of summer in the year of Yiwei, the first year of the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu, he returned to the region of the Yellow and Luo Rivers.
He brought approximately four hundred Sanskrit texts of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Pitakas, totaling five hundred thousand stanzas;
one set of the true likeness of the Vajrāsana;
and three hundred grains of śarīra.
The Empress Dowager, revering the Dharma and honoring the person, personally went out to meet him outside the Upper East Gate.
The monastics of Luoyang prepared banners and streamers and arranged drums and music to lead the procession ahead.
By imperial decree, he was stationed at Foshouji Monastery,
where all the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought were ordered to be translated.
Initially, he collaborated with the Khotanese Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda to translate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
After the Jǔshì era, he himself began the translation.
From the first year of Jǔshì, the Gēnzǐ year, until the third year of Cháng'ān, the Wǒmǎo year,
he worked at Fúxiān Monastery in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and Xīmíng Monastery in the Western Capital (Cháng'ān).
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-rāja-sūtra*,
the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*,

Auspicious Night:

Impermanence;
the eight states of no leisure and the state of leisure;

And in the *Vinayasamgraha* and other texts,

Subsequently, in the first year of the Shenglong era (the year of Yisi), when Emperor Zhongzong ascended the throne,

Furthermore, at Dafuxian Monastery, he translated four scriptures in six fascicles, including the *Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Bodhisattva Gandharvarāja of the Victorious Light Devaputra* and the *Sūtra on the King Adorned with All Merits*.
The śramaṇa Pantu read the Sanskrit text;
the śramaṇa Xuansan received it by pen;
and the śramaṇa Dayi verified the text.
The śramaṇas Śaṅghabhadra and Lìzhēn and others verified the meaning;
Cúí Tí, Minister of War, and Lú Càn, Palace Aide, and others polished the text;
and Yáng Shènjiāo, Grand Supervisor of the Imperial Library, Prince Consort, Duke of Guànguó, supervised the project.
Emperor He held the Buddhist scriptures in high esteem and composed a preface to extol them,
titled "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang’s Dragon Ascension.
The Emperor then presided at the West Gate of Luocheng.
He issued a proclamation to all the rulers to ensure that newly translated scriptures were clearly cited and referenced.
In the second year, the Bingwu year, he returned to the capital in the imperial entourage.
By imperial decree, a separate Translation Institute was established within Dajianfu Monastery to house him there.
In the third year, the *dingwei* year, the Emperor summoned him into the palace,
where he sat together with nine other śramaṇas translating scriptures during the ninety-day summer retreat.
The Emperor remarked that in the past, when he resided in Fangbu, he had been in a state of profound distress and destitution, with no one to turn to for refuge.
Through his prayers to Bhaisajyaguru, he was granted divine blessings;
thus, this profound benefit was celebrated as it once again elucidated the great Way.
Consequently, he commanded his disciples to retranslate the text.
It was translated in two fascicles at the Dafoguang Hall under the title *Yaoshi liuliguang qifo benyuan gongde jing*.
The Emperor personally attended the Dharma assembly and transcribed the text by hand.
Furthermore, in the fourth year of the Jinglong era, the gengxu year,
he translated the "Merit of Bathing the Buddha Image" at Dajianfu Monastery.

The layman Gōutámba Vajra from Eastern India, Prince Āshùn of Kaśmīra, and others verified and translated it.

More than twenty individuals, including Li Jiao (Vice President of the Xiuwen Pavilion, Special Advance, Duke of Zhao), Wei Sili (Minister of War, Viscount Xiaoyao), Zhao Yanzhao (Vice Director of the Secretariat), Lu Zangyong (Vice Minister of Personnel), Zhang Yue (Vice Minister of War), Li Yi, and Su Ting (all Secretaries of the Secretariat), successively refined the text with literary elegance.

Although Jing translated across all three collections of the Tripiṭaka, he devoted his primary efforts to the Vinaya section.
In the intervals between his translation work, he privately instructed his disciples;
in all his activities, he valued promptness above all else.
His straining [of water] to remove impurities was particularly extraordinary compared to his contemporaries.
His practice was transmitted among his fellow students throughout the capitals of Jing and Luo.
How magnificent! It is truly a great event for the legacy of the Dharma.
He passed away in the second year of the Xiāntián era at the age of seventy-nine.

The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* in one hundred and twenty fascicles was translated through both single and combined efforts; its initial commencement was in the second year of the Shénlóng era, and its completion was achieved in the second year of the Xiāntián era. Thus, this collection consists of forty-nine sūtras, both newly and previously translated, which have been consolidated into a single work.
From among these, twenty-six assemblies comprising thirty-nine fascicles were newly translated by Bodhiruci;
the remaining twenty-three assemblies comprise eighty-one fascicles.
All of these have been included after collating them with the old translations;

it is the same text as the "Section on the Principle of Profundity" (*Liqufen*) from the tenth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, differing slightly in length and detail. It was produced at the Eastern Capital in the second year of the Changshou era.

His original name was Dharmaruci,
which means "Dharma-Desire" in the language of Tang;
Empress Wu changed it to Bodhiruci.
In the Tang language, his name was Jue’ai (Jñānapriya).
He was a native of South India and of Brahmin descent.
His clan name was Kāśyapa.
He was of peerless intelligence, and his countenance and spirit were exceptionally refined and extraordinary.
At the age of twelve, he left home to join the non-Buddhist sects.
The Master received instruction from Bhāsarvajña and studied his scriptural doctrines;
he subsequently attained profound mastery of *śabda-vidyā* (phonology and grammar) and was particularly well-versed in *sāṃkhya* and *nyāya*.
He understood the principles of yin and yang, calendrical calculations, geomancy, astronomy, incantations, and medical prescriptions as clearly as if they were the palms of his hands.
Having reached the age of sixty, he considered himself capable of acting independently and offered his person as a wager for a debate with the monks.
At that time, there was a Tripitaka Master of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school named Yaśoghoṣa.
Knowing that his faculties were ripe, he proceeded to engage him in debate;
before many rounds had passed, the other was utterly defeated in both rhetoric and reasoning.
Only then did he realize that the sun of the Buddha’s wisdom is of such lofty brilliance that it cannot be matched by the glow of a firefly.
The ocean of Dharma is so deep and vast; how could it be moistened by a mere drop?
Thereupon, he submerged his entire being in reverent service, devoting himself exclusively to the study of the Buddha-vehicle.
He upheld the precepts without flaw, his will and integrity lofty and steep.
Chonghui was profoundly learned and possessed vast and deep understanding;
within five years, he had mastered the Tripitaka.
Hearing of his elegant reputation from afar, the Emperor dispatched an envoy to invite him.
Before he could even send a messenger back, the white clouds suddenly bore him away.
It was only when Empress Wu ascended the throne that he finally set out for the imperial capital,
arriving at the metropolis in the second year of the Changshou era (the Gui-si year).
In that same year, at Fo-shou-ji Temple, he translated the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*.
A śramaṇa from the King’s envoy of Central India, Dharmabhadra, jointly proclaimed the Sanskrit original.
The śramaṇa Zhantuo and the layman Brahmin Li Wuchan served as translators of the vernacular.
The śramaṇa Huizhi acted as the verifier of the oral translation;
the śramaṇa Chuyi and others served as scribes;
and the śramaṇa Sixuan and others composed the written text.
The śramaṇas Yuance, Shenyi, and others verified the meaning;
Sun Pi, Vice Director of the Office of State Guests, served as the supervisor.
Later, at the Eastern Monastery in the Great Zhou, he translated the *Bhūtakoṭiprajñāpāramitā*.
Vajramukuṭa, Mahāyānagayākūṭa,
Guṇamati, and Sumati.
The *Mañjuśrī-acintya-viṣaya-sūtra*,
the *Sundarī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and others;
furthermore, at the Buddha-śāsana-vihāra.
Translated as: The Dharma Gate for Protecting Life;
the Six-Syllable Divine Mantra; Prajñāpāramitā.
The Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī;

The *Guhyasusthita-sūtra* and others,

totaling nineteen works comprising twenty fascicles.
The *Shamen xinggan deng* (Equal Translations of the Conduct of Śramaṇas) was translated [by him].
Later, arriving during the reign of Emperor Hè, in the second year of the Shénlóng era (the Bingwǔ year), he accompanied the imperial entourage back to the capital.
By imperial decree, he was settled at Xīchóngfú Temple.
He then translated the *Mahāratnakūṭa-amoghapāśa-vikurvāṇa*,
the *Ekākṣara-uddhāra-uṣṇīṣa*,
and the *Sahasrabhuja-sahasranetra-mātṛ-dhāraṇī*.
The *Sūtra of the Wish-Fulfilling Wheel*,
the *Mañjuśrī-ratnakara*,
the *Vajra-jvālā*, and other such scriptures.
And the Mahāratnakūṭa.
This sutra consists of forty-nine assemblies in total;
however, translators of previous generations excerpted individual assemblies and translated them separately, without completing the entire collection.
In the past, during the Zhenguan era, Dharma Master Xuanzang traveled to India and returned with Sanskrit manuscripts.
At Hongfu Monastery, he translated the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*,
which is the first assembly of the twelfth section of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
Later, after the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* had been completed at the Yuhua Palace Monastery, the virtuous monks earnestly requested that he translate the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
Master Xuanzang remarked,
"The merit of translating the *Ratnakūṭa* shall not fall short of that of the *Prajñāpāramitā*."
"My life is already at its end, and I fear I shall not complete this task.
Although he pleaded earnestly and without ceasing, I finally began the translation from the interlinear notes.
After reaching only a few lines, I sighed and lamented, saying:
This sutra has no affinity with the sentient beings of this land;
my own strength is exhausted and I am unable to accomplish it,
so I have consequently desisted.
On the following day, Paramārtha arrived bringing the Sanskrit manuscript with him.
Emperor Wu ordered Paramārtha to continue the unfinished work of Xuanzang;
he subsequently gathered many eminent scholars and summoned renowned Confucianists.
I have examined the scriptures translated in previous dynasties and compared them with the newly arrived *jia* (interlinear) editions;
where the translations of former generations could be verified as identical, they have been appended.
Since ancient times, no complete translation of the original manuscript had been produced;
furthermore, old interpretations had long obscured the detailed text.
Thus, beginning in the second year of the Shénlóng era (the Bǐngwǔ year), the assembly was first convened.
It concluded at the banquet held in the second year of the Xuantian era of Emperor Ruizong,
the Gui-chou year; among these, twenty-six assemblies comprising thirty-nine fascicles were newly translated by Paramārtha.
These are the Trisamaya Assembly,
the Anantavyūha Assembly,
and the Amitāyus Tathāgata Assembly.
The Assembly of Akṣobhya Tathāgata;
