The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* assembly and the *Vaiśālī-pradeśa-ṛṣi-sūtra* assembly were first initiated on the day of the title-bestowing ceremony at the Foguang Hall within the Imperial Palace; Emperor Wu personally presided over the Dharma assembly and acted as the scribe to receive the essential meanings of the scriptures.
The hundred officials sat in attendance while the consorts and queens viewed it together;
even seeking among the ancients, nothing could surpass this.
Upon the succession of the throne by Emperor Ruizong, [the image] was further enshrined in the White Lotus Pavilion of Beiyuan and the Gānlù Hall of the Imperial Palace.
Biekaishou also received it in his own hand.
It was translated from the Sanskrit by the śramaṇa Sijing and the great leader of East India, Ishvara, along with Zhizhongshu, Dupogu, and others.
The śramaṇa Dharma from North India and the śramaṇa Prajñācūḍa from South India verified the Sanskrit meanings;
the śramaṇas Huijue, Zongyi, Pujing, Lifang, and others transcribed the text.
The śramaṇas Shengzhuang, Fazang, Chenwai, Wuzhuo, Shenliang, Huadi, and others verified the meaning;
the śramaṇas Chengli, Shenjian, Yunguan, and others subsequently arranged the text.

The text was polished by Xu Jian (Duke of Donghai Commandery), Director of the Household for the Crown Prince; Lu Can (Earl of Gu'an), Tutor to Prince Bin; Lu Zangyong (Baron of Donghai), Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs; Su Jie (Baron of Yewang), Secretariat Drafter; Peng Jingzhi, Minister of Rites; Wang Jie (Baron of Qi County), Left Assistant in the Imperial Library; Yan Wenzhi, Vice Director of the Court of the Imperial Treasury; and He Zhizhang, Doctor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Lu Xiangxian, Vice Director of the Secretariat and Marquis of Pingyu, and Wei Zhigu, Palace Attendant and Duke of Julu, served as supervisors of the translation.
Xue Chongyin, former Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Yang Zhongsu, Gentleman of the Palace Attendants and Baron of Hongnong, served as supervisors of the protection.
Once the transcription was completed, the original manuscript was presented to the Inner Palace.
Emperor Ruizong, who governed the myriad regions abroad while venerated the Triple Gem within,
personally composed a preface to be placed at the beginning of the scripture.
In total, he translated fifty-three works comprising one hundred and eleven fascicles.
Once the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* was completed by Samghapāla and Dharmaruci, they no longer translated further scriptures.
He delighted his spirit through Zen contemplation and nurtured his will through the Golden Elixir;
though his lifespan exceeded a hundred years, his cultivation of the Way remained unimpaired.
He maintained the recitation of scriptures and walking meditation, never ceasing from morning until night.
In the twelfth year of the Kaiyuan era, he accompanied the imperial entourage to Luoyang.
By imperial decree, he was stationed at Changshou Temple;
because it was added to the residence where Fazhi had stayed, the temple was renamed Kaiyuan.
In the ninth month of the fifteenth year,
he turned to his disciples and said,
"This body of bubbles and illusions is daily approaching decay and ruin."
"Though one may dwell for a long time, in the end all things are subject to decay.
I have spent my years in self-nourishment, hoping to avoid decline;
yet now that I am gradually approaching old age, it is in vain to merely prolong my time."
Thereupon, for twenty days, he neither drank nor ate, severing all use of medicine and food.
Although nearly fifty days had passed, his countenance and spirit remained unchanged.
On the third day of the eleventh month, he then requested scented water for a bath and changed into fresh, clean garments.
On the morning of the fourth day,
he took up various sutras from the Sanskrit originals, holding each one aloft upon his head and offering praise for each.
On the fifth day, at the time of the midday meal, he arrived.
He addressed his attendants, ordering them all to disperse:
"I shall retire briefly to a place of quietude; do not make any noise.
Thereupon, within the pure chamber, he lay down on his right side and passed away suddenly.
He was one hundred and fifty-six years old.
Were it not for his accumulation of superior deeds and his casting off of worldly toil,
how could he have preserved such a long life?
Whether departing or remaining, one must rely solely on oneself.

Having heard these words, the Emperor’s heart was moved by deep admiration; he sighed with profound grief for a long time and subsequently conferred upon him the posthumous title of Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Daqing).
He was posthumously titled the Tripitaka Master Kaiyuan Yiqiebianzhi.
An imperial decree dispatched the inner attendant Du Huaijing to the Eastern Capital to supervise the funeral,
and the Imperial Treasury was ordered to provide all necessary items for the burial expenses.
He caused them to be provided in infinite numbers.
Thereupon, the ceremonial processions, feathered insignia, banners, streamers,
and flowered canopies filled the streets and alleys beyond counting.
He subsequently moved the remains for interment at Longmen and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
One fascicle of the *Pañcavargika-karman*, titled *The Original Text of the Mahīśāsaka-karman*—this one work in one fascicle is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Ai-tong was of the secular surname Zhao;
he was originally a native of Tianshui.
He inherited the ancestral lineage and rectified past grievances.
Having entered the monastic order at a young age, he became renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya;
he lectured on the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya, becoming a teacher followed by disciples from both near and far.
Formerly, during the Song dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Jue-shou of Kaśmīra translated the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya and produced one fascicle of the Karma-vastu.
As time passed, its original manuscript has fallen into disrepair and become fragmentary.
Seeking it without success, the scholars were left without a basis for practice.
Consequently, they excerpted one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā* from within the *Mahāvinaya*,
which was widely circulated and propagated by the scholars of that school.
The *Xinyi Huayan Yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Newly Translated Avataṃsaka), two fascicles. This one work in two fascicles is extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan was a native of Jingzhao.
He was a preeminent disciple of Dharma Master Huayan-zang.
Diligent in his studies and free from indolence, he was proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning;
he was particularly adept in the Avatamsaka school.
As the newly translated scriptures lacked phonetic glosses and definitions,
those who read them had no basis upon which to rely for understanding.
Consequently, Yuan extensively consulted various character dictionaries and compiled this work in two fascicles.
This is so that those who study it need not seek teachers from afar to resolve the meanings of the characters.

*The Sūtra on the Definitive Karmic Obstructions Spoken of the Sublime Dharma*, one fascicle; second translation, identical in text to the *Sūtra Praising the Merits of the Mahāyāna* translated by Master Xuanzang; translated at the Laoyin Aranya in Shibi Valley, Zhongnan Mountains, in the sixth month of the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era. *The Dhāraṇī of the Gate of Producing the Boundless*, one fascicle; eleventh translation, identical in text to the *Sūtra of the Immeasurable Gates of the Subtle and Secret Retention*; translated at Feng'en Temple in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era. *The Sūtra of King Siṃhasauḍasa’s Abstinence from Meat*, one fascicle; translated at Feng'en Temple in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era. *The Essential Compendium of Various Sūtras on the Mahāyāna Practice of the Bodhisattva Path*, three fascicles; translated at the Laoyin Aranya in Shibi Valley, Zhongnan Mountains, on the twentieth day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era. The above four works comprise six fascicles, and their original texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan was the hostage son of the King of Khotan.
His surname was Yuchi and his given name was Lulu (pronounced lu with the second tone). Having arrived in the Great Tang in his youth, he early on enjoyed honorable rank and emolument.
He was appointed as General of the Left Guard (Zuolingjunwei Dajiangjun), Grand Marshal of the State (Shangzhuguo), and enfeoffed as Duke of Jinman Commandery.
By nature he was simple and sincere, with integrity and faithfulness dwelling in his heart;
he requested to donate his residence to establish a monastery in honor of the state.
On the eleventh day of the fifth month in the second year of the Shénlóng era, an imperial edict granted his request.
Furthermore, he reflected upon himself: born in a foreign land, he had grown up in the Central Kingdom;
by good fortune, he has served four successive reigns, reaching the pinnacle of honor and glory.
Fearing that he might continue to receive such generous emoluments and unworthily bask in extraordinary favor,
he then resolutely requested to leave the household life, hoping thereby to repay the profound grace [of the Emperor].
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the second year of the Shénlóng era, an imperial edict in black ink (mòzhì) stated:
In the nature of human beings, there are none who do not covet and cherish rank and emolument;
yet your aspiration is to renounce the mundane world and leave the household life,
following the traces of the *araṇya* and undertaking the practice of *dhyāna*.
Upon suddenly reviewing this memorial, I sighed in admiration and felt deep appreciation.
I have specially granted your request to fulfill your lofty aspiration on the fifth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Jinglong era, which coincides with the Emperor’s birthday.
Having left his home and shaved his head, he took the dharma-name Zhìyán.
He then requested to reside at the Zhìxiāng Monastery hermitage on Mount Zhōngnán to cultivate the Way.
There, he continued to practice with an empty mind, engaging in quiet meditation, seated contemplation, and walking meditation.
With diligent asceticism dwelling in his heart and profound contemplation accumulated through long seclusion,
he was further endowed with a mastery of both Chinese and Sanskrit scriptures that illuminated even the most subtle mysteries.
There were no true expositions of the *Ratnakūṭa* or secret verses of the Tathāgata that he did not receive repeatedly.
For a long time, he has been entrusted with the task of revising and examining imperial edicts;
moreover, he has frequently received the Emperor’s personal instructions to serve as a proofreader and translator.
He currently resides in the Shíbiè Valley in an āraṇya, practicing the dhūta austerities.
In the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era, at Shibi Lianruo and Feng'en Monasteries,
he translated four works, including the *Deciding Karma Obstructions Sūtra* (*Niścitakarmāvaraṇa-sūtra*).
These were all characterized by a balance of literary elegance and substantive depth, capturing their profound significance.
Furthermore, he translated one chapter of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī and six chapters of dhāraṇīs from the Lotus Sūtra, such as those of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva.
At that time, there were copies of the scriptures in which newly transcribed dhāraṇīs had been inserted.

Please do not take offense. The *One-Scroll Sūtra of the Great Dhāraṇī of the Mother of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas, Cundī*, translated by Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta (Nichiō), is the second version produced; its original manuscript is the same as that of the *Four-Scroll Ritual for Recitation Briefly Extracted from the Vajraśekhara Yoga*. Also, the *One-Scroll Sūtra of the Five-Syllable Heart Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva* from the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, and the *One-Scroll Essential Methods of Yoga for Avalokiteśvara and Cintāmaṇicakra Bodhisattva*. These three sūtras were all translated from Sanskrit manuscripts using abridged excerpts of the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*; they are not complete versions. Thus, these four works in seven scrolls are all extant.
The śramaṇa Vajrabodhi (Vajra-bodhi; in the Tang language, "Vajra-Wisdom") was a native of Mālaya in South India—a country known here as the Land of Light—and belonged to the Brahmin caste.
His country was situated near Mount Potalaka, the palace of Avalokiteśvara.
Having left home to become a monk in his youth, he traveled throughout India.
Although he was extensively learned in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings, he was particularly adept at *dhāraṇī*;
within this dharma-gate, there was rarely anyone who could equal him.
Wandering and teaching according to conditions, he benefited sentient beings wherever he went.
Hearing that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing in Great China,
he eventually embarked on a ship and traveled east until he reached the coastal regions.
In the eighth year of the Kaiyuan era, he finally arrived at the capital.
Thereupon, he extensively propagated the esoteric teachings and constructed maṇḍalas;
according to the ritual procedures, all were accompanied by miraculous and auspicious responses.
The śramaṇa Yixing deeply revered this secret dharma and frequently sought instruction from him.
Each time, the Master pointed out the details one by one and further established a maṇḍala for him to confer empowerment.
Yixing reverently received this dharma and requested its translation for circulation.
In the eleventh year, the Guihai year (1023),
at Zisheng Monastery, he translated the *Yogacaryābhūmi-bhāṣya-vidhi* and the *Saptakoṭi-dhāraṇī*.
The chief Brahmin of Eastern India, Ishvara, who served as a direct secretary, acted as the interpreter.
Scribe: the śramaṇa Wengu of Mount Song.
In the eighteenth year, the Gengwu year, at Dajianfu Monastery, he brought forth the Five-Syllable Heart Mantra of Mañjuśrī and the Essential Yoga of Avalokiteśvara.
The śramaṇa Zhizang translated the terminology.
Furthermore, he appended new mantras to the existing *Sūtra of the Heart of the Great Peacock King* (Suixiu).
His mastery of the dhāraṇī mudrās was such that they were efficacious wherever he went.
It was indeed this person through whom the secret teaching was transmitted.

*The Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, ten fascicles; one work in ten fascicles.
Its original manuscript is currently extant.
The śramaṇa Shi Huaidi was a native of Xunzhou.
He resided at Nanlou Temple on Mount Luofu in the province of Jizhou.
This mountain was a place where immortals and sages dwelt;
he studied the sutras and śāstras for a long time and became widely learned in many fields.
I have also roughly investigated the Nine Schools and the Seven Summaries;
however, because I reside near the edge of the sea,
there have frequently been Indian monks staying there.
As he pursued his studies, his command of the written and spoken language became thoroughly proficient.
Previously, when the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci was translating the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*,
Daoxuan was summoned from afar to serve as the verifier of the meaning (*zhengyi*).
Having completed his mission, he returned to his native land.
Later, while traveling through Guangzhou, he encountered a Buddhist monk whose name he did not know;
the monk brought a bundle of Sanskrit scriptures and requested that they translate them together.
It was compiled into ten fascicles;
this is precisely the *Mahābuddhotpattisikhara-daśasāhasrikā-śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
I guided the transcription of the sūtra’s essential meaning and also collated its literary structure.
When that Indian monk had finished transmitting the scriptures, no one knew where he had gone.
Later, he happened to arrive here while traveling with a southern envoy.

The *Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-vikurvaṇa-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra* in seven fascicles; the seventh fascicle is the *Japa-vidhi*. The *Subāhu-paripṛcchā-tantra* in three fascicles (translated into Chinese as the *Sūpo-hu Tongzi*, also known as the *Subāhu-vinaya*, or in two fascicles). The *Susiddhikara-sūtra* in three fascicles (translated into Chinese as the *Miaochengjiu-fa*). These, together with the *Subāhu*, both belong to the *Dhāraṇī-vinaya*; one must not peruse them without having entered the Great Maṇḍala, for to do so would be equivalent to violating the precept against listening surreptitiously to the Vinaya—thereby constituting a theft of the Dharma. The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sarvārthasiddhi-paramahṛdaya-dhāraṇī-śravaṇadhāraṇa-vidhi* in one fascicle, translated from the Sanskrit original. A brief partial translation of the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of All Meanings" from the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*. The above four works comprise fourteen fascicles, and their texts are all extant.
The śramaṇa Śubhakarasiṃha—
translated into Chinese as Shàn Wúwèi (Good Fearless)—
was a native of Central India.
A scion of the Śākya lineage,
his demeanor was refined and noble, and his intelligence surpassed that of his peers;
he thoroughly investigated the Five Vehicles and fully mastered the Three Studies.
He thoroughly mastered the source of dharanis and meditative contemplation;
there were no arts or specialized skills he did not understand.
Furthermore, as his primary vocation was the propagation of the Dharma, how could he have feared hardship or peril?
He then set out from Central India to travel to the Eastern Lands;
upon reaching the borders of Northern India,
his reputation had already reached the imperial capital.
The present Emperor, seeking out men of virtue and talent,
dispatched envoys to welcome him;
this was in the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Bingchen year.
He brought a great number of Sanskrit manuscripts to Chang'an.
Initially, they were deposited in the southern courtyard of Xingfu Monastery;
subsequently, by imperial decree, he was ordered to reside at Ximing Monastery.
In the fifth year, the Ding-si year, at the Bodhi Monastery, he translated the *Ākāśagarbha-śravaṇadhāraṇī-dharmaparyāya* in one fascicle.
The śramaṇa Siddha served as the oral interpreter,
while the śramaṇa Wuzhuo composed the text and recorded the transcription.
The Sanskrit manuscripts brought by Wúwèi were all ordered by imperial decree to be sent into the palace;
for this reason, he was unable to translate the various scriptures extensively.
Previously, the śramaṇa Wúxíng had traveled west to India, and having completed his studies, he was returning home.
Upon reaching Northern India, he unfortunately passed away.
The Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought with him were ordered by imperial decree to be welcomed back;
they were subsequently collected and preserved at Huayan Temple in the Western Capital.
Wuwei and the śramaṇa Yixing obtained several copies of Sanskrit sūtras and various dharanis and sublime gateways from him;
these had never been translated before.
In the twelfth year, he accompanied the imperial entourage to Luoyang and was stationed at Dafuxian Temple; thereupon,
he served as the śramaṇa Yixing’s assistant in translating the Mahāvairocana Sūtra.
The complete Sanskrit original of this sutra consists of one hundred thousand verses;
what is now presented is merely an abridgment of its essentials.
The śramaṇa Bao Yue translated the language.
The śramaṇa Xing served as the scribe to receive his instructions and also revised and composed the phrasing and logic;
the resulting texts balanced the refined and the plain, perfectly harmonizing with their profound meaning.
He also produced the two scriptures, the Subāhuparipṛcchā and the Susiddhi.
Possessing a fearless nature, he cherished tranquility and simplicity, using meditative concentration to delight his spirit.
From time to time, he engaged in Chan contemplation and encouraged those who were beginners.
With compassion in mind, he guided and attracted others without fail.
Whenever people questioned him with doubts, he analyzed them without impediment.

In the eighteenth year, the *Gengwu* year, at the East Pagoda Cloister of Xichongfu Monastery, he compiled the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* (Record of the Propagation of Buddhism during the Kaiyuan Era) in twenty volumes: the first volume containing the General Catalog, and the subsequent volumes containing the Separate Catalog. He also compiled the *Xu Dade Nei Dian Lu* (Continued Record of Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang) in one volume; the *Xu Gujin Yijing Tuji* (Continued Illustrated Account of Translations of Scriptures Past and Present) in one volume; the *Ji Gujin Fodao Lunheng* (Collection of Debates between Buddhism and Daoism Past and Present) in one volume; and the *Ji Zhujing Li Chan Yi* (Collection of Rituals for Repentance and Liturgy from Various Scriptures) in two volumes. Altogether, these comprise five works totaling twenty-five volumes.
Compiled by Zhisheng.
Zhisheng had early on entered the ranks of the Buddhist clergy with the resolve to propagate the Great Teaching;
however, his talent was slight and his strength meager, so he was unable to fulfill his original aspiration.
In the brief span of a moment, many seasons of cold and heat have passed;
yet I have been unable to propagate the True Dharma or shoulder the burden of Bodhi.
Recently, however, I have been perusing the Tripitaka and further exploring various records.
Observing its errors and those points that seemed unsatisfactory,
I have ventured this bold and somewhat florid composition to complete this record.
Although the literary phrasing lacks elegance, the facts herein have a reliable basis.
However, my humble views have not yet been broadened, and there are naturally many omissions and deficiencies.
The *Xu neidian lu* and other works are appended at the end of this main section.
I hope that future scholars will not find cause for reproach.
From the Later Han dynasty down to the present imperial court, there have been a total of nineteen dynasties. The Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras,
vinayas, and śāstras, along with the collected works and biographies of worthies and sages produced during this period,
comprise two thousand two hundred and seventy-eight sections in all.
In total, there are seven thousand forty-six fascicles.

Among these, one thousand one hundred twenty-four works comprising five thousand forty-eight fascicles are currently extant and included in the canon (*piṭaka*). As for the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* translated by Mandaraka during the Liang dynasty, it was already recorded within the Prajñā section; furthermore, because it was also compiled into the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, it is recorded again here in this catalogue. According to its actual count, [the total remains as stated].

However, among them, one thousand one hundred twenty-three works totaling five thousand forty-seven fascicles represent the number of those currently seen and in circulation; these include forty works totaling three hundred sixty-eight fascicles, which were all compiled within this land [of China] rather than being translations from Indic originals. Furthermore, one thousand one hundred forty-eight works totaling one thousand nine hundred eighty fascicles represent the number of those that are missing.

The two catalogues currently available comprise two thousand two hundred and seventy-one works in seven thousand twenty-seven fascicles; this falls short of the previous total by seven works and one thousand nine fascicles.

As for the differences: the *Vinaya Preface* translated by Wuguyan during the Eastern Jin was incorporated into the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; the one-volume *Devadatta Chapter* translated by Fayi during the Xiao Qi dynasty [is likewise distinct].
Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty, Zhìdé translated the *Repetitive Recitation Verses on the Universal Gate Chapter* in one fascicle;
these should both be incorporated into the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Also, during the Sui dynasty, Jñānagupta translated the *Chapter on the Silver Lord* and the *Chapter on Entrustment* together as one fascicle.
These are merged into the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
Regarding this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, there is the four-fascicle version translated by Dharmakṣema of Northern Liang,
and the seven-fascicle version translated by Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* was translated in five fascicles by Jueta during the Zhou dynasty.
During the Sui dynasty, the śramaṇa Baogui took the first three versions and combined them into eight fascicles.

Thus, the aforementioned three sūtras in the *Shanfan lu* (Record of the Elimination of Redundancy), together with these seven works totaling nineteen fascicles, accord perfectly with the total count, without any deficiency.

"I, You, relying on my own meager and shallow abilities, have long depended upon the Dharma-gate."
Gazing up with longing toward the profound winds [of the Buddhas], he vowed to propagate the teachings in this final age.
Whenever dawn or dusk arrived, he would recite and uphold the scriptures; during the autumn and summer retreats, he would lecture and explain them.
There was never a time when his mind did not race toward the Garden of Amrā (An-yuan) and his spirit leap with joy at the Sacred Peak (Ling-yue).
Thereupon, with humble and earnest resolve, he traced the waves back to their source and compiled what he had heard,

To compile it is to illuminate the original sources of the fundamental records;
to explain it is to ensure that the chronological tables and the prefaces to the scriptures do not fall into oblivion.
In the General Preface, the excellence of his assembly provides ample evidence through the biographies;
in the Narrative, the character of that man may be seen.

The regulations compiled by Dao You in his catalog are worthy of admiration;

For instance, within the "Diverse Records of Scriptures Transmitted Before and After" in the first fascicle:
In the old translation, the term *tathāgata arhat samyaksaṃbuddha* appears;
in the new translation, it is rendered as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is one error.
If one speaks in terms of the correspondence between the old and new translations: the old scripture says *tathāgata arhat samyaksaṃbuddha*,
while the new scripture says *tathāgata arhat samyaksaṃbuddha*.
In the old translations, it is rendered as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
in the new translations, it is rendered as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These two meanings differ entirely and cannot be interchanged.
Furthermore, Dharmarakṣa and Zhu Fahu were in fact one and the same person.
*Dharma* means "Dharma" (the Teaching), and *rakṣa* means "to protect. Thus, [Dharmarakṣa] signifies "Protector of the Dharma."
It is divided into two parts.
There are two errors:
in the catalogs of translated sutras and śāstras, whenever the titles alone are similar, they are immediately labeled as "retranslations."
Furthermore, he failed to carefully distinguish between the Great and Small [Vehicles], mixing them together;
this is the third error.
The *Preface to the Collection of Saṃgharakṣa* states that the work was compiled by "Zhonghu" (Saṃgharakṣa).
"Saṃgha" means "assembly," and "rakṣa" means "to protect. Thus,
"Saṃgharakṣa" refers to the person who compiled the scriptures.
The preface was composed by the translator, who titled it "Zhonghu" (Protected by the Multitude).
This is an error;
such a deviation from the original is extremely grave, and it is also a blemish upon this precious gem.

Subsequently, there are the *Excerpts and Collections* (抄集錄), totaling one hundred forty-four works in six hundred twenty-seven fascicles;
the *Excerpts and Collections by Sages and Holy Ones of the Western Regions* (西域賢聖抄集), totaling forty-eight works in one hundred nineteen fascicles;

and the *Excerpts and Collections by Various Virtuous Masters of This Land* (此方諸德抄集), totaling ninety-six works in five hundred eight fascicles. These comprise the biographies and records transmitted after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Record of the Eight Divisions, totaling sixty-eight sections and one hundred eighty-five fascicles;

Record of the Biographies of Sages and Holy Ones from the Western Regions, totaling thirteen sections and thirty fascicles; Record of the Biographies of Virtuous Masters of This Land, totaling fifty-five sections and one hundred fifty-five fascicles;
and the Ninth Division, the Record of Works Composed after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, totaling two sections and one fascicle.

One hundred and nineteen sections comprising one hundred and twenty fascicles consist of the writings of sages and worthies from the Western Regions, divided into fifteen sections totaling nineteen fascicles.

One hundred and four sections comprising one hundred and fifteen fascicles consist of the writings of various virtuous masters of this land, divided into one hundred and four sections totaling one hundred and fifteen fascicles.
The above constitutes nine catalogs.
A total of two thousand two hundred and fifty-seven sections and five thousand three hundred and ten fascicles;

however, when calculated, there are two thousand two hundred and fifty-four sections and five thousand one hundred and ninety-one fascicles. Upon a detailed examination against the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue), the sections and fascicles differ from the *Zonglu* (General Catalogue); thus, they are divided into six fascicles.
General Record, Number Seven.
Compiled in seven fascicles, the editor states:
I have examined and searched through this record.
It is not without error;
for instance, Dharmarakṣa— translated into Chinese as Fahu—
is in fact one and the same person.
The catalogue is divided into two parts;
it states that two fascicles of the *Susiddhikara-sūtra* (translated by Zhu Fahu) were separately produced and compiled as a retranslation.
Not knowing the terminology of the Brahmī or Jin scripts is the first error.
This is as seen in the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Twenty-two Clarifications).
In total, these are divided into two sections within the *Jinglü* (Scriptures and Vinaya) Catalogue:
the twenty-two fascicles of the *Vinaya* are included in the Vinaya section,
while the single fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-prakaraṇa-śāstra* (Mingliao lun) is included in this Treatise section.
The title of this single scripture is divided into two parts in the upper register;
the second part is an error.
That "Twenty-two" is actually half of the title of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
To claim now that there are twenty-two fascicles is a grave error.
As for the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (She lun) in twelve fascicles and the one in fifteen fascicles, these two versions are not different;
to maintain both texts while claiming they are redundant translations is incorrect.
The third error is including such works as the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* and the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* in the section on Doubtful Scriptures.
The fourth error is [the same].
I cannot present this in full detail;
it is briefly recounted as follows.

Within the fifteen fascicles of the *Sui Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (The Kaihuang Record of the Three Jewels), the title reads *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through Successive Dynasties). It was compiled by Fei Changfang of Chengdu, a scholar-translator at Xingshan Monastery in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era. This is the first volume of the *Lidai Sanbao Ji*, covering the reigns of successive emperors from the Zhou dynasty through the Qin, beginning from the tenth year of King Tai of the Zhou dynasty, the Jia-wu year.
Up to the twenty-sixth sovereign, Ziying, the son of the First Emperor of Qin, in the year Jiawu, there were a total of four hundred and eighty-one years.

Regarding the second volume of the *Lìdài sānbǎo jì* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Ages), the chronological sequence of the emperors begins with the first year of the Former Han, the Gāodì era, the year Yīwèi, following the New King [Xīnwáng] of the Former Han and continuing through the Later Han.
Up until the twenty-fourth year of Jian’an during the reign of Emperor Xian of the Later Han,
the year Jihai, there had been twenty-six sovereigns for a total of four hundred and twenty-five years.

According to the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Successive Dynasties), from the third entry on imperial reigns— beginning with the first year of Huangchu of Emperor Wen of Wei, the year Gengzi— and continuing through the Wei, Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Zhou, and Sui dynasties:
Reaching the year Ding-si, the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty,
there had been forty-four sovereigns for a total of three hundred and seventy-eight years.

This concludes the fourth section of the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Successive Dynasties) concerning the translation of scriptures, beginning from the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the year Ding-mao.
From the end of Emperor Xian’s reign until the end of the dynasty, there were eleven successive rulers spanning one hundred and fifty-two years.
During this period, twelve individuals— both Chinese and foreign, monastics and laypeople—
along with works whose translators were lost in antiquity, produced a total of three hundred and thirty-four scriptures and vinaya texts in four hundred and sixteen fascicles.
The Record of the Three Jewels through Successive Dynasties, Volume Five: An Explanation of the Scriptures Translated during the Wei,
Han, Southern Wei, and Wu Dynasties by Ten Monastics and Laity,
including Sūtras, Vinaya, Karmavācanā, and those of uncertain or lost translators.
A total of three hundred and twelve sections and four hundred and eighty-two fascicles.
From the *Lidai Sanbao Ji*, Volume Six, on the Translation of Scriptures, under the Western Jin dynasty (right section).
Thirteen individuals, both Chinese and foreign, monastics and laypeople alike,
[translated] the previously unattributed sūtras, precepts, and other texts,
totaling four hundred and fifty-one works in seven hundred and seventeen fascicles.
Record of the Three Jewels Through the Successive Dynasties, Volume Seven: Translations of Scriptures During the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
There were twenty-seven individuals—both Chinese and foreign, monastic and lay—who produced scriptures during this period, including those that were previously attributed to lost translations.
A total of two hundred and sixty-three works in five hundred and eighty-five fascicles.

This is the eighth volume of the *Lìdài sānbǎo jì* (Record of the Three Jewels through Successive Dynasties), concerning the translation of scriptures during the periods of Fúqín, Yáoqín, and the two subsequent Qín dynasties.

Sixteen individuals from both Chinese and non-Chinese regions belonging to the Śākya lineage produced a total of one hundred and sixty-four works in nine hundred and four fascicles, including sutras, śāstras, and biographies.

This concludes the ninth volume of the *Lìdài sānbǎo jì* (Record of the Three Jewels through the Successive Dynasties), covering the translations of scriptures during five successive dynasties: Western Qin, Northern Liang, Northern Wei, Northern Qi, and the Chen.
A total of twenty-seven individuals, both ordained and lay,
produced three hundred and two works in eight hundred and fifty-five fascicles, including the Tripiṭaka, records, and texts of unknown translators.
*Record of the Three Jewels Throughout the Successive Dynasties*, Volume Ten: Translators of Scriptures during the Song Dynasty.
Twenty-three individuals—monastics and laypeople, Chinese and non-Chinese—produced scriptures, vinaya, śāstras, biographies, catalogs, and other works.
In total, there are two hundred and ten works comprising four hundred and ninety fascicles.

According to the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels through Successive Dynasties), volume eleven, these are the translated scriptures from the three successive dynasties of Qi, Liang, and Northern Zhou.
The number of monastics and laypeople involved is fifty-one.
The Sūtras, Vinaya, Śāstras, and biographies and records,
totaling one hundred and sixty-two works in one thousand three hundred and twenty-six fascicles.
From the *Lidai Sanbao Ji*, volume twelve, on the Translation of Scriptures, by the Right [Official] of the Sui Dynasty.
There were nineteen persons, both Chinese and foreign, monastics and laypeople,
who produced newly translated texts as well as revised versions of various old treatises, biographies, and ritual codes,
totaling seventy-five works comprising four hundred and sixty-two fascicles.
The Thirteenth Record of the Catalogue of the Tripitaka Compiled through Successive Dynasties:
Mahāyāna Works, totaling five hundred and fifty-one works in one thousand five hundred and eighty-six fascicles. Mahāyāna Sūtras with Translators:
three hundred and thirty-four works in eight hundred and eighty-five fascicles. Sūtras with Lost Translators: two hundred and thirty-five works.

The *Lìdài sānbǎo jì* (Record of the Three Jewels through the Successive Dynasties) records that there are three hundred and two volumes of translated *vinaya*, comprising thirty-one works totaling nineteen sections and forty volumes;

four hundred and one works of translated *vinaya* whose translators are unknown, comprising twelve sections and fourteen volumes; five hundred and four works of translated *abhidharma*, comprising forty-nine works totaling two hundred and thirty-eight volumes;
and six works of translated *abhidharma* whose translators are unknown, comprising two works totaling seven volumes.
Section Fourteen: Catalogue of the Hīnayāna Works Included in the Canon. Five hundred and twenty-five works in one thousand seven hundred and thirty-nine fascicles.
It is an error to state that there are seven hundred and twelve fascicles. Regarding the Hīnayāna Sūtras: 1. Translated works:
one hundred and eight works in five hundred and twenty-seven fascicles. 2. Sūtras of Lost Translation: three hundred and one [works].
16 works totaling 482 fascicles of Vinaya with translators; 39 works totaling 185 fascicles of Vinaya with lost translators;
31 works totaling 67 fascicles of Abhidharma with translators;
21 works totaling 351 fascicles of Abhidharma with lost translators; and 61 [works].
The *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era) contains ten sections totaling twenty-seven scrolls.

The first scroll, the *Neidian Lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures), states that according to the *Fang Lu* (Fang Shen’s Catalogue), the total number of sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographies is two thousand one hundred and forty-six works in six thousand two hundred and thirty-five scrolls;
however, when calculated for inclusion in the canon, there are seventy-four works in three hundred and seven scrolls. These are consistent with the *Neidian Lu*.
The catalogs differ from the aforementioned; combined with the general table of contents, they form a total of fifteen fascicles.

Regarding the thirteenth and fourteenth fascicles, which contain the catalog of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures included in the canon—listing one thousand seven hundred and sixty works in two thousand three hundred and twenty-five fascicles—the figure of three thousand three hundred and ninety-two fascicles found in the Fang-lu (Fangshen) manuscript is an error in calculation. These are the Buddhist scriptures.
The Record states:
"Among the works compiled by [Dao]fang that have entered the canon,
the coarse and the precious are intermingled."
To claim that what exists amidst such abundance cannot yet be verified is not to say there is no basis for reliance;
nor can one arbitrarily prune and compile [the records]. The compiler states:
I have examined the *Chángfáng Rùzàng Lù* (Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon by Zhìcháng), and find its factual accounts to be confused and erroneous.
Regarding those works whose origins were doubted as being spurious, yet were all included in the canon,
I privately believe this was improper.
This is similar to the *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* and the *Bhadra-kalpika-samādhi-sūtra* found within the *Mahāyāna Catalogue*.
This is a single sutra with two titles;
currently, two versions exist,
one of which is erroneous.
The *Subhūtiparivarta* and the *Cháng'ān pǐn* (Chapter on Cháng'ān) are both alternative titles for the *Prajñāpāramitā-saṃgraha*;
it is an error to preserve these as two separate works.
The *Sūtra of the Devaputra Susīma* and the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Devaputra Susīma on the Four Matters* are two names for the same scripture;
it is recorded twice in two sections,
which is a third error.
The *Hastipadopama-sūtra* is an alternative title for the *Apraṇihita-sūtra*;
both names are preserved, though there are four errors [in the transmission].
The *Bodhicaryāvidhi-sūtra* (菩提無行經) is an alternative title for the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhisattva-sūtra* (文殊問菩提經).
Both versions are preserved;
there are five errors [in the former].
To incorporate the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhist treatises into the Mahāyāna constitutes six errors. Furthermore,
within the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) catalogues, the *Dharmatrāta-dhyāna-sūtra* and the *Aśubha-bhāvanā-sūtra* are both part of a single scripture.
The contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) is designated according to the dharma,
whereas Dharmatrāta establishes the title based on the person;
thus, both designations coexist.
Seven errors:
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (T.1548), fascicle 61;
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (T.1435), fascicle 59.
The two versions do not differ.
As for the sixty-first fascicle, the preface to the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya* by Vimalākṣa has been placed at the end;
otherwise, there are no differences whatsoever.
Now it is said that this is a retranslation;
both versions exist together,
yet eight errors remain.
The twenty-two sections of the Vinaya are contained within the Vinaya-piṭaka;
the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra is included in the Śāstra catalog.
This single title is divided into two parts.
The ninth error:
those twenty-two [volumes] of the Vinaya are actually the title of half the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*).
Today, only twenty-two fascicles of the Vinaya remain extant.
This is an error upon an error.
Within the *Dai lu* (Successive Records) of the *Saṃgītiparyāya-abhidharma-śāstra*, it states that it was translated during the Song dynasty by Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas.
Regarding those works included within the Canon, it is said that they have lost their original sources;
there are ten errors due to discrepancies between earlier and later versions,
while the remainder are recorded in the catalogs.
I cannot provide a detailed account here.

The *Sui Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures of the Sui Dynasty) in five fascicles was commissioned by imperial edict in the second year of the Renshou era; the Great Virtuous Monks of Xingshan Temple, along with the Śramaṇas who translated scriptures and scholars, compiled it, totaling two thousand one hundred and nine works in five thousand fifty-nine fascicles.
The original single volume contained no other translations; in total, it comprised three hundred and seventy works in one thousand seven hundred and eighty-six fascicles.
This is the first fascicle of the aforementioned collection.

The re-translations consist of those that were translated once, some twice, and even up to six times; in total, there are two hundred and seventy-seven works comprising five hundred and eighty-three fascicles.

The *Xian sheng ji zhuan* (Collected Biographies of Worthies and Sages), compiled by worthies and sages and translated according to its origins, comprises forty-one works in one hundred and sixty-four fascicles.

Of these, the two volumes preceding the second volume—comprising two and three-tenths of the total—consist of six hundred and eighty-eight works in two thousand five hundred and thirty-three fascicles, which are recorded as being included in the canon.
Separate texts produced within the main collection were excerpted and circulated separately, totaling eight hundred ten works in one thousand two hundred eighty-eight fascicles.
This is the third volume on the right.

Regarding those works of doubtful authenticity whose names resemble those of orthodox teachings but whose content involves human fabrication: they comprise two hundred and nine sections totaling four hundred and ninety-one fascicles.

From the fourth volume onwards, the first two volumes and two portions of the third—totaling one thousand nineteen sections and one thousand seven hundred and seventy-nine fascicles—need not be transcribed.

The old catalog of the missing texts contains the titles but lacks the actual scriptures; in total there are four hundred and two works comprising seven hundred and forty-seven fascicles, which we request be sought after.
This is the fifth volume on the right.
Its preface states briefly:
Do not transcribe those that are suspected of being spurious or forged.
As for the remaining three parts, they have been included in the Tripitaka;
these have now been compiled into the *Fǎbǎo jí* (Collection of Dharma Jewels).
The *Liujing zhuzi* (Biographies of Pure Abiders) and similar works follow the same precedent as the *Lüchao* (Abridged Extracts) in being categorized as separate biographical collections.
Other works include the *Sengzhuan* (Monastic Biographies) and so forth.
The phrasing draws from literary and historical sources and is not pure or correct;
although the events may be traced, their meaning is not worth recording.
The *Neidian lu* states:
At present, the complete transcriptions of the Tripitaka are widely circulated in the imperial capital.

While the titles of the sutras are listed in their proper order along with their translators and dates, more than half have been omitted, making them insufficient for consultation. Those who compiled this record remarked: [as follows].
I have examined this catalog and found it is not without errors; for instance,
the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Propagation of the Way* and the *Sūtra of the Dragon King Anavatapta*.
These are two titles for a single sūtra,
both attributed to Zhu Fahu’s translation;
both versions have been preserved.
The first point is an error.
Furthermore, the *Puyao jing* (Sūtra of the Universal Radiance) in eight fascicles states it was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;
yet, in the records of missing texts, it is again stated that the *Puyao jing* in eight fascicles was also translated by Zhu Fahu.
The two catalogues [of the Taishō Tripiṭaka] both record this omission as an error.
Furthermore, the *Pu-yao jing* (Lalitavistara-sūtra) in eight fascicles is described in the *Ru-zang-lu* (Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon) as a standalone text.
The Record of Missing Texts further states that this was a retranslation.
There are three errors regarding the discrepancies and corruptions between the missing text and the preceding and following sections.
The twelve-fascicle and fifteen-fascicle versions of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated by Paramārtha differ only in the number of fascicles;
their textual content, however, is no different.
Both editions currently exist.
The fourth error:
The *Mīśāsaka-karmavācanā* is recorded redundantly at both the beginning and the end within the *Qiūběn lù*.
The fifth error.
The *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows* (*Suixuan wangsheng jing*) and the *Treatise on the Bequeathed Teachings* (*Yijiao lun*) and so forth were compiled among the spurious and doubtful;
this is the sixth error.
The remainder is contained within the catalog.
It cannot be recorded in full detail.

The *Dàtáng nèidiǎn lù* (Record of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang), ten fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery in the first year of the Línḍé era (the Jiazi year), contains the first section:

the *Lìdài zhòngjīng chuányì suǒcóng lù* (Record of the Sources from Which Various Scriptures Were Translated Throughout Successive Dynasties). This refers to the various scriptures produced in different eras and their respective translators.
Since all compositions without exception accord with the Dharma and are subsumed within the scriptures, they follow the scriptures in their appearance.
During the Later Han dynasty, twelve monastics and laypeople transmitted and translated [the teachings], producing three hundred and thirty-four works in four hundred and sixteen fascicles;
one hundred and twenty-five works in one hundred and forty-eight fascicles were lost as to their translators. During the Former Wei dynasty...
The scriptures and vinaya texts translated by six monk-translators comprise thirteen works in twenty-five fascicles;
those translated by four monastics and laypersons during the Southern Wu state of the Sun clan comprise one hundred and forty-eight works in one hundred and ninety-five fascicles;
and lost translations comprise one hundred and ten works in two hundred and ninety-two fascicles. (West)

During the Jin dynasty, thirteen monastics and laypeople produced translations of sutras, precepts, and other works totaling four hundred and forty-six fascicles in seven hundred and thirteen scrolls;
eight lost-translator scriptures comprise fifteen scrolls.

During the Eastern Jin dynasty, twenty-seven monastics and laypeople produced translations of sutras, commentaries, and other works totaling two hundred and sixty-four fascicles in five hundred [scrolls].
Seventy-four fascicles; fifty lost translations totaling fifty-four fascicles;
forty scriptures and commentaries translated by eight monks during the Former Qin Fu dynasty totaling two hundred thirty-nine fascicles;
fifteen scriptures translated by one monk during the Later Qin Qifu dynasty totaling twenty-two fascicles; and [fifteen] lost [translations].
Translated scriptures: eight works in eleven fascicles, translated during the Later Qin (Yao) dynasty by eight monks.
Scriptures and commentaries produced by nine monastics and laypersons during the Northern Liang (Juqu) dynasty:
thirty-four works in two hundred and seventy fascicles. Works of unknown translation.
The scriptures translated during the Song dynasty consist of twenty-four monastics and laypeople, producing two hundred and seventeen works totaling five hundred and three fascicles.

The scriptures and commentaries translated during the Qi dynasty consist of twenty monastics and laypeople, producing twelve works totaling three hundred and ninety-six fascicles. The scriptures translated during the Liang dynasty... [text continues]
Laypeople: twenty-one individuals produced eighty-nine works in nine hundred and two fascicles, including sūtras, vinayas, and biographies (*zhuan*).
During the Yuan clan’s Later Wei dynasty, fourteen monastics and laypeople produced eighty-eight works in two hundred and ninety-eight fascicles, including sūtras, śāstras, and records (*lu*).
During the Gao clan’s Later Qi dynasty, two monastics and laypeople produced [sūtras].
The treatises consist of eight sections and fifty-two fascicles, translated and transmitted during the Northern Zhou dynasty under the Yuwen clan by eleven monastics and laypersons;
these include sutras, treatises, and works on astronomy totaling thirty-two sections and one hundred five fascicles.

During the Chen dynasty, three monastics and laypersons transmitted and translated these works, producing fifty-four sections and two hundred fifty-one fascicles, including sutras, treatises, biographies, and commentaries.
During the Sui dynasty, twenty-five individuals, both monastics and laypeople, produced one hundred and six translations of sutras and treatises totaling six hundred and thirty-three fascicles.

During the present dynasty (the Tang), twelve monks and others produced one hundred and seventeen translations of sutras and treatises totaling one thousand six hundred and sixty-eight fascicles. Altogether, these comprise eighteen dynasties.
The various sūtras produced therein total two thousand four hundred and eighty-seven sections.

There are eight thousand four hundred and seventy-six fascicles; the total number at the beginning of the first fascicle differs from the total number in the middle of the tenth fascicle, and when compared with various editions, the counts also vary in their discrepancies—it remains unclear which of these is correct.
The above first record is divided into five fascicles, from the first to the fifth.

The second, titled "Record of Single and Multiple Translations and the Survival or Extinction of Persons and Eras Throughout Successive Dynasties," refers to the fact that translations produced at different times vary in their authors and eras;

furthermore, due to the upheavals of war and disorder, both monastics and laypeople were dispersed. This record now provides a comprehensive accounting and reconciliation of these circumstances, hence it contains accounts of both single and multiple instances.
The list of Mahāyāna sūtras— both single and multiple translations, including those whose translators are unknown or lost, as well as records of their presence or absence—
comprises three hundred and eighty-six works totaling one thousand one hundred and fifty-two fascicles and eighteen thousand five hundred and twenty-two sheets.
The list of Mahāyāna vinaya texts— both single and multiple translations, including records of their presence or absence— comprises twenty-two works.
Thirty-four volumes of Mahāyāna treatises, including both single and multiple translations, along with a record of what has been translated and what is missing,
totaling seventy-two works in five hundred scrolls and nine thousand two hundred and twenty sheets; and two hundred and four works of Hīnayāna sūtras, including both single and multiple translations,
along with a record of what has been translated and what is missing, totaling five hundred and forty-four scrolls and seven thousand six hundred and seventy sheets.

Four sheets [of records] for the Small Vehicle Vinaya texts, including both those translated and those not recorded, totaling thirty-five works in two hundred and seventy-four fascicles and five thousand eight hundred and thirteen sheets;

and thirty-three works in six hundred and seventy-six fascicles and twelve thousand one hundred and seventy [sheets] for the Small Vehicle Śāstras, including both single and multiple translations, as well as those translated and those not recorded.

Seven sheets of paper for the *Collection of Records of Worthies and Sages*, comprising forty-seven works in one hundred eighty-four fascicles totaling two thousand seven hundred and sixty sheets; the above record is divided into the sixth and seventh volumes.

Record of the Classification of the Scriptures of Successive Dynasties and Their Inclusion in the Tripiṭaka, Part Three. This refers to the section on the Sūtras, which, being numerous in volume, has its essential outlines fully set forth.
They are entered into the canon according to their fascicles, grouped by category; thus, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are distinguished, and the single and multiple translations are recorded.

Altogether, the sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and biographies comprise eight hundred and one works, totaling three thousand three hundred and sixty-one fascicles, amounting to fifty-six [thousand] characters.
One thousand one hundred and seventy sheets, three hundred and twenty-six fascicles of Mahāyāna sūtras translated once:
two hundred and four works, six hundred and eighty-five fascicles, eleven thousand four hundred and forty-three sheets, sixty-six fascicles;
Mahāyāna sūtras translated repeatedly: two hundred and two works, four hundred and ninety-seven fascicles, seven thousand two hundred and ninety sheets.

Forty-nine bundles of Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) sūtras: first translation, one hundred and eight works in four hundred and thirty-five fascicles, totaling six thousand six hundred and ninety sheets; thirty-nine bundles of Small Vehicle sūtras:
re-translations, ninety-six works in one hundred and fourteen fascicles, totaling nine hundred and seventy-seven sheets; six bundles of Small Vehicle vinaya: thirty-five [works].
Section Two: Seven hundred and forty-four fascicles, five thousand eight hundred and thirteen sheets, twenty-eight bundles.
Mahāyāna Treatises: seventy-four works, five hundred and two fascicles, nine thousand one hundred and thirty sheets, fifty-two bundles.
Hīnayāna Treatises: thirty-three works, six hundred and seventy-six fascicles, twelve thousand one hundred [sheets].
77 sheets, 68 fascicles; *Xian-sheng ji-zhuan* (Collected Biographies of Worthies and Sages), 49 works, 184 scrolls, 2,084 sheets, 18 fascicles.
The above one catalog constitutes the eighth volume. The compiler states:
"Upon examining the numbers and sequences of this catalog compared with the preceding catalog, there are both similarities and differences regarding the number of works and scrolls."

The Mahāyāna Vinaya previously cataloged should now be incorporated into the Sūtras; furthermore, as the single and multiple [versions] are intermingled and the sequence is inconsistent, by what standard can they be determined?

The *Lìdài zǒngjīng jǔyào zhuǎndú lù* (Record of the Essential Extracts and Recitations of the Various Scriptures of Successive Dynasties), Volume IV, states that the purpose of recitation and study lies in seeking the essential and the broad; verbose texts and redundant meanings are not intended for immediate application. Therefore, I have selected and extracted from each section those passages that provide universal access. As for the remaining duplicate versions, they remain preserved but have not yet been examined. The authentic Mahāyāna Sūtras comprise 254 works in 795 fascicles, totaling 13,079 sheets. The Mahāyāna Vinaya comprises 20 works in 32 fascicles, totaling 430 sheets. The Mahāyāna Śāstras comprise 63 works in 445 fascicles, totaling 8,115 sheets. In total, there are 337 Mahāyāna works comprising the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
One thousand two hundred and sixty-seven fascicles, twenty-one thousand six hundred and twenty-five sheets.

The Hinayana sutras comprise one hundred and eighteen sections totaling four hundred and thirty-three fascicles and six thousand seven hundred and thirteen sheets; the Hinayana vinaya comprises thirty-five sections totaling two hundred and seventy-four fascicles and five thousand seven hundred and eighteen sheets; the Hinayana śāstras comprise twenty-nine sections totaling five hundred and sixty-five fascicles and nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven sheets. This is the total for the Hinayana sutras, vinaya, and śāstras combined.
In total, there are one hundred and eighty-two works, comprising one thousand two hundred and fifty-two fascicles and twenty-two thousand four hundred and twenty-eight sheets.

The *Collection of Transmissions of Worthies and Sages* consists of forty-three works, totaling one hundred and seventy-seven fascicles and two thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven sheets. Catalogue of the Bodhisattva Tripiṭaka, Part One, Section One. Regarding the Bodhisattva Piṭaka (*bodhisattvapiṭaka*):...
This is the teaching expounded by the Mahāyāna.
As for the Teacher who expounds it, his Dharma-body is eternally present, neither ceasing nor arising.
As for the principle expounded, it is the vast and true suchness (tathatā), which transcends names and is free from marks.
In general, there are differences among the Three Baskets;
specifically, there are twelve sections.
These begin with the initial aspiration for enlightenment and conclude with the tenth stage.
The discourses on the three knowledges and eight liberations,
and the texts on the six perfections and four means of integration—
if such categories constitute the name of this collection, it is called the Tripitaka.
Beginning from the *dingmao* year of the Han Emperor Ming’s reign until the *gengwu* year of our Kaiyuan era,
a total of six hundred and eighty-six works were found circulating.
In total, there are two thousand seven hundred and forty-five fascicles,
arranged into two hundred and fifty-eight bundles,
compiled as the Mahāyāna Dharma-treasury.

The general and specific categories are fully listed as follows: The *Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka* consists of five hundred and sixty-three works in two thousand one hundred and seventy-two fascicles, arranged in two hundred and three bundles. The *Bodhisattva Vinaya Piṭaka* consists of twenty-six works in fifty-four fascicles, arranged in five bundles. The *Bodhisattva Abhidharma Piṭaka* consists of ninety-seven works in five hundred and eighteen fascicles, arranged in fifty bundles. Regarding the *Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka*, there are four hundred and thirty-two Mahāyāna sūtras—comprising both single translations and combined translations of multiple versions—totaling one thousand eight hundred and eighty fascicles, arranged in one hundred and seventy-nine bundles. When consulting various ancient catalogs, all of them prioritize single translations.
In this present catalog, those scriptures translated multiple times are placed at the beginning.

The reason for doing so is that the texts and meanings of these repeatedly translated scriptures are fully complete, and their terminology and characteristics have been definitively established; therefore, they are designated as the primary section.
Furthermore, in the old catalogs, these were simply termed "re-translations" (chóngyì).
I have now changed the designation to "re-translations of single and combined versions" (chóngdān héyì),
because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* consists of nine assemblies as single texts.
Seven assemblies were translated more than once;
twenty assemblies of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* were single translations,
while twenty-nine assemblies were retranslations.
To state it directly: because the re-translation does not fully encompass the meaning,
as is the case with other scriptures,
it is therefore termed a "re-translated, single, and combined translation."
Furthermore, in ancient translations of the sūtras, the titles were invariably absent at the beginning.
As the eras and dates of the translators grew increasingly distant, they could no longer be traced;
it was for this reason that the designation "lost translation" (shiyi) came into being.
Now, having consulted various ancient catalogs and determined what is correct or erroneous,
I have clearly indicated the era and the translators at the beginning of each scripture;
those whose translations were lost are recorded in the catalog.
It is my hope that the Bequeathed Teaching of the World-Honored One will endure for the full span of sixty thousand years.

The Prajñā Section: The new and old translations of the Prajñā section, along with its derivative sutras, are all compiled here, totaling twenty-one works in seven hundred and thirty-six fascicles, arranged in seventy-three bundles. The Prajñā sutras are established at the beginning because they are called the "Mother of all Buddhas. In previous catalogs, these were compiled without a fixed order; however, in this catalog, the sutras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are arranged according to their respective classes. Regarding the Hīnayāna Vinayas, they are ordered according to their fundamental and derivative texts. Among the Mahāyāna Śāstras, those that comment on the sutras are placed first, while those that collect and explain the meaning are listed afterward. Regarding the Hīnayāna Śāstras, they follow the sequence of the Sarvāstivāda school: the *Jñānaprasthāna* is placed first, followed by the six *Pādas*, and the various branches such as the *Mahāvibhāṣā* are compiled at the end. The collected works of sages and worthies are divided into two parts: internal (Buddhist) and external (non-Buddhist). Since there are differences between the Western Regions (Da Xia) and China (Shenzhou), the categories are kept distinct so that readers may easily understand them.

Furthermore, according to Sengrui’s preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Smaller Version) from the Yao Qin period,
this scripture exists in four versions of the original text;
these are the Buddha’s teachings, delivered at different times, varying in length according to his skillful adaptation to the needs of those he was transforming.
The extensive version consists of one hundred thousand verses,
while the abbreviated version consists of six hundred verses.
This *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Perfection of Wisdom) is equivalent to the "Middle" version among those found in India.

Based on this middle version, it is known that its Sanskrit original is the same as that of the second assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, this is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, a commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

These are the four sūtras listed above.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the fourth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Regarding the *New Path of Practice Sūtra* (*Xin Dàoxíng jīng*) translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa, its title exists but the text itself is not extant; even if it were present in the various canons, it would be identical in content to the *Svalpākṣara-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, differing only in its title. Therefore, it is not reproduced here. Of the eight translations produced over time, five have survived and three are missing.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* (Sheng Tianwang Banruo Boluomi Jing), seven fascicles; translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Chen dynasty. This is the first translation of this sūtra.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the sixth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The two aforementioned scriptures comprise eleven fascicles in a single volume.

The *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, in two fascicles (or one fascicle), twenty-one pages; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa of Funan during the Liang dynasty. This is the first translation of the aforementioned sūtra.
It is also titled the Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra.
The initial text lacks the tenfold light;
the latter text contains the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.
The *Wénwényán shūshīlì tóngzhēn* (The Mantra of the Youthful Mañjuśrī) is also included in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, as the forty-sixth assembly (*parivarta*).
This was done because its title is identical to that of a later scripture.
Fearing there may be errors, I have published this again.

*The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Spoken by Mañjuśrī*, one fascicle, twenty sheets; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty. Included as a supplement among the third set of translations. The above is one sūtra.
The initial passage contains ten successive lights;
the subsequent passage lacks the *samādhi of one practice*.
The text states that "Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince," is the one [who speaks].
The first part praises the virtues of the bodhisattvas and enumerates their names;
this original version is somewhat more extensive.
Furthermore, these two sutras also differ in their relative detail and brevity.
The two aforementioned sūtras are different translations of the same text as the "Mañjuśrī-parivarta," the seventh assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

The second translation is the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-anuttara-viśuddha-piṇḍapāta-sūtra* in two fascicles—also titled the *Sarvadharma-māyā-nirmāṇa-nirvedhaka-samādhi-sūtra*—translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Xianggong at Nanhai Commandery. This is the single sūtra [listed] on the right.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the "Nāgaśrī" section of the eighth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Comparing the new and old versions, the older scripture is slightly more extensive; of the three translations, two remain while one is missing.

*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin [Later Qin] at Śrāvastī. First Translation. *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Yuanwei [Northern Wei]. Second Translation. *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpārmitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India at the Jetavana Grove during the Chen dynasty. Third Translation. *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang at Śrāvastī. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* as the Fourth Translation. *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of the Empress Wu of the Great Tang at the city of Yaśas. Newly included in the canon as the Fifth Translation. The above five sūtras are the same text translated differently.
Its fourth fascicle is capable of severing [delusions] through Prajñā.
It was translated by the Śramaṇa Xuanzang at the Hongfa Terrace in Yuhua Palace, accompanying the Emperor, in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era.
Later, in the fifth year of the Xianqing era,
he translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* at Yuhua Monastery;
this was precisely the ninth section, the "Vajracchedikā" (The Diamond Cutter).
Since the complete text has already been included [elsewhere], it shall not be translated again.
According to the precedent of various scriptures, those that should be incorporated into the great collections are treated as separate productions;
they must not be redundantly recorded within this catalog.
Because the name of the translator, the śramaṇa Yijing, is identical [to that of the author],
there may be confusion; therefore,
I have again set forth these three masters who composed treatises to provide a unified commentary on this sūtra.

*The Sūtra on the Prajñāpāramitā of True Reality*, one fascicle. Translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci from India. Recorded as the second translation in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. This sūtra is a different translation of the same text as the "Section on the Principle of Prajñā" (*Prajñā-nyāya-vibhāga*) in the tenth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Furthermore, in the Sanskrit texts of the Western Regions, there exist both an extensive and an abridged version;
thus, the meaning of the text regarding the principle of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is identical, let alone the difference between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

The *Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra on the Prajñāpāramitā for Protecting the State*, two fascicles (alternatively said to be one fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the second translation, while two other translations are missing. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Mahāvidyāmantra Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is recorded as the first translation in the *Chujing Ti* (Catalogue of Sūtra Titles) and was subsequently included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The *Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; this is recorded as the second translation in the *Neidian Lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures). Regarding these two sūtras, they share the same original text but differ in translation; of the three successive translations, two survive and one is missing. As for the *Prajñāhṛdaya Sūtra*, older catalogues list it as a single independent work, whereas a new examination reveals it to be a re-translation. Although the general meaning of these three sūtras—the *Benevolent Kings’ Prajñā* and the others—is consistent with the complete versions of the major [Prajñā] texts, they are not contained within those major texts. They are categorized as branches rather than being derived directly from them.
The thirteen scriptures above, totaling fifteen fascicles, share one volume.

In the Ratnakūṭa section, all the various assemblies and duplicate versions have been compiled in sequential order, comprising eighty-two sections in total; because these are composed of various sections, their original counts are preserved. The upper register contains one hundred and sixty-nine fascicles in seventeen volumes. The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, one hundred and twenty fascicles in twelve volumes, was translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang dynasty and has been newly included in this catalog. Altogether, this scripture consists of forty-nine assemblies, combining both new and old translations, as well as both single and composite versions.

Combined [with the ancient version], this forms one collection consisting of twenty assemblies in total; including both the new and old versions, there are twenty-nine assemblies in the single-text edition. Among these, twenty-six assemblies were newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, while twenty-three assemblies were ancient translations. Having compared the Sanskrit manuscripts with the ancient Chinese translations and those by Bodhiruci, they have been compiled together according to their assembly order, as detailed below.
The First Assembly on the Threefold Restraint, in three fascicles; newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang, being the second translation.
This new translation is a re-edition based on the same original text as the old *Mahāvaipulya-triśikṣā-sūtra*, though differing in its translation.
From the first fascicle to the third fascicle.
The second, the *Anantavyūha-parivarta*, in four fascicles, newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The above is a newly translated single-text edition.
From the fourth fascicle to the seventh fascicle.

The third assembly, the *Guhyakapāda-vajrapāṇi-parivarta*, in seven fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty; this has been collated and included here as a single ancient translation.
From the eighth fascicle to the fourteenth.

The two fascicles of the Fourth Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty, were verified as identical to those in the catalogue of Dharmottara and included here; these are old translations consisting of single independent texts.
Originally titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Dream*, it has been newly renamed *The Assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa Devaputras*.

It constitutes volumes fifteen and sixteen. Upon careful examination of the phrasing and syntax, it is found to differ somewhat from the translation by Zhu Fahu; the catalogs of Changfang and others all state that its translator is lost, while the catalog of Fashang attributes it to Zhu Fahu. For now, I have provisionally determined this according to Fashang’s record.

The Fifth: The Assembly of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, in two fascicles, newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty; this is the eleventh translation. This new translation, a reissued version, is a different translation of the same text as the *Old Sūtra of Immeasurable Purity and Equal Enlightenment*, the *Great Amitābha Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.
Volumes seventeen and eighteen.

The sixth assembly, the Akṣobhyatathāgata-parivarta, in two volumes, newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang; this third translation is a re-translation of the same text as the previous *Akṣobhyabuddhakṣetrasūtra*, differing only in its version.
Volumes Nineteen and Twenty. The Seventh Assembly:
The Adornment of the Armor, in five fascicles. Newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The above is a newly translated single-text edition.
From the twenty-first fascicle to the twenty-fifth.

The eighth assembly, "The Non-differentiation of the Essence of the Dharma-realm," in two fascicles, translated by the Liang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Mandaravaśa; this second translation has been collated and incorporated here as a duplicate of the old translation.
This is a different translation from the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva during the Yao Qin dynasty;
it corresponds to the same original text, though the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh fascicles are missing from the Qin translation.

The Ninth Assembly on the Ten Dharmas of the Mahāyāna, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei. This second translation has been collated and included alongside the previous version; it is a re-edited duplicate of the former.

This is a different translation of the same text as the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra* translated by Liang Zhongkai; it corresponds to what is stated at the beginning of that work, "Bhagavān. The title of the twenty-eighth fascicle, which attributes the translation to Saṃghavarman, is an error.

The Tenth: The Mañjuśrī Universal Gate Assembly, one fascicle; newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty; the third translation. The above is the new translation, a reissued version.
This is a variant translation of the same text as the old *Pumenpin jing* (Universal Gate Chapter Sutra) and others;
it constitutes the twenty-ninth fascicle.

It is the fifth fascicle of the "Appearance of Radiance Assembly" (*Chuxian guangming hui*), newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang. The above is a newly translated single-text edition.
From the thirtieth to the thirty-fourth fascicle;

twelve fascicles from the twelfth assembly, the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Verified against the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures) and included herein. The above are single-text translations from the old Tang dynasty.

From the thirty-fifth to the fifty-fourth fascicles, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-parivarta* was included in the "Re-translations" (chóngyì) according to the *Dàzhōu lù*. To claim that it is a different translation of the same text as the three-fascicle *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* is a grave error. Although the titles are identical, their length differs entirely; upon examining the textual meaning, they are further divergent. As for the three-fascicle *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, it is also included herein—namely, the *Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-parivarta*—and has now been reclassified from its former status as a "re-translation" to a "single translation" (dānyì).

The Thirteenth Buddha’s Discourse on the Assembly Concerning Abiding in the Womb, one fascicle; newly translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang Dynasty, the second translation. The above is the new translation, the reissued version.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Jiubaotai jing* (Sūtra on the Old Womb).
It corresponds to the fifty-fifth fascicle.

It consists of two fascicles titled *The Fourteenth: The Buddha’s Discourse on the Assembly on Entering the Womb*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, and has been included here after collation. The above is a single-text translation from the old Tang dynasty.
