The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* exists in either six or ten fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmakṣema of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin dynasty, together with Buddhabhadra; this is the fourth translation. The aforementioned sutra is the earlier portion of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, extending through the end of the "Mahāsaṃnipāta-paripṛcchā" chapter; it is a different translation of the same original text. Including the "Te-p'i" (Funeral) section, there are seven translations in total, four of which are missing.
The two aforementioned scriptures comprise eight fascicles in one volume.
The *Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* in two fascicles—also known as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, or in three fascicles—was translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin;
this is the first translation. The *Catuḥkumārasamādhi Sūtra* in three fascicles, or simply titled [the *Catuḥkumāra Sūtra*]...
The Sūtra of the Four Youthful Ones, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty; this is the second translation.

The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations. According to various catalogues, there is also a *Sūtra of Lamentation* in two or three fascicles, said to be a different translation of the same text as the *Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
However, the source of its translation is not recorded. Examining its text...
The *Jù* (Phrases) is identical to the *Fāngděng Níhán* (Vaipulya Nirvāṇa) and differs from it in no way;
however, while the first chapter of the *Fāngděng Níhán* is titled "Lamentation" (*Āiqì*), this work takes only that chapter title as its own name.
Compared to the *Fāngděng Níhán*, it lacks three chapters, yet otherwise there is no difference between them. Since the latter is cumbersome, it has been omitted and not recorded here.

The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* in five fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas together with Fazhi during the Northern Qi dynasty; this single volume is placed in the same case as the three preceding sūtras totaling ten fascicles. These three sūtras, including the *Vaipulya-nirvāṇa*, belong to the branch lineages of the *Nirvāṇa*.
Outside the five great divisions, there are various retranslated scriptures: two hundred and seventy-three works in five hundred and fifty-eight fascicles, arranged in fifty-one bundles.

The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* (大方廣莊嚴經), twelve fascicles; also known as the *Abhijñāvikrīḍita*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty; recorded in the fourth volume of the *Dazhou Catalogue*. This is the second translation. The *Puyao Jing* (普曜經), eight fascicles; also known as the *Vaipulya-pūrvaprabhava*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty; this is the second translation. Two other translations are missing. These two sūtras are the same text translated differently. Although the *Dazhuangyan Jing* was compiled as a single independent translation in the *Dazhou Catalogue*, there are some who place the *Puyao Jing* within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka; both of these views are erroneous.
The two preceding sutras comprise twenty fascicles in two volumes.

*Fahua sanmei jing* (The Lotus Samādhi Sūtra), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Liangzhou during the Song dynasty. This is a single-text version [of a branch of the *Lotus Sūtra*]. *Wuliangyi jing* (The Sūtra of Infinite Meanings), one fascicle; spoken prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmagatayaśas of India during the Xiao Qi dynasty. This is the second translation; of the two translations, one is missing. *Santam pundarīka jing* (The Sūtra of the True White Lotus), one fascicle; a different recension containing small portions of the "Treasure Stupa" and "Devadatta" chapters. Sengyou’s catalogue states that it was lost from Master Dao’an’s record as a sūtra of unknown translation; it is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue and included in the "Supplemental Collection. *Miaofa lianhua jing* (The Lotus Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma), eight fascicles and twenty-eight chapters, or seven fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the fifth translation. The aforementioned four sūtras comprise eleven fascicles and are kept in the same volume. This [volume] contains the beginning of the fifth fascicle of the *Miaofa lianhua jing*: the "Devadatta" Chapter.

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Xiao Qi dynasty, the foreign Tripitaka master Dharmapṛthivī, together with the Śramaṇa Faxian, the Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng) of Yangdu, translated this sutra at Waguan Temple.
The Sanskrit original of this Dharma was brought from Khotan.
Its eighth fascicle, beginning with the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*), contains verses repeated from the time of Emperor Zhou Wu by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta from North India.
Translated at Longyuan Monastery in Yizhou.
The Qin edition was missing this portion;
it was subsequently added to the compilation.
Furthermore, the six dhāraṇīs of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and others from the eighth fascicle were retranslated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang;
they are included within the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning) and are not listed separately here.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Correct Dharma Lotus Sutra) in ten fascicles, also known as the *Vaipulya Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or in seven fascicles, one set; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin—this is the third translation. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in seven fascicles, consisting of twenty-seven chapters, or in eight fascicles; translated and revised by the two Dharma Masters Kuṃārajīva and Jñānagupta, both Tripiṭaka Masters from India during the Sui dynasty, with the addition of the preface and the *Neidian lu*. Regarding these three sutras, they share the same original text but differ in their translations. The brief preface to the revised version states: [The preface follows...]
The translation by Dharmarakṣa is titled *Zhengfahù* (Protection of the True Dharma), while that by Kumārajīva is titled *Miaofa* (Wondrous Dharma).
Upon examining both texts, both contain omissions.
Regarding the omissions in Dharmarakṣa’s version:
These are the verses of the "Universal Gate" chapter.
As for what Kumārajīva omitted:

the latter half of the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter; the beginnings of the two chapters on "Pūrṇa" and "The Dharma Master and Others"; the "Devadatta" chapter; and the verses of the "Universal Gate" chapter.
Kumārajīva moved the entrustment (*parindanā*) to appear before the Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*);
in two versions of the *Dhāraṇī*, both are placed after the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*).
The differences and similarities between these versions are such that words cannot fully express them.

I have privately observed that the verses from the "Devadatta Chapter" and the "Universal Gate Chapter" were subsequently produced by former sages to supplement what was missing and have circulated widely; I look up to their legacy and take their established models as my standard.

In the first year of the Renshou era of the Great Sui dynasty, the year of Xinyou (701 CE), at the request of the śramaṇa Shangxing of Puyao Monastery, [the translators] together with the two Dharma Masters Kumārajīva and Jñānagupta at Daxingshan Monastery re-examined the Indian palm-leaf manuscript.
This version included the beginning of the two chapters on Pūrṇa and the Dharma Master, yet it was still lacking the "Simile of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter.

Furthermore, an additional half-portion follows the *dhāraṇī* on entering the stūpa and the subsequent section on supernatural powers; it concludes with an entrustment (*parindanā*) and a re-binding of the final [seal].
The wording and phrasing differ slightly.
Some corrections have also been made;
if you should consult this text, I hope you will not harbor any doubts.
Together with these added sections, there are now six translations in total.
Three [copies] are missing from the three registers.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* in three fascicles—also known as the *Acintyavimokṣa* or simply the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*—was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; it is the sixth translation. The aforementioned two sūtras in ten fascicles are contained in the same volume.

The Vimalakīrti Sūtra, in two fascicles or three fascicles, translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty; the second translation is the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* in six fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. According to the *Neidian lu*, there have been seven translations in total for these three sūtras of the same text with different translations, four of which are now missing.

*Mahāvaipulya-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Vimalakīrti-putra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* or the *Susīma-kumāra-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. First translation: *Mahāyāna-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Vimalakīrti-putra-sūtra*. Translated by Prince Upasena of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Liang dynasty. Third translation. These four preceding sūtras comprise ten fascicles in a single volume.

*The Scripture of the Youth Subāhu*, two fascicles; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui Dynasty; this is the fourth translation. The above three scriptures are translations of the same original text with different versions. It was an error for the *Zhou Catalogue* to place the *Scripture of the Youth Subāhu* among the single-text works. Of the four translations, the second version is missing.

The *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in eight fascicles, also known as the *Mahāyāna Karuṇā*, is of unknown translator; it is now appended to the Qin Records. This second translation, together with the two aforementioned sūtras totaling ten fascicles, is contained in the same volume.

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Pity Lotus Sutra), ten fascicles, one set; translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. This is the fourth translation. The two aforementioned sutras are translations of the same original text with different renditions; of the four translations produced over time, two are missing.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra* in ten fascicles, one set; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon as the fifth translation. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* in eight fascicles and twenty-four chapters; compiled and produced by the Śramaṇa Baogui of Daxingshan Temple during the Sui dynasty; this constitutes the fourth version. These two sutras are the same text with different translations; their prefaces briefly state:
Furthermore, there are three extant versions of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The first was translated by Dharmakṣema during the Liang dynasty; it consists of four fascicles and contains eighteen chapters.
The second was translated by Jñānagupta during the Zhou dynasty; it consists of five fascicles and comprises twenty chapters.

Later, during the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated at Jiankang four chapters: "The Distinction of the Three Bodies," "The Extinction of Karmic Obstacles," "The Dhāraṇī of Utmost Purity," and "Fulfilling Wishes by Relying on Emptiness."

In the preface, [Dao]zu remarked on the emergence of twenty-three chapters and sighed over how this scripture—so secret and profound—is now lacking any concluding entrustment (*parindanā*) in its later sections.
Although there have previously been three translations, [this remains incomplete].
My original doubts were not yet fully resolved.

I have long contemplated the Sanskrit texts, praying for the opportunity to encounter them; now that the Great Sui dynasty governs the realm, these new scriptures have arrived, and by imperial decree, the relevant authorities have been charged with translating them in succession.
In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, when his dharma assembly was briefly interrupted,
he invited the Tripiṭaka Master from the country of Gandhāra in Northern India— whose name is translated here as Zhìdé—
to serve as his preceptor.

I searched again for the later version and indeed found the "Chapter on Entrustment" (Zhūlèi pǐn) as well as the "Chapter on the Silver-Master Dhāraṇī" (Yínmǔ tuóluóní pǐn). These were translated at Dàxīngshàn Monastery in the capital.
Together with the previously published portions, they comprise twenty-four chapters in total.
It was written in eight fascicles.
The scholar Fei Changfang of Chengdu acted as the scribe (*bishou*).
The monk Shi Yancong of Riyang Monastery, who was proficient in Sanskrit, performed the collation and revision.
The compiler states:

as for the four fascicles by An Shigao," [they are omitted].
The seven-fascicle version by Paramārtha and the five-fascicle version by Jñānagupta both contain omissions.
Therefore, these three sūtras are not recorded here with redundant repetition.
According to the catalogs of Baochang and others,
during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the Tripitaka Master from India, Narendrayaśas, translated one version.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* was expanded into five fascicles under the title *Jīnapramāṇa-mahāprajñā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Examining this title closely now,
it is not a complete translation.
However, within the four-fascicle scripture translated by Wu Chen, two additional chapters were subsequently expounded;
the "Chapter on Lifespan" further continues the text, while the "Chapter on Great Eloquence" extensively elaborates upon the dhāraṇī methods.

therefore, it is called the *Further Extensive Life Span Great Eloquence Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Thus, these constitute the combined six-fascicle sūtra.
The preface states that Shouliang and Da-bian further supplemented its omissions.
By this it is proven that this is merely a continuation of the missing portions,
not a separate translation.
Furthermore, the preface to the sutra states that it was translated in five fascicles by Jñānagupta.

However, the catalogues of Fang and others state that as for Yaśogupta—this [Jñānagupta] and the other [Yaśogupta] were both masters of the Tripitaka who, at that time, translated together and recorded their work interchangeably; thus, both versions are equally valid.
Regarding the six-fascicle version of the *Compendium Sūtra* (*Jiebu jing*), as compared with this eight-fascicle version to clarify their similarities and differences:

first, one chapter in the six-fascicle sūtra is inverted; second, when compared with the new eight-fascicle sūtra, the meaning of the text concerning the "entrustment" (*parindanā*) in these two versions is entirely different.

the reason for this is not yet clear.

This also accords with two versions of the new translation, though there are slight differences between them.

Incorporating these with the sutras, there are five translations in total; two remain in the canon while three have been included in the *Shanfan lu*.

The *Tundun-tuoluo suowen jing* (Sūtra on the Questions of Tuṇḍanetra) is in two fascicles, or sometimes three, translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han. The first translation consists of ten fascicles for the above two sutras, which are kept together in one volume.

The *Mahādruma-kiṃnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles, also titled *Acintyavarga-nirdeśa*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the second translation. The two aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, in two fascicles; also titled *The Chapter on the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*, or in three fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. First translation. *The Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way*, in four fascicles; also known as *The Combined Sūtra on the Divine Footsteps of the Way*, or in two or three fascicles. Translated by the Tripitaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin. Second translation. These two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different renditions. Of the three successive translations, the third version is missing.
The three aforementioned scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one bundle. The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* (Jewel Rain Sutra) in ten fascicles constitutes one bundle;

it was translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci from South India and others. It is the third translation recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. The *Ratnamegha-parivarta-sūtra* (Jewel Cloud Sutra) in seven fascicles was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa from Funan together with Saṃghavarman during the Liang dynasty; this is the first translation. These two scriptures are different translations of the same text; among the three translations—new and old—the second version is missing.

The *Avivartacakra Sūtra* in three fascicles (or four fascicles without the character "遮"), translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty; the first translation. The above two sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*The Sūtra on the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma*, four fascicles. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it as a distinct scripture from the Liang region. It is listed as the second translation in the Northern Liang catalogue: *The Extensive and Majestic Pure Non-retrogressive Wheel Sūtra*, four or six fascicles, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Zhiyan of Liangzhou together with Baoyun. This is the third translation. These three sūtras are the same text translated differently. Its inclusion in the Zhou catalogue among the single-text sūtras as the *A-vui-yue-zhi-che jing* (Skt. *Anuvyañjana-sūtra*) is an error.

*The Scripture on the Seal of Entering and Not Entering Samādhi*, one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. First Translation: Preface and Record. The preface and record at the beginning of this scripture states: On the day of Renwu, the first month of the year Janglǒu (the second year of the Xinghe era of the Wei), when the moon was in the mansion of Shù and the calendar marked Jiǎzǐ, the śramaṇa Gautama Prajñāruci and the śramaṇa Tánlín translated [this text] consisting of 9,193 characters at the residence of the Duke Gāo, the Minister of the Interior and Grandee of the Same Rank. All catalogs state that this was translated by Bodhiruci; this is an error. Now, I rely on the preface and record as the correct version. *The Scripture on the Seal of Entering and Not Entering Samādhi*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yìjìng during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Táng. Newly compiled and entered into the records. Second Translation. Record: These two scriptures are the same original work with different translations. The old translation was listed as a single independent work in the *Zhōu lù* (Catalog of the Northern Zhou); the new examination establishes it as a duplicate translation.
The four aforementioned sutras comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

*Samādhi of the Collection of All Virtues* (等集眾德三昧經), three fascicles (or two fascicles), translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; first translation. *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Collecting All Merits* (集一切福德三昧經), three fascicles, translated by the Yao Qin Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva at Chenziji Monastery; third translation. These two sutras are the same text with different translations; of the three successive translations, one version is missing.

The *Cittadhāra-brahmadeva-sūtra* (Holding the Mind Sutra on Brahmā Deva), four fascicles—also known as the *Sūtra on Adorning the Buddha-Dharma* and alternatively titled the *Sūtra on Equally Governing All Dharmas*—translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty; alternatively in six fascicles and seventeen chapters. The first translation [of this title] consists of the three aforementioned sūtras totaling ten fascicles, contained in the same volume. According to the preface to the *Si-yi-san-mei-jing* (Sūtra of Increasing Benefit) by Shi Sengrui of the Yao Qin dynasty, it states: "I respectfully examine the previous translation; while its phrasing is quite elegant, its essential meaning is obscure. Upon consulting various catalogs, it appears that during the Wu dynasty, the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian (courtesy name Gongming) translated numerous sūtras, yet there is no version of the *Si-yi-san-mei-jing* among them. The *Chi-xin-jing* (Holding the Mind Sutra) which shares the same title as the *Si-yi-san-mei-jing* is actually the translation by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. Thus, Sengrui’s claim that "Gongming previously translated [it] and lost it" is an error.

The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (also simply called the *Suyi jing*) in four fascicles; Sengyou states it is the *Suyi yi jing*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the second translation. The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in six fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty. This is the second translation. These three sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* has a commentary (*śāstra*) in four fascicles.
The first two sutras comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

*Dharanidhara-bodhisattva-sūtra*, four fascicles (sometimes with the characters "Jiawen" [Additional Inquiry] added, or three fascicles), translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin—First Translation; *Lokadhara-sūtra*, four fascicles (also known as *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*, or three fascicles), translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin—Third Translation. These two sutras are the same text with different translations; of the three successive translations, the second version is missing.

*Jì zhū fāngděng xué jīng* (Sutra on the Universal Learning for Deliverance), one scroll; alternatively titled *Wú xué* (Without Learning). Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. First translation. *Dàchéng fāngguǎng zǒngchí jīng* (Mahāyāna Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sutra), one scroll; alternatively titled *Wú chéng* (Without Vehicle). Translated by the Sui Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vinitaruci. Second translation. The above two sutras are the same text with different translations. The Zhou Catalogue lists them as separate texts, but a new examination has classified them as retranslations.
The four preceding scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

*The Scripture on Mañjuśrī Manifesting the Treasure Store* (3 fascicles), also simply titled *The Treasure Store Scripture*, or in 2 fascicles; first translation by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. *The Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Scripture* (3 fascicles, or 2 fascicles); translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra. Fourth translation. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same text. Of the four successive translations, two are missing.

*Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa-sūtra*, two fascicles; also titled *Sarvabuddhacaryā-praveśajñāna-vairocana-garbha-nirdeśa-sūtra*, or four fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñāyaśas and others during the Northern Zhou dynasty. First translation. *Mahāyāna-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, two fascicles; also titled *Sarvabuddhaviṣayajñānapraveśa-vairocanagarbha*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara from Central India during the Great Tang dynasty. Second translation. Both of the above sūtras are the same original text with different translations.
The four aforementioned sūtras comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (Deep Secret Liberation Sūtra) in five fascicles was translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty; the current edition is the first translation of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in five fascicles, produced by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang according to the *Neidian lu*. The current edition is a re-translation. These two aforementioned sūtras comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

*Jiejie jing* (Sūtra on the Analysis of the Sections), one fascicle; translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen dynasty. The above-mentioned sūtra is an alternative translation of the first five chapters of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, appearing here as the first fascicle.
*Saṃtati-vimokṣa-bhūmi-pāramitā-sūtra*, one fascicle;

also titled *Vimokṣa-nītārtha* or *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. This aforementioned sūtra is an alternative translation of the final two chapters of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, appearing as volumes four and five.
The four scriptures listed above are different translations of the same original text; two are complete versions and two are initial translations. 1.

The two scriptures above are different translations of the same original text.

The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra in Four Volumes, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty; the second translation. [These] five sūtras in ten volumes are contained in the same fascicle.

*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, ten fascicles, one set; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty—alternatively, three translations exist. *Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, seven fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang dynasty; newly included in the catalog as the fourth translation. the second translation, *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-varṣa-sūtra* (one fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of Central India during the Sui dynasty;
the internal title of which reads *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-sūtra: Requesting Rain*.
Chapter Sixty-four. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui Dynasty. From the *Neidian lu*, Volume Three.
The three sutras listed above are translations of the same original text with different versions.

The above two sutras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom* (one fascicle), also titled *The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom of the Precious Field*, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty; this is the first translation. *The Scripture on the Tathāgata’s Seal of Wisdom* (one fascicle), also titled *The Scripture on the Dharma-body of All Buddhas*; its translator was lost from Sengyou’s catalogue, and it is now appended to the Song catalogue; this is the second translation. These two scriptures above are the same text with different translations.
The *Shangliujing* (Six Upper Scriptures), ten fascicles, in one volume;

the *Daguandingjing* (Great Consecration Scripture), twelve fascicles, in one volume—or alternatively, the catalog of the "Da" character records it as nine fascicles, which is not yet clear [in its provenance]. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bo Shili Miltuo of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty, with some portions translated separately. The individual fascicles are each distinct scriptures, listed in full as follows:
Volume One: The Sūtra of the Consecrated Three Refuges, Five Precepts, and Protective Amulets.
Volume Two: The Sūtra of the Consecrated Spells of Seventy-two Thousand Divine Kings for Protecting Bhikṣus.
Volume Three: The *Consecrated Dharani Sutra of the One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Spirit Kings Who Protect Bhikṣuṇīs*.
Volume Four: The *Consecrated Dharani Sutra for Protecting the Body with the Hundred Knot Spirit Kings*.
Fascicle Five: The Scripture on the Mantras for the Guardian Deities Who Protect the Left and Right Sides of the Consecrated Palace and Residence.
Fascicle Six: The Scripture on the Four-Directional Divine Mantras Concerning the Causes and Conditions of Consecrated Tombs.
Volume Seven: The Great Divine Spell Sutra of the Consecration for Subduing Māras and Sealing [Evil].
Volume Eight: The Great Divine Spell Sutra of the Consecration of the Maṇi-Inheritance.
Volume Nine: The Divine Spell Sutra of the Consecration for Summoning the Dragons of the Five Directions and Controlling Pestilence and Toxins.
The Tenth Scroll: The Sūtra of the Brahma-Deva’s Oracle for Empowerment.
The Eleventh Scroll:
The Sūtra of Empowerment for Vowing Rebirth in the Pure Lands of the Ten Directions; alternatively titled "Chapter Eleven: Universal Extensiveness."
The *Bie xing suiyuan wangsheng jing* (Sūtra on the Separate Practice for Rebirth According to One’s Vows) is the twelfth fascicle.

The *Guanding bachu guozui shengsi dedu jing* (Sūtra on the Consecration for Eradicating Past Transgressions and Attaining Deliverance from Birth and Death), which is the old version of the *Yaoshi jing*, refers to the Buddha’s journey to Vaiśālī; this is the first translation.
The *Yaoshi rulai benyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru), one fascicle, was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui dynasty.

The second translation in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures): *Yao shi liu li guang rulai benyuan gongde jing* (The Sutra on the Merit of the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha), one fascicle;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. The third translation in the *Neidian lu*:

*Yao shi liu li guang qi fo benyuan gongde jing* (The Sutra on the Merit of the Original Vows of the Seven Buddhas, Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha), two fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing at the Foguang Hall within the Imperial Palace during the Great Tang.
The fourth section of newly translated works included in this collection consists of the three sutras listed above,

which are different translations of the same original text as the *Sūtra on Deliverance from Suffering and Birth through the Removal of Transgressions* (Dizhuguo-zishengdedu-jing) found in the twelfth fascicle of the *Abhiṣeka* (*Guanjing*). Among these,
the two-fascicle version translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing is as follows:
Furthermore, it includes the original vows and mantras of the six Buddhas;
the remainder of the text is largely identical to the translation by Master Xuanzang.
As for that earlier version of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*—
Various catalogs all state that this was translated by the śramaṇa Huìjiǎn of Lùnyè Monastery during the Song dynasty;
however, upon examining its text, it is simply the twelfth fascicle of the *Guǎngdìng* [version] extracted and circulated separately.
There is no other original version.
As for the *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One's Vows*,
various catalogs sometimes state it was translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu period.
Some say it was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;
the version currently in circulation is the "Puguang-pin" (Chapter on Universal Extensiveness), the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahā-abhiṣeka-sūtra*.
There is no other separate edition. Since these two sūtras are both contained within the great collections (*mahā-vaipulya*), [they are not considered distinct works].

As for the separately produced circulating versions, they have been deleted and not recorded. *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han (First Translation).

*Puchao sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence), three fascicles—or four fascicles with the word "Mañjuśrī" added at the beginning—translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa (Second Translation). *Fangbo jing* (Sūtra of the Alms Bowl), one fascicle; a separate translation of the "Chapter on Raising the Bowl" from the *Puchao jing*. Regarding the first fascicle, Sengyou’s catalogue states that it was among the "Translated by Unknown Authors" in Dao’an’s catalogue. Dao’an noted that it originated from the Vaipulya section; it is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue. The above three sūtras are different translations of the same text. There have been six translations in total across the earlier and later periods, of which three are missing. The above six sūtras comprise ten fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll Eleven, Part One of the Separate Records, Appendix: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Six Hundred Fascicles in Sixty Sets. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang at the Yuhua Palace Monastery. The Diagram of the Translation Hall is shown to the right; this is that sūtra.

comprising sixteen assemblies across four locations;
translated into the language of Tang, it comprises six hundred fascicles.

the Tang translation comprises seventy-eight fascicles and eighty-five chapters.

From fascicle 566 to fascicle 573.

*The Scripture on the Dharma-Door of Great Purity*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin (the first translation). *The Scripture on the Dharma-Door of Great Adornment*, two fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui dynasty (the third translation). translated during the Later Han dynasty by an unknown translator. Second translation. One version lacks the visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. *The Sutra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle;

also called the *Sutra on the Visualization of Immeasurable Life*; a different version from the preceding and following sutras; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kāṅ-liang-ye-she (Guṇabhadra) of the Western Regions during the Song dynasty.

Translation One; Translation Two. Missing: *The Sutra of Immeasurable Life* (also titled *The Sutra of Amitābha*), one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. First Translation; Second Version missing.

*The Sutra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Acceptance*, one fascicle, also simply called *The Sutra of Praising the Pure Land*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
Record of Translated Inner Scriptures, Part Two: Translations. The two scriptures above are different translations of the same original text.

As for the *Short Amitāyus Sūtra* translated by Guṇabhadra, its original manuscript could not be found; even if it exists within the various collections, it is identical to the text of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and no different.
The eleven sūtras above, totaling thirteen fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

The *Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Sūtra on Rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven* (one fascicle), also known as the *Maitreya’s Sūtra on Rebirth Above*, was translated by the layman Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty; it is a single-text edition. Although this aforementioned Sūtra on Rebirth Above is a standalone translation, it is included here following the sequence of the *Sūtra on Becoming a Buddha*.

*Maitreya-buddhatva-sūtra*, one fascicle; a different version from the following sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the second translation; of the two translations, one is missing. *Maitreya-āgama-sūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost; recorded in the *Fashang-lu*; now appended to the Eastern Jin record. This is the third translation. *Maitreya-avataraṇa-sūtra* (also known as the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*), one fascicle; begins with "The Great Wisdom Śāriputra"; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the fourth translation. I have respectfully relied upon the two records, the *Changfang-lu* and the *Neidian-lu*, which both state that this is the *Maitreya-avataraṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding the initial mention of "the Greatly Wise Śāriputra":
this sutra was originally translated by the śramaṇa Shi Daobiao of Chang’an;
it was subsequently revised by the śramaṇa Daozheng of Jiangzhou during the Xiao Qi dynasty.
Now, upon careful examination of this account, some may say it is not so.
That Shi Daobiao was merely a monk under Master Kumārajīva who interpreted the meaning of the texts;
he was by no means the primary translator.
Even if this were merely a provisional translation,
how could its textual meaning be considered incomplete?
It was only when the Qi dynasty arrived that the administration strictly mandated further revisions and deletions.
The years and months have passed a great distance,
and the accounts are inconsistent;
since that work was edited by Daozheng, it is difficult to rely upon as a standard.
The sub-commentary on the sutra states that it is "in the Qin language";
thus, this is a translation from the Qin period, free from confusion.
It was previously recorded in Kumārajīva’s catalog, from which it originated.

*Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born as a Buddha*, one fascicle; translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang. This is the sixth translation. The three aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions; there have been six translations in total, of which three are missing.

*The Scripture on the King of Valiantness of All Dharmas*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kapiśa during the Song dynasty. Second translation: *The Scripture on the High King of All Dharmas*, one fascicle—also titled *The Scripture on the Meaning-King of All Dharmas*; translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei. Preface and Record, Third Translation. The aforementioned preface and record state: "In the fourth year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, the year being Renxu, on the twenty-third day of the sixth month of late summer, the cyclical sign being Yiwei, the guest-translator from India, the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci, together with the śramaṇa Tanlin, first translated [this text] at Dingchang Temple under the patronage of Grand Commandant Dou. It consists of 8,449 characters. All other catalogs claim it was translated by Bodhiruci, which is an error. Now, I rely on the preface and record to establish the correct version. Furthermore, the fact that the *Scripture on the High King of All Dharmas* is listed as a single-fascicle work in the Zhou catalog is an error.
The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different renditions; of the three successive translations, one version is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Ultimate Truth* (Paramārtha-dharmavijaya-sūtra), one fascicle, translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. Preface and Record, First Translation: The preface and record at the beginning of this sūtra state that on the first day of the ninth month of the fourth year of the Xinghe era (the Renxu year), a Jiazi day, the śramaṇa Dharmaruci and the śramaṇa Tanlin translated [this text] consisting of 5,576 characters at the residence of the Duke Gao, the Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Marshal. All other catalogs claim it was translated by Bodhiruci, which is an error. Now, I rely on the preface and record as the correct authority.

*The Scripture on the Questions of the Doubts of the Rishi Mahātejo’rcis*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. This is the second translation. The two scriptures above are translations of the same original text with different translations.

*Shunquan fangbian jing* (Sūtra on Accordance with Skillful Means), two fascicles; also known as *Zhuan nüren pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Female Body), or one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. Second translation: *Leyingluo zhuangyan fangbian pin jing* (Sūtra on the Chapter of Skillful Means Adorned with Joyful Garlands), one fascicle; also called *Zhuan nüren pusa wenda jing* (Sūtra of the Questions and Answers of the Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Female Body). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin. Postscript to the Sūtra. Third translation: The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions. Regarding the *Leyingluo zhuangyan jing*:
Upon examining various catalogs,
some state that it was translated by Kumārajīva during the Yao Qin dynasty,
while others claim it was translated by Fǎhǎi during the Song dynasty.
According to a postscript to the sutra, the bhikṣu Huidharma invited Dharmayaśas from the Qin Monastery in Kaśmīra to translate the *Vibhāṣā* from the Hu language into Qin.
The location of this "Qin Monastery" in Kaśmīra remains unknown.
Since it was translated by Dharmayaśas, it should be free from error.
Various catalogs all state that Dharmayaśas was highly proficient in the *Vibhāṣā*, and his contemporaries collectively referred to him as "the Vibhāṣā Master."
Therefore, Sengyou’s catalogue states that the translator of the *Śāriputrābhidharma-vibhāṣā* was this very person.
"She" (Śe) and "shi" (Śī) are merely close in sound.
In Sengji’s catalogue, the four translations previously appended to the record of Saṃghayaśas have been removed; two of these translations are missing their texts.
The eleven preceding scriptures, totaling twelve fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

The *Ṣaḍpāramitā-samuccaya-sūtra* (Six Perfections Collection Sutra) in eight fascicles—also known as the *Ṣaḍpāramitā-aparimita-sūtra*—or in nine fascicles, was translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui of the Wu dynasty; it is a re-translation of a combined version. The *Sudāna-jātaka-sūtra* (Sutra of Prince Sudāna) in one fascicle—also called the *Sudāna-sūtra*—was translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin; the Zhou catalog lists it as a single translation, but this is now considered a re-translation. This latter scripture is a variant translation of the section on the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) from the second fascicle of the *Ṣaḍpāramitā-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Śyāma* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sūtra of the Filial Son Śyāma*. The *Sengyou Lu* states that it was among the scriptures of unknown translators in the catalog of Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the Western Jin catalog as the second translation. *Śyāma’s Sūtra* (one fascicle), translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Shi Shengjian. This is the fourth translation. These two sūtras are the same text, appearing in the second fascicle of the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* within the section on the Perfection of Giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), though they are different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Prince Mupo*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. This is the first translation. *The Sūtra on the Prince Mupò*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Mupo*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty. This is the third translation. These two sūtras, included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), are of the same original text.
The *Jiùsèlù jīng* (Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer), one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty];

recorded in the *Fǎshàng lù*. The above sūtra is an alternative translation from the "Perfection of Vigor" (*vīrya-pāramitā*) section of the fourth fascicle of the *Chū liùdù jīng* (Sūtra on the Six Perfections).

The seven preceding scriptures comprise fourteen fascicles in one volume. Regarding the *Navarṇamṛga-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Nine-Colored Deer), its inclusion as a separate work in the Zhou catalog is an error. 1. *Akṣara-kośa-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Jewel Casket Without Letters), one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. First translation. 2.

*Mahāyāna-vyañjana-vigata-samantaprabhā-garbha-sūtra* (The Mahāyāna Scripture of the Universal Radiance Treasury Free from Words), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India at the West Taiyuan Monastery during the Great Tang dynasty. Third translation according to the Great Zhou catalog. 3. *Mahāyāna-samantaprakāśa-garbha-akṣara-dharmamukha-sūtra* (The Mahāyāna Scripture of the Universal Illumination Treasury: The Dharma Gate Without Letters), one fascicle; a re-translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as the fourth translation. These three scriptures are different translations of the same text. It is an error in the Great Zhou catalog to state that they are different translations of the same text as the *Mahāvaipulya-ratnakoṭa-sūtra*. Of these four successive translations, one translation is missing.

*The Scripture of the Old Woman*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture of the Old Mother* or *The Scripture of the Old Girl*. Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). First translation: *The Scripture of the Old Mother*, one fascicle. Lost among the translations in Sengyou’s catalog; now appended to the Song catalog. Second translation: *The Scripture of the Six Excellencies of the Old Mother*, one fascicle; also called *The Scripture of the Old Mother*. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song [Dynasty]. Third translation. The above three scriptures are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra of the Youth Candraprabha* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sūtra of the Youth Candrasūrya* or *The Sūtra of Śunika*, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; first translation. *The Original Sūtra of Śunika’s Son* (one fascicle); recorded as *Douben*, which is an error, or alternatively titled *Wurir*; translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra; second translation. *The Supplemental Compilation: The Sūtra of the Elder Devarakṣita* (two fascicles), also known as *The Sūtra of the Elder Śrīgupta*, translated by the Sui Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas; fourth translation. One version is missing. The three aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text with different renditions; although they share the same source, they differ significantly in their length and detail.
There are mutual increases and decreases [in the texts].

Furthermore, among the translations by Zhi Qian, there is one fascicle of the *Śunirjīva-sūtra*, which is said to be a different translation of the same original as the *Candraprabha-kumāra-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
Now, upon examining the phrasing and sentences [of both], [they are found to be identical].
The two sūtras are not different;
the father’s name was Shenri and the son’s title was Yueguang.
These two fascicles are divided based on the names of the father and son.
Since the two versions are identical, they are not presented side-by-side.
As for the *Śunirjīva-sūtra*, it is sometimes found within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka,
where it is said to have been extracted from the Āgamas.
Although the *Ekottarika Āgama* contains the account of the householder Śrīgupta,
the story of the youth Candraprabha is not included therein;
this too must be an error.
*The Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Bodhi-apracāra-sūtra* or simply the *Bodhi-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. First translation. *The Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle; also called the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. Second translation.
1. *Ekottara-gajaśīrṣa-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Vinītadeva during the Sui dynasty.
2. *Mahāyāna-gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Zhou dynasty.
3. [Untitled] (Recorded in the *Dazhou lu*). The above four sūtras are different translations of the same original text.
In the *Fanjing tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures) by the śramaṇa Jingmai, a separate version of the *Bodhi-sūtra* in one fascicle is recorded;
furthermore, in the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue), there is another *Bodhi-apracāra-sūtra* in one fascicle.
These two sūtras are both translations by Master Kumārajīva and are alternative titles for the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhisattva-sūtra*; thus, they have not been recorded redundantly.

*The Scripture on the Elder’s Son Jīvaka*, one fascicle; also known as *The Scripture on Jīvaka*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han. First translation. *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Departure*, one fascicle; also called *The Scripture on the Vowed Boy* or simply *The Scripture on Departure*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of the Western Jin. Third translation. *The Scripture on the Departed Boy*, one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhi Fadu of the Western Jin. Fourth translation. Two translations are missing. The above three scriptures are the same text with different translations. Furthermore, in the *Dazhou Catalogue*, a separate entry for *The Scripture on Jīvaka*, one fascicle—translated by An Shigao—is recorded; this is a different title and should not be listed as a duplicate.

*Vatsasūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. Recorded as the first translation in Fashang’s catalogue. *Kṣīraprabhāsa-buddhasūtra*, one fascicle; also called the *Kṣīraprabhāsasūtra*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Recorded as the second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations; they differ slightly in length and detail. Among the four translations, two are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Stainless Noble Woman*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Womb Treasury Sūtra*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty; recorded by Nie Daozhen as the second translation. Regarding this sūtra: it is said to be the same text as the *Womb Treasury Sūtra*, both attributed to Zhu Fahu’s translation. Upon examining the two versions, the wording and phrasing are entirely identical, differing only in their titles. Therefore, only one version is preserved here.

*The Sutra on the Woman in the Womb Listening to the Dharma*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sutra on the Unadorned Woman*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. Third translation: *The Sutra on Transforming the Female Body*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. Fourth translation. The above three sutras are the same text with different translations; the first two are somewhat abbreviated, totaling five translations, two of which are missing.
The twenty-one sūtras above, totaling twenty-two fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Liang Dynasty; the complete text, second translation, with a postscript to the sūtra. Regarding this *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*:
I have carefully consulted the records of Changfang and others,
all of which state that in the second year of the Yongding era of the Chen dynasty (the Dingchou year), the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha produced this sūtra at Jingtu Monastery in Nankang Commandery.

The postscript states: On the eighth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Shaothai era of the Liang dynasty, the year being Dingchou, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated [this work] at the request of Liu Wentai, the Interior Historian of Nan-kang, in Pinggu County.
Now, upon examining the chronological records (*nianli*) of various schools, they differ and contradict one another.

The *Nianli* of Baochang ends with the fifth year of Chengsheng, the Bingzi year, at which point the Liang dynasty ceased. The dates for Zhenluan and Wang Daogui extend until the second year of Shaotai, the Bingzi year, when it was changed to the first year of Taiping.
In the second year of Taiping, the year Dingchou, it was changed to the first year of Yongding.
The *Chen Shixian Lishi* (The History of Chen Shixian) establishes the title as the State of Chen and includes a chronology; it is unknown who authored it.

It is recorded that in the third year of the Yunsheng era, the year Jiashu, it was changed to the first year of the Dading era; this continued until the Later Liang dynasty, after a total of eight years had passed, before the reign title was finally changed.
However, none of the four dynastic calendars list a third year of the Shaotai era.
Since these four versions are all different,
it is not yet clear which constitutes the correct account.
It may be that the third year of Shaothai of the Liang dynasty, the Dingchou year, was indeed the first year of Yongding at the beginning of the Chen dynasty.
In the calendrical records, only the later titles are noted while the earlier names are not recorded;
for now, I shall follow the scriptural records and designate this as a translation from the Liang dynasty.

*The Unprecedented Scripture*, one fascicle. Translator lost during the Later Han; it was erroneously included in the old catalogs among the single-text works of the Hīnayāna. *The Extremely Rare Scripture*, first translation, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog), third translation. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same text. They are the first chapter of the aforementioned *Anuttaraśraya-sūtra* (Scripture on the Supreme Reliance), appearing in its first fascicle.

*The Scripture on the Definitive Compendium* (one fascicle), also known as *The Scripture on the Definitive Dhāraṇī* or *The Scripture on the Resolved Dhāraṇī*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin; the first translation. *The Scripture on Slandering the Buddha* (one fascicle), translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei; the second translation. These two scriptures are different translations of the same original text.

*The Scripture on the Dharma-body Asked by Mañjuśrī in the Ratnakūṭa Samādhi*, one fascicle; translated during the Later Han by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master from Parthia (the first translation). *The Scripture on the Essential Nature of Entering the Dharmadhātu*, one fascicle; translated during the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta and others, Tripiṭaka Masters from India (included in the *Shiyi* supplement as the second translation). The above two scriptures are different translations of the same text.

*The Tathāgata-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Northern Wei dynasty; the first translation. *The Mahāvaipulya-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Zhou dynasty; the second translation. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations. They are recorded in the catalog of the Great Zhou.

*Mahāyāna-śatapuṇya-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty; recorded as the first translation in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. *Mahāyāna-śatapuṇya-vyūha-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle. Re-translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as the second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*Mahāyānacaturdharmasūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty at Dongtaiyuan Temple; recorded as the first translation in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. *Bodhisattvacaturdharmasādhanasūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty at Hongfu Temple; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as the second translation. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

The *Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-vaipulya-sūtra* (or simply the *Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*), one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty—this is the first translation. The *Anuttara-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang—this is the second translation as recorded in the *Neidian lu*. These two sūtras are translations of the same original text with different versions; they differ slightly in length, one being more extensive and the other more concise.

*The Sūtra of the Three Turnings of the Previous Life*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin (first translation). *The Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Northern Wei (second translation). The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Receiving the Prediction*, one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju; first translation. *The Sūtra on King Utpalavaktra Receiving the Buddha’s Prediction and Being Named Subhūṣita*, one fascicle, also simply titled *The Sūtra on King Utpalavaktra*, translated by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa from the Western Regions Zhu Tanwulan; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection); second translation. These two sūtras above are the same text with different translations. From the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* (Sūtra on the Supreme Basis) below, nineteen sūtras were listed in the *Dazhou Catalogue* as independent works; they have now been identified as duplicate translations.

*The Scripture on Reverence for the True Dharma* (or *The Scripture on Reverence for the Right Dharma*), one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhasanta of the Northern Wei. First translation. *The Scripture on Good Reverence*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on Good Reverence* or *The Scripture on the Teacher of Good Reverence*; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty. Second translation. The above two scriptures are translations of the same original text with slight differences in length and detail.

*The Sūtra Praising the Merits of the Mahāyāna*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. *The Sūtra on the Definitive [Extinguishing of] Karmic Obstacles through the Sublime Dharma*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery during the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog as the second translation. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. The former version of the *Sūtra Praising the Mahāyāna* was a single independent work, whereas this is now a re-translation.

The twenty-three preceding sūtras comprise twenty-four fascicles in one volume. *Jianwang jing* (Sūtra on Admonishing the King), one fascicle—also titled *Daxiao Jianwang jing*—translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng; this is the first translation.

*Rulai shijiao shengjunwang jing* (Sūtra on the Tathāgata Teaching King Śatrujit), one fascicle—also simply titled *Shengjunwang jing*—translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; this is the second translation according to the *Neidian lu*. *Fo wei shenguang tianzi shuo wangfa jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha Expounding the Royal Law for King Prasenajit), one fascicle—also simply titled *Shenguang tianzi jing*—translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang and newly included in the catalog; this is the third translation. These three sūtras above are the same text with different translations. It is an error to record the *Jianwang jing* in the Hinayāna section and the *Shengjunwang jing* in the Mahāyāna section as being "single-text" (unrelated) works.

*Mahāvaipulya-sūtra-rāja*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. First translation. *Parivarta-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhasanta during the Northern Wei dynasty. Second translation. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty—First Translation. *Mañjuśrīcarita-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty—Second Translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Peṭa Tree*, one fascicle; translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian (Third Translation). *Sūtra on the Noble Path of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang (Sixth Translation). [Recorded in] the *Neidian lu*. Of the two sūtras above, they are the same text with different translations. There have been six translations in total, four of which are missing. It is an error for the *Sūtra on the Noble Path of Dependent Origination* to be listed as a separate work in the Zhou catalog. Furthermore, there is the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination at the City of Hearing*, one fascicle; its text is identical and not different from the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Peṭa Tree*, differing only in name. Only one version of this latter is currently extant.

*The Sūtra on the Rice Seedling*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *The Sūtra on the Completion of Birth and Death*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of Wu. Zhi Qian himself provided a commentary. Three translations exist, one of which is missing. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations; it cannot be determined which came first.

*The Scripture on the Samādhi of Self-Vow* (Zìshì sānmèijīng), one fascicle. A note beneath the title states: "Chapter Four: Sole Realization," extracted from the *Pure Conduct of Bhikṣus*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han; included in the *Supplemental Collection* (Shíyí) as the first translation. *The Scripture on the Tathāgata’s Sole Realization of the Samādhi of Self-Vow* (Rúlái dúzhèng zìshì sānmèijīng), one fascicle. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; the second translation. The above two scriptures are the same text with different translations. Of the three translations in total, one is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Ablution of the Buddha’s Image*, one fascicle; also called *The Sūtra of the Eighth Day of the Fourth Month* or simply *The Ablution Sūtra*. Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), Translation No. 1. *The Mahāsthapati Sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on the Ablution of the Buddha’s Image*. Translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Shi Shengjian. Translation No. 2. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Merit of Constructing Images*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *The Sūtra on Making Buddha Images*, also known as *The Sūtra on King Udayana Making Buddha Images*, one fascicle; translator lost, currently in the Han catalogue. It is recorded in the Zhou catalogue among the single-fascicle texts of the Hīnayāna, and the claim that it was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmakṣema is an error. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations; their chronological order cannot be determined.

*Longshi nü jing* (The Sūtra of the Daughter Nāgadattā), one fascicle; alternatively, without the character "nü" (daughter). Translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian. First translation. *Longshi pusa benqi jing* (The Sūtra on the Previous Life of the Bodhisattva Nāgadatta), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Longshi nü jing* or *Longshi ben jing*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. Second translation. The two sūtras above are translations of the same original text with differences in length and minor variations.

*The Scripture of the Eight Auspicious Divine Spells*, one fascicle (sometimes omitting the character "divine"); translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi *upāsaka* Zhi Qian—First Translation. *The Scripture of the Eight Yang Divine Spells*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Scripture of the Eight Yang*; newly examined as a re-translation; translated by the Western Jin Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa—Second Translation. *The Scripture of the Eight Auspicious Ones*, one fascicle; translated by the Liang-period Funan Tripitaka Master Saṃghavarman—Fourth Translation. *The Scripture of the Names of the Eight Buddhas*, one fascicle; translated by the Sui-period Indian Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta and others—Fifth Translation. The above four scriptures are the same text with different translations. Their introductory narratives (*nidāna*) are largely identical, though the names of the Buddhas differ slightly. Among these five successive translations, one version is missing.

*Yulanpen jing*, one fascicle; also called *Yulan jing*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. *Ba’en fengpen jing*, one fascicle; translator lost; now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. These two sutras are translations of the same original text with different versions; it is difficult to distinguish which came first, though they differ slightly in their breadth and brevity.

*The Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Image*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhākarasiṃha of India during the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the canon as the first translation. *The Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Image*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing during the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the canon as the second translation. The two sūtras above are translations of the same original text with different versions; the latter version is slightly more extensive.

*Jiaoliang shuzhu gongde jing* (Sūtra on the Measurement of the Merit of Rosaries), one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhākarasiṃha of India during the Great Tang Dynasty, newly included in the canon. First translation. *Shuzhu gongde jing* (Sūtra on the Merit of Rosaries), one fascicle; within it is stated that this is the "Method for Measuring the Merit of Rosaries from the Manjuśrī Dhāraṇī-piṭaka," translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang Dynasty, newly included in the canon. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.
The twenty-nine sūtras above comprise twenty-nine fascicles in one bundle. The *Amoghapāśa-vikurvaṇa-mantra-sūtra* in thirty fascicles occupies three bundles;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang, it was newly included in the catalog as the fourth translation. The *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle was translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui dynasty; this is the first translation. The *Amoghapāśa-mantra-hṛdaya-sūtra* in one fascicle was translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; it appears in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures) as the second translation. These two latter sūtras are different translations of the same text. They correspond to the "Introduction Chapter" of the aforementioned Great Sūtra, which the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci previously translated as a single fascicle titled the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-hṛdaya-sūtra*, though its original manuscript has not yet been recovered.

The *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-īśvararāja-sūtra* in three fascicles, also titled the *Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-mantra-rāja-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of India during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon. First translation. The *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle, also known as the *Pumen* (Universal Gate), translated by Li Wuchan, a Brahmin from Northern India, during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon. Second translation. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. These are excerpts from the Sanskrit manuscript and do not constitute the complete work; they share the same title as the preceding three sūtras but are distinct versions.

*The Sūtra of the Divine Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Eyes and a Thousand Arms*, two fascicles (or one fascicle), translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhitong of Zongchi Monastery during the Great Tang; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement). First translation. *Sūtra of the Mother Dhāraṇī Body of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes*, one fascicle (also known as *Qianbi Qianyan*); translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations. The first translation’s palm-leaf manuscript was intermingled, resulting in some loss of textual order.

The Sūtra of the Great, Perfect, and Unobstructed Heart of Great Compassion of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes, in one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānagupta from Western India during the Great Tang Dynasty. This is a supplementary single-text edition. Although this Heart Sūtra is a standalone text, it is included here following the preceding *Sūtra on the Body*.

*The Scripture on the Secret Treasury of Divine Mantras of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan; newly compiled and included in the canon, first translation. *The Scripture on the Cintāmaṇi Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated during the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnaciṃtā of India; newly compiled and included in the canon, second translation. The nine scriptures above, totaling twelve fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī-mantra of the Wish-fulfilling Mind of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon as the third translation. *The Sūtra of the Cintāmaṇicakra Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Great Tang, newly included in the canon as the fourth translation. The above four sūtras are the same text with different translations. Although these four versions of the sūtra vary in length—some being more extensive and others more concise—they are all based on the Sanskrit original and do not fully exhaust its meaning. Among those produced by Yi Jing, this version is the most concise.

*The Mañjuśrī-mūla-ekākṣara-dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *The Ekākṣara-mantra-rāja Sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of the Great Tang Empress Wu; newly included in the canon as the second translation. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

Furthermore, the twelve Buddha names at the beginning of the first fascicle of the *Scripture of the Names of Five Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas* are identical to those of the aforementioned *Scripture of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas* and are not distinct from them. The *Ekādaśamukha-hṛdaya-mantra-sūtra* is a different translation of the same text as [the preceding work] collected among the scriptures; its ritual methods (*vidhi*) are somewhat more extensive.

The *Mārīcī-devī-sūtra*, one fascicle—sometimes titled with the "Small Character" (Xiaozi) prefix—is of lost translation; it is now appended to the Liang dynasty catalog’s "Supplements" (*Shiyi*). The aforementioned scripture is the first part of the tenth fascicle of the *Ji jing* (Collected Scriptures), being a partial variant translation of the *Mārīcī-devī-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra of the Five Dhāraṇīs*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. According to the *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures*, this was a combined translation. Regarding the "Five Dhāraṇīs," they are: (1) the *Dhāraṇī of the Thousand Recitations* which can extinguish all sins; (2) the *Six-Syllable Dhāraṇī*; (3) the *Divine Dhāraṇī Spoken by Seven Koṭis of Buddhas*; (4) the *Divine Dhāraṇī that Follows the Intent of All Tathāgatas*; and (5) the *Heart-Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*. As for the *Dhāraṇī of the Thousand Recitations*, there is also a separate transcription of it that constitutes a distinct sūtra; however, since it is already included herein, it is not listed separately. It is incorrect for the *Record of the Great Zhou* to divide these into five separate sūtras.

*The Sūtra of the Thousand-Turn Dharani Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhitong of Zongchi Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty.
