and the Six-Syllable Dhāraṇī from among the miscellaneous dhāraṇīs.

These are different translations of the same original text. *The Great-Hearted Cundī Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty; listed as the first translation in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. *The Great Radiant Cundī Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Mother of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi of Southern India during the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the catalogue as the second translation. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Compared to the older version, the newer ones are somewhat more extensive. Nevertheless, even according to the Sanskrit originals used for translation, they are still not exhaustive. Among the five primary dhāraṇīs and the miscellaneous dhāraṇīs, only the mantras themselves have been translated, with no other ritual methods provided.
*Jing* (Scriptures), Volume 20, in two fascicles: the upper fascicle contains seven scrolls and the lower fascicle contains thirteen.

*Guānzìzài Púsà Suíxīn Zhòu Jīng* (The Sūtra of the Heart-Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva), one scroll; also known as the *Duōlí Xīn Jīng*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhītong of Zongchi Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the catalog. This aforementioned *Guānzìzài Suíxīn Zhòu*...
The first five spells from the *Zhoushou wushou jing* (Sūtra of the Five Spells),
the initial随心咒 (spell that accords with the mind) of Avalokiteśvara from the *Zazhou jing* (Sūtra of Miscellaneous Spells),
and the fifth [chapter] of the *Jijing* (Collected Sūtras).
Since these were translated earlier, they are compiled here. *Zhongzhong zami zhujing* (Various Miscellaneous Incantation Scriptures), one fascicle;

alternatively, some editions omit the word "jing" (scripture). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Northern Zhou dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) as part of the combined translations of miscellaneous incantations, totaling twenty-three items in all. Six incantations from within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. *Xuanta miezui tuoluoni* (Dhāraṇī for Extinguishing Sin through Circumambulating Stupas).
One: A mantra for extinguishing transgressions through a single prostration and for the Buddhas of the ten directions to come and welcome one at the end of life.
One: A mantra for making offerings to the Triple Gem.
One: An Avalokiteśvara mantra for repentance.
1. A Vajra-spell for snakes;
2. A spell for lifelong meditative tranquility;
3. A spell for swelling.
One Vajra-mantra for curing the illnesses of malevolent spirits;
one thousand-fold dhāraṇī;
and one Avalokiteśvara Heart-mantra.
There are four dhāraṇī spells of seven *koṭi* Buddhas:
one is the "Spell that Follows the Intent of All Tathāgatas," and one is identical in origin to the "Six-Syllable Dhāraṇī Spell" found among the five spells.
1. One Recitation of the Triple Gem Refuge Mantra.
*Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by Du Xingyi, Court Gentleman of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
Recorded as the first translation in the *Dazhou lu*. *Uṣṇīṣa-viśiṣṭa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle. The Great Tang.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of Central India during the Tang Dynasty; appended as a supplementary translation.
The *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Buddhapālita of Kapiśa during the Great Tang;
recorded in the catalog of the Great Zhou as the third translation. The *Parama-vijayabuddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī-karmāvaraṇaviśodhana-sūtra*, one fascicle. Great [Tang].
The *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated for a second time in the Eastern Capital by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Tang Dynasty;

alternatively titled with the word "Mantra" added: the *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*, newly compiled into the catalog as the fifth translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang.
These five sūtras above are translations of the same original text.
*The Sūtra of the Secret Retention of Immeasurable Gateways*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on Attaining All-Knowledge through Realizing the Way and Subduing Māra*.
Translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian. First translation. *The Sūtra of the Retention Born from Immeasurable Gateways*, one fascicle;
alternatively titled *The New Sūtra of the Secret Retention*. Translated by the Eastern Jin-period Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India.
The fifth translation is the *Ānandamukhanirhāradhāraṇīsūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Immeasurable Gateways*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty, it was included as a supplement.
The sixth translation is the *Aparimitadvāramārapramardanadhāraṇīsūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively simply called the *Mārapramardanadhāraṇī*.
The *Ānandamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated during the Song dynasty by the Śramaṇa Guṇadatta of the Western Regions together with Xuanchang—this is the seventh translation.
The *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Northern Wei dynasty—this is the eighth translation.
The [same] *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty.
The ninth translation, *The Sutra on the Solemn Production of Bodhisattvas*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty.
The tenth translation, *The Sutra of the Dhāraṇī of the Gate of Boundless Production*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of Zhixiang Monastery during the Great Tang;
newly included in the canon. The eleventh translation, as listed above.
Eight sūtras of the same original but different translations are recorded in the catalogs of Seng Chang and others among the works of Dharmabhadra (Jue Xian).

Furthermore, there is one scroll of the *Xin weimi chi jing* (New Sūtra on the Subtle and Secret Retention), which is the *Chusheng wuliangmen chi jing* (Sūtra on the Retention of the Gate of Producing Immeasurable [Dharmas]). It is also included among the works of Guṇabhadra (Gongde Xian).
Additionally, there is one scroll of the *Chu wuliangmen chi jing* (Sūtra on the Emergence of the Retention of the Gate of Immeasurable [Dharmas]), which is the *Ānandamukhanirhāradhāraṇī*.

Since these scriptures are of such great volume, the eleven translations—distinguishing between new and old—are not preserved separately; three translations are missing from the record. *Shengtang biyin tuoluoni jing* (1 scroll), translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang;

recorded as the first translation in the *Neidian lu*. *Miaobi yinzhuang tuoluoni jing* (1 scroll), translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Khotanese Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda; newly included in the records as the second translation. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same text. Regarding the *Shengtang biyin jing*, it was previously recorded as a single independent work, but a new examination has determined it to be a duplicate translation.
The seventeen sūtras above comprise seventeen fascicles in one volume.

*Anantapāramitā-dharmamukha-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Ananta-sūtra*—translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin dynasty; first translation. *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-bodhisattva-paripṛcchita-sarvadharmapraveśānantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the layman Wan Tanyi of the Northern Qi dynasty; third translation. The two sūtras above are translations of the same text with different versions; of the three successive translations, one is missing.

*The Vajra-Supreme Taste Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas during the Northern Wei dynasty; the first translation. *The Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui dynasty; the second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Flower-Cluster*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *The Divine Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Flower-Accumulation*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. It was erroneously included among the single-text works in the Zhou catalogue. These three sūtras are the same work with different translations; it is impossible to distinguish their chronological order.

*The Scripture of the Six-Syllable Mantra King*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue (First Translation). *The Scripture of the Divine Six-Syllable Mantra King*, one fascicle; translator lost, included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) and now appended to the Liang catalogue (Second Translation). These two scriptures are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī Mantra Spoken by the Seven Buddhas as Asked by the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha*. Translator lost; currently appended to the Liang Record. First translation. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). *The Tathāgata-upāya-kauśalya-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty. Second translation. The above two sūtras are translations of the same text with different versions. Regarding the *Tathāgata-upāya-sūtra*, the old catalogs list it as a single independent work, while the new examination classifies it as a re-translation.

*The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī of Holding Phrases* (1 fascicle), also known as *The Dhāraṇī of Phrases*, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as the first translation. *The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī-bhājana* (1 fascicle), also known as *The Dhāraṇī of Bhājana*, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* as the third translation. *The Scripture on the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King of the East* (1 fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India and others during the Sui dynasty; recorded in the fourth entry of the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog). The above three scriptures are different translations of the same original text. The first two are abbreviated, while the latter scripture is somewhat more extensive. Of these four translations spanning the earlier and later periods, three remain and one is missing. Regarding the *Scripture on the Supreme Lamp King*, the old catalog records it as a single independent work, whereas a new examination reveals it to be a duplicate translation.

*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Skillful Means of the Wholesome Dharma*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Secret Wholesome Gate of the Vajra*, one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *The Sūtra of the Divine Incantation of the Dharma-Gate for Protecting Life*, one fascicle; translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci; recorded in the Great Zhou catalogue as the third translation. These three sūtras are the same text with different translations. It cannot be determined which of the first two came before the other. As for the *Sūtra of the Dharma-Gate for Protecting Life*, its inclusion in the Great Zhou catalogue among the single-text entries is an error.

*The Sutra of the Vimalaprabhāsa-mahādhāraṇī*, one fascicle. Translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Western Region śramaṇa Mito-shan and others; newly included in the canon as the second translation. Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan initially translated it under the title *The Dhāraṇī Sutra of the Stainless Pure Light*, but as the original manuscript has not yet been recovered, that version is omitted. *The Sutra of the Dhāraṇī Spell for Invoking Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to Subdue Poisonous Harm*, one fascicle. Also simply titled *The Sutra of Invoking Avalokiteśvara*. Translated by the foreign layman Zhu Nanti of the Eastern Jin. This is the second translation; of these two translations, one is missing. The aforementioned nineteen sutras, totaling nineteen fascicles, are contained in the same volume.
*The Sutra on the Inner Treasury of a Hundred Jewels*, one fascicle; also called *The Sutra on the Inner Treasury of a Hundred Items*.
Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han Dynasty. This is the first translation; the second translation is missing.

*The Sutra on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in the Warm Chamber*, one fascicle; also simply called *The Warm Chamber Sutra*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty. Compiled as a supplement.
The *Sūtra on Sūrata* (one fascicle), translated during the Former Liang by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Shilun;
this version is missing from the first and subsequent translations. Third Translation:
The *Sihamei Jing* (one fascicle), also known as the *Bodhisattva Daoshu Jing* or the *Daoshu Samādhi*; this version is missing from three of the four preceding translations.
Translated during the Wu dynasty by the Yuezhi lay practitioner (upāsaka) Zhi Qian. First translation; two translations exist, one of which is missing.
*Bodhisattvajanmabhūmi-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Cāmarakṣa-sūtra*—translated during the Wu dynasty by the Yuezhi lay practitioner Zhi Qian.
[The entry for] Zhou is a single text erroneously placed first. First translation; the two translations consist of one complete text and one missing. *Catuḥpratisaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle.
Scroll from the Western Jin Dynasty, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. Second Translation; one of two translations;
the other is missing. *Śirīmatī-bhaginī-sūtra*, one scroll; also known as *Śirīmatī-strī-sūtra*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa.
First Translation; one of two translations; the other is missing. *Sampūrṇaprabhāsa-samādhi-sūtra*, one scroll; also called *Sampūrṇaprabhāsa*. Third [translation].
*Mei* (possibly referring to the *Chengju guangming jing*, "Sūtra of Perfectly Accomplished Radiance"), translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty;
the second of two translations, one of which is missing. *Baowang jing* (one fascicle), also called *Baowang tongzi jing*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty;
the first of two translations, one of which is missing. *Pusa xing wushi yuan shen jing* ("Sūtra on the Fifty Causes and Conditions of the Bodhisattva’s Deeds").
*One fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty.* First translation; the second translation is missing.

*Bodhisattva-practitioner Sūtra*, one fascicle, also titled *The Sūtra on the Elder Vaiśya’s Inquiry into the Practice of Contemplating the Body*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Bo Fa Zu of He-nei during the Western Jin Dynasty.
First translation; the second translation is missing. *Sūtra on the Fields of Merit for All Virtuous Ones*, one fascicle, or...
The *Clouds of All Fields of Merit Sūtra* (also simply titled the *Sūtra on the Fields of Merit*), translated by the Western Jin śramaṇas Dharmamati and Dharmaprajñā;
the first of two translations, one of which is missing. The *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Eastern Jin Indian Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra;
the third of three translations, two of which are missing. The *Buddhavacana Sūtra*, one [fascicle].

Volume [1]: Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty; First Translation. One of two translations is missing: *The Sūtra of King Suvarṇavarṇa*, one fascicle;
translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty; Second Translation. One of two translations is missing:
*The Sūtra on the Exposition of the Deeds of the Laity and the Clergy*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin Dynasty.
The second translation; among these two translations, one lacks the *Ekottara-buddhanāma-sūtra* in one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Sui dynasty.
The second translation; among these two translations, one lacks [the aforementioned]. The seventeen sūtras above comprise seventeen fascicles and are contained in the same volume.
*Chengyang zhufu gongde jing* (Sūtra on the Praise of the Merits of All Buddhas), three fascicles; also known as *Jizhufu hua* (Collection of the Flowers of All Buddhas) or four fascicles.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kikkaya of the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Northern Wei dynasty. This is the third translation; two other translations are missing.

*Suzhenti tianzi jing* (Sūtra of the Son of Heaven Susaddanta), three fascicles; also called *Wensishi jing* (Sūtra of the Four Questions). Or two fascicles. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty.

The first translation by Hu; one of the two translations is missing. *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*, one fascicle—also simply called *Māyā-sūtra*—or in two fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanying of the Xiao Qi dynasty. The second translation; one of the two translations is missing.
*Juekongzaihuan-jing* (Sūtra on Eliminating Fearful Calamities), one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin dynasty. The second translation; both translations are extant.
*Yi-quē-pò-jīng* (Sūtra on the Missing Pai), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Pò-jīng-chāo* (Excerpts from the Sūtra of Pai), translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].
Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) as the second translation; there are three translations in total, two of which are missing.

*Guānshìyīnpúsà shòujì jīng* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva), one fascicle; also known as *Guānshìyīn shòujué jīng* (Sūtra on the Decision of Avalokiteśvara). Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tánwúchí of Hónglóng, Song [Dynasty].
The third translation by Wujie; two of the three translations are missing. The above six scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume.
The *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Sea Dragon King Sutra) in four fascicles, or sometimes three, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin—this is the first translation;
two translations exist, one being missing. The *Śūraṅgamasamādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles, also simply called the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, or...
Two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; the ninth translation among nine, with eight missing.

*The Scripture on the Method for Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva*, one fascicle—said to be excerpted from the *Scripture on Profound Merit* (*Gambhīra-guṇa-sūtra*), also known as the *Samantabhadra Contemplation Scripture*;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty; the third translation among three, with two missing. *The Scripture on the Contemplation of Bhaiṣajyarāja*.

*The Scripture of the Two Bodhisattvas, Rājā and Bhaiṣajyarāja*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of the Western Regions during the Song dynasty—this is the first translation;
one of the two translations is missing. *The Scripture on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on What Was Spoken*;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty—this is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. The above five scriptures.

Ten fascicles in one volume. *The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and Severing the Bonds* (10 fascicles), also known as *The Scripture on the Ten Stages and Severing the Bonds*, in eleven or fourteen fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty. Of the two translations, one is missing. *The Essential Collection of All Buddhas* (2 fascicles), also simply called *The Essential Collection*; translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty. Of the two translations, one is missing. *The Scripture on Unprecedented Causes and Conditions* (2 fascicles), also simply called *The Unprecedented Scripture*; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanjing of the Xiao Qi dynasty. Of the two translations, one is missing. The above three scriptures comprise fourteen fascicles in two volumes.

The *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-sūtra* in twelve fascicles, or fourteen fascicles, or sixteen fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the second translation, while one of the two translations is missing. The *Cāru-divākara-vimala-samādhi-sūtra* in two fascicles—sometimes lacking the word "samādhi" or appearing in three fascicles—translated by the lay believer Nie Chengyuan of the Western Jin dynasty; this is the second translation, while one of the two translations is missing. These two aforementioned sūtras comprise fourteen fascicles in two volumes.

The *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* in thirteen fascicles—also titled the *Bhadrakalpa-samādhi-sūtra*—exists in versions of either seven or eleven fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. Of these two translations, one is missing. From the *Vimalaprabhā-śuddha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* below, thirty-six sūtras are listed; although they are said to be re-translations, only a single copy of each remains, while all others have been lost and cannot be recovered despite diligent search.
Mahāyāna Sūtras Translated Individually: One Hundred and Thirty-one Works in Two Hundred and Ninety-three Fascicles, Arranged in Twenty-four Sets.
*Mahādharmapradīpa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, twenty fascicles, two sets;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui Dynasty. *Mahātejas-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, twenty fascicles, two [sets].
*The Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas*, twelve fascicles (or thirteen fascicles), translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui Dynasty;
*The Sūtra of the Names of Three Thousand Buddhas of the Three Kalpas*, three fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty;
*The Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Past Adornment Kalpa*, Fascicle One; and *The Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Present Bhadrakalpa*.

The *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Future Star宿 Kalpa*, Scroll Middle and Scroll Lower; translator lost, included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) and now appended to the Liang Record.
These two sūtras comprise fifteen scrolls in two fascicles. The names of the Buddhas of the three kalpas appear in Changfang’s *Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon*.
They have now been combined into a single volume. Among these, the names of the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa (Worthy Kalpa) are derived from the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra*.
Combined as a double translation, the following is the single-text version of the *Buddhanāmasūtra* (The Names of Buddhas), arranged here according to its categories.

The *Sūtra of Five Thousand Five Hundred Buddha Names*, eight fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of Central India during the Sui dynasty; and the *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Merits and the Buddhas’ Protective Recollection*, two fascicles, said to have been extracted from various sūtras, or four fascicles, translated during the Cao Wei period with the name of the Tripiṭaka Master lost; these two supplementary texts are included here. The aforementioned two sūtras comprise ten fascicles in one volume. Regarding the *Sūtra on Inconceivable Merits*, it is an error in the *Da Zhou Catalogue* to state that it is the same text as the *Sūtra Asked by the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Light*.

*The Flower Hand Sūtra* (13 fascicles), also known as *The Sūtra Collecting All Roots of Goodness*, in ten, eleven, or twelve fascicles; one volume. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. *The Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra* (4 fascicles), also known as *The Vaipulya Dānadhāraṇī Sūtra*; translated by the monk Fa-zhong of the Northern Liang dynasty at Gaochang Commandery. Recorded in the *Baochang Lu*. *The Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* (4 fascicles); translated by Prince Śubhakaravarman of the Cīna country during the Yuan Wei dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Power Adornment* (3 fascicles); translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s Meaning of the Mahāvaipulya Round Enlightenment* (1 fascicle); translated by the Kaśmīri monk Buddhatrāta during the Great Tang dynasty. These four preceding sūtras, totaling twelve fascicles, are compiled together in this single volume.

*The Scripture on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, ten fascicles (or eight fascicles), one volume; alternatively, the title lacks the character "Hai" (Ocean). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Regarding this *Scripture on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou* states it was translated by Guṇabhadra during the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty. However, having carefully examined the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalogue), it records that this was translated by Dharmakṣema of the Eastern Jin, and not by Guṇavarman of the Song; thus, the *Great Zhou Catalogue* is in error. Furthermore, it states that this work is the same text as the single-fascicle *Scripture on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin, compiled here as a duplicate translation. Since the version translated by Master Kumārajīva has long been lost and its fascicle count differs entirely, they cannot be directly correlated. For now, I have followed various ancient catalogues and included it within the single-fascicle section.

*Mahā-upāya Buddha-ṛṇa-pratyupakāra Sūtra*, ten fascicles; translator lost, listed among the Later Han records. *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā Sūtra*, three fascicles; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin records and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). These two sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, share one volume. According to the *Dazhou Record*, it states that the seven-fascicle *Baoen Jing* is of the same original text as the single-fascicle *Dafangbian Baoen Jing* translated by Zhi Chen during the Han dynasty; and that the three-fascicle *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā Jing* is of the same original text as the single-fascicle *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā Jing* translated by Nie Daozhen during the Western Jin. Since these two single-fascicle versions of the *Baoen* and *Pūrva-caryā* sūtras were previously missing and their fascicle counts differ entirely from the current versions, they cannot be directly correlated. Therefore, they are compiled here within the section for single-fascicle texts according to various traditional catalogs.

The *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* in six, seven, or eight fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei; and the *Sarvadharmāvalokanacaryā-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty. These two sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, are bound together in one volume.

The *Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra* (*Pusa chutai jing*), five fascicles—also simply called the *Womb Sūtra* (*Tai jing*)—or eight fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty; the *Sūtra on the Extensive Manifestation of the Samādhi for Spreading the Way* (*Hongdao guangxian sanmei jing*), four fascicles—or without the word "samādhi"—also titled the *Anavatapta Dragon King Sūtra* (*A'nuotada longwang jing*) or the *Sūtra on Entering the Diamond-like Inquiry into the Concentrated Mind* (*Ru jin'gang wen dingyi jing*), comprising twelve chapters and translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty. Regarding these two sūtras, the Renshou, Da Zhou, and other catalogs all state that they are different translations of the same original text as the *Anavatapta Dragon King Sūtra*.
Both sutras state that they were translated by Zhu Fahu and are thus classified as retranslations. However,
according to Sengyou’s *Lu*, Zhu Fahu produced only the two-fascicle *Anoutada jing*.
The sub-note states that it is also titled *Hongdao guangxian sanmei jing*.
Among the records of Daochang, there is a two-fascicle *Hongdao guangxian sanmei jing* translated by Zhu Fahu of Central India.
The sub-note states that it is also titled *The Sūtra on Ānanda Inviting the Buddha*.
The *Táng nèidiǎnlù* records both sūtras as translated by Master Hù.
Furthermore, the two catalogs of Chángfáng’s *Nèidiǎn* record them accordingly.
Translated anonymously during the Western Jin dynasty.
There is also a two-fascicle *Anavatapta-nāgarāja-sūtra*;
upon comparing the texts of these two scriptures now, there is no difference between them whatsoever.
However, because titles were established in various ways,
the numerous catalogs differ;
some even record two sūtras under a single title.
In some cases, titles were inscribed interchangeably,
yet at that time no one realized the error; thus,
the confusion and proliferation grew deeper by the day.
Now that one has been discarded and the other preserved,
I hope there will be no further errors or omissions;
I have retained a single copy and included it within this compilation.

The *Sūtra on the Merit of Giving Lamps*, one fascicle; also known as the *Sūtra on Lighting Lamps*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi dynasty. These three preceding sūtras comprise ten fascicles in a single volume.

The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty. Regarding this *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, the *Dazhou Catalogue* states that it is a different translation of the same text as the seven sūtras such as the *Śikṣānanda-śikhā* (translated by Dharmarakṣa). This is an error; one must not hastily equate them as duplicate translations merely because their titles appear similar. According to the *Sui Catalogue*, the *Śikṣānanda-śikhā-sūtra* was extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, and the six sūtras including the *Aṅgulimālīya-paścāttāpa* were likewise excerpted from the aforementioned great collection. Since they are not different translations of the same original text, they should remain categorized as individual sūtras according to tradition.

*The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Wúsuǒyǒu* (Anupalaṃbha-bodhisattva-sūtra), four fascicles; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui dynasty. *The Sutra of the Fifty Calculations of the Perfection of Wisdom* (*Mingdu wushi jiaojì jīng*), two fascicles; alternatively titled without the characters "Perfection of Wisdom" (*Mingdu*) or without the fifty characters; translated by the Parthian Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. These three sutras, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*Zhongyin jing* (Sūtra on the Intermediate State), two fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty. *Dafagujing* (Sūtra of the Great Dharma Drum), two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. *Wenshushili wenjing* (Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Questions), two fascicles; also simply called *Wenshu wenjing*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty. *Yue Shangnü Jing* (Sūtra of the Girl Candrottarā), two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India and others during the Sui dynasty. *Dafangguang Rulai Mijizang Jing* (The Vaipulya Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury), two fascicles; translator lost, now appended to the records of the Qin dynasty. These five sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume. Regarding the *Dafangguang Rulai Mijizang Jing*, the records of the Great Zhou state that it is a different translation of the same text as the *Dafangdeng Rulai Zang Jing* (The Vaipulya Sūtra of the Tathāgata-garbha). However, upon examining the phrasing and the essential meaning, they differ significantly; therefore, it is treated as a separate version.
*Mahāyāna-Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, three fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Great Tang dynasty;
recorded in the catalog of the Great Zhou. *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Good and Evil Karmic Retribution*, two fascicles;
also titled *Mahāyāna-Tattvārtha-sūtra*; translated by the foreign śramaṇa Bodhimitra; the date of its production is unknown; recorded in the Great Zhou catalog.
The following are now appended to the Sui Catalogue: *The Lotus-Face Sūtra*, two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui Dynasty.
*The Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Wen-shu-erh-shih-wen ching*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) along with the *Mahāyāna-pratimā-lakṣaṇa-puṇya-sūtra*.

*The Extensive Sūtra of the Secret Dhāraṇī of the Great Jewel Pavilion’s Secure Abiding*, three fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang; newly entered into the catalog. *The One-Syllable Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin King Sūtra*, five fascicles (also known as the *Five Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Sūtra* or four fascicles), translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang; newly entered into the catalog. *The Great Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the One-Syllable Heart Mantra for the Age of Dharma Decline*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajñādeva of North India during the Great Tang; newly entered into the catalog. These three sūtras, totaling nine fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

The *Mahābuddhōṣṇīṣa-tathāgataguhyahetupratipattinirdeśasarvabodhisattvasamyak-sarvākāra-lalitavistara-sūtra* in ten fascicles, one volume: translated in the Great Tang by the śramaṇa Huaidi of Xunzhou together with Indian monks at Guangzhou; newly compiled and entered into the canon. The *Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-vikurvaṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra* in seven fascicles: translated in the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India together with the śramaṇa Yi-xing; newly compiled and entered into the canon. The *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra* in three fascicles (also known as the *Subāhu-vinaya*, or in two fascicles): translated in the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India; newly compiled and entered into the canon. The above two sutras, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*Susiddhikara Sūtra*, three fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the canon. *Mūlamandala Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled without the word "Sūtra"; translator lost; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) collection; now appended to the Liang dynasty catalog.

The *Vajraśekhara-yoga-saṃkṣipta-japa-vidhi* in four fascicles, also known as the *Sūtra*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi of South India during the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the canon. These three scriptures, totaling eight fascicles, are bound together in one volume.

*The Scripture on the Divine Incantations Spoken by the Seven Buddhas*, four fascicles (alternatively titled *The Scripture on the Incantations Without Words Spoken [by the Seven Buddhas]*). Translated during the Jin dynasty; the name of the Tripiṭaka Master is lost. It is now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. Regarding this *Scripture on the Divine Incantations of the Seven Buddhas*, the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou* classifies it as a re-translation, stating that it is the same text as the single-fascicle *Scripture on the Divine Incantations of the Seven Buddhas* translated by the foreign Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. However, since the text of this single-fascicle version has long been missing and its number of fascicles differs, they cannot be directly correlated. Therefore, I have included it here according to the old catalogues within the section for single-fascicle texts.

*Mahā-maṅgala-artha-deva-mantra-sūtra*, two fascicles (or four fascicles), translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanyao, Director of the Office for the Regulation of the Sangha under the Northern Wei; recorded in Fashang’s catalogue. *Mañjuśrī-ratnakara-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang; newly included in the catalogue. *Vajraprabhā-jvālā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Great Tang; newly included in the catalogue. *Āṭavaka-mahāyakṣasenāpati-buddhotpāda-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost, included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection); now appended to the Liang dynasty catalogue. *Amitābha-dundubhisvara-rāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost, included in the *Shiyi*; now appended to the Liang dynasty catalogue. *Mahāsamantabhadra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle.
*The Sutra of the Great Seven-Jeweled Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle; translated during the period of lost translators, included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), now appended to the Liang Record.
*The Sutra of the Six-Syllable Great Dhāraṇī Mantra*, one fascicle; translated during the period of lost translators, included in the *Shiyi*, now appended to the Liang Record.
*The Sutra of the Divine Mantra for Dwelling Peace*, one fascicle; translated during the period of lost translators, included in the *Shiyi*, now appended to the Liang Record.

*The Maṇirohaṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated during the Later Han dynasty by an unknown translator. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) as translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

*The Sūtra of Divine Incantations Spoken by the Master Bhadra*, one fascicle; the record states it was spoken by the illusionist "Wusuoshuo. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

Included in the *Shiyi*. *The Dhāraṇī Incantation for Protecting All Children*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. *The Dhāraṇī of the Heart of All Buddhas*, one fascicle.

Scroll: *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra for Deliverance from Suffering and Calamity*, one scroll, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed in the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.

*The Eightfold Name Universal Secret Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one scroll, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed in the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. *The Lokeśvararāja Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one scroll, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang;

listed in the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. *The Six-Gate Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one scroll, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed in the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [End of] the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
*The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Pure Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhitong of Zongchi Monastery during the Great Tang.
Included in the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou*, among the nineteen sūtras totaling twenty-three fascicles in the same volume.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Wisdom Torch*, one fascicle; translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan, Devendraprajña;
recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. *The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Assembly of All Buddhas*, one fascicle;

translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan, Devendraprajña; recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. *The Great Self-Existent Dhāraṇī of Immediate Attainment through Recitation*, [one fascicle].
*Dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha from Northern India.
Also known as *The Dhāraṇī of the One Hundred Thousand Seals Attained*, one fascicle;
translated during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda from Khotan. Newly compiled and included in the catalog: *The Sūtra for Saving Those with Averted Faces*.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Incantation for Burning Hungry Ghosts*, one fascicle; also known as *The Incantation for Bestowing Food upon Hungry Ghosts*.
This concludes with the incantation for bestowing water. Translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan;
newly included in the canon. *The Dhāraṇī Incantation of King Alaṃkāra*, one fascicle. Translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Incense King Bodhisattva*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon;
*The Sūtra of the King Adorned with All Merits*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon;
*The Dhāraṇī King Sūtra for Eradicating Karmic Obstructions*, one fascicle, [translated by] the Great... [Tripitaka Master Yi Jing].
*The Sūtra on the Auspicious Night*, one fascicle, newly compiled and included in the canon by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing and newly compiled for inclusion.

*The Dhāraṇī of the Supreme Mind of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha Capable of Fulfilling All Wishes and the Method for Seeking the Power of Hearing and Retention*, one fascicle, from the "Chapter on Accomplishing All Meanings," translated during the Middle Tang period.

The Chapter on the Five-Syllable Heart Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva from the Vajraśekhara Sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of India; newly included in the catalog. One fascicle.
Translated during the Great Tang Dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi of South India.

Newly included in the catalog. The Essential Yoga Method of Avalokiteśvara-Yogamālā Bodhisattva. One fascicle. Translated during the Great Tang Dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra of South India. Newly included in the catalog.
Volume [of] the *Newly Compiled Catalog*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi of South India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
The aforementioned three sutras, including the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra*, along with the preceding four volumes of the *Yogācāra* [texts], all derive from the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*.
The Sanskrit original of that sūtra consists of one hundred thousand stanzas; these four sutras are abridged essential excerpts and do not constitute the complete work.

*The Scripture on the Buddha’s Grounds*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. The *Neidian lu* records that there is a commentary of seven fascicles. *The Scripture Briefly Explaining the Instructions Given by the Buddha as He Was About to Enter Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle; also called *The Scripture on the Buddha’s Imminent Parinirvāṇa* or *The Scripture on the Bequeathed Teaching*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. There is a commentary of one fascicle. Regarding this *Bequeathed Teaching Scripture*, it was frequently recorded in older catalogs within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) Vinaya or compiled among the Lesser Vehicle Sūtras. However, because the commentary translated by Dharma Master Paramārtha explains it primarily through the lens of the Mahāyāna—such that the specific tenets of the Lesser Vehicle are not prominent—it has now been moved and included here.
*The Sūtra on the Birth of the Bodhicitta*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty, etc.
*The Buddha-mudrā Samādhi Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty;
included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). *The Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the layman Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin Dynasty; included in the *Shiyi*.

*Pusa benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Previous Lives of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Wuqi* (Without Arising). Translated by the Western Jin layman Nie Daozhen. Included in the *Shiyi*.
*Kianfo yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas), one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin.

Recorded in the *Fashang lu*. *Xianshou jing* (Sūtra of the Virtuous Head), one fascicle; also known as the *Xianshou furen jing* (Sūtra of the Lady Virtuous Head). [Begins with] "Qi... [fragmentary].
*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Candraprabha*, one fascicle, translated by the śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qin dynasty;
alternatively titled *The Boy Candraprabha* or *The Boy Candra*. Translated by the lay devotee (upāsaka) Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. Note:
This *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Candraprabha* is listed in the *Dazhou Catalogue* as a retranslation, being recorded as having the same original text as the *Sūtra of the Boy Candraprabha*.
This is an error; since the meaning of the text is entirely different, it has been translated as a single entry.

*Śraddhā-prajñapti-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Heart-Illumination), one fascicle—also known as *Citta-prakāśa-brāhmaṇī-bhikṣuṇī-bhakta-dāna-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Brāhmaṇī Wife Citta-prakāśa Offering Rice Water)—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *Daśadig-andhakāra-vināśana-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Extinction of Darkness in the Ten Directions), one fascicle—also called *Daśadig-andhakāra-nirvāṇa-sūtra*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *Mṛgamātṛ-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Deer Mother), one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Furthermore, within various catalogs there is another work titled *Mṛgaputra-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Deer Son), one fascicle, said to have been translated during the Wu period by the foreign Upāsaka Zhi Qian. Its text and phrasing are identical to the aforementioned *Mṛgamātṛ-sūtra*; they differ only in their titles, so they are not listed twice.

*Māraparājaya-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Defeat of Māra), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Together with the twenty-six preceding scriptures, these twenty-six fascicles are contained in one volume. *Rājaputra Śrīprabha-sūtra* (The Scripture of Prince Śrīprabha), one fascicle;

also known as *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-śrīprabharājaputra-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. Regarding this *Rājaputra Śrīprabha-sūtra*, the Catalogue of the Great Zhou classifies it as a retranslation. This is an error, as it is claimed to be a different translation of the same text as the *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* (or *Sudhana-sūtra*). However, since the wording and meaning differ, it is treated as a standalone text.
*Mahāyānopadeśa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty.
*Dṛḍhamatī-bhaginī-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *Sthiramatī-bhaginī-sūtra*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui dynasty.
*Sārthavāha-devaputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle—or alternatively titled *Apraśna-śabda*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui dynasty.
*The Sūtra of the Supreme King of All Dharmas*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of India during the Sui dynasty.

*The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita-rāja*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sūtra of the Eight Maṇḍalas*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Nadi of India during the Great Tang dynasty; recorded in the *Da Zhou Catalogue*. *Bodhisattva Vimalamati*.

*The Sutra on the Rites for Paying Homage to the Buddha-Dharma*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Nadi of India during the Great Tang Dynasty, included in the *Collection of Omissions from the Record of the Great Zhou*.
*The Sutra on the Merit Arising from Upholding the Names of the Seven Buddhas*, one fascicle;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang Dynasty, included in the *Record of Inner Scriptures*. *The Sutra on the Buddha’s Prediction of the Duration of the Dharma at His Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle; alternatively...
[The Scripture on the Samādhi of Silent Illumination and Divine Transformation, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang;
the Chart of Translated Scriptures. The Scripture on the Prediction for Cāṃpeyya, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang;
the Chart of Translated Scriptures. The Scripture on Neither Increasing nor Decreasing, translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei.]
One fascicle; some say two fascicles, which is an error. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
*Sūtra on the Merit of Building Stūpas*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Included in the *Dazhou Catalogue* as part of the "Supplement. *Sūtra on the Merit of Circumambulating Buddha Stūpas*, one fascicle; also called *Circumambulating the Stūpa*.
*Gongde jing* (Sūtra on Merit), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the era of the Great Tang Empress; newly compiled and entered into the canon. One fascicle.
*Dacheng sifa jing* (Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Four Dharmas), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the era of the Great Tang Empress;

newly compiled and entered into the canon. One fascicle. *Youde nü suowen dasheng jing* (Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of the Virtuous Daughter), translated during the era of the Great Tang Empress. One fascicle.
*Mahāyāna-saṃsāra-sarvabhava-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated during the Dazhou era by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India;
newly included in the catalog under the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang.

*Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Suvarṇavarṇa*, one fascicle, translated during the reign of the Empress of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing; newly included in the catalog. The Buddha... [text ends]
*The Sūtra on the Seal of the Dharma Spoken for the Nāga King Sāgara*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon.
*The Sūtra on King Siṃhasauḍasa’s Abstinence from Meat*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery during the Great Tang, newly included in the canon.
*The Sūtra on the Offering of Wax Candles after the Parinirvāṇa*, one fascicle; also titled *The Four Classes [of Disciples]*.
The *Guanla jing* (Sutra on the Offering of Wax) also simply states "Guanla jing," translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Heaven.

According to the catalogs of the Great Zhou and others, this *Guanla jing* was considered a re-translation; however, the claim that it is an alternative translation of the same original text as the *Yulanpen jing* is erroneous.
Now, having examined the differences in the wording, it is established as a distinct, independent text.

*The Scripture on the Names of the Eight Buddhas*, one fascicle; also known as *The Scripture of the Eight Buddhas*. Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. The aforementioned twenty-two scriptures comprise twenty-two fascicles in a single volume. Regarding the *Scripture on the Names of the Eight Buddhas*, the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou* states that it is a different translation of the same text as the *Scripture of the Eight Auspicious Mantras*; this is an error. Although the number eight is the same, the locations where they were preached differ entirely, and their purposes are distinct; therefore, it stands as an independent work.
*The Bodhisattva’s Internal Practice of the Six Pāramitās Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Internal Six Pāramitās Sūtra*.
Translated by the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao of Linhuai during the Later Han dynasty, it was originally included in the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) section and later added to the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Omissions).

*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Bodhisattva Throwing Himself to a Starving Tiger and Erecting a Stūpa*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s catalogue states that it records the act of giving one's body as alms to a starving [tiger].
The *Hu jing* (Tiger Sutra), translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Fasheng of Gaochang during the Northern Liang dynasty; postscript to the sutra.

The *Jingang sanmei benxing qingjing buhuai bumie jing* (Sutra on the Vajrasamādhi’s Innate Purity, Indestructibility, and Immortality), one fascicle, newly co-translated and appended to the *Sanqin lu*.

Also known as the *Jingang qingjing jing* (Vajra-Purity Sutra). The *Shizi yue fo bensheng jing* (Sutra on the Previous Life of the Buddha Siṃhacandra), one fascicle, newly listed as a work of lost translation and appended.

The *Sanqin lu* (Record of the Three Qin), the *Youjingang qingjing jing* (Sutra of the Right Vajra Purity), and various catalogs all state that the former was translated by the foreign Upāsaka Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty, though it was lost after the Han and its name subsequently reappeared.
Regarding the *Shiziyue fo jing* (Sutra of the Buddha Siṃhacandra), various catalogs all state that it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
Upon careful examination, however, the phrasing and wording of these two sutras are not those translated by Qian or Fahu.
These appear to have been translated by Master Kumārajīva and others since the Qin and Liang periods;

as they are now considered to have lost their original sources, they are appended to the Qin Records. *The Sūtra on the Wife of the Elder Dharmavatsa*, one fascicle; translator unknown. This title appears in An Shigao’s *Record of Heterodox Scriptures from the Liang Territory*, and it is now likewise appended to the Liang Records. *The Sūtra of the Kingdom of Sālā*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra of the King of Sālā*. Translator unknown. It is now appended to the Eastern Jin Records. The above two scriptures.
In the *Fashang lu*, both [texts] are stated to have been translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Now, upon close examination, the phrasing and wording of these two sūtras are not those translated by Master Kumārajīva.

They appear to have been translated during the Jin or Wei periods. Regarding the *Fazhi qi jing* (Sūtra on the Wife of Fazhi), its title already appears in Master Dao’an’s *Liangtu yijing lu*; it is now likewise appended to the Liang records.
The *Sālavatī-sūtra* is appended to the Jin Records.

The *Daśamaṅgala-sūtra*, one fascicle, is of lost translation and is now appended to the Qin Records. The *Ātreyī-dārikā-siṃhanāda-nītārtha-sūtra*, one fascicle, is of lost translation and is now appended to the Liang Records;
it is included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Omissions) section of the *Yiqiezhi guang* (Light of All-Knowledge).
*The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of the Immortal’s Compassionate Mind and His Abstention from Eating Meat*, one fascicle;

translator lost, now appended to the Qin record. *The Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, two fascicles (or one fascicle); translator lost during the Northern Liang dynasty, included in the *Shiyi* supplement. *The Scripture on the Extinction of the Dharma*, one fascicle;
a scripture with a lost translator in Sengyou’s catalog, now appended to the Song record. *The Scripture on the Profound and Great Dedication*.
One fascicle; missing from Sengyou’s catalogue, it is now appended to the Song catalogue. *The Scripture of the Prince of Heaven and the Demon Bilara* (one fascicle);
sometimes the characters "Prince of Heaven" are omitted, and it is also called *Piluo*. Sengyou’s catalogue states that this was among the missing scriptures of Master Dao’an;
it is now appended to the Qin catalogue as a supplement. *The Scripture on the Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct for Upāsikās* (two fascicles); likewise [appended].

It is simply called the *Jingxing jing* (Sutra on Pure Conduct), or sometimes without the word "jing" (sutra). Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it as a distinct sutra from the Liang region;
it is now appended to the Liang catalogue. The *Badarenjue jing*, one fascicle, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han.
According to Baochang’s catalogue, there is also the *Sanpin dishi jing*, one fascicle, also known as the *Dishi xue you sanbei jing*.
*The Sutra on the Four Classes of Disciples* (or *The Sutra on the Four Classes of Disciples*, also known as *The Sutra on the Training of the Four Classes*), one fascicle;
translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Wu. Translated during the Western Jin dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa, according to the *Fashang Lu*.
*The Sutra on Future Transformations* (or *The Sutra on the Consciousness of Future Transformations*), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty.
*Past Buddhas’ Almsround Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Sūtra on the Past World*, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa.
*Twelve Dhūta Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Śramaṇa Dhūta Sūtra*, translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra.
*Jyotiṣka Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra.
The *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* (translated by Luo), one fascicle. Sengyou’s catalogue states that it was a work of unknown translatorship during the period of Master Dao’an;
it is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue.
Regarding this *Rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra*, the *Dazhou Catalogue* and other records state that it is extracted from the *Āgama*.
I have carefully examined the four Āgamas and found that this sūtra does not exist among them.
Although the narrative concerning King Dīrghāyu in the sixteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama* shares some thematic similarities, its meaning and content differ entirely;
as this is a Mahāyāna text, it has been compiled here.

*Fǎchángzhù jīng* (Sūtra on the Permanence of the Dharma), one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that this was a lost translation by Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the Western Jin records. Twenty-three sūtras in twenty-five fascicles share this same volume, beginning with the *Upāsikā-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra*. Among these ten sūtras, the older catalogues all classified them within the Hīnayāna section. However, upon examining their literary principles, they are found to involve much of the Mahāyāna. Fearing that the ultimate truth might be obscured by being placed among the "Small" [Vehicle], I have moved them here.
The *Bodhisattva-vinaya-piṭaka* (The Bodhisattva’s Treasury of Discipline) consists of twenty-six works in fifty-four fascicles, arranged in five bundles.
Now, "precepts" (*śīla*) is the general term for the prevention of transgressions.
The pure precepts of a bodhisattva restrain only the mind,
whereas the discipline of a śrāvaka prevents transgressions of body and speech; therefore,
there are cases where a bodhisattva incurs a mass of faults due to external conditions, leading to the reproaches and formal censures of others.
Bodhisattvas and Mahāsattvas do not have such things at all.
The Buddha speaks directly for them so that they may practice accordingly;
since there is no basis for violating the precepts, the matters of reprimand and formal conclusion are omitted.
I have excerpted those passages from various Mahāyāna sūtras that clarify the points of training (*śikṣāpada*).
These are here designated as the Bodhisattva-vinaya-piṭaka.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vidhi-sūtra* (or *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*) in ten fascicles—also known as the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra*—in one volume of eight fascicles, was translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. At the beginning of this sūtra is a verse of homage, which is extracted from the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" section within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Formerly, the Śramaṇa Fashang, the Chief Administrator of the Shaoshuan Monastery during the Northern Qi dynasty, replied to an inquiry from Goguryeo, stating:
"The *Dichizhi* was received by the Bhikṣu Asaṅga from Maitreya."
Asaṅga was none other than the Bodhisattva Asanga.
Furthermore, according to the Record of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou,
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* consists of eight fascicles and contains twenty-seven chapters.
It is divided into three sections.
The first section consists of eighteen chapters;
the second section consists of four chapters.
The third section consists of five chapters.
The text does not provide alternative titles for it; however, in this current edition, it is sometimes titled *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* and sometimes titled *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.
Now, upon examining the scriptures, it is found that there are many names for this work;
the text states that it is called the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-mātṛkā*,
and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The name "Unfailing Manifestation" (*Abhedyapradarśana*) is the root of unobstructed pure wisdom (*anāvaraṇaviśuddhajñāna*).
Yuo (the Master You) stated that it is not the case that no other names are produced;
furthermore, this has been verified by examining various catalogs.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema exists separately;
it is an error to call it the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.

The *Bodhisattva-kuśala-śīla-sūtra* in nine fascicles—also called the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* in one account—or in ten fascicles, was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty and others. Regarding this single scripture, all catalogues state that it is a different translation of the same original text as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.
Now, examining the principles and the text, it is clear that they are not without distinction.
The *Śīla-sūtra* has a "Preface Chapter" at the beginning and a "Practice and Adherence" section at the end.
Neither the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* nor the *Śīlaparivarta* contains [the text in question];
however, within the *Śīlaparivarta* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there are both the text for receiving the bodhisattva precepts and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.
The *Kṣāntiśīla-sūtra* (or *Bhadraśīla-sūtra*) does not contain it at all.
Aside from these, the textual meaning is largely the same.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Dichizhi) has been extracted from the various records of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and compiled into this treatise.
Since there are such discrepancies, I have not yet dared to establish a definitive title.
Furthermore, according to the *Record of the Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou, it is stated that this is named the *Śīla-sūtra* and is also called the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
It is called the Bodhisattva Vinaya-moral code;
it is called the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is called the root of all wholesome dharmas.
It is named the Land of Peace and Bliss;
it is named the Collection of All Pāramitās.
In total, there are seven names.
The first fascicle begins with the *Upāliparipṛcchā-śīlasaṃvara-dharma*.
Only at the start of the second fascicle does the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) appear.
There are thirty distinct chapters in sequence; furthermore, there is a separate edition titled the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.
Now, upon examining the original text of the scripture and comparing it with Sengyou’s record, they differ.
At the beginning of the scripture there is "Thus have I heard," yet there is no account of Upāli questioning the method for receiving the precepts.
It consists of only nine fascicles.
The *Upāliparipṛcchā-śīla-saṃvara-dharma* is none other than the single later fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.
If one takes this as the first fascicle, it accords with the record of Sengyou.
However, since this version of the *Bhūmi-sūtra* has been separated from its original for a long time, it is now suddenly compiled into ten fascicles; one might fear that doubts will arise.
This *Śīla-sūtra* likewise follows the *Bhūmi-vastu* by dividing it into three sections.
The first section is titled "Bodhisattvabhūmi" and contains thirty chapters.
The second section is titled "Tathatā-vyavasthāna" and contains four chapters.
The third section is titled "Niṣṭhāgamanabhūmi" and contains six chapters.
Yǒu says: "The sequential arrangement of the chapters may perhaps cause confusion for those who consult it.

One fascicle of the *Jingyezhang jing* (Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions), whose translator is lost, is now appended to the Qin catalogue as a single volume. These two sūtras [the *Jingyezhang jing* and the preceding one] totaling ten fascicles share a single case. Regarding the *Jingyezhang jing*, Fǎshàng’s catalogue states it was translated by Zhú Fǎhù; however, upon examining its phrasing and syntax, it differs entirely from the stylistic flow of the sūtras translated by Master Fǎhù, and is therefore considered a work of lost translation.

The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* in seven fascicles, also known as the *Householder Bodhisattva Precepts*, exists in versions of five, six, or ten fascicles; it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty at Guzang. The single-fascicle *Brahmajāla Sūtra* was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is a second translation, whereas the previous version lacked the section on receiving the ten wholesome precepts. The single-fascicle *Sūtra on Receiving the Ten Wholesome Precepts* was lost to translation after the Han dynasty and was included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). These three single-fascicle sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.
*The Bodhisattva’s Ornament of the Fundamental Vows Sūtra*, two fascicles (sometimes without the word "Bodhisattva"), newly compiled as a Vinaya text;
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty—this is the first translation among three, two of which are missing.

*The Buddha-Treasury Sūtra*, four fascicles (also known as the *Sūtra on the Selection of All Dharmas*), or in two or three fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
*The Single-Volume Bodhisattva Precepts Text* (translated by Kumārajīva), one fascicle: extracted from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* chapter, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty, and subsequently included as a supplementary translation.
*The Second Translation of the Bodhisattva Precepts Text*, one fascicle: extracted from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; [spoken by] Maitreya.
The Bodhisattva’s Discourse on the Record of the Translated Inner Scriptures by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, Volume Three.
Regarding the two aforementioned sutras, they are different translations of the same original; there have been three translations in total, with one translation currently missing.

*The Ritual Text for the Bodhisattva Precepts* (Bodhisattva-śīla-karman), one fascicle; excerpted from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva and translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. *The Sūtra on the Good Precepts of Bodhisattvas* (Bodhisattva-kuśala-śīla-sūtra), one fascicle; a single-text edition translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśa during the Song dynasty, based on the questions of Upāli. [Recorded in] the *Baoshang lu*. The above six sūtras and ten texts are contained in the same volume.

*The Bodhisattva’s Inner Precepts Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty. Recorded as a single work in the *Fashang lu*. *The Upāsaka’s Five Precepts and Dignified Conduct Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty. Recorded as a single work in the *Baocang lu*. Regarding the above, it is an error for various catalogs to include this *Upāsaka’s Five Precepts and Dignified Conduct Sūtra* among the Hīnayāna Vinaya texts. The former [the *Bodhisattva’s Inner Precepts Sūtra*] is the root text of the Bodhisattva precepts, while the latter [the *Upāsaka’s Five Precepts and Dignified Conduct Sūtra*] contains the ritual for receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, as well as the methods for relinquishing them and performing repentance. Since these do not belong to the Hīnayāna school, they have been moved and included here.

*Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *Viśuddha-śīla-sūtra*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin (first translation). *Vimala-vinaya-vaipulya-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin (second translation, recorded in the catalog of Fashang). *Śānta-svara-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Tathāgata-bhāṣita-viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra*—translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Fahai (third translation). Fourth translation [missing]. These three sūtras share the same original text but differ in their translations; of the four successive translations, one is missing.
*Mahāyāna Tri-saṃvara-pāpadeśanā Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui dynasty.
*Record of Inner Scriptures*, single-fascicle edition. *Bodhisattva Pañcadharma-pāpadeśanā*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Bodhisattva Pañcadharma-pāpadeśanā Sūtra*; translator lost;
now appended to the Liang dynasty record as a single-fascicle edition. *Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra*, one fascicle; Liang dynasty, [transcribed by] Fu.
*Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of the Southern [Dynasty].
*Bodhisattva-śīla-upavāsa-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin;
a second translation exists, while two other translations are missing. *Mañjuśrī-pāpadeśanā-sūtra*.

One fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Five-Part Confession of Transgressions*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty. Of the two translations, one is missing.
*The Scripture on Śāriputra’s Confession of Transgressions*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Scripture on Confession of Transgressions*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. Of the three translations, two are missing. Section Three: Dharma and Vinaya.
*Meijing* (Sutra on the Unconscious), one fascicle; also simply titled *Falüjing* (Sutra on the Dharma and Vinaya), translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian;
second translation, one of two translations, the other being missing. *Shíshàn yèdào jīng* (Sutra on the Path of Ten Wholesome Actions), one fascicle;

translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan; newly included in the catalogue as a single-fascicle text. The above fourteen sutras comprise fourteen fascicles.

In this same volume, I have carefully consulted the old catalogues. Among the Mahāyāna Vinaya texts, the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* and the *Kāśyapa-sūtra* are now included within the *Ratnakūṭa-parivarta*, and thus are not listed here again.

The *Mahāvaipulya-triśikṣā-sūtra* is the same text as the *Tri-vidhi-saṃvara-parivarta* of the *Ratnakūṭa*, and the *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* is the same text as the *Upāli-parivarta* of the *Ratnakūṭa*. Now...
As these have been compiled and included within the Ratnakūṭa section, they are not recorded here.
The Bodhisattvapitaka contains ninety-seven works in five hundred and eighteen fascicles, arranged in fifty bundles.
The Bodhisattva-abhidharma consists of two categories:
first, those that explain the sūtras; second, those that elucidate the essential nature and characteristics of phenomena (*dharmas*).
In the older catalogs, these were recorded together and compiled in a confused manner.
The present collection is divided into two categories:
those explaining the sūtras are listed first,
while those elucidating the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are compiled afterward.
It is hoped that there will be no confusion or intermixture, so that readers may easily understand.
There are twenty-one works of Mahāyāna commentaries on sūtras and śāstras, totaling one hundred and fifty-five fascicles in fifteen bundles.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* consists of one hundred fascicles, or alternatively one hundred ten, or seventy fascicles, arranged in ten bundles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, this is a standalone work composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna as a commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Master Kumārajīva stated that if it were translated in its entirety, it would comprise one thousand fascicles; however, because the intellectual capacity of the people of Qin was weak, he abridged it, retaining only one-tenth of the original.

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, twelve fascicles (or fifteen fascicles), one volume; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci and others during the Northern Wei dynasty. This is a standalone work. Regarding the commentary composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*—which is the "Ten Grounds Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*—the preface to this treatise states that Bodhiruci and Ratnamati were translating together within the palace halls of Luoyang, with Buddhayaśas serving as the oral interpreter and the Emperor personally receiving the text in writing. However, it is not the case that both the records of Bodhiruci and Ratnamati contained this work in the *Chángfáng lù*. Now, they have been combined into a single volume and are included in the record of Bodhiruci.

The *Sūtra on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva* Treatise, in five, six, seven, or ten fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty. This is the single-text edition that comments upon the *Sūtra on the Questions of Maitreya*.
This is the forty-first assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.

The four-fascicle *Mahāyāna-ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra*, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei, represents the first of two translations; one of the two is missing. [The above] explains the old single-fascicle *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
This is the forty-third assembly of the *Ratnakūṭa*, specifically the *Sūtra on the Four Dharmas of the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin*.

One fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena and others of the Northern Wei dynasty. The preface and record are contained in this single volume. The above is the commentary on the "Ratnaśikhin Chapter" of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.

Now, regarding the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, which is the forty-seventh assembly, the *Lunxu ji* (Record of the Preface) states: On the first day of the ninth month in the year of Xinyou, the third year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, on the day of Gengzi, it was translated within the Jinhua Temple in the city of Ye by the Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena, a Kṣatriya of royal lineage from the country of Uḍḍiyāna; and by the Brahmin Gautama Dharmaruci from the country of Central India, together with the Dharma-protector, the Great Virtuous One, General of the Chariots and Cavalry, Acting Minister of State, Palace Attendant, and Chief Censor Gao Zhongmi of Bohai, who was a lover of the Dharma, and the Śramaṇa Tanlin. Monastics and laypeople joined forces for this task. The text consists of four thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven characters. All other catalogs claim that Bodhiruci translated it, but this is an error; we now follow the *Lunxu ji* as the correct record.
The three aforementioned treatises, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume. *The Commentary on the Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* (Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra), seven fascicles;

composed by Bodhisattvas such as Bandhuprabha and others, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded separately in the Neidian lu. *The Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra*, two fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Dharmagupta of the Sui dynasty. [Recorded separately in the Neidian lu. *The Verses on the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang and newly included in the canon. The three aforementioned treatises, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Śāstra*, three fascicles. Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya (Asaṅga) and explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei dynasty. First translation. *Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, three fascicles. Verses by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, commentary by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang dynasty. Newly compiled as the second translation. The above two treatises and their verses are translations of the same original text with different versions.
*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-vibhaṅga-grahaṇa-abheda-prajñapti-śāstra*, two fascicles;
composed by Bodhisattva Guṇadatta, also known as the *Guṇadatta-śāstra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
This single text appears in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. Regarding the four treatises and their verses mentioned above, although their authors differ, they all provide commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā*.
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there is also the ten-fascicle *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*.
