Upon examining its textual structure and principles, it was composed by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei as a commentary on Vasubandhu’s treatise; since it was not translated from an original Sanskrit manuscript, it is not included here.
Furthermore, there is the two-fascicle *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra-śāstra*, also known as the *Gāthā-śāstra*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of Central India during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Single volume, first translation. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*, composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati of Central India together with Senglang and others during the Northern Wei dynasty. Second [translation].
The first translation consists of the aforementioned five treatises in eleven fascicles, contained in the same volume.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* in two fascicles—beginning with a verse of homage—or in one fascicle, was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Northern Wei dynasty, together with Tanlin and others; it has been included here as a supplement. These two treatises are different translations of the same original text. As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* in five fascicles newly translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing, its original manuscript has not yet been obtained.
*The Treatise on the Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacinti* (4 fascicles), also known as the *Exegesis of the Sūtra of Superior Contemplation*;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty; single-text edition. *The Treatise on Nirvāṇa* (1 fascicle), composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
a brief commentary on the *Sūtra of Nirvāṇa*; translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmaprajña; date unknown.
In the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Inner Scriptures), appended after the first translation of the Yuan-Wei period, there is:

*The Treatise on the Verse "Originally Existing, Now Non-existent" from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle*, explaining a single verse of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Liang dynasty.

*The Treatise on the *Udānavarga* (Sūtra of the Final Teaching), one fascicle*, explaining the *Udānavarga*; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen dynasty. [Supplement] (Shiyi)
*Commentary on the Single-Volume Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei. *Treatise on the Sūtra of the Threefold Perfection*, one fascicle.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; includes commentary but lacks the sūtra text. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Masters Vimokṣasena and others of the Northern Wei.
Preface to the Single-Volume Translation. The initial preface to this treatise states:

"The Tripiṭaka Master Vimalamitra, a Brahmin from India, and the Dharma-loving Śramaṇa Gautama Liu-zhi, together with the Śramaṇa Tan-lin, translated [this work] at Jinhua Temple within the city of Ye during the third year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, when the year was Xin-you, the month was Ji-shu, and the day was Geng-wu."

On the thirteenth day, [I] translated one thousand ten words. A memorial submitted by Gao Zhongmi, General of the Household of the Righteous Cavalry, Grand Marshal with the Rank of Peer to the King, Censor-in-Chief, and Marquis of Bohai, requests that these records be venerated, protected, and circulated. All previous catalogs state that these were translated by Bodhiruci;
this is an error. Now, based on the sequential record, this is established as the correct version.

*The Commentary on the Sūtra of Turning the Wheel of Dharma*, one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; includes a sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) but lacks the root sūtra. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena and others of the Northern Wei dynasty. Preface and Record (Single Volume): The initial record of this treatise states: "Gao Zhongmi, General of the Flying Cavalry, Grand Marshal, Acting Minister of State, and Censor-in-Chief of Bohai, was skilled at seeking the principles of righteousness and selecting the true while rejecting the false. He therefore invited the Dharma Master Vimokṣasena and his disciple Gautama Liuqi to the Jinhua Monastery within the city of Ye. In the third year of the Xinghe era, the year being Daliang, the eighth lunar month, the first day of the cycle being Gengzi—the eleventh day—they translated [this work] consisting of three thousand nine hundred and forty-two words. The Śramaṇa Tanlin acted as the oral translator and recorded the proceedings. All other catalogs state that this was translated by Bodhiruci; this is an error. We now rely on this preface and record as the correct version.
The eight treatises above, totaling twelve fascicles, are contained in one bundle.
The Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-artha-śāstra consists of seventy-six works totaling three hundred and sixty-three fascicles, arranged in thirty-five bundles.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, one hundred fascicles, spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva, in ten bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded in] the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures) regarding single and combined translations. Regarding this *Yogācāra-śāstra*: during the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated it under the title *Shiqidi lun* (Treatise on the Seventeen Stages), but he reached only five fascicles before the work was interrupted due to obstacles. During the Northern Liang, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema translated the *Dichichi lun* (Treatise on the Stages of Yogic Practice), which consists of only ten fascicles; this is the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" section from within the "Maulī Bhūmi" (Basic Section). This present *Yogācāra-śāstra* represents the third translation. The original bundles for the first two versions were incomplete, and it was only with the translator of the Great Tang that the entire collection was finally made complete.

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings), twenty fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. [Two bundles. The *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra), one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattvas such as Jinabhadra; translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. [Catalog entry for a single volume. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-kārikā* (Verses on the Manifestation of the Holy Teachings), one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. [Catalog entry for a single volume. The *Dharmadharmatāvibhaṅga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Distinction between Phenomena and Their True Nature), one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya; translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. [Catalog entry for a single volume. The *Mahāyānābhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* (Compendium of Mahāyāna Abhidharma), seven fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. [Catalog entry for a single volume. The above four treatises, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same bundle.

The *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* in sixteen fascicles, a commentary compiled by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed as a single volume in the *Neidian lu*. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* in four fascicles, the original work of the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna with the commentary by the Brahmin Qingmu (Candrakīrti), translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin; listed as a single volume or in eight fascicles. These two treatises comprise twenty fascicles in two bundles.

*Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra-vyākhyā*, fifteen fascicles; originally composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and explained by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. This is recorded as a standalone work in the *Neidian lu*. It is the same commentary as the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, differing only in its specific explanations.

*The Treatise on the Twelve Gates*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. *The Treatise on the Eighteen Emptinesses*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. *The Diagram of the Translation of Scriptures*, one fascicle. *The Hundred Treatises*, two fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Āryadeva, explained by the Bodhisattva Vasu, and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. *The Root Text of the Extensive Hundred Treatises*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Āryadeva, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. These five treatises, totaling twenty fascicles in two volumes, are recorded as single works in the *Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures*.

The *Mahāyāna-śataka-vṛtti* (Extensive Commentary on the Hundred Verses of the Mahāyāna) in ten fascicles, based on the original by Āryadeva and the commentary by Dharmapāla; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded as a single work in the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Analysis of the Ten Stages) in fourteen fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; alternatively recorded as twelve or fifteen fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. [Recorded as a single work in the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures. The *Bodhicaryāvatāra-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom for the Equipment of Enlightenment) in six fascicles, based on the original by the Venerable Nāgārjuna and the commentary by the Bhikṣu Sthiramati; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui dynasty. [Recorded as a single work in the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures. The above two treatises comprise twenty fascicles in two volumes.
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, thirteen fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; alternatively, fifteen fascicles, one volume.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* as a single work.
*Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, fifteen fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; alternatively, ten fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra-anuvyākhyāna* (Commentary on the Middle Treatise) in two fascicles, translated by Kumārajīva as a single work;

composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga and translated by the Indian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Yuan Wei dynasty. Preface and Record, Single Volume. The aforementioned preface and record of the *Anuvyākhyāna* states:
"Gao Gong, the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat and General of the Household, invited the honored guest Gautama Prajñāruci to his residence to provide offerings."

Zhengtong Fufa, in response to Shi Tanlin’s production of this treatise on the meaning [of the *Śālistamba-sūtra*], composed it on the tenth day of the eighth month of the first year of Wuding (the Guihai year), at the hour of Bingyin. It consists of a total of 13,727 characters.
All catalogs state that Bodhiruci translated it; this is an error. Now, following the preface record, it is established as the correct version.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* in three fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga and translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha; the second translation [of the same]; and the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa-śāstra* in twenty fascicles in two volumes.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, two fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhanta of India during the Northern Wei dynasty—First Translation. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-mūla-śāstra*, three fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang dynasty—Third Translation from the Inner Canon Catalogue. The above three versions of the treatise are translations of the same original text.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* in fifteen fascicles, explained by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, or in twelve fascicles, translated by the Chen dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. This is the first translation. The aforementioned three treatises comprise twenty fascicles in two volumes. Furthermore, according to the *Renshou Lu*, the *Dazhou Lu*, and other catalogs, there was another copy of the *Saṃgraha* in twelve fascicles, forming a complete set, also said to have been translated by Paramārtha; upon collation, it was found to be identical to this present version. Therefore, only this single copy is preserved here.

*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, ten fascicles, commentary by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva; one set, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty (Inner Canon Catalogue, Second Translation). *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, ten fascicles, commentary by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva; one set, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang (Inner Canon Catalogue, Third Translation). The three aforementioned commentaries are translations of the same original text with different versions.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* in ten fascicles, explained by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva; one set, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. It is recorded in the *Neidian lu* as a single work. The right-hand portion [of this text] shares the same commentary as the three preceding treatises, differing only in its specific explanations.

*Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature), four fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. Single-text edition. *Dingji zang lun* (Treatise on the Definitive Treasury), three fascicles; translated by the Liang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. Single-text edition. Regarding the aforementioned *Dingji zang lun*, the catalog of the Great Zhou dynasty states that it was a "lost translation" without specifying the period in which it was rendered. Examining the style and structure of this treatise, it is evident that it is a sub-commentary among the works translated by Paramārtha. It is noted that the cataloguers of previous dynasties omitted it from their records. It is now included in the Liang dynasty catalogs as a work translated by Paramārtha.

*Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā*, one fascicle; composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. [Recorded in the *Neidian lu* as a single-fascicle work. *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, two fascicles (or three fascicles); composed by Vasubandhu, translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. This is the first translation. The four aforementioned treatises total ten fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

*Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, three fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded in] the Third Section of the *Neidian Lu*. The two aforementioned commentaries are translations of the same original text with different renditions.
*Mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Ultimate One Vehicle Jewel Nature), in four fascicles, or three, or five;

translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati of the Northern Wei Dynasty. Second Translation. [Of] two translations, one is missing. *Karmasiddhi-prakaraṇa* (Treatise on the Accomplishment of Karma), in one fascicle;
composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena et al. of the Northern Wei Dynasty. Preface and Record, Number One.
First Translation: The preface to the aforementioned treatise states that on the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month, in the year of Daliang (the third year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty),
under the cyclical sign Xinwei, the General of the Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Marshal, Acting Minister of State, and Censor-in-Chief, Gao Zhongmi of Bohai,
respectfully invited the Tripiṭaka Master from the kingdom of Udyāna, a native of Central India...
The Brahmin Gautama Liu-zhi, Shi Tan-lin, and others translated [this work] at Jinhua Monastery within the city of Ye; it contains 4,872 characters.
Although the name of the Tripiṭaka Master is not listed in the preface, according to the established regulations, this is indeed the work of Vimalākṣa.
It is an error for various catalogs to state simply that it was translated by Gautama Liu-zhi; here, we follow the record in the preface.
Correct.

One fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-karmasiddhi-śāstra*, composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. [Recorded in] the Second Volume of the *Neidian lu*. The two treatises above are the same text with different translations.

*Hetuvidyānyāyamukhaśāstra*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Śīlabhadra and translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Recorded in the first volume of the *Neidian lu*. Translated first. The five treatises totaling ten fascicles are bound in the same volume.

*Hetuvidyānyāyamukhaśāstra*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Śīlabhadra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon as the second translation. The two treatises above are the same text with different translations. The old *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* was recorded in the Zhou catalog as a single work, but a new examination has determined it to be a duplicate translation.
*Hetuvidyā-praveśa-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering Logic), one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
*Nirvedaka-śāstra* (Treatise on Manifesting Consciousness), one fascicle. The internal title states it is the "Chapter on Manifesting Consciousness" extracted from the *Nirākāra-śāstra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of India. This single-fascicle treatise is appended to the records of the Chen dynasty.
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle (also known as the *Xianshi lun*). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India. This treatise is a single volume;
its title is appended to the records of the Chen dynasty. *Vijñaptimātratā-śāstra*, one fascicle (also known as the *Pochexin lun*).
The first part states: "Consciousness-only has no external objects. Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei. First translation. Only.

*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle. The beginning states: "The Path of Cultivation is not shared with others. Both of the above two treatises were composed by Vasubandhu and translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
Second translation: *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and translated by the Tang Dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
Recorded in the *Fanjing tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures). Third translation. The three treatises above share the same original text.
The *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels through Successive Dynasties) does not state that these are the same text; upon new examination, they are identified as retranslations.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ratnasambhava-śāstra* in five fascicles, also titled the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-anuvyākhyāna-śāstra*, composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla and translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, has been newly included in the catalog as a single work. The *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* in one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, is included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) section of the *Neidian Lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures) as a single work. These nine treatises, totaling thirteen fascicles, are placed together in the same volume.
*Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), ten fascicles; composed by Dharmapāla and other Bodhisattvas; commentary on the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. One set. *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures), single volume. *Dafangdian zhangfu lun* (Treatise on the Great Man), two fascicles;
composed by Āryadeva Bodhisattva; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Daotai of the Northern Liang. *Fanjing tu* (Diagram of Scripture Translation), single volume. *Ruda* (Entering the Great).
*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga), two fascicles; composed by Sthiramati Bodhisattva; translated by the Northern Liang śramaṇa Shi Daotai.

Recorded as a single work in the *Neidian lu*. *Mahāyāna-tattva-aratnākara-śāstra* (The Jewel in the Hand of Mahāyāna), two fascicles; composed by Bhāviveka Bodhisattva; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.

Recorded as a single work in the *Neidian lu*. *Pañcaskandha-prakaraṇa* (Treatise on the Five Aggregates), one fascicle; composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva. Recorded as a single work in the *Neidian lu*.
Catalogue of the Inner Scriptures Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, Part Two:

Initial Translations Missing from the Original Edition *Mahāyāna-Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Five Aggregates), one fascicle, composed by Ārya Sthiramati; a different version from the preceding treatise, translated by the Tripitaka Master Jīvaka of Central India during the Great Zhou Dynasty.
*Sūtrālaṃkāra-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (The Jewel Garland of the King’s Righteous Conduct), one fascicle, a standalone work recorded in the Great Zhou Catalogue.
Volume [Number]: The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty;

a single volume, composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Liang Dynasty—First Translation. [The above seven treatises, totaling ten volumes, are contained in the same fascicle.]

*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, two fascicles; composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon. The above two treatises are the same work with different translations. The old *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* was listed as a single independent work in the Zhou catalog, but a new examination has determined it to be a duplicate translation.

*The Treatise on Generating the Bodhicitta*, two fascicles; also known as *The Sūtra on Generating the Bodhicitta*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Single volume. Regarding this *Treatise on Generating the Bodhicitta*, both the *Catalogue of Sūtras and Śāstras* and the *Catalogue of Śāstras* from the Great Zhou period list its title. It is now included in the section on śāstras as a work composed by a bodhisattva, though only one version currently exists. Some say it was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, while others claim it was taught by the Bodhisattva Maitreya; it remains uncertain which is correct.
*Treatise on the Three Non-natures* (Trisvabhāvanirdeśa), two fascicles; also known as the *Treatise on the Signless* (Nirābhāsasaṃgraha), sometimes in one fascicle;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. *Treatise on the Expedient Mind* (Upāyacitta-śāstra), one fascicle, comprising four chapters; alternatively in two fascicles;

translated by the Śramaṇa Jikaya of the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Northern Wei dynasty. This is the second translation; of the two translations, one is missing. *Treatise on Reality as It Is* (Yathābhūta-śāstra), one fascicle.

Title: *Yathārtha-śāstra-pratyuttara-parihāra-varga* (The Chapter on Refuting Objections in the *Yathārtha-śāstra*), translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Liang Dynasty.

A single volume. Also known as the *Nirākāra-viṣaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Object of Cognition Being Without Form) in one volume, or simply the *Viṣaya-cintā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Contemplation of Objects), translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.

According to the first fascicle of the *Fanjing tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures), this is a single-volume translation of the *Ālambana-parīkṣā-śāstra* (Treatise Examining the Object of Cognition), composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga; translated during the Great Tang.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang from the Inner Canon, Volume Two: Translations of Different Versions of the Same Text. Regarding the two treatises above, they are the same text with different translations;
the *Zhou Catalogue* did not state they were the same text, but a recent examination has determined them to be retranslations of the same work.

*Ālambanaparīkṣāvṛtti*, one fascicle; composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla and translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang. Newly included in the canon as a single volume. [Combined with] eight treatises totaling eleven fascicles in the same bundle.

*Vigrahavyāvartanī-śāstra*, one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vimalākṣa of Central India during the Yuan-Wei dynasty, together with others. Preface and Record (contained in a single volume). The preface to this treatise states: In the third year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty, the year being Daliang, in the month of Jianshen, on the day of Xinmao under the cycle of Guiyou, the Tripiṭaka Dharma Master Vimalākṣa of the Kṣatriya royal lineage from the country of Ujjayinī, together with the Brahmin Gautama Liu-zhi of the country of India, translated [this work] at Jinhua Temple within the city of Ye. It consists of a total of eleven thousand nine hundred and eight characters. The scribe was the Śramaṇa Tanlin. The claim in the *Qunlu* that it was translated solely by Gautama Liu-zhi is an error; we now rely on the preface and record as authoritative.
*Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, one fascicle; composed by the Noble Ureṅga, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of the Sui Dynasty.

*Dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty. *Ekottarika-śāstra*, one fascicle; [composed by] Nāga...
*The Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas: A Clear Gateway to the Mahāyāna*, one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated during the Northern Wei dynasty by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci.
*The Treatise on the Hundred Letters*, one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Āryadeva; translated during the Northern Wei dynasty by the Indian [monk] Tianzhu. *The Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures*:

Single-fascicle translations include the *Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas* (one fascicle), composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and translated during the Great Tang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. The *Treatise on the Hundred Letters* (one fascicle), composed by Bodhisattva Āryadeva and translated during the Northern Wei dynasty by the Indian [monk] Tianzhu.
*The Commentary on the *Hastavālaprakaraṇa*, translated and explained by Bodhiruci of the Tang dynasty, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen dynasty.

First entry in the *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures*. *The Hastavālaprakaraṇa*, composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang dynasty.
Newly included in the records. Second entry. The above two treatises are translations of the same original text with different versions.
The *Vigraha-vyāvartanī-vṛtti* was previously recorded as a standalone work; it has now been newly examined and reclassified as a new translation.

The *Hetuvidyā-śāstra-prakaraṇa* (or *Upādāya-prajñapti-śāstra*), one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Dignāga and translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang, has been newly included in the canon as a standalone work.
The *Sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-parīkṣā-kārikā*, one fascicle, composed by Bodhisattva Dignāga.
*The Verses on the Single-Volume Treatise on the Gates of *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā*, newly compiled and included in the canon, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang;
composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu. *The Single-Volume Treatise on the Staff*, newly compiled and included in the canon, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang;
composed by the Venerable Śākyaprabha. [Both works] newly compiled and included in the canon, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang.
*The Treatise on the Practice of Meditative Concentration through the Six Gates*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga, with commentary by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon.

*The Treatise on the Non-differentiation of the Dharma-realm of the Mahāyāna*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Sthiramati; translated by Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang.
*Catuḥśataka-śāstra-khaṇḍana* (Treatise Refuting the Four Schools of Heterodox and Hinayāna), one fascicle; translated by Zangtiyunbanruo during the Great Zhou period, from a single manuscript;
composed by Āryadeva Bodhisattva; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei.

*Nirvāṇa-khaṇḍana* (Treatise Refuting the Nirvāṇa of Heterodox and Hinayāna), one fascicle; translated as a single manuscript; composed by Āryadeva Bodhisattva; [translated] by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master of the Northern Wei.
The single volume translated by Bodhiruci from the Tibetan collection consists of sixteen treatises in sixteen fascicles, bound in one case.
This totals all Mahāyāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras currently in circulation.
In total, there are six hundred and eighty-six works,
comprising two thousand seven hundred and forty-five fascicles,
arranged in two hundred and fifty-eight bundles.
*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll 12, Part 2 of the Separate Record;
*The Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll 13, Part 3 of the Separate Record.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu Year.
2. Catalogue of the Śrāvaka Tripiṭaka: Records of Translations and Existing Texts.
Section Two: The Śrāvaka Piṭaka refers to the teachings expounded by the Hīnayāna.
The Teacher who is able to preach manifests birth and manifests extinction, responding to sentient beings and following conditions;
as for the teachings he expounds:
Thus, through the Nine Divisions, the Four Āgamas, the Abhidharma,
and the Vinaya, virtuous men and women receive these teachings and cast off the shackles of worldly toil.
Pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas revere it and thereby ascend to the other shore;
it is indeed the minor vehicle of the True Vehicle.
This is the transformation-city of Bodhi;
for inducing and advancing those of the initial resolve, nothing is superior to this.
Beginning at the Immortal Garden and extending to the Golden River.
That which is expounded by means of the "half-syllable" texts is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
this continues until the hundred rivers converge and the three carts are provided together.
Ascending together to wondrous enlightenment and attaining nirvana as one,
how could there be any distinction between small and great?
Truly, this is the gradual guidance of our Honored One.
Beginning from the Dīngmǎo year of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty and ending with the Gēngwǔ year of our Kaiyuan era,
these are the Tripiṭakas of the Hīnayāna that have been seen circulating.
In total, there are three hundred and thirty works,
comprising one thousand seven hundred and sixty-two fascicles,
arranged in one hundred and sixty-five bundles.
These are compiled as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, with their categories and specific divisions clearly set forth as listed below:

**Śrāvaka Sūtra Piṭaka:** 240 works, 618 fascicles, 48 bundles. **Śrāvaka Vinaya Piṭaka:** 54 works, 446 fascicles, 45 bundles. **Śrāvaka Abhidharma Piṭaka:** 36 works, 698 fascicles, 72 bundles. Within the Śrāvaka Sūtra Piṭaka, the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) sūtras—both those translated in multiple parts and those translated as single units—number 153 works, totaling 394 fascicles in 31 bundles. The *Catur-Āgama* sūtras are placed at the beginning because they constitute the fundamental texts of the Small Vehicle sūtras; the remaining sūtras are listed thereafter.

*The Dīrgha Āgama*, twenty-two fascicles, in two volumes; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī from the Yuezhi, together with Zhu Fonian, during the Yao Qin dynasty. The single volume is a re-translation. This collection of scriptures consists of four sections totaling thirty sūtras. As Sengzhao’s preface states: "The *Dīrgha Āgama* comprises four sections and four recitations, totaling thirty sūtras, which are compiled as one body."

The Madhyama Āgama, sixty fascicles (or fifty-eight fascicles), in six bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. To the right: this collection of sūtras consists of five recitations in total.

It comprises eighteen chapters in total, consisting of two hundred and twenty-two sūtras. According to the preface by Sengzhao to the *Madhyama Āgama*, it contains five recitations (*saṃyukta*) and four divisions (*nikāya*).

The *Ekottara Āgama* consists of fifty-one fascicles, or alternatively fifty, forty-two, or thirty-five; it is arranged in five bundles. It was translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva from Kaśmīra. This is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. Altogether, this section of the canon contains fifty chapters.

In total, there are four hundred and seventy-two sūtras. Regarding the individual preface by Sengzhao to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it states: "The *Ekottara Āgama* consists of eight recitations in four divisions.

The *Saṃyukta Āgama* comprises fifty fascicles in five volumes, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty, with certain sections retranslated by Zhu Fashun. To the right, this collection of sūtras...

Since the subjects discussed are diverse, there is no sequential order, nor distinctions such as those between the *Saṃyuktāgama* and other recensions. Sengzhao’s preface to the *Dīrgha-āgama* mentions the *Saṃyuktāgama*, the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, and the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya*.

Among the twenty fascicles of the *Saṃyuktāgama-sūtra* translated separately, which are included among the anonymous translations (*shiyi jing*), there is a sub-commentary containing characters in the Qin script. Although the translator’s name is not definitively known, it must have been translated during the Three Qin periods; thus, it is now appended to the Qin records. Regarding this collection of sūtras, although its textual content differs from the aforementioned sūtras and its sequence is disordered, [it remains part of the canon].
Upon careful investigation, it is found that these do not go beyond the aforementioned sutras;

this [work] merely extracts their essential points and thus constitutes a separate section. The various sutras following the *Buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* are all alternative translations of individual sutras from within the *Catur-aṅga-nikāya*.

*The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha*, two fascicles (also simply titled *The Nirvāṇa Sūtra*), translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazǔ of Hénèi during the Western Jìn; or *The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, three fascicles (or two), translated by the Śramaṇa Shì Fǎxiàn of Píngyáng during the Eastern Jìn. The current version is ascribed to Fǎxiàn’s translation, as described in the General Catalogue (*Zǒnglù*). There is also a *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* in two fascicles, sometimes without the character "bān" (pari-); this is newly classified as a work of lost translation and appended to the Eastern Jìn records. These three sūtras are listed above.
This appears in volumes two through four of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. It is a different translation of the same original text as the *Pūrvabhāga Cārikāsūtra*.

Regarding the *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, all catalogs state that it was translated by Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty; however, this is incorrect. Upon examining its phrasing and sentences, they are mostly archaic translations and do not at all resemble those translated by Guṇavara. Among the various canons, only the upper volume exists while the lower volume is missing. Consequently, it has been placed in the Jin-period catalog due to the loss of its source. Furthermore, there are some manuscript versions where the upper volume of the *Buddhaparinirvāṇasūtra* is identical in every sentence to the upper volume of the *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*; these are erroneous texts.

*Renben yusheng jing* (Sūtra on the Human Desire for Birth), one fascicle; translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is extracted from the tenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

It is a different translation of the same text as the *Mahā-upāya Sūtra* in the second division [of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*]. That various catalogs of former generations classified this *Renben yusheng jing* among the Mahāyāna sūtras was an error.

*Śīkṣānanda-ṣaḍabhimukha-praṇāma-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Śīkṣānanda-ṣaḍdvāra-vandanā-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. The above is excerpted from the eleventh fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

This is a different translation of the same text as the second part of the *Sujāta-sūtra*; compared to that original sūtra, this version is somewhat more concise. This sūtra is also found within the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*The Scripture of the Brahmin Āṣāḍha*, one fascicle. Also titled *The Buddha Opens and Explains the Characters*; alternatively titled *The Scripture of the Māṇava Āṣāḍha*. Translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian. The above is extracted from the thirteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the third fascicle of the *Amātya Sūtra*.

One fascicle, titled *The Brahmajāla Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views*, also known as the *Brahma Sūtra*, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The above is extracted from the fourteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the third fascicle of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra on the Fruits of the Śramaṇa*, one fascicle, translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above is from the seventeenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta* (The Discourse on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life) in three sections. The aforementioned eight sūtras comprise twelve fascicles in one volume.

The *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* (Discourse on the Origin of the World), ten fascicles, one volume, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of the Sui Dynasty; this is the fifth translation of the title. There is also the *Lokaprajñapti-hetuprabhava-sūtra* (Discourse on the Causes and Origins of the World), ten fascicles, one volume, which I fear might be confused with the previous version; it was translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta of the Sui Dynasty. According to the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang) and Jingmai’s *Jingtu*, it is recorded that during the Daye era, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta translated the ten-fascicle *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* at the Translation Hall in the Shanglin Garden in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). This was subsequently included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) section. Please verify according to the *Dajiang Neidian Lu* and Jingmai’s *Jingtu*. Both state that during the Daye period, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmagupta translated the ten-fascicle *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* at the Translation Hall in the Shanglin Garden of the Eastern Capital.
Now, having extensively searched through the various collections,
I have found two versions; while their general meaning is the same,
the wording differs slightly, and as for the chapter titles, there are occasional discrepancies.
The beginning of the former sutra states that the Bhagavat was in the city of Śrāvastī,
whereas the latter sutra states that the Bhagavat was in the city of Śrāvastī.
According to the Sanskrit terminology, the latter sutra is correct.
Now it is said that Xuematu and Jñānagupta each translated a separate version.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the aforementioned scripture,
the title states that the two masters Xuematu and Jñānagupta produced it together.
The former was translated by Jñānagupta,
while the latter is a re-translation by Dharmagupta;
since the texts of these two sūtras differ, [the distinction is clear].
For this reason, both recensions are preserved here.
Furthermore, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* also states that the Bhagavat was in the city of Śrāvastī; thus, we know they were both translated by Guṇabhadra.

Fearing that these two texts might be confused with one another, I have separately noted below that this is the *Qishi yinben jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Origins of the World). As for the *Lou tan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) in six fascicles—also called the *Da lou tan jing* (Mahālokānuvartana-sūtra)—or in five or eight fascicles, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Falu together with Faju: this is the second translation. The above three sutras are extracted from fascicles eighteen through twenty-two of the *Chang ahan jing* (Dīrgha Āgama).
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Caturvargika-lokadhātu-sūtra*.

The two-fascicle *Daśottara-dharma-sūtra* (also known as the *Bahudhātuka-mārga-varga-sūtra* or simply the *Daśottara-sūtra*) was translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty. The above [text] is from the ninth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*; it is a different translation from the same original text as the second section, the *Daśottara-sūtra*, differing slightly in its degree of detail.

The *Zhongbenqi jing* (Sutra on the Middle Origination) consists of two fascicles, though it is sometimes called the *Taizi zhongbenqi jing*. The title at the beginning of the sutra states that it is extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Dharmaphala and Kang Mengxiang during the Later Han dynasty. These three aforementioned sutras comprise ten fascicles in a single volume. Regarding the title of the *Zhongbenqi jing*, it claims to be extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*; however, upon searching the great edition of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, this specific sutra is not found there. It is possible that the Sanskrit manuscript was not fully translated; since it is stated to have been extracted from that [Āgama], it has been appended here at the end. The *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue) erroneously states that it is a different translation of the same text as the *Guoqu xianzai yinguo jing*, the *Xiuxing benqi jing*, and the *Ruixiang benqi jing*. Furthermore, regarding this *Zhongbenqi jing*, all catalogs agree that it was translated during the Later Han period. Yet, within the text itself, there are instances where Sanskrit terms are rendered into Chinese, stating "in the Jin language," which remains unexplained. How can this be?
The thirteen scriptures from "From the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa" onwards are all extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
They are separate scriptures with alternative translations.

*The Scripture on the Seven Knowledges* (or *The Scripture on the Seven Wisdoms*), one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. The above is extracted from the first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Sūtra on the Good Dharma at the Beginning*.

The *Sūtra of the Simile of Salt Water* (one fascicle), also known as the *Parable of Salt Water*, is now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an lost the record of its translator; it is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue. The above is excerpted from the first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Sūtra on the Simile of Water*.

*The Sūtra on the Guarding of the Causes for All Outflows*, one fascicle, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is from the second fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Āsravakṣaya-sūtra*.
One fascicle of the *Catuḥsatya-sūtra*, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is extracted from the seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Sūtra on the Analysis of the Noble Truths*.

The *Gaṅgā-sūtra*, one fascicle—also called the *Gaṅgā-upamā-sūtra*—was translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin dynasty. The above is extracted from the ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
These are different translations from the same original text as the *Campa Sūtra*.

The *Benshangyi zhi jing* (one fascicle), also known as the *Daxiangyi zhi*, was translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The *Yuanben zhi jing* (one fascicle) is of lost translation; it is now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text, appearing in the tenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
These share the same original text as the *Benji jing* (Sūtra on the Ultimate Limit).

1. *Dingshengwang gushi jing* (Sūtra on the Story of King Māndhātṛ), one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *Dingshengwang jing*. Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. 2. *Wentoujie wang jing* (Sūtra of King Vemacitra), one fascicle. Translated by the Northern Liang Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema. These two sūtras, which are different translations of the same text, were included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) and appear in the eleventh fascicle of the *Zhong ahan jing* (Madhyama Āgama).
This shares the same original text as the *Caturdvīpaka-sūtra*.

The *Yamaloka-pañcadevaputradūta-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled the *Ayaḥpuraniraya-sūtra*—was translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huijian. The *Ayaḥpuraniraya-sūtra*, one fascicle, was translated by the Eastern Jin dynasty śramaṇa from the Western Regions, Zhu Tanwulan; these two were included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.
Extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 12; this shares the same original text as the *Devadūta Sūtra* [in the *Dīrgha Āgama*], though it is somewhat more abbreviated than that original.

The *Guzhishishi Jing* (One Scroll on the Times of Ancient Worlds), translated by an unknown hand, is now appended to the catalog of the Eastern Jin. The above is extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 13.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Sūtra on the Original [Causes]*; compared to that original, this version is somewhat more concise.

The *Aṇiruddha-aṣṭānuśmṛti-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *Sūtra on the Concentration of the Mind through Dhyāna Practice* or simply *Sūtra on the Eight Recollections*—was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty. The above is from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Aṣṭānusmṛti-sūtra*.

The *Vigata-nidrā-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa, was included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above appears in the twentieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Sūtra on Sleeping with an Elder and Senior*, consisting of one fascicle.
Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao during the Later Han dynasty. The above is extracted from the twenty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Zhenren jing* (Sūtra of the Real Man).

*Qiuyu jing* (Sūtra on Seeking Desires), one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. The above is extracted from the twenty-second fascicle of the *Zhong ahan jing* (Madhyama Āgama).
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Sūtra on Impurity*.

One fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin; it was included in the *Supplement to the Missing* (*Shiyi bianru*) and appears in the twenty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
The first, *The Sūtra on the Brahmin’s Calculation of Water Purity*, is a different translation of the same text as the *Sūtra Requested by a Bhikṣu*.

One fascicle; the translator is lost, and it is now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin dynasty as part of the *Supplement to the Omissions*. The above [text] appears in the twenty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Udāyin-sūtra* (or *Vatsagotra-parivrājaka-sūtra*).

The *Duḥkha-skandha-sūtra*, one fascicle, was lost to translation; it appears in the Later Han Records and is included in the Supplementary Collection (*Shiyi*). The above is from the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Duḥkhaskandha-sūtra*.

The *Śreṇika-bhikṣu-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled the *Pañcaskandha-hetuvastu-sūtra*—was translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The *Duḥkhaskandha-hetuvastu-sūtra*, one fascicle, was translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin dynasty. These two sūtras, listed below, are different translations of the same original text and have been included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection).
The *Leksang jing* (Sūtra on the Perception of Pleasure), one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa, was included as a supplement;

it corresponds to the same original text as the *Hou kuyin jing* (Sūtra on the Aggregate of Suffering) in the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The above [text] appears in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Sañjñā-sūtra*.
*Āsrava-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty. The above is extracted from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Sūtra on the Attainment of Brahmacarya*.

One fascicle, titled the *Anutpāda-vāyu-sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; it was included in the *Supplement* (*Shiyi*). The above is from the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Anupada Sūtra*.
*The Sūtra on the Root of All Dharmas*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. The above is excerpted from the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
The first is a variant translation of the same original text as the *Dharmamūla-sūtra*.
The *Mahāprajāpatī-gautamī-phala-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huilan; the above is extracted from the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Gautamī-sūtra*.

The *Campā-bhikṣu-sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Campā-sūtra*—was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Faju) and was subsequently included in the supplementary collection. It appears in the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Campa Sūtra*.

The *Fu yin jing* (Sutra on Subduing Lust), one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju, has been included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) and appears here as the thirtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Yù xíngyù jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of Desire).

The *Mó rǎoluàn jīng* (Sūtra on Māra’s Disturbance), one fascicle—also known as the *Bì mó shì mùlián jīng* (Sūtra on the Evil Māra Testing Maudgalyāyana) or the *Mówáng rù mùlián lánfù jīng* (Sūtra on the Demon King Entering Maudgalyāyana’s Belly)—was lost to translation and is listed in the Later Han records. The *Bì mó shì mùlián jīng*, one fascicle—also known as the *Mó rǎoluàn jīng*—was translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty and was subsequently included in the *Shíyí*. These two sūtras above are different translations of the same original text.
The *Ratthapāla Sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled the *Arhat Ratthapāla Sūtra*—translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian;
the above thirty sūtras in thirty fascicles are contained in the same volume. These are from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Fascicle 31.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Ratthapāla Sūtra*.

The *Sons of Good Family Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Zhi Fadu, was included in the Supplementary Collection (*Shiyi*). The above is from the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same text as the *Sujāta-sūtra*.

It consists of one fascicle and was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Śīladharma (Shi Faju). It was included in the supplementary collection (*Shiyi*) and appears here as the thirty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Calculating Numbers*.

It consists of one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. It was included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) and appears in the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
A different translation of the same text as the *Āśivada Sūtra*.

*The Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, Compassion, and Renunciation*, one fascicle. Translator lost; now appended to the Eastern Jin Records as part of the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). *Sudatta Sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sūtra of the Elder Sudatta*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavidi of India during the Tianqi era of the Xiao Qi dynasty. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.
This is extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle thirty-nine.

It shares the same source text as the *Sudatta Sūtra*. The text of the *Maitracitta-vidveṣa-guṇa Sūtra* is somewhat abbreviated; some titles claim it is "extracted from the *Ekottara Āgama*, section twelve," but this is incorrect.

*The Sūtra on Training Spoken by the Buddha for the Old Brahmin of Yellow Bamboo Garden*, one fascicle. This was lost among the scriptures translated during the period recorded by Sengyou; it is now appended to the *Song-lu Shiyi* (Supplement to the Song Catalogue). The above is extracted from the fortieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Huanglu yuan jing* (Sūtra on the Yellow Reed Garden).
The *Fanmo yu jing*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty; the above is extracted from the fortieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Brahmāyu-sūtra*; compared to that original, this version is somewhat more concise.

One fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty; it has been included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above is from the forty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Śakrapraśna-samādhi-kuṭī-gāthā-sūtra*.

There is also one fascicle of the *Śuka-sūtra*, also titled the *Tuṭṭha-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. The *Sengyou-lu* states that this *Tuṭṭha-sūtra* was a work of unknown translatorship attributed to Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the Western Jin records as part of the "Supplement to Omissions. The two sūtras listed above are different translations of the same original text.
Extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 44.
This is the same text as the *Śuka-sūtra*.

One fascicle of the *Ityukta-sūtra*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin, has been included here as a supplement. The above is extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 45.
This is a different translation from the same source as the *Heart Sūtra*.

The one-volume *Yingfa jing* (Sūtra on Corresponding to the Dharma), translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa, has been included in the supplement (*Shiyi*) to the right-hand section, appearing in the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Dharmasūtra on Receiving [the Dharma] Later*.

The *Niraya Sūtra*, one fascicle—also known as the *Madhyama Āgama Niraya Sūtra*—was translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above is extracted from the fifty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
These are different translations of the same text as the *Chihhui ti jing* (Sūtra on the Ground of Delusion and Wisdom).

The *Upāli duosheshu jia jing* (One Scroll, Sūtra on Upāli Falling from the Śākya Clan) was lost among the translations in Sengyou’s catalogue; it is now appended to the Song catalogue. The *Zhāijīng* (One Scroll, Sūtra on Fasting), also titled *Chízhāijīng* (Sūtra on Observing the Fast), was translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty and was included in the *Shiyi*. The two sūtras above are different translations of the same text.
Extracted from the Madhyama Āgama, Volume 55.
It is the same text as the Upoṣadha-sūtra.

*Vaimasūra-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Song Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra; appended to the "Supplementary Collection" (Shiyi). The above is extracted from the Madhyama Āgama, Volume 57.
This is a different translation of the same original text as the *Vimāna-sūtra*.

It consists of one fascicle titled *The Sūtra on the Death of a Brahmin’s Son and His Unceasing Affection*, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao during the Later Han dynasty. It was included among the "Supplementary Omissions" (*Shiyi*). The above is from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Āditta-sutta* (The Discourse on Arising with Craving).

The *Daśa-grāmaṇī-aṣṭaka-purusa-sūtra*, one fascicle—also simply titled the *Daśa-grāmaṇī-sūtra*—was translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is extracted from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Yubachi jing* (Sūtra on the Eight Cities).

The *Jian jing* (Sūtra on Views), one fascicle, was listed among the "Translated by Unknown" texts in Sengyou’s catalogue; it has been included here in the supplement and is now appended to the Song catalogue. The above is extracted from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, where it is a different translation from the same original text as the *Jian jing*.
*Śalyopama-sūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) collection, now appended to the *Dongjin lu* (Catalogue of the Eastern Jin).
This work is from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* and is a different translation of the same original text as the *Śalyopama-sūtra*.

*Fǎpǔyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma), one fascicle; also known as *Jùfǎxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of Endowed with Dharma) or *Pǔyì jīng* (Sūtra of Universal Meaning). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. First translation. *Guǎngyì fǎmén jīng* (Sūtra of the Extensive Gate of Meaning), one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen dynasty. Third translation. One [of these] is missing. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Regarding the *Guǎngyì fǎmén jīng*, its initial title states that it is a separate translation of one chapter from within the *Zhōngāhán jīng* (Madhyama Āgama). Upon examination, this specific sūtra does not exist within the main body of the *Zhōngāhán*. It is possible that the Sanskrit manuscript was not fully translated. Since it is stated to have been extracted from that [Āgama], it has been appended here at the end. Its inclusion as a standalone Mahāyāna text in the *Dàzhōu rùzàng lù* (Great Zhou Catalogue of the Canon) is an error. Furthermore, in the *Fǎpǔyì jīng*, the name is rendered as "Shèlìrì" (Śāradvatī), while in the *Jùfǎxíng jīng*, it is "Shèlìfú" (Śāriputra); these differ by only one character, while the rest of the text is identical.
The seven scriptures listed above and the fifty-three scriptures below are all extracted from the Madhyama Āgama.

The *Jièdéxiāng jīng* (Sūtra on the Fragrance of Moral Virtue), one fascicle—also known as the *Jièdé jīng* (Sūtra on Moral Virtue)—was translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin dynasty. This [last] was extracted from the thirteenth fascicle of the Ekottara Āgama.
An alternative translation of the "Chapter on the Landowner" (*Gṛhapati-varga*).

*The Scripture on the Appearance of Four Persons in the World*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty; included in the *Supplement* (*Shiyi*). The above appears in the eighteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
A Different Translation of the Chapter on the Four Right Efforts (*Catvāri-samyakprahāṇa-varga*).

One fascicle of the *Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Queen’s Demise and Her Body Being Covered in Dust*, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Faju). The above is extracted from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Chapter on the Four Right Efforts.

*The Sūtra of the Girl Sumati*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above appears in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The *Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Avoiding Death* (一卷), translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han, is a slightly more concise version compared to this original sūtra;
it has been included as a supplement. The above is an alternate translation of the "Chapter on the Increase" from the twenty-third fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*The Sutra on the Five Kinds of Auspicious Retribution for Bestowing Food* (one scroll), also titled *The Sutra on Bestowing Physical Strength and Color*, or *The Sutra on Merit*; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalog. The above is extracted from the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha to Make Offerings*, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju; also known as *The Chapter on the Accumulation of Merit*. This is an alternative translation [of the same text]. It is excerpted from the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The *Dṛṣṭisamāna-varga* (等見品) is a variant translation that is somewhat more concise than the original sūtra; its inclusion in the Mahāyāna section by various catalogs is an error.

The *Sūtra on the Six Times a Householder’s Son Leaving Home to Become a Monk* (長者子六過出家經), one fascicle, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎn: the above is a variant translation of the "Chapter on Accumulation" (*Saṃcaya-varga*) from the twenty-seven-fascicle *Ekottarika Āgama*; this current sūtra is slightly more extensive.

The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled the *Magha-sūtra* or the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. This was included as a supplement among the thirty-two sūtras totaling thirty-two fascicles in the same volume.
*The Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations;
they appear in the thirty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, in the "Chapter on Power" (*Bala-varga*). This version is somewhat more extensive.

*The Scripture of the Malla Moving the Mountain*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Scripture of Moving the Mountain*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *The Scripture of the Four Unprecedented Dharmas*, one fascicle; also called *The Scripture of the Four Unprecedented [Dharmas]*, or omitting the character "fa" (dharma). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. The above two scriptures are alternative translations of the "Chapter on the Eight Difficulties" (*Aṣṭā-vighāta-parivarta*) in the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. They are separate translations of a single scripture, divided into two versions. These are somewhat more extensive than the current edition, which does not contain them all.

*The Sūtra on Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Wandering through the Four Crossroads*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Kang Mengxiang of the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty. The above is extracted from the forty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The entry for the *Bāpīrājaparivarta* (馬王品) in the Zhou Catalogue, which places it among the "Re-translations of Mahāyāna Sūtras," is an error.

The *Saptabuddhapitṛmātṛnāmasūtra* (七佛父母姓字經), one fascicle—also titled *Saptabuddhanāmasūtra* (七佛姓字經)—was translated during the Cao Wei period with the translator lost; the above [text] is extracted from the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
*An Alternative Translation of the Chapter on Unwholesome States*.

*The Cowherd Sūtra*, one fascicle; also called *The Herdsman Sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. The above is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on Cowherding" from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*; this text is somewhat more extensive.

The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, one fascicle, also known as the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. According to the *Fanying tu* (Diagram of Translated Scriptures), this is a variant translation of the "Cowherd Chapter" (*Gopālaka-varga*) from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*. Compared to the original scripture, this text is somewhat more concise. It is an error to include it in the catalog of Mahāyāna single-text translations.

*The Scripture on the Eleven Recollections of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Eleven Contemplations*. Translated by the Song dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra. Included in the *Supplemental Collection*. The above work is extracted from the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

Regarding the "Chapter on Paying Homage to the Triple Gem," this initial alternative translation consists of eleven contemplations. These two sutras are linked together; the first eleven matters have been verified as identical in both text and meaning, whereas the latter eleven matters have not yet been found upon investigation.

*The Sūtra on the Four Nirayas*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Four Great Nirayas*. Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The above was excerpted from the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The *Lǐ sānbǎo pǐn* (Chapter on Paying Homage to the Triple Gem) is a slightly expanded variant translation.

The *Ānábīndí huà qīzǐ jīng* (Sūtra on Anāthapiṇḍada Converting His Seven Sons), one fascicle, translated by the Parthian Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. The above is a variant translation of the "Chapter on Impermanence" in the forty-ninth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. This sūtra mentions only four sons; otherwise, the general meaning is largely the same.

*The Mahāprajāpatī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazǔ of Hénèi during the Western Jin dynasty. *The Buddha-mātṛ-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎn of the Song dynasty. These two sūtras, listed as supplementary additions, are the same text with different translations.
Extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Volume 50: "The Chapter on the Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī.

*The Scripture of King Brahmadatta’s Ten Dreams*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. *The Scripture of the King of Śrāvastī Dreaming Ten Things*, one fascicle; according to Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Chu sanzang jiji*), this was a scripture whose translator was lost during the period of Master Dao’an. It is now appended to the records of the Western Jin as part of the "Supplementary Collection" (*Shiyi*). The above two scriptures are the same text with different translations.

Extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 51. Chapter on the Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī. The *Sūtra on Ānanda’s Fellow Students*, one scroll, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han.

Regarding the aforementioned *Sūtra on Ānanda’s Fellow Students*, its title at the beginning of the text states it is extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Upon examining the original version (*mūla*), this sūtra is not found therein. Since it is stated to have been extracted from that [Āgama], it has been appended here at the end. From the *Sūtra on the Fragrance of Precepts and Virtue* downward, twenty-four sūtras are all alternative translations of separate sūtras from within the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

*The Scripture on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the catalog. This work is a variant translation of the second fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. Although this *Scripture on the Emptiness of the Five Aggregates* appears within the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, it was not separately produced as an independent text. It is preserved here so that it shall not be discarded; for this is a Vinaya citation of a Sūtra, rather than a Sūtra originating from the Vinaya.

*The Sūtra on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations*, one fascicle (or two fascicles), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. The above is a variant translation from within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. This sūtra consists of thirty sūtras from beginning to end; it is titled "Seven Stations and Three Contemplations" at the outset and "Accumulation of Bones" at the conclusion. Because it is designated by its initial title, the *Sūtra on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations* appears in the second fascicle, while the subsequent *Sūtra on the Accumulation of Bones* appears in the thirty-fourth fascicle. The remaining sūtras are scattered throughout various texts without being arranged in a single sequential order.

The *Āryadharmamudrā-sūtra*, one fascicle; also simply called the *Āryamudrā-sūtra* or the *Prajñāmudrā-sūtra*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. The above is an alternative translation from the third fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

*Saṃyukta Āgama*, one fascicle; translator lost; listed in the *Wei and Wu Records*. The above is extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. This is a different translation of that scripture. From beginning to end, it contains twenty-seven sūtras.

The first three sūtras appear in the fourth fascicle [of the standard version], though their sequence does not correspond. The *Saptasthāna-triparīkṣā Sūtra* (Sūtra on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations) stands at the end of this fascicle; its phrasing is largely identical to the preceding sūtras, though it is somewhat more extensive. The *Asthisañcayā Sūtra* (Sūtra on the Accumulation of Bones) is also included therein; it is unclear why these two sūtras overlap. The remaining sūtras are scattered throughout the expanded text. Various ancient catalogs all state that the translator is lost. Upon examining the phrasing, it is somewhat similar in diction and reasoning to the *Saptasthāna-triparīkṣā*; it appears to have been produced by An Shigao, yet no authentic record has been seen. For now, I follow tradition and list it as "translator lost."

*The Sūtra of the Simile of the Five Aggregates* (1 fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra of Being Driven by Water Froth*, or alternatively *The Sūtra of the Simile of the Five Aggregates*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. *The Sūtra of Being Driven by Water Froth* (1 fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra of a Great Mass of Froth in a River*, or alternatively *The Sūtra of the Simile of the Mass of Froth*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. These two sūtras were included as supplementary texts. Both are identical versions of the same work, appearing in the tenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Alternative translation:

*Buzishouyi jing* (Sūtra on Not Guarding the Mind), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Wuyi* (Without Mind). Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [dynasty]. The above is extracted from the eleven-fascicle *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama).
Alternative translation:

*Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated during the Jin dynasty with the translator lost; now appended to the *Dongjin lu* (Catalogue of the Eastern Jin) as part of the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Omissions). The above appears in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Alternative translations:

*The Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma* (one fascicle), also known as *The Sūtra on the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma*, translated by An Shigao, the Tripiṭaka Master from Parthia during the Later Han; and *The Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma* (one fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang and newly included in the canon. These two sūtras are the same text.
This is extracted from the fifteenth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

Although this *Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma* is translated differently [from the version in the *Vinayavibhaṅga*], it exists within the nineteenth fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayakṣudrakavastu*; however, it does not arise as a separate [independent] sūtra. Therefore, it is preserved without being discarded. This is a case where the Vinaya cites a Sūtra, rather than a Sūtra arising from the Vinaya. As for the *Cakravartana-sūtra*, its latter part is identical to its original while the former part differs; the reason for this remains unknown.

The Sūtra on the Eightfold Noble Path, one fascicle; translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty. The above is an alternative translation of the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
*The Nandika Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin dynasty. The above is extracted from the thirtieth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

There are two different translations of this sūtra in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*; here they have been combined into one, as the text is somewhat more extensive. It was previously recorded in the catalogs among single-fascicle works, but is now included here.

*The Sūtra on the Three Marks of a Horse*, one fascicle; also titled *The Good Horse Has Three Marks*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhīyào of the Western Regions during the Later Han. *The Sūtra on the Eight Manners of Horses Compared to Humans*, one fascicle; also simply titled *The Eight Manners of Horses*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhīyào of the Western Regions during the Later Han. These two sūtras both appear in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Alternative translation:

*The Scripture on Corresponding Characteristics* (Xiāngyìng xiàngkě jīng), one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Śikṣānanda [Shè Fǎjù]. This was recovered and included here from the aforementioned single-fascicle *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

Alternative Translation: *The Secret Essentials for Treating the Illnesses of Meditation* (one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Non-existence of Dharmas*, or two fascicles), translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. Regarding this sūtra, the title at the beginning states: "As asked by the Venerable Śāriputra, excerpted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, from the section on miscellaneous matters concerning araṇya-dwellers. Now, upon searching the original *Saṃyukta Āgama*, such passages are not found. It is possible that the Sanskrit manuscript was not fully translated. Since it is stated to have been excerpted from that [Āgama], I have included it here at the end. However, upon examining its literary style, it slightly overlaps with Mahāyāna sūtras; as it was previously cataloged among the *Jíchuán* (Collected Transmissions), I fear it may be misplaced.
The thirty-one sūtras above comprise thirty-one fascicles in one volume.
From the *Pañcaskandha-śūnyatā-sūtra* downward,
sixteen sūtras are all extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

Separate translations of the same scripture: 1. *Maudgalyāyanī-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Ānanda-huodao-nü-huo-jing* (The Scripture on Ānanda Being Deceived by a Woman Practicing Sorcery). Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. First translation. 2. *Maudgalyāyanī-xiejingzhong-liushi-jing* (The Scripture on Maudgalyāyanī Explaining Six Matters within the Body). Translator lost; currently appended to the catalog of the Eastern Jin. Fifth translation. 3. *Matang-sūtra*, three fascicles (or two fascicles). Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Zhu Lüyan together with Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. Recorded as the third translation in Fashang’s catalog. 4. *Shetoujian-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Taizi-ershiba-xiu-jing* (The Scripture of the Prince and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions) or *Hu’er-jing* (The Scripture of Hu’er).
