Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu. Fourth translation. The above four scriptures are different translations of the same original text. The first two are merely the latter part of a single chapter of the subsequent scripture, which has five translations in total, though one translation is missing.

*The Scripture on the Ghosts Questioning Maudgalyāyana*, one fascicle; translated by the Parthian Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han (First Translation). *The Scripture on the Miscellaneous Collection*, one fascicle; its textual principles differ slightly from the preceding and following scriptures. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin (Second Translation). *The Scripture on the Retribution of Hungry Ghosts*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of the Hells and Hungry Ghosts Spoken by Maudgalyāyana*. Translator lost; currently appended to the Eastern Jin records (Third Translation). The above three scriptures are different translations of the same original text. Of the four translations listed in sequence, one translation is missing.

*Ānanda’s Questions on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha*, one fascicle—also titled *Ānanda’s Questions Sūtra* or *Sūtra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha*. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. First Translation. *Dharmaparyāya on Arrogance*, one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. Second Translation. *Ānanda’s Analysis Sūtra*, one fascicle—also simply called *Analysis Sūtra*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin. Third Translation. The above three sūtras are different translations of the same original text. Regarding the *Dharmaparyāya on Arrogance*, it has been newly retranslated; thus there are four translations in total, one of which is missing.
*The Sūtra of the Five Mothers and Sons*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. First translation. *The Śamilara Sūtra*, one fascicle;

the Record of Sengyou states that Master Dao’an’s *Diverse Sūtras of Guanzhong* lists it in the *Sanqin Lu*. Second translation. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations. Regarding the *Śamilara Sūtra*, the Catalogue of the Great Zhou (Dazhou lu) states it was translated by Dharmakṣema. However, the Record of Changfang does not include this among his works; thus, the Great Zhou catalogue is in error.

*Yujie nü jing* (The Scripture of the Girl Yujie), one fascicle; also called *Yujie jing*. Sengyou’s catalogue states that it was a translation by Master An whose translator was lost; it is now appended to the Western Jin records. Originally appearing in the *Shiyi*, it was compiled into the *Yujie jing*. One fascicle; also known as *Zhangzhe yi fo shuo zifu wu jing jing* (The Scripture of the Elder Visiting the Buddha to Speak of His Daughter-in-law’s Lack of Reverence). Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin. Second translation: *Asuda jing* (The Scripture of Asuda), one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty. Third translation. The above three scriptures are different translations of the same original text.

*Xiūxíng běnqǐ jīng* (Sūtra on the Original Arising of Practice), two fascicles; also known as *Sùxíng běnqǐ* (Original Arising of Past Deeds). Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhú Dàlì and Kāng Mèngxiáng during the Later Han Dynasty. This is the third translation. [The following] sixteen sūtras, totaling nineteen fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*The Sūtra on the Auspicious Response of the Prince’s Original Enlightenment*, two fascicles; also titled *The Original Enlightenment and Auspicious Response*, or simply *The Auspicious Response and Original Enlightenment*. Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. This is the fourth translation. *The Sūtra on Cause and Effect in Past and Present*, four fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. This is the sixth translation. The above three sūtras share the same original text but differ in their translations. Of the first two sūtras, the texts are abbreviated and incomplete. Among the six translations in total, three are missing from the extant record.

*Fǎhǎi jīng* (Sūtra on the Ocean of Dharma), one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. Included in the *Shíyí* (Supplement) as the second translation. *Hǎi bādé jīng* (Sūtra on the Eight Virtues of the Ocean), one fascicle; translated by the Yao Qin Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva. Recorded in the catalog of Fashang as the third translation; included in the *Shíyí*. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations. Of the three successive translations, one translation is missing.
The Sutra in Forty-two Sections, one fascicle. Translated during the Later Han dynasty by the Indian śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna;
this is the first of two translations, the other being missing. The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Maiden Amrapālī and Jīvaka, one fascicle.

Sometimes the word "causes and conditions" (yin-yuan) is omitted, or it is simply titled the *Amrapālī Sūtra*. Translated during the Later Han dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia. The first [fascicle].
*Jièhuà dìyù jīng* (Sūtra on Teaching and Transforming in Hell), one fascicle; also known as *Dìyù bàoyìng jīng* (Sūtra on the Retribution of Hell).
Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. Of two translations, one is missing. *Nǔwáng xiongdi jīng* (Sūtra of the Dragon King Brothers), one fascicle;
also known as *Nán nǔwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Difficult Dragon King) or *Jiàng nǔwáng jīng* (Sūtra of Subduing the Dragon King). Of two translations, one is missing.
Translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian. First translation; two translations exist, one being missing.
*Jiāzhǎng yīnyuè jīng* (Sūtra of the Householder Svarasena), one fascicle; also called *Jiāzhǎng yīnyuè bùlánjiāshè jīng* (Sūtra of the Householder Svarasena and Uruvilvākāśyapa).

Translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian. First translation; two translations exist, one being missing. The nine preceding sūtras, totaling thirteen fascicles, are contained in the same volume. Their length is as follows:

This work, titled *The Sound of Delight*, was included within the middle volume of the *Zhou* catalog and classified under the Mahāyāna Piṭaka; however, having now examined its literary style and principles, it has been moved here.

The *Dhyāna-guhyaka-sūtra* (or *Dhyāna-guhyaka-dharma*), in three fascicles—alternatively titled *Dhyāna-guhyaka-dharma*—or in four fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the second translation; the other two translations are missing. Regarding this *Dhyāna-guhyaka-sūtra*, it was compiled and transmitted among the ancient catalogs. Upon examining it now, the three parts from beginning to end are extremely clear. While the upper and lower sections of the text mostly clarify dhyāna-contemplation, within it, the contemplation of the Buddha and other such practices clarify the matter of repentance for the eradication of grave offenses. Since these involve some slight overlap with the Mahāyāna and are not merely fabricated compositions, they are frequently found herein. Furthermore, among the various catalogs there is another work, the *Dhyāna-guhyaka-sūtra* in five fascicles, said to have been translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of the Song dynasty; its text is highly disordered and unfit for circulation, as described in detail in the *Shanfan-lu*.
*The Sutra of the Seven Daughters*, one fascicle—also known as *The Original Sutra of the Seven Daughters*—translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty];

first translation, three translations total, two missing. *The Sutra of the Eight Teachers*, one fascicle—translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]; first translation, two translations total, one missing.

*The Sutra of Yue Nan*, one fascicle—also known as *The Sutra of the Elder Yue Nan*—translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]; first translation, two translations total, one missing.
*The Scripture on the Difficulties of Attaining What One Desires*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Nian Chengyuan of the Western Jin.
First translation; two translations [of this title] exist, while two are missing. *The Scripture on King Ajātaśatru’s Inquiry into the Five Heinous Crimes*, one fascicle;
translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. First translation; two translations exist, while one is missing.
Supplementary Additions, included in the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. *Wǔkǔ zhāngjù jīng* (Sūtra on the Verses of the Five Sufferings), one fascicle;
also known as *Wǔdào zhāngjù jīng* (Sūtra on the Verses of the Five Paths). Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Dharmaruci during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

First translation; one of the two translations is missing. *Jiānyì jīng* (Sūtra of Firm Resolve), one fascicle; also known as *Jiānxīn zhèngyì jīng* (Sūtra of Firm Mind and Right Intention) or *Jiānxīn jīng* (Sūtra of Firm Mind). [The latter] follows.
*The Sutra on the Parinirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Han and the Anxi kingdoms (first translation);

two translations exist, one being missing. Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng (second translation); two translations exist, one being missing. *The Sutra on Advancing in Learning*, one fascicle;
also known as *The Sutra on Exhorting the Advancement of the Path of Learning*. Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. [Recorded in the] *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection).
Included in the second translation among three versions; two are missing. *Dedao ticheng xizhang jing* (Sutra on the Staff of the Ladder to the Way), one fascicle;

also simply titled *Xizhang jing* (Staff Sutra). Translator lost; now appended to the Eastern Jin record. Regarding this *Xizhang jing*, the *Da Zhou lu* states it was extracted from the *Za piyu jing*.
Since it is not found in the current major collections, it is difficult to establish a definitive standard; for now, it is included here.

*The Sūtra of the Poor Old Man* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra of the Poor Old Man*, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huìjiǎn; the second of two translations, one of which is missing. *The Sūtra of Samaja* (one fascicle), also titled *The Sūtra of King Śūradatta* or *The Sūtra of King Nanda*, translated by the Wu dynasty Indian śramaṇa Zhúlüyán; the first of two translations, one of which is missing. Regarding the above *Sūtra of Samaja*, the *Dàzhōu Lù* states that it was extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Upon examining that collection, however, it is not found therein; thus, it has been included here.

*The Sūtra on King Piṅgala’s Five Vows*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on King Puṣya*. Translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. This is the first translation; two other translations are missing. Note: The *Dazhou Catalogue* and other records state that this *Sūtra on King Piṅgala’s Five Vows* was extracted from the *Madhyama Āgama*; however, upon examining that text, it is not found there, so it has been included here.

*The Sūtra of King Vaidūrya*, one fascicle; translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. This is the second translation; the first translation is missing. Note: Regarding this *Sūtra of King Vaidūrya*, the *Dazhou Catalogue* and other records state that it is extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*. However, although the narrative concerning King Vaidūrya appears within the twenty-sixth section of the *Ekottarika*, the meaning and content differ entirely; therefore, it has been compiled here.
The first fifteen sūtras, totaling seventeen fascicles, are contained in one volume.

The *Seng jing* (Birth Sūtra) consists of five fascicles and contains fifty-five sūtras—or four fascicles according to another version—and was translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin; it represents the first of two translations, while the second is missing. The *Yizu jing* (Sūtra on the Meaningful Footsteps) consists of two fascicles and contains sixteen sūtras, translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu; this is the first of two translations, while the second is missing. These two preceding sūtras, totaling seven fascicles, are kept in the same volume. From the *Sishier zhang jing* (Sūtra in Forty-two Sections) downward, these twenty-two sūtras, although they are retranslations, are currently extant in circulation in their single versions; all others have been lost and scattered, and though sought after, cannot be found.

Small Vehicle Sūtras Translated Individually: eighty-seven works in two hundred twenty-four fascicles, arranged in seventeen bundles. *The Scripture on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma* (Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra), seventy fascicles, seven bundles.

Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei. Note: This *Scripture on the Stations of Mindfulness of the True Dharma* is listed as a "re-translation" in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. To claim it is a different translation of the same original text as the *Scripture of the Goose King Kāla* is an error. The *Scripture of the Goose King Kāla* was excerpted from this scripture; the former is a derivative work, while the latter is the primary text.

*The Compendium of the Buddha’s Past Deeds* (Buddha-pūrvayoga-saṃgraha-sūtra), sixty fascicles, in six volumes, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others of India during the Sui Dynasty. Note: This *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Past Deeds* was included in the catalog of the Great Zhou dynasty as a Mahāyāna re-translation. To claim it is the same text as the seven-fascicle *Sūtra on Past Deeds* but with a different translation is an error. The latter consists of verses of praise and differs significantly from this work. Some catalogs place it among the Mahāyāna sūtras, while others include it within the *Collection of Biographies* (Biqiuni zhuan). Fearing that such classifications might lead to confusion or misrepresentation, I have now moved it here.

The *Mūlaparivarta-sūtra* (本起經), seven fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; the *Udānavarga-sūtra* (興起行經), two fascicles, also titled *Sūtra on the Strict Admonitions of Past Causes*, with the title stating it was extracted from the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*, translated by the foreign Tripitaka Master Kang Mengxiang of the Later Han. Regarding this *Udānavarga-sūtra*, the Catalogue of the Great Zhou classifies it as a "re-translation," claiming it is a different translation of the same original text as the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Being Pierced in the Foot by a Wooden Spear*. However, upon examining the actual text, there are ten total narratives in total. The *Sūtra on Being Pierced in the Foot by a Wooden Spear* is merely one of these ten narratives. It has been excerpted and circulated separately—similar to the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* and other such works—and since it is not a re-translation, it stands as a single, independent text.

*The Sūtra on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution*, one fascicle, translated by Gautama Fazhi, Governor of Yangchuan Commandery during the Sui dynasty. The aforementioned three sūtras comprise ten fascicles in a single volume. Regarding this *Sūtra on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution*, the Record of the Great Zhou states that it is a different translation of the same text as the *Sūtra on the Retribution of Sin and Merit*; however, this is incorrect. Upon examining its phrasing and essential meaning, they differ significantly and are not the same; therefore, it stands as a separate text.

*The Scripture on the Great Ānāpāna-dhāraṇī* (also simply titled *The Great Ānāpāna Scripture*), in two fascicles; Master Dao’an also refers to it as the *Small Ānāpāna*. Alternatively, it exists in one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. According to the catalogs of the Great Zhou and others, there is also a version of the *Great Ānāpāna Scripture* in one fascicle, likewise attributed to An Shigao. Upon examining its phrasing, it is identical to the first fascicle of the *Ānāpāna-dhāraṇī Scripture*; since the text is entirely the same, it is not recorded here again.
*Śarīra-skandha-dhātv-āyatana-sūtra*, two fascicles (alternatively titled *Chú* [Elimination], which is likely an error;

or one fascicle); translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. *Sarvārtha-siddhi-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. *Ākrośana-sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. [These were] collected and included as supplementary texts (*shíyí*).
*The Sūtra on the Distinction between Good and Evil Origins*, one fascicle; translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Leaving Home*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Leaving Home*.

Translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. *The Sūtra on Āgama’s Right Practice*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on Right Intention*. Translated during the Later Han Dynasty.
*The Sutra of the Eighteen Nirayas*, one fascicle, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han; also known as *The Sutra of the Eighteen Hells*.
*The Sutra of Dharmas Receiving Dust*, one fascicle, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han.
*The Sutra on the Dharma-Contemplation of Dhyāna Practice*, one fascicle, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master [An Shigao] of the Later Han.

*The Sutra on the Elder’s Son’s Distress in Three Places*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sutra on the Elder’s Grief* or *The Sutra on Distress in Three Places*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
*The Sutra of the King of Gandhāra*, one fascicle (sometimes without the character "king")—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. *Sūma-* [fragment].
*The Sūtra of the Elder Ti* (one fascicle), translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].

*The Sūtra of Ānanda’s Four Matters* (one fascicle), translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]. *The Sūtra of Ajātaśatru* (one fascicle), translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].
*The Sūtra of the Four Vows* (one fascicle), translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].
The *Kālāma-brāhmaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty]; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). The *Śvāna-sūtra*, one fascicle;
Sengyou states it is identical to the *Śṛgāla-sūtra*; translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty];
included in the *Shiyi*. The *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*, one fascicle; formerly stated to be the same text as the *Ānanda-vibhaṅga-sūtra* and others.

[This] is incorrect. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin, it was included as a supplement in one fascicle of the *Bāguānzhāi jīng* (Sutra on the Eight Precepts of the Fast).
Translated by the layman Juqu Jingsheng of the Song dynasty, it was included as a supplement in one fascicle of the *Ājiūliú jīng* (Sutra of Ajita).

Sengyou’s catalogue states that this is an ancient scripture of Master Daoan; it is now appended to the Han dynasty records and included as a supplement in one fascicle of the *Xiàozǐ jīng* (Sutra of the Filial Son).
It is also called the *Xiaozibaoen jing* (Sutra on the Filial Son’s Requital of Kindness). Sengyou’s Catalogue states that Master Dao’an lost the record of its translator;
it is now appended to the Western Jin catalogue as a supplement. It is included in the upper volume among the twenty-two scriptures, totaling twenty-four fascicles in one bundle.
*The Sutra on the Five Hundred Disciples Speaking of Their Own Past Lives*, one fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the word "speaking" (*zishuo*). Also known as *The Sutra of the Beginning and End*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *The Mahākāśyapa Sutra*, one fascicle; alternatively, it lacks the character "Mahā" (*da*).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *The Sutra on the Four Self-Inflicted Injuries*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
*The Sūtra on Rāhula’s Forbearance*, one fascicle; alternatively titled simply *The Sūtra on Forbearance*.
Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. *The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha for Young Bhikṣus on Correct Matters*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. *The Sūtra on the Merits of the Bhikṣu Śaha*. Translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. At that time...
*The Scripture on Non-Timely [Death]* (or simply *The Scripture on Time*), one fascicle; translated by the foreign Dharma Master Yeluo (Yarola), though the imperial era of its production is unknown.
From the "Postscript to the Scriptures": All catalogs state that this *Scripture on Timeliness and Untimeliness* was translated by the Śramaṇa Faju of the Western Jin.
However, the colophon at the end of the scripture states: "The foreign Dharma Master Yeluo held the Hu (foreign) manuscript in his hand and orally [translated it]..."
This was personally translated by the Daoist practitioner Lü Tián of Liangzhou, who recorded it while in the city.
Now, relying on the scriptural record as authoritative, and since the imperial era remains unknown, it is appended here within the records of the Western Jin.
*Zì'ài jīng* (Sūtra on Self-Love), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Zì'ài bù zì'ài* (Self-Love and Non-Self-Love).

Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin. *Dōngxīn jīng* (Sūtra on the Central Mind), one fascicle; also titled *Dōngxīn zhèngxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Correct Practice of the Central Mind).

Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin. Included in the *Shiyí* (Supplementary Collection). *Jiànzhèng jīng* (Sūtra on Seeing the Correct), one fascicle; also known as *Shēngsǐ biàn* (Transformation of Birth and Death).

*Shi jing* (Sutra on Consciousness), translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; one fascicle. *Dayu shi jing* (Sutra on the Matter of the Great Fish), translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
one fascicle. *Anan qimen jing* (Sutra of Ānanda’s Seven Dreams), also simply titled *Qimen jing*, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
one fascicle. *He diao anan jing* (Sutra on the Hārītī Anāgāmin), translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; one fascicle.
One fascicle; also titled *He-diao* (or alternatively *Ke*) or *Deng-zhi Yin-yuan Jing* (The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Lamp-Finger).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. One fascicle;
*Fu-ren Yu-gu Jing* (The Sūtra of the Woman Who Encountered Misfortune), also titled *Fu-yu Dui Jing*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Shengjian of the Qifu Qin dynasty. Four [fascicles].
*Devendrasūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Liangzhou during the Song dynasty, together with Baoyun.
*Mahākāśyapa-daridra-mātṛ-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. *Dvādaśavarga-janmamaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. *Sūtra on the Retribution of Sin and Merit*.
*Ying jing* (Scripture on Correspondence), one fascicle; also known as *Lunzhuan wudao zui fu bao ying jing* (Scripture on the Retribution of Sin and Merit in the Revolving Five Paths).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. In the catalog of the Great Zhou, there is additionally a *Lunzhuan wudao zui fu bao ying jing* in one fascicle.
Upon examining its wording and phrasing, it is no different from this [present text]; however, the titles established differ in their brevity and detail.
As there are no differences in the textual variants, only a single edition remains.
*The Sutra of Five Non-Reciprocities*, one fascicle; also titled *The Great Meaning of the Five Reciprocities*, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng.
*The Sutra of the Buddha’s Greatness and the Sangha’s Greatness*, one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. *Yejī* [Sūtra].
*Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng. *The Sūtra of King Mela*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
*The Sūtra of King Madaka*, one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
*The Sūtra of King Candravyūha*, one fascicle (sometimes lacking the word "King"); translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
*Wǔ kǒngbù shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Terrifying Worlds), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Wú shì*. Translated by the Song layman Jūqú Jīngshēng.
*Dìzǐ sǐ fù shēng jīng* (Sūtra on a Disciple’s Death and Rebirth), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Sǐwáng gèngshēng jīng*. Translated by the Song layman Jūqú Jīngshēng.
Included in the *Shíyí* (Supplementary Collection). *Xīdài gēngzhě jīng* (Sūtra on the Lazy Plowman), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Gēng'ér*. Translated by the Song monk Sà... [text fragment].
*The Sūtra on the Elder’s Son Bianyi*, translated by the monk Shi Huijian of the Gate [of the Translation Bureau];
alternatively titled *The Sūtra on the Elder Bianyi*, or with the words "As Asked" added; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Fanchang of the Northern Wei.
*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Upright Upāsikā*, translated by the Brāhmaṇa Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei. [Total: thirty sūtras, thirty in number.]
These two scrolls are bound together in the same volume.

*The Sūtra on the Five Blessings of the Worthy One*, one scroll, translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazǔ of Hénèi during the Western Jìn dynasty; *The Sūtra of Questions from Heaven*, one scroll, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuánzàng of the Great Táng dynasty. [End of] the *Lù of Internal Scriptures*. Regarding these two sūtras, the *Worthy One’s Five Blessings* and the *Questions from Heaven*, both the *Catalogue of the Equal Records of the Great Zhou* and others included them among the Mahāyāna sūtras; however, upon examining their literary principles, they are found to pertain largely to the Hīnayāna school, and thus they have been moved here for inclusion.

*Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Yinyuán* (Causes and Conditions); translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *Hujing jing* (Sūtra on Purifying the Vows), one fascicle;
translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *Muhuànzi jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhi-Seed Beads), one fascicle;

alternatively written as *Huàn* or *Xuān*; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *Wúshàngchù jing* (Sūtra on the Unsurpassed State), one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue.

*Jin lu Lu zhi changzhe yinyuan jing* (The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of the Elder Lu Zhi of the Jin Dynasty), one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *Wu wang jing* (The Scripture of the Five Kings), one fascicle;
translator lost, now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin. *Chujia gongde jing* (The Scripture on the Merit of Leaving Home), one fascicle;

translator lost, now appended to the catalogue of the Three Qin. These have been included as supplementary entries. Of these, there are three circulating versions of the *Chujia gongde jing*, with the remainder [as noted above].
Although these two versions differ in their length, both are excerpted from the *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish).
It is said that the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha when he spoke this; it is now recorded in the *Biesheng lu* (Record of Separate Births).

This particular text states that the Buddha was in the country of Vaiśālī teaching the Licchavi Vīradatta. Within it, it further notes that "Vīradatta" means "Brave Army" (*yǒngjūn*) in the language of Qin.
Although the name of the translator is unknown, this must certainly be a translation from the Qin dynasty.
The *Candanavṛkṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle, is listed in Sengyou’s catalog as an ancient scripture of Master Dao’an;

however, the record by Fashang states it was translated by Kumārajīva, which is incorrect. It is now appended to the Han catalog. The *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra*, one fascicle, is listed in Sengyou’s catalog.
The *Pudawang jing* (Sūtra of King Puda), one fascicle, whose translator was lost according to Master Dao’an, is now appended to the catalogue of the Western Jin.

Master Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an [recorded] the *Fomiehu hou ganlian zangsong jing* (Sūtra on the Enshrouding and Burial after the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa), one fascicle—also known as the *Biqiu shi jing* (Sūtra of the Bhikṣu Teacher) or the *Shi biqiu jing* (Sūtra of the Teacher Bhikṣu)—as a work whose translator was lost by Master Dao’an. Master Sengyou’s catalogue [also attributes this] to Master Dao’an.

*The Scripture on the Mother of Demons* (Kauśika-mātṛ-sūtra), one fascicle; translated by an unknown translator, now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it as a work of unknown translation; it is now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue and included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement).

*The Scripture on King Brahmadatta* (Brahmadatta-rāja-sūtra), one fascicle; translated by an unknown translator, now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it as a work of unknown translation;

it is now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue and included in the *Shiyi*. *The Scripture on Parental Kindness* (Mātā-pitṛ-ṛṇa-sūtra), one fascicle; translated by an unknown translator, now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it as a work of unknown translation; it is now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue and included in the *Shiyi*.

*The Sutra on the Difficulty of Repaying Kindness*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sutra on Diligently Repaying Kindness*. Translated by An Shigao, a Tripiṭaka Master from Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
Included in the *Supplemental Collection* (*Shiyi*). *The Sutra of Sundarī*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sutra of the Brahmin*.

Translated by Zhi Qian, a lay devotee (*upāsaka*) from Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. *The Sutra of the New Year*, one fascicle. Translated by Zhu Tanwulan, a śramaṇa from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The *Dazhou Catalogue* and other records state that the three sutras beginning with "The Inability to Repay the Kindness of Parents" were translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*.
However, upon examining the extant version of the *Madhyama Āgama*, these sutras are not found therein.

Although a narrative concerning the *Poṣadha* (the observance of the full moon) does appear in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Ekottara Āgama*, its textual content and meaning differ entirely; therefore, they have been compiled here.

*The Parable of the Herd of Cows*, one fascicle, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Shi Faju. Regarding the aforementioned *Parable of the Herd of Cows*, the *Catalogue of the Great Zhou* states that it is extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*; however, as it is not found therein, it has been included here.

*Jiǔhéng jīng* (Sūtra on the Nine Premature Deaths), one fascicle; translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han. *Cánxíng sānshíqī jīng* (Sūtra on the Thirty-seven Practices of Dhyāna), one fascicle; alternatively titled with the character "pǐn" (chapter); translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han. *Bìqiū bì nǚ è míng yù zìshā jīng* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Who Attempted Suicide Due to the Evil Reputation of a Woman), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin. *Bìqiū tīng shī jīng* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Listening to Almsgiving), one fascicle; also known as *Tīngshī Bìqiū Jīng*; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. *Shēnguān jīng* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Body), one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. The above four sūtras, including the *Jiǔhéng jīng*, were included as supplements. The *Dàzhōu lù* states that they are alternative translations from the *Zá āhán jīng*. Regarding the *Shēnguān jīng*, it is said to be a separately produced version; however, upon examining the texts, no such work exists, so it has been compiled here.
*Anityatā-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Triparivarta-sūtra*. Translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang;
newly included in the canon. *Aṣṭākṣaṇa-sakṣaṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang;
newly included in the canon. *Dīrghanakha-parivrājaka-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle. [Translated] during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang.
*The Sūtra of Parables*, one fascicle, newly compiled and included in the catalogue by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang.
*The Brief Sūtra of Admonition*, one fascicle, newly compiled and included in the catalogue by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang.
To the right, it is stated that this *Brief Sūtra of Admonition* is said to have been extracted from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
The nineteenth fascicle of the *Yaṃsa-vastu* (Miscellaneous Matters) is an error; although it contains some abbreviated instructional texts, its meaning differs vastly from this [present work].
Since it was not produced as a separate version, it has been compiled here.

*The Sūtra on the Treatment of Hemorrhoids*, one fascicle; also titled *Hemorrhoids and Fistula*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog. Note: This *Sūtra on the Treatment of Hemorrhoids* also contains this mantra within the second fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-nidāna*. Some have classified it as a duplicate translation, but I maintain that this is not the case. That text states: "O Bhikṣus, this *Sūtra on the Treatment of Hemorrhoids* was already taught by me in another place, yet the purpose for which it was taught there was different, and the location was also not the same. This is a reiteration [of the teaching], not a duplicate translation. Thus, it is a re-statement, not a re-translation.
The thirty scriptures above comprise thirty fascicles in one bundle.

Regarding the Śrāvaka Vinaya Piṭaka: it consists of fifty-four sections totaling four hundred and forty-six fascicles, arranged in forty-five bundles. As for the "Vinaya Piṭaka": [it is as described above].
The Sūtra says:
"Because it is supreme;
because it is secret."
Because the Buddha alone has established this rule.
As it says in the Sūtras:
"When the disciples preach the Dharma..."
Alternatively, while some [versions] state that the devas preached the Dharma,
the Vinaya does not say so; rather,
it states that all was spoken by the Buddha.
Since ancient times, all various catalogs have classified the *Mātṛkā*, the *Sāmagrī-vinaya*,
and other such texts as belonging to the *Vinaya-piṭaka*.
Now, upon careful reflection, I fear this may not be appropriate.
All of these were composed by various sages and worthies following the division of the schools;
they were not proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Buddha,
nor were they compiled by the thousand sages.
The present compilation is divided into two categories:
first, the exposition of the five sections of the authentic Vinaya-piṭaka;
second, the exposition of the various śāstras belonging to the Nikāya-affiliates.
I hope that the roots and branches will not be confused and that the beginning and end will be clearly distinguished.
I trust that the various masters of the Way will again deign to revise and correct this.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in forty fascicles—or, as some say, thirty fascicles—divided into four volumes, translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhavarman of India together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty; this is a single-text edition. The above is one scripture.
This is the *Mūlavinayapiṭaka*,
which is the *Vinaya* of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Kāśyapa convened one thousand arhats.
It was compiled at the stone cave in the Bamboo Grove near Rājagṛha.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* consists of sixty-one fascicles in six bundles; the first fifty-eight fascicles were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra and others, together with Kumārajīva, during the Yao Qin dynasty. The final three fascicles, the *Pini xu* (Preface to the Vinaya), were subsequently translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Vimalākṣa during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The above scripture is the Vinaya Piṭaka of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was [compiled].

This was originally derived from the Sthavira school. Within this *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Vinayamātṛkā* (毘尼序) consists of three fascicles; some manuscript editions place it after the ninth recitation and before the tenth recitation, from fascicle 55 to 57, but this is an error. Now, having examined ancient manuscripts, they are all found at the very end. Therefore, we follow the ancient versions as the correct arrangement.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* in fifty fascicles, arranged in five bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* in twenty fascicles, arranged in two bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* in forty fascicles, arranged in four bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-nidāna-mātṛkā* in ten (or eight) fascicles, arranged in one bundle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon. The above four scriptures, together with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, all belong to the Sarvāstivāda school; however, their literary style and principles are not without differences from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
The reason for this is not known.

The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* (Wǔfēn lǜ) is also said to consist of thirty fascicles, or alternatively, thirty-four fascicles, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. These three volumes were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa from the Song dynasty, together with Zhu Daosheng and others. This is the single text mentioned above.
This is the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Mahīśāsaka school,
which emerged from the Sarvāstivāda school during the three hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in sixty fascicles—alternatively recorded as forty-five or seventy fascicles—divided into six bundles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the first scripture in the single-volume collection.
This is the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Dharmaguptaka school.
It emerged from the Mahīśāsaka school during the three hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
As for the Kāśyapīya school, they possess only a prātimokṣa-sūtra, and their vinaya-piṭaka has not yet been translated.
*Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Mahāsāṃghika Prātimokṣa*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
This is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. *Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle;
also titled *Mahāsāṃghika Prātimokṣa*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
*The Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Ten Recitations*, one fascicle, translated by Guṇabhadra; also known as the *Prātimokṣa Śīla of the Ten Recitations*.
Third translation; two of the three translations are missing. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
*The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Ten Recitations*, one fascicle; also known as the *Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa of the Ten Recitations*.
*Śikṣāpada-mūla* (The Root of the Precepts), compiled by the Śramaṇa Śīladhara of Chánggān Temple during the Song Dynasty;
one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog.

*Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-śīla-sūtra* (The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School); one fascicle. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog.

*The Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Mahīśāsaka School*, one fascicle; also called *The Mīśāsaka Prātimokṣa*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas and others of Jibin during the Song dynasty.
This single-text work constitutes the seventh sutra in the upper volume; all seven works in this fascicle comprise seven fascicles in total.

*The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Five-Part Vinaya*, one fascicle; also called the *Mīśāsaka Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa*. Compiled and brought forth by the Śramaṇa Shi Minghui of Jianchu Monastery during the Liang dynasty; recorded in the *Baochang Lu* as a supplement and included in the *Sifen Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; also called the *Sifen Prātimokṣa*. Compiled according to the Vinaya by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Monastery during the Great Tang; newly compiled and included in the canon. *The Sifen Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; also called the *Sifen Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa*. Compiled according to the Vinaya by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Monastery during the Great Tang; newly compiled and included in the canon. *The Sifen Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively called the *Dharmaguptaka Prātimokṣa* (or omitting the word "Bhikṣu"). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty. Single volume. Note: This Prātimokṣa originally lacks the verse of prostration.
The verses beginning with "There is one who enters the hall" and so forth are these.

Regarding the four-part *Bhikṣu* and *Bhikṣuṇī* Vinayas, several versions have circulated; however, they all deviate from the original texts by arbitrarily adding or omitting passages. Therefore, I have retained only the translation by Dharmayaśas of the Yao Qin period and the compilation based on the original text by the Grand Master of Taiyuan. All other versions have been discarded and not included in this record.

*Jiètuō jièběn* (Sūtra on the Code of Liberation), one fascicle; translated by the Bactrian Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty; belonging to the Kāśyapīya school. *Shānmí shíjiè fǎ bìng wēiyí* (The Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras and Their Deportment), also known as *Shānmí wēiyí jièběn* (Śrāmaṇera Deportment Code of Liberation); translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *Shānmí wēiyí* (Śrāmaṇera Deportment), one fascicle; sometimes titled with the character "sūtra" (*jīng*), which is largely the same as the preceding work but with minor differences; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Jibin during the Song dynasty. *Shānmíní líjiè wén* (Text on the Separation from Precepts for Śrāmaṇerīs), one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. *Shānmíní jièjīng* (Sūtra on the Precepts for Śrāmaṇerīs), one fascicle; translator lost, listed in the Later Han catalogue and included in the *Shiyí* (Supplementary Collection). *Shèlìfú wèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of Śāriputra), one fascicle; translator lost, now appended to the Eastern Jin catalogue. These ten single-fascicle sūtras, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.
*The Hundred and One Karmavācanās of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, ten fascicles, one volume;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon. *The Dharma of the Hundred and One Karmavācanās for Great Śramaṇas*, one fascicle;

originally from the *Ten Recitations Vinaya* (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya), listed in Sengyou’s Catalogue as a lost-translation scripture now appended to the Song Catalogue. *The Bhikṣu Karmavācanās of the Ten Recitations*.
One fascicle extracted from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), or two fascicles;
the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Sūtra on Upāli’s Questions to the Buddha) in one fascicle, compiled by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Sengqu at Zhongxing Temple in Yangdu based upon the Vinaya;

also known as the *Upāli-vinaya*, translated anonymously and recorded among the Later Han catalogues as a single volume; and the *Pañcavargika-karmavācanā* (Five-Section Ritual Manual) in one fascicle, titled Mi-sha-se (Mūlasarvāstivāda).

*The Original Karma-text of the Four-Part Vinaya (Sifen lü zajiemo)*, Volume One, newly compiled and included in the records by the Śramaṇa Shi Aitong of the Great Kaiye Monastery during the Great Tang;
titled *The Miscellaneous Karma of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya School*, beginning with the "Binding of the Precept Field" (*jie jichang*),
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Sengyai of India during the Cao Wei dynasty, collected as a supplement and appended to the *Dharmaguptaka Karma-text*.

*The Mopie* (Mo-pi-e), one fascicle, beginning with the "Establishment of the Great Boundary" (*Mahā-sīmā-bandhana*), or two fascicles; translated by the Anxi śramaṇa Tandi during the Cao Wei dynasty.
*The Four-Part Bhikṣuṇī Karma-dharma* (Sifen biquni jiemofa), one fascicle; Sengyou states it is the *Karma* of the Dharmaguptaka school, or alternatively called the *Miscellaneous Karma*;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. These seven scriptures, totaling seven fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

*The Random羯磨 (Karman) Compiled from the Four-Part Vinaya*, one fascicle, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Chongyi Monastery during the Great Tang; newly compiled and entered into the canon. *The Four-Part Bhikṣu Karman*, three fascicles; the title reads "Karman, Fascicle One," issued from the Four-Part Vinaya, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Monastery during the Great Tang according to the Vinaya; newly compiled and entered into the canon. *The Four-Part Bhikṣuṇī Karman*, three fascicles; the title reads "Bhikṣuṇī Karman, Fascicle One," issued from the Four-Part Vinaya, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Monastery during the Great Tang according to the Vinaya; newly compiled and entered into the canon. These three scriptures, totaling seven fascicles, are contained in the same volume. The aforementioned six works of *Karman* all derive from the Four-Part Vinaya; however, their texts differ in terms of length and the sequence of their arrangement.

The *Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra* in two fascicles is also called the *Mahāprajāpatī Receiving the Precepts Sūtra*, or simply the *Mahāprajāpatī Sūtra*. Its translator is lost; Sengyou’s catalogue states it was a separate scripture from the Liang region according to Master Dao’an, and it is now appended to the Northern Liang catalogue as a single-fascicle work. The *Kāśyapa Vinaya Sūtra* in one fascicle—also known as the *Mahābhikṣu Sūtra* or the *Sūtra on True and False Śramaṇas*—was translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. There is a second translation, and among various catalogues there is also a one-fascicle *Sūtra on True and False Śramaṇas* said to have been translated by the Song monk Huijian. This is the same text as the *Kāśyapa Vinaya Sūtra*; upon examining the phrasing, it is identical from beginning to end with the *Vinaya Sūtra*. Since there are no differing passages, it is not recorded here twice.

*The Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of Retribution for Violating the Precepts*, one fascicle. Extracted from the *Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana’s Questions on the Vinaya*; alternatively titled *The Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana’s Questions*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a separate work. *The Sūtra on the Precepts for Eliminating Calamities*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra on Subduing and Eliminating Calamities through the Precepts*. Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts for Upāsakas*, one fascicle; also known as *The Brief Treatise on the Five Precepts for Upāsakas*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. Of these two translations, one is missing. The above sūtras and vinayas constitute the Treasury of Proper Discipline (*Vinaya-piṭaka*).
The following sections from the *Śāstra* and other texts are termed "retinue" (*parivāra*) because they accord with the preceding primary tenets.
As for the *Karmavācanā* for the precepts and the mind, they are listed first because they are compiled strictly according to the essential text, without any additions or subtractions.

Regarding the *Vinayasamgraha* and other such works, based upon their original texts, there are frequent additions and subtractions which are here compiled below. 1. *Mūlasarvāstivada-vinaya-kārikā*, five fascicles; composed by the Venerable Viśākha;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon as a single volume. 2. *Mūlasarvāstivada-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu-saṃgraha-kārikā*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon as a single volume. 3. *Mūlasarvāstivada-vinaya-nidāna-mātṛkā-saṃgraha-kārikā*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon as a single volume. 4. *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu-sūtra*, one fascicle; translator lost; now appended to the Eastern Jin catalog as part of the "Supplementary Collection" (*Shiyi*). The above nine scriptures, totaling fourteen fascicles, are bound in the same volume.
*Vinaya-saṃgraha* (Fundamental Sarvāstivāda Vinaya Compendium), twenty fascicles, compiled by the Venerable Jayagupta;
alternatively, fourteen fascicles in two volumes, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang Dynasty; newly included in the canon as a single volume.
*Vinayamātṛkā*, ten fascicles, one volume, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of the Song Dynasty; a single volume.
*Pinaiye lü* (The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda), ten fascicles, one volume; also known as the *Ji yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Precepts).

Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Fu Qin period of the Yao Qin dynasty. A single-text edition. *Shanjian lü piposha* (The Vinayavibhāṣā of the Sūtra of Good Vision), eighteen fascicles;
alternatively called the *Vibhāṣā-lü* or simply the *Shanjian lü*. Translated by the foreign Śramaṇa Saṃghavarman of the Xiao Qi dynasty.
The *Dhāraṇa-yi-dan-ben Fo-a-pi-tan-jing* (Singular-Text Buddha-abhidharma-sūtra), two fascicles;

also called the *Fo-a-pi-tan-lun* (Buddha-abhidharma-śāstra), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. These two singular-text scriptures comprise twenty fascicles in two volumes.
Regarding the *Fo-a-pi-tan-lun*, various catalogs all state it consists of nine fascicles, though the reason for this is unknown; currently, only two fascicles remain according to the old catalogs.

Originally compiled within the Mahāyāna treatises, it has now been re-categorized here because its textual patterns and principles largely discuss matters such as the salvation of others and the reception of precepts, which correspond to this [section].
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* in eight fascicles is also called the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*;

its translator is lost, and it is now appended to the Qin Records. The single-fascicle *Mahābhikṣu-tri-sahasra-vaipulya-vinaya* in two fascicles is also called the *Mahāsaṃgha-vaipulya-vinaya*, in four fascicles; it was translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. These two aforementioned single-fascicle scriptures comprise ten fascicles in one volume, along with the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*.
The *Dazhou lu* states:
"During the Taian era of the Eastern Jin, Fulan translated [this work].
I have carefully examined the chronological records of successive emperors and find that there was no such era as Taian during the Eastern Jin period.

The Tai’an era fell during the reign of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin; although I have searched the records of his dharma-transmissions, I have not yet found them. Since the dates are already confused, they cannot be relied upon as evidence.
Furthermore, upon examining the text, all instances where Sanskrit terms were translated are referred to as "Qin language."
Therefore, this was translated during the Qin dynasty.
It is now classified as a work of lost translation and included in the Qin Records.
As for the *Sāhasrika-vaipulya-sūtra* (The Sutra of Three Thousand Dignified Manners):
In Sengyou’s *Record of Lost Translations*, these are divided into two sections,
each consisting of two fascicles.
Various catalogs, such as that of Daofang, state that the two versions were combined to form four fascicles in total.
Now only two remain; the other two no longer exist.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* in nine fascicles has a lost translator and is now appended to the Qin records. The single-fascicle *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* (also known as the *Ekottara-vinaya*) and the single-fascicle *Prakaraṇābhidharma-śāstra* (translated by the Chen dynasty Tripitaka Master Paramārtha from India) are both titled simply *Viniścaya-śāstra*. These two aforementioned scriptures, totaling ten fascicles, are kept together in one volume. This *Viniścaya-śāstra* was extracted from the *Prātimokṣa-śāstra* of the Saṃmitīya school.
That great treatise has not yet been translated; it consists of approximately six thousand stanzas.

A Dharma master of that school, an Anāgāmin named Guṇaprabha, relying upon the Vinaya-vibhāṣā and other works, composed a summary corresponding to the Vinaya in one fascicle, known as the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (The Compendium of Ascertainment).
This treatise explains twenty-two essential points of truth from the Vinaya Piṭaka;
it is called *Vibhaṅga* because it dispels the darkness of mind for those who practice the True Dharma and brings about thorough penetration of the meaning of the Vinaya.

In the *Fajing lu* (Catalogue of Dharma-jing) and the *Changfang ruzang lu* (Catalogue of Chang-fang for Inclusion in the Canon), both compiled by the Sui dynasty śramaṇas, these works are divided into two sections:
twenty-two fascicles of Vinaya texts are included within the Vinaya section, while one fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Mingliao lun) is recorded in the Śāstra section.
Furthermore, the "Twenty-two" [in the title] is actually the partial title of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
That it exists in twenty-two fascicles is a grave error;
it is indeed a grave error.

The Abhidharma-piṭaka of the Śrāvakas consists of thirty-six sections totaling six hundred and ninety-eight fascicles, arranged in seventy-two bundles; these various sections within the Abhidharma-piṭaka differ from one another.
While this has been circulated in this region for comparison with other traditions,
it now relies upon the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* as its primary source.
I take that treatise on the body (*kāya-śāstra*) as the starting point.
The *Pāda-śāstra* occupies the second position,
while the various branches such as the *Vibhāṣā* are arranged at the end.
Since the other schools are numerous, [the work] concludes with them.
It is difficult to categorize these matters,
so they shall await future generations;
herein there is no sequence of priority.

The *Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Eight Chapters of Abhidharma) in thirty fascicles, composed by Kātyāyanīputra; alternatively, in twenty fascicles and three volumes, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva of Kapiśa together with Zhu Fonian during the Fu Qin dynasty. First translation: the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* in twenty fascicles, composed by Kātyāyanīputra, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang dynasty in two volumes. Recorded in the *Neidian lu* as the second translation. The above two treatises are the same original text with different translations.
This is the fundamental Abhidharma-piṭaka of the Sarvāstivāda school,
composed by the master Kātyāyanīputra during the three hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In later generations, there were both extensive and abbreviated versions transmitted by followers.
This *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* is complete in both its prose and meaning;
those who transmit and study it call it the "Body Treatise" (*Śarīra-śāstra*).
Since the remaining six treatises each expound upon one branch [of the path],
they are called "feet" because they differ from the body [of the main work].
These were subsequently compiled and followed by the various schools.

1. *Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, twelve fascicles, composed by the Venerable Mahakausthila; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed as a single work in the *Neidian lu*. 2. *Abhidharma-sangīti-paryāya-pāda-śāstra*, twenty fascicles, spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; listed as a single work in the *Neidian lu*. 3. *Prajñapti-pāda-śāstra*.

There is a work in eighteen thousand stanzas composed by the Venerable Mahākātyāyana. "Kātyāyana" is translated as "Jianli" (Shearer) and "Yanzi" (Seed-descendant); it is a masculine surname among the Brahmins. This treatise has not yet been translated. The three aforementioned "Pādas" (Feet) were all composed during the Buddha’s lifetime. The *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Aggregate of Consciousness), sixteen fascicles, was translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; it appears as a single volume in the *Neidian lu*. Regarding the aforementioned treatise, it was produced within one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Composed by the Venerable Devaśarma (translated into Chinese as Tiānjí), an Arhat.

The *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Categories of Abhidharma) in eighteen fascicles was translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. This is the second translation recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The aforementioned treatise was composed by the Venerable Vasumitra (translated into Chinese as Shìyǒu) during the third century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

The *Saṃgītiparyāya-Abhidharma-śāstra* in twelve fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra together with Bodhiyaśas during the Song dynasty; this is the first translation. (Note: The two treatises above are translations of the same original text.)
The two aforementioned treatises comprise thirty fascicles in three bundles.

The *Ṣaḍ-abhidharma-dhātu-skandha-pāda-śāstra* in three fascicles was translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; it appears as a single volume in the *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures*. Regarding this one treatise: during the three hundred years following the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha...
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Together with the aforementioned *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*, it comprises nineteen fascicles in two volumes.

The *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* consists of sixty fascicles in six volumes—or alternatively eighty-four fascicles or one hundred and nine fascicles—and was translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman, together with Daotai and others. This is the first translation; this treatise was initially translated in one hundred fascicles to form its complete section.
The śramaṇa Daotǐng composed the preface.
During the annexation of Liang by Wei, forty fascicles were lost;
now, only sixty fascicles remain.
However, when the third *khandhaka* was completed, the latter five *khandhakas* were missing their originals.
Those who produced the new translation have fully restored all eight *skandhas*.
As for the versions consisting of eighty-four fascicles and one hundred and nine fascicles:
Later generations divided these sixty fascicles;
it was not originally incomplete.
Furthermore, according to the *Fayuan* by Sengyou of Liang:
In the second month of the eleventh year of the Tianjian era, an imperial edict was issued for Saṃghabhadra to further produce the remaining five *khandas* of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Although this account exists, the original text has not yet been seen.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, two hundred fascicles, twenty bundles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded in] the Second Volume of the Catalogue of Inner Scriptures. The above two treatises are the same original work with different translations.
This concludes the explanation of the aforementioned *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
Four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
five hundred great Arhats and others...
Composed in the kingdom of Kaśmīra. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, twenty-two fascicles;

composed by Vasubandhu, translated by the Chen dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India. First translation. *Abhidharmakośakārikā*, one fascicle (or two fascicles); composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu, translated by the Great Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. Second translation. Recorded in the *Neidian lu*. The translator Paramārtha’s version is missing. The above two treatises comprise twenty-three fascicles in three bundles.

The Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya, thirty fascicles, composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu; translated into three bundles by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded in] the Second Volume of the Catalogue of Inner Classics (Neidian Lu). The above two treatises and their verses are translations of the same original text with different versions.

The *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Principles Following the Abhidharma), eighty fascicles, composed by the Venerable Saṃghabhadra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, consisting of eight bundles; listed as a single work in the *Neidian lu*. The *Abhidharma-prakaraṇābhidharma-śāstra* (Treatise Elucidating the Abhidharma), forty fascicles, composed by the Venerable Saṃghabhadra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, consisting of four bundles; listed as a single work in the *Neidian lu*. These two treatises provide alternative explanations for the same verses of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, both composed by Saṃghabhadra. The Venerable Saṃghabhadra first composed the *Nyāyānusāra*, which was extensive and difficult to consult; he later composed the *Prakaraṇābhidharma*, which is concise and easy to understand, and thus provided this re-explanation.

The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* in four fascicles, composed by the Venerable Dharmottara (Dharmaśreṣṭhin), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kasmīra during the Eastern Jin dynasty; alternatively titled *Wulun*. The single-text *Abhidharmahṛdaya-sūtra* in six fascicles (or seven fascicles), composed by the Venerable Upaśānta, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India together with Fazhi during the Northern Qi dynasty. These two treatises, totaling ten fascicles, are contained in the same volume.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* in eleven fascicles—also known as the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-vibhāṣā*—was composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta; alternatively, it consists of fourteen fascicles and was translated by the Song dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman and others. This is the fourth translation; three other translations are missing. The three aforementioned treatises are all titled *Abhidharmahṛdaya*.
However, there are differences in the breadth and brevity of their respective expositions; the first fascicle of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states in its introductory note:
"The various masters' explanations of the meaning of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* by Dharmottara differ in both breadth and brevity."
The commentary by Dharmottara is the most concise;
that of Upaśānta consists of eight thousand verses,
and there is another master who has a commentary of twelve thousand verses.
These two treatises are known as the Extensive [Commentary]. Andhagiri explained it with six thousand verses.
Furthermore, the opening verse of the treatise says:
"I pay homage to the Victorious One, the Sublime Dharma."
I receive what has been taught upon the crown of my head.
I, Dharmatrāta, speak this because it was never previously taught.
The first four fascicles of the aforementioned three treatises constitute the original treatise by Dharmaśreṣṭhin.
The subsequent six fascicles are the commentary by Upaśānta;
therefore, at the end of that treatise it says:
"The Venerable Upaśānta, for the sake of benefiting his disciples..."
Therefore, it is known that this is indeed a commentary on the *Dharmatrāta-śāstra* (the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*). It is not the case that Dharmatrāta composed [this commentary] himself;
rather, the name "Dharmatrāta" appears in the title of the treatise because it was based upon his work.
Perhaps this is not the case;
the title in the middle of the treatise lacks these two characters,
and all catalogs refer to it as the *Dharmatrāta-abhidharma*.
Some say that the *Abhidharma* translated separately is by Dharmottara,
while the later *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* was composed by Dharmaśreṣṭhin;
compared to the former two treatises, the textual and doctrinal content of this one is somewhat more extensive.

The *Abhidharmāmṛta-śāstra* (Treatise on the Taste of the Nectar of Abhidharma), two fascicles; also known as the *Āmṛta-rasa-abhidharma*, composed by the Venerable Ghoṣaka, translated during the Cao Wei period by an anonymous Tripiṭaka Master. The *Anvaya-lakṣaṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Characteristics), one fascicle; also known as the *Guṇamati-anvaya-lakṣaṇa-śāstra*, composed by Dharma Master Guṇamati, translated by the Chen dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, in either one or two fascicles. The above three treatises comprise fourteen fascicles in two volumes.

*The Treatise Compiled by the Venerable Vasumitra Bodhisattva* (尊婆須蜜菩薩所集論), ten fascicles; composed by the Venerable Vasumitra, also existing in versions of fourteen or twelve fascicles; translated by the Kasmīrian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti and others during the Fu Qin dynasty. *The Single-Volume Treatise on the Three Dharmas* (三法度論), two fascicles—sometimes titled *The Treatise Without [the word] "Dharma"* (無論), sometimes called a *Sūtra*, and also existing in versions of three or one fascicle; translated by the Kasmīrian Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Regarding the second translation, one version is missing. As for this *Treatise on the Three Dharmas*, there are both the root text and a commentary (*śāstra*). The root text consists of three chapters and nine sections (*dharmapada*), while the commentary also comprises nine sections. Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu wrote a preface stating that the root text was originally composed by the Venerable Śrīlāta, while the commentary was compiled by the Mahāyāna lay practitioner (upāsaka) Saṃgharakṣa of India. However, the postscript to the scripture states it was compiled by the Mahāyāna bhikṣu Śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa. These two accounts differ slightly, and it remains uncertain which is correct.

*Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra*, two fascicles, composed by the Arhat Saṅghabhadra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded in the *Neidian lu* as a single work. *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa-śāstra*, fourteen fascicles, in two volumes.

*Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, twenty fascicles, composed by Harivarman; totaling two hundred and two chapters, or twenty-four fascicles in two volumes; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty as a single volume. *Lokasthiti-abhidharma-śāstra*, ten fascicles (sometimes without the character "lun"); one volume; alternatively said to be fifteen fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen dynasty as a single volume. *Vimuktimārga-śāstra*, twelve fascicles (or thirteen); [translated by Saṃghavarman of the Liu Song dynasty].

One fascicle: The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, twenty-two (or twenty or thirty) fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty; a single-text edition. The *Pañcavastu-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, two fascicles, also called the *Abhidharma-pañcavastu-śāstra*, composed by the Venerable Dharmatrāta and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśa together with Dharmagupta during the Yao Qin dynasty; according to the *Fanjing tu*, these two treatises as single-text editions comprise twenty-four fascicles in three fascicles. It is an error for the *Dazhou lu* to list the *Abhidharma-pañcavastu-śāstra* separately.

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* in fourteen fascicles, also known as the *Vibhāṣā-abhidharma-śāstra*, was composed by the Arhat Śītapāṇi and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kapiśa during the Fu Qin dynasty. The *Sāmmitīya-nikāya-śāstra* in three fascicles—sometimes without the word "nikāya" or stated to be in four fascicles—is of lost translation. "Sāmmitīya" means "Right Measure" (*samyak-pramāṇa*), referring to a treatise within the Sāmmitīya school. These two single-fascicle treatises, totaling seventeen fascicles in two volumes, are now appended to the Qin Records.

The *Fenbie Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) consists of four fascicles; it is also called the *Fenbie Gongde Jing* (Sutra on the Differentiation of Merits), or it appears in three or five fascicles. Its translator is lost, though it is included in the Later Han catalog as a single work. This treatise explains the meaning of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, ranging from the initial "Preface Chapter" to the "Disciples Chapter," where it stops after more than half [of the text] has been explained. Regarding the section on the Bhikṣu Rāja, the *Fashang Lu* states that it was translated by Zhu Fahu; however, this is not the case. Since the citations of the sutra and the explanations of its phrases herein are identical to the original sutra, it appears to have been translated by the same person as the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Yet, other catalogs all state that its source is lost. For now, we shall rely on this [record]. As for Sengyou’s record stating that it was compiled by Kāśyapa and Ānanda, this is also incorrect. Since the first fascicle of the treatise cites the explanations of foreign masters and the Sarvāstivādins, we know that it was not compiled by those two venerable ones.

The *Catuḥsatya-śāstra* in four fascicles, composed by Vasumitra and translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. The *Pratyekabuddha-hetupratyaya-śāstra* in two fascicles, translator lost; now appended to the Qin Records. The *Aṣṭādaśa-sūtra-śāstra* in one fascicle, newly classified as a lost translation and appended to the Qin Records. The above eighteen treatises constitute the first group of translations.
I have searched through various catalogs,
all of which state that this was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha during the Liang dynasty.
Now, upon close examination, it appears that the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha has already translated eighteen treatises.
It is not appropriate to translate this as a separate treatise on the differing tenets of the schools.
At the beginning of the treatise on the eighteen schools, after citing the "Section on Differentiation" from the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it subsequently states:
"Compiled by Dharma Master Kumārajīva," and only then follows the actual treatise.
If this were translated by Kumārajīva,
it would be inconsistent for him to cite the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchāsūtra*, as that scripture did not yet exist during the Qin period.

It is placed at the beginning; alternatively, it may be classified as a work of lost translation according to the *Bie lu* (Separate Record), with the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* serving as a reference.
There is no doubt that it was cited during the Qin period.
If it were a re-translation by Paramārtha, [it would have been listed accordingly].
In the commentary on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the character "Qin" (秦) should not have been present;
however, upon examining its literary style and structure, it appears for the most part to have been translated during the Qin period by Kumārajīva.
It is likely that various catalogs omitted this detail, leading to such doubts.
The commentary on the eighteen schools of the *Satyasiddhi* is the *Śāstravibhāga-viniścaya*.
Although this principle exists therein, I have not yet dared to point it out; I request that those of later generations who possess broad learning seek out the authentic record.

*The Treatise on the Different Tenets of the Schools*, one fascicle; also titled *The Treatise on the Different Tenets of the Schools*. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Chen Dynasty. Second Translation: *The Wheel of the Tenets of the Different Schools*, one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra; translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. Third Translation. The above three treatises are the same text with different translations.
The *Shangliu lun* (Discourse on the Six Superiorities), thirteen fascicles; same volume. 3.
The *Shengxian zhuan jilu* (Record of the Biographies of Sages and Worthies): the third section of the *Youben lu* (Catalogue of Works with Existing Texts) contains one hundred and eight works.
Five hundred and forty-one fascicles,
arranged in fifty-seven bundles.
These are the records of the transmission.
Compiled by holy and virtuous disciples after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
although these are not the authentic scriptures of the Tripiṭaka,
they nonetheless assist in propagating the profound transformation.
Within this, there are five general categories:
first, praising the virtues of the Buddha;
second, elucidating the true principles of the Dharma.
Third, describing the monastic conduct and rules;
fourth, refuting heterodoxy and protecting the Dharma;
fifth, the divergent tenets of external schools.
Those who praise the Buddha’s virtues include the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, the *Varṇārhavarṇastotra*, the *Śākyapravrajyāsūtra*, and so forth.
Those who elucidate the principles of the Dharma include—
The *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of Cultivating the Path) is equivalent to the *Jinglü yixiang* (Similarities and Differences between Sūtras and Vinaya) and other such works.
The accounts of the monastic practitioners consist of the biographies of Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, Faxian, Xuanzang, and others.
Those who destroy the heterodox and protect the Dharma include the *Bianzheng* (Discriminating the Correct), the *Hongming* (Propagating and Clarifying),
the *Poxie* (Refuting the Heterodox), and the *Bianhuo lun* (Treatise on Discriminating Delusions).
As for the heterodox systems of external schools,
these are the two theories of Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika.
When classified by their categories, none exceed these five.
The exposition in the fifth [chapter] applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, within this context, two additional examples are distinguished;
the translations from the Sanskrit original are presented first.
The transmission and propagation of this land shall be detailed hereafter,
so that the traditions of the East and West may not be conflated;
may readers thereby have their doubts dispelled.
The Collected Translations from Sanskrit Manuscripts.
Sixty-eight works.
One hundred and seventy-three fascicles.

Fifteen cases (zhì): *Buddhacarita-kāvya* (佛所行讚經), five fascicles, composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; also known as the *Buddha-pūrvayoga-sūtra* (佛本行經), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. Single-text edition: *Buddha-pūrvayoga-sūtra* (佛本行經), seven fascicles, also titled *Buddha-pūrvayoga-stotra* (佛本行讚傳), translated by the Śramaṇa Śīlabhadra of Liangzhou during the Song dynasty. The above [texts] are recorded in the Great Zhou Catalogue (*Dazhou lu*) as being included among the Mahāyāna re-translated scriptures.
It is an error to claim that the *Yun* (Cloud) [Sutra] is a different translation of the same original as the sixty-fascicle *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*.
The aforementioned two collections, totaling twelve fascicles, share one case.
The ten-fascicle *Saṃyukta-śataka-vastu-sūtra* constitutes one case; it was translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. It is included within [the canon].
The *Dianlu* (Catalogue) lists the *Shiyi* (Supplement) as being included within the twenty fascicles of the *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga), though some say it consists of nineteen fascicles;
it was translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Fu Qin period.

The single-fascicle edition of the *Xianyu jing* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish) consists of thirteen fascicles, though some versions have fifteen, sixteen, or seventeen; it was [translated] by the Śramaṇa of Liangzhou during the Yuan Wei period.
Huijue and others translated this single volume of the *Sūtra on the Translation of Scriptures* in Gaochang Commandery.

I have carefully consulted the preface to the *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) by the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Sengyou, which states: "The eight monks Huijue and others traveled abroad to seek the Way.

Upon reaching a great monastery in Khotan, they encountered a quinquennial assembly. The eight men listened separately and each recorded what they heard. Returning to Gaochang, they then compiled [the records]."
As for the *Upāsakaśata-sūtra* (The Hundred Discourses on Lay Practitioners), which is the aforementioned *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*:
