since all catalogs of former generations included it within the Sūtra-piṭaka, yet this current compilation is based on what has been heard from various sources, it differs from the original recitation of Ānanda. How does it differ from other such compilations?

Therefore, its inclusion in the orthodox Sūtra-piṭaka may be considered inappropriate; thus, it is now moved and appended to the section on collected biographies and records (*saṃyukta-vyākhyāna*). The same applies to the two sūtras, the *Udānavarga* and the *Śatavastuka*.
These are also separately collected works that were not part of the original recitations, yet they are appended here as well.
Of the two aforementioned collections, there are thirty-three fascicles in four volumes; the first three volumes each contain eight fascicles, while the fourth volume contains nine fascicles.

*Daodi jing* (Treatise on the Stages of the Path), one fascicle; sometimes titled with the character "Da" (Great) added. This is an excerpt from the *Xiuxing jing* (Sutra on Practice). Originally a brief foreign version, it was translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. It was included as a supplementary translation, being the second translation [of this material]. This single scripture is a partial, alternative translation of the later *Xiuxing daodi jing*. According to the preface by Dharma Master Dao’an, the śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa compiled the essentials of the scriptures into a single work consisting of twenty-seven chapters. An Shigao analyzed seven of the chapters collected by Saṃgharakṣa and rendered them into Chinese. Since both the chapter titles and their number are identical, we know that these are precisely the seven chapters produced by An [Shigao] and [Saṃgha]rakṣa. These seven chapters total eighteen sheets of paper. All catalogues state that they comprise two fascicles, which is an error.

The *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of Practice), in six fascicles—or alternatively titled simply the *Xiuxing jing*—or in seven fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin; this is the third translation. One [of the three] translations is missing. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.
Seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa of the Western Regions compiled [this work].

As for this "Saṃgharakṣa," it is the local dialectal term; in the Sanskrit of India, his name is Saṃgharakṣita. It is unreasonable to include him in the old catalogs as one whose works were classified among the sūtras.
This is no different from the compilers of the later *Sangharakṣa-saṃgīti-sūtra*.
How could one be included in the canonical scriptures while the other is compiled separately?
Since the precedent is thus, it is appended here.

*Saṃgharakṣa-saṃgīti-sūtra*, three fascicles (or five fascicles), compiled by Saṃgharakṣa; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kaśmīra and others during the Fu Qin period. Of the two translations, one is missing. The first three collections comprise ten fascicles in a single volume.

*The Sutra of One Hundred Parables* (Śataparivarta-avadāna), four fascicles, composed by Saṃghasena; or five fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇaviddha of India during the Qi dynasty. *The Single-Volume Sutra of the Original Karmic Conditions of the Bodhisattva*, three fascicles, composed by Saṃghasena; or four fascicles, or three fascicles, translated by the lay devotee (upāsaka) Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty. *The Essential Collection of Various Sutras on the Gate of Practicing the Bodhisattva Path in Mahāyāna*, three fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Temple during the Great Tang; newly compiled and entered into the canon. These three single-volume collections comprise ten fascicles in one volume.

The *Fufa zang yinyuan zhuan* (Biographies of the Causes and Conditions of the Transmission of the Dharma-treasury) in six fascicles—sometimes without the characters "yinyuan," or in four or three fascicles—was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ki-carya of the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Northern Wei dynasty; this is the third translation, while two other translations are missing. Furthermore, among the various catalogs, there is the *Zuochan sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation) in three fascicles—also titled the *Pusa chanfa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Methods of Meditation), or simply the *Chan jing* (Meditation Sūtra)—or in two fascicles; it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the first translation, while two other translations are missing. Additionally, within the various catalogs... [text continues].
There is also the *Āraṇyaka-xichan-fajing* (Forest-Dweller’s Scripture on the Method of Practicing Dhyāna) in two fascicles.
It is said to be a different translation of the same original text as the *Zuochan-sanmeijing* (Scripture on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation),
and it is also said to have been produced by Master Kumārajīva.
Upon examining the text, the beginning and end are identical in every respect;
they differ only in their distinct titles and are thus divided into two sections.
Since these are not separate translations, it is not appropriate for them to circulate as two independent works.
*The Sutra of the Buddha-Physician*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sutra of the Buddha-Medical King*. Translated by the Indian śramaṇa Zhu Lüyan and Zhi Yue during the Wu dynasty.
Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a single-fascicle work. *The Sutra of Miscellaneous Difficulties of the Sole Sun*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a single-fascicle work. *The Mahākāśyapa’s Journey to the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*.
*The Buddha Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on Kāśyapa Attending the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha*.
Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Eastern Jin. Single-text edition. *Bodhisattva’s Admonition Against Lust and Desire*, one fascicle;

also known as *The First Translation of the Sūtra*; the second translation is missing. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin. Four chapters. *The Sūtra on Learning the Dharma*, one fascicle.
*The Sūtra of the Single Volume on the Buddha’s Entry into Nirvāṇa and the Lamentation of Guhyapada the Vajrapāṇi*, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty;
one volume, translator lost, now appended to the Qin records.
*The Sūtra of the Single Volume on Kātyāyana Preaching the Verses on the Exhaustion of Phenomena*, according to Sengyou’s record, it states that Master Dao’an considered the translator lost.

Now appended to the *Xiqin lu* (Catalogue of the Later Qin): *The Sutra on the Buddha’s Treatment of the Body*, one fascicle; alternatively called *The Sutra on the Treatment of the Mind*. Sengyou’s catalogue states this is a scripture of unknown translator from the period of Master Dao’an;
it is now appended to the *Xijin lu* (Catalogue of the Western Jin). Appended to the *Shiyi* (Supplement) as a single-fascicle work: *The Sutra on the Treatment of the Mind*, one fascicle;
alternatively called *The Sutra on the Buddha’s Treatment of the Body*. Sengyou’s catalogue states this is a scripture of unknown translator from the period of Master Dao’an; it is now [appended].
The *Xi jing lu* (Record of the Western Jin) is appended as a single volume to the *Shiyi* (Supplement), compiled into the eleventh collection, volume eighteen, within the same fascicle.

The *Za bao zang jing* (Sutra of the Storehouse of Miscellaneous Jewels) consists of eight volumes—or, according to some accounts, thirteen—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kālaya from the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Northern Wei; it exists as a single version. The *Na xian biqiu jing* (Sutra of the Bhikṣu Nāgasena) consists of two volumes, though it is also simply called the *Na xian jing* in three volumes; its translator is lost, and it is listed in the first record of the Eastern Jin. It exists in two translations, one of which is missing; these two versions comprise ten volumes in the second collection, within the same fascicle.

*The Essential Methods for the Five-Gate Dhyāna Sūtra*, one fascicle, composed by the Great Dhyāna Master Buddhamitra and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kasmīra during the Song dynasty; appended as a supplement, this is the second translation. One of the two translations is missing. *Dharmatrāta’s Dhyāna Sūtra*, two fascicles, also titled *The Dhyāna Sūtra on the Meditation of Impurity: Expedient Means for Practice*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is a standalone text. Regarding Dharmatrāta and Buddhayaśas: they were both originally from Kaśmīra. Zhiyan, who traveled to the Western Regions, was a disciple of Buddhabhadra—the master of dhyāna in that country—and he also received fourteen sūtras concerning seated meditation and samādhi from the teachings previously studied by them.
Among the records of the Zhou dynasty, these were included within the canonical scriptures;
however, as they are not the word of the Buddha, they have now been moved here.
Although the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* (*Zá bǎozàng jīng*) collects the Buddha’s words, it also incorporates various other incidental narratives.
Because it was not spoken by the Buddha in its entirety, it is not included in the canon.

*Chánfǎ yàojiě* (Essential Explanations of Dhyāna Methods), two fascicles; also titled *Chányào jīng* (Sūtra on the Essentials of Dhyāna). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. Of the two translations, one is missing.
*Chányào hēyù jīng* (Sūtra on the Essentials of Dhyāna for Rebuking Desire), one fascicle; the title is given as *Chányào jīng hē*.

*Yùpǐn* (Chapter on Desires), translated during the Later Han with the translator lost; included in the *Shíyí biānrù dānběn nèishēnguān zhāngjù jīng* (Sūtra on the Verses of the Inner Body Contemplation) in one fascicle.

*Fǎguān jīng* (Dharma Contemplation Sūtra), translated during the Later Han with the translator lost; included in the *Shíyí biānrù dānběn* (Supplementary Collection of Single-Volume Works) in one fascicle.

*Sīwéi yàoluè fǎ* (Essential Summary of Contemplation), translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa; included in the *Shíyí biānrù dānběn* (Supplementary Collection of Single-Volume Works) in one fascicle, sometimes titled *Sīwéi yàoluè fǎ jīng*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection), second translation;
one of the two translations is missing. *Lishiyoujing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings), one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Kālodaka from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;
included in the *Shiyi*, second translation; two of the three translations are missing. *Jiu zapiyujing* (Old Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables), two fascicles; also called *Zapiyujing*.

The *Jijing* (Collected Sūtras), translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui of the Wu [Dynasty], was compiled as a supplementary collection and included as one fascicle of the *Danyben Zapiyu Jing* (Single-Volume Miscellaneous Parable Sūtra).
The *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) compiled by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han [Dynasty] consists of thirteen fascicles in its single-volume edition;
these are bound together in the same volume.

*Zapiyujing* (Miscellaneous Parables Sutra), two fascicles; also known as *Pusa durenjing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva Saving Humans). Translator lost; included in the Later Han record as a single-fascicle work from the *Shiyi*. Compiled into the *Zapiyujing*, two fascicles, by the Bhikṣu Daoli. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* as a single-fascicle work. *Ashewang piyujing* (Parables of King Aśoka), one fascicle; translator lost; now appended to the Eastern Jin record as a single-fascicle work from the *Shiyi*. Compiled into the *Ayuwang jing*, ten fascicles—or with the character "Da" (Great) added—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* as the second translation. The above four collections comprise fifteen fascicles and are contained in the same volume.

The *Aśokarāja-avadāna* in seven fascicles, also known as the *Mahā-aśokarāja-sūtra*, or in five fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Fashen of Parthia during the Western Jin dynasty; this is the first translation. The above two translations are different versions of the same text.
More than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was only upon the appearance of King Aśoka in the world that this tradition first emerged.

It is an error for the *Da Zhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalog) to include it among the Mahāyāna sūtras; furthermore, the claim in the *Chángfáng lù* (Changfang Catalog) and other records that Saṃghavarman produced a five-fascicle version of the *Aśokarāja-avadāna* is also an error. Since the preceding scripture is itself the *Avadāna*, it is inappropriate to record it twice.

*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Aśoka’s Son Losing His Eyes*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Dharmavardhana Losing His Eyes*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmanandi of India during the Yao Qin period of the Fu Qin dynasty; included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). Second translation; one of two translations, the other being missing. *The Explanations of the Extracts from the Four Āgamas*, two fascicles. Compiled by the Arhat Vasubhadra; translated by the Kuchean Śramaṇa Kumārajīva, Buddhabhadra, and others of the Fu Qin dynasty; included in the *Shiyi*. The three aforementioned single-fascicle collections comprise ten fascicles in total and are contained in the same volume.

The *Dharmapada-sūtra* in two fascicles, also known as the *Dharmapada-saṃgraha*, was compiled by the Venerable Dharmatrāta and translated by the Indian śramaṇa Veṅkaṭananda and others during the Wu dynasty. This second translation lacks one portion found in the first. The *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 1, states: [text follows].
As stated in the *Dharmapada*,
the Blessed One, for the sake of sentient beings, has expounded various teachings in many different regions and localities.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta— translated here as Fajiu (Dharmatrāta)— among the various expositions following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
established the Chapter on Impermanence for those teachings concerning the meaning of impermanence,
and so on, up to establishing the Chapter on the Brahmins for those concerning the meaning of the brahmins.
Therefore, it is known that this sutra was composed by Dharmatrāta.
Its inclusion in the Zhou-era catalog of the Tripitaka, where it is listed among the Mahāyāna sūtras and within the collected commentaries,
is a grave error resulting from repeated misplacement.

The *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* in four fascicles—also known as the *Dharmapada-mūla-prakaraṇa-sūtra*, or in five or six fascicles—was translated by the Western Jin śramaṇas Śīladharma and Dharmodgata. This is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. Regarding the similarities and differences between this and the aforementioned *Dharmapada-sūtra*: [text follows].
The preceding sutra merely compiled the verses without including the prose;
this subsequent sutra, however, includes the origins of the verses, explaining that the World-Honored One spoke them only after certain causes and conditions had arisen.
Compared to the preceding verses, this [version] is abbreviated and incomplete.
Furthermore, the preceding and succeeding verses vary in their respective expansions and omissions.
It is an error for the *Zhou lu* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) to include this among the Mahāyāna sūtras.

*The Kāśyapa Saṃnipāta Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection). First translation; two other translations are missing.
*The Biographies of the Compilers of the Tripiṭaka and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka*, one fascicle; translator lost. Now appended to the catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
*The Single-Volume Remnant*, included in the *Shiyi*. *The Sūtra of the Three Wisdoms*, one fascicle; Sengyou’s catalogue states it was translated by An [Shigao].

The *Pañcadharmapratipatti-sūtra* (also known as the *Abhidharma-duḥkhajñāna-sūtra*, though some editions omit the word "pratipatti") in one fascicle was translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty; it was recovered from among the lost texts and appended to the single-fascicle collection of the *Abhidharma*. The *Āgama-mukhabhāṣita-dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda* [in one fascicle] was also recovered from among the lost texts and appended to the single-fascicle collection of the Āgamas. *Yuan jing* (Sutra on Conditions), one fascicle; also simply titled *Ahan koujie jing* (Oral Explanation of the Āgama) or *Duan shier yinyuan jing* (Sutra on Severing the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination);
translated by the Anxi upāsaka An Xuan and Yan Fotiao during the Later Han dynasty. *Danben xiaodaodi jing* (Single-Volume Sutra on the Lesser Path of Practice), one fascicle;

*Li fayuan jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Beneficial Vows), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Liyu jing* (Sūtra on Vows) with the addition of the word "gāthā. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Omissions) as a single-fascicle work. *Liupusa ming* (Names of the Six Bodhisattvas), one fascicle.

The *Fang zang lu* (Catalogue of the Dharma Treasury) states that the *Liupusa ming* should also be recited and maintained. Translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost. Included in the *Shiyi* as a single-fascicle work, number 105.
*Daśastotra* (Ten Praises of the Buddha), one fascicle; composed by the Venerable Mātṛceṭa; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang;
newly compiled and entered into the canon as a single-volume work. *Āryāvalokiteśvarastotra* (Praise of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara), one fascicle;

translated during the era of the Empress of the Great Tang by the Śramaṇa Shi Huizhi of Foshouji Monastery; excerpted from the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalog) as a single-volume work included in the *Shiyi bian* (Supplementary Compilation).
The *Shang shi'er ji* (Twelve Collections of the Superior) in sixteen fascicles constitutes one volume.
The *Wuming luocha ji* (Collection of the Rākṣasa of Ignorance), also known as the *Wuming luocha jing* (Sutra of the Rākṣasa of Ignorance), is either one or two fascicles;

its translator is lost, and it was included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a single work, now appended to the Qin Records. The *Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa Zhuan* (Biography of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa), one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin.
*The Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, appended as a supplementary single volume.
*The Biography of Bodhisattva Āryadeva*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, appended as a supplementary single volume. *The Dharma of Vasubandhu*... [text truncated]

*Śāstrasaṃpradāya-śāstra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. This was included in the *Shiyi* (Supplement) as the second translation;
one of the two translations is missing. *Dharmapada-gāthā-saṃgraha*, one fascicle; spoken by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna for King Caṇḍaka;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty. Recorded in the old catalog of the Tang dynasty as the first translation. *Upadeśa*.

*Fazhe yu wang yaoyi jing* (Sūtra of the Essential Verses for Exhorting Kings), one fascicle. Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of India during the Song dynasty.
Included as a supplement in the second translation. *Longshu pusa quanji wang song* (Verses of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna’s Exhortation to Kings), one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang. Newly included in the catalog as the third translation. The above three collections are identical.
The verses from the two previous translations have been combined into a single fascicle within the various *sūtra* collections; they are now divided into two scrolls.

There is one fascicle of the *Bimbiṣāra-turaja-udāyana-rāja-dharma-deśanā-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty. Furthermore, there is a separate edition of the *Bimbiṣāra-rāja-dharma-deśanā-sūtra*, one fascicle.
The wording is identical to this;
therefore, it is not presented twice.

*The Dharma of Inviting Piṇḍola*, one fascicle (alternatively titled *Sūtra*); translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huijian. This is the second translation; one of the two translations is missing. *A Brief Analysis of Karmic Retribution*, one fascicle; composed by Bodhisattva Mahavira (Dayong). Alternatively titled *Compendium*; translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of the Song dynasty. Included in the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Collection) as a single-fascicle work. *Sūtra on the Transformations of the Future Spoken by the Bhikṣu Gaṅgita*, one fascicle. A work of lost translation from Sengyou’s catalogue, now appended to the Song dynasty catalogue as a single-fascicle work included in the *Shiyi*. *Record of the Dharma Spoken by the Great Arhat Nandimitra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tang dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. Included in the *Neidian lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures) as a single-fascicle work. *Seventy Treatises* (*Saptatiśāstra*), three fascicles (also known as the *Saṃkhya-śāstra*); alternatively in two fascicles. Translated by the Chen dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. This is a single-fascicle treatise.
It was composed by the non-Buddhist sage Kapila.

It elucidates the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*), namely the *Sāṃkhya-sūtra*, which is what is referred to as the "Kapila-śāstra. In the two catalogs of the Inner Canon by Jingtai and Daoxuan, there is a three-fascicle *Suvarṇasaptati-śāstra* translated by Paramārtha, and additionally a three-fascicle *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*. To claim that both of these titles refer to the same work is an error.

*The Treatise on the Ten Categories of the Victorious School*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [Recorded in] the *Diagram of Translated Scriptures* as a single work. Commentary: This treatise was composed by the victor Candranandana (Huiyue). It elucidates the ten categories (*padārtha*), which were originally set forth by the owl-ṛṣi (Ulūka). Although there were only six categories in the original treatise, Candranandana added four more to complete the ten. Because it encompasses both the fundamental and derivative aspects of the system, it is titled *The Treatise on the Ten Categories of the Victorious School*. The scriptures state that this is the Vaiśeṣika treatise. Its numerical categories surpass those of two other treatises; it is not a teaching of the Buddha, but belongs to the various non-Buddhist schools. Among these, these two are considered superior. It was translated so that those of broad learning might thoroughly understand the doctrines of heterodox paths.
The first fifteen sets comprise seventeen fascicles in one volume.
These are compilations of works composed in this land (*Jambudvīpa*);
there are forty such compilations totaling three hundred and sixty-eight fascicles.

The *Shijia pu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni) in forty-two fascicles consists of ten volumes; there is also a separate five-volume edition that differs from this one in its breadth and brevity. Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Sengyou of Jianchu Monastery during the Qi dynasty, it was originally recorded in the *Changfang lu* and has been newly included in the Canon. The *Shijia shi lüe pu* (Brief Genealogy of the Śākya Clan) in one volume—sometimes without the character "lue" (brief)—was compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang; it was originally recorded in the *Neidian lu* and has been newly included in the Canon. The *Shijia fangzhi* (Topography of Śākyamuni) in two volumes was compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang; it was originally recorded in the *Neidian lu* and has been newly included in the Canon. These three collections comprise thirteen volumes in two fascicles: the first fascicle contains seven [volumes] and the second fascicle contains six.

*Jīnglù yìxiàng* (Diverse Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya), fifty fascicles in five bundles: ordered by imperial decree in the fifteenth year of the Tiānjiān era of the Liáng dynasty for the śramaṇas Bǎochàng and others to compile and produce;
recorded in the Chángfáng Catalogue and newly included in the Canon. *Dúluóní zájí* (Miscellaneous Collection of Dhāraṇīs), ten fascicles in one bundle:
the author is unknown; currently appended to the Liáng Catalogue. The aforementioned collection of incantations is classified in the Dàzhōu Catalogue as a single Mahāyāna text.
Furthermore, to claim that the translator is lost is incorrect; upon examining the text, it is evident that this is a local compilation rather than a separate translation from a Sanskrit original.

This is known because texts such as the *Saptabuddha-mantra-sūtra* and the *Dhāraṇī-pātra-sūtra* were all translated during the entry [of scriptures] into the court, and the *Ārakṣa-kumāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* was translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei.
Furthermore, the *Dharanipata Sutra* and the *Sutra of the Most Victorious Lamp King* translated [herein] are of the same original text.
Since such sutras as these have all been collected and included, they are certainly not transmitted from Indic originals; they must be compilations produced here in this land.
It is unknown who compiled them, and thus this account is provided.

The *Zhujing yaoji* (Essential Compendium of Various Scriptures), twenty fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xuanyun of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty; newly edited for inclusion in the Canon, Volume One, Part A. The aforementioned two collections comprise twenty-two fascicles in total: ten fascicles in the first (upper) volume-set and twelve fascicles in the second (lower) volume-set.

The *Neidian Lu Xinbian Ruzang Zhongjing Mulü* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of the Inner Scriptures Included in the Canon) in five scrolls was compiled by imperial decree in the second year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty for the sake of śramaṇas and scholars engaged in translation; these two collections comprise twenty scrolls in two fascicles.

The *Dàtáng nèidiǎn lù* (Record of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang), ten fascicles, one bundle, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery of the Great Tang; newly compiled and included in the canon. The above four collections comprise twenty-one fascicles in two bundles: the first bundle contains eleven fascicles, and the second bundle contains ten fascicles.

The *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* (Kaiyuan Era Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings), twenty fascicles in two volumes, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the Western Regions of the Great Tang; the *Xinbian Ruzang Yiqiejing Yinyi* (Newly Compiled Pronunciation and Meaning of All Scriptures Included in the Canon), twenty-five fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xuanying, a translator of scriptures in the Great Tang; and the *Xinbian Ruzang Chunei Dianlu Xinyi Huayan Yinyi* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of Works Included in the Canon from Within and Without, with Newly Explained Pronunciations and Meanings of the Avataṃsaka), two fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Jingfa Monastery in the Great Tang—all newly compiled for inclusion in the canon. The *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* in twelve fascicles, compiled by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang; newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon from the *Neidian lu*. The *Collection of Ancient and Modern Debates on Buddhism and Daoism* in four fascicles (or three), compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxian of Ximing Monastery of the Great Tang; newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon from the *Neidian lu*. The *Continued Collection of Ancient and Modern Debates on Buddhism and Daoism* in one fascicle, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery of the Great Tang; newly compiled for inclusion in the Canon. *The Record of the Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem in the Eastern Lands*, three fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang; newly compiled from the *Neidian lu* (Inner Canon Catalog) and included in the canon. *The Treatise on the Śramaṇa’s Non-prostration to the Laity*, six fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Yanzong of Hongfu Monastery during the Great Tang; newly compiled from the *Neidian lu* and included in the canon. The *Biography of the Tripitaka Master of Ci’en Monastery of the Great Tang*, ten fascicles, one volume; compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huili and others of the West Taiyuan Monastery of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon. The *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Xu gaoseng zhuan), thirty fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty; extracted from the *Neidian lu* and newly entered into the Canon. Upper Collection, thirty fascicles, divided into four bundles: the first and second each contain eight fascicles, while the third and fourth each contain seven.

*Biànzhènglùn* (Discourse on Distinguishing Orthodoxy), eight fascicles, one set; compiled by the Śramaṇa of Longtian Monastery in the Great Tang, included in the *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures) and newly entered into the canon. *Bòxiélùn* (Discourse on Refuting Heresy), two fascicles or one fascicle; compiled by the Śramaṇa of Longtian Monastery in the Great Tang, included in the *Neidian lu* and newly entered into the canon. *Zhēnzhènglùn* (Discourse on Examining Orthodoxy), three fascicles; compiled during the era of Empress Wu by the Śramaṇa Xuán Yí of Foshouji Monastery, newly entered into the canon. *Shīménbiànhuòlùn* (Discourse on Distinguishing Delusions in Ten Gates), two fascicles or three fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇa Fùlǐ of Dàxīngshàn Monastery in the Great Tang, newly entered into the canon. *Hóngmíngjí* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]), fourteen fascicles; compiled by the Śramaṇa Sēngyòu of Jiānchū Monastery during the Liáng dynasty, included in the *Chángfáng lu* (Record of Chángfáng) and newly entered into the canon. The first collection consists of thirty fascicles, divided into four bundles: the first bundle contains ten fascicles; the second bundle contains seven; the third bundle contains seven; and the fourth bundle contains six.

The above six collections, totaling thirteen fascicles, are contained in the same volume.
From the *Śākyaputra-vaṃśa* downwards,
there are forty works totaling three hundred and sixty-eight fascicles;
all were compiled by virtuous scholars of this land.
Nevertheless, it truly serves as a fundamental guide for assisting and glorifying the Great Dharma and for maintaining it during the final age; therefore,
I have compiled this record and prepared it for wide circulation.
If one were to transcribe the canon according to personal preference and inclusion or exclusion,
then although other biographies may pertain to the Buddhist tradition,
they are not recorded here unless they belong to a protector of the Dharma.
In total, counting all the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of the Hīnayāna, as well as the collected biographies of worthies and sages currently in circulation,
there are four hundred and thirty-eight works comprising two thousand three hundred and three fascicles.

Five scrolls of the *Han Faben Neizhuan* (Inner Biography of the Dharma’s Origin in the Han), author unknown; three scrolls of the *Shamen Falin Zhuan* (Biography of the Śramaṇa Falin), compiled by the Śramaṇa Yancong. These two works were prohibited by imperial decree and not permitted to circulate; therefore, they are not included here.
*Catalogue of the Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era*, Scroll 14, Supplemental Record IV, Part 1.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu Year.
Section Two: Records of Translations for Which No Original Exists, Part One. Supplemental Records: Section Two, Part One, Records of Translations for Which No Original Exists.
Regarding those cases where there is a translation but no original text:
this refers to the scriptural texts of the Tripiṭaka teachings and the collected works of sages and worthies,
which belong to the category of those for whom the titles survive but the originals are missing.
Since the holy teachings first moved eastward, nearly a millennium has passed;
their substance and form have undergone frequent changes, and the transmission of the bells and tripods has shifted many times.
Furthermore, with the passing of Zhou Wuding, the ranks of the monastic community were decimated.
Consequently, the treasury of the Dharma-lamp has lost its brilliance and the sun of wisdom has hidden its light;
essential texts of the Tripiṭaka have for the most part become scattered and incomplete,
perhaps because recent translations from the Eastern Capital had not yet reached the Western Capital.
Some were newly produced and extremely rare;
though sought after, they could not be found, and their profound subtleties remained unheard of.
To have read through their titles in vain was a labor that left one with nothing but longed-for frustration; even to beat one’s breast in regret, it would be too late.
Now, having searched through various catalogs to record all that has been lost or omitted, I hope that renowned worthies will join me in investigating and seeking them out.

Including those from the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, as well as the collected works of holy sages, there are a total of one thousand one hundred and forty-eight titles comprising one thousand nine hundred and eighty fascicles for which original copies are missing.
Four hundred and eight sections of Mahāyāna sūtras,
totaling eight hundred and one fascicles, are missing; as are the missing sections of Mahāyāna vinaya.
Twenty-two treatises in twenty-five fascicles of Mahāyāna śāstras,
of which twenty works are missing.
Six hundred and five works totaling eight hundred and fifteen fascicles of the Small Vehicle Sūtras in forty-eight volumes are missing;
six hundred and five works totaling eight hundred and fifteen fascicles of the Small Vehicle Vinaya are missing.
Thirty-seven works in forty-two fascicles of Hinayana treatises;
nine works missing.
Sixty-five fascicles of the *Collection of Biographies of Worthies and Sages* (missing texts);
forty-seven works totaling one hundred eighty-four fascicles of Mahāyāna sūtras (missing texts); and two hundred works of Mahāyāna sūtras that are retranslations (missing texts).

The *Wupin jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) in five fascicles, comprising four hundred and eighty-four [verses], is the same as the *Xiaopin banruo* (Shorter Prajñāpāramitā). There is a new translation of the *Daofxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā) in ten fascicles, also known as the *Xiaopin*, or in seven fascicles; according to Sengyou’s catalog, it is titled the *Gengchuxiaopin* (Re-translated Shorter [Prajñāpāramitā]), translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. Furthermore, according to the catalogs of Baochang and others:
Regarding the statement that among the translations by Zhu Fahu there is additionally a seven-fascicle *Shorter Perfection of Wisdom Sutra* (Xiaopin jing), this is not correct;
for Master Hu already possessed the new translation of the *Practice of the Way Sutra* (Daofxing jing).
It is not appropriate to produce the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya* (Small Version) separately.
Furthermore, the commentary on the *Daoxing banruo jing* is also called the *Xiaopin*.
Moreover, in the catalog of Yixiansi Temple, there is a four-fascicle version titled the *Dazhidu wuji jing*.
It is also said to have been produced by Master Hu.
Since it shares the same root text as the *Daoxing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā), it would not be appropriate to translate it separately.

As both versions are redundant, they have not been preserved. The *Dazhidu jing* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) in four fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty, is the fifth translation. The three aforementioned scriptures share the same root text as the fourth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
There have been eight translations in total;
five versions are extant in the canon, while three are missing.

Regarding the number of scriptures translated by Kumārajīva recorded in the catalogs of Sengzao and others, there is mention of a *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (Fàngguāng bōrě) in twenty fascicles. This is not correct; since Master Kumārajīva had already translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Dàpǐn), it would be inappropriate for him to have produced a duplicate *Fàngguāng*. Any such record must be an error.

*The Sutra of the Supreme Pure Alms-Begging of the Bodhisattva Sumati*, in two fascicles; also known as *The Sutra on the Samādhi of Resolving that All Dharmas are Like Illusions*, or in one fascicle. Translated by the Śramaṇa Yan Fotiao of Linhuai during the Later Han dynasty. First translation. The above sutra is the same text as the eighth assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
There have been three translations in total;
two versions are extant in the canon,
while one is missing.

The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle (or two fascicles), thirty-one sheets; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin—this is the first translation. The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Liang dynasty—this is the third translation. Thus, there are three translations in total, both preceding and following.
One manuscript is preserved in the Imperial Library;
two manuscripts are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom* (Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra), one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly compiled and entered into the canon as the third translation. This is identical in content to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtra* and other similar texts.
There are three translations,
of which two versions are extant in the canon and one is missing.

The *Dàoxíng jīng* (Sūtra of the Practice of the Way), one fascicle. Master An stated that this is an excerpt from the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* compiled by a person of high wisdom from the Western Regions; An composed a preface for it. It was translated by the Indian śramaṇa Zhu Foshuo during the Later Han dynasty. Although this single sūtra is titled "Dàoxíng," its volume and length are quite small.
It should not be considered identical to the *Pūrvamārgacaryā* as having the same origin;
rather, it shall be recorded separately.

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle (sometimes without the word "Mahā"), translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi lay practitioner Zhi Qian. *Mahāprajñā-anuparivarta-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan. These ten works, comprising twenty-seven fascicles, were newly included in the catalog from below the *Wu-pin jing*; they are missing from the Prajñā section.

*The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han—First Translation. *The Sūtra of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment*, two fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bo Yan of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei—Fifth Translation.

Furthermore, in the records of Sengchang and others among the translations by Bo Yan, there is additionally one fascicle of the *Pingdengjue jing* (Sūtra of the Equal Enlightenment), which is identical to the aforementioned sūtra. There is no redundant duplication.

There is also a two-fascicle version of the *Wuliangshou jing* (Sūtra of Immeasurable Life), also titled the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Pure Equal Enlightenment), translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
This is the sixth translation, titled the *Wuliangshou zhizhen dengzhengjue jing* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Life, the Tathāgata, the Truly and Perfectly Enlightened One).
One fascicle. Also titled *The Scripture on the Joy of the Buddha-land* or *The Scripture on the Land of Ultimate Bliss*.

Translated by the foreign śramaṇa Dharmayaśas of the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the seventh translation. *The New Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, two fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
also said to have been produced in the second year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty. This is the eighth translation.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Baoyun of Liangzhou during the Song dynasty;
the ninth translation, the *New Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty and recorded in the catalog of Zhenji Temple;
the tenth translation. These seven scriptures above are the same text as the "Infinite Life Assembly" (Akṣobhyavyūha), the fifth assembly of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
This sutra has undergone eleven translations in total;
four versions are extant in the canon while seven are missing.

*The Sutra on the Chapter on the Training of Bodhisattvas in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya*, three fascicles, translated by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Zhidao Gen (Third Translation). [Note: This sutra is the same text as the sixth assembly, the *Acalatathāgata-parivarta*.
There were three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Non-differentiation of the Essential Nature of the Dharmadhātu*, two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; recorded as the first translation in Fǎshàng’s catalogue. This aforementioned sūtra is identical in its original text to the eighth [fascicle], the "Dharmadhātu-essence Assembly."
There are two translations, one of which is extant and the other missing.

*The Scripture on the Universal Gate*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; this is the second translation. The above scripture is the same text as the tenth chapter, the "Assembly of Mañjuśrī’s Universal Gate."
There have been three translations, two of which remain and one of which is missing.

*The Sutra on Adorning and Purifying the Buddha-land*, two fascicles; also called *The Sutra on the Pure Land*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazhu of Henei during the Western Jin dynasty. This second translation is the same text as the fifteenth chapter, the "Mañjuśrī-vyākaraṇa-parivarta."
There are three translations in total, two of which survive and one is missing.
*Bodhisattvapitaka-sūtra*, three fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty; this is the first translation. (The above is one scripture.)
This is identical in substance to the seventeenth assembly, that of Pūrṇa;
there are two translations, one preceding and one following, of which one remains extant and the other is missing.
The *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* (Fa jing jing), in two fascicles or one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty; this is the second translation.
Furthermore, according to the catalogues of Seng Chang and others, there is additionally the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Yuqia zhangzhe jing) in two fascicles, also translated by Zhi Qian.
This is the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra*. It is not a redundant repetition [of the following].

*Yugaprajñāparipṛcchā-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henei during the Western Jin dynasty; the fifth translation. *Yugavaiśya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty; the sixth translation. The three sūtras above are the same text as the nineteenth assembly, the *Yugavaiśya-parivarta*.
There have been six translations in total;
three remain extant and three are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Questions of the Maiden Prajñā* (one fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the era of Empress Wu of the Great Tang, newly included in the canon as the third translation. This aforementioned sūtra is identical in text to the thirtieth chapter, "The Assembly of the Maiden Prajñā."
There are four translations in total; three are extant and one is missing. 1.

*Ajātaśatru-rājadhītṛ-āśudharmabodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty (First Translation). 2. *Āśudharma-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty (Third Translation). 3. *Āśudharma-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Song dynasty (Fourth Translation). The above three sūtras are the same text as the thirty-second assembly, the "Assembly of the Bodhisattva Abhayamati."
There have been five translations in total;

two remain extant while three are missing. Furthermore, according to the catalogs of Sengzao and others, Zhu Fahu additionally translated one fascicle of the *Aśokadattā-avadāna* (The Sutra of the Gift of Aśoka by the Daughter of King Ajātaśatru).
This is merely a difference between the Sanskrit and Chinese pronunciations;
they should not be treated as two separate names. "Aśoka" is the Sanskrit term, while "Wuyushi" (Giver of No Sorrow) is the Chinese translation.
The fact that these two sūtras are recorded together is an error of the cataloguers. *Yàohuàn sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Illusion-like Samādhi), two fascicles, or one fascicle;

translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master Ān Shìgāo of the Later Han—First Translation. *Yàohuàn sānmèi jīng*, two fascicles; translated by the Xiyù Tripiṭaka Master Jītāmì of the Eastern Jin—Third Translation. *Yòuyào sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Illusion-like Samādhi), two fascicles; translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhīshīlún of the Former Liáng—Fourth Translation, following the *Shòuléngyán hòujì*. *Shèng shànzhùyì tiānzǐ suowèn jīng* (Sūtra on the Questions of the Noble Son of Heaven, the Well-Abiding Mind), four fascicles; newly compiled and translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty—Sixth Translation. The above four sūtras are the same text as the thirty-sixth assembly, the *Shànzhùyì tiānzǐ huì*.

There are five translations in total;
