*The Sūtra on Maitreya’s Inquiry into His Original Vows*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the second translation. The aforementioned sūtra is identical in text to the forty-second assembly, "The Assembly on Maitreya’s Inquiry."
There were three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing.

The *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra* in two fascicles, also titled *Jinglü jīng* (Sūtra on Pure Discipline), was translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui of the Wu dynasty. This separate version is the first translation; the aforementioned single sūtra is the same text as the forty-seventh assembly, the *Ratna-śikhara-bodhisattva-parivarta*.
This is the "Ratnaśikhara-parivarta" from the Mahāsannipāta-sūtra;
apart from its original text, there are two translations—
one extant and one missing.

*Śrīmālā-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahopāya-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty. First translation. The above sutra is the same text as the "Assembly of Lady Śrīmālā," the forty-eighth [assembly].
There have been three translations in total;
two remain extant while one is missing.

*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, three fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jayayasa during the Northern Zhou dynasty. Regarding this single scripture, although it is called *Ratnakūṭa*, as there is no original text available for collation, [its authenticity remains uncertain].
It is unknown with which [text] it shares the same origin;
for now, it is recorded here at the end.
From the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* downwards, there are thirty works totaling fifty-four fascicles.
The *Ratnakūṭa* section contains missing texts.

The *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, twenty-seven fascicles, translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han—this is the first translation; alternatively, there is a version in thirty fascicles with some new characters, or in twenty-four fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin—this is the second translation. These two sūtras are the same text.
There are three translations in total;
one version is extant in the canon while two are missing.

*Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty. This is the third translation. Thus, this single sūtra has four translations in total across its various editions.
Three versions exist and one is missing.

The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* consists of two fascicles—sometimes titled with the character "Da" (Great)—or one fascicle; it was translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Foshuo of India during the Later Han Dynasty. This second translation, the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* in one fascicle, is a re-translation of the final ten chapters.

Yǒu has one fascicle; there is no version in three fascicles. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi during the Later Han Dynasty, it is recorded as the third translation in the *Jìngtài lù*. The *Bānzhóu sānmèi niànfó zhāng jīng* (One Fascicle) is a separate translation of the "Chapter on Practice" (*Xíngpǐn*). The fourth translation is the *Bānzhóu sānmèi jīng* in two fascicles, which the Master Ān’s catalog states was translated again by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty. The above four scriptures are of the same original text.
There have been seven translations in total, of which three remain and four are missing; four are complete versions and three are abridgments. 1.

*A-ch’a-mo p’u-sa ching* (Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra), four fascicles, translated by the Indian śramaṇa Vighnanandin during the Wu dynasty. 2. *A-ch’a-mo p’u-sa ching*, four fascicles, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. 3. *Wu-jin-i ching* (Akṣayamati-sūtra), ten fascicles, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fashun during the Song dynasty. The above three sūtras share the same original text. The fifth translation [is listed here as part of the sequence]. (Note: The numbering in the source text appears to skip from the third to the fifth translation; the first two are the earliest versions, followed by the Song translation as the fifth in the sequence of extant works.)
There have been five translations in total;

two are extant in the canon while three are missing. Furthermore, in the catalogs of the *Chángfáng* and others, among the works translated by Dharmarakṣa, there is additionally a four-fascicle *Akṣayamati-sūtra*.
According to his catalog, Dharmarakṣa had already translated the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*;
it was therefore inappropriate for him to translate the *Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā* again.
The title of this *Akṣayamati-sūtra* states:
"In the Jin [dynasty], it was called 'Wujinyi' (Inexhaustible Intention).
A footnote in the catalog records:
Alternatively, it consists of four fascicles;
these are merely differences in the Sanskrit and Chinese titles.
In reality, this is a single sūtra for which two versions are preserved in the catalogs.
This is a grave error.
The *Smaller Akṣayamati Sūtra* in two fascicles was translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty.
Since this single sūtra is designated with the prefix "Small" (Xiǎo), it should not be the same text as the aforementioned sūtras.

The *Vaipulya Sūtra of the Lord Ākāśagarbha* in eight fascicles—also known as the *Questions of Ākāśagarbha*—or in five fascicles, translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Shi Shengjian. This aforementioned sūtra is an alternative translation of the "Ākāśagarbha-parivarta" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
Even if it exists within the Tibetan canon, it is a separate production;
the *Ākāśagarbha-parivarta* was not translated by Dharmakṣema.
It is either not a different translation, or it is indeed this very sūtra translated by Dharmakṣema.
The *Asādhya-niścaya-nirgata-samādhi-devaputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, five fascicles;

translated during the Northern Zhou dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñāyaśas, a Dhyāna Master. This work is currently suspected to be identical to the *Susthitamati-sūtra*. From the *Mahāsannipāta* section below, thirteen works totaling ninety-seven fascicles are missing from the Mahāsannipāta collection.

*The Sūtra on Entering the Tathāgata’s Inconceivable Wisdom*, three fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Chan Master Jñāyaśas of the Northern Zhou dynasty. [Recorded in] the second volume of the *Catalogue of Translated Scriptures*. The above sūtra has four translations in total.
Three versions survive while one is missing.

*The Scripture on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva* (1 fascicle), also titled *The Great Vaipulya Scripture* or simply *The Ten Stages Scripture*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin—this is the first translation; *The Great Vaipulya Bodhisattva Ten Stages Scripture* (1 fascicle), translated by the lay believer Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin—this is the second translation; *The Ten Stages Scripture* (1 fascicle), translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin—this is the third translation. These three scriptures share the same original text.
There have been five translations in total; two remain extant while three are missing. *The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Non-arising and Non-ceasing*, one fascicle.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of the Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon as a single-text edition. *The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the reign of the Empress Wu of the Great Tang; newly included in the canon as a single-text edition. *The Buddhapiṭaka Vaipulya Sūtra*, also titled *The Sūtra of the Inquiry of Vimalaprabhā*. Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Daoyan. Regarding this last sūtra, the catalogue of the śramaṇa Fajing of the Sui dynasty states: [text follows].
This is an alternative translation of the "Chapter on the Difficulty of Attaining" (*Duranuprāpaṇa-parivarta*) from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
This chapter is currently missing; it was in the sixth fascicle of the old translation and is in the thirteenth fascicle of the new translation.

The *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-sūtra* in one fascicle is also the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, though it is simply titled the *Mūla-karma-sūtra*. It was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the third translation, and together with the preceding and following versions, there are five translations in total for these chapters.

Four copies are in the canon and one copy is missing. Since the old *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was translated by Buddhabhadra, it would not be appropriate for this separate version of the *Karma-sūtra* to appear [as part of it].
Because the *Da Zhou Catalogue* lists it as being included in the canon, yet its text has not been seen.
Furthermore, this is what is being stated here.
Moreover, it is an error in the *Chángfáng lù* (Catalogue of Dharma Master Chángfáng) to claim that Zhīqiān retranslated the *Jìngxíng pǐn jīng* (Sūtra on the Chapter on Pure Conduct).
The footnote for the *Jìngxíng jīng* states:
First, the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-sūtra*.

Second, the two-fascicle *Bodhisattva-daśadharmasthiti-sūtra*, which is the "Ten Abodes" chapter translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin; this is the third translation. The above includes five translations in total, comprising both the main text and its preceding and succeeding versions.

Four original copies are held in the canon while one is missing; according to the catalogs of Changfang and others, there is additionally one fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*, said to have been translated by Buddhabhadra during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Examining this closely, since Sengxuan had already translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the "Great Text"),
it would not have been appropriate to produce this scripture separately;
thus, Daofang’s catalogue is erroneous.

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* in twelve fascicles; this is the "Ten Stages" chapter translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin dynasty, representing the second translation. The above includes five translations in total, both preceding and following this particular version.
Four original copies were in the imperial collection, while one copy was missing.

The *Luo-mo-jia jing* (Rāmāyaṇa-sūtra) in three fascicles is a portion of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*) chapter, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Faxian of the Western Regions during the Cao Wei dynasty; this is the first translation. The *Luo-mo-jia jing* in one fascicle is also a portion of the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty; this is the fourth translation. The above includes five translations in total, both preceding and following the present version.
Three versions are extant in the canon while two are missing; from the *Tathāgata-jñāna-acintya-sūtra* onwards, twelve works totaling twenty-seven fascicles are missing from the Avataṃsaka section.

*The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of Brahmā*, two fascicles. The old catalogues record it as *Hu-ban*; it is now rendered as *Fan* (Sanskrit). Alternatively, it consists of one fascicle. Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Loka Chen during the Later Han. First translation. *The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, two fascicles. A condensed version of the preceding chapters by the foreign Tripiṭaka Master An Faxian of the Cao Wei. Second translation. *The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of Wu; the "Preface Chapter" and "Chapter of Lamentation" constitute two fascicles. Third translation. *The Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, twenty fascicles. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhimeng of Yongzhou during the Northern Liang at Liangzhou. Sixth translation. The above includes the original Great Version of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* along with the newly translated latter portion, totaling seven translations in all.
Three versions are extant in the canon while four are missing; furthermore, the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue) cites the record of Zhu Daozu, stating:
"In the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Eastern Jin, Buddhabhadra translated the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in one fascicle at Daochang Temple."
Some say it consists of ten fascicles;
this refers to the first ten fascicles of the Great Version, ending with the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly. I have now searched through various catalogs and biographies.
As for the *Dharmapada*, it was translated by Faxian.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was also translated at Daochang Temple in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era.
All the various scriptures produced by Faxian were translated jointly with Buddhabhadra.
The titles and annotations in various catalogs frequently overlap;
since the time and place are identical, they certainly were not produced twice.
I have now merged them into one and shall no longer maintain separate versions.
The four sections totaling twenty-six fascicles from the *Brahmaparinirvāṇa-sūtra* are missing from the *Nirvāṇa* division.

The eight-fascicle *Pu-yao jing* (Lalitavistara) translated during the Shu period has a lost translator; it appears to have been produced in the Shu region. It is listed as the first translation in the Wei and Wu catalogs. There are versions of eight, six, or five fascicles. The third translation was made by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Zhìyán together with Bǎoyún. These two aforementioned sūtras share the same source text as the *Vaipulya-vyūha-sūtra*.
There are four translations in total;
two are extant and two are missing.

*The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty—this is the first translation. Regarding the above sūtra, there are two translations in total, preceding and following.

One version exists and one is missing. *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Lotus* in six fascicles: one edition includes the character "zheng" (correct). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Qiangliangjie from the Western Regions during the Wu dynasty. According to the *Fanying tu* (Diagram of Translations), this is the first translation. *The Sūtra of the Saṃpuṇḍarīka* in six fascicles: translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin during the Taishi era; this is the second translation.
I have carefully consulted the records of Sengchangfang and others.
According to them, this *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) was translated by Dharmarakṣa in the seventh year of the Taikang era.
According to the *Nie Daozhen lu*, it further states that the *Sapumintuoli jing* (Saptabuddhaka-sūtra) in six fascicles was translated in the first year of the Taishi era.
This appears in the *Zhu Daozu lu*; as it is the same scripture, it is inconsistent for it to appear twice.
Since their names differ, it remains uncertain whether their original forms were preserved or lost;
the reason for this is not yet clear.
It may be that *sārvabhaumapadmāni* is the Sanskrit term.
*Zhengfahua* (The Lotus of the True Dharma) is the name used during the Jin dynasty;
both the Sanskrit and the Chinese names are preserved here.

This was an error on the part of the cataloguers. *Fangdeng Fahua Jing* (The Vaipulya Lotus Sutra), five fascicles, translated by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Zhidao Gen; this is the fourth translation. The three scriptures to the right share the same original text.
Including the six translations of the *Addenda* and *Preceding Texts*, three remain and three are missing.

*The Sūtra of the Buddha Summoning with the Three Vehicles*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty. This aforementioned sūtra is an alternative translation from within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This should be the *Upamā-parivarta* (The Chapter on Similes).

It is the first translation of the two-fascicle *Old Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, translated by the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao of Linhuai during the Later Han dynasty. There is also a three-fascicle *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* (different from the former), which Daoxuan states is distinct from the *Vimalakīrti*.

Some editions contain the character "si" (思) [in the title], or consist of two fascicles; translated by the Upāsaka Zhu Shulan of the Western Regions during the Western Jin dynasty, this is the third translation. There is also the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* in one fascicle, alternatively titled the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty; this is the fourth translation. According to Sengyou’s catalog, there is further a one-fascicle *Abridged Vimalakīrti-sūtra*.
It is also said to have been translated by Zhu Fahu.
A note below states that Sengyou’s opinion was that the earlier version of the *Vimalakīrti* was redundant, and that Fahu had deleted the missing verses from it.
Since my current view does not differ from the former, I have not preserved this separately.
Furthermore, within the Zhou Catalogue, there is additionally a two-fascicle *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, which is also said to have been translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty.
It appears in the Changfang Catalogue; however, upon examining the Changfang Catalogue, the title of this sūtra is not found therein.

The record in the *Zhou* [catalogue] is erroneous. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* in four fascicles was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghapāla of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; this is the fifth translation. The above four sūtras share the same original text;
there have been seven translations in total, both earlier and later.
Three [versions] are preserved and four are missing.

As for the five fascicles compiled by the Western Jin śramaṇa Zhimin-du—combining one version by Zhi [Qian], two by Zhu [Fahu], and three others—it is not included because it was not a separate translation and its original manuscript is lost.

*Mahāvaipulya-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the second translation. Of the four translations of this single sūtra, three remain extant and one is missing.

*The Scripture on Dwelling in Seclusion*, ten fascicles; translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin—First Translation. *The Scripture on the Flower of Compassion*, ten fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Daogong of the Northern Liang—Third Translation. The above two scriptures are the same original text.
There have been four translations in total;
two survive and two are missing.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty—this is the third translation. In total, this single sūtra has undergone three translations across different periods.
Two versions exist and one is missing.

The *Mahāyāna-ratnamegha-sūtra* in eight fascicles was translated by the Śramaṇa Subhūti of Funan during the Chen dynasty; this is the second translation. The aforementioned scripture has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two versions exist and one is missing.

*Samādhi-saṃnipāta Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Śramaṇa Bo Fazu of Henei during the Western Jin dynasty. This is the second translation. The above sūtra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two versions exist and one is missing.

*Dhṛtarāṣṭra-bodhisattva-sūtra*, three fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the second translation. The above sutra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two [versions] are extant and one is missing.

The *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles—also titled *Xiànshì bǎozàng* (Manifestation of the Treasure Store)—or in three fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Fǎqīn of Āndù during the Western Jin dynasty; this is the second translation. The *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhīfǎdù of the Western Jin; this is the third translation. The above two sūtras share the same original text and comprise four translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Two versions exist and two are missing.

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty, is the first translation. The above sūtra has been translated four times in total, spanning both earlier and later periods.
Three versions are extant and one is missing.

*The Mahāvaipulya-nirnimitta-sūtra* in five fascicles—also titled *The Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-sūtra*, or simply *The Mahāmegha-sūtra*, or *The Great Cloud Sūtra*—in four fascicles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty. This is the first translation; the aforementioned sūtra has two translations, one preceding and one following.
One version exists and one is missing.

*The Scripture on the Non-Activity of All Dharmas*, one fascicle, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty; this is the second translation. The above scripture has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two [versions] exist and one is missing.

*Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Fǎqīn of Parthia during the Western Jin; this is the third translation. Furthermore, a second edition of the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, two fascicles, was retranslated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhú Fǎhù of the Western Jin; this is the fourth translation. The aforementioned [version] by Zhú Fǎhù was translated in the seventh year of the Tàikāng era of the Jin dynasty. It is the *Chāojīng* (Sūtra of Transcendence).
Subsequently, when the texts were retranslated, the original titles were further expanded; however, according to Seng'an's catalog,
there was only a further appearance of the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*,
while the *Samādhi-vikrāmiṇa* did not appear.
Regarding that [translation by] Zhi Chen,
because it was translated previously,
it is said that it was "further produced"; both versions are recorded in Sengyou’s catalogue.
*Ajātaśatru-sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; this is the fifth translation. The three sūtras mentioned above share the same original text.
Together with the *Pātra-praveśana-sūtra*, there are six translations in total.
Three [versions] are extant and three are missing. *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle;

excerpted from the seventh fascicle of the *Mahācandrapradīpa-sūtra*. Translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han. First separate translation. (The above includes both the large version and its preceding and following three translations.)
Two [versions] survive and one is missing.

*Xiangyi jing* (Elephant-Axle Sūtra), one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han; recorded as the first translation in Fashang’s catalogue. *Wusuoxiwang jing* (Sūtra on Having No Expectations), one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin; this is the third translation. These two sūtras share the same original text and comprise four translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Two versions are extant and two are missing.

One scroll of the *Jinguangshou jing* (Sūtra of the Golden Light-Head), translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Shilun of the Former Liang; this is the second translation following the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, newly compiled and included here. This single sūtra is the same text as the *Dajingfamen jing* (Sūtra of the Great Purity Dharma-Gate) and others, having undergone three translations in total.
Two [versions] exist and one is missing.

*The Gāthā of Amitābha Buddha*, one fascicle; translator lost, recorded in the Later Han catalog as the first translation. The above is the same text as the later *Amitābha Gāthā*; these are two translations, earlier and later.
One version exists and one is missing.

*The Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Kapiśī during the Song dynasty; listed as the second translation in Baochang’s record. The above sūtra has two translations, one preceding and one following.
One version contains [the title] while the other omits it.

*The Minor Sūtra on Amitāyus*, one fascicle; also known as the *Amitābha Sūtra* or without the character "Minor. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song dynasty; this is the third translation. The above is identical in substance to the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

There have been three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing. In the *Da Zhou Lu* (Catalogue of the Great Zhou Canon), there is a record of a *Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*; however, since its text is no different from that of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, it is considered a missing version.

*Maitreya-buddha-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Maitreya-āgami-janma-sūtra*. Seventeen sheets. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. First translation. Regarding the above sūtra, there are two translations, one extant and one missing.

*Maitreya-āgami-janma-sūtra*, one fascicle. Sengyou’s Catalogue states that it was lost among the translations attributed to Master Dao’an; it is now appended to the first translation in the Western Jin catalogue. *Maitreya-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-vastu-sūtra*, one fascicle. This title lacks the character "vastu" (事) in Sengyou’s Catalogue; it is a lost translation appearing in Baochang’s Catalogue. It is now appended to the second translation in the Eastern Jin catalogue. *Maitreya-avataraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty. This is the fifth translation. The above three sūtras share the same original text and comprise six translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Three translations are extant and three are missing.

*Dharmarājika-sūtra* (諸法勇王經), one fascicle; translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema during the Later Han dynasty. According to the *Fǎshàng lù*, this is the first translation. Thus, this single sūtra has undergone three translations over time.
Two texts exist while one is missing.

*The Expedient Means Sūtra of the Adornment of Joyful Necklaces* (Lè yīng luò zhuāng yán fāng biàn jīng), one fascicle; translated by the Wu-period Indian Tripiṭaka Master Kang Senghui—this is the first translation. Also known as *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Adornment of Necklaces* (Dàchéng yīng luò zhuāng yán jīng).

Also titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Transforming the Female Body*, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Fǎhǎi; this is the fourth translation. The two aforementioned sūtras are the same text with four translations in total, two of which survive and two of which are missing.
Among the catalogs such as those of Chángfáng, it is recorded that Zhú Fǎhù translated the *Sūtra on Skillful Means* (*Shùnquán fāngbiàn jīng*) in two fascicles.
Furthermore, he translated the *Suiquan nü jing* (Scripture on the Woman Who Follows Expedient Means) in two fascicles.
In the colophon of the *Shunquan fangbian jing* (Scripture on Accordance with Expedient Means),
it is further annotated that it is also titled the *Shunquan nü jing*.
Because the two meanings of "following expedient means" (suíquán) and "conforming to expedient means" (shùnquán) are similar,
Sengyou’s catalogue refers to it as the *Suíquán nǚ jīng* (Scripture on the Woman Following Expedient Means).
It is recorded in the separate catalogues but is not found among the works listed in Dao’an’s catalogue.
Therefore, it is known that this is indeed the *Shunquan jing* (Scripture on Following Expedient Means).
Most of the titles in the catalogs compiled by various schools were erroneous.
The *Suiquan nü jing* (Scripture on the Woman Following Expedient Means) has now been deleted and not established [as a canonical text].
*Śyāma-pūrvayoga-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Śyāma-sūtra*.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty during the third translation. The above includes four translations in total, combining both the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* and its individual versions.
Three translations are extant and one is missing.

*The Sūtra of the Jewel Casket* (Wuzi baobie jing), one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Northern Wei dynasty; this is the second translation. In total, there have been four translations of this sūtra, preceding and following one another.
Three [versions] remain and one is missing.
*Śilidali Yuejing* (一卷), one fascicle;

Sengyou’s Catalogue states that this was a translation of unknown provenance from An Gong’s catalogue and is now appended to the Western Jin section as the second translation. This single scripture is the same text as the *Yueguang Zhangzi Jing* and others.
There are four translations in total;
three survive and one is missing.

*The Scripture on the Vow of the Elder’s Son*, one fascicle, translated during the Cao Wei dynasty with the translator lost (second translation); *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Vow*, one fascicle, translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng (fifth translation). These two scriptures share the same original text and comprise five translations across different periods.
Three translations exist and two are missing.

*Vatsa-sūtra*, one fascicle—also called *Vatsaputra-sūtra*—translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin; this is the third translation. *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, one fascicle—alternatively titled *Kṣīraprabhā-sūtra*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin; this is the fourth translation. These two sūtras share the same original text and comprise four translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Two [versions] are extant and two are missing.

*The Scripture on the Adornment of the Woman*, one fascicle, translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty; first translation. *The Scripture on the Woman Heard from within the Womb*, one fascicle, recited and brought forth by the śramaṇa Shi Fahuā of the Xiao Qi dynasty; fifth translation. The above two scriptures are the same text, with five translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Three versions are extant and two are missing.

*The Scripture on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination at the City of Hearing* (1 fascicle), also known as *The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination at the City of Hearing*, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han—First Translation. *The Scripture on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination at the City of Hearing* (1 fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han—Second Translation. *The Scripture on the Twelve Links of Contemplating Dependent Origination under the Pei-tuo Tree* (1 fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin—Fourth Translation. *The Scripture on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* (1 fascicle), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavidi of India during the Southern Qi—Fifth Translation. The above four scriptures share the same original text and comprise six translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Two [versions] exist while four are missing;
their *Wencheng jing* is present within the canon, yet its text is identical to that of the *Baituosu xia jing*.
Furthermore, there is one fascicle of the *Shier yinyuan jing*.
Consequently, they extracted [the relevant passages] from the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*;
thus, these two sūtras were not transcribed into the canon,
and one must seek out separate versions elsewhere.
*Yiliao benshengsi jing* (Sūtra on the Differentiation of Fundamental Birth and Death), one fascicle.
According to Sengyou’s *Yuan*, this was a sūtra of unknown translator among the records of Master Dao’an;
it is now appended to the Western Jin records. Of the above, there are three translations of this single sūtra in total.
Two versions exist and one is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Sole Realization and Self-Vow Samādhi*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñātāmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. This is the third translation. The above sūtra has three translations in total, spanning earlier and later periods.
Two versions exist and one is missing.

*The Scripture of the Eight Auspicious Ones*, one fascicle, translated by the Song dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra; this is the third translation. The aforementioned scripture has five translations in total, including the preceding and following ones.
Four versions exist, with one missing.

*The Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India. This is the third translation recorded in the *Dazhou Catalogue*. To the right, this single sūtra exists in four total translations, comprising both new and old versions, as well as expanded and abbreviated recensions.
Three [versions] are extant and one is missing.

*Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Śrīmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; the first translation. *Māyūrī-vicitravidyārājñī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Śrīmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; the second translation. *Māyūrī-vidyārājñī-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmaruci of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty; the third translation. The above three sūtras share the same original text and comprise eight translations in total, including these preceding ones.
Five versions survive while three are missing; the first six are abbreviated, while the latter two are extensive.
As for Śrīmitra’s retranslation, the *Sampuṭa-mantra-sūtra* (Zashenzhou jing) should be a different recension.
Since I have not yet seen these scriptures, it is difficult to provide a definitive collation. 1. *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* (one scroll).

The old catalog states it was translated during the Wei or Wu periods, but the translator is lost. This is the second translation. 2. *Ānanda-mukha-sūtra* (one scroll). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Faqin of Parthia during the Western Jin dynasty. This is the third translation. 3. *Aparimita-māravidrāvaṇa-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (one scroll). Translated by the Śramaṇa Bai Fazang of Henei during the Western Jin dynasty. This is the fourth translation. The above three scriptures share the same original text; there are eleven translations in total, arranged chronologically.
Eight [versions] are extant and three are missing.

*The Mahā-spell*, one fascicle; *The Spell for Moving Mountains*, one fascicle; *The Spell for Subduing Demons*, one fascicle; *The Vīradeva-dhāraṇī*, one fascicle (the original text contains errors and corruptions regarding its title); and *The Spell of the Harmony-Knot*, one fascicle.

These fifty-two scriptures following the titles "Buddhas of the Ten Directions" were all newly collected in Sengyou’s Record from the Liang dynasty as translations of unknown origin; they are now appended to the Song Record.
Regarding the various scriptures translated from Indic originals whose translators have been lost,
although their titles appear among the catalogs, their texts have long since been lost and are no longer available for consultation. Furthermore,
it is truly difficult to definitively determine the distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Furthermore, even this rough classification involves considerable overlap;
I trust that learned scholars will examine and settle these matters.

Regarding the Mahāyāna Vinaya texts for which the originals are missing: twenty-two works in twenty-five fascicles. *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, two fascicles (or three), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Mengxiang from the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty. This is the first translation. Of the two translations—this one and the previous—one version exists in the canon while the other is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Original Action of the Bodhisattva’s Diadem* (Bodhisattvamaṇḍalāvadāna-mūlakarma-sūtra), one fascicle; translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan. Second translation: *The Sūtra on the Original Action of the Diadem*, two fascicles, also titled *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Diadem*; translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Daoyan. Third translation: [Title missing]. Of these three translations, one version remains in the canon while two are missing.

*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty. First translation. Of the three translations before and after this, two are extant and one is missing.

*Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin dynasty. Second translation. Of the four translations before and after this, three are extant and one is missing.

*The Scripture on the Method for the Bodhisattva’s Fast*, one fascicle; alternatively, without the word "scripture" (*jing*), it is also titled *The Scripture on the Method for the Fast of the Bodhisattva Worthy Head* (*Xianshou pusa zhai fa jing*), also titled *The Righteous Fast* (*Zhengzhai*), or *The Observance of the Fast* (*Chizhai*). Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. First translation: *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Righteous Fast*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Jñānagupta of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin. Third translation: The above is the same text as the *Scripture on the Bodhisattva Receiving the Fast*.
There are three translations in total;
one remains extant while two are missing.

The *Mañjuśrī-paścāttāpa-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *Mañjuśrī-pratideśanā-sūtra*—translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, is the second translation. The above constitutes the two preceding and succeeding translations.
One version exists while another is missing.

*The Sūtra on Śāriputra’s Repentance* (one fascicle), also simply titled *The Sūtra on Repentance*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin; this is the second translation. *The Sūtra on Śāriputra’s Repentance* (one fascicle), translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin; this appears in the catalog of Fashang as the third translation. Thus, there are three translations in total, both preceding and following.
One version exists and two are missing.

*Fǎlǜ sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Dharma-Regulations), one fascicle; translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. Recorded as the first translation by Fǎshàng. The above comprises the two translations, earlier and later.
One exists and one is missing. *Buddhānuśāsana-sūtra* (佛悔過經), one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *Pusa jie du shou tan wen* (單本菩薩戒獨受壇文), one fascicle;

translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin. *Pusa chanhui fa* (單本菩薩懺悔法), one fascicle; the Fang Catalogue states it is a different recension, translated by the lay devotee Nie Daozhen of the Western Jin. Single-fascicle version.

*The Text on the Precepts for Laymen and Laywomen Free from Desire*, one fascicle; also known as *The Text on the Twenty-two Precepts of Complete Practice*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

Single-text edition. *The Text on the Bodhisattva Precept Altar*, one fascicle; also known as *The Text on the Layman’s Precept Altar*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty.

Single-text edition. *The Twenty-two Precepts of Good Faith*, one fascicle; also known as *The Text on the Complete Practice of the Twenty-two Precepts for Laymen and Laywomen Free from Desire*, or alternatively titled *The Three Refuges*.

*Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kasmīra during the Song dynasty; one fascicle. (Noted as absent from Sengyou’s catalogue; Fang states it is a different recension.

*Sūtra on the Single-Volume Method for Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts*, translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost; one fascicle. *The Ten Methods for the Successive Stages of Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts*, translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost; one fascicle. *Bodhisattva Repentance Method*, translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost; one fascicle.

*The Bodhisattva Who Has First Aroused the Thought of Enlightenment Constantly Practices Five Matters During the Six Periods of Day and Night*, translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost; one fascicle. *Avaivartika-bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, translated during the Later Han dynasty, translator lost; one fascicle.

One fascicle; not in the old catalog; lacks the word "Bodhisattva"; translated during the Wei or Wu periods with the translator lost; a missing text of a Mahāyāna treatise; a missing text of a Mahāyāna treatise; twenty sections;

*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, one fascicle; the author is unknown; whether it is a single or multiple translation is not yet certain; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Ceylon during the Chen dynasty; *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-upadeśa*, five fascicles; the author is unknown; whether it is a single or multiple translation is not yet certain; translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog; the original manuscript has not yet been located; *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Ceylon during the Chen dynasty; second translation; the above two translations, earlier and later, [are listed].
One version exists and one is missing; the above four sections are commentaries on the sūtras.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in five fascicles was translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Liang dynasty; it is a re-translated version and shares the same original text as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Since the original text of this alternative translation is missing, it is unknown which of the *Seventeen Stages* (*Saptadaśabhūmi*) it corresponds to.

It is also unknown who the author of the one-fascicle *Mūlamadhyamaka-śāstra* was, whether it is a single work or part of a larger collection, and remains unverified. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India during the Liang Dynasty: *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*, four fascicles (or five fascicles). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty: [First Translation]. Regarding the above two translations, one exists while the other is missing; the *Catalogue of the Canon Compiled during the Great Zhou* lists it, yet despite my current search for the manuscript, I have not yet obtained it.

*Treatise on the Five Aggregates of the Mahāyāna*, one fascicle. Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu; translated during the Chen dynasty, lost [in the original], recorded in the *Chen Dynasty Catalogue of the Mahāyāna Temple*. First translation, newly appended to the Liang catalogue. The aforementioned Chen catalogue states:
In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Taizhian era of Emperor Chen, the śramaṇa Huibu arrived from the north.
He produced two translations,
one of which was preserved and the other lost.

*Upāyahṛdaya-śāstra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin dynasty; this is the first translation. Of the two preceding and succeeding translations, one remains extant while the other is missing.
*Trikāla-vibhaṅga-śāstra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Liang dynasty. *Pratividhāna-śāstra*, one fascicle;
it is currently suspected that this is the same as the *Tattva-saṃgraha-śāstra* found in the canon, hence its title there is *Tattva-saṃgraha-śāstra, Pratividhāna-pariccheda*;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty. *Nigraha-sthāna-śāstra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen dynasty.
*Triyānasiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle, translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.

*Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle, translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty. *Cetanā-karma-śāstra*, one fascicle, translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.
*Mahāśūnyatā-śāstra*, three [fascicles], translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.
Volume [X]: Translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty; a single volume combining the Five Treatises on Knowledge (*Pañcavidyā-sthāna-śāstra*):

1. Phonetics (*Śabda-vidyā*), 2. Medical Formulas (*Cikitsā-vidyā*), 3. Arts and Crafts (*Śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), 4. Incantations and Techniques (*Adhidaiva-vidyā*), 5. Seals and Talismans (*Mudrā-vidyā*).
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Ratnabhadra during the Northern Zhou dynasty. Single Volume: *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ten Stages), ten volumes, by Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva.
Compiled by Kumārajīva, translated during the Yao Qin dynasty; a single volume. The Right Changfang Record states:
"Master Kumārajīva had not yet finished translating this work during the Hongshi era.
The end of the scroll resembles the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samgraha*."

The *Jian'er Qin lu* (Record of the Two Qin Dynasties) and the *Chen chao dasheng si zang lu* (Catalogue of the Mahāyāna Monastery Collection of the Chen Dynasty) state that it has another name, the *Shizhu piposha* (Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā); it is now suspected that this is indeed the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* contained within the canon.

*Śrīprajñāṣaḍakṣarīsūtra-tryadhikāra-śāstra*, one fascicle; translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Great Tang by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci from South India; newly included in the catalog as a single-fascicle collection. *Pramāṇasamuccaya-śāstra*, four fascicles; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yi Jing of the Great Tang; newly included in the catalog as a single-fascicle work. Furthermore, the record of Fashang states:

Regarding the statement that "the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* in twenty fascicles was translated by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha in the second year of the Taiching era of the Liang dynasty," this must be an error;
it is most likely twelve fascicles.
This is an error of the scribes.
According to the records of Sengchangfang and others,
Paramārtha’s translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* dates to the Chen dynasty.
Since the Liang catalog no longer exists,
it is not preserved here.
In total, there are four hundred and fifty works comprising eight hundred and seventy-four fascicles of Mahāyāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras that are missing from their original texts.
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Volume 14, Supplemental Record IV;
*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, Volume 15, Supplemental Record V.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu year.
Section Two: Records of Translations for Which the Originals Are Missing.

Section Two: Records of Small Vehicle Sūtras with Missing Texts; Records of Small Vehicle Sūtras Re-translated with Missing Texts; Records of Small Vehicle Sūtras Re-translated with Missing Texts: one hundred and twenty-five works, totaling two hundred and sixty-five fascicles. *Madhyama Āgama* (Middle Length Discourses), fifty-nine fascicles. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmanandi during the Fu Qin dynasty. This is the first translation. Regarding this single sūtra, there were previously two translations; one version remains in the canon while the other is missing.

The *Ekottarika-āgama* (Zengyi Ahan Jing), fifty fascicles—Fang says forty fascicles, You says thirty-three fascicles, or sometimes twenty-four fascicles—translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmanandi during the Fu Qin dynasty; this is the first translation. The above scripture exists in two translations, earlier and later.
One copy exists in the collection, while one is missing. *The Sūtra of Kātyāyana* (Jiūmójīē jīng), one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra of Kātyāyana Resolving Difficulties* (Tóngjiāshè jiě nán jīng).

It is lost among the translations attributed to unknown translators in Sengyou’s catalogue (*Chū sānzàng jì jí*). The *Fǎjīng lù* states it is an alternative translation from the sixteenth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*. There is also a one-fascicle *Sūtra of Kātyāyana Resolving Difficulties*, also titled *The Sūtra of Kātyāyana*; Sengyou says it was translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Shengjian. Fajing notes that it shares the same source text as Kumārajīva’s *Kātyāyana Sūtra*, though Kumārajīva’s version lacks the *Kātyāyana* portion. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.
Extracted from the seventh fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
It shares the same original text as the *Bisuxu jing* (Sūtra on the Constellation Puṣya).
Both of these originals are missing.

*The Scripture on the Six Directions of Prostration*, one fascicle—also known as *The Scripture on Śukarāta’s Six Directions of Prostration*, or simply *The Scripture on the Six Directions of Prostration*—translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. The above is a combined edition of the *Sujāta-sūtra*, the eleventh chapter of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, which exists in three successive translations.
Two [texts] are extant and one is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Explanation for the Brahmin Āṣāḍha*, one fascicle, translated by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Śīla-vīrya (Shi Fayong). This includes the *Madhuvāsistha-sūtra*, the thirteenth sūtra of the *Dīrgha-āgama*.
There have been three translations of this work;
two remain while one is missing.

*The Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views*, one fascicle, also known as *The Brahmajāla Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty. This is combined with the *Brahmā-paripṛcchā Sūtra* from the fourteenth [chapter] of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
There have been three translations, two of which survive and one of which is missing.

The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) exists in six fascicles, five fascicles, or eight fascicles, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin; this is the first translation. The *Loutan jing* in eight fascicles was translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin; this is the third translation. The above also includes the *Jishi jing* (Sūtra on the Record of the World) from the fourth division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
There have been six translations in total, four of which survive and two of which are lost.

Regarding the *Daoyi faxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Will for the Path) in two fascicles, the Catalogue of Fang [Yong] states it was translated from the *Dīrgha Āgama*; alternatively, it may consist of one fascicle and was produced during the Later Han by an Anxi [Parthian] master.
*Mahādvādaśamukha-sūtra*, one fascicle (or two fascicles), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han;
annotated by Master Dao’an. The Fang Catalogue states it was excerpted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. *Alpadvādaśamukha-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han;
annotated by Master Dao’an. The Fang Catalogue states it was excerpted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. An [Shigao] of the Later Han, a Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia.

*Qīfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Seven Dharmas), one fascicle, translated by An Shigao. The old catalogs state it is the *Ābhidharma Qīfǎxíng jīng* (Abhidharma Sūtra on the Practice of the Seven Dharmas) or simply the *Qīfǎxíng jīng*.
Sengfang states it was extracted from the *Cháng hán jīng* (Dīrgha Āgama). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han.

*Dùzēngdào zhāng jīng* (Sūtra on the Increase of the Path), one fascicle. This title lacks the character "dào" (path) in the old catalogs. It is a variant translation of the *Shíbàofǎ* (Ten Dharmas of Retribution). Sengfang states: [it was extracted from the *Cháng hán jīng*]. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han.
*Yijue lü jing* (Sūtra on the Decisions of Meaning in the Vinaya), one fascicle; translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Anxi during the Later Han, from the *Chang ahan*.

Some editions omit the word "sūtra" (*jing*). It is also called the *Yijue lü fahang jing*. Sengyou’s catalogue states it was translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Anxi during the Later Han, and that it is excerpted from the *Chang ahan*.

*Mile jing* (Maitreya Sūtra), one fascicle; translated by An Shigao, Tripiṭaka Master of Anxi during the Later Han, from the *Chang ahan*. Master Dao’an stated it was excerpted from the *Chang ahan*. Sengyou’s catalogue records this.
The scriptures translated by Master Yun’an whose translators were lost are appended to the catalogue of the Western Jin;
they comprise fourteen works in twenty-eight fascicles, all of which belong to the *Dīrgha Āgama* and are incomplete editions.

*Catuḥsatya-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by the Tripitaka Master Kang Mengxiang of the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty. The above is also included within the seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* as the *Vibhaṅga-āryasatya-sūtra*.
There are four translations in total, including the preceding and following versions.

Two [texts] are extant and two are missing. *The Sūtra on the Māra King Entering Maudgalyāyana’s Belly*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on the Wicked Māra Testing Maudgalyāyana*. The old catalogues state it is the *Sūtra on the Māra King Entering Maudgalyāyana’s Belly*. Sengyou’s Catalogue states it is the *Ancient Classic Sūtra* of Master Dao’an. It is now appended to the Han Catalogue. This is combined with the *Sūtra on Subduing Māras* from the thirtieth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*.
There have been five translations in total;
three remain and two are missing.

*The Scripture of Rāṣṭrapāla*, one fascicle, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han dynasty. This is also included as the thirty-first scripture in the *Madhyama Āgama*. There have been four translations in total for the *Rāṣṭrapāla Sūtra*.

Two versions exist and two are missing. *The Scripture on the Householder Vikaṅkata’s Sixfold Prostration*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Scripture on the Householder Weihua*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jīvaka from the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Second translation: *The Scripture on the Householder Vikaṅkata’s Sixfold Prostration*, one fascicle. Translated by the lay practitioner Zhu Nanti from India during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Third translation: *The Scripture on the Son of Śreṣṭhin*, one fascicle; also known as the *Alternative Version of the Scripture on the Sixfold Prostration*. Translated by the Sramaṇa Shi Huijian of the Song dynasty. Fourth translation. The above is also included in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* as the *Śreṣṭhiputra-sūtra*.

There are six translations in total, two of which survive and four of which are missing. *The Sūtra on Falling into the Blue Pond*, one fascicle. Master Dao’an states it was translated from the *Madhyamāgama*;

Sengyou’s catalogue states it is a work of unknown translator by Master Dao’an, appended to the Western Jin records. *The Sūtra on the Seven Matters*, one fascicle. Master Dao’an states it was translated from the *Madhyamāgama*; Sengyou’s catalogue states it is a work of unknown translator by Master Dao’an, appended to the Western Jin records. *The Sūtra on Rāṣṭrapāla*, one fascicle. Master Dao’an states it was translated from the *Madhyamāgama*; Sengyou’s catalogue states it is a work of unknown translator by Master Dao’an, appended to the Western Jin records. (Note: This last sūtra is suspected to be the same text as the thirty-first [sūtra] in the *Madhyamāgama*, the *Rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra*.)

*Huanyu jing* (Sūtra on Joy), one fascicle. The *Fajing lu* states it is titled *Quanyu*; it is said to be from the twelfth volume of the *Zhongahan*. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it as a lost translation, attaching it to the Western Jin records. *Bufou wubai biqiu jing* (Sūtra of the Buddha with Five Hundred Bhikṣus), one fascicle. Master Dao’an stated it is from the *Zhongahan*. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it among his classical texts and attached it to the Han records. *Fanyou san shi yuchi buzuzu jing* (Sūtra on the Three Matters of Ordinary People: Folly and Insufficiency), one fascicle. Master Dao’an stated it is from the *Zhongahan*. Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an classified it among his classical texts and now attaches it to the Han records. The Buddha admonished the bhikṣus, saying: "With my divine eye, I observe the births, deaths, beauty, and ugliness of people in the world. Venerable ones..."

*Beizhe jing* (Sūtra on the Lowly), one fascicle. Master Dao’an stated it was translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*. Sengyou’s catalogue states: "Master Dao’an’s ancient manuscript of this sūtra is now appended to the Han catalogue. *Fǎpǔyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Universal Meaning of the Dharma), one fascicle; also called *Pǔyì jīng*. Translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. This is the second translation; the third translation is missing. The following fourteen works, totaling fourteen fascicles, are all incomplete versions belonging to the *Madhyama Āgama* section: 1. *Sìdì jīng* (Sūtra on the Four Truths) ... [and so forth for the remaining titles] ... [End of list] All are incomplete versions of the *Madhyama Āgama*.

*The Scripture on King Prasenajit’s Mourning for His Mother*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Scripture on King Prasenajit*. Sengyou calls it *The Scripture on King Poye-ni*. Translated by the Song layman Juqu Jingsheng. The above includes an additional version of the scripture, totaling four translations across its various recensions.
Two extant and two missing.
Found in Volume 18.

*The Sūtra on King Bimbisāra’s Questioning of the Buddha Regarding Offerings*, one fascicle; translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Northern Wei dynasty. The above includes one additional version of the same sūtra; there are thus four translations in total, two of which are extant and two of which are missing.
Extracted from the twenty-sixth fascicle.

*Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Aṅgulimālaka-sūtra*. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above includes one additional version of the same scripture, making five translations in total across its various recensions.
Three versions are extant and two are missing;
it appears in the thirty-first fascicle.

*The Scripture on Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Traveling Through Various Kingdoms*, one fascicle, also titled *Traveling Through the Four Crossroads*, translated by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa. The above includes one additional version of the scripture, comprising four translations in total across its various editions.
Two versions are extant and two are missing. This appears in the forty-first fascicle.

*The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s Mother*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī*. Translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng. The above includes an augmented version; in total, there have been five translations of this sūtra across its various editions.
Three texts are extant and two are missing.
These appear in the fiftieth fascicle.

The *Za jing* (Miscellaneous Sūtras) consists of forty-four sūtras in two fascicles; Master Dao’an states they were translated from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, though some say it is one fascicle. Translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. [Note: Some say this refers to the forty-four sūtras of the *Za jing*.
Since no specific title is indicated, it remains unclear from which fascicle this was extracted.

Regarding the *Bǎi-líng-shí-pǐn jīng* (Sūtra of One Hundred and Sixty Chapters) in one fascicle, the old catalogs state it is the *Zēngyī āhán bǎilíngzhāng jīng* (Sūtra of One Hundred and Sixty Chapters of the Ekottarika Āgama), translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han. Furthermore, the following seven works totaling eight fascicles—the *Bōsìníwáng sāngmǔ jīng* (Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Mourning for His Mother) and others—are all partial, incomplete versions of the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
*The Scripture on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*, one fascicle, ten sheets; translated by An Shigao, the Tripiṭaka Master of Parthia during the Later Han dynasty.
Regarding this scripture, all catalogs state that it was extracted from the *Saṃyuktāgama* and other collections.

During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the Indian śramaṇa Saṃghavarman arrived in Jiankang in the tenth year of the Yuánjiā era. At the Zhèngxiè Jīnglǜzàng Míngzáxīn Dàochǎng, Huìguān observed that Saṃghavarman possessed a profound understanding of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and could recite it with complete fluency. Although the previous Tripiṭaka masters had already translated it, [it was deemed necessary to produce a new version].
Before it could be transcribed,
he requested that it be translated again.
Baoyun conveyed the words, and Guan personally received them in writing.
One week passed before it was completed.
Thus, we know that those who practice through both insight and conduct constitute its fundamental essence.

"Excerpted scriptures" (zhīpài jīng) refers to those works extracted from within a major collection and circulated separately;
examples include the second assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others of this kind.
Now, the Dharma-gates are vast and expansive, their source and limit rarely fathomed;
the scriptural records are manifold and intricate, their boundaries never exhausted.
Therefore, there is transformation and guidance according to what is appropriate, and the bestowing of conditions in response to sentient beings.
Within the great compendiums, these are frequently used in abbreviated form according to the occasion;
those who search for them do not know their source,
and those who study them do not carry their meaning to completion.
Now, having synthesized various strands and brought them back to their respective categories,
I have further revised the old records by deleting, adding, or removing entries as necessary.
I have fully recorded the titles and provided detailed accounts of discrepancies and variations.
It is my hope that future scholars may examine these branches to know their source.
Fearing that this work may not yet be exhaustive, I look forward to the wisdom of those who come after.

The *Śikhaṇḍin-rāja-sūtra* establishes its title based on the initial circumstances, while the *Caraka-benmo jing* (Sutra on the Origin of Caraka) adopts its designation according to the subsequent text. Since they concern the same event, they cannot be divided into two; therefore, only one name is retained here.

These one hundred and thirty-two sūtras are all extracted from the *Saṃyuktāgama*, according to the two catalogs of the *Zhongjing lu* compiled during the Kaihuang and Renshou eras of the Sui dynasty.
Furthermore, there are eight sūtras,
namely: the Saptasthāna-triparīkṣā-sūtra and the Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-sūtra.
The Sūtra on Being Drifted by Water Foam;
the Sūtra on the Eight States of Horses;
the Sūtra on Correspondence and Compatibility.
The textual collation of these five sūtras reveals that they are alternative translations rather than separate productions.
Furthermore, there are several other sūtras,
such as the *Sūtra on the Eleven Marks of Mindfulness of the Tathāgata*.
The *Kāyagatāsati Sutta* (The Discourse on Mindfulness of the Body) and the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta* (The Discourse on Rebirth According to One's Intentions) are both found in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
This is an alternative translation.
The *Ekādaśākāra-sūtra* appears in the *Ekottarika-āgama*;
it is likewise an alternative translation.
Regarding the *Kāyavastu-sūtra*, I have examined it against the eight supreme sūtras and found it included in their cataloged records; therefore,
it has been excluded here.
The three sūtras concerning the dharmas associated with the precepts were included as separate texts in the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue);
they have now been verified and extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
As for the five sūtras concerning the young Brahmin, [they are likewise found therein].
Among the records of the Zhou dynasty, this work was missing from the collected texts;
now, having located its manuscript,
I have compared it and found it to be identical to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

Among these, the *Ekottarika-āgama* Sūtra on the Wealthy Householder and the *Sūtra on the Half Āmalaka Fruit* have already been recorded in the *Sui Zhongjing Lu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures of the Sui Dynasty) under the section of independent sūtras (*bie sheng jing*).

Section Four: A Record of the Elimination of Redundancies. One hundred and forty-seven works in four hundred and eight fascicles. Regarding the "Record of the Elimination of Redundancies": it refers to those works which, while possessing merit, are overly prolix and repetitive; thus, they have been abridged to remove the superfluous. Furthermore, there are those works that, though not without merit, are difficult to verify as authentic; these have likewise been omitted. This constitutes the fourth section of the *Separate Catalogue*. It comprises one hundred and forty-seven works totaling four hundred and eight fascicles. As for the "Record of the Elimination of Redundancies," it is intended to eliminate the excessive and the cumbersome.
