6. A Further Detailed Record of Doubts, Part Six. One hundred and fourteen sections, nineteen fascicles. Regarding the *Record of Doubts*:
it is a further detailed record of doubts.
Since the Brahma scriptures were first propagated in the East nearly seven hundred years ago,
the teachings have experienced periods of flourishing and decline, and their transmission has shifted from time to time;
the number of translated volumes, spanning earlier and later periods, approaches ten thousand.
Since the collection of fascicles is so vast, it is difficult to examine them all thoroughly.

Those who compiled the definitive records recorded what they heard as soon as they encountered it, yet they did not minutely investigate the fundamental tenets; thus, some principles may be subject to doubt.
Now, fearing that the genuine and the spurious may be intermingled and right and wrong may overlap,
I have therefore compiled this separate record to show to future generations.
It is my hope that men of profound insight and high talent will once again examine and finalize it with care.

*Vīra-samādhi Sūtra*, two fascicles; *Sūtra on the Determination of Sin and Merit*, one fascicle; *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Praṇidhāna-viśuddha-deśa-ṛddhi*, one fascicle—I personally examined its original manuscript and found it to be entirely not the word of the Buddha; *Sūtra on Saving and Protecting Life and Limb to Relieve People from the Calamities of Illness*, one fascicle—its textual style is similar to that of the *Sūtra on Saving from Disease*, and as one is authentic and the other is spurious, it remains doubtful whether it is truly the latter; *Sūtra on the Most Sublime and Victorious Samādhi*, one fascicle—its textual style is similar to that of the *Sūtra on the Most Sublime Initial Teaching*, and as one is authentic and the other is spurious, it likewise remains doubtful; *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi Sūtra*, one fascicle; *Sūtra on Pure Dharma Practice*, one fascicle; *Recorded Account of Confucius, Laozi, and Yan Hui Returning to Their Origins*, one fascicle, also titled *Sūtra on the Five Hundred Brahmins Asking about Existence and Non-existence*. This sūtra states: "The human body is produced from the five grains. The above eight works, totaling nine fascicles, beginning with the *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra*, [are listed here].
In ancient catalogs, these were all classified as spurious and false;
however, they were subsequently included among the authentic scriptures during the Great Revision (Dazhou jianding).
Upon examining them, it is found that the principles of their followers are largely inconsistent with the truth.
The meanings and phrases discussed in this treatise occasionally involve ordinary sentiments;
for now, these are appended to the section on Doubts and Difficulties for inclusion in the authentic record. Some say:
The fault of disparaging the holy teachings thus finds its locus.
The Buddha has given this sincere word; it is not a matter for reproach or challenge.
As the Sūtra says:
If one harbors doubts regarding what I have taught, they should not even accept it, let alone such works as these.
Following this principle, one must distinguish between the correct and the false. Furthermore, we await the collective deliberation of the virtuous to discern the true from the false.

As for the eight scriptures previously included in the spurious catalog, they are now classified as spurious; their sequence within this current spurious catalog is preserved without deletion. Among the scriptures deemed authentic by the Zhou catalog that were previously listed as spurious, there are several more whose original texts have not yet been seen; therefore, they are not discussed here.

*Fashè jīng* (Dharma Society Sūtra), two fascicles; the internal title reads *Yèbào lúnzhuǎn chángzhài yǐndǎo dìyù císhàn zhuāngyán fǎshè jīng* (Sūtra on the Dharma Society Adorned by Charity, Guiding the Rebirth in Hell and the Repayment of Debts through the Cycle of Karmic Retribution). This single sūtra is recorded in the *Dàzhōu lù* as having been translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhú Fáhù of the Western Jin dynasty.
I have carefully consulted the records of Sengchang and others;
among the translations by Dharmarakṣa, there is one fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-sūtra* (Fashè jīng), with a footnote at the end stating: [text omitted].
The *Shijiu* (Commentary on the Nine Classics) falsely suspects that this is likely the *Xiaofasheshijing* (Sutra of the Small Dharma Society) from the old spurious catalogues.
The original title of the preceding sutra further states:
"Translated from the Hu language by the Tripiṭaka Master Huanglu."
However, upon examining the intent and character of this text, it appears to involve human sentiments;
since its titles and annotations are inconsistent and difficult to standardize, I have provisionally included it in the *Yilü* (Record of Doubtful Texts) pending further detailed investigation.

Regarding the three-fascicle *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Passage), which was transcribed and compiled by Xiao Ziliang: there is a two-fascicle *Yiyi jing* (Sūtra of Beneficial Intent) among those recited by the nun Sengfani. It is suspected that this [Jingdu] sūtra is identical to that [Yiyi] sūtra. These two sections, totaling five fascicles, were included in the canon according to the *Dazhou lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue).
Upon examining the phrasing, it also appears to involve human sentiments;
the matter must be carefully scrutinized, and for now, I shall compile this as a record of doubtful points.

Among the scriptures recited by the bhikṣuṇī Saṃghanandā, there is one titled *Ullumbinī-sūtra* (One Scroll of the Ullumbinī Sūtra), which is suspected of being a forgery. This is the aforementioned single scripture.
The two catalogs of Changfang’s Buddhist scriptures state directly that it was presented by Mudaoxian in the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty,
without further elaborating on the details.
Since its original source is absent, it is difficult to determine whether it is authentic or spurious;
for now, it is appended to the Record of Doubtful Texts.
*Jingtu aluohanben jing* (The Sutra of the Almsgiving Bowl for the Ullambana Festival in the Pure Land), one fascicle, five sheets. The above is one such scripture.
Neither the new nor the old catalogs have ever recorded it;
yet, as it is currently circulated among the common people, it is being treated as an authentic scripture.
Upon closely examining its phrasing, however, one finds that it also reflects mere human sentiments.
This matter must be examined with great care; for now, it is appended to the Record of Doubtful Texts.
One fascicle of the *Sanchu jing* (Three Kitchen Sūtra):
the aforementioned sūtra has not been recorded in any of the old or new catalogs.
Nevertheless, upon examining the textual principles and considering human deliberation,
there have been numerous instances where practicing in accordance with them yielded verified results. Yet,
as these matters must be further scrutinized, they are for now appended to the section on Doubtful Matters.

7. Record of Falsehoods Confounding the True: An Auxiliary Record. Section Seven: The Record of Falsehoods Confounding the True. Three hundred and ninety-two works in one thousand and fifty-five fascicles. These so-called "false scriptures" were composed by those with heterodox views in order to confound the authentic scriptures.
Since the Great Master withdrew his form from view two thousand years ago,
the teachings of Māra have flourished in competition while the True Dharma has declined.
Consequently, there have been those of stubborn ignorance whose minds are deluded by evil views.
To forge various sutras to deceive the common people and for perverse words to confound the orthodox— how lamentable this is!
Now, fearing that the genuine and the spurious will be intermingled and right and wrong treated with equal indifference, [I write this].
It is like the precious gems of Mount Kunlun being mixed with common tiles and stones,
or Jambū-river gold being priced the same as lead and iron;
now that they are categorized and distinguished, the genuine and the counterfeit can be separated.
I hope that the Jing and Wei rivers will flow separately so as not to leave cause for future regret.

Although the sixteen-fascicle *Buddhanāma-sūtra* is authentic, it contains spurious interpolations; this twelve-fascicle version is what is currently known among the common people as the *Mātṛkā-rākṣasa-buddhanāma*.
It appears to have been compiled in recent times;
it was formed by selecting and interweaving passages from the twelve-fascicle version translated by Dharmaruci.
From within it, the titles of various sūtras were extracted.
Taking the names of later pratyekabuddhas, the names of bodhisattvas from various sūtras, and the names of arhats,
these are arranged as the sequence of the Triple Gem;
in total, there are thirty-two items.
After the ritual worship of the Three Jewels, there is always a section for repentance.
Following this repentance, the *Mātarah-rākṣasa* apocryphal scripture is further appended;
thus, vulgar and profane language is intermingled with the sacred words of the sages.
The Sūtra says:
"Take what is before and place it after; take what is after and place it before;
place what is before and after in the middle."
Placing it in the middle between the preceding and following sections is precisely correct.

Upon examining the compiler, he was entirely mediocre and ignorant; for instance, in the fourth fascicle, he states that there is no tradition of Dharma-xian (Faxian) translating scriptures in the South.
This biography is included among the Dharma-treasures;
it is a record of the travels of the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin dynasty,
as he journeyed to India.
It is an extreme error to place this text among the authentic scriptures.
Furthermore, as it says in the ninth fascicle: "Namo Pūrṇa, Namo Maitrāyaṇīputra."
This is the name of one person divided into two parts for chanting.
Next, "Namo Ānanda Rāhula" is the names of two people combined into one.
Such errors and delusions are truly numerous and cannot be described in detail;
they are briefly pointed out as above.
The masses of the ignorant imitate and practice them, and the heterodox factions transmit them together.
If I were not to specify this, I fear it might defile the True Teaching;
therefore, I have recorded it.
*The Essential Practice of the Sutra on Sacrificing the Body*, one fascicle, three pages and more; followed by the "Vow for Sacrificing the Body," totaling five pages. The above is one sutra.
It is unknown by whom it was composed;
heterodox factions were flourishing at the time.
The title at the beginning of the scripture reads:
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang.
According to the scriptures translated by the Master, this sūtra does not exist;
its spurious and erroneous nature is clearly evident.
Furthermore, I shall set forth four points to enlighten the ignorant mind.
First: the spurious scripture initially states, "In Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain."
The name "Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak) appears in ancient translations of the sūtras;
however, Master Xuanzang translated it as "Jiufeng" (Vulture Mountain) in all cases.
To say "Lingjiu" (Numinous Vulture) now is a manifest error.
I. Regarding the forged scripture, it further states:
"Beside the Śītavana cemetery on Vulture Peak Mountain.
According to various biographical records:
That Vulture Peak Mountain lies fourteen or fifteen *li* to the northeast of the inner palace city within the kingdom of Magadha.
How could there be a place for discarding corpses situated within the capital city?
Since this is not the case, both [versions] are exposed as false.
Furthermore, the spurious scripture states:
"The Buddha said that when he was the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara, his initial vow was to sacrifice his body."
Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata was the teacher who bestowed the prediction upon Śākyamuni Buddha at the completion of his second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
How could one who has received the prediction that he shall attain [Buddhahood] only be able to die and relinquish [his life] once he has attained it?
The facts contradict the principle, as the three types of falsehood are manifest.
First, within the spurious sutra it is further stated:
"If there were someone who slaughtered sentient beings throughout the entire Sahā world-system..."
The four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, slandering the Vaipulya sutras,
and stealing the property of the permanent endowment or the property currently held by the Sangha—
such transgressions as these collectively entail falling into hell.

If one could eliminate all karmic offenses simply by discarding the body, then those who slander the sutras or commit the heinous crimes (ānantarya) and ought to fall into the Avīci Hell would have their heavy retributions cleared away upon death by merely discarding the body, leaving no further grave consequences.

How does this differ from the false calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who claim that the stains of sin are eliminated by bathing in the Ganges River, and thus recklessly cast themselves into the water to seek rebirth in heaven and receive its blessings? To say that discarding the body at death eliminates sin is no different from such deluded views.
Fools commit evil deeds and seek to eliminate their transgressions through these means;
let the wise reflect carefully so as not to be deceived,
lest they sink forever into the miserable realms with no prospect of liberation.
The facts contradict the principles, as the four types of falsehoods are manifest; the corruptions are so numerous that they cannot be recorded in full.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-dharmādarśa-sūtra* (Yoga Fajing jing), in two fascicles or one fascicle, also includes a spurious preface; this is the first scripture [discussed].

That is, two additional chapters were added to the preceding text of the *Xiàngfǎ juéyí jīng* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Regarding the Semblance Dharma) from the old spurious record, forming a single sūtra as a whole.
The first chapter is titled "The Buddha, on the Verge of Nirvāṇa, Preaches the Dharma for Ānanda on the Abiding and Extinction [of the Teachings]."
This volume takes the *Buddha’s Final Nirvana Record of the Dharma’s Abiding* translated by Master Xuanzang,
revising and expanding it, and places it at the beginning.
Next is the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha’s Praise of the Contemplative Practice of the Dharmakāya."
The following is the "Chapter on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Sadāpradāna.
This chapter is identical to the old translation;
however, according to its textual flow and sequence, it does not connect coherently with the preceding sections.
In the first year of the Jinglong era (707 CE), the monk Shili of the Sanjie sect forged this work. In its preface,
he falsely claimed that the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci and the Tripitaka Master Baosiwei and others had translated it together at Chongfu Monastery.
Master Shili said: "There are Brahma-scriptures circulating that Master Zhi never saw or heard of;
because they were previously included among the spurious, I have recompiled this to clear away doubts."

Layered falsehood upon falsehood, the errors and corruptions are even more numerous. One can see this by reading it for oneself; there is no need for extensive narration. The compiler says: I once personally questioned the Tripiṭaka Master Liu-zhi regarding this matter.

The Tripiṭaka Master replied, "In my region, there were originally no Sanskrit manuscripts, and I have never translated this sutra. His disciple Prajñāgupta was of clear and keen insight and fully understood the circumstances. Fearing that because the ages had long passed, errors might corrupt the true teaching, he has pointed this out here to warn future generations. Furthermore, because the monk Shi-li engaged in petty disputes while young, the Emperor personally took concern and ordered him to return to lay life. Is this not a sign that Heaven did not grant its protection and instead sent down punishment upon such a person? Moreover, at the time of his death, his belly was as large as a jar, and evil omens arrived swiftly—how could one not be afraid?

*The Scripture on Maitreya’s Descent to Rebirth, Dispatching Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to Exhort Sentient Beings to Abandon Evil and Practice Goodness for Longevity and Happiness*, one fascicle (also simply titled *The Scripture on Longevity and Happiness*), ten sheets; *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-karuṇā Asking the Tathāgata at What Time He Should Appear in the World and Universally Proclaim [the Teaching]*, one fascicle, eight sheets; *The Scripture on Maitreya Attaining Buddhahood According to His Original Office*, one fascicle; and *The Scripture on the Essential Secret of the Vajra: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhadra-vṛkṣa Asking the Buddha*, also titled *The Scripture on the Origins of King Vaśavartin*, or including the character "Wu" (無), fourteen sheets—these four scriptures above were all forged by heterodox followers.

Regarding the claims therein that Maitreya Tathāgata is about to descend to be born, etc., I have carefully consulted the authentic scriptures: after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, when fifty-seven koṭis and six hundred thousand years have passed in the human realm, and the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa has increased to eighty thousand years, only then will Maitreya Tathāgata appear in the world. How could Maitreya descend to be born while the human lifespan is less than a hundred years? Such delusory falsehoods are used to seduce the ignorant and foolish.
Those of shallow understanding mostly accept this with faith;
because of this, they fall into ruin. How tragic it is!
Therefore, I have distinguished these points specifically so that you may examine them with great care.
After the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Ānanda preached for the fourfold assembly the *Sūtra on the Rituals for Paying Homage to the Buddha and Observing the Fasting Vow*, one fascicle;
it is also called the *Sūtra on the Rituals for Observing the Fasting Vow upon the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*. [Compiled by] Maitreya Maṇibuddha.
*The Scripture on the Enlightenment of Buddha-nature*, one fascicle; the colophon at the end of this scripture states:

*The Scripture on the Enlightenment of Buddha-nature through the Causes and Conditions of the Human Body*, or simply *The Scripture on the Enlightenment of Buddha-nature*, consisting of nine sheets. *The Scripture on the Upāsaka Precepts for Pure Conduct*, one fascicle;

alternatively called *The Scripture on the Upāsaka Precepts for Pure Conduct*, with the thirteenth chapter titled "On Responsive Manifestations" (*Ganying-pin*). [This] changes the *Scripture on the Bequeathed Teaching* (*Yijiao jing*) into...

*The Scripture on the Great Flood of the Jiǎshēn Year*, six sheets; this differs from the account of the waters in the *Record of the Buddha’s Alms Bowl* regarding the events of the Jiǎshēn year (two sheets).
*The Scripture of the Frog*, one scroll, "Chapter on the Blue Frog," approximately one and a half sheets. *The Scripture of Self-Reflection*, one scroll (two sheets).
*The Scripture on the Profound Weight of Parental Kindness*, one scroll; the preface cites Ding Lan, Dǒng Ān, and Guō Jù.

[These are] equal [in number]. Thus it is known that there are: one fascicle of the *Tathāgata-śāsana-rahasya-piṭaka-sūtra* (The Secret Essential Treasury Sutra of the Tathāgata’s True Teaching) consisting of three sheets;

one fascicle of the *Vinaya-piṭaka-sūtra* consisting of eight sheets; one fascicle of the *Uṣṇīṣa-sūtra*, whose internal title reads *Buddhabhāṣita-gambhīra-praṇīta-dharmārtha-śāstra-vyākhyāna-gambhīrārtha-saṃsāra-mārga* (The Treatise on the Profound and Sublime Meaning of the Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, Explaining the Profound Meaning of the Path of Birth and Death), consisting of seven sheets; one fascicle of the *Dhyānamukha-sūtra* consisting of five sheets; and the *New [Fascicle on] Jealousy*.
The *Fujing* (Sutra of the Wife), one fascicle, also known as the *Du fujing* (Sutra of the Jealous Wife). The aforementioned sutra was fabricated by a person of recent times;
its author’s name has been forgotten.
It was falsely created because a husband, out of his wife’s jealousy, sought to deceive her with this scripture.
Within that [text], it is stated that those who harbor jealousy receive extremely heavy retribution.

The *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra* in two fascicles is also simply called the *Aṅgula Sūtra*. Among the sūtras with names identical to those in the authentic canon, there is this *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra* in two fascicles;
I suspect this sūtra is a compilation by Xiao Ziliang based on the *Chónglóu Jìjīng* (The Staircase of Precepts Sūtra).
*Qingjing jushi zi duren jing* (Sūtra on the Pure Layman’s Son Saving Beings), one fascicle; also called *Qingjing shi jing*. *Madengqi jing* (Mātaṅga Sūtra), one fascicle.
*Biyu jing* (Sūtra of Parables), one fascicle, translated by Huilan of the Song dynasty.

Among these, there is a *Biyu jing* for which no original manuscript exists; as its title is identical to this one, their authenticity is confused, so both are retained here. *Muliang wen jing* (Sūtra of Maudgalyāyana’s Questions).
One fascicle; the title is identical to that of a true scripture, yet the language and meaning differ entirely. *The Scripture on the Extinction of Minor Dharmas*, one fascicle;

the text and meaning differ entirely from the *Scripture on the Extinction of Dharmas* in the true canon. *The Scripture on Ringing the Bell*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on the Dharma of Upholding the Precepts*, one fascicle.

*The Scripture on the Golden Scalpel for Opening the Mouth*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on Hell*, one fascicle. Translated during the Han dynasty with the translator lost; it contains [descriptions of] hell.
*Sūtra*, one fascicle—this is likely this very work; both versions are preserved for now. *Utpalaka-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle.
*Ānanda-puṇyavipāka-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, one fascicle. *Ānanda-vinaya-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, one fascicle (possibly identical to the *Ānanda-śīla-vinaya-paripṛcchā-śāstra*).
*Śramaṇa-śāstra*, one fascicle. *Pratyekabuddha-kevalayācanā-śāstra*, one fascicle. *Vinaya*... [text ends]
The *Qingwen lun* in one fascicle, the *Diyu zhuan* in one fascicle, and the lower portion of the *Yangju jing*—
these eighteen sections comprising nineteen fascicles all possess doctrines that contradict [orthodox principles],
and their spurious and false nature is manifest.
Since various commentaries and treatises have all cited [these works] without recognizing their falsehood,
I have compiled this record to transmit it to future worthies.
Should they awaken to the fact that these are not authentic, I hope they will join me in reforming this corruption.
Furthermore, the number of such apocryphal scriptures is truly vast;
we shall await further research to continue compiling examples of this category.
[The following entries] begin with the *Buddhanāmasūtra*.
Thirty-seven works in fifty-four fascicles.
These were never recorded in previous catalogs;
they have now been collected and included in the new Kaiyuan Catalog.
*Samādhi-pratipatti-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Mahāmaudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, or alternatively called the *Buddha-preṣita-samādhi-pratipatti-sūtra*.
*Bhikṣu Hui-ming-jing*, one fascicle; also known as the *Bhikṣu Hui-ming-jing*, or alternatively called the *Vimala-tattva-sūtra*.
*Niṭa-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Niṭa-huang-luo*.

*The Sūtra of the King*, also known as *The Sūtra of King Huangluo*, or *The Sūtra of the Myriad Characters on the Chest*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Sūtra of the Myriad Characters Manifesting on the Chest*.
*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Sahe*, one fascicle; the old catalogues call it *The Sūtra of King Sahe Bodhisattva*, or *The Sūtra of Sahe-sa*.
*The Catalogue of the Dharma Scriptures* states that its alternative name is *The Sūtra of the Universal Deliverance of the Nation*, [and] *The Sūtra of the Virtuous Faithful Woman*.
*Sūtra* in one fascicle; alternatively called the *Śraddhā-sūtra*. *Hushen-zhu-miao-jing* (Sūtra on the Wondrous Protector of the Body) in one fascicle;

also known as the *Dushi-hushi-jing* (Sūtra on Delivering and Protecting the World). Some claim it is the "Twelve Wondrous [Sūtras]," which is an error. *Du-hu-jing* (Sūtra on Delivering and Protecting) in one fascicle;

alternatively called the *Du-hufa-jing* (Sūtra on Delivering and Protecting the Dharma). The *Fajing-lu* (Record of the Dharma Scriptures) states it is the *Du-fahujing*. *Vīra-samādhi-sūtra* in two fascicles. *Śubharāja-śakramahārāja-sūtra*.
In two fascicles; alternatively called the *Sūtra on the Merit of the Honored Emperor Śubhavasu*, or as one fascicle.

The *Weiwu Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of Non-Existence) in one fascicle, or the *Weiwu Sanmei Arahagong Jing* (Sūtra of the Arhat Gong of the Samādhi of Non-Existence) in one fascicle, or called the *Xiangguo Arahagong Jing* (Sūtra of the Arhat Gong, the State Chancellor).
The *Huiding Puhuan Shentong Pusa Jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Universal Supernatural Power of Wisdom and Concentration) in one fascicle; the old catalog refers to it as "Wisdom" (*Hui*).
*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Universal Sovereign of the Lands and Spiritual Powers*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on the Sheathed Male Organ*.
The *Dharmakṣema Catalogue* states that it is also titled *The Sūtra on the Questions of the King of Body and Land:
Governing the State*. *The Great Aśoka Sūtra*, one fascicle; it says: "When the Buddha was at Vārāṇasī... *The Sūtra on the Four Matters of Liberation*, one fascicle; also known as...

*The Scripture on Delivering People through the Four Matters of Liberation*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of Mahā-Aniruddha*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of the Poor Woman Who Is Not [Possessed of] the Eight Mindfulnesses*, one fascicle;
and that titled *Nanda*—the old catalogs refer to it as the *Scripture of the Poor Woman Nanda*.

I have carefully examined the eleventh fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, which contains the account of the origins of the poor woman Nanda; if this work is identical to that, then it is not [this particular scripture].

*Jiuzhu jinxiang jing* (Sutra on the Forged Casting of Golden Images), one fascicle; *Sishen jing* (Sutra of the Four Bodies), one fascicle; *Puhui sanmei jing* (Sutra of Universal Wisdom Samādhi), one fascicle;
*Aqiu na jing* (Sutra of Aqiu-na), one fascicle—the old catalog states this is the *Aqiu na sanmei jing*; two separate sections; *Duzheng jing* (Sutra of Sole Testimony), one fascicle;
*Faben zhai jing* (Sutra of the Dharma-Foundation Fast), one fascicle—stated to have come from Xiliangzhou and transmitted by Moliluo; *Da biqiuni* (Great Bhikṣuṇī).
One fascicle of the *Śīla* (Precepts). The *Zhou lu* states: "A different version of the *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla-sūtra*, transmitted by Mili, a disciple of Śrīmitra.
[This follows] the *Dingxing sanmei jing* below;
[these constitute] twenty-five works in twenty-eight fascicles.

In the catalog of the Śramaṇa Mitian Shi Dao’an of the Fu Qin dynasty, there were twenty-six scriptures listed as "spurious" or "doubtful. Among these, the *Bao rulai sanmei jing* (The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Tathāgata Ratna) was originally included in the Master An’s list of spurious works; however, because this sūtra has a clear source for its translation and was previously translated twice, it has been incorporated into the "Authentic Catalog" (*zhenglu*), and thus [the previous entry] has been removed. Master An stated:
In the monastic traditions of foreign lands, all students kneel and receive the teachings orally.
If one has received ten or twenty turns of the same material from a teacher, one transmits it to later students;
should there be even a single character that differs [from the original], [the transmission is considered flawed].
They collectively investigated and prosecuted him, and as soon as they found an opportunity, they expelled him;
for in the monastic law, there is no leniency.
It had not been long since the sutra arrived in the land of Jin.
Yet those who delight in such matters mix sand with gold;
though they appear refined and elegant, they lack any means of rectification.
How, then, can one distinguish the true from the false?
For the farmer, the grain and the weeds exist together;
Hou Ji sighed at this.
Gold and jade caskets are sealed within the same chest.
Even Bian He felt such shame for his sake;
how could I dare presume to join the ranks of those who study?
Seeing the Jing and Wei rivers mingled together, and dragons and snakes advancing side by side.
How could one not feel shame for this?
I have now set forth my views on those works which are not Buddhist scriptures as listed above,
to be shown to scholars of the future.
All know this as base and contrary to principle.

The *Bhikṣu-āyus-dharma-caryā-sūtra*, one fascicle—also titled *The Sūtra on the Initial Preaching of the Āyus-dharma by the Tathāgata to the Five Bhikṣus*—is recorded in Saṃghayue’s Catalogue (*Sengyou lu*) as follows: [text continues].
The title of this sutra previously stated it was translated by Kumārajīva.
Sengyou, however, examined the scroll and found that it originally lacked a translator’s name;
furthermore, among the works produced by Kumārajīva, this sutra was not included.

Therefore, it is included in the Record of Doubtful Works (*Yilù*). The layman [Seng]yù requested the *Fótián jīng* (Sūtra on the Field of Merit) in one fascicle; Yù stated that the original title of this sūtra was translated by Dharmakṣema. However, since this sūtra is not among those translated by Dharmakṣema, it is included in the Record of Doubtful Works. The *Guǎngdìng dùxīng zhāohún duànjié fùlián jīng* (Sūtra on the Consecration of the Head, the Crossing of Stars, the Summoning of Souls, and the Reconnecting of Severed Bonds) in one fascicle: the *Fǎjīng lù* states that there is also a smaller version of this sūtra, and that both are entirely human compositions. The *Wéiwéidào jīng* (Sūtra on Non-action) in two fascicles: the catalogues of Chángfáng and others state it was translated by Dharmakṣema, yet they also say it is a spurious work with commentaries from later generations. The *Fǎjīng lù* of the Sui dynasty and the *Rénshòu lù* both state it is the *Dàchéng miàojīng* (Mahāyāna Wondrous Sūtra). Regarding the aforementioned single sūtra, I personally examined its manuscript.
It appears that this was compiled during the Han or Wei dynasties;
it was not translated from an Indic original.
Among the Zhou catalogues, it is included within the section of "Correct" (zheng) scriptures.
Now, because its name was confused with the True Sūtra, it was included in Daoxuan’s *Fajing lu* as a spurious record.
One scroll of the *Jueding zui fu jing* (Sūtra Determining Sin and Merit): the *Fajing lu* states that its alternative title is the *Hui fa jing*, while the *Renshou lu* states:

*Qínglí yǒuzuì jīng* (Sūtra on Parting from Sentiments and Avoiding Transgressions), one fascicle; the title is given as *Qínglí yǒuzuì jīng pǐn xià* (Lower Chapter of the Sūtra on Parting from Sentiments and Avoiding Transgressions).
*Shāoxiāng zhòuyuàn jīng* (Sūtra of Incense Offering and Prayer), one fascicle; also known as *Zhòuyuàn jīng*. *Ānmù zhòujīng* (Sūtra of the Divine Incantation for Entombment), one fascicle;
the *Fajing lu* calls it *Ānmù shénzhòujīng*, while the *Chángfáng lu* states it was compiled by Dào bèi of the Qi dynasty. *Kuàngyuèguāng púsà jì* (Record of Bodhisattva Candraprabha), one fascicle.

One fascicle; alternatively, there is the *Buddhapātra-śāstra* (Record of the Buddha’s Almsbowl) in one fascicle, also titled *Buddhapātra-śāstra*. [It contains] the account of the great flood in the Jiǎshēn year and the matter of Bodhisattva Candraprabha.

The *Mile xiàjiào jīng* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent to Teach) in one fascicle, or perhaps following the *Bāpí jì* (Record of the Almsbowl), there is the *Jiùshíliù zhǒng dào jīng* (Sūtra on the Ninety-six Kinds of Paths).
The *Fājīng lù* (Catalogue of the Dharma Sūtras) states it is the *Jiùshíwǔ zhǒng dào jīng* (Sūtra on the Ninety-five Kinds of Paths); this is recorded in the *Rénshòu lù* (Ren-shou Catalogue).
The title of the two-fascicle work reads: *Scripture on the Removal of the Miscellaneous Divine Incantations of the Ninety-five Kinds of Heretical Paths*.
The above records twelve scriptures.
According to Sengyou’s Catalogue:
Either because its doctrines are contradictory or because its prose and verses are shallow and vulgar,
it has been entered into the Record of Doubtful Works.

It is hoped that by weeding out the weeds and chaff, the Precious Dharma will be made manifest. Furthermore, the *Yùlù* (Record of Supplements) contains one fascicle of the *Guǎngdìng Yàoshī Jīng* (Guanding’s Version of the Bhaisajyaguru Sutra), stating that it was compiled by Huìjiǎn of the Song dynasty based on the sutra. However, since the original text of this sutra has already been translated four times—both new and old—the spurious record has excluded it.

*Tiwei boli jing* (The Sutra of Tiwei and Boli), two fascicles; compiled by the monk Tanjing of the Northern Region during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty. Previously there was a separate *Tiwei jing* in one fascicle, which differs entirely from this work in terms of authenticity. *Baoshche jing* (The Sutra of the Precious Chariot), one fascicle; alternatively titled *Miaohao baoshche jing*; compiled by the śramaṇa Tanbian of Huai Prefecture in the Northern Region and revised by the bhikṣu Daoshi of Qingzhou. [The following is] the *Biqiu yingong jing* (Sutra on the Bhikṣu’s Receiving Offerings).
Fourteen fascicles in sixteen volumes.
These are spurious scriptures found in Sengyou’s Catalogue of the Liang Dynasty.
Sengyou’s catalogue states briefly:
Yòu collated various scriptures and extensively gathered their similarities and differences;
based upon the sūtras and vinayas, he observed points of considerable doubt.
Indeed, the essence and intent of the true sūtras are harmonious, profound, and far-reaching.
The literary compositions of those who feign authority are shallow and confused in meaning;

there is nothing they can hide, whether it be jade or stone, crimson or purple. I have now distinguished those works of which I harbor doubts and annotated them in this record, while also marking at the end those falsely composed by recent authors.
Relying instead upon various miscellaneous scriptures, he composed titles for them himself; thus,
he neither advanced to hear the teachings while traveling to the Western Regions,
nor did he retreat to witness the translations produced by foreign masters.
I have heard that [the former] arose from the windows and doors [of his own tradition], while [the latter’s] seal of approval emerged from his own breast.
This is enough to cause deep trepidation in those who would mislead later students.
Since these matters were personally witnessed and heard by me, how could I dare remain silent?

Alas! Those of future generations should examine this with care. Furthermore, the *Yùlù* (Record of Supplements) contains one fascicle of the *Pútí fúzàng fǎhuà sānmèi jīng* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Dharma-Transformation of the Storehouse of Bodhi-Blessings) and one fascicle of twenty-one essential dharma-verses from various sutras; both are attributed to the śramaṇa Dàohuān. According to the records of Zhìlǎngfáng and others, Dàohuān also produced other spurious scriptures; therefore, these have been compiled here together with those others.

*Jiushang jing* (Sutra on the Nine Wounds), one fascicle; Fang says it is seen in the *Bielu*. *Bodhi fuzang fahua sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Dharma-Transformation of the Bodhi-Treasury of Merit), one fascicle; Fang says it appeared during the reign of Emperor Wu; it is seen in the *Sanzang ji* and the *Baochang lu*. *Qifo geshe jing* (Sutra of the Verses Spoken by Each of the Seven Buddhas), one fascicle; Fang says it is seen in the *Wulu*. *Shenzizhishen jie jing* (Sutra of Verses on Deep Self-Knowledge of the Body), one fascicle; Fang says it is seen in the *Wulu*; Sengyou says the translator is lost. *Zhongjing yaolan fahui ershishiyi shou* (Twenty-one Essential Dharma Verses from Various Sutras), one fascicle; compiled in the third year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty; seen in the *Sanzang ji* and the *Changfang lu*. The above consists of five works in five fascicles.
The *Chángfáng lù* states:
"Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daobei of the Xiao Qi dynasty.
Daobei later changed his name to Daoxuan."
Although these are seen in various catalogs, they are all classified as apocryphal scriptures (*yijing*).

Following the traditional arrangement, they are included here within Changfang’s catalog. Daobei further possesses one fascicle of the *Anmu zhoushou jing* (Sutra of the Incantation for Ancestral Tombs); although Sengyou’s catalog does not specify its author, it is clearly listed among the apocrypha, so it is not recorded here again.
*Jingtu jing* (Sutra on the Pure Land), seven fascicles;
translated in the first year of the Yongyuan era of the Xiao Qi dynasty, when [the translator] was nine years old. *Baoding jing* (Jewel-Peak Sutra), one fascicle;
translated in the first year of the Yongyuan era, when [the translator] was nine years old. *Zhengding jing* (Sutra on the Correct Peak), one fascicle.
In the first year of the Yongyuan era, he was nine years old when he produced one fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the first year of the Yongyuan era, he was nine years old when he produced one fascicle of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
In the first year of the Yongyuan era, he was nine years old when he produced one fascicle of the *Tṛṣṭhubha-guṇa-vyūha-sūtra* (or *Bhaiṣajya-vastu-sūtra*).
*The Sūtra of the Prince*, one fascicle; translated in the second year of the Yongyuan era when [the translator] was ten years old.
*The Sūtra of Gayāśīrṣa*, one fascicle; translated in the second year of the Yongyuan era when [the translator] was ten years old.
*The Sūtra of Vārāṇasī*, one fascicle; translated in the second year of the Yongyuan era when [the translator] was ten years old.
The *Youlupin jing* (Ullambana Sūtra), one fascicle, translated in the first year of the Zhongxing era; [the translator] was twelve years old at the time.
The *Yiyi jing* (Upāyakauśalya Sūtra), two fascicles, translated in the first year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty;
[the translator] was thirteen years old at the time. Zhiyuan, by imperial decree, produced the *Bore de jing* (Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), two fascicles.
In the first year of the Tianjian era, at the age of thirteen, Zhiyuan, acting on imperial instructions, produced one fascicle of the *Huayan yingluo jing*.
In the first year of the Tianjian era, at the age of thirteen, Zhiyuan, acting on imperial instructions, produced one fascicle of the *Sheng shizi hou jing*.
In the third year of the Tianjian era, at the age of fifteen, he produced one fascicle of the *Shoudaweijing*.
In the fourth year of the Tianjian era, the *Anāgāma-sūtra* in two fascicles was produced within the Huaguang Hall of the Imperial Palace;
it was produced when [the Master] was sixteen years old. In the fourth year of the Tianjian era, the *Sudharmasvara-siṃhanāda-sūtra* in three fascicles was produced;

it was produced when he was sixteen years old. The *Udumbara-sūtra* in one fascicle, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* in four fascicles, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in one fascicle, and the *Saptajanma-sūtra* with its preface in one fascicle—these twenty-one sūtras totaling thirty-five fascicles, together with the thirty-four fascicles previously listed, were obtained.
The Record of Sengyou of the Liang Dynasty states that [this work] was produced by the young daughter of Jiang Bi, a *taixue* doctor at the end of the Qi dynasty, known as Nizi.
Initially, when Nizi was in her early childhood (*tiaochen*),...
At times, he would sit in quiet meditation with eyes closed and recite this sutra; at other times,
he would speak of ascending to heaven,
or claim it was divinely bestowed.
His speech became fluent as if through lifelong habit;
he caused others to transcribe it, but it would suddenly cease after a short while.
After the passage of ten days and a month, it resumed again as before.
The monastics and laypeople of Kyoto all circulated accounts of his wonders.
When the current Emperor issued an imperial edict for an audience and questioned him regarding these matters,
he answered according to the facts no differently than an ordinary person.
However, he was deeply devoted to the True Dharma and practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) to a small extent.
When his parents wished to marry him off, he vowed not to comply.
Subsequently, he left the household life and became known as the monk Dharmayaśas.
He resided at Qingyuan Temple.
Having collected the orthodox scriptures and scrutinized various accounts,
Daoyou requested that those matters within his own observation be brought forth for inspection.
His family kept it secret and did not show it to others;
he obtained only three fascicles of the *Miaoyin Shizihou Jing* (Sūtra of the Lion’s Roar of Wondrous Sound) to include in his catalog of doubtful scriptures.
This nun passed away in the third month of the Jianguan era.
A person fond of rare things obtained her writings and commentaries;
those produced before and after her death total more than twenty volumes. Her maternal uncle, Sun Qi, considered them to be authentic scriptures.
As they circulated through exegesis and proselytization, were collected and transcribed, and once committed to brush and paper, they would surely remain in the world. Formerly,
at the end of the Jian’an era of the Han dynasty, the wife of a man from the Ding family of Jiyin suddenly appeared as if stricken by a seizure and was able to speak in the Hu language.
Furthermore, he requested paper and a brush to write it himself in the Hu script.

A foreigner from the Western Regions who saw this writing remarked that it was a sūtra-prognostication (*vyākaraṇa*), adding that upon investigating the distant past, such a thing was not non-existent.
However, its meaning was not from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], nor was there a master to translate it; thus, it harbors both the intent to accept and reject.

Changfang considered it a doubtful case because its cultivation has a specific origin, and he placed it among the "Correct" titles. Yet, the Renshou Catalogue, the Neidian Catalogue, and others, regarding it as not being a translation from an Indian original, have classified it among the "Spurious" records. Following the determinations of the Renshou Catalogue and others, I likewise include it here among the spurious works.

The *Gāowáng Guānshìyīn Jīng* (Sūtra of King Gao’s Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara), one fascicle; also called the *Xiǎo Guānshìyīn Jīng* (Short Sūtra of Avalokiteśvara), consisting of slightly more than half a sheet of paper. Regarding this one sūtra:
formerly, during the Tiānpíng era of the Northern Wèi dynasty...
Sun Jingde, a recruited soldier from Dingzhou,
had fashioned an image of Avalokiteśvara while on duty.
When his term was completed and he was about to return home to offer worship, he [made a vow].
Later, he was implicated by bandits;
unable to endure the torture, he falsely confessed to the crime. The next day, he was to be executed.
That night, he performed prostrations and repentance, weeping profusely.
Suddenly, as if in a dream, he saw a śramaṇa instructing him to recite the *Jiusheng Guanshiyin Jing* (The Sutra of Avalokiteśvara for Saving Lives).
This sutra contained the names of various Buddhas, stating that by reciting them one thousand times, one would be spared from suffering and calamity.
Jingde was startled awake; it was exactly as he had perceived in his dream, without the slightest discrepancy.
He then recited [the scripture] one hundred times.
The officials bound him and led him toward the marketplace.
As he walked and recited, he reached the thousandth verse just as he was led to his execution.
When the blade struck him, it snapped into three pieces without harming his skin or flesh.
He changed the blade and struck again.
After three changes of blades in total, the blade broke as it had before.
When the provincial governor questioned him,
he fully related the circumstances from beginning to end.
He reported the circumstances to Chancellor Gao Huan,
who then submitted a memorial on his behalf requesting that he be spared from death;
consequently, this [text] was widely circulated throughout the world.
This was what is known as the *Gāowáng Guānshìyīn Jīng*.
Jìngdé subsequently prepared a vegetarian feast to welcome the image,
whereupon he saw three marks of sword wounds upon its neck.

The compilers of the *Qi shu*, the *Bian zheng lun*, the *Neidian lu*, and other records state: "This sutra was included in the imperial catalog of the Northern Zhou dynasty and entered into the canon; it is not so now. [They argue: "Although this was divinely transmitted and did not result from a formal translation, how does it differ from what was recited by the monk Fashang previously? Why should that be classified among the spurious while this is included in the authentic records? Since the precedent is such, I have appended it here.
*The Sutra on the Adornments of the Retinue of Sarvajñatā*, one fascicle, twenty-odd sheets. Regarding this sutra,
Sengyou’s catalogue states that in the ninth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, the Daoist practitioner Miaoguang from Touduo in Yingzhou [transmitted it].
Although he had observed the precepts for seven years and feigned superior spiritual marks,
all the nuns and elderly women unanimously proclaimed him to have attained the Holy Path. Consequently,
the Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng) of that province deliberated on how to expel him.
He subsequently went secretly to the capital to reside at Puhong Temple, where he produced this scripture.
He also transcribed it upon a folding screen, which was covered with red gauze and offered to with incense and flowers;
the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, and the smoke from their offerings filled the air.
The origins of the matter were made manifest and an imperial edict was issued to Jiankang.
Upon the examination and verification of the confessions and documents,
it was found that he had abridged various sutras with many personal interpolations.
Lu Yan, who falsely fabricated the identity of the borrower and refined the wording of the petition,
and Miaoguang, whose clever deception merited the death penalty for execution—
both having conspired for ten years— were sentenced to penal servitude at that very year, on the twenty-first day of the fourth month.
An imperial edict was issued to the Sangzheng Huichao, ordering him to summon twenty eminent and virtuous masters from the capital who were capable of expounding the Great Dharma,
such as Sengyou and Tanzhun, to go together to Jiankang to debate the matter of Miaoguang.

Xiao Chao immediately received the imperial decree and, together with twenty individuals—including Tanzhun, Sengyou, Fachong, Huili, Huji, Zhizang, Sengmin, and Fayun—conducted the interrogation in the county.
The offenses of Miaoguang were investigated in detail according to the written petition;
the assembly of monks deliberated and, in accordance with the Vinaya, expelled him for punishment.
By imperial grace, his death was commuted.
Fearing that he might again cause confusion in a remote region,
[the authorities] detained him for a long time at the Eastern Prefecture.
Thereupon, they collected more than twenty copies of this scripture along with the folding screens and incinerated them at the county seat.

Nevertheless, as there remain scattered fragments that might confuse future generations, I have once again provided a brief account of the Elder Sarvajñāta—the father of Wondrous Light (Prabhāketu)—whose younger brother was named Vajraśrī; his disciple was named Siṃha, who compiled this record. In other records, the origins were described only briefly; here, I have set them forth in full detail so that the source may be thoroughly understood and all may together reflect upon and exhort one another.

The *Anāgāmi-sūtra* in two fascicles: I personally saw a single-fascicle version that constitutes a complete work, which was likewise composed by humans. To the right, according to the catalogs of various dynasties such as those of Sengchangfang and the *Shiyi lu*, both versions of this sūtra are recorded.
Within the *Sengfani song* (The Chanting of the Monastic Dharma), there are also two fascicles of the *Anāgāmin Sūtra*.
As neither possesses an original text to verify their authenticity, it is difficult to distinguish between them;
for now, their titles are preserved separately.
*The Scripture on Resolving Doubts in the Semblance Dharma*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on Pure Dharma Practice*, one fascicle;

*The Scripture on the Transformations of the Honored One of Dragon Lineage*, one fascicle—this is largely identical to the *Scripture on the Liberation of the Four Matters* in Master Dao’an’s spurious catalog;

*The Scripture on the Ten Great Vows of Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle—the *Renshou Catalog* states that it is also titled *The Scripture on the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara*; the full title is as follows:
*The Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara’s Ten Great Vows from the Ocean of Broad and Fierce Wisdom*, Chapter Seven Hundred;

*The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle; *The Mahāyāna Lotus Hayagrīva Rākṣasa Sūtra*, one fascicle, also known as *The Sūtra on the Retribution of Śramaṇas Asked by Bodhisattva Ratnabuddhi*;
*The Sūtra on the Emptiness-Purity Samādhi*, one fascicle, also titled *The Response of the Emptiness-Stillness Heaven*.

Regarding the *Ying Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi to be Attained), I have carefully consulted the catalogs of successive dynasties and find that it has already been translated twice. Fearing that these might be conflated or that false titles might be usurped, I have preserved both entries in their original form:
first, the *Puluo liao jing* (Bhadrakalpika-sūtra) in two fascicles; second, the *Dafazunwang jing* (Mahādharmarāja-sūtra) in thirty-one fascicles;

third, the *Shifangfo juehuxi jing* (Daśadigbuddha-vimati-nirṇaya-sūtra) in one fascicle; and fourth, the *Bafanggenyuan bashiliufoming jing* (Aṣṭadig-mūla-ṣaḍaśabuddhanāma-sūtra) in one fascicle. These are likewise [to be included].
*The Sutra Spoken by the Fundamental Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as a Proof*, one fascicle;

*The Sutra on the Original Arising of Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood*, seventeen fascicles (the *Renshou Record* states seventy fascicles); *The Sutra of Avalokiteśvara Bestowing Jewels upon Maitreya’s Descent*, one fascicle;
*The Sutra of Maitreya’s Subduing of Demons at His Attainment of Buddhahood*, one fascicle (also known as the *Sutra on Saving and Delivering Sentient Beings*).
*The Sūtra on Measuring Heaven and Earth from the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma*, one fascicle;
also known as *The Second and Ninth Chapter on Measuring Heaven and Earth from the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma Sūtra*. *Sūtra on Avalokiteśvara’s Verses on Rebirth*, one fascicle.

*Sūtra on the Adornment for Attaining Buddhahood by Extinguishing the Seven Sections*, one fascicle. *Sūtra Asked by the Bodhisattva Śūnyatā-vihārin*, one fascicle; also known as *The Extinction of the Dharma*.

The *Jin jing* (Exhaustion Sutra) also states that the Dharma has perished; the *Fajing lu* (Record of the Dharma Scriptures) says that this sutra is manifestly spurious and was certainly not translated by Zhu Fahu.
This refers to the *Youkongji suowen jing* (Sutra on the Questions of Youkongji).
I have carefully examined the various records, which have already been translated twice.
Fearing that false names might be falsely appropriated,
I have therefore preserved the titles of both versions.
There is also a one-fascicle *Dharmaviniścaya-sūtra* (or *Dharmakṣaya-sūtra*).
This is simply another name for the same work and need not be recorded again. It is an error that both the Great and Small Vehicle catalogs of spurious scriptures include this *Dharmakṣaya-sūtra*.

*Zhàomíng Púsà Jīng* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Illumination), one fascicle; *Jiātóu tuózì Zhàomíng Púsà Fāngbiàn Pìyù Zhìbìng Jīng* (Sūtra on the Expedient Means and Parables of the Bodhisattva Illumination Regarding the Practice of Dhūta for Healing Illness), one fascicle;
*Shǒuluó Bǐqiū Jiàn Yuèguāng Tóngzǐ Jīng* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Śūra Seeing the Youth Candraprabha), one fascicle; *Ānán Xiànbiàn Jīng* (Sūtra on Ānanda Manifesting Transformations), one fascicle;
*Bōrě Xuánjì Jīng* (Sūtra on the Profound Record of Prajñā), one fascicle; *Yōushēn Xuánjì Jīng* (Sūtra on the Profound Record of the Mysterious and Deep), one fascicle; *Xuánjì* (Profound Record).
The *Sūtra* in two fascicles; the Zhou catalogue records it as one fascicle. The *Mahā-saṃnipāta Sūtra* in four fascicles;

the Zhou catalogue records that its alternative name is the *Maitreya’s Descent to Rebirth and the Formation of the Great Good Saṃnipāta Sūtra*, or it is in three fascicles. The *Bodhicittotpāda Sūtra* in one fascicle; there are currently two fascicles extant, which are the authentic scripture.
Although these share the same title, they differ in the number of fascicles. [Also included is] the *Bodhisattva Seeking the Five Eyes Sūtra*.
One fascicle, translated by Nie Daozhen; this scripture bears this title, yet it further contains what is falsely forged while usurping the name of a genuine work.
Thus, both the authentic and the spurious versions exist. *Banniepan hou zhu biqiu jing* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣus After the Parinirvāṇa), one fascicle:
according to Sengyou’s catalogue, this is an alternative title for the *Xiaobanniepan jing*. *Xiaobanniepan jing*, one fascicle; also known as the *Dafamiejin* (The Great Extinction of the Dharma).
According to the record of An Shigao’s translations on the right, there is a *Kṣudraka-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Since this shares the same title,
and furthermore lacks a definitive original text for comparison, [its authenticity remains uncertain].
Furthermore, both [versions] are recorded together.
There is one fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Five Corruptions and Evil World*, as well as the *Great Sūtra on the Five Corruptions*, which should be this very same work.
Also, there is the *Sūtra on the Miraculous Transformations of Heaven and Earth*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra on the Ten Evils*, and the *Sūtra on the Loutan [Cosmology] of Avalokiteśvara*.
One fascicle of the *Xiǎolóu tán jīng* (Sūtra of the Small Tower); one fascicle of the *Xūmí sìyù jīng* (Sūtra of the Four Regions of Mount Sumeru);

one fascicle of the *Zhènghuà nèiwài jīng* (Sūtra of the True Transformation of the Inner and Outer), also known as the *Lǎozǐ huàhú jīng*; and the *Chuánlù* (Record of Transmission) states that during the Jin dynasty, the *Jìjiǔ* (Libationer) Wáng Fú composed the *Móhuà bǐqiū jīng* (Sūtra of the Demon’s Transformation of Bhikṣus).
Within Zhī Qiān’s catalog, this sūtra is listed; it is feared to be a forgery that has usurped the title of a genuine work. Furthermore—

The *Shanxin shenzhou jing* (Sutra of the Good Faith Divine Spell), one fascicle, is listed within the catalog of Kumārajīva; there is also a *Shanxin mahashenzhou jing* (Sutra of the Great Good Faith Divine Spell) in two fascicles.
As their titles overlap and it is uncertain whether they are authentic or spurious, both entries are retained for now.

There is also the *Wuzhuo jing* (Sutra of the Five Turbidities), one fascicle, as well as the *Xiao wuzhuo jing* (Minor Sutra of the Five Turbidities). It is likely that this [latter] sutra is the section on sins and blessings found within the *Huaxian jing*.
*Sūtra* in one fascicle; also simply titled *Huāxiān jīng* (The Sūtra of Fresh Flowers). *Wǔlóng huìguò jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Dragons’ Repentance) in one fascicle;

also known as *Wǔlóng huìguò hùfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Five Dragons’ Repentance for Protecting the Dharma), or *Kōnghuì huìguò jīng* (Sūtra on the Repentance of Emptiness-Wisdom). *Jièjù sānmèidàomén jīng* (Sūtra on the Gate of the Path of Precepts and Samādhi) in one fascicle.

*Zuìmiaoshuìdìng jīng* (Sūtra of the Most Sublime and Victorious Samādhi) in one fascicle. *Tiānzhú shāmén jīng* (Sūtra of the Indian Śramaṇa) in one fascicle. *Jiùhù shēnmìng jì* (Rescue and Protection of Life and Vitality)... [incomplete].

*Renbing kuejing* (Sutra on the Suffering and Calamities of Humans), one fascicle; also simply titled *Jiuhushenmingjing* (Sutra on Saving and Protecting Life) or *Hushenjing* (Sutra on Protecting the Body).
To the right, there is another copy of this sutra, titled *Dafo ding tuoluonijing* (Great Buddha-Crown Dhāraṇī Sutra).
The original states it was translated by the Brahman Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. With the addition of one incantation, the rest of the text is largely the same.

The compiler notes that the title of the scripture is unclear as to whether it is Paramārtha’s work; furthermore, if this were a re-translation by Paramārtha, the phrasing would differ entirely from the old version. Since only the incantation differs while the remainder is identical, it cannot resolve people's doubts. As there is no basis for investigation, it must not be compiled arbitrarily; therefore, it is listed here according to the original record.
*The Great Nara Sūtra*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on Wisdom and Right Practice*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Brahma-Emperor*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on Resting the Tomb*, one fascicle;

*The Sūtra on Settling the Household*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on Resting the Dwelling*, one fascicle (note: this differs from the *Sūtra of the Divine Incantation for Resting the Dwelling* found in the *Zhenglu*);
*The Sūtra of the Celestial Lord*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Divine Ship for Crossing the Sea of Birth and Death*, one fascicle.

*The Scripture of the Śrāmaṇera Saving the Ants*, one fascicle: I have carefully examined the fourth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra*, which contains the account of the śrāmaṇera saving the ants;
as it is identical to that [account], it is not a spurious work. Since this [present text] has not yet been seen, I shall preserve it for now.
*The Scripture on Bowing to the Buddha in the North*, one fascicle. *The Scripture on Reverent Merit*, one fascicle. The full title reads: *The Tathāgata’s Exhortation from Within the Golden Coffin*.
*Jielingjing* (Sutra on Accumulated Pure Adornments and Reverent Merit), one fascicle; *Aluohetiao Guowangjing* (Sutra of King Arahacchada), one fascicle;

*Wubai Fanzhijing* (Sutra of Five Hundred Brahmins), one fascicle—also titled *Yiyou Yiwujing* (Sutra of Both Existence and Non-existence); *Xiuxing Fangbianjing* (Sutra on the Expedient Means of Practice), one fascicle; *Jilingjing* (Sutra of the Verses of Command), one fascicle;

*Dushi Budijing* (Sutra of Transcending the World and Immortality), one fascicle; *Zhaifa Qingjingjing* (Sutra on the Purity of the Rules for Fasting), one fascicle; *Wuwei Fa* (Dharma of Non-action).

*Daojing* (Scripture on the Way), one fascicle; *Zhòumèijing* (Scripture on Incantations and Sorcery), one fascicle; *Zhèngzáijīng* (Scripture on the Righteous Fast), one fascicle, translated by An Shigao. The *Zhǔfǎhù lù* (Catalogue of Dharmarakṣa) also contains the *Zhèngzáijīng*;
fearing that it might conflate with other works and usurp a true title, its entry has likewise been preserved here.

*Shītálínjīng* (Scripture on the Śītavana Forest), one fascicle; *Zhāohúnpólíngjīng* (Scripture on Summoning Souls), one fascicle, also called *Zhāohúnjīng* (Scripture on Summoning Souls). The *Zhōu lù* (Catalogue of Zhou) states: [these are included].

*Zhāopò jīngfǎ shèjīng*, one fascicle. The *Fālù* states: "Having searched through ancient records, it appears there should have been a separate system for the *fǎshè* (Dharma-society), yet this scripture has not been seen;
thus, its full details cannot be established. To the right, this single-fascicle *Fǎshè jīng* has been encountered in three versions.
Although the setting [of the narrative] is the same, the wording is entirely different.

Right: According to the *Liang sengyou lu*, the *Sui fei changfang lu*, the *Tang daoxuan lu*, and others.
It further states that during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Shi Fadu brought it forth, but does not mention a translator.
It is unclear what the meaning of the word "brought forth" (chu) is here:
does it mean he compiled and produced it, or did he falsely claim to have produced it?
Its original source is further missing, making it truly difficult to authenticate.
For now, it is recorded in the *Fajing lu* (Dharmatrāta’s Catalog) among the spurious records.

One fascicle titled *Yi weiyi* (Divergent Dignified Conduct); the *Fajing lu* states that it was composed by Fadu, a disciple of Dharmayaśas during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. It contradicts the true Vinaya and deceives both monks and nuns; it is still practiced in Yangzhou to this day, hence I have specifically pointed this out. One fascicle titled *Wan fanfu lun* (Treatise on the Five Ordinary Beings); listed below the *Anagamin jing* (Sutra on the Non-returner).
Eighty-six works in one hundred and forty-one fascicles.

According to the *Record of Doubtful and Spurious Scriptures* within the *Catalogue of All Scriptures* compiled by the śramaṇa Fajing and others by imperial decree in the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, it says:
Furthermore, their names and titles deviate from the truth; some seize upon the golden words at the beginning only to propound rhyming prophecies at the end.
Some first discuss worldly arts and later resort to Buddhist terminology.
Others cite the auspiciousness and misfortune of yin and yang.

Some clarify the spirits, ghosts, calamities, and blessings; such instances as these are clearly false and deceptive. Now, it would be appropriate to keep them concealed in order to remedy the world's afflictions.

However, within the *Fajing lu*, scriptures such as the *Suiyuan wangsheng jing*, the *Yaoshi jing*, the *Brahmadeva Shencei jing*, the *Renwang jing*, the *Baorulai sanmei jing*, the *Zhancha jing*, the *Fanwang jing*, the *Wuku zhangju jing*, the *Anzhai shenzhou jing*, and the *Yijiao lun* are all classified among the doubtful and apocryphal. This is not correct. The three scriptures beginning with the *Suiyuan wangsheng jing* originate from the *Daguanding jing*, while the seven scriptures beginning with the *Renwang jing* have well-documented sources of translation. To include them among the doubtful and apocryphal is, I believe, inadmissible. Therefore, I have now included them in this "Correct Record" (*Zhenglü*), and they are no longer listed here [among the doubtful].

In the first year of the Tiāncè Wànsuì era of Empress Wu of the Great Táng, by imperial decree,

Regarding the spurious scriptures among the *Kanding zhongjing lu* (Catalogue of Determined Scriptures),
the *Zhou lu* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) states:
"Traditionally handed down from antiquity, it has been said that these are all false and erroneous."
Observing their phrasing, it is verbose and cluttered;
their principles are superficial and frivolous.
Though they pilfer the name of the Buddha’s teachings, [they lack the substance].
In the end, the true nature of human scheming was exposed.
That the various classes of beings have fallen into delusion and ruin is entirely due to this.

Therefore, I have compiled and itemized them as listed above. The compiler states: These eighty scriptures were never included in the ancient spurious catalogs; only the *Zhou lu* (Catalogue of the Zhou Dynasty) uniquely compiled them. Regarding the *Three Stages Buddhist Teachings* in four fascicles, the *Neidian lu* states that the *Separate Collection of the Three Stages* in four fascicles is this very work; it clarifies ten major sections in three fascicles. The *Changfang lu* states that the *Separate Collection of the Three Stages* in three fascicles is this very work. The *Roots and Capacities and Universal Medicine Dharma* in two fascicles is found in the *Dazhou lu*. There is also the *Thirty-Six Kinds of Mistakes Made by Failing to Recognize What is Before One’s Face* in one fascicle, which explains all thirty-six kinds of mistakes made by failing to recognize what is before one’s face. Altogether, the teachings of the Three Stages consist of four works.
The first consists of three stages in four fascicles;
the second consists of three stages in three fascicles;

This scroll clarifies the five turbidities of the world, the evil times of the final dharma (*mappō*), and the ten non-virtuous acts of sentient beings whose merit and practice are inferior.

it explains how they should rely on various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras to study under spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and learn to resolve upon bodhicitta. This single scroll extensively elucidates the faculties of sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*.

The *Dharma* and the *Miscellaneous Collections* comprise thirty-five works in forty-four fascicles in total.

Compiled by the śramaṇa Xingxing of Zhenji Monastery during the Sui dynasty, the *Changfang Lu* states they comprise thirty-five fascicles in total, while the *Neidian Lu* states they comprise forty fascicles in total. The spurious records of the Great Zhou dynasty list only twenty-two works in twenty-nine fascicles, failing to include them all. The Stele for the Flourishing of the Three Stages Teaching states they comprise over forty fascicles, yet does not separately list their titles, divisions, or fascicle counts. Now, having searched thoroughly and compiled them, the complete items are listed above as follows.
Although Xingxíng’s compilation cites scriptural passages, they all serve to bolster his own biased views and give rise to groundless fabrications.
Having deviated from the holy intent and further encroached upon the True Doctrine,
an imperial edict was issued in the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era prohibiting it and forbidding its dissemination.
As his followers became numerous and his influence spread far and wide, they formed factions through their shared practices, providing one another with abundant support.

They then established Xinxing as their religious leader and propagated distinct teachings and heterodox dharmas, which were similar to those of Tianshou; thus, they established a false Triple Gem. Although Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty suppressed them, he was unable to eradicate their fundamental roots.
In the first year of the Zhengsheng era of our Tang Empress [Wu Zetian], an edict was issued to determine which scriptures were spurious and to collect miscellaneous talismans and records,
ordering them to be sent to the Sacrificial Department (Cibu).
The aforementioned teachings, as they contradict the intent of the Buddha and claim to be heterodox, are hereby included among these.
This constitutes the limit for the spurious and mixed *fulu* (records).
Furthermore, according to an imperial edict from the second year of the Shengli era of Empress Wu,
those who study the Three Stages [Teaching] may only practice begging for alms.
Maintaining a long fast, abstaining from grain, upholding the precepts, and practicing seated meditation—
anything performed beyond these constitutes a violation of the law.
This is the decree of our Emperor Kaiyuan, the Martial and Valorous Sovereign.
The Sage’s virtue shines forth, universally benefiting the common people;
the Sage’s sun is radiant in heaven, leaving no hidden place unilluminated.
Knowing that they had turned away from truth and constructed delusions, he issued regulations to sever them.
On the third day of the sixth month in the thirteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the year of Yichou (725 CE),
an imperial edict was issued stating that the partitioned screens in the three-tiered courtyards (*sānjièyuàn*) of all monasteries must be removed,
so that they communicate with the main halls and the assembly of monks may dwell together without being permitted to reside separately.
All collected records of their conduct shall be strictly prohibited, severed, and destroyed.
If the administrators permit them to wander about converting others and fail to restrain them,
they shall be compelled to return to lay life.
Fortunately, having received Your Majesty’s enlightened decree to reform past errors, I have not dared to arbitrarily include them in the orthodox records.

All such entries have been expunged to serve as an example for future generations. As for the seven grades of breadth and brevity, they were derived solely from the scriptural collections; although they contain no divergent meanings, they represent the number of compilations by Xinxing. Since the current regulations prohibit their retention, I have not ventured to preserve them, yet I have recorded them here in this catalog.

Although this work extensively expounds the meaning of the sutras and differs from forged compositions, once a title has been established, it forms a distinct section and fascicle.

Fearing that future generations might fall into confusion, I have clearly annotated it in this catalog. The *Changfang lu* states: "The world at large collectively cites this as a doubtful scripture (yi jing). These are anthologies of various sutras, resembling a grove of numbers;
they are merely titled as being "established by the Buddha.

Regarding the aforementioned *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*:
The Record of Sengyou of the Liang Dynasty states:
In the seventh year of the Yongming era,
King Wenxuan invited Shi Sengrou of Dinglin Shangsi and Shi Huici of Xiaozhuangyan Temple [to the court].

The above constitutes the Avataṃsaka section, comprising forty-three works in two hundred and ninety-eight fascicles.

A collation of various catalogs confirms that these were all transcribed by Xiao Ziliang, Prince Wenxuan of Jingling and Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial during the Southern Qi dynasty; this is recorded in the Chángfáng Lù.

The King, being fond of extensive inquiry, personally compiled and edited this work, setting aside his own frugality to emulate the *Lishi* (Calendar of the Ages). He did not expect it to be transmitted to future generations;
yet, scholars followed one after another in copying and reading it.

As worldly people mixed in their own interpolations, they confused and corrupted the original text. Therefore, I have set forth the fundamental framework here, so that you may understand its origins in detail.

However, as for those titles that include the characters "copied" (抄), they all belong to this same category; if one carefully examines their beginnings and ends, they will be distinguished from one another.
The *Neidian lu* states:
"Since these differ from the titles of the original sūtras, the inclusion of 'copied' makes the distinction explicit, so that future seekers may know they have a specific source. Indeed.
Its flavor is all-pervasive and its principles are perfectly harmonious; it bridges the profusion of worldly customs and examines the diverse paths of human nature and desire.
Therein lies the Way.
Its meaning is neither dubious nor delusory.

Sengyou, Changfang, and others in various catalogs all annotated these as "doubtful scriptures" (*yi jing*). This was because they feared that such works might involve the dregs of decadence, losing their original essence.

Although it is titled *Fayuan jing*, it is included among the compiled works. The right-hand section begins from the "Six Meanings of the Buddha-Dharma").
There are fifty-four sections totaling five hundred and one fascicles;
these all bear titles that falsely claim to be authentic scriptures, with their wording increased or decreased,
or they are composed by mixing disparate doctrines under newly established titles.
If one were to collect them based on their correctness, there is fear that the "jade and stone" may be indiscriminately conflated;
yet if one treats them all as forgeries, there is evidence upon which to base the original source.
Between these two paths—acceptance and rejection—it is truly difficult to reach a definitive judgment.
Furthermore, this has been compiled according to the spurious entries at the end of the original record.
May future students, in their examination of it, take care to discern its merits and defects.

Catalogue of the Mahāyāna Canon, Part One: The Mahāyāna Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras comprise a total of six hundred thirty-eight works in two thousand seven hundred forty-five fascicles, arranged in two hundred fifty-eight bundles (*zhì*).
